# The Pagan World

## And the initial origin of their gods

Through what delusions <note>original: "verwhänungen"; refers to the false beliefs or presumptions of the ancient world</note> a certain imagined power was attributed to them, for which reason they were honored by the ancients. Thus, shrines, temples, images, and altars were erected for them, and innumerable names were given to them. Also, how certain **kings, emperors, cities, and estates** supported them with great wealth and riches, or at other times robbed, burned, tore down, and completely destroyed them. What quarrels, wars, and bloodshed arose on this account, gathered together from the writings of many highly esteemed and learned men (whose names are listed on the reverse side of this page).

### **Six books by Diodorus the Sicilian, the most**
renowned historian among the Greeks, the contents of which show the imagined beginning of the world, as well as its first habitation and the rule over all lands, with many stories, customs, laws, and practices regarded as unbelievable, which occurred up until the Trojan War. <note>Diodorus Siculus was a 1st-century BCE Greek historian; his "Bibliotheca historica" was a massive universal history.</note>

**The truthful description of the Trojan War by Dictys of Crete,** in which he himself was a commander over many people and recorded the events as they actually happened. <note>Dictys Cretensis was long believed to be an eyewitness to the Trojan War, though scholars now view the text as a later Roman-era invention.</note>

**The sculpted symbols of Horus—a King and Priest in Egypt three thousand years ago—** through which, before the invention of letters, all the secrets of the clergy and the worldly-learned were made known and displayed. <note>Refers to the "Hieroglyphica" of Horapollo, an attempt to explain Egyptian hieroglyphs which the Renaissance saw as mystical allegories.</note>

**Planetary Tables, in which those aforementioned gods are named in place of the seven** wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets of the classical solar system: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, plus the Sun and Moon.</note>; according to the findings of the astronomers, what they effect in the births of humans, in the character and inclinations of their lives, and what power they have over the weather and the growth of crops, presented here in a very brief form.

<margin>
Rare book. See Engel, Library, page 417. <note>original Latin: "Liber rarus. Vide Engel Libr."</note>
Feuer C. Library page 58. Bauer Library page 103.
Goetz [?] page 105.
</margin>

From this, the Christian reader may sense the goodness of God toward him, as one who is rightly instructed. He may also hear with pleasure many beautiful stories, teachings, and sayings, [and see] how miserably natural wit is blinded without the enlightenment of Divine wisdom; indeed, he may fathom the origins from which discord and strife in matters of faith and other important things have broken out throughout the ages. Decorated with many delightful illustrations.

# The Pagan World
## And the initial origin of their gods

The source / through what delusions certain imagined powers were attributed to them, for which sake they were honored by the ancients. So much so / that foundations, temples, images, and altars were erected for them, and innumerable names were given to them. Just as several **Kings**, **Emperors**, **Cities**, and **Estates** supported them with great wealth and riches, or conversely robbed, burned, tore down, and completely destroyed them. The disputes, wars, and bloodshed that arose on their account have been gathered from the writings of many learned and worthy men (whose names are on the reverse side of this page).

### The six books of Diodorus the Sicilian, the most famous historian among the Greeks, the contents of which show the supposed beginning of the world, as well as the first habitation and mastery of all lands, with many stories, customs, laws, and practices regarded as incredible, which occurred until the Trojan War.

The truthful description by **Dictys of Crete** <note>A legendary figure said to have fought in the Trojan War; his "journal" was a popular source for medieval and Renaissance accounts of the conflict.</note> concerning the **Trojan** war, in which he, being a commander over many people, recorded the events as they actually happened.

The sculpted symbols of **Horus** <note>This refers to Horapollo, the supposed author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, which Renaissance scholars believed held mystical, non-alphabetic secrets.</note>, a **King** and **Priest** in **Egypt** three thousand years ago, through which—before the invention of letters—all the secrets of the spiritual and worldly scholars were expressed and shown.

**Planetary Tables**, in which those gods named above are placed in the stead of the seven wandering stars; according to the teachings of the astrologers <term>Sternenseher</term> <note>literally "star-seers"</note>, what influence they have on the births of men, in the conduct and inclinations of their lives, and what power they have over the weather and the production of crops, is briefly presented.

<margin>
Rare book. See <note>original: "Vide"</note> Engel Volume IV, page 274.
Feuer l. B. <unclear>reading</unclear> page 58. <unclear>reading</unclear> Volume II page 103.
Goetze <unclear>reading</unclear> page 445.
</margin>

Decorated with many delightful woodcut illustrations.

# To the Noble and Steadfast / Georg
## von Stätten the Elder / my com-
## manding and gracious Lord.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap "E" intricately decorated with a landscape scene featuring a house and trees within the flourishing curves of the letter.</image-desc>

It has been ten years now, (Noble and Steadfast Lord <note>original: "Edler Vester Herr" — a traditional honorific for a member of the landed nobility or a high-ranking patrician</note>), since—as is Your Honor's custom to discuss those who have gained some fame in **Holy** and **Secular** writings while at the table—among others, the mention of **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC known for writing a universal history of the world</note> arose. Your high-minded judgment then suggested that, above other pagan historians, his books are so pleasant and profitable to read, especially for people occupied in government and secular offices. For these writings of his do not only show the magnificent deeds of the ancients, but also contain honest and fair decrees. Therein is found such a natural drive for honor that one must wonder where these peoples—ignorant of God’s commands—derived such a yearning for the good, with such a brilliance that even a Christian, instructed by the **Law of Moses** <note>original: "Esatz Mose"</note> and the free teaching of our Savior, could see in them where manhood, virtue, and fairness were followed. There, power arose, and the welfare of the Imperial Cities and Estates remained persistent. Indeed, a believer might perceive in these texts what a blessed life among us here on earth would be, if the pursuit of such love of honor in worldly matters were joined to the true knowledge of the certain will of God. 

I—perceiving your upright spirit toward God, the world, and your fatherland (as witnessed by all who know you, and confirmed by both hearsay and sight)—realized then that with these words you intended to encourage my modest understanding and to persuade me to translate such books of **Diodorus** into German for the good of our common Fatherland. I was immediately reminded by my own conscience how the significant favors I received from you had made me duty-bound to fulfill your pleasure and desire (which tend only toward honor) without further prompting. For this reason (I remember it well), I made a bold promise that at the next opportunity I would undertake this translation into German. This promise of mine I now fulfill—though after a long delay—with the hopeful confidence that my hard-earned contribution will compensate for the long postponement of this debt to you, as a merciful creditor. After all, even with a profit-seeking usurer, a little bit of crude ore <note>original: "stumes außer den graben ärtz" — literally "silent ore out of the pits/ditches"</note> from the pits sometimes appeases the annoyance of a long wait. Thus, I know well that it is not necessary for me to mention to you the additional labor I have performed beyond my promise, with the intent that I...

<summary>In this dedication, the author recalls a dinner conversation from ten years prior where Georg von Stätten praised the historian Diodorus Siculus, prompting the author to promise a German translation. I ask you to receive this in good spirit; otherwise, I would have to explain more extensively what moved me to this, or indicate with my defense how it is useful and for what it is serviceable. Since, until now, all my words and writings have been understood by you in the best way, all those who love the fear of God, honor, and art know that they are also loved by you. Wherever the opportunity arises, they are bound by your high generosity to offer back to you the gifts granted to them by God (if there is anything in those same gifts pleasing to you). And it is precisely my joy that you should be a judge here, so that with your judgment, you might recommend <note>original: "auffmütze" — here meaning to present with distinction or lend the weight of one's reputation</note> this work of mine to all the world. For who would not consider useful and good that which Lord Georg von Stätten holds as fruitful and prudent for the common good? Especially since it is and always was true that in the most famous city of the **Holy Roman Empire of the German Lands**, Augsburg, the service of God <note>original: "Handel Gotts" — referring to the religious life and ecclesiastical affairs of the city</note>, all wisdom, all discipline, all virtue, and all arts flourish alongside and within great wealth.

You, however, are such a citizen of that city—who (aside from the heritage of your lineage, which is nearly the oldest there) spent your youth in all noble exercises, traveling through many kingdoms and residing at the courts of the highest princes—that you were afterward found in the Fatherland to be a man of high understanding for the common good. In the Council, and sometimes with deeds and dedicated fortune alongside other citizens, you have been found faithful, loving, willing to serve, and helpful, right up to a respectable yet humble old age, remaining vigorous and quiet through a disciplined life. 

In addition, your household has always been regarded by honorable and sensible people as a school of learning for all honorable and modest moderation, and for all necessary, enjoyable, and useful questions concerning God, Nature, and Honor. This is not without the special testimony of Divine grace, which gifted you with an only son of the same kind, Georg, my favorable and dear young Lord <note>original: "Junckherre" — a title for a young nobleman or the son of a prominent patrician</note>. He has acquired such a knowledge of the **Greek** and **Latin** languages, as well as many others, and experience of many lands, and such an understanding that in the future, as befits such a citizen, he may be an advisor to his fatherland in joy and sorrow. From him, through his beautiful children—your grandchildren—you may draw and see comfort while still living, whereby your lineage must sprout and grow toward long-lasting honors.

I commend your current and increasing, long and everlasting prosperity of soul and body to God the Lord, while commending myself to the same. Dated Basel, the first of March in the year.

# To the Christian and art-loving reader / I wish

->Johan Herold / God’s grace, luck, and salvation.<-

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'W' at the beginning of the text, featuring an ornate design with foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

Were these six books written by me concerning the heathen gods <note>original: "Heydnischen Göttern" — referring to the deities of Greek and Roman mythology</note>—drawn from **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note>, **Horus** <note>likely referring to Horapollo, supposed author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, and other subsequent collected writings—presented only to learned men experienced in many languages, I would expect either praise (for the sake of what I have undertaken, which no other German before me has wished to take upon himself) or, at the very least, those men would read all of this without offense. It would not be unfamiliar to them, as those who have previously read such things in Greek, Latin, and other languages in the most gracefully composed order by **Lilio Giraldi** <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), an Italian scholar whose work on the history of the gods was a primary source for Herold</note>, whose lead I have followed as much as possible. However, since I intend herewith to serve the **common Germans** <note>referring to those who were literate in their mother tongue but lacked a classical education in Latin or Greek</note> who are not informed in foreign languages, it is necessary that I remind the Christian reader: I myself consider every perverted opinion and devotion—indeed, whatever power is withdrawn from God and attributed supernaturally to any creature—to be a separation from the holy Christian community.

For from my childhood until this hour, I have always believed (and by means of divine grace, this my faith and confession shall remain against the **gates of hell**) as follows: I confess God the everlasting, almighty Father, as a creator, bringer-forth, and indeed an author of all things, whether in Heaven, upon or under the Earth, or wherever else anything may be that can be seen, or what is invisible—conceived, imagined, or fathomed with understanding and reason—or what may not even be plumbed in its essence and being by the weakness and frailty of human wit. Over all of this, I acknowledge Him as a Lord, Arranger, and Creator, with a firm confession that He has given us humans clearly to understand through **Moses** <note>referring to the Book of Genesis</note> as much as is necessary for us to know regarding the beginning of all things. Whatever others have allowed themselves to dream concerning this is all the **juggling-game** <note>original: "gauggelspil" — a common Reformation-era term for deception or empty superstition</note> and trifle of human curiosity. I confess Him as the only one who rewards good and punishes evil, without whose permission no creature may be helpful or harmful to another.

For out of His grace—indeed, out of the Love which He Himself is and bears toward us—He chose a pure virgin, namely **MARY**, who was to conceive His Son without disturbance of her virginity or maidenhood, and to bear the same, so that He might take away the evil which mankind had loaded upon themselves through disobedience. This same **Christ Jesus** I confess and believe: that He, born through Mary, true God and man through the assumption of flesh, until reaching full mature age, preached the will of His Heavenly Father and quite freely His teaching—indeed, the **eternal Word**, which He Himself is—publicly to all the world. Afterward, at His appointed time, without sin or misdeed, He suffered the death which neither Sun nor Moon could bear to look upon; indeed, He was shamefully hanged on the **Cross** to reconcile our shame and our sin before God with His scorn endured before the world, and to make satisfaction for those who believe in Him. Thus buried, He—as the firstborn of the Christian rebirth—awakened Himself from death by power on the third day and arose, after which He ascended in a glorified body to His Heavenly Father, with whom He has been, is, and remains in eternity.

So I confess that the Father and Son have sent down to us the **Holy Spirit**, who flows from them, being true, co-essential, and everlasting God, to enlighten all people and, in the power of their triune unity, to establish an assembly <note>original: "versamblūg" — referring to the Church or the body of believers</note> which, until the end of this perishable world, shall fight knightly against sin, death, and the devil among **Jews, Turks, and false Christians**, according to the teaching of that same Spirit, with icy repentance and the remission of their committed misdeeds before God the angered...

As for my nature and mindset regarding the things that such a faith requires outwardly and toward one's neighbor, you, friendly and dear reader, may easily perceive from this: that I am an inhabitant of the highly praiseworthy city of **Basel** (which had its beginning with Lucius Munatius Plancus <note>original: "T. Minutio Basillo" — Herold refers to the Roman founder of Augusta Raurica, though the name is slightly garbled in the source</note> before a stone was even laid at the ruined fortress near the little village of **Augst**). I am also enrolled there as the lowliest of students, where the teaching of the ministers of the Church, the civil laws of the city, and its customs are founded upon the sole word of Jesus Christ. Through this, whatever pertains to spiritual and worldly administration lives in Christian love, freedom, and discipline. It maintains peace, friendship, and goodwill toward neighbors, associates, and foreigners; the pious are brought forward, while those who act against such things are punished according to their deserts following Christian admonition.

This has been recounted by me, dear reader, for this reason alone: so that you will not listen to those who think that by writing such things, one wishes to establish **idolatry** <note>original: "Götzenwerck"</note>. Once, **Augustine**, **Arnobius**, **Clement of Alexandria**, and **Theodoret of Cyrrhus** <note>original: "Cyrus"</note> struck down idol-worship (which at that time held all power and administration) with just such writings, as if using the heathens' own sword. **Epiphanius**, **Irenaeus**, and others pointed out the shameful delusions and abominable lives of the apostates <note>original: "Aberrennlingē" — those who wander away from Christian teaching</note> in their written books. In these, one could see how stubbornly they fought against the truth; and with these very writings, the authors rooted out such mischief more effectively than the authorities did with fire, sword, or torture.

Now, it is not my intention here to fight against the long-rejected views of Christians, Jews, or Turks; all my endeavor is directed toward how my dear fatherland—**Germany**, highly famed from olden times for its manhood and faithful loyalty—might, in this current enlightenment of the bright Word of God, also learn and grasp "worldly wisdom" (which is a gift from God for the use of love) in its own undivided language. For just as the **Egyptians** were the first in such arts—indeed, were considered the only ones—the **Greeks** stole these same arts from them and increased them greatly, until the **Romans**, along with worldly dominion, gracefully snatched them from the Greeks and improved them significantly. In our own times, this has instilled a yearning memory in the **Italians**, who have brought these arts to the highest splendor. And this is what **Plato**, **Cicero**, and **Pietro Bembo** <note>original: "Bembus" — a 16th-century Italian scholar and cardinal known for his work on the Italian language</note> (to be brief) did in their own languages, even though they were considered well-instructed and learned in other tongues. However, a love for art cannot be awakened except through the example of foreign skill and virtue, which then brings a zeal and incentive to learn, imitate, and even improve everything.

This image is most evident in history books; for in those same writings, one is free to mix in divine, worldly, and civil affairs, as much as each person has understanding. One may and must also write for oneself what is graceful in the use of language, from which it easily follows that whatever weighty occasion is offered to the **common man** (who also has a brain), he may use it to exercise his reason, to develop his skill, and to improve what he reads. Therefore, those who attempt to teach and instruct other people in an elegant way before they themselves know—or before it has been prescribed to them—why they should speak, undertake a vain labor. <meta>This page continues Herold's preface. Having established his personal background and faith in Basel, he now turns to a passionate defense of the German language. # Preface

The German language is currently spoken and written in a way that sounds more like "Babylonian" confusion than good German. Into our ears and into every line, whole wagonloads of grand-sounding titles and nicknames are crammed, alongside echoes begged from Spanish, Italian, Latin, and even more distant lands. Just as with modern fashion, a mockery is being made of this magnificent gift from God—our manly language—as if it were a game for apes. I would even dare to swear that more true German is found in an ancient, uncorrupted *Song of Hildebrand* <note>original: "Hiltenprandt" — an allusion to the Old High German heroic lay, which Herold sees as a model of pure language</note> than in these modern, thousand-page works of "Rhetoric," as they call them. 

This trend brings its own fitting reward: an unheard-of changing of baptismal and family names. It has reached the point where almost no German educated in the arts—out of a sense of honor for the German lands or his own family—dares to mention his fatherland or his surname in his own language when he brings forth something notable. While it is worthy of high praise to know foreign histories, good arts, and languages, it is conversely shameful to forget one's own nature—that is, the love for one's own German language—which even a mindless beast would not do. It is a disgrace to show no excellence in it, or even to suggest that our Fatherland lacks people who could grasp all possible and worthy arts in their native tongue. Some think a German is unfit for stargazing, land-surveying, or singing, even though arithmetic—the very foundation of these arts—has reached its highest peak among us. 

Should a German not know how to shape his own letters, his lovely manner, and his "flowers of speech" <note>A Renaissance term for rhetorical ornaments</note>, or how to clarify his intentions, when nearly all the world's languages and arts have become so familiar to us Germans? In proclaiming the Will of God, who can surpass them? Do they not have laws for lands and cities, with their specific and proper decrees? In the works of **Andreas Perneder** <note>A 16th-century legal scholar who wrote influential manuals in German</note>, you will see what he was able to contribute to the Law throughout his long life. In medicine, **Hieronymus Bock** <note>A famous physician and one of the "fathers of botany"</note> gives a good demonstration of what our language is capable of. 

But if you think that the speech of the Greeks and Latins—which they call **Poetry** <note>original: "Poeſim"</note>—is a thing you should not bother to imitate, it could easily happen that one replaces it with hopping tales that jump to many beats. As an example of this, I wish to set down here for you a translation of **Martial’s** *Happy Life* <note>original: "Martialis Wolleben" — Herold translates Martial's Epigram 10.47, a classic poem on the "good life"</note>, which I have rendered into German:

Would you know what makes a noble life?
Mark this well, my dearest Martial:
Wealth acquired not by toil, but left by ancestors,
A home of one's own, fields of decent size,
Freedom from lawsuits, rarely in the Council, a quiet mind,
Vigorous in strength, healthy in body and blood,
Simple yet wise, joined by equal friends,

<column-break/>

Obedient servants, a table not overladen,
Nights without care, not burdened with wine,
A gentle wife who brings neither shame nor harm,
Sleep that makes the night short, and being content
In your station, as God has ordained for you;
Conduct yourself so that you do not fear the final hour,
Nor ever wish for death from the bottom of your heart.

Therefore, I earnestly ask all readers who love honor and the arts to receive this work of mine in the best spirit. Also, let no German hide his talents, but rather let everyone practice and strive so that through the immortality of his name, our learning-hungry Fatherland may—even without the help of foreign tongues—have the opportunity and encouragement for all arts becoming of a Christian and an honest man in the future. Rest assured that all my thoughts, until the end God has set for me, shall be directed with tireless diligence and unstinting effort toward selecting and presenting what can be learned from the past histories of the whole world, and what benefit may be gleaned from them to assist our common Fatherland.

# Of the Heathen Gods
## and their supposed power, for which they were worshipped by the Ancients.

->The First Book.<-

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut initial 'E' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and stylized leaves, occupying the height of approximately eight lines of body text.</image-desc>To both Jews and Christians, through the special grace of the true, everlasting, eternal, and almighty God, the supposed power of the [heathen] gods—being failing and fictitious—has always been entirely ridiculous, and their worship (namely to the pious and sensible) has forever been utterly abominable. Indeed, even among the heathens themselves, those who sought after reason yet failed to attain true knowledge through their own presumption, there were some who refused to regard anything visible, anything with a beginning and an end, or anything subject to creation and destruction, as that which one calls God. And it seems to me not at all out of the way to show what several of the aforementioned have written about this, as we first present something wonderful and well worthy of contemplation regarding the name [of God].

Accordingly, the ineffable power, wisdom, and love are given written in the name itself, as when <term>Moses</term> <note>original: "Mose"</note> received the Law on Mount <term>Sinai</term>. He [God] indicated Himself with four letters that can neither be joined together nor spoken by a human voice, as is visible here where that very name is set down; for in Hebrew it is יהוה <term>Jehovah</term> <note>original: "Jova"; the Tetragrammaton</note>, and yet it cannot be fully interpreted or understood. Therefore, the Hebrews also say that God has no name that can be understood or spoken by us humans, for His own essence is His name—indeed, [they say] it is not His name. And just as His essence is unfathomable (for if we possessed that knowledge, we would be equal to Him), so too His name cannot be known. Therefore, because this name with these four letters is a unique and special name—having no suffix nor being derived from others, as all other names of that language are—one ascribes this very name to God.

# Of the Pagan Gods /
## and their supposed power, for which they were honored among the Ancients.

->The First Book.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap initial 'E' featuring intricate scrollwork and foliage patterns in a square frame.</image-desc>

To both Jews and Christians—by the special grace of the true, everlasting, eternal, and almighty God—the supposed power of the [pagan] gods has always appeared entirely ridiculous as a void and a fiction, and their worship (at least to the pious and wise) has always been utterly abominable. Indeed, even among the pagans themselves, those who sought after truth through reason—yet did not attain true knowledge out of their own presumption—there were some who refused to consider anything visible, anything that has a beginning or end, or anything subject to creation and destruction, to be that which is called "God." And it seems to me not at all misplaced to show what some of these mentioned authors have written on the matter, provided we first present something wonderful and well worthy of consideration regarding His name.

For this reason, and because the unspeakable power, wisdom, and love are written within the Name itself—as when Moses received the Law on Mount Sinai—He indicated Himself with four letters <note>This refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God.</note> which can neither be rhymed together nor pronounced by a human voice. This is visible if the name were set down here; for in Hebrew it is written as **יהוה** <note>original Hebrew: YHWH</note>, often rendered as <term>Joua</term> <note>An archaic transliteration of Jehovah.</note>, and yet it is not fully translated, nor can it be truly understood from that rendering. Therefore, the Hebrews also say that God has no name that can be understood or spoken by us humans, for His own essence is His name; indeed, the letters are not His name themselves. And just as His essence is unfathomable (for if we truly knew it, we would be equal to Him), so also His name cannot be known. Because this name, with these four letters, is a unique and specific name—not a descriptor or derived from others like all other names in that language—this name is attributed to God alone.

What other names were later given to God is now well known to the whole world. Now, let one take note of this: God is called <term>Deus</term> <note>Latin for God.</note> by the Latins; <term>Theos</term> <note>Greek for God.</note> by the Greeks (where the letters "Th" are counted as a single character); <term>Thut</term> by the Egyptians; <term>Syre</term> by the Persians; and <term>Esar</term> by the Etruscans. The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests or astrologers.</note> have called Him <term>Orse</term>; the Arabs, <term>Alla</term>; the Assyrians, <term>Adad</term>; the followers of Muhammad, <term>Agdi</term>; those in the newly discovered lands and islands call Him <term>Zimi</term>; and our dear ancestors, the true Germans, have named Him <term>Guot</term> <note>The author connects the German word for God (*Gott*) with the word for "Good" (*Gut/Guot*).</note>, based on what He is [goodness] rather than how He exists. it is found that it remained as four given letters throughout the whole world, signifying to people that they could neither conceive nor pronounce what He truly was.

And since this very name provides no essence, but rather serves as an indication of the Almighty God, we wish to proceed and hear what the ancients first held regarding God and how they honored Him before idolatry was introduced. But it is indeed true, as Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC who wrote the *Bibliotheca historica*.</note> writes, that it is not easy to seek out the first names of those by whom God was first honored, nor is it easy to fathom how they spoke of God's immortality. Yet to us Christians, by the special grace of God, it is quite simple and manifest to have and know the true knowledge of Christ; thus, for us, the descriptions of the heathens (for which reason this book is begun) should be received more as a trifle—even a mockery—rather than as something to be grasped as contrary to fundamental Christian knowledge.

What may be recovered from Holy Scripture regarding the first invocation of the true God, we shall also let rest here as a true and sufficient report. This was first given by God Himself (before all others, who later became rooted in unstable opinions through their own presumption) and prescribed through Moses. Zoroaster, a son of Oromasdes <note>original: "Oromasdi," referring to Ahura Mazda, the deity of Zoroastrianism.</note>—whom some estimate to be the son of Noah, Ham, and who lived much around the time of Nimrod—says in the books of his secrets concerning God: "God has the head of a hawk, for He is the most noble and steadfast among all those things that suffer no corruption or decay; He is uncreated <note>original: "vnerpoñ," likely meaning unbegotten or un-born.</note>, inseparable, most like and similar unto Himself, a form and leader of the good, even an outpouring of the same. He takes no heed of gifts, being best in Himself, most prudent, a father of justice, who knows righteousness and its dangers without any instruction; He is the right perfection of nature, a unique finder of true wisdom." But Mercurius Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic, long believed to be a contemporary of Moses.</note>—who lived in the time of Moses with the Pharaoh whom God drowned in the Red Sea—what he, as a pagan, wrote about God seems to me worthy of being placed first. He writes thus in the book *Of Divine Wisdom*:

> God is the most blessed, who is otherwise called the best spirit. He is the soul in the body, the mind <note>original: "gmůt," here representing the Greek *Nous* or divine intellect.</note> in the soul, the word in the mind; and yet God Himself is the procreator and father of all these things. The word, the image, and the mind belong to God; the body comes from the formation. The formation is the soul, and a little piece of the purest material <note>original: "plasts," referring to the substance that is molded or formed.</note> of the physical form; the soul is a piece, and the mind is a part of the soul; the mind is somewhat participant in God. God is also in everything, for everything, around everything, through everything: the mind to the soul, the soul to the form, the form to the vessel.

This Hermes, or Mercurius Trismegistus, also says: "And since our discourse has run to the point where we have begun to speak of the kinship and society between humans and gods, then recognize, my Asclepius <note>The student to whom Hermes addresses the dialogue.</note>, the power of man. The Lord and Father—or that which is highest in God—is that He is a creator of the heavenly gods, who are set up in the temples and allow themselves to be so near to mankind."

He says further: "Thus humanity is always mindful of its nature, also..."

it does not forget its origin, but always persistently wishes to imitate the Godhead in one thing: and just as the Lord our Father created His likeness—gods—and made them eternal, so does humanity shape its idols after the image of its own countenance.

To this, Asclepius <note>In the Hermetic dialogues, Asclepius is the student of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> replies to Trismegistus and says: "You speak surely, Hermes, of the images or carved idols?" Hermes says: "Yes, Asclepius, my words refer to these columns and images fashioned after the human form. And consider well within yourself in what error and ignorance you are stuck—though you are otherwise esteemed as a dear, highly wise man. You see for yourself that such images have a physical sensitivity, and as if they possess a spirit, they are full of it; they are great in their deeds and counter-actions, having a knowledge of future things and often foretelling them, which even all the prophets or soothsayers do not know. They sometimes punish and plague people with sickness, sometimes make them healed and healthy, sometimes joyful, and at times sad, according to what they deserve. Thus it surely cannot be hidden from you that Egypt is an imitation of Heaven (or, to speak more clearly of the matter) a place where all the practice and administration of heavenly things are directed and descend; indeed, to speak more accurately, our land is a temple of the whole earth. Nevertheless, since a prudent man should have knowledge of all future things, it cannot with any fairness be kept secret that a time is coming when it will appear as if Egypt, in a devout spirit, has honored the Godhead with church services in vain; and then such idolatry of the Egyptian land must be entirely shattered and held as vanity."

From all this it is easy to see that this Heathen <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, whom the author views as a pagan who nonetheless glimpsed the truth.</note> recognized a single, eternal, true God; but nonetheless, through the deception of the evil spirit—as Paul says—he became maddened in such knowledge and high reflection because of his ingratitude, such that he also describes other gods. Some of these, he claims, were made by the highest God (by which he undoubtedly means the Sun, Moon, Stars, Air, and that which we see in the heavens). But the other gods were made by men, whereby he means stone, wood, gold, and silver worked into the shape of a human. He understands these to be insensitive in themselves, but that evil spirits—incited by the unbelief of men—hide within them, deceiving human frailty into thinking that some punishment follows from negligent worship, or a reward follows from great displays of honor. Such an opinion arises from the wrath of God along with all the filth flowing from it. But so that the evil spirit must always give way to the truth, the <term>small spark</term> <note>original: "klein funcklin." A common philosophical concept (scintilla animae) suggesting a trace of divine light remains in the fallen human soul.</note> of true Divine knowledge was kept as an inextinguishable fire within this man, so that it was sufficient for the whole world until the coming of Christ to ignite the light of reason; for Hermes freely and openly confessed how such idolatry of the Egyptians would be utterly darkened, appear publicly as false, and be brought to ruin.

Yes, it is also certain that every error to which the evil spirit directs humanity must be revealed—indeed, revoked. For his words indicate that his ancestors sinned greatly against God with their idolatry; he speaks himself, not knowing where his words lead, and says:

Let us speak again of reason and of humanity, for reason is a Divine gift through which humanity is a rational...

### Concerning Heathen Gods

...named animals; then what was said of man—although they are wondrous—is yet not so greatly to be wondered at as this: that which exceeds all wondrous things with its own wonder, namely, that man could fathom the divine nature, and indeed, even create and bring it about. For our ancestors dwelt in great error; in the dealings of the gods they were unbelieving and did not devote themselves to the service and devotion of divine things. Yet they discovered an art to make gods. And to such a discovery, they mixed the powers according to the natures of the world. And since they were unable to create souls, they conjured the souls of spirits or angels <note>The author is referring to the Neoplatonic and Hermetic idea that statues could be "animated" by drawing celestial spirits into them through "theurgy" or ritual.</note> and thrust them into the holy images and divine mysteries, so that such idols could have the power to do good or evil. 

For your grandfather, my Asclepius <note>Asclepius the Elder, often identified with the Greek god of healing or the Egyptian Imhotep.</note>, who first discovered what pertains to medicine, has had a temple consecrated to him on the hill of Mansloth <note>original: "Mansloth"; likely a localized spelling or corruption of a place name in Egypt mentioned in early Hermetic Latin translations.</note>, where his worldly human self lies buried—that is, his body. But as much of him as remains—indeed, entirely as man is in the sensitivity of life, and that being his best part—has returned to heaven. Even today, he still provides help to people in their illnesses through his divine power, just as he gave counsel through medicine while living on earth. Likewise, Hermes—from whom I, your grandfather, take my name <note>The speaker here is Hermes Trismegistus, identifying himself as the grandson of an earlier Hermes.</note>—dwells, as you know, in the city named after him, Hermopolis (now called Benisaif <note>original: "Benisaif"; likely referring to Beni Suef in Egypt.</note>). He is honored there, and he helps and assists all people who make pilgrimages to him and visit his temple. So we know well that Isis, the wife of Osiris <note>The central figures of the Egyptian myth of resurrection; Isis was the goddess of magic and motherhood, Osiris the god of the afterlife.</note>, is gracious to some and does evil to others. For these earthly gods are more easily moved to anger than those who are made and mixed together from both the natures of man and the divine. Therefore, in Egypt, certain irrational animals are also consecrated to him; moreover, here and there in the cities named after them, their souls are honored, and whatever customs were established for them are carried out in those places.

From this, it is finally seen how this man falls from the knowledge of the true God into idols, sorcery, and such error, in that he attributes some soul to irrational animals, and yet frequently indicates that all such things are but an idle tale. As when he says Aesculapius <note>The Latin name for Asclepius.</note>, the grandfather of Asclepius, and Hermes (or Mercury), his grandfather, were born as men and thus buried as gods in heaven. He says the goddess Isis has human emotions—that she becomes angry and does other things that a human made of soul and body is accustomed to do—but he calls the soul a spirit instead, and the body an image made of wood and stone.

Now this Egyptian, or Hermes, is the last of the five Mercuries <note>The author follows the medieval tradition of "euhemerism," which argued that pagan gods were actually historical kings or sages who were later deified. Cicero famously listed five different figures named Mercury.</note> who are counted, and is also held to be a god among the Egyptians. They have also dedicated to him the first month of their year (which they begin in the Autumn month) and give it the name Theut <note>Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing.</note>; and the Saites <note>The inhabitants of Sais, an ancient Egyptian city.</note> honor him especially highly. He is also called Tris-megistus <term>Trismegistus (Thrice-Greatest)</term>, to signify that he was held to be King, High Priest, and the Wisest. This same man, speaking of God, concludes and says: "But God is one; the One needs no name, for He is the one who is without a name."

# The First Book.

Around the time of the Babylonian captivity <note>The period in the 6th century BCE when the Jews were exiled to Babylon.</note>, there was a prince in Miletus, a city now located in Anatolia <note>Modern-day Turkey.</note> called Melayo. He was counted among the Seven Sages of the world, being the first in both order and time. He held this view of God: that God was a spirit <term>gemüt</term> <note>In this context, the German "gemüt" refers to a divine Mind or Intellect.</note> that brought forth all things from water, and that He had no beginning or end.

### Anaximander.

A few years after him came Anaximander, an ingenious master of Nature—that is, the study of the properties of all things. He attributed nothing at all to a Divine Spirit, but rather believed the stars were the heavenly gods. However, Cicero <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher (106–43 BCE).</note> says that he also held the opinion that there were gods who lived and ruled for many years, but eventually died and gave way to others who followed them. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Christian bishop known for cataloging heresies.</note>, on the other hand, writes of him that he held the beginning of all things to be infinite, from which all things arise and into which all things are again dissolved.

### Anaximenes.

A fellow citizen of these two in Miletus, and living not long after them, was Anaximenes. He attributed everything to the air, believing it to be infinite, the origin of all causes, of all the gods, and indeed God Himself; and that all things are transformed back into it.

### Democritus.

At the time of the pious Esther <note>The biblical queen of Persia.</note>, there lived this Democritus, a citizen of Abdera—now called Polystilo in Rumelia <note>original: "Romanei"; a term then used for the Balkan territories of the Ottoman Empire.</note>. He held that God was a fiery spirit and a living soul of the world.

### Pythagoras.

Slightly more than two thousand and sixty years ago, this wise man lived on the island of Samos. He said that God is the unique Number <note>Pythagorean philosophy famously held that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note>, without which nothing has been created or made. He is a single beginning from which all things come; He was the first, subject to neither thoughts nor passions, invisible, and uncreated.

### Archelaus / Pherecydes.

These two attributed divine power to the Earth, believing that all things come and begin from her.

### Heraclitus.

This man from Ephesus in Ionia—the capital of which is now called Figena in the district of Quiscam by the Turks—held that the gods came from fire, and that God Himself was an intelligent fire.

### Anaxagoras.

He was born in Clazomenae in Thrace—which is now Marognen in Rumelia—and lived around the time of Heraclitus, when the Tarquins were driven out of Rome <note>The legendary expulsion of the last kings of Rome, traditionally dated to 509 BCE.</note>. He said that the Divine Spirit was the origin of all things we see, and that this same spirit was infinite and moved itself.

# Concerning the Heathen Gods

## Prodicus.

This man, born on the island of Ceos <note>original: "Zea." An island in the Cyclades.</note>, claimed that the Sun and Moon were gods because all vital power came from them.

## Diogenes and Cleanthes.

These two say that the air is a divine power, without which nothing could be made, nor could anything exist.

## Straton.

He believed that Nature, or the living essence of things, was God.

## Antisthenes.

This man was an Athenian who said that although the common people <term>pöuel</term> <note>Referring to the "populace" or the uneducated masses.</note> were taught that there were many gods, there was actually only one God by nature, who is the creator of all things.

## Chrysippus.

He was born in Tarsus <note>original: "Terassa."</note> in Cilicia <note>original: "Caramanien."</note>, the homeland of Paul the Apostle. He said that the "necessity of divine nature" was God. Sometimes he also proposed that the nature of physical things was God.

## Zeno.

This man was born in Citium on the island of Cyprus. For a time he lived in Rome, then moved to Athens where he taught about three hundred and fifty years <note>original: "vierthalbhundert jar."</note> before the birth of Christ. He taught his students under a porch or colonnade <note>original: "vor-schopff."</note> which the Greeks called a *Stoa*, which is why his followers are called the Stoics. Among other things, he said that God is the beginning of all things, a "body" or substance that is exceedingly pure and so wise that it permeates everything with its providence.

## Xenophanes.

He was an Ionian, the son of Orthomenis, from the city of Colophon—which is now called Altobosco, or "the High Forest," in the district of Chios <note>original: "Quisco."</note>. He lived nearly five hundred and fifty years <note>original: "sechss halb hüdert jare."</note> before the birth of Christ. Regarding God, he said: God is a single entity, and all things are one in Him <note>A reference to the pantheistic idea that "All is One."</note>.

## Parmenides.

He was from Elea, the son of Pyres <note>original: "Pyteti."</note>, and lived about four hundred and fifty years before Christ's birth. He said that there was a fiery, shining ring or crown that surrounded the world, and that very thing was God.

## Empedocles.

He was born in Agrigento <note>original: "Gargatho."</note> in Sicily and was a student of Pythagoras. He recognized no other god than what he named as Jupiter, Juno, Aidoneus, and Vesta <note>original: "Vestis."</note>, which he equated to the four elements: fire, earth, air, and water. He believed that these, along with their eternal strife and opposition, were the beginning of all things; otherwise, he held there was no God. Now, this very man could, as long as he showed no honor to God...

...wanted it known <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of a philosopher, likely Empedocles.</note>, because he was experienced in medicine and the natural arts. A person who had fallen into a faint during the plague and had lain for some time without signs of life, he later—as some believed—revived and awakened from death. Thus, he came into great esteem and fame among all people. So that this fame would remain with him, he went secretly to Mount Etna, which is now called Mongibello and spews fire. He willfully jumped into the abyss at the very top, with no other hope than that he hoped, if no one knew where he had gone, they would consider him a God. What great cleverness, O God! See, this wise man wants to be called God because of a simple medicine that he gave to the sick, which he borrowed from You. You, who give life and take away death, he will not acknowledge. Such is the wisdom of this world.

## Plato.

He was a quite magnificent, brave man, and the most learned among the Greeks, and the most grateful to his schoolmaster <note>Referring to Socrates.</note>. He was born in Athens, where he also gathered a following for his teaching, which remains even to this day with great worldly fame and is esteemed by learned people. They are called the Academicians because this <gloss>Plato held his school near Athens</gloss> in a pleasant, solitary place where there was a beautiful meadow and garden with shrubs and sprouting trees called <gloss>the Academy <note>original: "ἀκαδημία"</note></gloss>. This man recognized God as God as He is in Himself: that He is the creator, origin, sustainer, life, and perfection of all things. This is not to be wondered at, for this Plato traveled to Egypt to learn something true about God, and there he learned all the secrets of the priests. Moreover, he also read the books of Moses, about three hundred and eighty years before the birth of Christ. Indeed, this man wrote so magnificently of God that even some heathens believed John the Evangelist had taken the beginning of his Gospel from Plato. <gloss>But who would deny that the Spirit of God could have breathed into Plato the very same thing that He intended for John to write?</gloss>

## Speusippus.

This man was a sister’s son to Plato and also his heir. He said: God is a powerful, living nature that ordered and ruled all things.

## Aristoteles.

This highly learned man had nearly reached his fortieth year by the time of Plato's death. He had also heard him as a student for about twenty years in Athens, though he was <gloss>born in Macedonia</gloss> in an obscure village called Stagira, not far from the harbor or the landing place that is now called Doari. After the death of Plato, when Xenocrates took over the school of the Academy, Aristotle also went to Athens and, as a learned man, he established himself at a place called the <gloss>Lyceum <note>original: "Lyceū"</note></gloss>, which we might call the "Wolf’s Place" <note>The name Lyceum is derived from Apollo Lyceios, a title of the god often associated with wolves.</note>. There he held school, instructing his disciples while walking here and there. From this, the name of his following, the <gloss>Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticorū," meaning "those who walk about."</note></gloss>, grew. But one perceives here what the world's wisdom is, for in all schools, our ancestors and also the learned of our times have understood that whatever they wish to show as natural or divine must be proven precisely with his writings.

## Alcmeon.

Croton—now called Cotrone in lower Calabria, located on the Tarentine Gulf—produced this man, who was a young follower of Pythagoras <note>original: "Pithagore"</note>, a physician, and the first to reveal the internal causes of things <note>likely referring to his pioneering work in animal dissection</note>. He said that the sun, the moon, the other stars, and the mind were God. He could not conceive (as Cicero says) that with this teaching he was ascribing immortality to mortal things.

## Ecphantus.

This man was a Sicilian, born in Syracuse <note>original: "Serragosa"</note>; he said God was the mind and bodily power.

## Theodorus.

He was a fellow citizen of Democritus at Polystilo <note>Likely Abdera in Thrace, the home of Democritus.</note>, living about four hundred years before the birth of Christ. He said he could find nothing to indicate to him that there were any gods, or if there were, he did not know what they might be like. He received his reward, however, for he was driven out of the city and country by the Athenians, and his books were burned.

## Diagoras.

Opposite Crete <note>original: "Candien"</note> is the island of Millo, once called Melos; it was there this man was born. According to the noble arts of the time, he was held to be a wise man and a teacher (as Lactantius <note>A significant early Christian author and advisor to Constantine.</note> writes), yet he denied that God existed anywhere. 

There are some who write that once he entrusted something to someone for safekeeping, and that person later denied receiving it and refused to return it. This affected the man so deeply that, despite how God-fearing he had been before, he spoke out, saying: "There is no God, for if there were one, he would not let such a sin go unpunished in that rogue." Thus, I am inclined to believe that since he could not openly challenge the Athenian laws and their lax oversight, he mocked their gods and the very idolatry to which they clung with such superstition, as if to say: "They fear and honor idols of stone and wood, and if they omit anything in the sacrifice or service of these, they consider it a great sin. But if there were a true fear of God among them, such trickery <note>original: "bscheysserei"</note> would not be permitted to pass." 

Truly, he showed by his deeds that he despised idol-work; for at one time, when he had a great lack of wood and did not know how he should cook his food, he seized a wooden image of the god Hercules and said: "Now then, Hercules, you must face your thirteenth labor <note>original: "dryzehend Taͤpfstuͤck"</note>; defend yourself, or you must be my cook here!" Good Hercules did not move, so Diagoras quickly took his axe, split Hercules into logs, and cooked his meal with them. When the common people became aware of this, they called him "the Atheist" <note>original: "Gottlosen"</note>. <header>The First Book.</header>

...the temple of Juno <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Hera.</note> was visited by many on pilgrimages and possessed many kinds of hung-up tokens <note>votive offerings left by those saved from danger</note>, as well as inscribed tablets. On these were shown the names of those who, having suffered shipwreck in the waves of the sea, had swum out or otherwise escaped, having vowed to come there with a gift which they performed once they had been delivered from danger. 

Now, when Diagoras was asked and addressed by one of his good friends: "My dear Diagoras, do you not think—if the gods took no notice of human affairs as you claim—that so many would have escaped the fury of the sea, those who made their vows here and, as you well see, have placed their tokens here?" 

"You have made your point," said Diagoras, "but how many are there who drowned and could not stick their memorials here?" 

Later, as he and his company set sail again to return home and the tide came strongly against them, those who were in the ship with him said: "We have this monstrous storm from no one else but you, O you who despise the gods; it serves us right—why did we let you board?" 

"Ha!" he said, "look over there, twenty more ships are being tossed to and fro by the waves. Am I in all of them?" Now, this man lived about four hundred years before the birth of Christ.

## ->Theodorus.<-

This man is from Cyrene in Africa; he was a famous person who lived about three hundred years before the birth of Christ. He said that everything told about the gods was a fable, for there were none of them. He was called "the godless" <note>original: "gottloß"</note>, and everyone shunned him, although he also gained followers.

## ->Epicurus.<-

This man lived during and after the life of Alexander the Great <note>Reigned 336–323 BCE.</note>, and his name gave rise to a following called the Epicureans. They are slandered as godless companions choked in all manner of lusts. This is because it is boasted that he claimed all welfare and the highest good lay in pleasure. This he certainly did not understand as the pleasure of the body, for he led a temperate life and denied that anyone who did not lead an honest, modest life could have a pleasant life. 

But everyone has everyone else as friends and enemies, and it can easily happen that one who just wanted to swallow you out of love becomes hostile toward you. Thus, his detractors easily took what he said about the pleasure and rest of a free mind, independent of the world, and interpreted it as the kind of lust that the common man calls pleasure. Regarding God, however, he spoke thus: God is indestructible and eternal, but takes no part in human or worldly affairs, using these words: "The gods are always of one color, neither harsh nor soft, without anger, without joy." <note>This reflects the Epicurean view of divine indifference (ataraxia), suggesting gods exist but do not intervene in human life.</note> 

And to speak of it briefly, although the ancients who were held to be wise men recognized and found that there was a God, they were entirely unable to fathom what and how he might be. Many quarreled over his nature, his sense, form, location, and disposition. Therefore, Xenophon <note>A student of Socrates and a noted historian and philosopher.</note> also said: God could not be seen in his true form; for that reason, one should not scrutinize him, because, as Arcesilaus <note>A Greek philosopher and founder of the Second Academy, known for his skepticism.</note> says: God alone follows the truth, but man may never rightly achieve it.

What, however, the Egyptians in general, as well as the Moors, Atlanteans, and Phrygians held regarding God and the gods, is unnecessary to recount here...

<header>Concerning Heathen Gods</header>

...[to tel]l, because Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC, known for his monumental 'Library of History'.</note> gives a sufficient account of them.

Furthermore, what kind of gods this or that land worshiped and honored—how, why, and with what means—we will also describe more extensively hereafter. Yet I cannot neglect to mention here that many peoples besides the Jews would not permit images of the gods, or of that which they held in place of God. And to name our own dear ancestors, the Germans, before others, Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – c. 120 AD), a Roman senator and historian.</note>—who lived in the time of Emperor Trajan, about a hundred years after the birth of Christ—writes thus:

> They also consider it unsuitable for divine power, and that it cannot be adequately honored, if one were to enclose the gods within walls and barriers in temples, or wish to carve and fashion them in human form.

Thus it follows that until the time when the true service of God appeared most clearly and salvation-giving, through the luster of the incarnate Word of God, Germany remained without images. This the evil enemy <note>The author refers to the Devil.</note> could not endure, but directed the peoples between the Rhine, Elbe, and Danube to erect a pillar in memory of the army leader Hermann <note>Likely referring to Arminius, the Cheruscan leader who defeated the Romans at the Teutoburg Forest; the 'Hermanns-pillar' or Irminsul was a major Germanic sacred site.</note>, who fought so gallantly for his fatherland, which they called "Hermann’s Pillar" (from which some, I know not why, wish to make a Hermes or Mercury).

If, however, someone says that images of Mercury, Mars, Isis, and I know not what other gods are found elsewhere, he must not attribute this to the Germans; for they are found in no place except where the Romans held their splendor and garrisons. How little value they held among the Germans is shown by the fact that they are built into walls here and there in place of ashlar and cornerstones, rather than being placed or set in special locations or noble chambers. The same happened with the image of Svantevit <note>A four-headed Slavic deity of war and fertility worshiped on the island of Rügen.</note> in Rügen, when the Papal grace and preaching came into Germany with Archbishop Boniface, who is called our Apostle. For he [Boniface] could not point out enough of the true invisible God; the common man wanted to learn with Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many mystical and philosophical writings were attributed.</note> to make so many—indeed more—visible gods. Thus it is found that Germany never wanted to have any idolatrous images and also accepted images of saints quite late.

So too the city of Rome stood for over a hundred and seventy years before they ever erected an image of the gods. And since we have come to remember the Romans, it is not irrelevant to say what their learned men held concerning God.

## Marcus Varro.

This man, as Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) who often quoted pagan sources to support Christian arguments.</note> writes, was the most learned among the Greeks and Romans; Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who discusses Varro extensively in 'The City of God'.</note> also grants him the fame of being the most learned, saying that this man read so much that it is a wonder how he had the leisure to write so much, and he wrote so much that it is equally unbelievable that he had time to read anything. He was a high-born Roman, held in high esteem in the time of Cicero, and followed the Academy <note>The Academic school of philosophy, which often emphasized skepticism or the difficulty of certain knowledge.</note>. He wrote of the origin and life of the old city of Rome, recorded the course of the ages, what the mysteries of divine service were, and also from where the names and surnames of gods and men arose. He set down in writing their lineages, offices, and their origins—what belonged to the priest, the master of the house, and the soldier—as well as the landscapes, villages, in what places and how each was situated. Thus Cicero confessed that that which he wrote was [derived] from

# The First Book.

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar often called "the most learned of the Romans."</note> is well-regarded, even considered the very best; praise is given to him for his inventive understanding and his singular skill in all the arts. Now, this very man said: He considers that God is the soul of the world, and that the world itself is God.

->**M. T. Cicero.**<-

~~Let he who has the desire read Plutarch in German translation, concerning the life of Cicero; there he would perceive the form and nature of a wonderful, precious man.~~ <note>This passage was struck through in the original manuscript.</note> Concerning God, he says: God is a free, unbound spirit, who is separated from any accumulation of any kind of mortality, and who perceives and weighs all things.

->**C. Plinius.**<-

This man was a significant and visible wonder-work of nature, for he described the wonders of Nature so extensively that the whole world marveled at his skill; and he himself must have been struck with awe at that which was previously created so skillfully through the wisdom of God. Now this Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note>, who lived in the time of Vespasian, knew and investigated all created things and creatures so well—their essence, form, powers, and effects. But (and here one must be seized with horror), he was not able, or perhaps not willing, to recognize the One who provided all of this. Oh, the wonderful judgment of God! Oh, the unfathomable counsels of Divine wisdom! Here God wishes to have nothing hidden from this man, yet He keeps the ultimate cause hidden from him. For who knows anything if he does not recognize God? Dear reader, hear what this man speaks so shamefully of the same.

I consider it merely human folly <note>original: "blödigkeit"</note> (he says) to wish to seek an image or form of God. For whoever God truly is (if indeed a God exists at all), and wherever he may be, he is nothing else than all perception, all that is seen, all that is heard, pure soul, even the very spirit itself, in all of his own being. To believe that there are many gods is a childish madness. God is simply when one mortal provides help to another mortal. I almost do not know which is better for mankind: whether to believe, as some do, that there is no God at all, or to honor such shameful gods with such foolish pageantry that it is an outright disgrace. But as we live, it nonetheless guides the human race somewhat to believe that there must be gods who punish sin, so that wantonness might be somewhat dampened. And so that he might pour out his lack of understanding all at once, he says further, like a godless man:

Human folly, which is imperfect by its very nature, has this one thing with which it may comfort itself: That God cannot do all things. For He cannot inflict death upon Himself, nor can He make it so that twice ten is not twenty, etc. Oh, the terrifying punishment of God! Here, out of his failure to recognize such high gifts, Pliny mocks his merciful God rather than being willing to be thankful and acknowledging of Him.

->**An Unnamed Author.**<-

"Therefore I call upon you, you highest begetter and sower of all..."

# Of Pagan Gods

...to whom alone all divinity is attributed—which is granted to other gods by all peoples, either collectively or individually—and in as many languages as you are agreed to be called upon. But how you wish to be named or called is not for us to know. It may be that within you is a power and a common divinity poured into the world, mixed into fire, air, earth, and water, to which no external harmful pressure may come, so that you are moved by yourself. Or perhaps you are a power raised above all heavens, through which you oversee these your works, as if from a high castle of Nature. For at once all goodness and all love are in you; therefore you desire nothing other than what is right, and you have no reason to refuse the same, because you are able to fulfill it; and if there were something that you would not grant to those who have deserved so well of you, then either your power or your goodness would be failing.

¶ Now I would be well-advised to omit the opinions concerning God held by those whom we call the Latin and Greek poets, for the reason that their talk has no foundation and their sayings are wavering; but because Clement of Alexandria <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), a Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260 – 339 AD), the "Father of Church History" who often cited pagan authors to show they foreshadowed Christian truths.</note>, and others were not ashamed to cite some of them herein, the labor should not vex us either, and we will first begin with Orpheus, who is the oldest.

## Orpheus.

He lived almost thirteen hundred years before the birth of Christ, in the time of Abimelech <note>original: "Ammelechs." Abimelech was a figure in the biblical Book of Judges.</note>, the Judge in Israel; he speaks of God thus:

->In heaven sits God, encompassing the earth<-
->Beginning, middle, and end; He is the worthy essence<-
->Otherwise you may never express Him<-
->My limbs wish to break<-
->When I turn my mind toward Him<-
->And consider the highest art of His power<-
->The gods and the spirits fear Him<-
->He knows no decline whatsoever.<-

## Hesiod.

This one also lived eight hundred years before Christ was born; he speaks of God thus:

->You are a King and a Lord<-
->Of all that which shall never die.<-

## Pindar.

He was a citizen of Thebes (now Stibes in Boeotia) and lived some five hundred years before Christ's time; he says of God thus:

->Let it be a certain purpose for you<-
->That God is the origin of all things<-
->For in that there is no lack<-
->He is that which shall be, what was, and is.<-

## Parmenides the Great.

<margin>*</margin> Not long after this one, he lived and spoke of God in his poem thus:

->He is unborn, and therewith<-
->Free from all decline and destruction<-
->He is whole, only-begotten, and<-
->Firm; to Him no beginning is known.<-

## Diphilus.

## Aeschylus.

Approximately four hundred and seventy years before Christ, there lived this man, an Athenian, who speaks of God in this way:

> ->God is the earth and also the air<-
> ->The Heaven, which has no rift<-
> ->He is at once all that<-
> ->Which is, or which ever was<-
> ->All that is mortal or frail<-
> ->Is apart from Him, at all times.<- <note>Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BC) was one of the three great Greek tragedians. This verse reflects a pantheistic view where God is synonymous with the fabric of the universe.</note>

## Euripides.

His contemporary and fellow citizen was **Euripides**, who held the following view of God, where he says:

> ->Do you see this heaven high<-
> ->Which is so wide, and yet has no end<-
> ->Believe that this is the worthy God<-
> ->Who thus moistly encloses the earth.<- <note>Euripides (c. 480–406 BC) refers here to the "aether" or the atmosphere, which ancient Greeks often identified with the divine breath or presence surrounding the world.</note>

For a long time now among us Germans, there has also been a patched-together booklet in circulation under the title **Sibyl's Prophecy**. Although few know what or who the **Sibyl** actually was, because she spoke so reasonably about God, it seemed to me not entirely in vain to set down some of her sayings here—though first I must describe what everyone should think of such women in the future. For there were two opinions even among the ancients regarding them. First: it is believed that because there was once a priestess of the idol **Apollo** at **Delphi** who prophesied and was named **Sibyl**, all subsequent prophetic women kept the name **Sibyl**. After that, others say that this is a name joined together from two words; for in Greek *God* <note>original: "σιὸς" (sios) — a Doric form of "theos".</note> means "gods" and *counsel* <note>original: "βουλὴ" (boule)</note> means a "counselor." As if to say, she is the one who brings forth the counsel of the gods.

The learned count ten of these **Sibyls**, as **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar whose list of Sibyls became the standard reference for Christian writers.</note> says. The first was born in **Persia** in a city called **Noe**; her father was named **Berosus** and her mother **Erymätha**; her true name was **Sambetha**, and she wrote twenty-four books concerning Christ the Lord. The second was a **Moor** from **Libya**. The third lived at **Delphi** and was named **Athennis**; **Diodorus** mentions her in another way. In **Cumae**, in the Kingdom of **Naples**, lived the fourth, who was called **Herophile**. The fifth was from **Erythraea**, named **Athenais**, in the time of **Alexander**. The sixth was named **Phyto**, from **Samos**. The seventh was named **Amalthra**, and was at home in **Cumae**. The eighth was a woman of the **Hellespont**, in the time of **Solon**, from the village of **Marmissa**, called **Lampusia**. The ninth was from **Phrygia**; the tenth was at home in **Tivoli**, named **Albunea**.

# Concerning Pagan Gods

...things, of which all deity alone is possessed, which is attributed to other gods among all nations, either collectively or individually; and as many languages as there are, you are invoked with them. But what you wish to be called or named is unknown to us. It may be that in you there is a power and mind <note>The abbreviation "gm" likely stands for *Gemüt*, meaning mind or spirit.</note> that is divine, infused into the world, mixed into fire, air, earth, and water, to which no external, transient pressure may come, so that you move yourself. Or you are perhaps a power exalted above all heavens, through which you oversee these your works as if from a high castle of Nature. For at once in you is all goodness, all love; therefore you desire nothing other than what is right, and have no reason to refuse the same, because you are able to do it; and if there were something that you would not grant to those who have deserved well of you, then either your power or your goodness would fail.

Now I would be well-minded to omit the opinions of God from those whom we call the Latin and Greek Poets, for the reason that their talk does not hold firm and their sayings are wavering; but because Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, and others were not ashamed to cite several of them here, the labor shall not vex us either, and we will begin first with Orpheus, who is the oldest.

For a long time among us Germans, a stitched-together booklet has circulated under the name *The Sibyl’s Prophecy*. Although few people know what or who the Sibyl was, since she did not speak so inconsistently regarding God, it seemed to me not entirely in vain to include several of her sayings here. The eighth was a Hellespontine, from the village of Marmessos, called Lampusia in the time of Solon. The ninth was from Phrygia, and the tenth was at home in Tivoli <note>original: "Tiboli"</note>, named Albunea.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

Now, regarding these Sibyls, the prevailing opinion is that their writings were mixed together and not attributed to any one specifically, but were all given under a single name. As I intend to show further with God’s help, when the six books of *The Sibyl’s Prophecy* (translated from Greek into Latin by Sebastian Castellio <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) was a French theologian and a famous humanist scholar who produced influential Latin and French translations of the Bible.</note> and by me into German) are brought to light. But what the Sibyls held regarding the one God, we wish to set down here as well.

### **Sibylla** *Erythrea.* <note>The Erythraean Sibyl was a priestess of the Apollonian oracle at Erythrae in Ionia.</note>

After the rebuilding of the *Capitolium* <note>The main temple and citadel of Rome.</note> or Town Hall in Rome, which had burned down through the negligence of the guards about one hundred and thirty-six years before Christ’s birth, the Romans sent Publius Gabinius, Marcus Octacilius, and Lucius Valerius to Erythrae to fetch the writings of the Sibylline oracles. Thus they brought back about a thousand lines of them, among which were several that read as follows:

> There is one single God. Who
> Alone rules. So is He also more
> Singular, for everything else that is
> Is comprehensible; He at no time
> Was born; also the Creator of
> Heaven, Sun, Moon, stars, earth, water.
> He made mankind, gave him His image.
> He remains whatever lives, both tame and wild.

### **Sibylla** *Chumea.* <note>The Cumaean Sibyl, the most famous of the Sibyls in Roman tradition.</note>

After she had spoken long and much about what God had commanded her to convey to mankind, she said further: "Thus speaks the Lord of Himself:"

> I, I am alone God the Lord,
> Outside of Me there is no God anymore.

Now, however, so that I do not make the reader weary, I will proceed to bring forth one or two examples showing that the false gods, against their own will, spoke and answered truthfully about the true God. For when Apollo <note>The Greek god of prophecy; here, the author refers to the oracular responses given in his name.</note> was once asked by someone who God was, or what He might be, he said:

> God comes from Himself. He has
> Never had a teacher. He exists
> Eternally. No mother brought Him into the world.
> Whoever would try to describe Him fails.
> In light He dwells always, forever and ever.
> That very thing is God, I tell you.

Nicocreon, the tyrant in Cyprus <note>Nicocreon (died 311 BC) was the last king of Salamis in Cyprus.</note>, once had this Apollo asked what or how God might be; then he gave this answer:

> God is everywhere. If you seek His limbs,
> You find them always here and there.
> The adorned heaven signifies His head;
> His breast and belly are the wide sea;
> The soil of the earth is His thigh;
> His ears are the air;
> The bright radiance of the Sun (believe me)
> Is His eye, before which nothing is hidden.

### The Second Book.

<image-desc>A large, elaborate ornamental calligraphic initial 'W' featuring intricate, interwoven lines and scrollwork.</image-desc>
As was sufficiently shown in the first book, certain distinguished persons—highly regarded by the learned and accepted as masters by the ancients—have, out of human reason, foolishly spoken of God (if I may say so) and thereby falsely misled others. Not all that can be found on this subject has been placed here, for there is an uncountable amount remaining that would be tedious to recount, since, as the saying goes: *As many minds, so many heads.* <note>A translation of the Latin proverb *Quot homines, tot sententiae* (As many men, so many opinions).</note> It is enough to record here that even among the Heathens <note>The term "Heathen" (German: *Heyden*) was used by Renaissance writers to refer to the non-Christian peoples of antiquity, particularly the Greeks and Romans.</note> there were many magnificent men who knew well that there is but one single God, and that all other gods were merely a fabricated fable and human invention; indeed, even the devils and evil spirits must confess this. Therefore, we shall now proceed and take in hand the classification of such false gods.

<margin>Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> says openly that the nature of the gods was accepted in this way—and not without reason—by the wisest among the Greeks and Latins: wherever some benefit or something useful to the human race occurred, they knew such must flow from the kindness of the true (though unrecognized) God; therefore, they honored the gift of God by the name of a god.</margin>
Firstly, some divide these gods very briefly into six types: Heavenly, Earthly, Hellish, those of the Sea, of the Springs, and of the Flowing Waters.

Then there are those who divide them into three parts: Gods, Demigods (half-human, half-god), and Heroes.

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar known for his works on Roman religion.</note> separates the known gods from the unknown; likewise, the Athenians held that some were native gods and others were foreign <term>guest-gods</term> <note>Original: *Gastliche götter*. This refers to the Greek practice of incorporating foreign deities into their own local worship.</note>.
