# Of the Heathen Gods
## The Consentes: The Supreme Ones.

The most prominent, however, in the divine dominion are estimated to be twelve in number, half of whom are men and the other half women. They were also called *Consentes*—that is to say, the Councilors—by the ancients, for the reason that they took counsel on all matters with Jupiter. They are those whom Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), a writer often called the father of Roman poetry.</note> recounts as follows:

->Juno, Vesta, pure Minerva,<-
->Ceres, Diana, fine Venus,<-
->Jupiter, Mars, Mercury,<-
->Vulcan, Apollo, Neptune.<-

To each of these was also assigned their own month of the year and their sign of the sun <note>zodiac sign</note> in the heavens. Likewise, a part of the human body, the powers of the elements, the birds in the air, the fish in the water, the animals upon the earth, and the ores beneath the earth were granted, attributed, and dedicated as their portion. However, among the star-gazers <term>astrologers</term>, a different division is found, which we shall leave to its proper place; instead, we shall describe several of their powers that most closely resemble nature, as follows hereafter and as has been found by various authors.

## <term>The Selected <note>original: *Selecti*; refers to the *Dii Selecti*, a group of twenty principal Roman deities considered more powerful than the common gods.</note></term>

Thus you have these eight gods, whom they call the "Selected," because the ancients believed they possessed some power and influence in the heavens, upon the earth, and beneath the earth. These were their names:

-> Janus, Saturn, Genius <-
-> Pluto, Bacchus, the Sun, the Moon, the Earth <-

These eight, counted alongside the previous ones <note>likely referring to the twelve *Dii Consentes* mentioned on a previous page</note>, brought the total number to twenty. For this reason, some grouped them together as husband and wife, in this manner:

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jupiter | Apollo | Mercury | <term>Liber <note>The god of wine and fertility, often identified with Bacchus.</note></term> |
| Juno | Diana | Minerva | Ceres |
| 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| Saturn | Mars | Vulcan | <term>The Sun <note>original: *Sol*</note></term> |
| <term>The Earth <note>original: *Tellus*</note></term> | Venus | Vesta | <term>The Moon <note>original: *Luna*</note></term> |

Since in natural, worldly matters, each aids and supports the other in their influence, whereas the remaining ones were unique in their specific duties and actions, they left them without wives. These were:

-> Janus, Neptune, <term>Genius <note>In Roman belief, a *Genius* was a protective spirit or divine nature inherent in every person, place, or thing.</note></term>, Pluto. <-

Now, concerning the supposed might, powers, and influences of these gods—as the most prominent among them—we intend to describe them in the following six books according to an established order, as far as time permits, yet with the utmost diligence.

# The Second Book.
## Jupiter.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting the god Jupiter. He is seated on an ornate throne, bare-chested and wearing a crown. He holds a long scepter in his left hand and a bundle of lightning bolts in his right hand. To his left stands an eagle, and to his right is a young boy (Ganymede) holding a drinking vessel. At the base of the throne lies a defeated giant.</image-desc>

Now that it has been shown which gods the heathens called the highest and most powerful, I wish to describe in particular what was held regarding each of them. And first, concerning Jupiter, whom they called the beginning of all things and also the lord of all that exists. For just as the soul rules the body, so (says Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD known for his allegorical interpretations of Greek mythology.</note>) does Jupiter rule the entire world. For this reason, although the ancient wise men well knew that God is one and alone, they nonetheless gave him many surnames. Above all, the Latins called him Jupiter, meaning a "helper" <note>original: *Jupiter*; derived from the Latin *Juvans Pater*, meaning "Helping Father."</note>, while the Greeks called him *Zos* <note>original: *Ζωσ*; a variant or corruption of *Zeus* or *Zen*, which the author connects to the Greek word for "living."</note>, which signifies a source of life. We shall also present the other surnames hereafter. Cicero writes thus of him: One counts and speaks of three Jupiters. The first and second, some claim, were in Arcadia; one had a father named Aether <note>The personification of the upper sky or "upper air."</note>, the other Coelum <note>The Latin word for "Sky" or "Heaven."</note>. The third was born in Crete or Candia <note>Candia was the Venetian name for the island of Crete.</note> and was a son of Saturn; indeed, his grave is said to still be found there. Varro, however, speaks of well over three hundred Jupiters who were put forward here and there to be worshipped through the superstition of the ancients.

His image was commonly seen sitting upon an ivory royal throne, entirely bare from the head down to the belt. In his left hand, he carried a royal staff <note>a scepter</note>; in the right hand, a thunderbolt which he shot down upon the giants, who then lay dead beneath his feet. Next to him stood an eagle on one side, which led a beautiful boy <note>This is Ganymede, the cupbearer to the gods.</note>; this boy held a beautiful drinking vessel in his hand and offered Jupiter a drink from it. He was also covered from the waist down.

Some, such as the Cretans or Candiots, depicted him without ears; the Lacedaemonians <note>The people of Sparta.</note> gave him four ears. In the City of the Sun in Egypt <note>Heliopolis.</note>, they fashioned him out of gold in the form of a youth who was not yet bearded; they gave him a whip in his right hand with which he strikes, and in the left a ray of light along with several ears of corn. Others depicted him in the form of a mature and brave man.

Martianus Capella <note>A Latin author from late antiquity known for his encyclopedic work on the liberal arts.</note> depicted his Jupiter with a flaming crown upon his head; over this, he spread a small red veil and a white shirt. As an outer garment, he gave him a robe of azure color that was set and embroidered with little stars. In his outstretched right hand, he held two globes: one golden, the other of amber <note>original: *Augstein*; an archaic German term for amber.</note>. With the left hand, he leaned upon a lyre <note>original: *Geygen*; literally "fiddle," but in this classical context referring to a stringed instrument like a lyre or cithara.</note> with nine strings. He wears greenish boots and steps upon a net.

With this painting, they wished to signify several things: Firstly, that by his sitting, one should judge how unchangeable and steady his power is. That he was bare on the upper part should be understood to mean how he is so visible, wonderful, and bright in his heavenly creations—moreover, visible to the angels alone...

# Of Heathen Gods
<sig>X</sig>

visible; for this reason he is covered from the waist down, so that much of his eternal nature <note>original: "vnanfängklich," meaning without beginning.</note> cannot be recognized or fathomed by the lower creatures. And because in man the heart is situated on the left side, he carries the royal scepter in that same hand, as an indication that the king and creator of all things—the soul and the understanding—resides in all. That he shoots the lightning bolt with the right hand signifies his omnipotence and glory; for what is swifter <note>original: "trüngerlicher." While this can mean "deceptive," in the context of lightning it refers to its sudden, piercing, and overwhelming nature.</note> than the bolt? Thus the right side is always held to be more honorable. The Giants at his feet signify that no earthly power may stand before him, nor can any successfully rise up against him. 

And because the eagle is by nature a hot-blooded creature or bird, and moreover desires the heights and soars upward, they have painted it beside him. By this they give us to understand that fervent love and the fear of God—a pure soul—is directed toward heaven and carried there by the youth <note>Referring to Ganymede.</note> who sits upon the eagle; this is the loveliest and most acceptable drink offering to Him. To exclude the idle fables which say that Jupiter abducted Ganymede for the sake of his beauty, Xenophon <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and historian.</note> clearly shows that he was taken up for the sake of his rich soul. 

That the Candiotes <note>People of Crete (Candia).</note> painted him without ears was intended to show that it is not fitting for the ruler of all things to listen to one more than another; rather, he should know beforehand how to help everyone according to their needs in response to their cries. Those who gave him four ears reported that he maintains all things by hearing from the four corners of the world.

Martianus <note>Likely Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author whose work "The Marriage of Philology and Mercury" was a standard textbook on allegory.</note>, however, who observed the nature of Jupiter, intends with the crown of flames to show his fiery nature; with the red veil, its luster. And because his star is so pure, the two spheres held out signify that his influence—a great foresight, a fruitful and skillful power—brings such qualities to one born under his path; that he also makes the earth lovely and green is signified by the green boots.

Some crowned him with leaves because his nature is lovely, and his branches are forever greening, lush, and useful. Others placed an oak wreath upon him to signify the memory that before he brought mankind into a brave and respectable community, they had eaten acorns. Concerning the image that was set in his place in the City of the Sun, we shall speak in another place; but now we shall recount some of his surnames.

## ->Pater. Father.<-

He was called "Father" primarily because he shelters all his creatures with a fatherly, friendly grace, and furthermore rules everything with foresight, serving as a guide and leader of an honorable and godly life.

## ->Jupiter. Helper.<-

He is called this because in Latin *iuvare* means "to help," as if one were to say *Juvans pater*, which is the "helping father" who fatherly assists mankind, agriculture, fruits, and everything that has life. For this reason, he was also called *Jupiter Pappens* or *Pappas* by the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia.</note>, which means nothing other than "Father." From this, we Germans (having changed a few letters) say *Aette* or *Tätte* <note>Archaic or dialectal German terms for "Dad" or "Father."</note>; the Hebrews say *Abba*; all of which mean "Father." From this, the words *Papst* <term>Pope</term> or *Pfaff* <term>Priest or Parson</term> were brought forth.

# The Second Book.

## Rex. King.

He was called a King; for in Lombardy, which is now called La Burdia <note>Likely a reference to Longobardia. The text mentions a city in "Grecien" (Greece), which may be a historical confusion by the author or a reference to a specific lost source.</note>, there stood a temple that was consecrated to Jupiter the King. Likewise at Sardis in Lydia, there was also a temple where Cyrus, the king of Persia, sacrificed to Jupiter the King <note>original: "Jupiter dem künig geopffert"</note>.

## Omnipotens. Almighty.

Almighty—thus he is named by Virgil, Soranus, Orpheus, Homer, and, as Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian and lexicographer of the 5th or 6th century.</note> says, the Athenians.

## Optimus, Maximus. The Best and Greatest.

Among the Latins, he was always called upon with all earnestness and devotion as the Best and the Greatest, because it is within his will and power to show goodness to the world. And under this title, King Tarquinius Priscus of Rome vowed to build him a temple, which was later raised from its foundations by Tarquinius Superbus; however, after he was driven out, this temple was later consecrated by Horatius, a burgomaster <note>original: "Burgermeyster"; in this Roman context, it refers to a Consul.</note>.

## Dius. Of the Air.

Among the other seven wandering planets or stars, there is one that is the highest and most beneficial—indeed, the healthiest—assigned to Jupiter; for this reason, he is also at times named and called for the healthy air <note>original: "gfunden lufft," meaning the clear or wholesome atmosphere.</note>, as a cool, lovely star that the Greeks call *Dios* <note>original: Διός</note>; thus the name has remained with him.

## Victus. Victorious.

The ancients believed that all things must fall before him; therefore, when Papirius fought against the Samnites near Aquilonia, and the battle stood very hard, he vowed to Jupiter the Victorious <note>original: "Joui dem Sigparen"</note> that if he helped him to strike the enemy, he would—before he drank any drink—offer up a vessel of mead to him. Thus he held the victory, and over thirty thousand of the enemy lay fallen. A holiday was also held on the thirteenth of April in honor of Jupiter; for when the Romans warred with the Sabines, Quintus Fabius vowed a temple to this Jupiter, which was built on the Palatine Hill. Likewise, Jupiter was also honored under this name by the Greeks, for they had a temple in Epirus called the *Niceum*, for *nike* <note>original: νίκης</note> signifies "victory." There, at one time, the Macedonian king struck his camp while fighting against the Romans.

## Inuictus. Unconquerable.

Augustine says in the seventh book of *The City of God* <note>original: "Statt Gottes"</note> that Jupiter was also honored under this name. He also had a temple in Rome in which a consecration festival <note>original: "kirchweyh"</note> was held on the thirteenth of June <note>original: "Brachmonats," the old German name for June, the "fallow month."</note>.

## Imperator. The Commander.

At Praeneste <note>original: "Prenestina"</note>, not far from Rome, Jupiter had a [temple] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note> under this name.

## Custos. The Guardian.

<margin>before he was Emperor</margin> Some say a temple was erected to this Jupiter by Domitian for this reason: when the reign of Vespasian was beginning, and the Vitellians <note>Supporters of the rival Emperor Vitellius during the civil wars of 69 AD</note> had taken the Capitol, Domitian was hidden by the sexton or bell-ringer. One of his freedmen dressed him in priestly clothes, and he mingled among the priests so that he later escaped and fled to good friends until his father became the supreme Lord. Then he tore down the sexton’s house and built for Jupiter—whom he calls <term>Conservatorem</term> <note>The Preserver or Sustainer</note>—a small, simple chapel, and had an altar made upon which was written all that had happened to him. When he himself had become Emperor, he erected a great and magnificent temple to this Jupiter and had himself depicted sitting in the god’s lap.

Furthermore, one finds coins struck or minted under the name of Nero which have on one side a seated Jupiter who carries a lightning bolt in his right hand and a spear in his left, with the inscription <note>original: "IVPITER CVSTOS"</note> JUPITER THE GUARDIAN.

## Capitolinus. He of the Capitol.

This name—and the temple in which the image stands—has always been the highest, most honored, and most devotedly visited, where all the gifts and offerings of kings, princes, and lords from all lands were given. But the name comes from this: that a temple was built to Jupiter in the city of Rome, indeed in the fortress or citadel of the same, upon the hill that was previously called Saturnius and later Tarpeius. For when Ham the son of Noah—whom some call Saturn—came to Janus in those parts where the city of Rome now stands, he built a small town on a hill there, from which the little hill and town obtained his name. 

Now, in time, as the descendants built a citadel, fortress, or castle on the hill, they also established a convent of nuns <note>The author refers to the Vestal Virgins using contemporary 16th-century Christian terminology</note> or a cloister for virgins upon it. Thus it happened that the Sabines came into conflict with the city; they overran the city and besieged the castle. Tarpeia, a nun and daughter of Spurius Tarpeius the castellan, secretly conspired with the enemies, asking that they give her their "weapons and beautiful gilded jewelry" <note>An allusion to the golden bracelets the Sabines wore</note> if she delivered the castle and opened the gates to them. The enemies agreed, but once they were let in and she demanded her reward, they grew disgusted by the traitress and threw their weapons and jewelry—their heavy shields—upon her so violently that she was crushed and suffocated under them. Thus the fortress was afterwards called Tarpeia. 

When, some time later, they were digging to build another temple, they found the skull of a murdered Volscian who had been buried there, who was perhaps named Tolus; after that, the place was named <note>original: "Caput Tolij"</note> the Head of Tolus <note>Etymological legend for the name "Capitol"</note>. Thus at times this Jupiter was called Tarpeius...

...once called Capitolinus <note>Referring to the Capitoline Hill in Rome</note>, and over time this temple was so adorned that some write: as far as heavenly things are distinguished from earthly ones, so far did this temple surpass all wondrous buildings and ornaments of the world. Tarquinius Priscus <note>The fifth King of Rome (r. 616–579 BC)</note> vowed to build this temple to **Jupiter the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Beſten vnd Grőſten Jupiter," translating the Latin title Jupiter Optimus Maximus</note> while he was fighting the Sabines, as was said before. The statue, however, was made by a potter named Turritanus, who was at home in Fregella, a city located at the place that is now perhaps Pontecorvo or Atripalda, not far from Rome. And so it was made of earthenware, glazed and painted in the most beautiful fashion; for this, Tarquinius Priscus commissioned him (as Pliny writes).

Since I have come this far, it seems right to me not to omit how this temple came to be. In the last battle that the Roman King Tarquinius Priscus fought against the Sabines (which now comprises the Duchy of Spoleto), he vowed in his hour of need that if victory should be granted to him, he would found a temple to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. When he had succeeded, he intended to prepare the site on a hill. However, it was uneven, sharp, full of peaks and crags, and also entirely steep, so that it was difficult to climb; furthermore, there was no wide, flat space at the top. Therefore, he had many pillars and support columns raised and built up masonry level with the peak of the mountain; afterward, he poured and filled the empty gaps with soil and gravel until it became a level plain. All the common people were forced into hard labor <note>German: "fronen" – referring to the *corvée*, or unpaid labor required by a lord or king</note> for this. Because the work lasted so long (for he also constructed the water drains <note>Referring to the Cloaca Maxima, the Great Sewer of Rome</note>), the citizens became so resentful that some killed themselves to escape the labor. To prevent this, the King had the dead bodies crucified and left unburied to be cast before wild beasts and birds. The citizens were so deeply horrified by this that they chose to endure the toil and cost of the building rather than bear such disgrace. Just as he was preparing to begin the temple, he fell ill and died before he could lay the foundations.

His grandson, Tarquinius Superbus <note>Tarquin the Proud, the seventh and final King of Rome</note>, after he had taken the city of Sezza <note>Setia</note> on the Pontine Sea and captured a significant amount of plunder, undertook to finish the building started by his ancestor. He summoned all manner of craftsmen and artists. When they began to dig, a wondrous thing occurred: as they dug very deep to lay the foundations, they found the head of a man who had only recently been killed; his face was still quite lifelike, and it even sweated warm blood. When Tarquinius saw this, he ordered the digging to stop and sent messengers far and wide for the soothsayers of the land, asking them what this signified. They, however, did not know how to answer. They told the King he should send to Tuscany <note>Etruria</note>, where there were very certain soothsayers, and they pointed out which one there was the most famous. Thereupon the most prominent citizens were sent to him as ambassadors. When these men arrived at the place where the soothsayer lived, a young boy met them by chance. They addressed him, asking that he help them as the Roman embassy and present them to the soothsayer. The youth said, "Dear Lords, he whom you seek is my father. He is busy now; you must wait a little, then you may go to him. But I advise you to tell me in the meantime what cause brings you here, so that I might give you some instruction on how you should deal with him, so that you do not fail in the..."

...that he would question you and perhaps confuse you with his answer, for you do not know how to speak with such people; however, much depends on how one asks or answers there. If you stick to this answer, he will not be able to outwit you and will well understand that he cannot turn away from you that which is destined for you; and then he will speak clearly as to what it signifies, hiding nothing."

When this message and instruction had been given by the youth, they followed it and answered in such a way that the soothsayer was forced to give this answer: "Now go forth, dear friends, and tell your citizens that it is ordained by God that the place where this head was found shall be a capital city <note>A play on words: "head" in Latin is *caput*, leading to the name *Capitol*</note> for the whole of **Italy**." Thus was this mountain and temple called the **Capitol**.

When this message was reported to the King and the community at **Rome**, he permitted and commanded the master-builders and laborers to proceed. He raised the temple very high and at great cost, but he could not finish it, for in the meantime he was driven out and chased into exile.

In the third year thereafter, however, when **Valerius Publicola** and **Marcus Horatius Pulvillus** were Mayors <note>The text uses "Burgermeister," but refers to the Roman Consuls</note>, and the temple had been fully built and each of them wished to dedicate it, **Valerius** was drawn away into war through the trickery of **Horatius**. Thus **Horatius** dedicated the temple on the thirteenth day of the Harvest Month <note>September</note>, four hundred and two years before the birth of **Christ**. But as he, with all due labor and devotion, was holding the doorpost, the brother of **Valerius** arrived and said: "Lord Mayor, your son has perished in the field," thinking he might turn the man away with such sad news. But the Mayor continued with his dedication and speech, answering only: "Throw the corpse wherever you wish." Thus was this temple built and dedicated, upon which King **Tarquinius Priscus** had bestowed such great effort, and **Superbus** <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the last King of Rome</note> spent forty thousand crowns. He made three small chapels within it: in the middle was **Jupiter**, and on both sides were **Juno** and **Minerva**, all under one roof and vault. Its front part faced South <note>original: "Mittag," literally midday</note> and had a porch with three rows of high columns; at the sides, it was vaulted upon two columns. This was done because **Tarquinius** had good knowledge of the **Etruscan** church ceremonies and secrets, and wished to give it to be understood that **Jupiter** held the middle in the air, **Juno** the lowest toward the earth, and **Minerva** the highest toward the fire <note>The author is likely associating the three gods with the Aristotelian elements or celestial spheres</note>.

# The Second Book #

Now, since this temple was burned in the time of **Sulla** and **Marius**, it was decorated anew. The image of **Jupiter** was made somewhat larger, placed higher, and positioned toward the rising sun, differently than it had been before. This was done in the hope that, if the image looked toward the square and market in **Rome** along with the **City Hall** <note>original: "Ratthaůß", referring to the Roman Curia or Senate House</note> toward the east, all plots secretly hatched against the city and the public would be revealed and discovered. Accordingly, the temple was improved and renewed by **Sulla**, who brought several marble columns from **Athens** for that purpose. **Catulus** made the covering or tiles of the roof from bronze plates which had been gilded; some of these may still be seen at **St. Peter’s Minster** <note>St. Peter's Basilica</note>, which **Pope Honorius** took from that very place. Likewise, **Q. Catulus** reconsecrated this temple.

So that you may know, however, what customs the ancients had in the consecration of their temples, I find that among the old **Romans**, a *Candelabrum* <term>Candelabrum: A lamp-stand or candle-stick</term> was what they called a candle-stick, and a *Delubrum* <term>Delubrum: A shrine or temple, or specifically the base for a cult image</term> was called a "god-stand." For just as in the part where a candle is placed they call it a *Labrum* <note>meaning a lip or basin</note>, making it a *Candela* [candle], so when an idol is placed in a stand, it is called a "god-stand" from *Deo* [God] and *Labro*. Now, to consecrate such a temple, chapel, or altar, the common people had to be called together and asked who seemed suitable among those whom the **Mayors** and **Guild-masters** <note>The author uses 16th-century German terms like "Burgermeister" and "Zunfftmeyster" to describe Roman magistrates and officials</note> had proposed by order of the **Council**. A Mayor or General was almost always chosen for this. When the one who was to perform it was named, a day and hour were determined on which all the people should gather and attend the church-consecration.

Then the **High Priest** <note>the Pontifex Maximus</note> came and lit a fire-pan, before which stood a trumpeter or piper. He placed the one who was to perform the consecration at the threshold of the door and exhorted him to take care and not fail by a single letter in his speech, otherwise the consecration would be worth nothing; he was also to repeat the words diligently after him. So the man repeated the words after him, grasping the door-threshold with one hand, while with the other he offered some grass plucked from a sacred spot, which they called *Sagmen* or *Verbena* <note>Latin terms for sacred branches or plants used in rituals</note> (which was the same as the **Iron-wort** <term>Iron-wort: Vervain (Verbena officinalis), a plant long associated with healing and sacred rituals</term> that old women now dig up on **St. John’s Day** and use for many superstitions) and spoke thus:

->**Jupiter**, you the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Jupiter du Bester vnd Gröster", translating the Latin title Jupiter Optimus Maximus</note> (or if it were another god, he named him by his name and surname as he was called), this temple, together with its belongings, cell, chapel, table, altar, and stand, I release and free from all claims of the common man and human worldly law; and whatever was possessed, given, and promised to this place, spiritual or worldly, I hereby promise and dedicate to you.<-

The **Greeks**, when they consecrated a temple, or an altar and idol, dressed many women in clothes of various colors and patterns; these women carried large pots full of vegetables <note>original: "gmůeß", referring to a pottage of legumes or grains</note> around, which they distributed and gave away to the bystanders after the office was completed. So much for consecration—if a word or deed was missing at the temple, it was worth nothing. However, in the case of consecrating an altar or image, the grasping of the posts could be omitted. But no person could consecrate anything for themselves who was not chosen by the community, for it was not considered consecrated if it was not unanimously recognized as holy.

This temple was afterwards set on fire, plundered, and burned by the **Germans** <note>Referring to the Germanic tribal soldiers or the Vitellian forces during the civil war of 69 AD</note> when the **Vitellians** and **Flavians** went to war with one another,

Thus it was rebuilt again by **Vespasian** in this manner: He had a counselor and very distinguished man with him named **Lupus Vestinus**, whom he commanded to be the master builder. This man called together the soothsayers, by whom he was advised as the gods wished: that the ruins and the fallen building should all be cleared away and cast into the sea and marshes, and the temple should be placed on the previous site, for nothing at all should be changed from its previous form. Accordingly, on the **twenty-second of July**, in the seventy-eighth year after the birth of Christ <note>original: "Heumonats" (Hay month), the traditional German name for July</note>, while the heavens were bright and beautiful, the entire site was strewn with flowers and, as far as its boundaries were to reach, it was draped with garlands and small veils. The soldiers marched onto the site and prayed for good fortune. Afterward came the **Vestal Virgins** <note>original: "nonnen Veſtis"</note> with young boys and daughters who still had both father and mother living <note>In Roman ritual, children with two living parents, known as "patrimi et matrimi," were required for their ritual purity</note>; these all carried water from springs, brooks, and rivers to wash the building site.

**Helvidius Priscus**, the <term>Schultheys: a chief magistrate or praetor</term> of **Rome**, was chosen to pray for atonement, and the High Priest **Plautus Aeliatius** had to dictate the words to him (as I will tell later in the book concerning the divine offices and ceremonies). He sacrificed an ox and a cow, laid the entrails upon a piece of turf, and prayed to **Jupiter**, **Juno**, and **Minerva** that they should help bring the matter to a fortunate end, grant grace to carry out the construction, and allow the church or temple to be entrusted to them through the devotion of the people. And so, he touched the rope to which the ashlar stones <note>hewn, squared stones</note> were hung to be pulled up. Immediately the other officials—such as the Councilmen, Priests, Knights, and the common men, especially the most prominent—pulled up the first and largest stone with great joy, which the **Emperor** himself laid. The wealthy all threw into the foundations native silver, gold, and ore; for the soothsayers had previously warned the people to see that no stone, gift, or gold previously dedicated to another use should be given there. Thus, this temple was erected in its previous form, except that it was somewhat higher, which was permitted by the priests, and otherwise nothing was deemed to be missing from the original.

This very temple caught fire afterward in the fifth year, when it was already completed and **Vespasian** had died. **Domitian**, however, his son, restored it again within eleven years afterward and gilded everything that was inside, so that it cost him over seven million and six hundred thousand crowns. To conclude briefly, this temple was a cathedral and foundation that could not be compared to any other in the entire world. Among other things, the gifts of kings were seen therein: a golden vine that had grapes made of precious gemstones, which was given as a gift by **Aristobulus**, a son of **Alexander** the <note>The text says "Indian King," likely a historical error or misspelling of "Iudiſchen" (Jewish), referring to the Judean King Alexander Jannaeus</note> King, which was valued at three hundred thousand crowns. Likewise, King **Antiochus** of **Syria** gave a candelabra made of precious stones of great value, from which one may perceive what magnificent treasures were spent there. Besides this, whenever the **Romans** captured a city or land, they robbed and stripped all other temples to decorate this one. Also inside were the images of all the Kings of **Rome**, of **Scipio** who defeated **Antiochus**, **Sulla**, **Aemilius Lepidus**, **Metellus**, **Cornelius**, **Fabius Maximus**, **Brutus**, **Africanus**, **Cornelia**, and others without number; and the four bronze columns that now stand at **St. John Lateran**. And in previous years, a small church stood on this very spot, called **San Salvatore in Maximis**. <header>The Second Book.</header>

...out of gilded [materials]. There are also such [Capitols] in **Toulouse** in **Spain** <note>original: "Tolosa in Spanien." Though Toulouse is in modern-day France, it was often associated with the borders of the Spanish provinces in older geographies</note>, in **Capua**, and in **Benevento**. There was also once a **Capitol** in **Cologne** in **Lower Germany**, on the site where the **Church of Our Lady** <note>The Church of St. Maria im Kapitol, built upon the foundations of a Roman temple</note> now stands.

## Fulminator: The Ray-Shooter <note>original: "Der Stralſchieſſend"</note>

Both the **Latins** and the **Greeks** gave **Jupiter** the names **Fulminator** <note>Latin: the Thunderer</note> and **Keraunios** <note>original: κεραύνιος; Greek: the wielder of the thunderbolt</note> because he destroyed the entire lineage of **Oenomaus** with thunder. Similarly, he has been called the **Thundering** and the **Lightning-dealer**, because in the region where he is honored, his flashing among the planets draws the clouds together, creates lightning, thunders, and strikes. For when **Seleucus**, the King of **Syria**, built the city of **Seleucia** by the sea and the thunder struck there, the common people believed the thunder was a god who had descended; they began to sing joyfully and honor **Jupiter** whenever it lightened or thundered.

Likewise, the Emperor **Augustus** built a temple to **Thundering Jupiter** because once, while he was waging war in **Cantabria** and was being carried at night in a litter, a bolt of lightning struck and scorched the litter in which he lay; it also struck dead the servant who was carrying him from the front. Now, when the temple was completed, everyone wanted to honor the Emperor by offering sacrifices in this new church. Because of this, **Capitoline Jupiter** appeared to the Emperor in a dream, looking angry because this new building was taking so many devout people away from his own temple. The Emperor replied that this **Thundering Jupiter** was merely his <term>Sacristan: an official in charge of a temple or church; original: "Mößner"</term> or gatekeeper, for he stood directly in front of the other **Jupiter's** temple. The next morning, he had the tower hung with small bells as a sign; for it was the custom (as it still is today) to hang small bells or chimes on towers to announce when someone entered a house.

## Feretrius: The Bearer-Master <note>The name Feretrius is traditionally derived from the Latin "ferre," to carry (the spoils), or "ferire," to strike (the enemy)</note>

**Romulus**, the first king of **Rome**, marched out against the **Caeninians** <note>original: "Ceniner"</note>, who lived about a mile from the city and who scouted and plundered the area around **Rome** with their livestock. He fell upon them so quickly and unexpectedly that as they fled toward their city, the enemy was so close behind them that **Romulus** entered with them. Before the citizens could truly recognize the enemy, **Acron**, their king, took his bodyguards and several chosen soldiers and charged at **Romulus**, intending to drive him out of the city and kill him.

But **Romulus** offered him single combat and slew him, hewing off his head and stripping him of all his armor, weapons, and gear. He carried these toward the city to a hill on the **Capitoline Hill**, where an oak tree stood at which the shepherds were accustomed to sacrifice. When he arrived there, he marked out a place with his feet and walked around it—about ten feet in length and no more than five in breadth—and gave the god his title, saying: "Now then, **Jupiter Feretrius**, look, here **Romulus** the King brings you royal armor and spoils. As I have purposed in my mind and marked out here, I wish to build you a temple, which I now promise and vow to you. This shall be a storehouse and chest for the rich and glorious spoils—namely, the weapons stripped from defeated kings and princes by those who succeed me in this Realm and who face enemies as I have done."

This temple was hereafter the first to be erected and consecrated in Rome. And Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>original: "Dionysius auß Alicarno"</note> says it is not far off the mark if one calls this Jupiter the "Thunder-hurler" <note>original: "τερψικέραυνον" (terpsikeraunon); Greek epithet meaning delighting in thunderbolts</note>, because he encompasses all of nature within himself and draws [all things] upward with his movement. One might also call him the "Spoils-bearer" <note>original: "σκυλοφορον" (skylophoron)</note> or the "Trophy-holder" <note>original: "τροπαιουχον" (tropaiouchon)</note>, which three words, when translated, mean: the Pursuer, the Spoils-bearer, and the Master of Victory Signs. 

Nearly three hundred years later, Cornelius Cossus, the mayor and general, slew Lartes Tolumnius, a king of the Veientines, and hung his armor and gear there, beside the trophy of Romulus. After this, over two hundred years later, Marcus Claudius Marcellus stabbed the Gallic king named Viridomarus <note>original: "Werdmayr"</note> and offered his embroidered, gold-melted armor and weapons to this Jupiter—the third and final [to do so]. 

Plutarch thinks that because the Latins adopted and mispronounced many words from the Greeks, they also called a stretcher <note>original: "feretrum"</note>—which the Greeks call a grave-pit—a "funeral bier" <note>original: "todten Bar"</note>. From this, they derived [the name] for Jupiter, because all the victory signs taken from enemies were carried by the Romans on a bier or stretcher. Thus, Jupiter could be translated here as "Master of the Bier" <note>original: "Barameister"</note>. In conclusion, this temple site in Rome is now called **Saint Mary in Ara Coeli** <note>original: "Sanct Maria in Ara Coeli"; the church on the Capitoline Hill built on the site of the Temple of Juno Moneta, near the site of the ancient Jupiter temples</note>.

### *Latialis.* The Latin.

This Jupiter has his name and temple from this: that Tarquinius Superbus, when he became the leader and general of the Latins, made an eternal alliance with the Volscians and Hernicians. He proposed to build a temple that would be common to the Latins, Volscians, Hernicians, and Romans, though the Romans, as the founders, would have all authority over it. He chose a site in one of these regions, on a mountain near Alba <note>Mount Albanus</note>, and established a feast day or church-dedication where the leaders of these nations would gather annually. 

Each brought his contribution of cattle and other things to be distributed among the common people. He also established a fair or annual market there, where they would feast honorably with one another; many sacrifices were made there, and the alliance was constantly renewed. This was then called the **Latin Festival** <note>original: "Latinisch feyer"</note>. The sacrifice offered for the entire alliance was a bull, of which each envoy of the allies was given his share, and such an animal was sacrificed on behalf of them all by a Roman priest. A certain number of lambs had to be sent from one city, a measure of milk from another, a heap of cheese from this one, and milk-cakes <note>original: "milchkuchen"</note> from that one, which were then distributed.

Athanasius and Lactantius claim that at times, humans were sacrificed to this Jupiter. Festus says: King Latinus of Alba, when he fought in a battle against King Mezentius of the Caerites, never reappeared, and no one knew where he went; he was thus called Jupiter Latiaris. However, Propertius believes he is the Capitoline Jupiter.

### *Stator.* The Stayer.

There is a place and church in Rome called **Saint Mary in the Pain of Hell** <note>original: "Sancta Maria in der hellen pein"; likely a reference to Santa Maria in Inferino, a site near the Roman Forum</note>, where a temple once stood that was [dedicated] to Jupiter by Romulus...

established under the aforementioned name. For when the Sabines had taken the Tarpeian Hill <note>The Capitoline Hill, where the Tarpeian Rock is located.</note>, Romulus came to do battle with them; but when his troops were driven into flight and he himself was hard-pressed, he cried out with a loud voice: "O Father of gods and men, do not let the enemy break in any further; take away the terror from the hearts of the despondent Romans; stay them! Oh, stay them, so that they do not flee so ruinously. Here, here (if you hear me), I will establish a temple to you under the name of 'Jupiter the Stayer' <note>original: "Stellenden Jupiters"</note> as a memorial for those who come after, that through your help this city was saved." Just as if Jupiter had heard these words, the Romans turned back, rallied together, charged against the enemy, and drove them into flight—until the Roman women (who, as maidens, had been carried off by the Romans during a public spectacle, which was the cause of the war) ran between the two sides and made peace. Seneca says that Jupiter was called "the Stayer" because he preserves and stays all things in their place through his divine grace and goodness. On certain coins of Antoninus Pius and Gordian <note>Emperors Antoninus Pius (r. 138–161 AD) and Gordian III (r. 238–244 AD).</note>, a naked figure is struck on the reverse side, standing upright, leaning on a spear with the right hand and holding a thunderbolt in the left, with this inscription: TO JUPITER THE STAYER <note>original: "IOVI STATORI"</note>.

The feast and celebration of this Jupiter was held on the twenty-seventh day of June <note>original: "Brachmonats"</note>, as may be read in Ovid and others.

Roughly four hundred and thirty years later, Marcus Atilius Regulus, the Consul <note>original: "Burgermeister"</note>, marched against the Samnites (who are now called the people of Abruzzo, the Lucerini). The battle became so fierce that a great multitude perished on both sides. He threw up his hands toward heaven and cried out that if the Romans would cease their retreat, he would build a temple to Jupiter the Stayer. Livy believes that Romulus only consecrated the ground <note>original: "kirchhoue"</note> and built nothing upon it, but that Atilius completed it. However, some point out that there was another temple of this name near Saint Anastasia; others say it stood between Saint Nicholas "among the rope-makers" <note>likely the church of San Nicola in Carcere or San Nicola degli Incoronati</note> and Our Lady of the Sun.

# Pistor. The Baker.

On the Capitoline, there also stood a chapel in the name of "Jupiter the Baker" <note>original: "Brotbecken"</note>. This comes from the time when the Gauls had captured Rome and were besieging the Capitoline Hill. Since they could not find a way to scale the mountain nor take it by force, they intended to starve out those lying within. Then Jupiter warned one of the men in the garrison in a dream that they should bake bread from all kinds of grain and throw it over the cliffs down among the enemy. This was done; and when the Gauls saw it, they believed those in the castle were well-provided with food and supplies, so they broke camp and despaired of capturing the fortress. For this reason, a temple was established at the place where the vision had come to the soldier. Some wish to claim that the statue called the *Marforio* <note>One of the famous "talking statues" of Rome, a colossal 1st-century AD personification of a river.</note> was an image of Jupiter, but I am more inclined to believe it represents the Rhine. For although there are things seen around the bottom that look like bread loaves <note>original: "weckechts"</note>, one can clearly see that it resembles a hurdle or mat woven of rushes, criss-crossed and checkered—smooth at one ear and rough at the other, with its diamond patterns.

# Of Heathen Gods
## Lapis. The Stone.

Jupiter received this very name of a stone because it was customary to swear oaths by God. It was the practice of the Romans, whenever they entered into a treaty with someone, that the appointed lords had to swear in the manner I will describe here, just as they swore to the Carthaginians.

"If I perform this covenant and oath faithfully and without any deception, then may God help me in all things. But if I act otherwise, or intend any injustice or evil, then may God protect everyone else while I alone perish, and may I never again find fortune—neither in my own ancestral laws and customs, nor in my own house or home, nor in my own churches, nor in my own burial place. Indeed, I must vanish just like this stone." With these words, he threw away the stone or pebble <note>original: "Kißling," meaning a flint or river pebble</note> that he carried in his hand.

Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian of the 2nd century AD.</note> says: "This was the custom and the wording of the oath among the ancients: 'If I knowingly do wrong, then may God, who looks down upon me from the heights, protect this city and fortress, and cast me away just as I fling this stone from me.'"

The Carthaginians had a similar custom for swearing. Hannibal held a lamb in his left hand and a pebble in his right, and said: "I pray to the gods that if I use deceit here, they may slaughter me just as I murder this lamb here." With these words, he struck the lamb dead with the pebble. The Athenians also swore upon a stone, as Aristotle indicated in his book on civil laws. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note> also notes that those who swore by the stone were perjurers if they did not keep what they had confirmed thereby. Oh, what wretched misery! What would Augustine say to us now, when he would hear young and old, high and low, every day naming the blood, the wounds, and every good deed of God—as well as all the limbs and sufferings of Christ—to support lies and intentional, premeditated deceit? Circumcise, O God in heaven, our uncircumcised hearts and our unclean lips.

For this reason, Jupiter was also honored by the Greeks under the name *Horkios* <note>original: ὅρκιος, meaning "of the oath"</note>, regarding the swearing of oaths. Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> says that in the town hall at Olympia, there was an image of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> which held a thunderbolt in each hand, as if to show both parties who were dealing with one another that if one among them failed his oath, punishment would not be far behind. For it was before this very image that one had to give and take the oath in this manner: The priest brought forward a boar, then the one who wished to swear took a dagger in his right hand and cut off some bristles, which he offered to Jove; then he raised his hand toward heaven and said: "You God of heaven and earth, you Sun, and all you of the Underworld who listen for the punishment of perjury, take heed. If it be that I use no deceit, then bless me well; but if I swear falsely here with my knowledge, then let the curse and punishment that must follow the perjurer come upon me. And as I do to this boar, so may God do to me." Then he slit the boar's throat and threw it into the nearest water or sea, so that the fish should consume it.

There was also another way among the Greeks to enter into alliances. For they took a glowing iron in their hand and prayed to God that the covenant [would last] as long...

...should last so long until the iron should come forth again; and with these words, they cast it into the sea <note>original: "Möhr," here referring to the sea or deep water. This refers to a famous oath by the Phocaeans who swore never to return to their city until the iron they threw into the sea floated back to the surface.</note>.

In Sicily, at the place called the Pool of the Palici <note>original: "Palicorum stagnum," a site of ancient volcanic springs in Sicily</note>, now called the Naphtha pools, the water would sometimes bubble up to a height of eight cubits, so that anyone unfamiliar with the custom would think it was about to flood the land; but just as it welled up, it would settle back down again. At this same spring, if someone wished to swear an oath, a scribe would write the matter he wished to attest upon a small tablet, seal it, and throw it into the spring. If he swore truly, the tablet floated to the top; if he swore falsely, the letter sank immediately. Furthermore, a sulfurous steam and fire rose out of this swampy pool, which would instantly burn the perjurer to ashes.

The Persians, when swearing an oath in their wartime dealings, took a shield <note>original: "tartsche," a type of medieval shield</note> and upon it they stabbed and killed a bull, a boar, a wolf, and a ram; in that same blood, the allies wetted their swords, and the Persians their spears.

->Fidius. The Trustworthy.<-

The image of this Jupiter <note>Jupiter Fidius, the god of oaths and good faith</note> is made thus: A marble stone was carved out, much like a window, in which three busts were to be seen. The one on the right was in the form of a peaceful man; on the left was a female figure also dressed in civic clothing, wearing a laurel wreath on her head, offering her right hand into the right hand of the male figure. In the middle was a beautiful young boy, most lovely to look upon, over whose head was written <term>FIDII SIMVLACHRVM</term> <note>original Latin: "The Image of Fidius"</note>; by the figure on the right <term>HONOR</term> <note>original Latin: "Honor"</note>; and on the left <term>VERITAS</term> <note>original Latin: "Truth"</note>.

->Philius. The Friendly.<-

The Greeks held this one to be a god of their friendship.

->Aliterius. The Averter.<-

The Greeks say that at one time there was such great hunger in their lands and cities that the poor broke into the bread-boxes of prisoners and stole their nourishment. However, Jupiter warded these people away from the communal mills so that they could take nothing from them; for this reason, he was honored under this name.

->Diespiter. Father of Day.<-

Because Jupiter brings birth and fruit into the light of day, they gave him this name. Or, as Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar and writer.</note> says: This one is the lowest and is devoted to the earth, from which all things sprout and grow; he is also their beginning and end.

->Lucetius. Giver of Light.<-

Following this opinion—that he brings us into the light and helps us, granting and offering life—they gave him this name. Otherwise, among the Greeks, one finds him called *Lencaus* and *Aethrius* <note>Likely referring to "Leukaios" (Bright) and "Aethrios" (of the Clear Sky).</note>, as the bright and clear one.

## Elicius. The Summoner.

Valerius Antias writes: When King Numa Pompilius could not bring it about to hear thunder whenever it suited him—and he always wished to know how to handle such things—he hid twelve pure, chaste youths in a cave by a spring, following the command and instruction of Egeria <note>Egeria was a nymph or goddess who, according to Roman legend, was the counselor and wife of Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome.</note>. He knew that the gods Faunus and Martius Picus <note>Ancient Italian prophetic forest deities.</note> would come there to drink when they were thirsty; he also gave the youths ropes to bind them. Alongside this, he had several vessels full of precious wine placed here and there. Now, when the two gods came and wished to drink, they found such a pleasant and fragrant drink that their curiosity led them to drink until they were full and fell asleep. Thus, the twelve youths bound them so that they knew nothing of themselves. When they had slept off the wine, they taught the King with what sacrifice he might lure <term>Elicius|from the Latin 'elicere', meaning to draw down or summon forth</term> and bring Jupiter down to earth. Thus, the King performed that same sacrifice from Mount Aventine with great devotion, so much so that Jupiter appeared to him. The King asked how he might turn the strikes of thunder from himself; Jupiter thought for a long time, but finally said: "You must pay with a head that the lightning has struck." "Yes," said the King, "with the tuft of hair" <note>original: "schopff," meaning a tuft or shock of hair.</note>. Jupiter spoke: "A human [head]." The King replied: "With hair it shall be done." Jupiter said: "It must be living so that it moves." Pompilius answered: "Then let it be a fish head." When Jupiter saw that he had been deceived by such speech, he cried out: "Numa, you have outwitted me! For I intended it should cost a human head with the tuft and hair, but since you have gotten the better of me, well then, do it your way, and use that bidding whenever you want thunder."

Livy indicates how the King provided and consecrated an altar to Jupiter on Mount Aventine. Otherwise, Plautus calls him *Prodigialis* <note>original: "Prodigialem," the god of omens or prodigies.</note>, that is, "The Warner," to whom one must always sacrifice incense or a salted flat-cake. This Jupiter also had his worship in Cyprus, where he was called *Elatios* <note>original: "ελατιον," likely referring to Zeus Elatios, the "High" or "Driving" god.</note>.

## Viminalis. The Reed-Hill Dweller.

There is a hill in Rome, not far from the Baths of Diocletian <note>The largest of the imperial baths in Rome, built around 300 AD.</note>, upon which stands the Church of Saint Susanna, called the Viminal. It was always, and remains today, full of reeds <note>original: "bintzen" (Binsen). The Viminal Hill is named after the 'vimina' (osiers/reeds) that grew there.</note>. An altar was erected to Jupiter there, from which he takes his name; and because the altar stood not far from a beech tree that was old and shady, he was also called "at the Old Beeches," and *Fagutalis* <note>From 'fagus', the Latin word for beech tree.</note>; the sacrifices performed there were also called *Sagutal* <note>Likely a variant of 'Fagutal', referring to the sacrifices at the Fagutal shrine.</note>.

<header>The Second Book</header>

# Veiouis, Veiupiter, Vedius. Good-Harm <note>original: "Gütschad." This archaic German compound likely combines 'gut' (good) and 'schade' (harm), reflecting the contradictory or 'inverse' nature of Veiovis, often seen as a small or sinister Jupiter.</note>.

The syllable *Ve* <note>original: "Ve"</note> in Latin sometimes brings a reduction and sometimes an increase, as in the word *Vehemens* <note>Vehement or powerful.</note>. This is made from *Veh* and *Amans* <note>Loving.</note> and signifies that someone places all their love and desire firmly upon one thing. It might also well be said to come from *Veh* and *Mens* <note>Mind.</note>, with the letter *e* placed between them to make it sound better; this signifies a gentle spirit that is firmly set upon something. Here, then, is the increase. *Veh-cordia* <note>original: "Veh/cordia," referring to *vecordia*, meaning senselessness or lack of heart.</note>, however, brings a reduction, where one does not have enough heart to act uprightly; for the little word *Veh* is used mostly in fear and heard in sorrow, when one’s strength leaves them, which also happens in excessive desire or joy. 

Thus, the Romans gave this Jupiter this name in the very year when Hannibal <note>The Carthaginian general who famously invaded Italy.</note> departed from Italy and was defeated in the barbarian lands. Also, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> writes, a statue made of cypress was erected to him in the Capitol in Rome in the five hundred and fifty-first year after the founding of the city. This statue has horns and several arrows in its hands, with a ram at its feet. Mars also sacrifices a goat <note>original: "geyß." While the text attributes the sacrifice to Mars, Roman ritual typically involved sacrificing a goat to Veiovis "in the human manner."</note> to him, and his chapel stood between the Citadel and the Cathedral Chapter on the Capitol in Rome. Thus, it is almost to be presumed that the Romans erected the image out of joy—because the burden of the Carthaginians was somewhat lessened for them, and misfortune had fallen upon their necks at that time, bringing them into sorrow—seeing him as an increaser of their own salvation and a reducer of the enemies' welfare.

## Maius. The Greater.

The Tuscans <note>The Etruscans, an ancient Italian civilization known for their influence on Roman religion.</note> honored Jupiter under this name because of his majesty and magnificence.

## Inuentor. The Finder.

Eurystheus <note>The king who commanded Hercules's labors.</note> commanded Hercules, among other tasks, to drive the oxen of Geryon <note>A giant with three bodies living in the far west (Spain).</note> out of Spain. On his return, he came with them into Italy to the place called Palantium <note>The Palatine Hill in Rome.</note>, where there was good pasture; he let them graze and, being weary, fell asleep. A robber who lived there in a cave, named Cacus, found the fine booty and pulled several of them by their tails into the cave, so that their footprints would not point inward, and he might better hide them. When Hercules woke and found some missing, he searched for them, paying no mind to the footprints pointing outward. He slipped into the cave and first found Cacus, who denied having the cattle. Furthermore, when Hercules wanted to search further, Cacus called upon other neighboring people for help, as if Hercules were doing him violence. The oxen heard Hercules’s voice and lowed and mooed, so that Hercules found them, struck Cacus to death, and destroyed the cave because it had been used for robbery. He performed penance for the killing, washed away the sin with the water of the Tiber, and erected an altar to this Jupiter where the place now called *Schola Graeca* <note>original: "Schola Greca," likely referring to the area near the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin in Rome.</note> is located, near Saint Paul’s Gate in Rome. There he sacrificed a young bull and departed. Whenever two people enter into marriage, they sacrifice to this god.

## Arbitrator. The Mediator.

This Jupiter had a porch with five columns in Rome.

<header>On Pagan Gods</header>

### Prædator. The Plunderer <note>original: "Teyl vnd Gmeinhaber" — literally 'Participant and Share-holder'</note>.

When the Romans went out to war, they promised the gods a portion of the booty; for this reason, a temple was also erected to this Jupiter.

### Adultus. The Mature <note>original: "Gstanden oder Mañbar" — 'Stood' or 'at the age of manhood'</note>.

This name was also given to Jupiter, under which he was honored when people entered into marriage. By this, they wanted to make it understood that such a thing should not be undertaken before the years of maturity.

### Opitulus. The Succorer <note>original: "Helffend" — 'Helping'</note>.

He was named thus because he shows help to those in need.

### Impulsor. The Overthrower <note>original: "Vmbstossend" — 'Overturning'</note>.

Because he overthrows all pride.

### Centumpeda. The Hundred-Footed.

Because every thing stands more firmly the more feet it has; and since Jupiter is immovable, they gave him this name.

### Almus. The Nourishing <note>original: "Ernhörend" — here meaning 'sustaining' or 'feeding'</note>.

He was given this name because he nourishes all things.

### Rumius. The Suckler.

*Ruma* <note>original: "Ruma" — a Latin term for the breast or teat</note> means "teat" in German, from the Latin word, and because all animals are raised through suckling, this name was also attributed to him.

### Supinalis. The Overturner <note>original: "Stürtzend" — 'Casting down'</note>.

And since he overturns all sin and evil, they called him the Overturner.

### Tigillus. The Support <note>original: "Vnderstützend" — 'Under-propping'</note>.

And because he holds and maintains everything in Heaven and Earth together, just like a support beam in a large building, they gave him this name.

### Dapalis. The Feaster <note>original: "Brasser" — 'Glutton' or 'Reveler'</note>.

This name was given to Jupiter because no expense should be spared in sacrificing to him; even today, it is said that "priests' banquets" are bravely feasted upon <note>The author is likely making a contemporary Reformation-era jab at the perceived gluttony of the Catholic clergy</note>. Regarding how one should sacrifice to him, <term>M. Cato</term> <note>Marcus Porcius Cato, known as Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), a Roman statesman and author of 'De Re Rustica' (On Agriculture)</note> writes of farming and says:
> Every year you shall cheerfully offer to Jupiter the Feaster a large jar with a well-measured amount of wine. On that same day, you shall also let your oxen and ox-drivers, and those who must pull the plow, have a holiday, and say: "Accept this, Feaster; it is truly right that I and my household prepare good vessels for you. And now be merry, for I sacrifice to you from a large-bellied jar of wine; come, drink it away, feast bravely!"

### Vltor. The Avenger <note>original: "Rachsam" — 'Revengeful'</note>.

At our Lady of the Round <note>The author refers to the Pantheon in Rome, which was dedicated to St. Mary and the Martyrs in the 7th century</note>, or the Rotunda in the city of Rome, there is a

He is also said (as Dio <note>Likely referring to the historian Cassius Dio</note> relates) to have had a chapel on the Capitoline Hill.

## Zeus. The Life-Giver.

The Greeks have often expressed this name of Jupiter with a single syllable, such as when they call him *Zeus*, *Zen*, *Deus*, *Sdeus*, *Zan*, *Zes*, *Zas*, *Dis*, *Din*, *Dan*, and *Dzeus* <note>original Greek: $\zeta\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\varsigma, \zeta\dot{\eta}\nu, \delta\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\varsigma, \sigma\delta\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\varsigma, \zeta\dot{\alpha}\nu, \zeta\dot{\eta}\varsigma, \zeta\dot{\alpha}\varsigma, \delta\iota\varsigma, \delta\iota\nu, \delta\alpha\nu, \delta\epsilon\upsilon\varsigma$</note>. These small words almost all suggest that he is a life-giving power, giving life to all that exists, both through his fiery power and through his vital moisture, both of which are attributed to him.

## Dictæus. Of Dicte.

On the island of Crete <note>original: "Candien"</note> there is a promontory called Dicte, facing out toward the Libyan Sea <note>original: "Barbarischen mör"</note>, very near to Mount Ida. He had a temple there for a reason described in a certain fable.

Saturn was accustomed to devouring his children as soon as they were born. Rhea, Saturn’s wife and Jupiter’s mother, hid her pregnancy from her husband and gave birth to the child Jupiter <note>original: "Jovem"</note> without Saturn's knowledge. She gave him to the Curetes <note>original: "Curetern" — mythical armored attendants</note> who lived on this mountain to keep him safe. Whenever Saturn passed by, they began a clanging and a din with drums and bells so that he could not hear the crying child; thus he became so deafened that he did not know where the child was or what was happening. The bees followed this sound and nourished Jupiter with their honeycombs. For this reason, it is said that Jupiter made them so clever that they maintain an order and arrangement in their lives, just like a well-ordered kingdom or city.

## Idæus. Of Ida.

Here the historians and others have a dispute. One side claims the name comes from Mount Ida located in Phrygia, where Paris shared his judgment regarding the three goddesses; the other says it is the Ida in Crete. Now, there is a stronger suspicion that it refers to the mountain in Phrygia; for there, near Troy and the town of Celenen <note>Celaenae</note>, King Midas erected an altar to this Jupiter for the following reason: An earthquake arose which cracked the ground so often and so wide that it swallowed many people and houses in Celaenae. The king was told by soothsayers that he must throw his most precious treasure—that which he loved most—into the chasm, and then it would close. Although Midas kept no jewel back and threw everything into the abyss, it still would not end. Anchurus, the King’s son, understood well that there was no treasure more precious than life itself. He went to his father and also to his wife Timothea to bid them farewell, sat upon his horse, and leaped into the hole. Immediately it closed up, just as it had appeared before. Therefore, King Midas built an altar to this Jupiter there, and in that place a rock grows which, at a certain time of year, turns entirely to gold.

## Aegiochus. He of the Goat-Shield.

The Greeks tell many trifles here, saying that Jupiter, when he...

## Milichius. The Gracious.

**C**ornutus calls him the joyful, friendly, and kind <note>original: "Milichius," from the Greek *Meilichios*, meaning "the Easy-to-be-Entreated" or "Gracious"</note>, because he is joyful and friendly toward those who have desisted from sins and apply themselves to what is good. On the other hand, he is kind toward sinners whom he does not reject if they turn back to him.

In Athens, this Jupiter was held in especially high honor when his feast day came. Everyone flocked to it, and the common people all made magnificent sacrifices according to their means; they did not only sacrifice but gave many gifts and engaged in strange games and pastimes, though these occurred outside the city. Regarding this, there was once a citizen of Athens of a noble old family—who was a victorious champion at Olympia—who desired to have the rule over his fatherland. When he consulted Apollo about this, the answer was that he must wait until Jupiter’s greatest festival was held to seize the fortress <note>the Acropolis</note>. Therefore, he once called upon Theagenes, the tyrant of Megara (now Megror), his father-in-law, for secret help. When the Olympic festival was held in the Peloponnese, he fell upon the fortress, but the matter failed him because it was not the right festival <note>The citizen was Cylon of Athens; he mistook the "greatest festival of Jupiter" for the Olympics, whereas the oracle likely meant the Diasia festival of Jupiter Milichius</note>. Thus he received his reward: he had to flee, and his followers either died of hunger or were murdered.

This Jupiter has no image, but he was honored in a crude, pointed pillar of fire <note>referring to an aniconic stone pillar or pyramid shape</note>. Not far from Naupactus, which is now called Lepanto, there lay upon a mountain a small spot called Myonea. There, this Jupiter had a sacred grove or thicket and an altar; they sacrificed there at night, and before the sun rose, the sacrifice was entirely consumed.

In Argos, a statue of this Jupiter also stood, which Polyclitus carved. Likewise, by the river Cephisus, there is also a temple and altar of this Jupiter, where Theseus himself—because he had executed Sciron the murderer and other such evil rogues—received absolution from the descendants of Phytalus <note>the Phytalidae, a priestly family who purified Theseus of blood-guilt</note>.

## Sthenius. The Strong or Hard.

There was a feast day in honor of Danaus at Argos, on which one had to have flutes and pipes, as well as wrestling, jumping, and similar great expense and effort. Later, this was changed and dedicated to this Jupiter <note>original: "Sthenius," from the Greek *Sthenios*, meaning "the Powerful"</note>. At Troezen, there was a hill toward Hermione where this Jupiter’s altar stood; but Theseus made the discovery <note>of his father's tokens</note> there, and he himself was later honored there.

## Phratrius. The Clan-Brother.

In April, the Athenians held a festival that lasted four days in a row, about which I will speak later when I write of similar feast days. Now, during that same time, the second feast day was dedicated to this Jupiter, for every guild <note>original: "Zunfft," here referring to the *phratries* or ancestral clans of Athens</note> brought him its sacrifice.

<header>The Second Book.</header>

### Alysius. The Banisher of Evil.

On Mount Dicte <note>original: "Dicto"</note> in Candia <note>modern-day Crete</note>, Jupiter was honored with a grove <note>original: "Thau od Forst," likely referring to a sacred grove or woodland</note> and temple because he drives away all evil.

### Mæragetes. Master of Death.

By his own will, this Jupiter received this name and was honored as the one who has power over the life and death of men <note>original: "Mæragetes," from the Greek *Moeragetes*, the "Guide of the Fates"</note>.

### Aegyptius, Nylus. The Egyptian or the Nile.

Among the Egyptians themselves, this word signifies virtue and everything good; moreover, the Nile gives strength and fertility to the entire land. For this reason, Jupiter acquired this name, as is noted by Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC Greek historian</note> and others.

### Tarsos. At Tarsus.

Because Jupiter had a high religious foundation <term>stifft</term> <note>referring to a temple or established religious seat</note> there, he also bore this name. This city lies in Cilicia, now called Karamania, and Tarsus is the homeland of Saint Paul.

### Plusios. The Wealthy.

All wealth and gifts come from God; therefore, the Greeks gave Jupiter this name <note>original: "Plusios," from the Greek *Plousios*, meaning wealthy</note>. He also had a temple in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>.

### Hyperdexius. The Protector.

On the island of Lesbos, now called Mytilene <note>original: "Metelin"</note>, there was a field where a temple to Jupiter stood; thus, he retained this name <note>original: "Hyperdexius," meaning "the one who holds his hand over" or protector</note>.

### Hæcatombæus. The Giver of a Hundred Sacrifices.

Because in the month of April, a hundred oxen were always sacrificed to Jupiter at once—and that month was named accordingly—this name arose. In Crete, or Candia, at Gortyna (now called Gurtina), not far from the Labyrinth <note>the legendary maze of the Minotaur</note>, he has a temple. This place is still somewhat inhabited and once had a beautiful castle with many water pipes that carried water into the city. One still finds more than two thousand pieces of fallen columns and statues there, which provide evidence of the magnificent waterworks and temple, as Benedictus Bordon <note>Benedetto Bordone, a 16th-century Italian cartographer and author of a famous book on islands</note> describes.

### Elæus, Elieus. The Elean.

Although the Olympian Jupiter also took his name from the city where the playing field was located—called Elis—he was also honored under these two names in Cyprus and Thebes, which have remained associated with him.

### Olympius. The Olympian.

Just as the Capitoline Jupiter was held in high honor among the Romans, so too was the Olympian Jupiter held in exceptional regard among the Greeks; for this reason, necessity requires a somewhat more extensive account of it. The Peloponnese, although not entirely so, is almost an island, where they

## Sthenius. The Strong or Hard.

A festival was held in honor of Danaus at Argos, upon which there had to be much playing of shawms and pipes, as well as wrestling, jumping, and similar great expense and effort. All wealth and gifts come from God, which is why the Greeks gave Jupiter this name; he had a temple in Lacedaemonia <note>the region of Sparta</note>.

In this land is a region once called **Elis** / now **Belvedere** / and we Germans might well call it the **Whungow** <note>likely "Wungau," a localized German name used to approximate the geography of Elis</note> / it stretches somewhat toward **Sicily**. This region was ruled after the **Great Flood of Deucalion** / by **Aethlius**, a son of **Jupiter** and **Protogenia** / after him his son **Endymion** / then **Epeus** his grandson / from whom the inhabitants were called the **Epeians** / then in his place came his brother **Aetolus**, who did not stay long / then **Eleios** became King / who built the city of **Elis** and named the region after himself. His son **Augeas** devoted himself to cattle pastures / of which he had so many that he covered the entire land with manure / and made it almost uninhabitable / so he promised **Hercules** / that if he would clean the land for him / he would give him a portion of the kingdom. Immediately Hercules directed the river **Peneus** into the land / which washed away and flooded the manure in such a manner...

<header>The Second Book.</header>

...so that he either cleansed it or brought it to use, and produced much fruit. Augeas <note>King of Elis, famous for his stables which Hercules was tasked to clean</note> believed he should reward the labor and not the cleverness of the act; therefore, Hercules had to invade the region with a gathered army, conquered it, and established near a mountain called **Olympus** <note>Though the text says Olympus, the games were held at Olympia in the region of Elis</note> a fire or festival in memory of the deed, and founded a school there, where all fencing masters, wrestlers, jumpers, singers, and the like could practice. This foundation and holiday fell into disuse over time until roughly the seven hundred and seventy-eighth year before the birth of **Christ** <note>The traditional date for the first Olympiad is 776 BC</note>, at which point the **Greeks** began to count the years of historical events by recording this festival—just as the **Romans** later did by the terms of their Mayors <note>referring to the Roman Consuls</note>, and as we do by the birth of Christ. The difference was that the Romans appointed new mayors every year, and we increase the number from year to year; the Greeks, however, when they began to count the first **Olympiad**, would say: "The first, second, third, or fourth year of the first Olympiad." Thereafter came the second Olympiad, which also counted four years, and then they established the third, and so on throughout; thus, the time was always calculated from one Olympiad to the following four years, and one hundred ninety-four Olympiads passed until the time of Christ. And after **Ipylus** <note>Iphitos, the King of Elis who restored the games</note>, from the lineage of **Hercules**, restored this festival, the entire landscape around **Elea** (of which he was King) was dedicated to **Jupiter** <note>the Greek god Zeus</note> by all the Greeks. Thus, anyone who troubled this land and city with war, fire, or plunder—or if such things befell it and they did not come to its rescue to the best of their ability—that person would be an enemy and under a ban by all Greeks. Furthermore, if anyone came to wage war against others and passed through that land, he and his military folk had to surrender all weapons to the locals until they reached the border; but if someone marched into it with an army, he had to pay fourteen crowns minus six *bazen* for every man, which then amounted to two **Minas** <note>an ancient unit of currency</note>.

The games which Hercules first established to be practiced there were five in number: jumping; running; throwing stones or iron bars; slinging; and shooting with the small shaft <note>likely referring to javelins or archery</note>. Also carrying, lifting, and pulling, where one had to apply all his strength. Finally, wrestling. Whosoever competed in these five pieces and achieved the best result was called a **Pentathlon** or **Quinquertio** <note>original: "Quinquertio," a Latin term for the pentathlon</note>, which may be translated into German as "One Skilled in Five." Over time, the Greeks added the "Whirling-Run" <note>possibly a circular race or chariot maneuver</note>; also racing on horses without saddles; and in a chariot pulled by two horses, or one horse, two mules, two mares, or sometimes even a single foal. Likewise, fighting with clubs, running in armor, or with a shield <note>original: "tartschen," a type of tournament shield</note>. The people of **Elea** also trained young boys for such games. This festival began on the eleventh of the **Month of June** <note>original: "Brachetmonats," the traditional German name for June</note> and lasted five days in succession; on the sixteenth day, the prizes were awarded. At that point, they began to count the new Olympiad. I am well aware that some say it begins there after the Autumn, when day and night are equal again; that may be so, for many reasons which are not necessary to recount here. Now, whoever wished to go to this festival could do so, with the exception of women; for if one were found there, she was thrown off a cliff called **Typens** <note>Mount Typaion</note>. Otherwise, the general public came there to fight; but those who wished to conduct trade or merely watch also had their lodgings here and there in the cities.

From all the cities of the Greeks, ambassadors also gathered with their contributions at a place in **Eli** <note>Elis</note> where the old fencing school once stood; there they had a house that was called the **Greeks' City Hall**, built at the common expense...
