-># Of Pagan Gods<-

built, and there the envoys <note>delegates from the various Greek city-states</note> had to remain together for ten months to deliberate and consider how the games should be conducted and how to manage the contestants. Not far from there is the **Plethrium** <note>original: "Plethrū"; a part of the gymnasium at Elis</note>, where those who wished to compete practiced for thirty days. Whoever wished to run would sometimes put on boots and run through the sand, so that when it came to the actual race, he would be all the lighter. If one wished to jump, he would hang weights upon himself, and so on. They also ate only beef for a time beforehand and no other dainties, believing this would make them strong. They abstained from all women and also had to swear that they had prepared and practiced well for ten months prior. This oath was taken before the statue of **Jupiter, the Hearer of Oaths** <note>original: "Eydhörenden Jupiters"; referring to Zeus Horkios, the protector of oaths</note>, of whom we spoke before. A contestant also had to declare his lineage, how he had conducted himself throughout his life, what trade he practiced, and prove that he was an honorable and upright man.

Now, as the time drew near, the masters of the games were present. At first, two were always chosen from the **Eleans** <note>inhabitants of Elis, the region where Olympia was located</note> by a unanimous vote of the envoys; after some years, their number was set at nine, soon after at ten, later it returned to eight, then back to ten. These men had a silver box containing beans. On two beans was the letter **A**, on another two the letter **B**, and so on, two of each letter were cast in. Then the slips of those who wished to compete, having given their names in writing, were placed in another box. After being well-mixed, the names and letters were drawn together. For example, if **Hans** and **Caspar** <note>The author uses common German names of his own time to explain the ancient Greek system to his readers</note> had entered their names: Hans's name is drawn, and then, perhaps after a hundred other slips are pulled, Caspar’s name is drawn. If, in the meantime, Hans was assigned an **A** from the bean box, and Caspar eventually also drew an **A**, the two must compete against each other. If Hans wins and another man named **Michael** also draws an **A**, he must face the one who was previously victorious. This continues until one man remains who has defeated all others so that no one else challenges him, or no one else is left; then he has won the victory.

From such a victory, one receives a small **Olive tree wreath**, which was then considered a higher honor than a **Triumph** in **Rome** or winning the "first thanks" <note>the top prize or recognition</note> in a **Tournament** among the **Germans**. It is indeed true that afterwards, a statue was erected for him in the **Temple of Jupiter** at the common expense of the **Greeks**, detailing how he had prevailed and conquered. Thus, **Xerxes** <note>The King of Persia who invaded Greece</note> should not have judged that noble youth so despondently based on the words of his wise men. For when Xerxes was defeated by the Greeks at the "edge of the blade" at the hot springs <note>likely referring to the Battle of Thermopylae or the broader conflict around Plataea</note> in **Plataea**, and some poor Greeks were brought to him from the field (having gone there because of their poverty) to serve him, the **Persians** asked them where the other Greeks were. They replied: "In **Elis**, where they are watching the competitive games and wrestling." When they were further asked what a man might win there, they replied: "An olive wreath." Then **Tigranes** <note>A Persian general</note> cried out loudly: "O **Mardonius** <note>Another high-ranking Persian commander</note>, what kind of men have you led us against, who fight not for the sake of wealth, but for the sake of fame and honor!" Indeed, that youth spoke rightly once. Who has ever been more highly praised than one of these contestants when he returned home victorious? And if **Virtue**, **Moderation**, **Honor**, and **Piety** were not constantly fading in all lands, while **Splendor**, **Gluttony**, **Deceit**, and **Impudence** increased, I would wonder why it is that in our times (when all other things have reached their peak) the **Tournament** has so greatly declined? But let a greater man speak on that.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Olympic Games, specifically focusing on the penalties for cheating, the rewards for victors, and the physical description of the temple complex at Olympia.</meta>

-># The Second Book<-

If anyone who registered as a competitor used any trickery or deceit, the city from which he was born was fined several thousand crowns. From this money, they would fashion a statue and place it in the temple of **Jupiter** <note>Original: "Jovis"; referring to the Zeus Zanes, statues of Zeus paid for by fines and intended as a warning to athletes.</note>, so that in the future everyone would be deterred by the sight of it. Those who practiced deceit were also whipped—be they the judges who were to award the prize, or the competitors themselves. For the judges of the games also had to swear before the statue of Jupiter (as heard above) that they would regard neither favor, passion, nor bribes, but would award the prize according to justice, and would keep their mouths eternally clean regarding why they judged one man worthy or why they did not crown another. Also, the fellow cities themselves were punished if they did not send their envoys, for it was held as though they despised the festival.

When a competitor returned home, he was given ten thousand crowns from the public treasury, and a seat at the lords' table <note>He was granted "prytaneion" honors, meaning free meals at the public expense for life.</note> for as long as he lived. They would erect a statue for him, and if he had achieved the victory in all contests, the likeness had to be exactly and entirely his own image. Sometimes he was brought in on a high wagon with four stallions, not through the proper gate, but they would tear down a portion of the city wall for him. They wished to signify by this that cities which produced such citizens did not need many walls, for they had people who knew how to fight and how to win. However, he always had to risk his life for a simple wreath of olive leaves, which he did not keep for himself as soon as he came home, but hung it up to honor his fatherland in a temple or in the town hall. For this reason, when **Astylus** <note>Astylos of Croton, a famous runner of the 5th century BC.</note> had achieved victory in this contest three times, and twice—bribed by money—had himself proclaimed a citizen of **Syracuse**, the **Crotonians** (his native people) tore down his house and courtyard, built a prison for rogues upon it, and had his statue smashed to pieces.

This competition ground was four hundred feet <note>Original: "schůch"; literally "shoes," a historical measurement of length.</note> wide on all sides and lay by the river **Alpheus**. It was about seven and a half miles from **Elis**, in the territory of the city of **Pisa** in the region of **Olympia**, which **Hercules** chose for this place and named after his teacher.

There, the **Eleans** built a temple to Jupiter after they overran, conquered, and plundered the **Pisans** (because the Pisans had attempted to seize control and authority over this festival from the Eleans). This occurred approximately five hundred and seventy years before the birth of Christ; thus the Eleans became wealthy from the goods of their enemies.

Before the temple, there is an olive grove or dark little forest, which is consecrated and named **Altis** <note>Original: "Altin"; the sacred heart of the Olympic sanctuary.</note>. On the outside, the temple is surrounded by columns, built entirely of hard marble as it was found in that region. It is forty-eight feet high, ninety-five feet wide, and nearly two hundred and thirty feet long, covered with stone slabs. The master builder was named **Libo**, a Pisan. At each corner, the temple has a golden sacrificial vessel, and at the peak, a golden statue of **Victory** <note>Nike</note>, under whose feet lies the **Gorgon shield**. On the outer columns hang the gilded shields, and on the front gables are depicted all the stories of **Pelops** and other things lovely to behold. It has bronze doors of hammered work, and inside, there are also columns that support beautiful and fair vaults, through which one must pass to reach the Altar of Jupiter. This altar is high, and one must climb several steps to reach it.

Whoever wishes to run puts on boots, as it were, and runs through the sand there, so that he might be all the lighter during the actual race when it counts. If one wishes to jump, he hangs weights upon himself and makes himself heavy, etc. <note>The author refers to *halteres*, stone or metal weights held by ancient long jumpers to increase momentum.</note> They also ate beef for a time beforehand and no other delicacies, believing they would become strong from it. They abstained from all women and also swore that they had prepared and practiced well for ten months prior; this oath was taken before the statue of **Jupiter the Oath-Hearer** <note>Original: "Eydhörenden Jupiters"; referring to the statue of Zeus Horkios where athletes swore to follow the rules.</note>, of whom we spoke before. He also had to declare his lineage, how he had conducted himself throughout his days, what trade he practiced, and demonstrate that he was an honorable and upright man.

When the time drew near, the **Judges of the Games** <note>Original: "Kampffherre"; known historically as the Hellanodikai.</note> were there. At first, two were always chosen from the people of **Elis** <note>Original: "Eleern".</note> by the unanimous voice of the envoys; after several years, nine were appointed; soon after, ten; later it returned to eight, then back to ten. These men had a silver box in which there were beans; upon two of them was the letter **A**, upon another two the letter **B**, and so on, always two of each letter were cast in. Then they took the slips of paper from those who wished to compete and had submitted their written names, placed them in another box, and let them be drawn once they were well mixed together. Whichever name and letter came out together—for instance, **Hans** and **Caspar** <note>The author uses common German names of his own time to explain the ancient Greek pairing system to his readers.</note> have submitted their names; Hans's name is drawn, and after a hundred other slips are drawn, Caspar's name comes out. Hans prevails; then another is drawn named **Michel**, who also brings forth an **A**; he must then face the one who previously prevailed. This continues until there is one who has finished off and overcome the others, so that no one else wishes to face him, or no one else is left; then he has won the victory.

For such a victory, one receives a small **olive wreath**, which is then held in higher esteem than a **Triumph** in **Rome** or winning the first prize in a **Tournament** among the **Germans**. It is indeed true that afterwards, a statue was erected for him in the **Temple of Jupiter** at the common expense of the Greeks, depicting how he prevailed and conquered. Thus, **Xerxes** should not have considered that noble youth so utterly disheartened because of the high wisdom of his speech. For once, this youth spoke rightly. Who has ever been more highly praised than one of these very competitors when he returned home victorious? If only virtue, manhood, honor, and piety did not fade more and more in all lands at all times, while pageantry, gluttony, deceit, and impudence increased, I would wonder where it comes from that in our times (when all other things have reached their peak) the **Tournament** has so completely declined. But let a greater man speak of that.

<header># The Second Book</header>

If any **competitor** <note>Original: "Kämpffer." Refers to the athletes participating in the games.</note> who enrolled himself used any trickery or fraud, the city of his birth was fined several thousand crowns. From this money, statues were made and placed in the **Temple of Jupiter** <note>Historically known as the Zanes, these were bronze statues of Zeus paid for by fines levied against athletes who cheated.</note> so that in the future, everyone might take warning from them. Those who practiced fraud were also flogged, whether they were the judges who were to award the honors or the competitors themselves. For even the judges of the games had to swear before the image of Jupiter—as was mentioned above—that they would regard neither favor, effort, nor gifts, but would grant the honors according to equity and keep their deliberations eternally secret <note>Original: "ewigklich reynen mund halten," literally "keep a clean mouth," meaning they must not reveal why one was honored and another not.</note> regarding why they deemed one worthy or did not crown another. Furthermore, the partner cities themselves were punished if they did not send their envoys, for it was considered as if they held the festival in contempt.

When a victor returned home, he was given ten thousand crowns from the public treasury and a place at his lord's table for as long as he lived. A statue was erected for him, and if he had achieved the best results in all the contests, the likeness had to be exactly identical to him. Sometimes he was brought in on a suspended chariot with four stallions, not through the proper gate, but instead a part of the city wall was torn down for him. This was intended to show that a city which produced such citizens had little need for walls, for they had people who knew how to fight and conquer. Yet, he first had to risk his life for a little wreath of **olive leaves** <note>Original: "Ollaub" (Öllaub).</note>, which he did not keep for himself upon returning home, but hung up in a temple or the town hall to honor his fatherland. For this reason, when **Astylos** <note>Astylos of Croton, a famous athlete of the 5th century BC.</note> had achieved victory in this contest three times, and twice—bribed by money—allowed himself to be announced as a citizen of **Syracuse**, the people of **Croton** (where he was born) tore down his house and property, built a rogue's prison upon it, and had his statue smashed to pieces.

This competition ground was four hundred feet on all sides and lay by the **Alpheus** river. It was seven and a half miles from **Elis**, within the jurisdiction of the city of **Pisa** in the region of **Olympia**, which **Hercules** chose for this site and named after his teacher.

There, the people of Elis built a temple to **Jupiter** when they marched against, conquered, and plundered the **Pisans** (because the Pisans had attempted to seize the foundation and authority of this festival from the Eleans). This occurred approximately five hundred and seventy years before the birth of Christ, and the Eleans became wealthy from the property of their enemies.

In front of the temple, there is an olive grove or a darker little forest which is consecrated and called the **Altis** <note>Original: "Altin." The sacred grove at Olympia.</note>. On the outside, the temple is surrounded by columns, built entirely of hard marble found in that very region. It is forty-eight feet high, ninety-five feet wide, and about two hundred and thirty feet long, covered with stone tiles. The master builder was named **Libo**, a Pisan. At every corner, the temple had a golden sacrificial cauldron, and at the summit, a golden statue of **Victory** <note>The goddess Nike.</note>, beneath whose feet lies the **Gorgon shield** <note>The Aegis, featuring the head of Medusa.</note>. On the outer columns hang the gilded shields; on the front of the doors are depicted all the stories of **Pelops** and other things most lovely to behold. It has bronze gates with chased work, and inside, there are also columns that support handsome and beautiful vaults, through which one must go forward to the **Altar of Jupiter**. That same altar is high, and one must climb several steps to reach it.

<header># Of Heathen Gods</header>

<meta>catchword: heart</meta>

ascend. The statue of **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note> is also made of gold and **ivory**, crafted with great elegance. His head is crowned as if with a wreath of olive leaves; in his right hand, he holds a statue of **Victory** <note>original: "Victoria"; the Greek goddess Nike.</note> (of whom we shall speak in the section on Victory), which is also made of ivory but wears a golden cap along with a golden crown. In his left hand, he carries a most lovely scepter, set with pearls and precious stones. Atop the scepter sits a golden eagle. His sandals and clothes are all made of gold; his cloak is adorned with **embossed animals** <note>Original: "tribnen thiern." This refers to repoussé work, where metal is hammered into relief from the reverse side.</note> and floral patterns. His throne is decorated with pearls and other precious stones, and also inlaid with ebony and ivory in the shapes of many strange animals. At each foot of the throne is a figure of Victory that seems to leap joyfully. The eight braces that support the throne are cast so that at the base they depict the **Theban children** <note>A reference to the myth where the Sphinx kidnapped the youths of Thebes.</note> snatched by the **Sphinxes**; and **Apollo** and **Diana** <note>The Greek Artemis.</note> are shown shooting the children of **Niobe** to death. The throne is not hollow in the middle but is supported by small golden columns. At the top of the back of the throne, on one side, is the figure of **Graciousness** <note>Referring to the Charites or Graces.</note>; on the other, the figures of the **Hours** <note>The Horae, goddesses of the seasons.</note> are cast so that they extend above the head of the statue. Down below, under Jupiter's feet, are lions and the battle of **Theseus** with the **Amazons**. Likewise, on the steps, there are various wonderful images. The space under the statue on the floor is made of black stone; the slabs around the altar are made of speckled marble, black and green. This area is anointed with **oil** <note>The oil was used not just for ritual, but to preserve the ivory from the humidity of the marshy Olympic grove.</note> so that the dampness of the dark ground does not harm the ivory. A woolen curtain, dyed scarlet and embroidered with **heathen designs**, hangs before this altar; it can be pulled up and down as one wishes.

**Phidias**, the sculptor of Athens, created this image. It is said that once, when he earnestly called upon Jupiter to give him a sign if this work were made according to his will, a bolt of thunder immediately struck the roof above without causing any other damage. However, when others asked Phidias how or from what he had modeled the likeness, he is said to have answered that he took it from three of **Homer’s** verses in the first book of the **Destruction of Troy** <note>The Iliad. The verses describe Zeus nodding his head, causing Olympus to shake.</note> which mention the eyebrows and hair of Jupiter. Nevertheless, **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> felt that he did not manage the proportions quite right; for although the chapel is high, the seated statue is so tall that he would have to push his head through the roof if he were to ever grow tired of sitting and wish to stand up.

This temple also has a sacrificial altar, which is made solely from the **ashes** of the hindquarters of the animals sacrificed to him, mixed with water from the **Alpheus** <note>The river Alpheios near Olympia.</note>; for one is not permitted to moisten or touch the ashes with any other water. The lower base surrounding it measures about one hundred and twenty-five feet in circumference. There are steps, one following the other, but none extend further back than thirty-five feet. The altar itself is about twenty-four feet high. The **Eleans** <note>The people of Elis, who administered the Olympic Games.</note> sacrifice there every day, as may anyone else who wishes; however, no woman is allowed to go higher than the base. Annually, on the nineteenth of **February** <note>Original: "Hornungs."</note>, the ashes are cleaned from the altar of **Diana** which stands in the council house of the stadium, and then the ashes are mixed again to plaster over whatever has crumbled. Furthermore, the **kites** <note>Original: "Arweyhe." The sacrifice is a black **ram**, and therefore the head belongs to the **master of the wood** <note>original: "holtzherrn"; an official responsible for the timber used in sacrifices.</note>. I also cannot well skip over the fact that near the **competition grounds** <note>original: "Kampff platz"; referring here to the hippodrome where races were held.</note>, opposite the Town Hall, there is a fenced-in meadow in which the **racehorses** are kept. At the back it is broad and wide, but at the front it is narrow and pointed. At the front, by the exit, is a wooden **dolphin**. On both sides there are stables, for which the racers draw lots; and at the front a chain is stretched across so that no horse may break out. 

Whenever this festival comes, they build a new altar of bricks in the middle of the wide section at the back; above it is a wooden **eagle** with outstretched wings. It is designed so that the person required to start the race triggers <note>original: "flücket"; literally "plucks," referring to pulling a lever or cord.</note> the eagle with a specially made mechanism, so that the eagle swings high up and gives a signal to all those standing around as to when he wishes to let them go. 

When the eagle thus soars, the **barriers** <note>original: "schrancken"; the starting gates.</note> at the front open, and they let the two who were matched against each other run their horses. And as they come to the exit, the dolphin ducks down to the ground; then they must both stand still at the outermost barrier until it rises. At that moment, it is required that each man use his skill and ability.

...jesting. These same heralds also had to contend with one another in shouting; whichever among them had the best voice, that same one called out the victors.

The racecourse is wider on one side than on the other; therefore, right at the start, there is a small mound like a round altar, which they call **Taraxippum** <note>original: "Taraxippum"; from the Greek *Taraxippos*, meaning "The Disturber of Horses."</note>, that is, "Horse-Fright." As soon as the horses reach this spot, they become terrified and then immediately frantic, and yet no one knows why. This causes them at times to smash the **little carts** <note>original: "Kärtzlin"; light racing chariots.</note> or sleds, dragging the racers along and wounding them quite badly. For this reason, the racers commonly offer sacrifices to this "Horse-Fright" so that he might be merciful to them.

And although it might be thought that **German sledding** <note>The author is comparing the ancient chariot races to the 16th-century German tradition of recreational winter sledding.</note> had its origins in this racing, I wanted to include a small illustration here so you might see the difference. Regarding the danger, there is no comparison at all; for consider the lightness and nimbleness of the little cart, the speed of the small wheels, the swiftness of the horses, and the crack of the whips. You would clearly see what a horse with a heavy, dragging sled-load can do against these, where four horses run without any hindrance. One can still sense how our ancestors, in manly exercises—even in jest—always gave much of their intellect and liked to show themselves off. Just as **Tacitus** <note>The Roman historian Publius Cornelius Tacitus, whose works described the customs of Germanic tribes.</note> speaks of their jumping, which was much more dangerous than that of the Greeks; it was performed by naked youths between and upon bare swords, without any hope of gift or reward. Some trace of this remains in the **sword dance**. Likewise, the **fencing schools** <note>original: "fächtschulen"; these were organized guilds or training centers for martial arts, often associated with the "Marxbrüder" guild.</note> are more common among us Germans than elsewhere, having special locations such as **Frankfurt am Main**, which city has the privilege of appointing and ordaining fencing masters.

**Nero**, for whom nothing was too much, presumed in these very games to harness ten horses to a single little cart; however, he once fell quite violently and, although he was put back on, he had to give up before he reached the finish line.

Now, Jupiter was called **Olympian** after Mount Olympus, which is so high that at around three o'clock in the morning the rising of the sun can be seen from there. For this reason, this mountain is often taken by the poets to be **Heaven** itself, wherein Jupiter reigns, sees all things, hears, leads, and arranges everything according to his pleasure. What treasures and ornaments he had in this temple of his, there is neither time nor space to recount here.

A temple was also erected to this Jupiter in **Athens**, as they say, by **Deucalion** <note>The legendary survivor of the Great Flood in Greek mythology, often seen as a founder of civilizations.</note>. **Perseus**, the Macedonian king, undertook to expand and rebuild this temple with such liberality that even **Livy** <note>The Roman historian Titus Livius.</note> speaks of it. How highly this king honored the gods and how generous he was may be shown by the foundations and the begun construction of the temple dedicated to the Olympian Jupiter in Athens—more so than any other works. For its like was not on earth, and in its magnificence, it would have been worthy of the greatest of the greatest gods, had it been brought to completion.

The statue therein was made of gold and ivory only in the face; the rest of the body of the statue was made of clay and plaster. It was crafted by **Theocosmos of Megara** <note>original: "Thecosmos von Megara"; a 5th-century BC Greek sculptor.</note>.

# The Second Book

Likewise, this same King <note>Likely referring to Antiochus IV Epiphanes, known for his grand building projects.</note> began a temple in **Antioch** that was covered all over with golden plates—on the walls as well as the gilded ceiling—and dedicated it to this Jupiter.

About a quarter-mile from this city of **Syracuse** (now called Siracusa in Sicily), a small village and temple were established for this Jupiter, where some columns may still be found. Although it was at times occupied by **Nicias** and the Athenians, and later by **Marcellus** and the Romans, it nevertheless remained un-plundered. **Timoleon** <note>A Greek general who liberated Syracuse.</note> established a bishopric or high priesthood there and endowed it so richly that it lasted a long time. In **Patras**, this Jupiter also has a temple in the marketplace; there he sits upon a beautiful throne, and **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> stands beside him. This Jupiter is also called "of the Pisaeans," being located near their city.

## Physicus: The Naturalist <note>original: "Physicus"; from the Greek *physikos*, meaning one who understands the laws of nature.</note>

The ancients named him thus, either because he reveals the needs of nature and makes them understood in all things, or because they regarded him as the **air** <note>In ancient philosophy, Jupiter was often identified with the element of air or the "ether" that surrounds the world.</note> which sustains all natural things.

## Panomphaeus: The Hearer of All <note>original: "Panomphæus"; a title meaning "the sender of all voices or oracles."</note>

He holds this name because he hears the concerns of the entire world and understands in whatever language he is called upon; indeed, all peoples and tongues call upon him as their helper. Or, it is because he is the breath and the air, which is the cause of every voice; for no voice can travel unless it has air. Some claim he is called this because he is the sole master of all **prophecy** <note>original: "wharsägens."</note>; others are merely his servants and can say no more than he allows them.

**Ovid** <note>The Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso.</note> indicates that this Jupiter had an altar before the ears of Troy were even built, located between the two headlands: **Sigeion** (which is now called the "Cape of the Janissaries") and **Rhoiteion** (now called Saint Maria), between the two waters of the Simois and the Scamander.

## Caraeus: The Carian. Militaris: The Warrior. <note>original: "Caræus" and "Militaris."</note>

In Asia, in the land now called **Anatolia**, there is a province called **Caria**. In it was a city named **Mylasa**, where Jupiter had three temples. One was under the name **Osogoa**; the other, because of the alley and street upon which it stood, was called **Labraundus** <note>A reference to Zeus Labraundeus, often depicted holding a double-headed axe.</note>. Although he was named "The Warrior" in that same place, the temple was of ancient construction, as was the statue itself. Together with those from the surrounding districts, the people of Mylasa honored him greatly; young and old, high and low, clergy and laity, they would always walk a mile and a half in a devout procession to offer sacrifices there. Only noble citizens could be accepted into the office of the priesthood. Furthermore, they had another temple where Jupiter was "at home" in Caria; it was a common church for the whole land, which the Lydians and Mysians also shared. In a friendly and brotherly manner, they maintained all the needs of that place at their common expense. In former times, the royal court of the Kings of Caria was also located there. Some say he was called **Carios** as the "Head Lord," because he is the highest and supreme. As for the one named "The Warrior," King **Mithridates** offered sacrifices to him in this manner after he drove the reinforcements of **Murena** <note>Lucius Licinius Murena, a Roman general who fought Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note> out of Cappadocia.

## Hoplosimos <note>original: "Hoplosimos"; likely a corruption of the Greek *Apomyios*, meaning "the averter of flies."</note>

From whence this name comes, or in what regions Jupiter was honored under this name, even those who have made mention of it do not know. Although it seems to me that it concerns the hatred of flies—as if one should write *Hoplo Myos* <note>original: "Hoplo Myos"; here the author attempts an etymology linking "Hoplo" (weapon/protection) and "Myia" (fly).</note>—which could be translated as "the protection against flies." Although there are those who believe he is called *Homoplasios* here, a name knit together from Latin and Greek, where *Homo* means a human and *Plasios* comes from *Plastice* <note>original: "Plastice"; from the Greek *plastikos*, meaning to mold or shape.</note>, signifying a sculptor or image-maker, as if one wished to say "The Shaper of Humans" or "Human-Maker," because the creation of the first humans is attributed to Jupiter. 

It is also not hidden from me that a giant named **Hoplodamos** is said to have raised this Jupiter after he was hidden in **Crete** by his mother **Rhea**; perhaps he was the same giant who was his schoolmaster. Whether the name comes from that source, those who are not satisfied with these explanations may search further. Now, a good indication is given that as soon as the sacrifice was made to Jupiter, the flies fled. Furthermore, that same altar upon which they sacrificed was the very one belonging to the **Olympian**; likewise, the other altar of **Juno Alear** <note>original: "Juno alear"; likely referring to Juno Alea, an ancient title of the goddess.</note> was not far off, and they sacrificed to both at once, which is why he was also called *Hoplos myia* <note>original: "Hoplos myia"; the Fly-Averter.</note>. However, I wish to leave no one’s judgment bound to mine. 

This Jupiter had a temple in **Caria**, and when his priest was murdered at one time and no one knew who had done it, they say that the severed head, lying in its own sweat <note>original: "schweüß"; likely referring to the discharge of fluids from a fresh corpse.</note>, spoke: "**Cercy** is the murderer." This man was sought for a long time until someone of that name was found and executed. If this is true, it is more a miracle <note>original: "wundzeiche"; a sign or wonder.</note> than something natural, though some believe it is natural that a dead body—having been murdered or struck to death and already bled out—should sweat again when the killer comes near it. This is common within twelve hours, but after that time, it is very rare, so that it seems like a miracle, yet it arises from this: 

The killer sets all his powers and vital spirits <note>original: "lebliche geyste"; the "animal spirits" believed in medieval medicine to animate the body.</note> within him in anger against the one he wishes to kill. Conversely, the spirits and vital powers of the victim set themselves in fury against the perpetrator, even entering into the evildoer—that is, mixing with his powers—so the corpse must grow cold so that it can no longer bleed. But afterward, when the killer comes to the corpse, both powers and vital spirits weigh and struggle against each other, wishing to inhabit the dead person’s own previous dwellings again. They return to their place—that is, into the blood—which they stir and heat so that it may flow. But those who write of this allow these vital powers no more than twelve hours, and then only in strong and well-natured people, saying...

### Ascreus the Just

In Lydia, this Jupiter was worshipped and called "the Just." Also, the first fruits were all given to him, perhaps named Ascreus because *Ascrea* was taken for Justice, or because he also had a temple at Ascrea.

### Morius the Holy

The Greeks call a homicide *phonos* <note>original: "φόνος"</note>. It is said that Mars struck dead the son of Neptune, named Halirrhothius, near the place called the Academy and the school of Plato in Athens. In that same place, a small olive grove was planted which was called *Moria*; it was under a ban <note>In this context, a "ban" refers to a sacred enclosure or territory where the trees were protected by religious law.</note>, for whoever cut anything there or damaged it was given over to every curse and evil, and held as an abomination by everyone. It was so sacred that the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> themselves, when they invaded the city of Athens, spared the forest. Also, little wreaths were given out from these olive trees to those who won the victory in the Panathenaic games (about which we wish to speak in its proper place).

### Expiator the Giver of Penance

How homicides were atoned for among the ancients, we do not wish to keep silent later on; now, for that same purpose, the help of Jupiter was called upon. Just as King Croesus did there, when Adrastus the Phrygian killed his son Atys, he remembered this Jupiter. This Jupiter also had his altar and image on the Olympian grounds.

### Muscarius, the Hater of Flies

Jupiter was sacrificed to and offered honor so that he might drive away the flies, which in summer times are so very impetuous in some places, as happened in Arcadia by the temple of Pallas. Likewise, there was also a chapel to this Jupiter in Rome, which **Hercules** founded. Neither fly nor dog entered there; that same chapel stood on the Cattle Market <note>The Forum Boarium.</note>, and was demolished only a few years ago. There, the image of **Hercules**, bronze and gilded, was also found. On the Olympian grounds, there was also an image of this Jupiter and an altar consecrated by **Hercules**; for when he was taking his leisure there and the flies caused him so much unrest, he sacrificed to this Jupiter, and they all retreated across the Alpheus water. Pliny wonders at this, because otherwise no animal has so little sense or understanding. Therefore, it is quite a wonder that if one sacrifices an ox to the "Hater of Flies" at the Olympic festival, they all depart from the land together, as thick as if they were a cloud.

In the Cyrenian region, there are so many flies that they even bring the plague <note>The author uses "schelmen," a term for pestilence or rogue diseases.</note> into the land when they fall and die; therefore they sacrifice to this god, so the pestilence flies out of the land. They call him *Acaron* <note>original: "Acaron"; likely a reference to the Philistine city of Ekron, associated with Beelzebub.</note>. Among the Jews, Beelzebub was called the "God of Flies," but that does not belong here. And this Jupiter is sometimes called *Myiagras* <note>Greek: "Fly-catcher."</note>, sometimes *Apomyios* <note>Greek: "Fly-averter."</note>, and as mentioned above, *Hoplosmyios*.

# Of Heathen Gods

## Ctesios the Acquisitive
<note>original: "Cteſios Der Gwinſüchtig"</note>
Since Jupiter is meant to be a lord, creator, and the origin of all things, and since he gathered the scattered world together and taught people how to live with one another—doing this or that task, and how each person should do something to meet their own needs or help another for a fair payment—the Greeks gave him this name <note>From the Greek *ktesios*, meaning "of possessions" or "of the household wealth."</note>. He was especially highly honored at Athens, where they made offerings to him with costly wine, all kinds of fruits, and oil.

## Nicephorius of Nicephorium
<note>original: "Nicephorius Der zü Nicephoren"</note>
Sigenwald, or Nicephorium, is a grove located in Mesopotamia and planted by King Eumenes. This Jupiter had a temple there; he also prophesied to the Emperor Hadrian that he would yet come to the Empire.

## Altius the Altier
<note>original: "Altius Der Altier"</note>
Near the Olympic grounds there is a grove or a consecrated forest called Altis; from this very place, Jupiter received this name.

## Areius the Predatory
<note>original: "Areius Der Räubiſch"</note>
Passaron is a city in Thesprotia, in the region called Butrinto, a village roughly around Dodona <note>An ancient sanctuary famous for its oracle.</note>. There, this Jupiter had a temple and an altar. In that same temple and at the altar, the Kings of the Epirotes <note>People of Epirus, a region in Greece.</note> had to swear to the people to rule according to the law and fairness; likewise, the people swore to be obedient and subject to the King.

## Palestes the Wrestler
<note>original: "Paleſtes Der Kämpffer"</note>
When Hercules established the Olympic games and decreed that these pastimes should be held every fifty months, no one would challenge Hercules because he always wanted to fight himself. Jupiter himself came and disguised himself as a wrestler; he contended with his son for a long time until he finally revealed who he was. Then Hercules prepared an altar for him, etc.

## Maelissaeus the Melissean
<note>original: "Mæliſſæus Der Meliſſer"</note>
Amalthea and Melissa were two sisters who nourished and raised Jupiter with milk and honey. Therefore, he received his naming from these, his nurses.

## Maemactes the Winter
<note>original: "Mæmactes Der Winter"</note>
He received this name from the winter month <note>The Greek month *Maimakterion*, roughly November/December.</note> precisely because he begins at that time to become rough and gloomy in his course, and to bring confused weather.

## Herceus the Enclosed
<note>original: "Herceus Der vergättert"</note>
He is so named because of the houses of wealthy people; for in those houses, the image of Jove was commonly enclosed within gates or lattices <note>The author connects the Greek *herkeios* (of the courtyard) to the German *Gatter* (gate or lattice).</note>. By this, it was also often determined whether someone was of noble lineage or not. This same—

# The Second Book

Some write his name without the letter H, and so he must be called Erceus <note>original: "Erceus"; from the Greek *Herkeios*, meaning "of the courtyard," referring to Jupiter as the protector of the family enclosure</note>; this is then said to mean that he drove all evil away from the houses in which he was depicted.

## Hospitalis the Hospitable
<note>original: "Hospitalis Der Gaſtlich"</note>

In the Empire of Trebizond <note>A Greek successor state of the Byzantine Empire on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note>, which was once Cappadocia but is now occupied by the Turks, and not far from the promontory of Jasonium (now called St. Thomas), there lived a nation called the Genetae. Right on that same promontory, they had a magnificent foundation in honor of this Jupiter. Hospitality has always been held in such high honor among the heathens that even people who otherwise despised the God in heaven and considered his thundering to be mere foolishness believed they would receive more good fortune if they maintained and honored the laws of hospitality.

For this reason, our dear ancestors, the Germans, have always and at all times been held in high renown throughout the world, above all other nations, for their hospitality. For they considered it a great sin if they did not provide lodging for a person (whoever he might be) and share with him according to their full ability. Indeed, if someone had consumed everything he had with his guest, he would then show the guest another neighbor—the most well-to-do one he knew—and go with him from house to house until the guest went on his own path and way, well-provided and satisfied. If the guest desired something for his journey, they refused him nothing. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at—indeed, it is a marvel—that Plato indicates in his laws how this Jupiter is also angered if anyone disrupts an established friendship. For when people accept and confirm a friendship with one another, Jupiter is the patron of that fellowship <note>original: "Zunfftbrüder"; literally "guild-brother," implying a sacred bond</note>, and he is the witness of hospitality.

Now, we shall seek to describe (as far as time permits) how the ancients honored this Jupiter so highly. If someone wished to be the guest of another—that is, when two people bound themselves so that whenever the journey took one of them to the place where the other was at home, he should have everything he needed: lodging, food, drink, clothing, and entertainment (excepting only the host's wife and children)—he was to have, use, and enjoy these things just as if they were his own. However, so that no deception might occur, each gave the other a jewel, a token, or a sign <note>Often a *tessera hospitalis*, a small token of wood or metal broken in two so each party had a matching half</note>, which he had to carry with him and present if he intended to visit the other; he was also not allowed to lodge at any other inn. Now, such brotherhood or hospitable friendship was established for many reasons. Sometimes one person happened to become acquainted with another through an embassy, through trade, or where someone was struck by need on the road—being sick, poor in money, without provisions, or the like—and was taken in by a good man until he became healthy, provided with a bed and shelter, food and drink, and sent back home with provisions and help. This is how Titus Quintius the Roman treated Badius the Capuan during a great illness, when Badius fell sick in Rome while on business; Titus nursed him and sent him home honorably. Sometimes it happened that one person took another as a guest because of his virtues, as did the son of Pharnabazus, the governor in Bithynia <note>An ancient region in northwest Asia Minor</note>. For when Agesilaus, the King of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, held a parley with his father and conducted himself so bravely in word and deed toward him, and they departed from one another, the youth ran after Agesilaus and said:

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jupiter Hospitalis by exploring the historical and legal rituals of guest-friendship (known as *xenia* in Greek) in Greece and Rome, leading into contemporary examples of diplomatic protocol and chivalry.</meta>

# Of Heathen Gods

"Agesilaus, if it pleases you, I would like to be yours, and you shall be my guest-friend." "I accept," said Agesilaus. "As a token of this," said the youth, "take here my little spear." In return, Agesilaus gave him his horse's breast-ornament and crupper <note>harness decorations for the front and back of the horse</note>, which were very beautiful and decorated all over with studs; with these, the youth rode away in joy after his father.

Now, concerning such hospitable friendship: if it were to be diminished or broken, it was considered a great shame. If it ever happened that two such guest-friends were to come into conflict with one another, they could not fight—neither in the city, nor in the country, nor even on the battlefield—whether by legal action or physical force, until each had first returned and delivered back to the other his token. For this reason, in the writings of Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note>, when T. Quinctius Crispus lay in the field against the Romans (at the time the Capuans had defected to Hannibal), and Badius, his guest-friend, offered to fight him or break a spear with him, he spoke thus:

> I will find plenty of enemies against whom I can show my might; you, too, will not lack a man upon whom you may test your fortune. Therefore, it is unnecessary to skirmish with you now. Do not think I say this out of cowardice; I had thought you were calling me out to hold a friendly, hospitable conversation with me. You need not worry; I would have been willing to comply if the law, the custom, and the tradition of the guest-friend's vow did not prevent me.

Likewise, Germanicus, the adopted son of Emperor Tiberius, would not undertake any physical action against Piso until he had formally renounced their guest-friendship in writing; from this, the "warning letters" <note>original: "verwarnūgs brieff"; also known as letters of defiance or *Fehdebriefe*</note> of great lords today largely have their origin. Sometimes cities also entered into such friendships with specific individuals. For example, when the Romans sent an offering to the Temple of Apollo at Delphi with three ambassadors in one ship, they were captured by Liparian pirates and taken to the island of Lipara. There, the governor of Lipara, Timasitheus, invited them as guests, escorted them with several ships to Delos, and then back to Rome. Because of this, gifts were sent to him from the public treasury, and he was accepted as a guest-friend of the Roman state.

In Greece, wherever there was a well-ordered city, it had its own public inns in which guest-friends and ambassadors of the city were received. These houses were provided with vessels, beds, wine, and bread. When someone arrived, they were invited as guests on the first day; afterward, they were sent eggs, chickens, vegetables, and fruit for as long as they stayed there. Whatever else they bought, however, the guests paid for from their own pockets; and this they called *Xenia* <note>original: "Xenia"; Greek for "guest-gifts"</note>.

In Rome, whenever or from wherever a foreign embassy arrived, they first had to ride to the Temple of Saturn. There the treasurers were stationed, who wrote down their names; then, they were sent honors called *Lautia* <note>original: "Lautia"; the Roman term for the formal hospitality and gifts provided to foreign envoys at public expense</note>. If anyone among them was sick, they had to be cared for; if someone died, they were buried at the expense of the public treasury. From this comes the custom still among us in the cities where we give gifts of wine to strangers, and where innkeepers must report to the authorities which guests they have staying with them.

And these tokens of such guest-friendship remind me much of the societies or brotherhoods of St. George and St. Michael; the former receives the Golden Lamb from the Romans <note>likely a reference to the Order of the Golden Fleece, though the author associates it with Roman origins</note>, and the other the Golden Shells from the French kings. For when Lord Andrea Doria (whom they call *Andream d’Orien*) shook off the service of the French Crown, he sent back his insignia <note>his collar or token of the order</note> to the King, so that he might be free to march against him in the service of the Emperor.

# The Second Book

In conclusion of all this, it has always and forever been considered a harmful and great sin whenever someone insults their host or their guest, or if someone received as a guest commits a disgrace or other misdeed in the host’s lodging, or shows him ingratitude; the "Hospitable Jupiter" <note>Jupiter Hospitalis</note> was always called upon for vengeance in such matters.

### Dodoneus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; He of Dodona.

Near Gomenitsa in Epirus, there once was a city called Dodona. In that same place was the oldest temple and house of prophecy found in Greece. The city and temple were situated in an open field surrounded by much moss. It is said that Deucalion and Pyrrha <note>the survivors of the Greek flood myth, similar to Noah</note> first offered sacrifices there after the great deluge that poured over Greece, seven hundred and eighty-two years after the true general Great Flood.

Now, near the city is an oak forest that is very thick and dark; in the middle of it stood an oak tree that was considered holy and consecrated. Near this same tree stood two very high columns. Upon one stood a brass or bronze kettle; upon the other was a figure of a child that appeared to float, holding a bronze switch <term>rütlīn</term> <note>a small rod or wand</note> in its hand. The wind constantly drove this figure around so that it struck the kettle over and over, from which a steady ringing sound echoed.

Whenever someone came who wished to ask how things would go for him, the priestesses <term>Pfāssine</term> <note>originally the Selli, a group of prophets</note> assigned there would answer. These women always lay upon the ground and were never permitted to wash their feet; for this reason, they were called "Tomuri" (from which this Jupiter was sometimes called Tomarios or Tamarius). They would say that Jupiter had ordained this or that. The questioner then believed this, imagining that he had heard the speech coming from the oak itself, even though he could not have understood it over the noise of the kettle. There was also a spring not far from this oak which would light any torch or lamp if it were thrust in unlit, but it would extinguish burning ones even from a distance.

Two young women named Semiramides are said to have come from Egypt; one went to this region and the other to Libya, and thus established this practice of prophecy. From this, a rumor was spread that two doves had flown over the sea, and one had settled on the oak and spoken, saying that everyone would find an answer there for what they asked. But Herodotus <note>the Greek historian</note> holds the opinion that two young maidens came who taught the people the devotions and customs of the Egyptians. For ever afterward, there were women there who performed the idol-worship, such as Promenea, Timareta, Nicandra, and others. He was also called "Molossus" because Dodona was located in the land of the Molossians.

### Ithometes &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; He of Ithome.

In Messenia in the Morea <note>the Peloponnese peninsula</note>, there is a city situated about five miles above Koroni in the Peloponnese, by the stream which once took its name from the city when it was called Messana, but is now called the Stream of Koroni. In this very city, the castle once stood that was called Ithome, named after a water goddess <note>a nymph</note> who is said to have raised Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. Her name was Ithome, and she had a sister named Neda, from whom the water that runs through that same mossy area got its name. Every day, water must be carried from this river into the temple. Every year, a new priest is appointed; he keeps the statue with him in his house until the church consecration festival <note>the annual feast day</note> comes, at which time his service begins. The master craftsman Agelades made this statue.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

As these [the Messenians] had waged war with the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> for many years, and both sides had suffered greatly, it happened that a prophecy was given to them: that whoever should be the first to sacrifice one hundred tripods <note>three-legged sacrificial vessels</note> to Jupiter—whether they or the Lacedaemonians—victory over the other would be granted to them. Now, since the Messenians were not wealthy enough to have them made of bronze and wished to have them turned from wood instead, a Lacedaemonian named Debalus <note>likely Oebalus or a variation of Daedalus</note> anticipated them with a trick. He made one hundred such tripods out of clay as best he could, put them in a sack, and went one evening into the city disguised as a hunter with a wild-game net. During the night, he performed a sacrifice and slipped away early. What followed afterward—the defeat against the Lacedaemonians and the deaths—the Messenians attributed entirely to this deception. Therefore, their captain Aristomenes later sacrificed three hundred men at once, and among them Theopompus, the Lacedaemonian King, to this Jupiter as revenge.

It happened that once, by the wind, a fire was carried into a forest not far from Leuctra (which is now called Istechia), and there it burned a great heap of trees. And so, when the ashes were washed away and carried off by the wind and rain, the statue of this Jupiter was discovered.

## Atabyrius. He of Atabyros.

A mountain lies on the island of Rhodes which is quite high, being the highest in those parts. Although Timaeus <note>a Greek historian</note> also honors a mountain of this name in Sicily, where bronze bulls once stood which were said to low whenever something unjust occurred on the island. From one of these mountains, this Jupiter is said to have taken his name, though Lacedemonius says this name came to him from his host and ally in war. For when Jupiter gained the upper hand and took all power for himself, he bore himself so magnificently and was so raised up in pride that he established churches, temples, and altars for himself in many places. Also, whenever he came into a province, he drew kings, princes, lords, and cities to himself through the bonds of hospitality <note>guest-friendship</note> and in whatever other way he could. When he then departed from them, he commanded that a temple be erected to him and also to the one who had received him as a guest, so that the memory of the alliance entered into might remain all the more eternal. From this, he was named after his hosts, being called Athabyrius, Labradeus, Laprius, Casius, Molion, and many other names.

## Apelantius. He of Mount Apesas.

Nemea was a city in Argos, which is now a small village in those parts called Scutica, not far from the waterfall at Legina; and not far from this city lay a mountain called Apesas, named after a lord who had a fortress upon it. There Perseus first sacrificed to Jupiter, so that this name originated from that place.

## Laphystius. He of Laphystium.

Oron in Morea <note>the Peloponnese</note> is a fortified village and city which Andrea Doria <note>Andreas de Oria, a famous Genoese admiral</note> wrested from the Turks in our time, which the Spaniards later cleared out and left desolate to the Turks, on account of the scoundrel

About half a mile from that same place, there stood a hill or small mountain upon which there was a grove <note>original: "Dhan oder förstlin," a small forest or sacred grove</note>, in which a stone image of this Jupiter stood. There, they say, Athamas once intended to sacrifice the siblings Phryxus and Helle, his children. There they sacrificed the ram to this Jupiter, and his descendants maintained this custom for a long time. Xerxes did not wish to enter this grove, nor would he allow any of his men to go inside, for reasons that Herodotus relates, which are not necessary to describe here.

## Trophonius. The Trophonian.

Lebadia, which is now called La Badia, lies in Boeotia and is in Greece proper. There was a cave <note>original: "hülin"</note> there called the Cave of Trophonius. Strabo and Livy say that Jupiter was honored there, and although almost all other scholars mention the cave and its prophecy, they do not name a Jupiter there. However, it seems to me not out of place to write here about what kind of hole and phantom <note>original: "fantasey," likely referring to the superstitious nature of the oracle</note> it was.

Some claim that Trophonius was a master builder and an ingenious stonemason in Lebadia, who built an underground temple in honor of his fatherland. Those who wish to know the future travel there and sit naked before the cave; they are then sucked under the earth by a vapor, yet they carry certain cakes <note>original: "küchen," typically honey-cakes</note> in their hands, which they throw to the monsters and vermin they encounter in the cave. Then, after they have heard and inquired, they are cast out again, sometimes nearby and sometimes quite far away at another location.

Still others say that Agamedes, the King of Stymphalus (which is now called Wussy <note>a contemporary 16th-century name for the region</note>), fathered a son with a woman named Epicafte, whom he named Trophonius. Now, the father and son were so highly renowned for their building and stoneworking that they were contracted to build the temple at Delphi. They also built a treasury for Augeas of Elis in which he kept his gold and jewels; however, they had placed a stone in such a way that they knew how to move it to enter the treasury, and then how to put it back when they wished to leave. The treasure decreased, and Augeas could not understand how it happened. Just at that time, Daedalus came from Crete, having been driven out by Minos; Augeas asked him for advice on how he might catch the thieves. Daedalus quickly prepared a trap <note>original: "rüstet jne bald"</note> in which Agamedes was caught. When Trophonius saw that his father could not be freed, he cut off his head so that he might not be recognized. Nevertheless, the matter came to light after a long time, and Trophonius fled to Lebadia, where he built the cave and lived in it all his life until he died. After his death, the world was deluded into thinking that Trophonius was worthy of being sacrificed to as a god, and that he gave certain answers to everything he was asked.

Some add another version, saying that Trophonius was swallowed alive by an earthquake during his flight, and that some years later, when a great plague did much damage in Boeotia, they were answered by God <note>meaning a pagan deity or oracle</note> that they should sacrifice to the soul of Trophonius, and so the...

->### Concerning Heathen Gods<--
<meta>catchword: If someone</meta>

stopped the dying <note>referring to the end of the plague mentioned on the previous page</note>. But because they did not know where he was to be found, they saw a swarm of bees <note>original: "jmen"</note> emerging from the earth and immediately thought his grave must be there. They thrust a man into the hole, who first encountered two dragons; he threw several cakes into their maws, so they did not harm him, and he came out again uninjured.

If Pausanias is to be trusted as a witness, one may read here what he writes happened to himself, for he descended into it. First, when someone wishes to go in, he must stay for several days in the outer building and temple that is above, which is consecrated to the Good Spirit and also to Good Fortune. While he remains there, he maintains himself in all things moderately and purely; he is not allowed any warm water, but must instead bathe in the river Hercynna. He is given enough meat from the daily sacrifices, for he himself must sacrifice before Trophonius and his children. Likewise to Apollo, Saturn, Jupiter the King, and Europa (who is said to have otherwise been Ceres and a nurse to Trophonius). At every sacrifice, the priest is present to inquire what the signs indicate—whether the person will have a good journey, or if he will not be well-received by Trophonius. Then, on the night when one wishes to descend, he must first sacrifice a black ram <note>original: "schwarzẽ wider"</note>. If its entrails show good omens, he may then expect a good journey; for even if the first sacrifices showed good signs, and this one does not go well, they consider it all in vain. With this, he calls upon Agamedes again. If the sacrifice is favorable, the priests lead him at night to the water of Hercynna, where two boys—children of citizens, about thirteen years old—baptize him and anoint him well with oil. After he has bathed, the priests lead him to the consecrated spring which is not far away; there he must take the Draught of Forgetfulness <note>original: "Dolldrunck," referring to the spring of Lethe</note>, so that he immediately forgets all he has done in his life. Afterward, they give him another drink <note>the spring of Mnemosyne or Memory</note>, which is said to have the power so that he may never forget everything he experiences in the hole. Then the image of Trophonius is brought before him, which Daedalus carved and which the priests keep in secret, showing it to no one except those who wish to enter the cave; he honors and prays to it, and then he departs in a linen shirt, which is well-girded with a silk band.

Now, the mouth of the cave is above the grove <note>original: "Dhan"</note> on a mountain. The entrance is made of white stone and has an opening like a small altar, nearly three feet wide at every corner. Above the opening stand several fire-pillars <note>likely decorative obelisks or pillars for torches</note>; hanging from them are small doors or latches, made quite pleasingly. As soon as you enter the hole, you find a curve or a chasm that is not natural but made quite skillfully like an oven-hole; it is about six feet wide and no more than twelve feet deep, as one might estimate. But down to the bottom there are no built stairs; instead, they give the person a small ladder made for the purpose. Then, he who wishes to descend stoops down, holding honey cakes <note>original: "ghonigt küchen," used to appease the sacred serpents</note> in his hands; he braces himself with his knees against the sides of the cave and slides down. The rest of his body quickly follows his feet, just as water flows over a cliff. Once they have come inside, future things are revealed to them, though not to one in the same way as to another. When someone wishes to come out again, he turns his feet toward the mountain and travels back out through the entrance. They say that no one has ever perished within, except for a guard of Demetrius; he descended not out of devotion, but to retrieve a treasure from within. It is said his corpse reached as far as the small door, but the cave would not cast him out entirely.

# The Second Book

When someone finally emerges from the hole, the priests take them and place them upon the **Chair of Memory** <note>German: "stůl der Gedächtnuß"; this refers to the throne of Mnemosyne, the goddess of memory</note>, which is located not far from the entrance. They ask the person what they saw and heard there. Then they lead them to the Chapels of the **Good Spirit** and **Good Fortune** <note>German: "Capellen des gůten Geysts vnd Glücks"</note>. Because the person has just come out, they are often in such a state of terror that they recognize neither themselves nor anyone else. After a while, when the person comes back to their senses, they remember all their previous experiences and begin to laugh. Whatever a person has seen or heard must then be recorded on a tablet for preservation.

¶ They say that Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, also descended into this place. It is said that once someone has been in this hole and returned to themselves, they never laugh again; they remain constantly solemn and sorrowful. However, quite a few claim that Trophonius was an ambitious man who sought to gain an immortal name for himself—much like the philosopher Empedocles <note>Empedocles was said to have leapt into Mount Etna to appear as if he had vanished into godhood</note>. It is suggested he prepared a hollow in the earth for himself and gave answers from it to those who came to question him; however, when he later died of hunger in that hole, a spirit took up residence in the hollow and gave answers in Trophonius's place.

Cicero states that Trophonius and Agamedes built a temple for the Delphic Apollo. As their payment, they asked for whatever was most beneficial to mankind. Apollo promised them this reward, and three days after the consecration of the church—just as everyone was praising their work most highly—they were found dead, having passed away in their sleep.

## Catæbates the Wonder-Worker
<note>Catæbates: from the Greek "Katabates," meaning "The Descender," usually referring to Zeus as the bringer of lightning</note>

¶ Some give him this name because, by his power, he often descends to and beneath the earth in a bolt of thunder. Others say that he often lowered himself from heaven for the sake of human women. Because of this, the playwright Aristophanes attributes a dung beetle to him, as if he were wallowing in filth, mocking him in this way. Regardless, he had an altar in the Olympium <note>the great Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens</note>.

## Citheronius, the One at Cithaeron

¶ Alcomenes is said to have taught this Jupiter how to use a trick to bring Juno back to him after she had left him in a fit of anger and refused to stay with him any longer. He had a wooden image carved <note>German: "Dedalon"; likely referring to a Daedala, a wooden cult image</note>, and the women of Cithaeron and throughout all Boeotia led it to Jupiter as if it were a bride. Juno then ran out with the women of Plataea, intending to crash the wedding. From this event, it came to pass that they were reconciled. But since this story concerns Juno more closely, you may search for this history under her entry, where you will also find its significance.

## Croceatis, the One at the Red Cliff

¶ This is a stone quarry where red marble is mined, not far from the suburb of Pagus or Gythium in Morea <note>the medieval name for the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note>. This stone is used for all magnificent and costly buildings, and it is especially good for structures built in water. Outside, in front of the quarry, stands a stone image of Jupiter.

## Arbius, the One at Arbia

¶ On the island of Crete <note>German: "Candien," the Venetian name for Crete</note>, there is a mountain called Arbius where Jupiter was worshipped, and thus he kept the name; he was also called Asius.

## Dolichæus &emsp; &emsp; He of Doliche.

In Syria Comagena, roughly around Casracata by the Euphrates, there lay a city called **Doliche**, where this Jupiter was worshipped; from this, he received this name. However, the island of **Doliche** is likely now **Castellrugio** <note>Now known as Kastellorizo</note> opposite the island of Cyprus, about ten miles to the north.

## Aegiphagus &emsp; &emsp; Goat-Swallower.

**Nicander** calls him thus <note>The Greek epithet *Aigiphagos* literally means goat-eater</note>, certainly in one of the books he wrote that is either not currently available or not yet commonly published. I have already said enough about **Juno** under this name; it may be that **Hercules** sacrificed to both his father and his stepmother at once.

## Meſſapeus &emsp; &emsp; He upon Mount Messapius.

**Strabo** points out this mountain, which is not far from the hill of **Taygetus**, near **Mizithra** <note>The medieval name for Mystras, near ancient Sparta</note> or **Lacedaemon**; below it in the wide field, there is said to lie a grove or forest consecrated to this Jupiter, named after **Messapus**, the lord of this land, or as some would have it, after one who was sacrificed to him.

## Labradeus &emsp; &emsp; He with the Throwing-Axe.

In the place where we spoke of the warrior, this Jupiter is also worshipped; **Lactantius** says that it happened with him as it did with **Trophonius**, having also received his worship as a guest. But the image there carried no scepter, nor any thunderbolt; the reason being that when **Hercules** killed the Amazon **Hippolyte**, he took, among other things, a battle-axe from her and gave it to his mistress **Omphale**. The kings of the **Lydians** thereafter carried this instead of a scepter, until **Candaules** thought it was unseemly for a king to carry a woman’s weapon; he gave it to **Gyges** to carry, who later drove him from the kingdom and killed him. Thus, he later built a temple to Jupiter and placed a battle-axe in the hands of his image, calling him **Labradeus**, because an axe is called *labrys* <note>original: "Labre"</note> in the Lydian language.

**Aelian** says he received this name because of a great rain, and by the same temple is a spring full of tame fish that wear little necklaces and gold rings in their fins. A **Carian** saber hangs upon this image as a memorial that the Carians were the first to invent the forging of war-armor and to let themselves be hired for money to serve other lords in the course of wars—a rough, predatory, and mercenary-like <note>original: "Landßknechtiſch", referring to the Landsknecht mercenary soldiers</note> people.

Not far from **Alexandria** in **Egypt**, which is now called **Scanderia**, lies a mountain once called **Casius**, now **Albere**, toward **Damietta**; there is also a city of that name at the foot of the mountain. There a temple was built by **Casius**, the son of **Cleomachus**; by the same, or not far from it, through...

...due to the treachery of the Egyptian King, the great **Pompey** was stabbed and beheaded; his body was buried on this mountain within the temple. <note>Referencing Mount Casium, where Pompey the Great was killed and where a temple to Jupiter Casius stood.</note>

## Triphilius &emsp; &emsp; Of the Three Tribes.

**Diodorus** also speaks of this Jupiter, whom you may look up; however, **Strabo** claims that **Pisa**, located in **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese</note> in the **Alpheus Valley**, of which we spoke regarding the Olympian Jupiter, had three places: one called **Olympia**, the second **Triphylia**, and the third **Cauronia**. From these, the entire landscape later received its name, as if from three guilds or three different peoples. And because such great honor was shown to Jupiter there, they say he was given this name. His deeds were described by the poet **Euhemerus** and hung upon a pillar in his temple, which Jupiter himself had erected out of pure gold. <note>Euhemerus was famous for the theory that gods were originally great kings or heroes, a philosophy known as Euhemerism.</note>

## Endendros &emsp; &emsp; He of the Trees.

The people of **Rhodes** named and worshipped him thus, just as Jupiter **Sardessius** was held in high esteem near **Lyrnessus** in **Lycia**, which is now called **Briquien**. <note>The name *Endendros* literally means "in the tree."</note>

## Chrysaoreus &emsp; &emsp; He of the Golden Sword.

In **Anatolia**, which was once called **Asia**, by the **Pamphylian Sea**—near the gulf now called **Macri** <note>The Gulf of Fethiye</note>—there was a city named **Stratonicia**, which is now called **Statouiza**, built most exquisitely by the **Macedonians**. Nearby, in a wide field, stood a temple in honor of this Jupiter, shared by all the **Carians**. When matters concerning the land or other necessities arose that affected them all, they would meet for council at this foundation; they also hold their annual church-consecration festival and a wedding-like feast there.

## Chthonius &emsp; &emsp; The Earthly.

In **Corinth**, this Jupiter had a statue, and in **Olympia**, he had an altar. <note>This title usually refers to Jupiter in his role as a god of the underworld or the fertility of the earth.</note>

## Taranteus &emsp; &emsp; He of Tarentum.

In **Bithynia**, there was a city called **Tarentum**, in which Jupiter was honored and from which he retained this name.

## Aristæus and Icmæus.

**Aristæus** is said to have been a son of **Apollo** and **Cyrene**. He was the one who, among the ancients, discovered how to pasture and tend to sheep, how to derive use from their wool, milk, and cheese, and also how to keep and raise bees. When, at one time, there was a great dying of cattle on the island of **Zea** <note>The island of Kea</note>, he was summoned and gave them instruction on how to help the livestock and drive away the parching heat. Thus, out of the honor given to him for this good deed on the island, he erected an altar and established certain sacrifices to Jupiter. Because of this, Jupiter is named **Aristæus** and **Icmæus**, "the Dispeller," because the evil, stagnant, and poisonous air was driven away at that time. On this island of **Zea**, there were four small towns: **Iulis**, **Phoeessa**, **Carthæa**, and **Coressus**. Two of them, **Carthæa** and **Iulis**, remained standing for a long time, and the inhabitants of the other two moved into them. The entire island had a law which read: "He who cannot live well shall not live poorly..." <note>Referring to an ancient law of Kea where the elderly or infirm would voluntarily take hemlock to avoid being a burden.</note>

...did not desire it. Their scholars interpret the reason as follows: because the island was narrow, never very fertile, and the population was large, those who were sixty years old—who because of their age could no longer live healthily, happily, or vigorously—should put themselves to death with a poisonous draft of **aconite**. <note>Aconite, also known as wolfsbane, was the plant traditionally used for state-sanctioned euthanasia on the island of Ceos.</note> Now, in the time of **Pompey**, there was an elderly lady who, according to the law, wished to depart to leave room and space for the young. Pompey, arriving on the island by chance, heard of this and summoned the lady. He spoke to her kindly, and with all sorts of encouragements to live, he intended to persuade her to desist from her undertaking. But it was all in vain; for after he had spoken long and much, she answered him:

"Lord, you should not imagine that I would undertake such a deed without long and timely consideration. I have once and for all set before my own eyes what inconstant fortune may ever present to a person as 'good,' and have clearly perceived that such things are nothing but a poisoned bowl. Through this, those who think themselves well-composed waste away and die all the more grievously, yet as if through a pleasant sickness. Until now, fortune has not offended me, so it has not yet made me suspicious that it is secretly plotting to deeply grieve me. I do not wish to wait for that slap in the face. Even if our law—which is unfortunately lacking in serious weight—were not so strict with me, I believe, O Lord, you know how to judge for yourself what great blessedness it is when someone dies in their highest prosperity, before they encounter the malice of fortune or become an object of men's pity, at which point the soul and all powers depart from the body with pain and resentment. Therefore, do not prevent me from doing what the custom of the land and the rights of citizenship permit me, and what my own heart advises me is best." With this, she obtained leave from **Pompey**, followed through with her undertaking, and fulfilled the laws of the land.

## Phyxius &emsp; &emsp; The Protector of Fugitives.

Because he is a refuge for the oppressed, he bears this name <note>original: *Phyxius*, from the Greek 'phyxis' meaning flight or escape</note>. For when the floods gained the upper hand in **Thessaly** and some people escaped, they afterwards sacrificed to **Jupiter** under this name and honored him greatly. Some, however, claim the name is **Phrygius**, asserting that when **Phrixus** rode away on the **Ram with the Golden Fleece**, <note>original: *Goldfäligen*</note> he made his sacrifice to **Jupiter** and thus established the name.

## Hypsistos &emsp; &emsp; The Highest.

There was a gate in **Thebes** called the "Highest Gate." There was also a religious foundation there dedicated to **Jupiter**. Likewise, there was a statue of him near **Corinth** and another in **Olympia**; thus he is rightly called the Highest.

## Homolius &emsp; &emsp; The Unifier.

That he unifies all things <note>original: *vereinbare*</note> is attributed to **Jupiter**, which is why he bears this name. They worship him in **Thebes** and other places in **Boeotia**. There are those who say there was a prophet named **Homolion** who had a daughter, **Ennyus**; he sent her to **Delphi** to be a prophetess, and she gave **Jupiter** her father's name.
