<note>This section lists various local names for Jupiter, the king of the gods, based on where he was worshipped or the specific legends associated with him.</note>

## Hymettius, Parnethius, Heliconius

There are two mountains in **Attica** named **Hymettus** and **Parnes**, and a third called **Helicon**. On all three of these mountains, Jupiter was honored. He had an image made of olive wood on Parnes and an altar on Mount Helicon.

## Soatas the Armor-Bearer

Among the people of **Thespiae**, there was an image of Jupiter that was worshipped for a specific reason. It happened that a dragon was devouring the entire countryside. Jupiter commanded that a young boy be chosen by lot every year to be thrown to the dragon. The lot eventually fell upon a youth named **Cleostratus**. A man named **Menestratus**, who loved the youth dearly, forged a breastplate of bronze with backward-pointing spikes <note>German: "widerbürstigen anglen," referring to hooks or barbs designed to catch in the dragon's throat</note> and dressed the boy in it. Cleostratus was willing to suffer for his fatherland and ran directly into the dragon's maw. Both he and the dragon died on the field of battle. Because of this, the Thespians erected an olive-wood image to "Jupiter the Deliverer" on that spot.

## Hypatus the Highest

The city of **Glisas** in **Boeotia** lay upon a mountain called **Hypatus**. On that mountain, a temple was established to this Jupiter, with an altar in the porch called the **Erechion**. To him, nothing living was sacrificed; instead, they offered all kinds of fruit and sweet cakes, but without wine. They also offered a specific cake called a **Pelanos**, made from fine starch flour, containing frankincense and drops of gum. For his labor, the priest was offered a **Kreuzer** <note>A small silver coin used in the Holy Roman Empire; here used to represent a small, standard fee</note>.

## Triophthalmos the Three-Eyed

Since Jupiter possesses power over both the heavenly and earthly realms, they say that in **Troy**, King **Priam** had a "three-eyed" image. Two eyes were in their usual places, and the third was on the forehead. This image stood in the middle of the royal court, and the king fled to it for sanctuary when Troy was captured. When the Greeks divided the spoils of war among themselves, this image fell to **Sthenelus**, who took it with him to **Argos**. Some believe it had so many eyes to demonstrate that the Lord God sees all things in all places.

## Anchelmos at Anchesmos

Near **Athens**, there was a hill they called **Anchesmos**. It was not very high, and because Jupiter had a shrine there, he kept that name.

## Epidotes the Bountiful

Because God gives all good gifts, they also called Jupiter by this name, and the people of **Mantinea** erected a temple to him, as **Pausanias** <note>A famous Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD</note> writes. **Mantinea** (also called Antigonia) is a city now called **Mundi**, located in **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note>.

## Polieus the Civic

So then [Athens], now a small village—which is a pity—was once called Athens, the very eye of all Greece, a fountain spring of all human... <note>original: "meneschlie," likely "menschlichen" (human wisdom or arts), cut off by the page break</note>

...human wit and arts in war and peace, a covenant of the world. In that same city, there was an image with the name of this Jupiter, which **Leochares** <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 4th century BC</note> had carved. They sacrificed to this god in the following way: they placed wheat and barley mixed together upon the altar without any protection. Then a bull, which has been destined for sacrifice, approaches; as soon as he touches the grain, they call for a designated priest. He strikes the ox on the spot, throws the axe onto the altar, and flees. The other priests act as if a crime has been committed and pretend they do not know who did the damage; they bring the axe before the court, as if the axe should be judged in place of the perpetrator. **Pausanias** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer</note> says here: that in the times when **Erechtheus** was the city leader in Athens, the first "Ox-Slayer" <note>original: "Buphonus"; referring to the ritual of Bouphonia</note> sacrificed an ox to this god, threw the axe from him, and fled from the Attic countryside. Then the judges declared the axe "not guilty"; Pausanias says he does not wish to reveal the secret of this custom or its cause.

## Panhellenius &nbsp;&nbsp; The Common God of the Greeks.

The Athenians had a temple built to this Jupiter by the Emperor **Hadrian**. However, the true temple of this Jupiter was on the island of the Aeginetans, now called **Egina** <note>original: "Ligina"</note>, which was established for this reason: **Aeacus** was a son of Jupiter, fathered by the nymph **Aegina**, a daughter of **Asopus**. Jupiter gave him this island. **Juno** became indignant that her husband’s bastard should rise so high; she sent a plague <note>original: "schelmen," here meaning a pestilence or evil</note> over the whole island so that every person there died. And so that Aeacus would have even greater sorrow, he alone remained alive. As he ran about a forest, mindless with grief, he came upon an anthill <note>original: "omeyßhauffen"</note> and begged his father Jupiter that, if he were truly his son, he should not let him perish so completely. Thus, according to his desire, living humans were made from the ants <note>These people became known as the Myrmidons, from the Greek word for ant, *myrmex*</note>. This fable only demonstrates that all things are possible for God, and for one who trusts in God, help and grace never fail. Otherwise, this little tale could be interpreted this way: because it is a stony, rocky island, and the inhabitants dug out the soil and turf everywhere and carried it to the heights to make fields, they were given the name of "Ants."

Now it happened soon afterward that a great drought came to the whole land of Greece, so that nothing would grow or turn green. Therefore, a common embassy of the Greeks was sent to **Delphi** <note>original: "Delphon"</note> to ask what should be done. They were answered: Jupiter must be appeased; however, for him to hear the prayers of the troubled, it was necessary that Aeacus should intercede and offer sacrifice. So the envoys of all the Greeks came to Aeacus and petitioned him to reconcile them with his father. Thus he sacrificed and offered his prayer, and enough rain came. Therefore, the Greeks built a temple to this Jupiter on a small hill on the island, in which they also placed the image of Aeacus along with those who had come as ambassadors. Hadrian’s temple was built quite magnificently with one hundred and twenty columns of red marble; the walls and all the vaults, and very beautiful libraries <note>original: "bůchbhaltũgen"</note>; he had them gilded in all places and covered with alabaster, the shimmering marble.

## Scotinas &nbsp;&nbsp; The Darkened One.

Not far from **Lacedaemonia**, which is now called **Mistra** <note>original: "Mizithra"</note>, lay a small grove or fir-wood <note>original: "Dhan"</note> that took its name from this god—or perhaps Jupiter took his name from it.

### Ambulius &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Of the Walkway.

In the same city <note>Referring to Sparta, where Jupiter Ambulius was worshipped</note> were several basins made in a square, and others dedicated to this god as the one who had his altar in the walkway <note>original: "umbgāgé"; likely referring to an ambulatory or a place of passage</note>.

### Euanemus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Fair-Wind.

Similarly, they had an image of Jupiter because he gave favorable winds.

### Cappotas &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Reliever.

Gythium is one of the eighteen free cities in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note>, now called the Pagaeer Corner, located on the Gulf of Laconia <note>original: "Colochiner güessen"</note>. About a horse-run's distance <note>A traditional measure of distance, roughly a stadium</note> from the city is a cliff called **Cappota**. There, when **Orestes** <note>The son of Agamemnon, pursued by the Furies</note> was mad, he rested for a while upon the cliff and came back to his senses; thus, they dedicated this rock to Jupiter and named him after it.

### Homogynus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Uniter.

Aegium <note>original: "Egyum"</note> was once a small town on the Gulf of Patras. It had a temple by the sea where **Agamemnon** held the general assembly of all the Greek princes. There, they deliberated on the war—how it should be waged against **Priam**, and how the abduction and shame of **Helen** might be avenged. **Phurnutus** <note>Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD</note> calls him **Homogynus** <note>Meaning "of the same race or family"</note>. He was always honored in great families for everything that belonged together.

### Splanchnotomos &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Metalworker.

On the island of Cyprus, near the city of Tamassos <note>An ancient city famous for its copper mines</note>, this Jupiter received his worship and name from the metalworkers <note>original: "Oerztknappen"; though the Greek name *Splanchnotomos* literally means "the cutter of vitals"</note>.

### Gamelios &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Matchmaker.

Because it was believed that Jupiter was the one who brought all marriages together and maintained them in prosperity, he was given this name. However, he was only honored this way by the Greeks, which is why **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the church father</note> mocks **Chrysippus** <note>A famous Stoic philosopher</note> there and says: "He gives a wise man foolish advice which he wants: a wise man should take a wife so that he does not anger this Jupiter." For in that way, among the Latins <note>The Romans</note>, no one who was a wise man would be allowed to marry, since none among them knows of this Jupiter. They also called him **Teleius**, which means "the mature" or "the marriageable"; he had an altar and a squared column at Tegea under this name. They also called him **Genethlius**, which is the "Protector of Little Children," as if he were the one who took care that children were conceived and well-raised in marriage.

### Aratrius (otherwise Dagon) &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Plow-Shower.

Among the Syrians, this Jupiter was honored as the one who first showed how to use the plow and how to cultivate grain.

### Hecalesius &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Of Poor Hecale.

This Jupiter received his name from a poor old woman <note>Hecale, who according to legend hosted Theseus before his battle with the Marathonian Bull</note> who, not far...

### Enæsimus, Efimus
->The Gracious. The Aimer.<-
<note>original: "Zilstölled"; likely referring to one who sets a goal or aim.</note>

In **Coronea**, located in **Boeotia**, Jupiter was honored under the first name. He received the second name from the idolatrous worship paid to him on a mountain on the island of **Cephalonia** <note>original: "Zafalona"</note>, which was once fought over and captured by the Venetians. That mountain is very high, but the island surrounding the mountain lies so low that it is often flooded by the turbulence of the sea.

### Athous
->The One on Mount Athos.<-

**Athos** is a very high mountain on the Aegean Sea, which is now called the **Archipelago**, located in the corner and promontory of **Macedonia**. In our times, it is also called the **Holy Mountain** <note>Mount Athos is still known as the "Holy Mountain" (Agion Oros) today due to its many monasteries.</note>. On its summit, this Jupiter has his chapel, just as he was also worshipped on Mount **Nynnatio** and named after that mountain.

### Lupercus, Lycæus
->The Wolfish.<-

In **Rome**, on the **Palatine Hill**, where the small church of **Saint Theodore** now stands, this Jupiter once had a temple. His image there was entirely naked, girded with a whip. In this attire, people would run about during the festivals of Jupiter. Some believe the temple stood where **Romulus and Remus** were heard <note>or found</note> by a she-wolf. Others say that a grove <note>original: "Dhan oder hölzlin"</note> stood there where the Arcadian god **Pan** sometimes dwelt, and it was called "The Wolfish." It was honored for this reason: because he protected the sheep from wild beasts.

In **Greece**, however, on the mainland island of the **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese</note>, where **Arcadia** is situated, there is a mountain called **Olympus** by some, but **Lyceus** by others. There, this Jupiter had a temple, for some claim Jupiter was raised in that place. For this reason, it is also called the Holy Mountain. The nurses of this Jupiter are said to be the water goddess **Thisoa**, along with her companions **Neda** and **Agno**. In front of the temple, there is a grove. If anyone enters it without the knowledge of the priests or without the prescribed sacrifices, they shall not live out the year. It is also said that no living animal that walks in that forest ever casts a shadow. There is also a spring there that is very much like **Mount Pilatus** near **Lucerne** in **Switzerland**. For if one stirs it even a little with a piece of wood or throws something into it, a thick mist rises into the heights, bringing hail and storms.

This mountain, temple, and Jupiter also received the name because **Lycaon** the Pelasgian and **Cecrops**, the King of the **Athenians**, lived at the same time, but they did not hold the same customs in sacrifice. For Cecrops performed his sacrifice to **Jupiter Hypatus** <note>The Highest</note> with cakes and honeyed tarts; but...

<header>The Second Book.</header>

...but Lycaon murdered a young child on this mountain and altar, burned it there, and poured out the blood. For this reason, he was immediately transformed into a wolf. It is also claimed that the first city upon which the sun ever shone was built there and was named **Lycosura** <note>Lycosura was an ancient city in Arcadia, claimed by Pausanias to be the oldest in the world.</note>.

There are some who tell another reason for this Jupiter's name and worship. They say Lycaon conducted his rule in a very just and pious manner; and so that he might more easily and without special effort raise his subjects to fairness and all goodness, he told his people that Jupiter went to and fro in the world to distinguish between what was good and evil, and that he often came to Lycaon himself as a guest. Now, since he had many children, he said on one occasion that Jupiter was coming; therefore, they should prepare a good meal as a sacrifice and receive the God well. The children, out of curiosity to find out whether the God who knew all things would actually be there, took a child, murdered it, and prepared its flesh like any other sacrifice, hoping Jupiter would know nothing of it. But immediately thunder came and struck dead all those who had given counsel or deed to this murder. It is also said that some of those who had unknowingly eaten of this sacrificed child were transformed into wolves; those among them who then ate no animal or flesh for ten years thereafter became human again, whereas the others who had eaten flesh remained wolves <note>This refers to the legend of Lycanthropy, where the term "wolf" is used for those who fail the moral test of the gods.</note>.

# Hamon The Sandy. Unknown.

Because the creator and lord of all things, the one God, is something eternal, secret, unknown, and not to be fathomed, the Egyptians called Jupiter **Amun**, who is called **Hamon** or **Amon** by our people. This is because a story was invented that he was found by a shepherd in the sand among some herds; for this reason, his image is painted with ram horns <note>original: "Wider hörner"</note> at the temples. What **Diodorus** writes of him, I will let rest for now. **Herodotus**, however, says that when Jupiter was so often begged by his son **Hercules** to show himself as his father just once, he would not do it; instead, he cut off the neck of a ram, pulled the skin from its head, and placed it on as a mask, putting the rest of the skin on his body, which is why he is still painted in this way.

Now, this Jupiter had a temple in an exceedingly vast desert in **Africa**, where neither foliage nor grass grows, but rather everything is sand for many hundreds of miles in all directions behind the region of **Cyrene**. This temple was located where the **Ammonites** dwelt, in a forest of olive and other tall trees, with beautiful flowing waters, right in the middle of the sand—quite pleasant—barely more than a German mile <note>A historical unit of distance, roughly 7.5 kilometers.</note> in circumference. This temple also rose to fame through the speaking of doves, just like the one at **Dodona**.

Not far within the sands from the temple, there is a spring called the **Source of the Sun** <note>original: "Sonnen quel"; known in antiquity as the Fons Solis.</note>. At sunrise, it runs out blue; at noon, when the heat is greatest, it is coldest; in the evening, it begins to become warm; at midnight, it boils; and the higher the sun rises toward the day, the colder it becomes; but in its setting, it turns toward the heat. **Perseus**, **Hercules**, **Cambyses**, and **Alexander** sought out this temple with particular pleasure—the first two in person, **Cambyses** with a great army and even greater loss, and **Alexander** with a significant number of people, quite successfully.

# Of Heathen Gods

Many believe his image was painted with ram's horns <note>original: "widerhörnern"</note> because his answers and prophecies were completely obscured and confused, as well as very secret, for they were given only through signs and gestures.

Caesar, in his translation of Aratus, believes the sign of the Ram in the sky is that which preceded Dionysus or Liber <note>Liber is the ancient Roman god of wine and freedom, often identified with the Greek Dionysus</note> when he traveled through the African desert and showed him the way; for this reason, Liber built a temple in his honor.

## Assabinus — The Gatherer of Cinnamon

In the place where cinnamon grows in thick, rough thickets, the local people are not permitted to harvest it unless Jupiter allows it. To understand when he is pleased, they sacrifice to him the heads and knees of twenty-four oxen, twenty-four goats, and twenty-four sheep. Then the priest announces the time they should begin, divides the harvest with a small scoop <note>original: "schäffelini," a small vessel for measuring</note> made for that purpose, and reserves for the God his portion. Also, one must not harvest it before sunrise or after sunset. The mountains of Assabina, however, are located in fertile Arabia, where today the land of Yemen <note>original: "Mamonta," likely referring to the region around Mocha</note> lies around Aden and Ta'izz, where the King of Aden rules. Similarly, the Sabeans <note>An ancient South Arabian people</note> in that same region also had their own Jupiter, whose temple was always open, and all incense had to be brought there first under penalty of death. From this, the priests took a portion according to measure. This Jupiter was called Sabin.

## Anxyrus — The One at Terracina or Buhschorn

Terracina is a small town situated by the sea, separating the Roman dominion from the Kingdom of Naples. There, the image of Jupiter was honored in the form of a beardless youth; for by this, they meant to signify that no razor had ever touched him <note>Anxyrus, or Anxur, was a local deity of the Volscians later identified with Jupiter as a youth</note>.

## Eleutherius — The Free

Many are of the opinion that this Jupiter was called *Liberator* <note>original Latin: "Liberator," meaning the Deliverer or Redeemer</note> among the Latins. He was held in particularly high honor among the Athenians because he had freed and redeemed them from the Medes <note>The Persians</note>. Likewise, the people of Plataea had a chapel, altar, and image of this Jupiter, which was erected after the Greeks were liberated from the yoke of the Medes by Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan general</note>, and sacrifices were offered to him in the middle of the city's marketplace. Half a mile from the city, the common Greeks had a marble altar and also a snow-white image of this Jupiter made from the same marble in a meadow. There, a festive game was held every year where armored riders would tilt and race to win rich jewels in memory of the victory achieved in bloody strife when they gave battle to Mardonius <note>The Persian commander at the Battle of Plataea, 479 BCE</note> in those parts with the help of the common allies.

The Greeks did the same after the victory they gained against the Macedonians, also erecting an altar to this Jupiter.

Thraseas and Seneca, the natural philosophers, offered their blood to this Jupiter when they were put to death at the command of Nero <note>The Roman historian Tacitus records that as Seneca the Younger committed suicide on Nero's orders, he sprinkled his blood on the floor as a libation to "Jupiter the Deliverer"</note>.

# The Second Book.

## Soter — The Preserver or Savior.
<note>The Greek title *Soter* means Savior or Deliverer.</note>

After Hercules had overcome the Minyans, he erected an altar to this Jupiter. Similarly, the Athenians had a temple dedicated to him in their Town Hall <note>original: "Rathauße"</note>, in the porch of which stood all manner of artistic statues and paintings. Also, Alexander the Great, when he learned that his fleet had returned from the Indian Sea <note>original: "Indischē mhor"</note> without harm, offered sacrifices to this God. Aristotle also commissioned several statues of him at the end of his life. Diocletian minted coins under this name; the engraving on one side featured a standing figure holding two lightning bolts <note>original: "strål"</note> in the right hand and a spear in the left, with the inscription: TO JUPITER THE PRESERVER <note>original Latin: "IOVI CONSERVATORI"</note>. There is also another coin where Jupiter holds a statue of Victory in his right hand and an upright spear in his left, with these words: TO JUPITER THE PRESERVER OF THE WORLD <note>original Latin: "IOVI CONSERVATORI ORBIS"</note>.

The Emperor Licinius also struck a coin which featured a naked figure on one side, though a mantle hung from its neck; it carried a spear in the left hand and a round globe in the right, upon which stood a winged figure of Victory holding a crown or wreath in its right hand and a palm branch in its left. At the feet of this Jupiter was an eagle with outstretched wings on the right side, while on the left side lay a male figure as a captive with his hands bound behind his back; upon this was the number XIV <note>likely a regnal year or mint mark</note>, and around the border: TO JUPITER THE PRESERVER <note>original Latin: "IOVI CONSERVATORI"</note>.

King Aetius, a son of Anthas, erected an altar to this Jupiter at Troezen, near the Leginus Lake by Predena. In Achaia, not far from Patras, where the city of Aegium once stood, this Jupiter had a small column <note>original: "Dhāulin," likely a diminutive of "Säule"</note> at the marketplace, along with an altar and a chapel <note>original: "cāppelin"</note>. Inside were two bronze <note>original: "öhrine," meaning brazen or made of bronze</note> statues of him: one newer and bearded, and the other, which was the older and proper one, beardless. Every year they chose a new priest, who had to be a very handsome beardless youth; however, if a beard began to grow during his term, he was removed, and another chosen one took his place. In Corone, in the open market, this Jupiter also had a bronze statue, as he did in Messene (now called Mosenichtia or Petalidia). In the harbor of Epidaurus (now Malvasia), a statue was erected to this Jupiter along with a temple that was famous far and wide; the Mantineans also had one. In Londario, which was once called Megalopolis, a beautiful temple adorned with columns was consecrated to this God. We have spoken before of the "Armor-bearer" <note>original: "Banzertrager"</note> and mentioned that he also bore this name and had a temple and statue at Thespiae; you may look for it there.

## Sosipolis — The City Guardian.
<note>The Greek *Sosipolis* translates to "Savior of the City."</note>

In Magnesia in Asia, there was a temple to this Jupiter, as can be inferred from the fact that the city, to honor the harp-player Anaxenoi, allowed him to wear this Jupiter's scarlet mantle. Otherwise, we find another legend concerning Sosipolis: that the Eleians in Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note> honored him constantly and with great devotion, serving him with great fear as if he were always present among them. In his temple, a respectable, elderly woman continuously performed her offerings, wearing a white veil that covered her head and face. The Eleians also swore all their oaths by this God. How such idol-worship began, I shall explain. It happened that the Arcadians once invaded the Eleians with a great army...

The Eleans, however, proved themselves brave; they marched out against the enemy, and as the battle-cry began, a woman appeared carrying a child in her arms. She stepped toward the Elean captains and spoke out boldly and without fear. She said that only a few hours had passed since she had brought this child into the world, and it had appeared to her in a dream that this child would be the companion and protector of the Eleans and would help them achieve victory. The captains were pleased with the matter; they took the child and placed it, entirely naked, between the two advancing armies. As the Arcadians pressed upon them with great hatred, this child suddenly turned into a serpent <note>original: "Drachen." In early modern German, "Drache" usually referred to a serpent or snake rather than the winged beast of later fantasy.</note>. The Arcadians were terrified by this, but the Eleans took heart; the former fled while the latter pursued them, thus achieving victory. Now, it seemed to the Eleans that they saw the serpent crawl into a hollow beneath the earth, and at that very spot, they built him a temple. But whether this <term>Sosipolis</term> <note>From the Greek *Sōsīpolis*, meaning "Savior of the City."</note> has anything in common with Jupiter is something a more idle person may investigate further.

## Konias — The Dusty.
<note>Derived from the Greek *konis*, meaning "dust."</note>

In Athens, this Jupiter had a temple that was not covered by a roof <note>The lack of a roof allowed dust to collect, giving the god this epithet.</note>.

## Larissæus — He of Larissa.

Near the city of Argos, in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, there was a mountain or high hill, almost surrounded by other hills, upon which this Jupiter had his temple.

## Cenæus — He of Cenaeum.

The island of Euboea is now called Negropont <note>The Venetian name for the island, used commonly until the 19th century.</note>. It has a promontory that was once called Cenaeum, now named the "Little Head" of Litar <note>likely modern Cape Lithada</note>. There, Hercules is said to have built a temple after he had conquered Oechalia and won Iole to be his wife.

## Charnon.

A temple was erected to Jupiter by this name not far from Mantinea <note>OCR reads "Mudinn," likely a corruption of *Mantinēe*.</note> in Arcadia, near the tomb of the prince Epaminondas.

## Tamynæus — He of Tamyne.

Near Athens, there lies a region called Eretria; there stood a city called Tampia, named Tamyne by others, in which Jupiter had a temple and an image.

## Aethneus — He of Mount Etna.

In Sicily, by the burning mountain once called Aetna and now called Mongibello <note>From the Latin *mons* and Arabic *jabal*, both meaning "mountain."</note>, a temple was built to this Jupiter who had overcome the Giants; from this mountain, he received his name.

## Scyllius — He of Scyllaeum.

In Candia <note>The medieval name for the island of Crete.</note>, there was a mountain called Scyllaeum. There, the Cretans also maintained the worship of Jupiter at times, from which this name comes to him. Likewise, in Egypt, at the place called Hermonthite, he was honored and kept the same name. Also at Lycorea, which some consider a city near Mount Parnassus.

# The Second Book.

Parnassus / which some call a pass in the city of Delphi / there Jupiter was also worshiped and has kept this name. Likewise, he was worshiped at Males in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula.</note> at the promontory / where the dangerous passage still is / and he held that same name there as well.

# Bel.

The Assyrians and Babylonians generally called him Bel / because *El* signifies the Sun among them / and for that reason they, along with the Phoenicians, call him *Hel* or *Bel*. In the Carthaginian language / he is said to be called *Bal* / which means as much as Saturn / or the Sun <note>original: "Sol"</note>. However, there have been many of these Bels / yet they were always understood to be in the place of Jupiter / the God whom they held to be the highest; they say he taught men star-gazing <note>original: "sternsehe" — astronomy or astrology</note>. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a Church Father.</note> says Arbelus was a man / who during his lifetime was also called God by his followers / who, along with the neighboring Assyrians, later offered sacrifices to him / and showed him divine honors. Cicero maintains that the fifth Bel / was Hercules. What Diodorus says on this matter, you may find in his own writings. 

This Bel had a temple in Babylon with bronze doors / the temple was a square measuring a quarter-mile on all sides / in the middle of it stood a tower of hard marble / six hundred feet <note>original: "schüch" — literally 'shoes,' an old measurement similar to a foot.</note> high / and just as thick / upon that same one stood another tower / and upon the second a third / and so on from the fourth up to the eighth; they were full of steps on the outside and vaulted / through which one could climb to the heights and rest. At the very bottom is a chapel / quite magnificently decorated / and a golden table upon the altar. No image is inside. This foundation had a very large income / but it was burned by Xerxes. Alexander the Great wanted to have it rebuilt. Similarly, this Jupiter had his temple and worship at Apamea in Syria. What else is written in Holy Scripture regarding this Bel / and the interpreters of the same / I will let rest for the moment / as it is common knowledge to many.

# Nemeetes — He of Nemea.

About eight miles from the harbor of Corinth in the Morea / there was once a forest and a small town by the name of Nemea / where Jupiter had a very delightful temple in a grove <note>original: "Hähnlin" — likely a diminutive of "Hain" (grove).</note> of cypress trees. At this temple, the Greeks held a game and festival every four years / with no less splendor and expense than the Olympic ones; it was contested in the same manner / as at Olympia / the prize <note>original: "danck"</note> was a wreath of celery <note>original: "Epfich" — smallage or wild celery, the traditional crown of the Nemean Games.</note>.

This festival, however, first arose as an anniversary for one who had died / in this manner. Seven Kings of the Argives / marched with armed hands to support Polynices / who had besieged his brother Eteocles in Thebes / but when they came into Thrace / they found a woman <note>original: "weyßbild" — literally 'white-figure,' an archaic term for a woman.</note> near Lemnos / they begged her to show them where they might find water to drink. The good lady, named Hypsipyle / was quite willing / and wished to lead the lords to where they would find water; so that she might be faster / she laid her foster-child / Archemorus, the son of the priest Lycurgus / down on a patch of grass / and while she showed the princes the watering hole / a serpent came, coiled around the child, and choked it. When the princes became aware of the tragedy upon their return / they killed the worm <note>In this period, "worm" often referred to snakes or dragons.</note>. Now, it had been previously prophesied by Amphiaraus / that this child would be a certain sign to the princes of this war / of their impending misfortune. Yet to comfort the good Hypsipyle / they established [the games]...

# Of Pagan Gods

Seven princes established athletic games at the place where the child <note>This refers to the infant Opheltes, whose death was seen as an omen by the Seven Against Thebes.</note> had perished, and they named them the Nemean Games. Long afterward, when Hercules hunted and killed a lion in that same place, he revived these games, improved them, and dedicated them to his father, Jupiter. At first, the judges over these games were the Deceleans, and later the Corinthians. Every three years passed, and in the fourth, these games would begin. The Argives, who provide the founder and High Priest there, announce the games and conduct everything just as the Eleans <note>The officials who managed the ancient Olympic Games.</note> do in the Olympic Games. However, the masters of the games are dressed in mourning clothes; also, before the games begin, the funeral images of many heroes and brave men who have passed away are carried about. It is also said that a lord named Molorchus had an only son whom a lion living in those parts had killed and torn to pieces. When Hercules came to him and heard the pitiful lamenting from his host, and the great grief he held for his son’s sake, he executed the lion to repay his host for his hospitality. Afterward, in memory of the deceased and of his own deed, he established these games in honor of his father.

On the twelfth day of the new moon <note>The first month of the lunar calendar.</note>, these athletic games began. If it happened, however, that these games were held in winter due to some delay, then armored riders competed on racing chariots.

### Elacataeus — He of Mount Elacateus.

In Thessaly, there was a mountain of this name, upon which Jupiter had a temple and from which he received his name.

->Mechaneus — The Craftsman.<-

In Argos, there is a workshop <note>original: "werckgaden" — a shop or place of manufacture.</note> in which the image of this Jupiter was found; and by that same image, the Argives are said to have sworn never to return home alive unless they had destroyed Troy.

->Comyrus.<-

At Halicarnassus (which is now called Messi <note>A medieval name for the region near Bodrum, Turkey.</note>), this Jupiter was honored under this name, perhaps provided with a temple there by Artemisia, the wife of Mausolus <note>Famous for building the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>.

->Bageus — The Great and Nimble.<-

In Phrygia, this Jupiter had his place of worship.

->Samnius — The Wine-Cask.<-

Aristophanes <note>The Greek comic playwright.</note> gives Jupiter this name.

->Asbamaeus — He of Asbamaea.<-

In Cappadocia, not far from the city of Tyana, this Jupiter had his temple. Nearby was a lake that produced a spring which swelled up high, yet never overflowed its banks.

->Marnas — The Virginal.<-

The people of Gaza in Syria honored this Jupiter.

->Cynethaeus — The Hunter.<-

Because he taught the Arcadians how to hunt, he was named and honored as such among them. Although the Cynethaeans were a rural people in Arcadia, they erected a nine-foot <note>original: "neünschüig" — literally nine 'shoes' tall.</note> statue to Jupiter at Olympia, which carried a lightning bolt <note>original: "straal" — literally a beam or ray, referring to the thunderbolt.</note> in each hand; perhaps Jupiter received his name from that very place.

# The Second Book

## Hicetesius — The One Beseeched
Because he is kind and, out of grace, accepts and hears the prayers of sinners, he received this name. <note>original: "Hicetesius." From the Greek 'hiketēs,' meaning a suppliant or one who comes seeking mercy.</note>

## Cosmetes — The World-Ruler
The Lacedemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> honored this Jupiter and erected a temple to him in their citadel. His image is the first to be cast from bronze, yet it is not made from a single piece; rather, each limb is made separately so they may be joined together.

## Salaminius — He of Salamis
Famagusta, a very famous city in Cyprus, was once called Salamis. Tacitus writes that Teucer came there while fleeing his father’s wrath and built a temple to Jupiter.

## Epacrius — Upon the Heights
Because temples, pillars, statues, and chapels were commonly erected to Jupiter or other gods upon the summits of mountains, he also received this name. <note>original: "Epacrius." Derived from the Greek 'akros,' meaning the highest point or peak.</note>

### Epicarpĭus — The Fruit-Giver
This Jupiter was honored on the island of Negropont. <note>The medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea.</note>

### Tharamis — The Bloodthirsty
Some claim those in Asia called him by this name because human beings were sacrificed to him. <note>Likely a reference to Taranis, a Celtic deity often associated by Roman-era writers with Jupiter and grim rituals.</note>

### Mandragoras — The Slumberer or Infuriator
The plant Mandragora <note>The mandrake root, famous in folklore for its sedative and hallucinogenic properties.</note>, as they say, induces sleep and makes a person act as if they were full of wine; for this reason, they say Jupiter has this name, because he makes people act mad.

### Abretanus — He of Abrettene
The Abrettenes, a people in Asia <note>Specifically in Mysia, Asia Minor.</note>, erected a temple to this Jupiter into which no pig was permitted to enter.

### Phaeton
The star of Jove <note>The planet Jupiter.</note> is called by this name by all astronomers.

### Elaphrius
Under this name, he was honored in Crete.

### Velsurus
In Thrace, they had a very ancient temple in a place of this name, where this Jupiter was highly honored; Cicero makes mention of this.

### Nephelegenetes — The Cloud-Gatherer
He is often called this by the poets because his star brings a certain moisture among the elements. <note>original: "Nephelegenetes." A classic Homeric epithet for Zeus as the bringer of rain and storms.</note>

### Metietes — The Wise, The Counselor, The Prudent
Under this name, the Cretans also honored him.

# On the Heathen Gods
## Ypsimedon the Overlord. <note>original: "Ypsimedon Oberherr." From the Greek 'Hypsimedon,' meaning 'ruling on high.'</note>

Because he rules and manages all things, he is named thus. From certain mountains, he also had specific names, such as from the mountain Cragus in Lycia, and Drymnos in Pamphylia <note>Regions in what is now southern Turkey.</note>. Among the Tyrians, he was called Pro-mantheus, from his power of prophesying. In other places, he was called Gyrapsius; likewise Ahor, and many other names are given to him.

->Exacesternus: The Physician.<- <note>original: "Exacesternus. Der Arzt." Likely from the Greek 'exakester,' meaning a healer or one who makes amends.</note>

Because he has the power and authority to make people healthy, he also received this name.

->Eypnos, Epipnos: The Good Inspirer, the Sleeper, or the Giver of Good Dreams.<- <note>original: "Eypnos, Epipnos, Guter inblaser/Entschlaffer/Gut träummacher." Derivatives of 'Hypnos' (sleep) and 'Epipnous' (inspired/breathing upon).</note>

It was attributed to him that he would give and breathe in good, gentle words, and likewise that he would bring forth good dreams; therefore, he had this name.

->Epyrnytius, Epistaterius, Talaos, Palinæos.<-

Exactly because he is a supervisor of all power, he has this name in Chios and Crete.

->Medineus: He of Medin.<- <note>original: "Medineus Der zu Medin." Likely a reference to a specific local cult site.</note>

The Lycians honored him by this name.

->Pallantius<-

He was honored in Pontus, at Trebizond <note>original: "Trapesond." A major city on the Black Sea coast.</note>.

->Panoptis: The All-Seeing.<- <note>original: "Panoptis Der Allding sehend." From the Greek 'Panoptes.'</note>

In Achaia <note>A region in the northern Peloponnese of Greece.</note>, this Jupiter has his temple and service.

->Epicenius: The Common One.<- <note>original: "Epicenius Der Allgmein." From 'Epikoinos,' meaning common to all.</note>

Under this name, he was honored among the Salaminians <note>The people of the island of Salamis.</note>.

## Epibemios the High-Seated. <note>original: "Epibemios Der Hochsitzend." Likely from 'Epibōmios,' meaning 'upon the altar.'</note>

On the island of Siphnos, Jupiter was honored near a tower that stands right in the middle of the island called Isambola. From that same place flows a water that moistens a beautiful pleasure garden all around it, which is full of all kinds of fruits.

->Mazeus<-

In Phrygia <note>A kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia.</note>, he was honored under this name.

->Epopsius, Epopetes, Pancrates, Panchares.<- <note>Titles meaning 'The Overseer,' 'The All-Powerful,' and 'The All-Gracious.'</note>

Thus the Athenians named and honored him, of which mention is made under other names.

->Ecelidos and Zeter.<-

He had these names in Cyprus.

->Erros and Errinis.<-

These names mean that he is a Preserver and a Redeemer.

->Euphonius, Eridemius, Thalassius, Epichrades, Maritæos, Epiclidius, Epiclopius, Palamæon.<-

These names you will find here and there, along with their worship, such as in Rhodes, Sidon, Chios, and other places; they signify much the same as was mentioned before...

# The Second Book

Previously mentioned under various other names. These pertain to a good reputation, punishments, women, deadly matters, trickery, and the like.

->Alastor: The Remorseful Conscience.<- <note>original: "Alastor. Reüchßgwissen." From the Greek *Alastor*, meaning an avenging spirit or one who does not forget.</note>

Because he punishes sin and makes a person recognize their own conscience, he was named thus.

->Forensis: He of the Marketplace.<- <note>original: "Forensis. Der vff dem Marckt." From the Latin *forum*, the public marketplace.</note>

Under this name, Jupiter was honored in many places, such as in Olympia, among the Thebans, and likewise at Lacedaemon <note>The ancient name for the city-state of Sparta.</note>. This occurred because altars, temples, and statues were erected to him in the marketplace, as town halls were commonly located in such places. Jupiter was meant to remind the councilmen how faithfully they should deliberate for the common good, respecting what is upright and fair, since they had God as a witness. Furthermore, both the buyer and the seller were reminded by this name to trade uprightly and honestly.

->Monitor: The Admonisher.<- <note>original: "Monitor. Der Ermhaner." Latin for one who warns or advises.</note>

There was an altar on Mount Parnes <note>original: "Parnetio." A mountain range in Attica, Greece.</note> among the Athenians, consecrated and held in high esteem under the name of Jupiter the Admonisher.

->Euamemius: The Fair-Blower.<- <note>original: "Euamemius. Gütblaßt." Likely a corruption of the Greek *Euanemos*, meaning "of the fair winds."</note>

Wherever the ancients wished to call upon a good wind, they offered sacrifices to this Jupiter; he also had his temple not far from Lacedaemon.

### Cuculinus: The Cuckoo. <note>original: "Cuculinus. Der Gutzgauch." From the Latin *cuculus* (cuckoo). *Gutzgauch* is an archaic German term for the bird.</note>

Not far from Hermione—which is now called Damalia in Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>—at the promontory of Scyllaeum <note>original: "Schilli."</note>, there once lay a city called Halice. It is said that Jupiter transformed himself into a cuckoo there, from which the place, the hill, and also the temple received their names. Although I was not inclined to recount every shameful fable of Jove, I cannot hide the reason why he is called "The Cuckoo" here. For they say that when Jupiter was still a youth and Juno was still a maiden, they went wandering apart from the other gods on Mount Thronax. When Jupiter saw her there alone, he fell into a passion and stirred up a storm so that all the other gods hid themselves, while Juno shut herself in a small house on the mountain. Jupiter transformed himself into a cuckoo and flew into Juno’s lap so that she would be less frightened. She took pity on it and covered it; then he revealed himself as he truly was. She resisted granting his will for fear of her mother, so he promised her marriage; they became one, and from this, the mountain received its temple and its name. See what "free" gods these are! But see also how dangerous it is to leave young maidens alone in their curiosity. Indeed, see what a free adulterer Jupiter is; for the sake of mortal women, he becomes gold, a bull, or a pig <note>The author likely means "swan," as in the myth of Leda, though the German text says "Schwein" (pig).</note>, yet to honor his own spouse, he becomes a cuckoo. A clever person will easily understand the rest.

->Ilapinastes: The Banqueter.<- <note>original: "Ilapinastes. Der Rundzecher." From the Greek *Eilapinastes*, meaning a feaster or one who provides a banquet.</note>

Cyprus has always been a house of pleasure; for this reason, the "hammer-meals" <note>An archaic term for a social feast or drinking bout.</note>, drinking circles, and similar societies and festivities were attributed to this Jupiter, as if they proceeded from him, yet in an orderly fashion.

# Of the Pagan Gods

Now, Jupiter had many of these and other surnames <note>original: "zünämmen." These are epithets or titles added to a deity's name to describe a specific function or local connection.</note>, derived from his nature, from the places where he was honored, and also due to certain events. However, though it was done without understanding and out of false delusion, the true God was nonetheless meaningfully intended under these same names. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> also says, and Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD), an early Christian author from Carthage who often critiqued Roman religion.</note> agrees with him, that there were over three hundred Jupiters who were worshipped in the world. That is to say, this was the number of names that were attributed to Jupiter. These are not all to be found today, yet few would be missing—one would still find that number of names, or even a greater one, if the space and time were available to search for them. I trust the reader will be satisfied here if I add what title the poet Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek musician and prophet; here, the author refers to the "Orphic Hymns," which early Christian scholars often cited to show glimpses of monotheism in paganism.</note> gave to him. These titles rightly belong to the true God, yet out of blindness, they were attributed by Orpheus to God's own creature. The words, translated roughly, read as follows:

> Jupiter alone encompasses all,
> What air, earth, sea, and also at once
> The high and round heaven encloses within itself,
> Yes, also what is beneath the ground.
> What is without end, what is God, immortal,
> What has been, and what shall be entirely,
> Jupiter holds all within himself,
> Beginning, middle, and end. That is he.
> The first, and so he remains. Also his gift
> Is all the wealth and property of the world.
> He is a foundation for the earth,
> A support for the heaven that shines there.
> King and source of all things,
> A single power, old and young.
> A single God, great lord,
> A royal body, and nothing more,
> Through whom is upheld and maintained
> What day, night, fire, earth, air, and mist perceive;
> In summary, what is and what shall be,
> Of this his majesty is completely full.

-> End of the second book of the Pagan Gods. <-

# The Second Book

In order that I leave nothing out that is pleasant to read, and to provide an account of the planets to the Germans (who may have a curiosity for such things), I have included them here among these gods and set down their tables. The reason for this is so that you might know in your future studies where each of these seven stars is placed and how they move according to their own shifting courses. These are called the "Wanderers" <note>original: "Schweyffer" or "Irrenden." The author is explaining the Greek etymology of the word "planet," which means "wanderer."</note>, or the "Straying Stars," or "Travelers," however you wish to name them, for this small Greek word *Planeta* gives you that meaning.

Also, for the understanding of these drafted tables, you should know that the "World" is named not only as we usually speak of it—sometimes for the time in which we speak, as in "since the world began" <note>original: "Von ye welten här."</note>. It is also not named for people alone, as when we say, "There was a great world of people there." Likewise, it is not used only in place of the ground beneath us, as when we say, "In the whole wide world." Rather, when we give the World its right name according to the understanding of its kind and nature, we mean by its naming the Earth, Water, Air, and Fire—and the circular, partitioned orbits of the seven wandering, circling stars, which the Greeks and Latins called *Planets*. Included in this also is the stiff, unmoving firmament of stars <note>The "fixed stars" which appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, unlike the planets.</note>, which is called the *Firmamentum* in Latin. Only then do we have the "Heavens," a name by which we Germans also sometimes call the Air and the circular paths of the stars—as when the air is clear and bright, we say: "It is a lovely heaven." Likewise, "The heaven is entirely blue," even though this is nothing other than the Air itself. Still, at night, seeing the stars shining, we say: "The heaven is so full of stars." Yet the true and right naming of "Heaven" points toward that place we desire to reach for eternal joy after this life. Of that place, no mention or explanation is needed here.

## Of the Earth.

Regarding the four lower circles, of which the Earth is one, much detail is not necessary, except to say that because it is the heaviest, it is the lowest part of that which the Heaven encloses. By its name, we mean not only the soil but the entire globe of the Earth with its mountains. It is entirely spherical <note>original: "syn wäll," meaning circular or globular.</note>. This can be gathered from the fact that the sun rises later in some places than in others, which is primarily proven by eclipses. For instance: those in the East may see an eclipse of the moon at four o'clock in the night, while those toward the West <note>original: "Nidergang," literally "the going down" of the sun.</note> see it at two o'clock. For roughly every hundred and twenty miles from East to West, the sunlight varies by one hour. This same thing is found from North to South; for the further North <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally "midnight," a common German term for North.</note> you travel, the higher the "Seven Stars" <note>Likely referring to the Big Dipper or the Pleiades, used to judge latitude.</note> appear to you; but the further you turn toward the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally "midday," the term for South.</note>, the lower and more invisible they become to you.

If you were to say it is not spherical because of the many mountains and valleys, or because certain curves of the sea go into it, then consider the vast, encompassing width of the Earth compared to such things; one can see that they amount to nothing, or at least very little.

Take this example: if you have a ball that is not perfectly polished and smooth, but has some corners or bumps, and you stand twenty, thirty, or forty paces away from it, you will not notice its unevenness, but will see it as a sphere. Furthermore, if the Earth were not spherical, the sun and stars would cast shadows at the moment they rise that would be the same as the shadows at noon—which is not the case.

If you say the Earth is round, then the sun in its rising would not follow the surface...

<meta>catchword: appear</meta>

...appear, but rather like an arc; this happens at once and is indeed so. However, the immense distance, because of which we cannot see its full appearance as it extends outward, prevents us from perceiving that shape.

The Earth's weight is so great that it falls toward its own center and heaps itself together; because it is then constrained within the circular paths of the other spheres <term>seinwälle</term> <note>literally "round-waves" or "spheres," referring to the celestial orbs</note>, it must become spherical. It is also situated in the middle of the world; compared to the immovable circle of the stars, it is like a tiny dot in the center of a spherical field. For if you were to place it in any other spot—toward the East, West, South, or North—the result would be that the Sun and Moon would rise unevenly, appearing perhaps at midday or not until midnight.

The Earth is also immovable; because of its weight, it cannot move upward, nor can it sink any lower than it already is. If it were to shift to the sides, as we have said, the stars would not be able to show us a reliable or certain path. Alfraganus <note>Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works were foundational in medieval Europe.</note> and Archimedes almost agree in their calculations that the circumference of the earth is six thousand three hundred of our German miles, or thirty-one thousand five hundred Italian <note>original: "welscher," a term used for Southern/Romanic foreign lands, particularly Italy.</note> miles. In this calculation, one thousand steps make one Italian mile, and five feet make one step. In the heavens, three hundred and sixty degrees <note>original: "stapfflen," literally "little steps."</note> are counted, each one representing eighteen and a half German miles, or eighty-seven and a half Italian miles. The thickness <note>The diameter.</note> of the Earth comes to two thousand German miles; that is, from the place where we stand, straight through to the place directly beneath our feet.

## Of the Water.

The sphere or roundness of the Water follows the roundness of the Earth. The reason is that although water is heavy, it is not as heavy as the Earth; thus, it lays itself upon the earth, surrounds it, and forms a circle, as can be observed. If you sit in a ship on the sea and set your eyes on a target in the distance while you are standing at the bottom of the mast, and you sail part of the way toward it, you will see such markers less and less the further you go. However, if you climb up to the crow's nest <note>original: "mastkorb," the basket at the top of the mast.</note>, you can see it a bit longer. From this, it is easy to note that the water is round. If your journey is toward the North, you will always see the "Wagon" <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major, commonly called the "Himmelswagen" (Heavenly Wagon) in German-speaking lands.</note> standing higher the further you travel toward Midnight <note>North.</note>.

I will not hide from you that some consider the Earth and Water to make a single sphere or globe, so that the previous measurement remains the same. But the water or the sea is mobile in its roundness, as one clearly sees and feels by the fact that it has its tide every six hours, flowing in and out.

## Of the Air.

Since the Earth and Water make a sphere, the Air that surrounds them both must also be spherical and round. The Air is mobile and also has its rotation along with the revolving heavens. This can be seen when "peacock tails" <note>An old term for atmospheric phenomena, possibly comets, meteors, or the Aurora Borealis, which appeared to fan out like a peacock's tail.</note> and similar fires ignite in the air and are whirled around, just as is seen with the stars at certain hours, appearing now in this place and then in another.

This is measured against the [...] because the Air fills everything [...] Fire, if it did not have its vastness, would consume everything.

### The Second Book
# Concerning Fire

Some contend that Fire and Air form a single sphere together; however, it is certain that Fire must also be <term>globular</term><note>original: "synwell," meaning perfectly round or spherical</note> in its own right. Due to its lightness, it constantly seeks to rise upward; however, it cannot pass beyond the sphere of the Moon, which is also globular. Below, it is driven by the Air to all places, so that it must remain enclosed within its own sphere. This is easily understood in relation to the other elements because Air fills everything, leaving no void, and if Fire did not have its assigned space, it would consume and destroy everything.

### Description of the Seven Circular Wandering Stars

<image-desc>A cosmological diagram consisting of seven concentric semi-circular arcs representing the celestial spheres of the planets. Each arc is labeled with a traditional astrological symbol. From the outermost arc to the innermost, the symbols are: Saturn (♄), Jupiter (♃), Mars (♂), Sun (☉), Venus (♀), Mercury (☿), and the Moon (☾). Below the moon's arc at the center of the diagram is a circle representing the Earth.</image-desc>

You should not think that these seven wandering or "erring" stars <note>In the 16th century, "planets" were called "wandering stars" because they moved against the background of the fixed stars.</note> move by themselves; rather, it is their <term>celestial spheres</term><note>original: "gezürck der whände," literally the "circle of the walls."</note> that turn, while the stars themselves are fixed and firmly attached in their places. Furthermore, these stars are in themselves nothing other than a thicker and more compressed part of each respective sphere. The rest of the sphere is otherwise invisible due to its thinness, but the star becomes visible at that specific point where the material is most thick and tightly gathered.

## Saturn

Among this number, Saturn is the highest and first. He is a daily, masculine star who is excessively cold and dry. His <term>houses</term><note>The zodiac signs where a planet is most "at home."</note> are Capricorn and Aquarius; his <term>exaltation</term><note>The sign where the planet's influence is most powerful.</note> is Libra at the twentieth degree; his <term>fall</term><note>The sign where the planet's influence is weakened.</note> is Aries. He rules the element of Fire by day in Sagittarius. He is the <term>master of Air</term><note>The ruler of the Air triplicity.</note> by day in Gemini and by night in Libra. His <term>terms</term><note>original: "sätz," referring to specific degrees within a sign assigned to a planet.</note> are the second step in Virgo and Pisces, the fourth in Cancer and Capricorn, the fifth in Aries, Taurus, Sagittarius, and Aquarius, the sixth in Gemini, Scorpio, and Libra, and also the seventh in Leo. He has his first <term>aspect</term><note>original: "anplick," referring to the geometric angles between planets.</note> in Leo and Pisces, the second in Libra, and the third in Taurus and Sagittarius. His "joy" is in Aquarius and also in the twelfth house. His friends are Jupiter and the Sun, along with the <term>Dragon's Tail</term><note>The South Node of the Moon, associated in some traditions with Saturnian energy.</note>; his enemies, however, are Mars and Mercury. His appearance is stronger when rising than when setting. In the sixth sign he stands against the Sun, and in the eighth against the Moon; you have a table of his effects [elsewhere].

## Jupiter

The second after Saturn is Jupiter. His powers and effects regarding births, weather, and other matters follow on the reverse side of this page.

# Of the Heathen Gods

Jupiter is also a diurnal <note>meaning active during the day</note> star, warm and moist. His houses <note>original: "behausung" – the zodiac signs where a planet is most "at home"</note> are Sagittarius and Pisces. His exaltation is Cancer in the fifteenth degree <note>original: "stapfflen" – literally "steps," referring to the degrees of the zodiac</note>; his fall <note>the sign where the planet's influence is weakest</note> is also the fifteenth degree in Capricorn. He rules over the fire signs by day in Leo, and over the Earthly signs by day and night in Aquarius. His terms <note>original: "sätz" – specific subdivisions of a zodiac sign ruled by a planet</note> are in the fourth degree of Virgo and Pisces; in the fifth of Scorpio and Sagittarius; in the sixth of Aries, Gemini, and Leo; in the seventh of Cancer, Libra, Capricorn, and Aquarius; and in the eighth of Taurus. His joy <note>a sign where a planet's nature is particularly well-suited</note> is in Sagittarius and the eleventh house. His first aspect <note>original: "anblick" – how a planet "looks" at others or specific degrees</note> is in the tenth degree of Gemini and Capricorn, the second in Leo and Pisces, and the third in Sagittarius. His friends are all other planets except for Mars. He also has the Dragon’s Head <note>term: Dragon's Head (the North Node of the moon, usually considered beneficial)</note> as a friend, while the Dragon's tail <note>the South Node, usually considered malefic</note> is his enemy. His light is stronger at rising than at setting. In the fifth sign he stands against the Sun, and in the ninth against the Moon.

## Mars

The third planet, Mars, is a masculine yet nocturnal star, hot and dry. His houses are Aries and Scorpio. His exaltation is the twentieth degree of Capricorn, and the twentieth degree of Cancer is his fall. Over the Earthly signs he rules by day and night in Capricorn, Aquarius, and Scorpio, and by night in Cancer. His terms are in the second degree of Libra, in the third of Taurus, in the fourth of Sagittarius and Capricorn, in the fifth of Aries and Aquarius, in the sixth of Leo and Scorpio, in the seventh of Libra, Cancer, and Virgo, and in the ninth of Pisces. His first aspect is in the tenth degree of Aries and Scorpio, the second in Gemini and Capricorn, and the third in Leo and Pisces. He has his joy in Scorpio and the sixth house. His friend is Mercury; otherwise all others hate him, even more so than Jupiter and the Sun. The Dragon’s Head is also not favorable to him, whereas the tail is his friend. At rising he is somewhat more powerful than at setting. In the fourth sign he stands against the Sun, and in the tenth against the Moon. Regarding his effects, you have a specific table.

## Sol (The Sun)

This is a hot, parching <note>original: "dōriendes"</note> diurnal light; his house is Leo. The nineteenth degree of Aries is his exaltation, and Libra, in that same degree, is his fall. Over the fire signs he rules by day in Aries and by night in Leo. His terms are Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn. The first aspect is in the tenth degree of Virgo, the second in Aries and Scorpio, and the third in Gemini and Capricorn. He has his joy in Leo and the ninth house. Jupiter and Venus are his friends; his enemies are Mercury and the Moon, and also the Dragon’s tail. The table of his powers you will find in other places.

## Venus

This is a feminine nocturnal star of warm moisture. She has her house in Taurus and Libra; her exaltation is in the twenty-first degree of Pisces; her fall is in Virgo. Over earthly things she rules by day in Taurus; over watery things by day in Cancer and by night in Scorpio. Her terms

### ->Mercurius.<-

☿ This one is at times feminine and then masculine; now moist and then dry; active by day and by night; he is valued for his radiance. ### ->Luna.<-

☽ This is a feminine, nocturnal, moist light, yet one warmed somewhat by foreign heat <note>a reference to the Moon reflecting the Sun's light</note>; her house is ♋ Cancer; her exaltation is the third degree of Taurus; and her fall is in Scorpio. In the third sign she stands against Mercury. You have her table in its place. 

Now, these celestial spheres <note>original: "syrwält" – likely referring to the *sphaera* or the "ornamental world" of the planetary orbs</note> of the planets turn themselves about and are moved from the West <note>original: "Niedergang"</note> toward the East <note>original: "Offgang"</note>, contrary to the first movable rotation <note>term: Primum Mobile (the outermost sphere that moves all others from East to West daily)</note> which, as we shall say in its place, runs from East to West. That they—namely the five which are called planets excluding the Sun and Moon—steer themselves from West to East is found in this: that the other stars, in their course and whirling, always maintain a steady position and form, while these change themselves continually, standing now near, then far from this or that star. And because it would be unseemly for the stars to fly about as a bird flies, one must note that the globe or celestial sphere is driven around for that reason. Thus one sees clearly that each of the wandering stars <note>the literal meaning of "planets"</note>, the faster and longer it runs its course, always nears the West even more.

# Of the Heathen Gods
<note>The "heathen gods" refer to the planets, which bear the names of Roman deities.</note>

They are, as it is said, "burnt" <note>term: combustion (when a planet is so close to the Sun that its influence is hidden or weakened)</note> when they are closer than fifteen degrees <note>original: "stapfflen" – literally "steps," referring to degrees of the zodiac</note> to the Sun; they are entirely suppressed when they run within twelve degrees of the Sun. If a planet runs alone and is not joined to any other planet, it is "void" <note>original: "lhår" – likely "leer" (empty); in astrology, "void of course" means the planet makes no aspects before leaving its sign</note>. They are "in appearance," however, when they show their own course and that of other stars by night or day. They are entirely "enclosed" and "besieged" <note>term: besiege (when a planet is positioned between two "malefics" or harmful planets like Mars and Saturn)</note> when they come between two contrary or evil planets. Sometimes they move toward one another, throwing their rays <note>original: "stroūmē" – streams or beams of light</note> at one another; sometimes they are separated by several degrees, as far as their rays can reach. Occasionally, one will not yield its power to the other, as when three of them come into one sign, and the strongest one—who weaves his light between them—does not let the others draw closer until he has passed them both. It also happens at times that they transfer their light from the superior <note>the slower, outer planets</note> to the inferior <note>the faster, inner planets</note>; then, when two join as one, they take the light from others and press it against someone else. Thus, it is common that one leaves his nature to the other when he enters the other's own house and sign; indeed, they receive one another in this way. Sometimes the higher planet gives his light to the lower one who is burnt by the Sun, bringing it back to him along with his power.

The "aspects" <note>original: "gegen schein" – literally "counter-shining"</note> of these planets are simply a coming-together found within one sign, at a specific degree, and even down to a minute fraction. There are five such aspects, which are recorded as follows:

* <image-desc>Sextile symbol (asterisk)</image-desc> The sextile aspect <note>original: "gezenglanz"</note> of the sixth corner is moderately good and signifies some friendship between them.
□ <image-desc>Square symbol (quadrature)</image-desc> The square aspect signifies malice and enmity between them.
△ <image-desc>Triangle symbol (trine)</image-desc> The triangular aspect is very good and lucky, bringing them friendship.
☍ <image-desc>Opposition symbol</image-desc> Direct opposition, where they stand in a straight line facing one another's light; entirely evil, hostile, and unlucky.
☌ <image-desc>Conjunction symbol</image-desc> This sign is otherwise used for the "New" <note>the New Moon</note>, but here it signifies a coming-together of the planets.

These wandering stars <note>planets</note> are also assigned to man and his limbs <note>term: melothesia (the mapping of zodiac signs or planets to parts of the human body)</note>:
> **Saturn:** Right ear. Bladder. Bones. Phlegm. Spleen. Cartilage. Eyelids.
> **Jupiter:** Lungs. Windpipe. Seed <note>semen</note>. Sense of touch. Arteries.
> **Mars:** Left ear. Kidneys. Genitals.
> **Sun:** Sight. Brain. Heart. Pulse-vein of the right side.
> **Venus:** Liver. Flesh. Sense of smell.
> **Mercury:** Mind. Speech. Tongue. Reason. Gall. The seat <note>rectum/anus</note>. Fingers.
> **Moon:** Neck. Throat. Stomach. Belly. Womb. Left side. Hips.

## The third book.

Since I have now collected the surnames and naming of Jupiter—as far as time has allowed—and since Juno is named after him as his spouse, because the star <note>The planet Jupiter</note> is assigned to her, and the air has much in common with the inclination of Jupiter, I will now begin to speak of her. First, I will describe her surnames, and thereafter I shall describe in what form or image she was presented to the fools <note>original: "toretchen" – a diminutive of "fools," referring to the unlearned who worshiped idols</note>.

# Of the Heathen Gods: Juno.
<meta>catchword: that otherwise</meta>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the goddess Juno. She stands upon a pedestal, crowned with lilies and holding a long scepter in her right hand. She is bare-chested but partially draped in a transparent veil. Behind her head is a prominent rainbow. To her left is a peacock, and a lion's skin lies at her feet. The base of the platform depicts two additional peacocks in profile.</image-desc>

She was painted as a fine, lovely, well-statured woman sitting upon a costly throne; she carried a scepter in her right hand, and a rainbow stood above her head. At her feet, she had two peacocks; she wore a crown of lilies <note>original: "Gilgen" – an archaic German term for lilies</note>, and in her left hand, she held a pair of shears <note>associated with her role as a midwife</note>. A lion’s skin lay beneath her feet. She also wore beautiful boots, along with a lovely small veil that hung down from her head and covered her private parts; otherwise, she was bare. By this, the ancients wished to show that the air preserves the human form and its abilities in a vigorous and long-lasting state; and furthermore, because nothing on earth can live without the air, she holds the royal staff and the lily-crown to signify this pleasant power. The shears signified that she came to the aid of those giving birth, for with the respite and relief provided by the air, women in labor find recovery. The rainbow signifies the many colors with which the air changes according to the weather, and the peacocks signify that they signal these same changes with their cries.

## Hera, the Air, or the Beloved.

Because the fire heats the air, the ancients said that Jupiter and Juno were a married couple. They created a poem stating that Jupiter bound her with golden chains and hung iron anvils from her. This was to show that no matter how close the air is to the fire, it nonetheless is mixed below it <note>original: "nidiſch," likely a variant of "niedrig," meaning lower in the elemental hierarchy</note> with the two elements of water and earth, both of which are quite heavy compared to the upper air.
   Some claim that Hera was otherwise called Hecate, meaning the beloved or the gracious, because she was held in such high esteem by Jupiter. There are also those who believe she is called Hera as a name for "holy," because she is a protectress of marriage, which is a holy thing. The festivals of the Heraea were held for her at Argos, which are otherwise called the Hecatomb <note>original: "Hecatombe" – a great public sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen</note>.

## Lucina, Lucetia: The Light-bringer.

The ancient people and gods assigned eyebrows and eyelids to Juno; and because the eyes are shielded and protected by them, she retained the name of the "Light-bringer." Or, it may be because she shines above the earth and assists the conceived fruit <note>the fetus</note> until it comes into the light. Plinius <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> believes she received the name from her grove, which is called *Lucus*, where she was first honored. The image of this Lucina was once struck upon the coins of Faustina, the daughter of Antonius <note>Antoninus Pius</note>. It shows the image of a respectable woman dressed in a gown <note>original: "schauben" – a fur-trimmed robe or mantle worn by the upper classes</note> and covered with a cloak, holding a bowl in her right hand and a spear in her left, with this inscription: **TO JUNO LUCINA** <note>original Latin: "IVNONI LVCINAE"</note>.
   In Rome, she had a temple where the Church of St. Lawrence in Lucina now stands; her feast was held every month, on the first day of each month.
   In Athens, she also had a chapel, though under the name that she was not Juno herself, but rather her daughter, brought there from the land of the Muscovites or Tartary <note>referring to regions of modern Russia and Central Asia</note>. Her images always wore clothes reaching down to the soles of her feet.

The people of Aegium had her image made of wood, covered with a cloak down to the feet, though the face was of stone, as were the hands and feet where they were visible; the image held one hand raised, and in the other, she held a burning torch, to signify that the pains of childbirth <note>original: "kindßwhe" (Kindeswehe)</note> heat one no differently than a burning fire. In *Argos*, in *Boura* (not far from *Athens*), in *Kleitor* in *Arcadia*, and in *Hermione* (now called *Damala*), she also had a temple where no man was permitted to look upon her image. At the very top of Mount *Cronius*, where they kept all their treasure, they also had a temple to this *Lucina*, whom they named *Olympia*. In *Pellene* in *Achaia* and in *Tegea*, they also erected her temples and altars.

## Egeria the Bringer-Forth.

Festus says that she was honored under this name as one who was helpful to women in labor to cast out or bring forth <note>original: "fürzůbringē"</note> the fruit of the womb.

## Iuga the Joined.

Just as a yoke joins two animals together, so the "yoke of marriage" was called *Coniugium* <note>Latin: "marriage" or "joining"</note> by the ancients. From this, she retained the name, as if she presided over marriage. For this reason, there is still a street in *Rome* once called the "Yoke-Way" <note>The *Vicus Iugarius*</note>, because a specific temple of *Juno* under this name was located there; it was likely in the district where our Lady of Consolation, or *St. Maria de Consolatione*, now stands.

The Greeks called her *Zygia* or *Zygiam* <note>Greek: "The Yoker"</note>, as she who joins the wife to the husband in a yoke.

## Gamelia the Nuptial.

The Greeks gave her this name, and those who were entering into marriage offered sacrifices to her. It is said that King *Cecrops* was the first to establish this in *Athens*, and he also dedicated the month of January to her under this name <note>Referring to the Greek month *Gamelion*, which overlaps with January</note>.

## Teleia the Established.

Mount *Cithaeron* is located in *Boeotia*, and upon it was built a city called *Plataea*; there, this *Juno* had a particularly beautiful foundation and was called "the Established" <note>original: "Gstandne" – likely translating the Greek *Teleia*, meaning "The Mature" or "The Perfected," referring to a married woman</note>. Her image was of a singular size, and the entire temple was remarkably appointed in its architecture and decoration, being almost entirely adorned with marble. At *Londario*, which was *Megalopolis*, she also had a temple.

They say that *Temenus*, a son of *Pelasgus*, raised this *Juno* while he ruled near *Stymphalus*, and he erected three temples to this goddess under the names of the Maiden, the Established <note>The Wife</note>, and the Widow.

## Iterduca and Domiduca: The Way-Leader and Home-Leader.

Martianus Capella names her thus because, in her name, daughters are led to the bridegroom and into his house.
