# Of Heathen Gods

## Unxia, the Anointer.

The ancient custom of the Romans was that when the bride arrived at the groom's house, she anointed the doorposts with fat <note>original: "schmeer" (lard or grease)</note>. From this, the goddess retained this name. Some say she used oil, and others say wolf's fat. However, it was only anointed once.

## Cinxia, the Girder.

This name of hers was observed and honored with great devotion, for the custom was that the groom would not ungird <note>To unfasten the bridal belt or girdle</note> the bride until he wished to lie down with her.

## Socigena, the Companion-Maker.

Because Juno brought the groom and bride into companionship and fellowship, Martianus <note>Martianus Capella, a late Roman author whose work on mythology was popular in the Middle Ages</note> gave her this name.

## Populona, the Communal.

As the "common people," Juno is honored under this name because nations <note>original: "völcker" (peoples)</note> spring from marriage. It might perhaps not be so far-fetched if one considered the area around Piombino, where Jupiter had his sanctuary at Populonia; Juno was also honored there and took her name from that place.

## Magna, the Great.

In Amandiacha—that is an island sometimes called Samothrace, about four miles long and wide—they say this Juno was born and raised. She also had an ancient temple there, which the shipmates of the Argo <note>The Argonauts</note> built, and they brought the image of this goddess there from Argos. At the spot where she was said to have been born, there was also a thicket of wild vines. Her image was carved by Smilides of Aegina, a contemporary of Daedalus.

Ovid says she had a peacock which was held in great honor for a long time and nested in a tree beneath the Esquiline Hill. She is also called Maxima <note>The Greatest</note>, Bona <note>The Good</note>, and Domina <note>The Mistress/Lady</note>, and is addressed by other names by Virgil.

## Regina, the Queen.

Juno had a temple in Rome on the Aventine Hill, which was established and endowed by Camillus <note>Marcus Furius Camillus, a Roman general and statesman</note> from the spoils he captured at Veii (where Martignano now stands). Livy writes of this as follows: When all the worldly goods were bagged and plundered, they turned to the robbing of the temples. The treasures of the gods were taken away along with their images, though this was more like a respectful relocation than a hostile robbery. From the bright crowd, brave youths were chosen who, having been cleanly bathed and dressed in white, were required to carry Juno, called "The Queen," to Rome. When they entered the temple with devotion, they approached the image with fear, for previously none but the hands of the priests were permitted to touch it. Afterward, growing bold—as if they were possessed by the spirit or moved by a soldierly daring—they said: "Juno, do you wish to go with us to Rome?" Soon <note>original: "Bald" (the catchword for the following page)</note> the others said she had nodded her head and said yes, and all Rome shouted for joy. Thus...

She was placed unharmed on the Aventine Hill <note>One of the seven hills of Rome</note>, where the founder Camillus <note>Marcus Furius Camillus, the Roman general who conquered Veii</note> had vowed her to remain in her eternal dwelling. When Cnaeus Flaminius <note>Likely Gaius Flaminius, 3rd century BCE</note> waged war against the people of Piedmont <note>Northern Italians; original: "Pemontefer"</note>, he vowed and established a temple to this Juno on the Capitoline. At Ardea—which has kept its name—located about two miles from Rome, this Juno was also honored; Marcus Ludius <note>A Roman painter mentioned by Pliny the Elder</note> painted her temple there.

## Moneta &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Admonisher.

As all things pass away, so it has happened with Rome; yet the fallen buildings lying in heaps still give witness to the beauty and power of this old city. Indeed, even in its ashes <note>original: "gnist" (sparks or embers)</note>, it is somewhat more lovely than other cities in all their splendor and built-up state. There, below the Capitoline, stands a Town Hall <note>The Palazzo dei Conservatori</note> where the *Conservatores* <note>City magistrates of Rome</note> are stationed. This building has been opened and decorated by many Popes, painted through and made quite pleasant. Some believe that the temple of this Juno was once located there, or perhaps in the gardens just behind it. Livy says that Lucius Furius <note>Lucius Furius Camillus, son of the great Camillus</note>, while leading an army against the Aurunci <note>An ancient Italian tribe</note> because they were raiding the Romans, vowed a temple to this Juno during the heat of battle and had to build it after the victory. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says that when the Romans were short of money during the war they waged with King Pyrrhus and the Tarentines, they called upon Juno for advice on what to do. She is said to have answered them: If they fought uprightly and honorably without any deceit, they would have no need to worry about money. When this came to pass, they erected this temple to her and kept all the coins they minted within it. Some say that great earthquakes <note>original: "Erdpidem"</note> occurred in the city at one time, and while many in great terror did not know what to sacrifice or which God to appease so that the earthquakes would cease, a voice was heard from the citadel <note>the Arx</note>: They should sacrifice a pregnant sow <note>original: "schweinsmütter"</note> to Juno. This was done and it helped; therefore, a temple was built at the place where this voice was heard. In this temple, the linen cloths <note>The *Libri Lintei*, ancient Roman records of prophecies and magistrates</note> were kept, in which the prophecies of the Romans were written.

## Sospita &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Preserver.

This Juno had a temple in Rome on the Palatine Hill <note>The most central of the seven hills</note>; no concubine <note>original: "kebsweiß"</note> was allowed to touch her altar. At Lanuvium, which is located about two miles from Rome, this Juno was held in especially high honor. Her image was clothed in a goatskin, she held a small spear and a small shield, and wore pointed shoes <note>original: "gschnåblet schůch"; likely the *calceoli repandi* seen in Roman art</note>. The people of Lanuvium were admitted to Roman citizenship, but with the condition that the sanctuary <note>original: "stifft"</note> of this Juno, along with its banners <note>original: "Phånlin"</note>, should also be common to the Romans. Not far from this temple lay a dragon in a cave, which a maiden fed with her own hands.

By the Capitoline in Rome, and not far from it, there is a street called *Monicanaria* <note>Likely the Vicus Canarius or "Dog Street"</note>; on that same street, this Juno had a temple, which people

## Novella: The Newness or the Calendarer.

She is also otherwise called the Calendarer <note>original: *Calenderin*</note>, for she was always called upon by the priests on the first day of the coming month. Previously, the Laurentines <note>the ancient inhabitants of Laurentum in Latium</note> held their usual appointed holidays and sacrifices to her. And because we have come to this topic, we wish to speak here of the word "Calendar," which is common yet not so well understood. The little word *Calo* <note>Latin: *calo*</note> means "I call," and although it is a Greek word <note>$\kappa\alpha\lambda\tilde\omega$ (*kalō*)</note>, it was known among the Latins.

Now, the Romans liked to keep their holidays—which they established for every idol—secret from the common people. For this reason, Romulus established a special Council House for this purpose on the Capitoline Hill; it was called the Calaber Court <note>Latin: *Curia Calabra*</note>. To that place, the High Priest, the King’s Chaplain, or the Choir King <term>Chorkönig: a translation of the Latin *Rex Sacrorum*, a priest who carried out the religious duties formerly held by the kings</term> was sent once he had observed on which day of the month the moon would be new. When he had then made this known to the other priests, the King, and the Choir King, they offered sacrifices, and the High Priest called the people together in the aforementioned Calling Court, or *Calabra*, and announced to them how many days lay between then and the Nones. These Nones <note>one of the three specific marker days of the Roman month</note> were named such because after they passed, there were always nine days remaining until the Ides; *Novem* means nine, or *Nonus* the ninth. 

Commonly, there were either seven or five days between the first day of the month—which they called the Kalends <note>original: *Calendas*</note>—and the Nones. If five days fell in between, the priest shouted "I call" <note>original: *Calo* or *καλῶ*</note> five times; but if seven fell in between, he shouted the same seven times. Then the people knew when they should return to hear what holidays, sacrifices, feast days, or workdays were scheduled for that month. 

Now it happened that the moon usually became new on the thirteenth or the fifteenth of the month; then the first day was added to the past month and called the Kalends, which was then the first of the beginning month. Afterward, in March, May, July <note>original: *Newmonat*</note>, and October <note>original: *Wynmonat*, literally "Wine month"</note>—each of which has thirty-one days—they counted five days until the sixth day, which was called the Nones. From that day, there were seven more days until the Ides, or the new moon <note>The author here associates the Ides with the "new" moon, though historically it usually marked the full moon</note>. Thus, the Kalends counts as one day, five days in between, then the Nones, then seven more after that; add them to the Ides and you find fifteen days. Following this, in the aforementioned months, they counted sixteen days afterward, which they named according to the following month. For example, in March, on the day after the Ides, they said: "the seventeenth Kalends of April," "the sixteenth Kalends of April," thus counting backward until the thirty-first. Where they otherwise would have said "two Kalends," they said *Pridie Calendas*, which means "on the day before the Kalends." They also used this little word *Pridie* <note>Latin: the day before</note> on the day immediately before the Nones and the Ides, saying *Pridie Nonarum*, *Pridie Idus*, *Pridie Calendarum*. Therefore, you must always understand that when you say the eighteenth Kalends, seventeenth Kalends, or sixteenth Kalends, it refers not to the month you are currently in, but to the following one—though you count the days of the month you are in. For example, if you write "on the seventeenth Kalends of April," it signifies that you have dated your document on the sixteenth day of March. Now, this calculation also ends in the months that likewise have thirty-one days, such as in Janu-

# The Third Book.

...January, August, and December <note>original: *Christmonat*, literally "Christ-month"</note>. In April, June <note>original: *Brachmonat*, the "fallow month"</note>, September <note>original: *Herbstmonat*, the "harvest month"</note>, and November <note>original: *Wintermonat*</note>, there are only thirty days. In February <note>original: *Hornung*, a name referring to the "shedding of horns" or the month's brevity</note>, which in common years has only twenty-eight, it has one more in a leap year, namely twenty-nine. Regarding the reasons for these changes, I do not think it good to remain silent.

First, the year was strangely divided among the ancients. The Egyptians divided it into four months; the Arcadians into three months; the Acarnanians into six months; and the Italians into thirteen months, which contained three hundred and forty-seven days. However, Romulus, at the beginning of his reign, also wished to properly order the year. Therefore, he took every day on which the new moon could be seen as the first day of the month. But because—due to the moon’s orbit— the new moon might appear somewhat earlier or later, he had to give the preceding month more or fewer days, depending on when the new moon was discovered. Thus, it happened that these months were unequal in their days. Now, Romulus made the year only ten months long, giving six of them thirty days each, and the remaining four thirty-one days each. This brought the total to three hundred and four days. Because of this, it soon became obvious that the moon’s orbit did not agree with this number of days. Consequently, they wished to have twelve months, and King Numa added fifty-one days; to this, they took one day from each thirty-one-day month (which was six days), and thus brought together fifty-seven days. These they divided into two months, giving one twenty-nine days and the other twenty-eight. They brought the year to twelve months and three hundred and fifty-five days. Thus, the Romans had one day more than the Greeks. This odd-numbered day they gave to January, because they held the odd number to be the most holy, and January was dedicated to the heavenly gods. 

For where the Greeks had ordered their year into three hundred and fifty-four days, they could not align it with the sun’s course, for they were still short eleven days and six hours annually. They took these eleven days and six hours from each year, which in eight years amounted to three months of ninety days, so that each month had thirty days. They added those same three months to the ninth year, which was their leap year, and it had four hundred and forty-four days. These days they called <term>ὑπερβάλλοντας</term> <note>original: *Hyperfalontas*, from Greek *hyperballontes* meaning "exceeding" or "added"</note>, that is, the "adorned-on" days; but the months they called <term>ἐμβολίσμους</term> <note>original: *Embolismos*, meaning "intercalary" or "inserted"</note>, that is, the "inserted" months.

When the Romans tried to follow the Greeks in this, they failed; they were off by eight days because they had given January the odd day (as said above) within the three hundred and fifty-five days and had not accounted for it. Thus, they had to intercalate so many days into the ninety days over twenty-four years that it amounted to one hundred and fourteen days. From this, it often happened that the months which were intended for summer fell in the winter. When the matter still would not succeed, they went further and gave their priests the power to mix in the leap days. These same priests allowed themselves to be bribed with money by the usurers and money-changers, announcing the leap days according to their own will, so that they might favor the rich usurers by shortening the deadlines for payments. Thus, the matter remained just as broken as before.

At the time when Gaius Julius Caesar came to Egypt—as he was otherwise a very subtle-minded man—he also learned how the sun’s course does not complete its designated circle in the heavens in less than three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours. Upon his return to Rome, he distributed the year thusly:

->**Of Heathen Gods**<-
15 A.

He gave to January, August, and December <note>original: *Jenner, Augst, Christmonat*</note> two additional days each. To April, June, September, and November <note>original: *Brach, Herpst, Wintermonat*</note>, he gave one day each. The others he left unchanged, except that every four years, an extra day should be intercalated <note>inserted into the calendar</note>. This day was to be attached to February <note>original: *Hornung*</note>, which previously had only twenty-eight days, during the bissextile <note>original: *Bissextili*, from the Latin for 'twice sixth,' referring to the way the leap day was counted</note>, which is the leap year. However, that same day was to always be inserted before the last five days of February as a memorial, because the ancients were accustomed to adding their extra days there, as in their year this month was the last and was treated as if it were discarded <note>In the oldest Roman calendars, the year ended in February rather than December</note>. Although Caesar achieved this with great effort, he first had to intercalate ninety days to fix the existing errors, making one year fifteen months long.

Once he had brought the year into this order and ensured that the leap day should always be set after the passing of the fourth year, he had this division proclaimed throughout the world, and everyone was well satisfied with it. But just as he had it announced, he was stabbed to death. Because of this, the priests <note>the *pontifices*, who oversaw the Roman calendar</note> immediately made another error: they did not let the fourth year finish, but instead inserted the leap day at the beginning of the fourth year. Thus, in thirty-six years, twelve days were intercalated where only nine should have been. When Emperor Augustus realized this, he forbade including any leap day for the following twelve years; and when that period of maintenance had passed, he brought the cycle into its correct course. And so that what was to be done would not be forgotten, he had it engraved in bronze tables for eternal memory.

It would perhaps not be out of place for us to set down the entire year here, just as it was determined in days and months by Julius Caesar. However, I wish to warn the reader that for the first six months, I have included the festivals and the specific rising, setting, and weather of the stars as they were recently discovered in Rome. But because the remaining six months did not have such additions in my source, I have added from other writers what seemed most prominent to me. The first number signifies the lunar cycle <note>the Golden Number used to track the moon's phases</note>; the second number is the day of the month; the seven letters represent the Sunday letters; and the third number provides the countdown to the Nones, Ides, and Kalends <note>the three marker days of the Roman month</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific festival calendar of December to a historical and mythological explanation of the Roman months. It details the transition from the ten-month calendar of Romulus to the twelve-month lunar calendar established by Numa Pompilius, explaining the etymology and various imperial renamings of each month.</meta>

<header>Of Pagan Gods</header>

So that you may receive further instruction from what was said at the beginning—how Romulus had a year of ten moons <note>A "moon" here refers to a lunar month.</note>—I will write here for you which was the first month in the year, how they followed one another, what names he gave them and why, and also how their names were changed at various times thereafter.

1. **Martius** or **March**, named after the god Mars, whom Romulus believed to be his father; it has 31 days.

2. **Aprilis** or **April**, named after Venus, who was the mother of Aeneas, from whom the lineage of Romulus descends; it has 30 days. **Neroneus**, named after the Emperor Nero. <note>Several Roman emperors attempted to rename the months after themselves or their titles, though most of these changes did not last beyond their reigns.</note>

3. **Maius** <note>May</note>. Some claim it was so named by Romulus to honor Jupiter and his supreme majesty. Others say he named it after the goddess Maia. Still others believe it was for the *Maioribus*, that is, out of love for the Senate <note>The "elders" or ancestors.</note>; it has 31 days. **Claudius**, for the Emperor Claudius wanted it named after him.

4. **Junius** <note>June</note>. This is said to have previously been called *Junonius* among the Latins <note>After the goddess Juno</note>. But Romulus is said to have named it so out of love for the youth <note>The *Juniores*</note>. Others say Junius Brutus drove out the kings during this month, and this name was kept in his memory; it has 30 days. It was also called **Germanicus**.

5. **Quintilis**, so named because it was the fifth from the beginning of the year; it has 31 days. **Julius** <note>July</note> comes from Julius Caesar, because he was born on the 12th of that month.

6. **Sextilis**, because it was the sixth month in the year; it has 30 days. **Augustus** <note>August</note>, for the reason that all his highest deeds were accomplished in this month of August. **Commodus**. Nothing was too much for this Commodus, which is why he wanted to erase the memory of Augustus and have this month named after himself.

7. **September**, according to the count, as it was the seventh; and it begins to become rainy or wintery and damp; it has 30 days. **Tiberius**: the Senate in Rome honored this Emperor with it. **Germanicus**, because he was victorious over the Germans in war. **Tacitus**, from the Emperor Tacitus. **Herculeus**, by command of Commodus, who also wanted to be called by that name, and because he was named Emperor in that same month, as well as **Germanicus**.

8. **October**, that is the eighth moon of Romulus's year; it has 30 days. This month was called **Livius**. **Domitianus**, after the Emperor. **Invictus** <note>The Unconquered</note>, by command of Commodus, because he was made a priest in every religious foundation in that month.

9. **November**, this follows as the ninth in the count from the first month and was reckoned among the winter dampness; it has 30 days. **Exuperatorius** <note>The All-Surpassing</note>, after a surname of Commodus, for in this month he was named Emperor along with his father and donned the garments of a man.

10. **December**, this was the last or tenth in the year of Romulus; it has 30 days. **Amazonius**, so named by Commodus out of love for his mistress Marcia, who went about dressed like an Amazon.

Now follows the year of Numa, that is, the two months which he added to the count of Romulus; for he attached fifty days to the year as previously mentioned. He also took one day from each of the six thirty-day months mentioned above, so that he distributed fifty-six days into two months, giving each twenty-eight days, and one of these he placed at the beginning of the year.

1. **January** <note>original: "Jenner"</note>; he named it thus in honor of Janus, the two-faced god, as if this month looked backward at the past and forward into the coming year; it has 29 days.

2. **February** <note>original: "Februarius"</note>, named for the god Februo, because it was to be the month of atonement, and the city should cleanse itself in that same month, confessing and being devout to pray for forgiveness for their sins; it has 28 days.

Soon Numa reconsidered and gave January, or the first month, one more day to indicate that he followed the Pythagoreans in favoring odd numbers and held them in high regard. But he left the even number for February <note>original: "Hornung," an old German name for February meaning "bastard" or "lowly-born," as it was the shortest month.</note> as a rejected, sorrowful month, keeping it for the leap-day <note>original: "Schalten," referring to the intercalation of extra days.</note> as was mentioned above.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Roman calendar, moving from the specific monthly duties listed in the previous table to a broader historical and mythological explanation of how the calendar was established and made public. It specifically details the transition of the calendar from the secret knowledge of priests to a public tool for the common people.</meta>

# Of Pagan Gods

Thus you have the division of the entire year as Julius Caesar established it. Although the lunar cycle, or the "Golden Number" <note>A 19-year cycle used to determine the date of the new moon.</note> as we call it, did not align perfectly—for in two hundred and twenty-two years, it shifts by more than a day—I nevertheless did not want to omit that number, nor the solar cycle or the literal notation <note>The "dominical letters" used to find the day of the week for any given date.</note>. For the lunar cycle is useful for calculating when the New Moon falls, while the solar cycle is used for the rotation of feast days and for knowing when to insert the leap day. How that is to be done is not recorded here, as it is not the present subject. Nevertheless, I will not keep from you that in Rome, the division of the year was also found carved in marble—which you might well call a "Peasant’s Calendar"—and it is undoubtedly an ancient thing, containing the following information.

But to return to my original speech regarding the Kalends <note>The first day of the Roman month.</note>, you should also know that the feast days or days of sacrifice, which the priests previously announced on the Mondays <note>The author uses "Monday" (Montag) loosely here to refer to the day of the moon/Kalends.</note>, were made public and prescribed for everyone by Gnaeus Flavius, the city scribe. This was done with such great rejoicing and favor from the common man that through their support and power, even though he was not of high birth, he was made an Aedile <note>original: "pawherzen." A Roman magistrate responsible for public buildings and festivals.</note>. Because of this, the councilors and the nobility were so indignant—and when he was later elevated to Guildmaster—they were so enraged that they threw the rings from their hands in protest.

Now, this was very beneficial to the common man; previously, he had to wait for court days and run after the priests, perhaps even giving them gifts, if he wanted to know when those days were, which caused him much lost time. Flavius helped them with this act, so that they no longer needed to chase after anyone, but could attend to their work while knowing the court days and holidays. However, this only occurred about four hundred and fifty years after the founding of the city of Rome.

Regarding the feast and sacrifice days, as well as their customs, we shall speak elsewhere. Yet you should know that the first day of every starting month, as mentioned, was dedicated to Juno. There was always an indulgence <note>A remission of religious debt or a period of grace.</note> in her temples, and one had to offer sacrifices to her on that day. This was because the ancients considered Juno and the Moon to be one and the same thing, which one could observe on that day. Or it was because the Moon wanders through the air, which Juno rules. Thus it is heard that the Nones <note>The 5th or 7th day of the month.</note> indicated that the "New" or the "Jous" [Ides] would come nine days later—though some claim they were so named because something "new" <note>original: "news," a play on "Nones" and "New."</note> was noted then. The word "Jous" <note>The Ides, which the author links to Jupiter.</note> is an old Tuscan word, signifying trust in Jupiter; it indicates that through the setting of the sun, the light has not entirely died, but the moon is illuminated by her, holding together the brilliance of the night and the day. For this reason, all "Jous" days [Ides] are dedicated and consecrated to Jupiter, the Father of Day.

## Februalis
## The Purifiers.

§ February, which is otherwise called "Hornung" or the Month of Indulgence, holds this festival for Juno, so that women seeking indulgence from her might be purified. From this, she has retained this name.

## Caprotina
## The Maid-Leader.

When the Gauls and Germans, under Brennus and others, moved about and plundered the whole world, a troop of the same folk also came to Rome, captured the city, and plundered it, except for the fortress of the Capitol...

<header>### The Third Book.</header>

almost nothing was left whole; yet they were driven off by Camillus. <note>Marcus Furius Camillus (c. 446–365 BC), a Roman soldier and statesman honored as the "Second Founder of Rome."</note> Even so, the city could only recover from the assault with great difficulty. Therefore, the neighboring enemies bordering the city took an opportunity to wage war on Rome and exhaust it. They appointed a warlord named Posthumus Livius, a very wealthy citizen of Fidenae—which was a city located about one mile from Rome. He camped not far from the city, and from there he sent his envoys to Rome to announce his message to the Council. If they wished for anything of the plundered city to be left to them, then they, the neighbors, should be answered and delivered their wives and daughters. The Councilors were in great distress as to what answer they should give, or how they should handle the matter. Then a servant girl stepped forward named Tutilla; <note>original: "Tutilla." More commonly known in Roman sources as Tutula or Philotis.</note> she said she wished to go voluntarily to the enemy with other servant girls as her companions, and behave as if they were the noble ladies and freeborn daughters. Thus, they were dressed in the clothes of the ladies and freeborn daughters, and the men and children followed after them, weeping and lamenting loudly, so that the enemy would more easily believe that they were the rightful women. Livius distributed them among the units in the camp. The maids pretended that they had a great festival that they had to observe; the enemy was willing, helped them, and drank heavily; they were merry. In the evening, when everyone was drunk and dazed, and sleepy from the wine, the maids acted as if they wished to perform a sacrifice. They climbed a wild fig tree, and from there they gave the Romans a signal that everyone in the camp was without care <note>i.e., off their guard</note>. Thus, the Romans fell upon them from the city and struck down the unsuspecting enemy. To be thankful for this good deed, they set all the maids free, provided for their marriages, and gave them dowries from the public treasury. They permitted them to go about dressed as they had been when they entered the camp, and thus established this festival, calling it <term>Caprotinas</term> <note>original: "Caprotinas." Referring to the *Nonae Caprotinae*, celebrated on July 7th.</note> after the fig tree, to honor Juno, who had thus instructed the maids. The temple and altar of this Juno were outside the city.

## Curis: The Spear-Bearer

In former times, instead of a royal crown, great lords carried small spears or scepters. For this reason, such a small scepter was always painted or sculpted in the hands of Juno as a queen. Since she had a very old temple on a hill in Rome, the name of that same hill, the <term>Quirinal</term>, came from this Juno; for the Tuscans <note>Etruscans</note> said <term>Curinalis</term> <note>original: "Curinalis." Derived from the Sabine word *curis*, meaning spear.</note> because they did not have the letter Q. With a small spear, one had to part the bride’s hair, because Juno presides over marriage; yet this spear had to be one that had been stuck into a gladiator who had been stabbed to death with it. This was intended to signify that fruitful children should be produced from the marriage, because Juno also carried a spear.

## Zeuxidia: The Joiner

They also speak of a very old temple that Juno had at Argos; for when she was once received in a friendly and honorable manner by the king there, and had seen the land—that it was good for farming—she went into Egypt and sent certain oxen of <term>Apis</term> <note>The sacred bull of ancient Egyptian religion.</note> the King out of Egypt to Argos, with instructions on how they should be yoked together and how the fields should be farmed. Now when the matter succeeded for the king in Argos, he built a temple to this Juno and called the fields of grain "Juno's flowers"; for from this "yoking together" she is called <term>Zeuxidia</term>. <note>original: "Zeuxidia." From the Greek *zeugnymi*, meaning to yoke or join.</note>

<header>Concerning Pagan Gods</header>

# Tropæa: The Victory-Markers

Those who were victorious in wars commonly erected commemorative columns or signs in their temples; because of this, they received this name <note>original: "Tropæa." From the Greek 'tropaion,' a monument erected to signify the 'turning' or defeat of an enemy.</note>.

## Lacinia: The Goddess on the Lacinian Promontory

Calabria—which was once called Greater Greece <note>original: "Groß Grecia," referring to Magna Graecia, the coastal areas of Southern Italy colonized by Greeks.</note>—has a corner or promontory once called Lacinium, now called the "Cape of the Columns" <note>original: "Capo Colonne."</note>. A king once lived there who conducted great highway robberies and was named Lacinius; he was killed and punished for this by Hercules, who then ordained a sanctuary there for Juno.

This temple is about one mile from the city of Croton <note>Modern-day Crotone in Calabria.</note>. Although this city was two and a half miles in circumference, its air was so exceptionally healthy that a proverb arose from it, saying: "He is healthier than a Crotonian." Furthermore, this city produced such brave and noble men that it was said: "The least among the Crotonians is worth more than the foremost among all other Greeks." Nevertheless, Livy <note>Titus Livius (64 BC–AD 17), a famous Roman historian.</note> values this temple more nobly and highly than the city itself; he says it was held in high regard by all the surrounding peoples. It had a thick sacred grove <note>original: "Phan," meaning a fane or sanctuary.</note> around it, surrounded by high firs and pines, and adorned with other beautiful trees. In the center, however, were entirely pleasant meadows and pastures, in which all kinds of cattle belonging and consecrated to the sanctuary wandered without any shepherds and grazed unprotected. At night, however, they ran back to the stall where they belonged, herd by herd, one with the other. They were never harmed or captured by wild beasts or robbers. Great profit was gained from this, such that a large column cast of pure gold stood there, alongside other unspeakable riches and great treasure.

This temple was also covered with marble tiles, which Fulvius Flaccus <note>Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, a Roman general who was censor in 173 BC.</note> had removed, wishing to cover the Temple of Equestrian Fortune <note>original: "Reüterischenn Glücks," referring to Fortuna Equestris.</note>—which he had founded—with them. When the Senate heard of this, he was forced to return them to their former place. He, however, went mad, and his two sons were stabbed to death.

No matter how great the storm winds were, the ash could never be blown off the altar of this temple, which stood under the open sky prepared for sacrifice. Hannibal <note>The Carthaginian general during the Second Punic War.</note> had a summer camp by this temple and erected an altar there with beautiful white marble tablets, upon which he wrote all that he had ever done and accomplished in war. Yet he desecrated it in that he had all the Italians who would not travel with him upon his departure—and who had fled into this temple—hewn down within it.

In Rome, not far from the gate of St. Lawrence, which was once called the Esquiline <note>original: "Exquilia."</note>, this Juno also had a grove and a temple.

## Feronia: At Feronia, or the Summoner

A fortress located not far from Soracte; this mountain on the Tiber is nearest, about one or two miles from Rome, and is now called St. Sylvester’s Mount. A city was once located there called Feronia, not far from which a sanctuary was situated...

### The Third Book.

...named after her and dedicated to Juno, featuring a beautiful sanctuary that was shared by the Sabines <note>An ancient Italic tribe living in the central Apennine Mountains.</note> and the Latins. It held established market days every year where everyone gathered—some to fulfill their vowed pilgrimages, others to buy, and still others to sell. It also attracted a great crowd due to the tricks performed there by the Hirpini <note>original: "Hirpiner." A group of priests who performed rituals at the sanctuary of Soranus/Feronia.</note>. These priests of the same sanctuary would occasionally behave as if they had been driven into a frenzy by the Goddess; they would rake through glowing ashes or otherwise walk with bare feet over iron and burning coals without being harmed. Regarding this, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> himself says that this was no miracle nor did it come from God, but rather that the Hirpini—who were otherwise called "wolves"—used an ointment on the soles of their feet so that the fire could do them no harm.

This city is said to have taken its name from the word *Feror* <note>Latin for "I am carried" or "I am tossed."</note>, which means to be tossed to and fro upon the sea. For when Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> established laws that were far too punitive, those who never dared to keep them fled with their homes and belongings and settled in other places. After they had been tossed about for a long time, they finally found this region upon their first landing; there, according to their vow, they built a city along with a temple and dedicated it to the "Goddess of the Arriving" <note>Juno Feronia.</note>.

There is also more than one temple, though this was the most prominent temple and sanctuary dedicated to Juno under that name. For the Holy River, or *Petra Sancta* <note>Holy Stone; likely referring to Pietrasanta near Lucca.</note>, not far from Lucca, was also a sanctuary of Feronia in ancient times, as King Desiderius <note>The last king of the Lombards (reigned 756–774 AD).</note> testifies. They honored and held this Juno as their helper for those who were counted as free and released from servitude; for in the temple, they would shave their heads and grant them their freedom <note>Referring to the Roman ritual of manumission, where a slave's head was shaved and they were given a 'pileus' or felt cap as a symbol of liberty.</note>.

She undoubtedly had a temple in Rome as well, for certain taxes were ordered to be collected there from the freedmen. Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> mentions this, noting that a gift was made from those funds and a sacrifice sent to the Goddess.

Similarly, she had a spring and a grove not far from Terracina, which were held in high honor and possessed great wealth until Hannibal plundered them. It is also said that once, when that same grove caught fire and almost the entire woods were scorched, the inhabitants wanted to carry the statue to another place; however, the blaze suddenly ceased, and the forest turned green again.

### Aegophagia: The Goat-Eater

Only the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, as Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> says, honored and represented Juno under this name. They claim that Hercules first built the temple for her among them and instructed them to sacrifice goats due to a lack of other livestock. This happened because Juno—when he fought against the sons of Hippocoon <note>Hippocoön was a King of Sparta who usurped the throne from his brother Tyndareus.</note>—did not hinder him at all as she had on other occasions, but was entirely helpful to him. The reason Hercules fought against Hippocoon and his sons arose because, after the death of Iphitus, Hercules came to them to atone for the killing and asked them to grant him absolution, which they refused. Furthermore, when a dog they kept at the house bit and injured Hercules' companion, Deonus, as he was passing by, Deonus threw a stone and killed the dog. The sons of Hippocoon then ran out and beat Deonus to death with clubs. Because of this, Hercules later killed them all.

# Of Pagan Gods

## Samia: She of Samos.

I made mention of this goddess when I wrote of Juno the Great, but what was left out there was that a river named Imbrasio <note>The Imbrasos river on Samos.</note> flows on this island, which was previously called Parthenicus—just as the island itself was once named. Thus, this temple likely stood by the water, which brought her this name. Her statue there was also fashioned in the clothing and form of a bride. This island was also called Pelasga, and Juno was sometimes named after it. There was even a proverb made about this island: that one might find "hens' milk" <note>An ancient Greek and German idiom for something rare, exquisite, or a land of extreme plenty.</note> there because of its fertility.

## Argiva: She of Argos.

This Juno had a temple at Argos which Eurydice—a daughter of Lacedemon and the wife of Acrisius—had built. However, they also say that Juno was born at Argos. For this reason, a high festival was held for her called the Hecatombe <note>original: "Hecatombe." A Greek sacrifice of one hundred oxen.</note>, which we shall speak of later. As the temple stood somewhat outside the city, on the wedding festival day, the wagon of Juno had to be pulled and guided with her priestess inside by white oxen. 

But when, at one time, no white bulls could be obtained, and the requirement could not be met, the priestess had two young sons named Cleobis and Biton <note>original: "Cleobis vnd Bizon."</note>. These two she yoked together like bulls, and they pulled the wagon toward the temple. When the youths had completed the journey in place of the oxen, the mother knelt down and prayed to Juno that she should give her sons a proper reward for this devotion. Then these youths fell into an eternal sleep, which ended their lives. Because of this, many later believed that death was the very thing the gods might give to a person as the most useful gift. To Argos, all the Greeks came together annually to offer this sacrifice to Juno and held a game there; whoever did best received a bronze shield and a small wreath of myrtle as thanks.

## Prosymnia.

Napoli in Romania <note>Refers to Nafplio in the Peloponnese, Greece; "Romania" was a term used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for various territories of the former Roman/Byzantine Empire.</note> is a well-known harbor or landing place in Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula.</note>, once called Nauplia. About three miles from there are two cities in the land: Argos and Mycenae. Between them, a temple was situated in ancient times at a place called Prosymnia, named after a woman who was Juno's nurse and a daughter of Asterion. This temple was otherwise called the Heraion <note>original: "Hereum."</note>, from the name Hera or Juno. 

The mountain or hill on which this temple stands is called Euboea; it has a hill opposite it called Acrea, named after two women who were sisters of this Prosymna (after whom the entire region around the temple is named). A small stream, the Free Brook <note>original: "Eleutherion."</note>, runs below the temple; the servants of the temple and others who wish to sacrifice there use this water. The master builder was a citizen of Argos named Eupolemus. Inside, on the vaulting and the area above the columns, the lineage of Jupiter and other gods is depicted, as well as the War of the Giants, shown with carved figures. Likewise, the destruction of Troy is shown. In the vestibule are the statues of the heroes and priestesses who tended to this temple, along with other decorative pieces. The statue of Juno was made by Polycleitus <note>One of the most famous bronze sculptors of Greek antiquity.</note>.

made of ivory and gold <note>original: "helffenbeyn vnd gold"; a chryselephantine statue.</note> which sits upon a beautiful, high throne of the same material. She wears a crown upon which the Graces <note>original: "Holdsäligkeiten"; the Charites, goddesses of charm and beauty.</note> and the Hours <note>original: "Stunden"; the Horae, goddesses of the seasons and natural order.</note> appear in embossed work. In one hand she holds a pomegranate, and in the right a scepter upon which sits a cuckoo <note>original: "Güggauch."</note>; this comes from the fable we mentioned regarding Jupiter <note>referring to the myth where Zeus disguised himself as a cuckoo to woo Hera.</note>. Beside this image was another very old statue made of wild pearwood, dedicated to this same Juno, which once stood at Tiryns.

A very rich sanctuary <note>original: "stifft."</note> was located there; for the wedding of Hebe and Hercules is depicted and formed there entirely of pure silver. There is also a large peacock made of solid gold, inlaid with pearls and precious stones, which Emperor Hadrian donated to that place, as well as a large golden crown and a golden mantle, which were gifts from Nero.

### Alea. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; The Fugitive.

Chiarenza <note>modern Kyllini.</note>, which was once called Sicyon and is situated not far from Corinth, possessed this sanctuary. It was built by Adrastus (who fled from his brother Pronax and came to his grandfather Polybus in Sicyon, where he later became king).

### Hoplosmia.

Regarding this name, we have said enough in the section on Jupiter <note>An epithet relating to Juno as a goddess of weaponry or protection.</note>.

### Fluonia. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; The Month-Divider.

Those women who had conceived and were relieved of their monthly flow <note>original: "Monatsfluss"; menstruation.</note> believed this happened through the help of Juno; therefore, they offered sacrifices and honored her under this name.

### Leucolena. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; White-Armed.

The poets and others have given Juno this name because of her beauty, in order to praise her with it <note>original: "Leucolena"; from the Homeric Greek "leukōlenos."</note>.

### Acrea. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; She of the Heights.

It was mentioned above how a small hill at Argos was called Acrea <note>original: "Acrea"; from the Greek "akra," meaning a high point or citadel.</note>, where the citadel or fortress of the Argives once stood; Juno had a temple there. But it is also found that not far from the Corinthian harbor of Lechaeum—now called Lestriocozi—there was a promontory or corner called Acrea. A very old temple of this Juno stood there, to which Medea fled with her two sons, Mermerus and Pheres, who had been stoned by the Corinthians.

### Bunea.

Above the city of Corinth lay a hill and old fortress called Acrocorinth, in which many a sanctuary, chapel, and altar was consecrated. Among others, this Juno also had a temple there, built for her by Bunus, the son of Mercury and Alcidamie; when Aeëtes <note>original: "Aetas."</note> moved to Colchis, Bunus wished to be King of Corinth.

### Pharygea. At Pharygia.

Magnesia, where Euripica is now situated, on the gulf once called the Pelasgic Gulf <note>original: "Sinus Pelasgicus"; the modern Gulf of Volos.</note>, is a city located by the sea. It was first called Taripha, then Scarphia, and finally Pharygia. There, Juno had a temple built by the Argives <note>People from Argos.</note>, who were a people once ruled by Pelasgus <note>The mythical ancestor of the Pelasgians, the earliest inhabitants of Greece.</note>. For there are several famous cities named Argos. First, the one we are discussing here; the second, built by Orestes near Durazzo <note>Modern Durrës in Albania.</note>; the third in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula.</note> near Mycenae, where Prosymnia was at home; the fourth in Thessaly on the river Achelous <note>original: "Acheloo"</note>, of which we have made mention regarding the Argive woman; the fifth was on the island of Nisyros <note>original: "Nysaro"</note>. This island had five villages and a burning mountain <note>A volcano.</note> which is so hot halfway up that one cannot climb it without wooden shoes <note>original: "holzschůh"; clogs used to protect the feet from geothermal heat.</note>. Additionally, it has a hot spring and, in a wide field, a deep lake from which they boil salt. It is located about three miles from the land and the city of Cnidus <note>original: "Cnido"</note>, which is now called Capo Crio, in Anatolia in the governorship of Quisco. The sixth Argos is near Troezen. The seventh is at Mount Argaeus in Cappadocia, now called Artagopensa, in the Empire of Trebizond. Cities of this name are also located in Scythia, Caria, Phocis <note>original: "Phuacien"</note>, and Macedonia.

### Dyrphia. Dyrphian.

On the island of Negropont <note>Modern Euboea.</note> there is a mountain called Dyrphyus <note>Mount Dirfys.</note>; she was worshipped there and received her name from it.

### Parthenia. The Maiden.

She is said to have this name from Mount Parthenius in Arcadia, and also for other reasons as I have indicated in the section on "Juno the Established" <note>original: "Gstandnen Juno"; likely referring to Juno Stata.</note>.

### Ipnusia. Hypnusian.

In Samos there was a small district of this name; she took her name from it because she was worshipped there.

### Candrena. At Candara.

In Paphlagonia <note>An ancient region on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia.</note> there was once a city called Candara, where Juno was worshipped and acquired this name.

### Cytheronia. Of Cithaeron.

Cithaeron was a king who ruled in the regions where Achaia and Boeotia now lie, by the river Asopus <note>original: "Asopo"</note>, which is called Darbon. Not far from there lies a mountain named Cithaeron after him. This same king built a temple at Plataea for both Jupiter and Juno. To explain why they both—Jupiter and Juno—are called "Cithaeronian," this little tale <note>original: "mëhlin"</note> is put forward:

It happened once, for some unknown reason, that Jupiter and Juno had a disagreement. Consequently, she withdrew to Euboea and left Jupiter. Jupiter sent after her, wishing to reconcile with her through kind words, but Juno remained stubborn <note>original: "plaict sich"</note> and would hear nothing of it. The good Jupiter was anxious and went to Cithaeron to ask for advice on what to do (for at that time Cithaeron was regarded as a very wise man). He...

<header>The Third Book.</header>

advised Jupiter <note>original: "Joui"</note> that he should have a wooden image carved and have it carried on a cart with two oxen, as if a bride were being brought to him. When Juno heard of this, she quickly set out with other women and ran to the cart; in a great fit of jealousy, she tore the clothes off the image. There she discovered the trick and the deception; nevertheless, she burned the wooden bride and allowed herself to be reconciled with Jupiter, returning to live with him. Plutarch and Eusebius tell this little fable with slightly different words, but in this same manner. They intend this domestic quarrel between Jupiter and Juno to signify the disrupted elements and their storms, which cause great damage to natural growth unless they are moderated by a harmonious course. For where the fiery, hot nature of Jupiter <note>Jupiter here represents the element of fire or the sun.</note> takes the upper hand, everything must wither; likewise, all things rot where Juno—that is, the airy moisture <note>Juno here represents the element of air or water.</note>—is the master. For this reason, in Boeotia <note>A region in Greece.</note>, when the rainy nature took the upper hand and flooded everything, and then the heat dried it up again, they said the two gods had become one again. However, first the oak tree sprouted and brought forth fruit; this was the same image that Jupiter had made. Because of this, they thereafter always carved such images for their sacrifices, as shall be heard in its proper place.

## Ammonia. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; The Sandy One.

As the housewife and consort of Jupiter <note>original: "Jouis"</note>, she was also honored under this name; in Elis, she had her altar and sacrifice. <note>The name likely refers to the Egyptian-Libyan god Ammon, whose oracle was in the desert sands.</note>

## Boopis. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; The Large-Eyed.

The poets and others have attributed large and also beautiful eyes to Juno, from which she takes this name. <note>original: "Boopis"; often translated from Greek as "ox-eyed" or "cow-eyed," signifying majesty.</note>

## Tetthlæ.

Among the Plataeans, Juno also had a temple under this name, which was given to her there.

## Europia.

Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian.</note> gives her this name and leaves it at that.

## Telchinia.

Diodorus writes of this one in his description of the island of Rhodes. For the Telchines, as Strabo mentions, were the first blacksmiths or coppersmiths, and they also made images for this Juno.

## Cypria. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; In Cyprus.

In Holy Mary of Loreto, to which there is a great pilgrimage as is known to many, there stood in former times a small town called Catellum <note>Possibly referring to Cupra Marittima or a nearby Roman castellum.</note>. In the entire March of Ancona <note>A region in central Italy.</note>, it was a trading city and a house of commerce; it had a temple called Cupra or Cypra, and it is from this that this Juno took her name.

## Gabinia. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; At Gabii.

In Gallicano, which is situated about two miles from Rome and was once the city of Gabii, Juno was highly honored and thus received this name; however, the temple lay somewhat outside the city.

## Rhescyntus. She of Rhescyntus.

Nicander <note>A Greek poet and physician from the 2nd century BCE.</note>, when he speaks in his *Theriaca* <note>original: "Triacks"; a famous poem about venomous stings and bites.</note> regarding the bite of the water-lion <note>likely referring to a "Cenchris," a type of spotted serpent.</note>—which causes a person to completely rot with its bite, and strikes with its tail to cause fiery sores and swellings—says it is otherwise called Cenchrynes and moves between the islands of Samos and Mytilene. He claims that directly opposite lies a mountain called Rhescyntes, and that Juno has a temple upon it. I would almost believe this to be the mountain Rhodope, which is now called Silver Mountain in the Teplice District in the Vogtland <note>original: "Wossen"; the author is attempting to identify ancient Greek geography with local German landmarks.</note> and has many silver mines; for the river Ibar flows there, which was once called the Hebrus. I also well know that some consider the Maritsa <note>original: "Moritza"</note> to be the Hebrus, which flows into the sea near Gallipoli.

## Anchia. The Blooming One.

In Argos there is an ever-blooming place with beautiful flowers; there stood a temple dedicated to this Juno by Bacchus. He had set out against the Argives and Perseus with several women from the islands located in the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea.</note>; and when he lost some of them in battle, he erected a grave for them there and established this temple in their memory, to honor Juno. This is as much as shall be said for now regarding Juno.

<header>The Third Book.</header>

# Apollo and the Sun.

<image-desc>Two woodcut illustrations side-by-side. The left image depicts the god Apollo as a crowned man playing a violin-like instrument (a fiddle). At his feet lies a slain three-headed dragon. To his left stands a laurel tree with a raven perched in the branches and a bow with a quiver of arrows leaning against its trunk. The right image shows a man in a tall, pointed hat—Apollo in his role as a divine shepherd—tending to a herd of cattle in a landscape with a tree and mountains in the distance.</image-desc>

As we now come to Apollo, Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman, who discussed the nature of the gods in his writings.</note> recounts that there are four such figures. He says the most ancient among them was born of Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcano"</note> and was considered a guardian of the city of Athens. The second is a son of Corybas in Crete, who quarreled with Jupiter for the rule of that island. The third was sired by Jupiter from Latona, and he settled at Delos. The fourth he calls an Arcadian, who also established the laws of the land in that place.

Now, although there were many who later took the name of Apollo, he is credited with four attributes in which he is praised above all others. He is a harpist; secondly, he is an inventor of medicine and a physician; thirdly, a shooter and archer; and fourthly, they held him to be a soothsayer. He was so supreme in these arts that he was elevated to the status of a god of all these things.

His form was painted as a beardless youth wearing a three-pointed crown on his head, a fiddle <note>original: "geygen"; though a violin is anachronistic for antiquity, the author uses the contemporary instrument of his time to represent Apollo's lyre.</note> in his left hand, and in his right a bow for shooting. Under his feet lay a three-headed dragon which he had shot; the laurel tree, upon which a raven sat, stood beside him.

And because he was sometimes taken in place of the Sun—the overwhelming heat of which causes disruption and decay in the air, from which the "rogue" or the pestilence <note>The author links the sun's heat to the miasma theory of disease.</note> arises—they gave him the rays or arrows. For this reason, it is still called the *Butsch* <note>original: "Butsch"; a colloquial term for a plague-boil or the plague itself.</note> among us. Some attribute his perpetual youth to the fact that the Sun constantly draws moisture up into the air, from which rain is formed, and the world is thereby renewed and washed clean; for this reason, he is depicted as young.

Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who frequently interpreted gods as allegories for natural forces.</note> grants that this Apollo is the Sun in the heavens and is Liber <note>An Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus or Dionysus.</note> upon the earth. Beneath the earth, he is Apollo. Therefore, he has three signs: a lyre, which signifies the harmony <note>original: "zusamen hellung"; referring to the "music of the spheres."</note> of the heavenly orbits; a griffin as an earthly sign; and the rays as a harmful god of the underworld. Some give him a raven instead of the griffin, but Phornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher known for allegorical interpretations of myths.</note> contradicts this because that bird is black and unclean, whereas a swan is better suited to the brightness of the Sun, added to which the swan has such a lovely voice.

# Of Heathen Gods

The laurel tree, which is attributed to him, is always green, burns easily, and purifies; all of this best resembles and agrees with the grace, heat, and beauty of the Sun. The tripod signifies the perfection of this number and the three circles in the heavens, in one of which the Sun runs and completes the year, which is called the Zodiac; the other two at the sides, it reaches. The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> also painted and sculpted this god with four ears, and likewise with four hands, as a generous and mild being. Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often wrote about pagan customs.</note> says the ancient heathens held Apollo in secret as the "only god," which is why the true image of Apollo in the temple at Delphi was a pillar. Furthermore, it was understood that the fire which flared up there had no exit nor entrance in those places.

Arnobius <note>An Early Christian apologist.</note> claims that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome.</note> did not include Apollo among the number of the Roman gods. Nevertheless, we shall proceed and speak of this name, Apollo.

Plato believes that he received his name from the flickering and shooting forth of the Sun's rays; among the Thessalians, he was thus called "Aplon," which refers to the act of prophecy, which means "Simple" or "Plain." <note>The author is likely referencing the Greek word 'Haploun,' meaning simple or unified.</note> Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher.</note> adds that he is called <term>alpha</term> <note>original: "α"</note> and <term>pollos</term> <note>original: "πολλος"</note>, which signifies "not many," as if to say that his splendor and beauty were not shared by many, but belonged to him alone. For this reason, he is also called "Sol" by Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar.</note>, as the "only one" <note>original: "solus"</note> who shines there. One also finds those who believe he has his name from the abundance of fire or light he possesses, with which he ignites all the stars. Some say he moves daily from one place to another, running very swiftly from the Sunrise to the Sunset, and alone ignites all other starlight; these meanings have their roots and derivations in Greek words. Besides this, some name him such because he destroys and kills living things, as was said above, when he poisons the air with excessive heat. It is indeed true that grace and loveliness are attributed to this Apollo, because his shine and power—when he is taken in place of the Sun—revive all things and bring much more benefit than harm; for this reason, he carries grace in his right hand, and the arrows and bolts in his left. He is also esteemed as a physician, because the moderate, natural heat of the Sun chases away all sickness.

## Apelles. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Averter.

The ancient Romans also knew this well, which is why they gave him the name Apelles, which means "The Averter" <note>From the Latin 'pellere,' to drive away; the name refers to Apollo as a protector who drives away disease.</note>, as Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian.</note> indicates. For the same reason, the Athenians also honored him. But to speak first of those honors he received in Rome, you should know that this Apollo had several temples and images in Rome; the first temple dedicated to him was not far from the herb market <note>The Forum Holitorium</note> near and outside the Carmental Gate <note>original: "Thor Carmente"</note>. Some believe the church now located there is the one called "Our Lady" and "of the Capitol" <note>Likely referring to Santa Maria in Campitelli or Santa Maria in Aracoeli.</note>. As it appears to me, this occurred nearly two hundred and forty years after the death of Numa, under the Guild-masters who also held the office of Burgermeister: Marcus Fabius Vibulanus, Marcus Folio, and Lucius Sergius, who, as some say, vowed a temple to Apollo to ward off a plague. He had another temple near the Flaminian Circus <note>original: "Reñplatz Flaminij"</note>, where the ropemakers now twist their cords and the lime kilns are built; some believe the site of the Church of St. Apollinaris is there. It is also well to be presumed that this Apollo was first brought by the Romans fro...

...called Vaticanus, for the sake of soothsaying <note>The author connects "Vatican" to the Latin *vaticinari*, meaning to prophesy or foretell.</note>, where the Vatican hill now stands; and afterwards a temple was built there to Apollo, not far from and very close to where St. Peter’s Basilica now stands. Indeed, some write that the Church of St. Petronilla stood on that very spot, which Pope Paul I dedicated to the daughter of Peter. Above it, a beautiful marble tomb of red porphyry stone <note>A rare, purple-red volcanic stone prized by Roman emperors.</note> was found by the Way of St. Sebastian, in which was written:
->TO PETRONILLA, SWEETEST DAUGHTER<-
<note>original: "PETRONELLAE FILIAE DVLCISS."</note>

Augustus also erected a temple to this Apollo after he had overcome Antony and Cleopatra, and he adorned it with gold, silver, ivory, statues, shutters, and towers so magnificently that nothing more precious was seen in Rome. He also established a library there, making it public and consecrated; at the festivals, he arranged five-year games with racing and jousting, as at Olympia, and established priests there to tend the temple. He was also otherwise called *Navalis* <note>meaning "of the ships," referring to the naval victory at Actium.</note>. It burned down in the year 360 after the birth of Christ; it almost happened that the Sibylline prophecies <note>A collection of oracular utterances kept in the temple of Apollo.</note> would have perished with it. Not long ago, the chapel of St. Lucy stood there, which has now also been torn down.

On the Horse Hill <note>original: "Roßberg"</note>, which was once called the Quirinal and is now called Monte Caballo—named after the two marble horses that King Tiridates of Armenia gave to Nero—there also once stood a temple of Apollo, behind where the palace of Cardinal Caraffa is now built. And one otherwise reads in Suetonius <note>A Roman historian (c. 69–122 AD).</note> of a temple of *Apollo Tortor* <note>meaning "Apollo the Torturer."</note>, the location of which is unknown. In the Church of Our Lady in Porticu (or the porch), which was once called the Portico of Octavia, stood an image of Apollo, and he held a ray in his right hand. Otherwise, at the market of Augustus, where St. Hadrian now stands at the three markets, there was also an image of him made of ivory. Furthermore, Lucullus brought an image of this Jupiter <note>The author likely means a colossal statue of Apollo, as Lucullus is famous for bringing the "Colossus of Apollo" from Apollonia.</note> to Rome from the region of Pontus (now Anatolia), which was forty-five feet high; it had stood in the city of Apollonia, which is situated on the Rhyndacus water (now called the Lycus). It still lies in pieces in Rome, in the Palace of the Conservators below the Capitol; I have even touched and measured several of those same pieces myself. Some write it cost one hundred and fifty talents, which would be ninety thousand crowns.

## Cœliſpex.
->Sky-gazer / Researcher /<-
->Slipper-bearer.<-

In Rome, on the eleventh street by the Great Circus, Apollo had a temple, founded or renewed by Caesar. Because of the statue that looked up toward heaven as if counting the stars, and because it wore slippers, it was called *Cœlispex* <note>original: "Celispey," from the Latin for "heaven-watcher."</note> and *Sandalarius* <note>meaning "the one with sandals."</note>. This building almost suggests to Nero that it was also the "Torturer." However, we do not wish to be closed to further correction here.

## Pæan.

When the Athenians called upon this god at Delphi for help so that they might resist the Amazons—at which time Theseus was still their king—the priest gave them as an answer that they should call upon the god while striking with this word, and cry out continually **io acae**, which is **Io Paean.** <note>A cry of victory or a prayer for help to Apollo.</note> In German, this might be translated as: "Hands up! Strike in!"

Others believe it comes from the little words <term>Ieios</term> <note>original: "Jeios"; a Greek epithet for Apollo often associated with a cry for help or healing.</note>, which signifies "healing," and then <term>Paean</term> <note>original: "paian"; a title for Apollo as the physician of the gods.</note>, which means "stilling," as if he stilled all pain with his healing power; and they prayed to him in this way so that he would not overheat the air, nor cause decay, nor bring the plague <note>original: "den sterbend," referring to the "dying" or pestilence.</note>.

### Hulios. &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; Bringer of Health.
<note>original: "Vlios"; likely derived from the Greek "Oulios," meaning "health-giving" or "destructive," depending on the context of the god's power.</note>

Because Apollo was esteemed as so salutary, he also earned this name as an origin of health; the Milesians <note>Inhabitants of Miletus, an ancient Greek city in Ionia.</note> sacrificed to him for this reason. Similarly, Theseus sacrificed to this Apollo when he intended to face the Minotaur <note>original: "Ochsenreisen," literally "Ox-giant," referring to the half-man, half-bull monster of the Cretan labyrinth.</note> in Crete.

The Milesians, whom people now call those of Melayo, once had a temple of Jupiter. It was erected after the Branchidae <note>A clan of priests who served the oracle at Didyma.</note> betrayed the temple on Mount Didyma <note>original: "Didanio."</note> and handed it over along with the treasure, which Xerxes later burned. For this reason, the Milesians built this temple so massive that nothing else in the world was its equal; because of its sheer size, it could not be covered by a roof. It took up as much space as many a small town. Inside and out, it had a precious grove or forest, and it was quite magnificent, adorned with beautiful decorations throughout.

### Libystinus. &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; Lybian.

At Cape Passaro, or the Passaro Head, a promontory of Sicily that was once called Pachynum—and a village lay not far from it called Sparcasurno, or "Smite the Oven"—Apollo once had a temple under this name. When the Lybians first sailed to the island and arrived at the promontory, Apollo brought a pestilence <note>original: "schelmen"; here referring to a plague or "rogue" sickness.</note> among them, so that they nearly all died there. For this reason, the inhabitants gave him this name.

Macrobius <note>A Roman provincial who wrote "Saturnalia," a source for much classical lore in the Renaissance.</note> adds here that something similar occurred in Rome when the festivals and first theatrical games <note>original: "schimpffspil," referring to the Ludi Apollinares.</note> were held for this Apollo. While they were being held, the enemy attempted to invade the city. Many arrows and other missiles came out of the clouds into the enemy and drove them away, so that the Romans achieved such a swift victory that they were able to return to the games and finish them completely. Thus you find here that Marcus <note>Referring to Marcius the Seer, whose prophecies led to the establishment of these games.</note>, a soothsayer who wrote several prophecies for Apollo that were previously unknown to the Romans, ordered these games to be established. Cicero testifies to this in his first book *On Divination* <note>original: "von der Weyssagungen."</note>, where he mentions Publius and Martius, the two brothers and soothsayers, who brought this to light in their poems.

### Loxias. &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; Crooked-running.

Because the sun runs in a crooked, diagonal circle and roundness from its rising to its setting, and from midday onwards casts its rays upon us transversely, this name was given to Apollo. Some claim he has this name because his soothsaying is so inconsistent and of a confused understanding <note>Refers to the notoriously ambiguous and "oblique" nature of the Delphic oracles.</note>.

# The Third Book.
<meta>catchword: today</meta>

...gia, Aidia, Pelasgia, Cerham, Chamydia, Cynethun, Pirpilo, <note>These are ancient names for the island of Delos, such as Ortygia, Asteria, and Lagia.</note> and finally named **Delos**; it lies far from Negropont <note>The medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea.</note> across the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea.</note> at a distance of about one mile. On this island, the ancients said that **Apollo** was born and raised. The island, as some write, emerged through an earthquake and for a long time floated back and forth upon the sea until it finally settled and remained where it now stands. It also sits high and is visible and prominent among all the other islands of the **Cyclades** in the Archipelago, appearing like a king over them. Near it lies **Rhenea**, located so close that **Polycrates**, the tyrant of Samos and lord of the surrounding islands, once joined them together with a chain and dedicated them to Apollo of Delos.

In the island of Delos, a temple was erected by **Hercules**, in which the **Meropes** <note>A legendary people or clan.</note> helped him; others say it was built by **Erichthonius**, the son of **Cecrops**, in the year 2456 after the beginning of the world. In that same temple, the statue of Apollo was fashioned in this manner: In his right hand, he carried a defensive bow; in the other, he led the three **Graces** <note>original: "Holdsäligkeiten"; the Charites, goddesses of charm and beauty.</note> who carried musical instruments—one a lute, the second a flute, and the middle one a reed pipe. The altar upon which sacrifices were made was constructed entirely of horns taken from the right side of the heads of animals; they were also miraculously intertwined and joined together in such a way that it was counted among the wonders of the world. 

Now, on this same altar, one was not permitted to sacrifice any living animal. It was also forbidden to keep anyone in the island or city who was in the throes of death, or to allow them to die there, or to bury them. It was considered a great crime if a dog were brought into this island or heard therein. Dying people and dead corpses all had to remain and be kept on the island of **Rhenia**, which lies directly opposite at a distance of a bowshot. If the Delians overlooked this, the <term>dying-one</term> <note>original: "der sterbend"; likely referring to the god Apollo in his role as a bringer of plague or "the striker," or perhaps a personification of the pestilence itself.</note> came among them and punished them for their sins. For this reason, **Pisistratus** <note>The tyrant of Athens.</note> once had this island purified, such that as far as he could see from the temple, he had the graves dug up and whatever dead bodies or bones he found carried away to Rhenia. 

And when that was not enough, a long time afterward, the **Athenians** had to purify it even more thoroughly, casting out all graves throughout the entire island. They gave a command that those in danger of death must be taken to Rhenia before they died, lest any impurity arise. And so that such customs and commands would not fall into decline or be forgotten, they renewed the festivals, celebrations, and competitive games that had been established there in ancient times. Every five years, there was to be wrestling, singing, and racing (Homer also mentions these festivals in the *Hymn to Apollo*, therefore they must be very old). The Athenians also arranged for those living in the surrounding islands to visit with their wives and children, traveling there for the games, specifically the wrestling match, where a palm branch was given as a prize to the victor. This branch came from the tree said to be the first palm tree to grow in all of Greece, having sprouted in Delos. Above the city of Delos and above the temple was a mountain called **Cynthius**, from which Apollo and **Diana** received their names, being called **Cynthius** and **Cynthia**. At the foot of this same mountain lay a spring which was of the same nature as the **Nile** in Egypt: it rose, flowed over, and receded just as the Nile does. Both islands together comprise about two miles in circumference, and there is still...
