## Concerning the Heathen Gods

Today in Delos, at the place where the temple once stood, great ruined buildings can be seen, many fallen marble columns, and a stone statue that cannot be set upright in any way. Rhenea is beautiful and fair, and well-built. The customs and the manner of offering sacrifice in this temple were allegedly brought and taught by two young women, Hyperotha and Laodice from Scythia—from the Hyperboreans, who are undoubtedly called Muscovites <note>The author is identifying the legendary northern "Hyperboreans" with the Russians/Muscovites of his own era.</note> today. Along with them, two other young daughters, Argis and Opis, are said to have come from there, who showed these things to the daughters of Delos and trained them for daily service. 

When the fame of this temple first began to spread, and **Theseus** sought to release the **Athenians** from the annual burden (for they had to send seven young men and as many maidens to Minos in Crete, or Candia, to be killed because of the death of his son), he vowed that if he should return to Athens in peace and free of tribute, he would establish and endow an annual festival <note>The "Theoria," a sacred embassy or pilgrimage.</note> for **Apollo** in Delos. Having succeeded, he fulfilled his vow, decreeing for all time that every year on the seventh day of October <note>original: "Weinmonats"; literally "wine month," the traditional German name for October.</note>, the ship in which Theseus sailed to Crete should be sent with a blessing to Delos. This ship was preserved for nearly nine hundred years, from the time of Theseus until **Demetrius Phalereus**, being repaired whenever it was damaged. The ship was called the **Paralis**. 

Often, when it was sent on its annual voyage to Delos, it remained away for a full month. During this time, it was forbidden to put anyone to death, whether by law or otherwise, nor could anyone be arrested during that period <note>This "sacred truce" famously delayed the execution of the philosopher Socrates.</note>. If it stayed away so long, it was often because the winds were contrary to the ship. The costs of the voyage, along with the great gifts with which the ship was loaded to honor the God, were paid by the treasurers from the public purse. Once, while this ship was anchored at Sunium (now called the Little Pillar-Head, or Cape Colonna) ready to sail, it was seized by the **Aeginetans** (now called Egina) and carried away along with many noble men. This later cost the Aeginetans many lives, for the Athenians eventually defeated them with seventy sails against seven hundred ships.

Such annual voyages were made not only by the Athenians, but also by the cities of the surrounding islands and the mainland, who sent their ships, beautifully adorned and with songs of praise, to Delos. When each arrived, it pulled in closest to the temple. For this reason, **Nicias**, in order to create order when he was the Admiral, did not dock closest to the temple, but landed at Rhenea. He prepared everything needed for the sacrifice and gifts there and threw a bridge from one island to the other (which he had previously caused to be made in Athens according to the correct measurements). In the morning, he crossed this bridge, which was decorated all over with gold, tapestries, and flowers, leading his youths and daughters into Delos in order, accompanied by sweet singing for the sacrifice. He also erected a palm tree made of bronze <note>original: "årtz"; brass or bronze.</note> for the God, and purchased a field and the foundation nearby for a thousand crowns. This he dedicated to the temple, so that the fruit it yielded annually would go to the foundation to provide a feast for those arriving on this annual pilgrimage.

The Greeks held this temple in such high honor—either for the safety of their situation or for the sake of the sanctuary—that they deposited all the funds they collected in their common assemblies there, as a defense against foreign enemies and the Medes <note>The "Medes" refers to the Persian Empire. This refers to the Delian League, where Delos served as the treasury for the Greek city-states.</note>...

### The Third Book

...which they placed into a common treasury <note>original: "pfenning kasten"; literally "penny box," referring to the public funds of the Delian League.</note>. Thus, the first assessment under the pious **Aristides** <note>Aristides "the Just" (c. 530–468 BC), an Athenian statesman known for his fairness in calculating the tributes of the Greek city-states.</note> amounted to two hundred seventy-six thousand crowns, which were deposited there. All the envoys of the Greeks also gathered there whenever they wished to hold a general assembly regarding the freedom of the land or to deliberate on matters of particular importance.

Furthermore, foreigners held this temple in such high honor that it remained unplundered throughout all wars. For when **Darius**, the King of the Persians, dispatched **Datis** to Greece with a powerful army—on horse, on foot, and by ship—and he brought nearly all the surrounding islands under his control and plundered them, robbing their temples and endowments, the Delians fled to **Tenos** <note>original: "Tenion"; the neighboring island of Tinos.</note>, which is an island situated about two miles away. But as the ships of Datis hastened toward Delos, Datis pressed on ahead of them and allowed no one to land at Delos; they were all forced to harbor at **Rhenea**. When he learned of the flight of the Delians, he sent his heralds to speak to them thus:

> You hallowed and spiritual men of Delos, it weighs heavily upon me that you have fled from me, for I am wrongly judged by you as one who desires to do you harm. I do not know that I have ever given cause for such suspicion. For I know well of my own accord (though also by my King’s command) that I should neither trouble nor hostly attack the place or the inhabitants where two gods <note>Apollo and Artemis, who according to myth were born on Delos.</note> were born. Therefore, return with free and safe passage; no harm shall come to you.

And immediately upon sending this message, he offered and burned three hundredweights of incense upon the altar.

After his departure, there was an earthquake at Delos, which was given as an omen of the great discord that later arose among the Greeks from disunity and civil war. And when Datis discovered in a dream that one of his captains had stolen an image from Delos, he had all the ships searched, and when he found it, he transported it back to Delos in his own ship. The entire island was also always a singular marketplace for the Greeks, especially after the Romans captured and destroyed **Corinth**; then the wealthiest citizens who had escaped and survived moved to this island. They built and planted there in the most costly manner, whereby it became a center of trade and a warehouse for all commerce, whether by land or by sea, for it was well-situated for both the Greeks and the Romans. The **Athenians** guarded it and served as its protectors. 

But at the very last, when the Roman war with **Mithridates** <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus (120–63 BC), a major antagonist of the Roman Republic.</note> began, and **Menophanes**, his general, learned that there was a sanctuary at Delos where fugitives and other wrongdoers sought refuge, this general—perhaps out of contempt for the God, or perhaps by his king’s command—approached the island. When he learned that the city and temple of Delos were unprotected by walls and that many people were within, yet unarmed, he attacked. He went ashore and slaughtered both foreigners and locals, robbed the temple, plundered the city, and captured a great treasure. He carried away all the votive offerings and jewels <note>original: "Götzengaben vñ Kleinotter"</note>, sold the women and children, and razed the city and temple to the ground, as one who cared more for gold and goods than for the God. **Gaius Verres**, who left no temple unrobbed and no ornament or court in Europe and Asia unplundered, also went to the island by night while serving as a quaestor <note>term: Schultheiẞ (Magistrate/Official). Here the author refers to Verres’s role as a subordinate to Dolabella.</note> to **Dolabella**. Under the cover of darkness and mist, he had the most beautiful and ancient statues and ornaments carried out of the temple and onto the ships. The inhabitants dared not complain of anything before Dolabella.

# Of the Heathen Gods

...they did not know if it was by his command (for he was also present). They attributed it to God. **Cicero** says that such a violent storm arose that no one could remain on the sea; indeed, because of its fury, there was almost no peace in the city until the robber **Verres’s** <note>Gaius Verres (c. 120–43 BC) was a Roman magistrate notorious for his extreme corruption and for looting artworks from Greek provinces.</note> ship was cast ashore and shattered. Thus **Dolabella** <note>Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella, a Roman official and associate of Verres.</note> found the loot and ordered it to be placed back into the temple, so that he might depart afterward. **Strabo** says that even in the time of **Augustus**, although the Romans had retaken the island and restored that empty nest to the **Athenians**, the temple and all the buildings still lay in ashes. Likewise, **Pausanias**, who lived in the time of **Hadrian**, says that since nothing more remained for which a pilgrimage there was worth considering, not a single person lived there anymore. Thus, while **Athens** is inhabited to this day, nothing remains in **Delos** but landmarks and old ruins.

The answers and signs given from this temple were famous above all other prophecies of **Apollo**, because they were revealed clearly and brightly with specific words, without being obscured. **Cicero** also describes a laughable prank, saying that the **Delians** were so well-informed in hatching and raising young chickens that they made a professional trade out of it. Many of them supported themselves by it, and they were so remarkably quick-witted <note>original: "gätz gschwind"; meaning exceptionally sharp or clever.</note> that among many thousands of eggs, they knew and could tell exactly which hen had laid this or that egg. Otherwise, there is a proverb: *An egg is an egg,* or *One egg looks like another*; yet these men knew one egg from another, just as a mother, by the twinkling of the eyes, recognizes her two twins (who otherwise look alike) from one another, even if no one else can distinguish them. I myself wonder how those who have compiled books of proverbs have until now forgotten these **chicken breeders**. For what would better suit a rhyme about one who wants to know everything—even if his wits occasionally fail him—than to say: "He has it as certain as a Delian chicken breeder." Now **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous humanist who compiled the *Adagia*, a massive collection of Greek and Latin proverbs.</note> cites this speech of Cicero, but he leaves his book of proverbs unadorned by the *Delian Chicken-coop* <note>original: "Gallinario D. lio"; referring to the Latin term *Gallinarius Delius* used by Cicero.</note>, though he otherwise makes use of several places nearby. **Varro** and **Columella** <note>Roman authors who wrote famous treatises on agriculture and animal husbandry.</note> also mention them.

Now we have said enough about the island; to speak now of **Apollo**, I must show how his birth and its significance were presented and interpreted by the ancients.

**Zeus**, one of the Giants who possessed and named the island of **Teos** <note>The text likely refers to the Titan Coeus, Latona’s father in standard mythology, though the author here calls him "Zeus, one of the Giants."</note>, begat **Latona**. While she was still a maiden, **Jupiter** seduced her, which is why the war of the Giants against the gods arose. This so greatly angered **Juno** <note>The Roman name for Hera, the queen of the gods and wife of Jupiter/Zeus.</note> that she would allow Latona no safe place on the entire earth, but instead sent forth a **Dragon** <note>Python, the monstrous serpent.</note> who had to pursue the pregnant woman everywhere she went. Finally, Latona fled to the island that was called the **Quail** <note>original: "Wachtel"; referring to the island Ortygia, from the Greek *ortyx* for quail.</note> or **Ortygia**, and it floated back and forth upon the sea. There she gave birth, just before the dragon **Pytho** could catch her, to her daughter **Diana**. Diana was so large and powerful that, instead of a midwife, she helped her mother bring her brother **Apollo** into the world. Apollo, even as a newborn, was already so equipped with strength that he shot the dragon that had chased his mother with arrows. He then began to give answers to everyone who came to him regarding their questions about future things. Some interpret this to mean that after the great floods in the time of King **Ogygis** <note>A legendary king of Attica or Boeotia, associated with a primordial flood that predated the one of Deucalion.</note>, almost...

<header># The Third Book.</header>

...at the departure of the Children of Israel from Egypt, traveling across all of Thessaly, <note>original: "Thessalien"</note> great damage was done. Also, as these events receded, the waters would not dry up, but for a long time left a dampness and fog from the rising heat of the sun. Because of this, in many places around the Egyptian Sea and in Greece, neither the sun nor the moon could be seen at all. At last, when the mists thinned somewhat and were no longer so thick—especially around the islands where, by natural cause, mists cannot be as thick as on the land—it happened that on one particular day, precisely on this island of **Ortygia**, <note>An ancient name for Delos, often associated with "quail."</note> the light of the moon was glimpsed, followed immediately by the brilliance of the rising sun. Thus, everyone was gladdened, saying that the sun and moon, which had been considered lost, were back again, appearing as if newly born into the day. For this reason, they named the island **Delos**, which signifies a "showing" or "manifestation." <note>original: "erzeigung"</note> 

To give this poetic story an impressive appearance, they took a woman named **Latona** <note>Also known as Leto, the mother of Apollo and Diana.</note> who happened to have given birth to twins at that same time. The dragon **Python** <note>original: "Phyto"</note> also signifies nothing other than the swirling clouds and foggy vapors tossed to and fro by the wind, which are darkened before the light of the sun and moon. The fact that **Juno** <note>Hera, often representing the air or the earth in these allegorical readings.</note> created this same dragon signifies that sometimes Juno is understood to represent the earth, and at other times the sea, out of which such vapors rise. That **Diana** was born first signifies that the moonlight precedes the brilliance of the sun, and that the moon, like a midwife, receives the sun’s rays in its horned, curved light. Together, they kill the dragon with their heat, by which they dry up the moisture. The fact that **Apollo** gives answers signifies that long afterward, the temple was built as mentioned above, and people allowed themselves to be deluded into believing that prophecies were given there. Also, that some call the island the "navel of the earth" <note>original: "nabel des erdpodens"</note> should not be understood as if it were situated in the center of the world's geography.

## Epidelius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Landing.

In former times, a small spot lay on the promontory of **Malea** in the **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note> where **Malvasia** <note>The fortress-city of Monemvasia.</note> is now, and it was named **Epidelius**. For, as heard above, when **Menophanes**, the captain of **Mithridates**, plundered the island and temple of Delos, someone threw the statue of **Apollo** into the sea out of contempt. It was washed by the sea to that shore. When the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> found it within their territory, they preserved it with great devotion and erected a temple for it there.

## Phaneus. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Appearing.

The island of **Chios**, which was once called **Aethalia**, **Chia**, **Macris**, and **Pityusa**, is now called **Chios** <note>original: "Schio"</note> and is still subject to the **Genoese** (to whom it was given by **Michael Palaiologos**, the Emperor of Constantinople, two hundred and ninety-two years ago, along with the city of **Smyrna** which lies opposite it in **Anatolia**). This same island has a promontory called **Phaneum**, now **Capo Mastico**, where there is a very deep harbor. A temple of this Apollo was located there, with a grove of palms, so that he is said to take his name from this mountain. However, some also say the mountain is named thus because **Latona**, while fleeing, came to the promontory and there first caught sight of the island of **Delos**. **Gaius Verres** also plundered this temple and stole the statues, as **Cicero** testifies. **Macrobius** believes his name...

# Concerning the Heathen Gods

...comes from the fact that the sun appears new every day. **Phornutus** <note>A Stoic philosopher also known as Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, known for his allegorical interpretations of Greek myths.</note> however, says it is because the sun makes all things visible and revealed. Some wish for him to be called **Anapheus**, after the island of **Santorini** <note>original: "Sanct Erini"</note> which is not far from **Crete**, <note>original: "Candien"</note> lying about eight miles away, and was anciently called **Anaphe**. Within that place, there was once a temple of this god.

## Phœbus. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Pure.

Because the sun is so pure and clear, they call him **Phœbus**; and as some say, it is because he purifies men of their misdeeds. Some say the name comes from his grandmother, the mother of **Latona**. <note>The author likely means Phoebe, the Titaness who was the mother of Leto (Latona).</note> Others say it is because he gives light and life, which in Greek would be called *phos* and *bios*. <note>original: "φως vnd βιος"</note> **Cornificius** says his name refers to the meaning that he shoots and wounds with great force. <note>Likely referring to the sun's rays as arrows.</note>

## Aigenetes, Argenetes, Archogenetes.

On the island of **Rhodes**, <note>original: "Rodis"</note> about two miles toward the north where **Filerimos** <note>original: "filerno"</note> now lies, there was a city called **Kamiros**. Both there and between **Lindos**, there stood a statue cast from bronze dedicated to **Apollo**. It was made and erected by **Chares of Lindos**, <note>original: "Carete dem Lindier"</note> a famous master craftsman. It stood one hundred and five feet high until it fell during an earthquake in the time of **Ptolemy Philopator**, <note>Ptolemy IV, reigned 221–204 BCE.</note> as some claim; others say it fell and broke at the knees in the time of **Pompey the Great**. The image was so large that there were few who could wrap their arms around its thumb. The master spent twelve years making it, and it cost two hundred and forty thousand crowns. Somewhere on its chest, the statue had a mirror in which one could see all the ships departing from **Alexandria** in Egypt. Some nine hundred years ago, the **Saracens** (in the time of the **Emperor Phocas**) loaded the pieces onto nine hundred camels and carried them away.

Now, the people of Kamiros worshipped this very Apollo in place of the sun, giving him names as the one who rises new every day, as the one who begets, sees, hatches, brings forth, nourishes, and increases all things. And although I know some write that **Lindos** and **Kamiros** were joined together by the god **Ialysos** to make the single city of **Rhodes** out of three before this **Colossus** was fully erected, it nonetheless remains that they always honored Apollo specifically in one statue or another. 

Likewise, in **Sicily**, there is still today a landing place and suburb called **Schiso**, <note>Modern Giardini Naxos.</note> which was once called **Naxos**, built by the Athenians under their leader **Theocles** and destroyed by **Dionysius the Tyrant**. There, an altar was erected to **Apollo Archegetes**, <note>Apollo the Founder or First Leader.</note> to which sailors made their vows. This Apollo also had a temple in **Megara** made of baked stones, which the **Emperor Hadrian** later renewed in marble. His image there, however, is made of **ebony wood**, which—being without fruit or foliage—is said to grow and become large under the earth, never shooting forth into the sun. Much of this is found in the Rhineland, and now some small watches <note>original: "vhrlin" — likely referring to portable timepieces or small table clocks.</note> are brought to Germany which are said to be encased in this wood.

...snatches—as a wolf snatches sheep—or because it makes all things prophetic and visible, they have given him this name. Also, the ancient Greeks called the brightly appearing, pressing daylight before the rising of the sun *Lyceum*. <note>The author is connecting the Greek word *lykos* (wolf) with *lyke* (light), an ancient etymological association for Apollo Lyceus.</note>

Thus, there is a city in the land of Egypt, formerly called **Lycopolis** and now called **Munia**, <note>Modern day El Minya.</note> where signs still exist showing that the sun was highly honored there, but was called **Lycu**; a wolf was worshipped in its place because this animal, just like the sun, draws all things to itself and sees in the night just as well as in the day—much as the sun gives its daylight to other places when it is night for us.

In **Athens**, there is a place—which was later the school of **Aristotle**—where an ancient temple stood dedicated to **Apollo Lyceus**, taking its name from **Lycus**, the son of **Pandion**.

**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note> reports further that under this name, **Apollo** also had a temple at **Argos** in **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese.</note> which was quite famous and costly. It held two statues: one that **Danaus** had commissioned to be made of wood along with the temple, which had perished through age, and another carved by **Attalus** the Athenian that stood there in his time. The reason **Danaus** built this temple was as follows: When **Danaus** came to **Argos**, he entered into a dispute over the sovereignty with **Gelanor**, the son of **Sthenelus**. Although the common people held many negotiations, they could not reach a decision against **Gelanor**, who claimed all rights by force. A day was appointed to deliberate on what should be done. As the time of the appointed day drew near, just as it was dawning and the cattle were being driven out of the city, a wolf appeared and fell upon the herd. It fought primarily with a bull that had undertaken to protect the herd. When the common people saw this struggle, they said: the bull is **Gelanor**, and the wolf is **Danaus**; for just as the wolf is hated by men, so **Danaus** was driven out from his own and sought to seize the property of another, whereas **Gelanor** fought hard for his "herd." As a great crowd gathered, it was decided that he whose animal won the fight should rule. Thus, the bull was defeated, and **Danaus** kept the kingdom. For this reason, he believed that **Apollo** had sent this wolf into the herd, and therefore he erected the temple to him. 

Some claim that **Sicyon** <note>original: "Sicionien"</note> is now **Basilica**; others say it is **Chiarenza** in **Morea**. **Pausanias** says there was a fallen temple there in his time, once consecrated and dedicated to this **Apollo** for this reason: at one time, the wolves did such great damage to the sheep that the citizens could gain no benefit from them. They were then instructed by **Apollo** to seek a dry log in a certain place, peel it, take the bark, and place it as bait within meat for the wolves. As soon as the wolves ate it, they all died from it. They kept the peeled log in the temple for a long time, but the priests could never say what kind of wood it actually was.

It has a flowing water once called **Xanthus**, now **Sirbis**, which pours into the **Macri** gulf. <header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

Apollo brought great fame, renown, and honor to the entire province [of Lycia], as both Diodorus and Herodotus mention. These Lycians had a law and custom that was found nowhere else: the children were named after their mothers. Likewise, if one were to be considered noble, he had to possess nobility from his mother's side; the father's heritage counted for nothing. Whether this temple is the same one that Strabo <note>Greek geographer, c. 63 BC – 24 AD.</note> attributes to Latona <note>Apollo’s mother.</note> is not something to be settled at this time. In any case, there were many other temples in Patara as well as this one. It is said that at the small headland where Patara extends into the sea, a man named Lycus found a chest carried there by the waves of the water. When he opened it, there was a painting inside of Apollo with his attributes: rays, a bow, and a lyre. Because of this, he immediately founded and built the temple as a memorial.

## Lycoctonos. Wolf-slayer.

Among the Athenians, there was once a law that whoever killed a young wolf in the province of Attica (which is now called the Duchy <note>The author refers to the Duchy of Athens, a Crusader state.</note>) was given a talent—that is, six hundred crowns. But to the one who brought in an old wolf, the reward was doubled. They were such enemies to the wolves; and because Apollo was otherwise considered a patron and protector of shepherds, they believed he was naturally opposed to wolves. Thus, he received this name. It is also to be noted that the wolf—which is otherwise dedicated to Mars—is banished by Apollo. They say that in Argos, on the marketplace, this Apollo had his temple.

## Lycobanta. Lycegenetes.
->Day-tracker / Year-bringer.<-

Homer calls Apollo by this name because he tracks the day and brings the early brilliance, leading the year through the zodiac. From this, it is said that the Sun is particularly inclined toward the wolf, and Apollo has a special delight in that animal, because his mother Latona turned into a wolf when she gave birth to him, in order to escape Juno. For this reason, a bronze wolf <note>original: "öhriner wolff"</note> was erected in the temple at Delphi to commemorate this story. However, there are those who say it does not signify the transformation of Latona, but rather a different event: once, some church-thieves broke in, stole the treasure, and buried it. When no one could discover where it was, a wolf came into the temple, grabbed a priest by his garment, and led him to the treasures, where the wolf began to scratch at the earth. Thus they dug after it and found what was lost.

## Lycoreus.

They say that when the Great Flood of Deucalion <note>The Greek version of the Great Flood story.</note> came to Thessaly—of which more was mentioned previously—the wolves gathered together and ran toward a mountain. Whoever followed them there escaped, while all the others drowned. There, a city called Lycorea was built, and in it, a temple to Apollo. Yet some write that this city stood above the temple at Delphi, and that Apollo’s name comes from there because his son, Lycoris, built it.

# Latous, Latoius, Latonigena, Latonius.

->Son of Latona.<-

The poets and other writers give Apollo all these names because of his mother’s hair <note>Likely a reference to his maternal lineage.</note>. For Latona is otherwise a name for the Night; and as Apollo appears at the end of the night—at the moment the Sun rises as if out of the womb of the night—she is assigned to him as a mother. Furthermore, the Night is called Latona because through sleep, she introduces the forgetting of all things <note>A play on the Greek *Lethe*, meaning forgetfulness, which sounds similar to *Leto* (Latona).</note>. In this context, Jupiter is called his father because the Sun has its course in the heavens and through the air—for which Jupiter is also sometimes taken to represent.
Between Megara and Corinth, exactly where one lordship and border divides the other, this Jupiter had a temple.

# Opsophagus. The Gourmand.

Celius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), an Italian scholar who wrote the *Antiquae Lectiones*.</note> indicates that the people of Elis gave this name to Apollo and honored him under it; no doubt because the Sun, with its eternal course, ripens and "consumes" all things—indeed, just as the Sun brings things to fruition, it also persists with unperishing stability.

# Epicurius. The Helper.

Megalopolis, which is now called Londari in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, had in the Valley of Lycaean Jupiter an exceedingly beautiful bronze statue of this Apollo, which stood about twelve feet high. This same statue, however, came from Phigalia (which is now called Neospiti in Arcadia). Near that same city, about a gunshot’s distance away, a magnificent temple decorated with beautiful marble was built for this God, such that even the roof was made of marble tiles. The reason for this was their claim that Apollo had helped them at a time of pestilence. The master builder of this temple was Ictinus <note>The famous architect of the Parthenon in Athens.</note>. Bassae was the name of the place where it stood, and later, during the wars of the Greeks, the city and temple were plundered, and the statue was taken to Londari.

# Spodius. Of the Ashes.

In Thebes in Boeotia (which is now Ediles), there is a stone or rock where they say Hercules was lulled to sleep by Minerva during his madness—at the time he wished to kill Amphitryon <note>Hercules' mortal stepfather.</note>. Having sunk down upon that very spot, an altar of ashes <note>The name "Spodius" comes from the Greek *spodos*, meaning wood-ash.</note> was erected and consecrated to this Apollo. Certain divinations and oracles were also performed there.

# Delphinius. The Dolphin.

Some say that Apollo transformed himself into a dolphin when Castalio the Cretan, together with his followers, was driven out by his own people and sailed forth to seek a new seat. They say Apollo swam before them until they reached Cirrha (now called Aspropiti), located on the Gulf near Patara; for Crissa lies between Suola (called Anticyrrha) and Aspropiti, and that is where they landed. Plutarch says that Apollo sent them a dolphin and did not swim before them himself.

For previously, every manslayer had to be a permanent fugitive from the state; or, if he were caught in the place where he committed the killing, he had to die there. The Aeginetans dedicated one month in the year to this Apollo, in which they offered sacrifices to Jove and celebrated; some believe it is April, but they called it *Ikisten* or *Domatites*.

## Delphic. ->At Delphi.<-

Since in all the world there was no more famous sanctuary among the heathens that could equal this sanctuary at Delphi—and because high and low-born persons from all over the world brought their most important concerns there and fetched answers, either in person or through messengers—I cannot refrain from giving a somewhat more detailed account of it.

The city of Delphi is located in Phocis, just two miles above the previously mentioned Aspronisi. There, in ancient times—even as far back as the time of Joshua <note>The author synchronizes the founding of the oracle with the biblical era of Joshua, successor to Moses.</note>—there was a chasm and a rift in the earth. As the shepherds were tending their livestock nearby, there were some goats, one of which went to the cave; and as she peered into the cave, she became strangely joyful, and also had a different voice than before, leaping and acting strangely. A shepherd named Coretas saw them go there; it seemed to him that something was not right, so he crept after her one time. There he found the chasm. He immediately became frantic, as if he were possessed, yet he spoke of things to come. When he came to himself again, he told other people. Thus a crowd gathered, driven by curiosity, until everyone realized that those who looked inside became somewhat out of their senses; therefore, they held it to be an earthly prophecy and considered it a place where a divine spirit dwelt.

For a good while it continued that if someone wanted to know the future, two would go together, and one would be sent ahead to hear what the matter was. But eventually, many fell into the pit out of lack of caution and perished. To prevent this, the inhabitants appointed a woman named Themis to do what was necessary and tell the answers to those who asked. So that she might stand over the chasm without worry or danger, they forged an iron tripod <term>tripod: a three-legged stool or stand</term>, upon which she could sit and receive the vapor of the spirit without falling. Soon after, those who wished to be devout attributed the true prophecy to Apollo, following the departure of Themis. Therefore, they placed a maiden in that same spot named Phemonoe, who was the first priestess of Apollo. To give it more prestige, they made her a hut or small church out of olive branches brought from the Tempe <note>The Vale of Tempe in Greece, sacred to Apollo.</note> (that is, from the pleasant valley in Thessaly by the river Peneus, where the place Lago Fichio now is). This was the first temple.

Afterward, as some claim, when this temple became dry and unsightly, a citizen of Delphi named Ptera built a temple for Apollo out of nothing but honeycombs. And because *Ptera* signifies a wing <note>original: "flügel"</note>, it was said afterward that this temple was made of bees' wings mixed with honeycombs. And although *Pteris* otherwise signifies the herb we call Forest Fern <note>original: "Waldfharn"</note>, I am very much of the opinion that from the same, so that it...

Since it was not always convenient for everyone to travel so far to gather olive branches, and perhaps because at that time no olive trees yet grew in these lands. Later, after this temple also became too dilapidated, a certain devout and wealthy man was found who took on the expense and built an entirely **brazen** <note>original: "öhrinen"; meaning bronze or brass.</note> temple for this Apollo. I can well believe, however, that it was hardly larger than what was required for the priests to have their place. We may let the fable pass which says that **Vulcan** <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and smithing.</note> built it; it might rather be that the master builder held this name. And this very temple—during the time of **Obed** <note>A biblical figure, the father of Jesse and grandfather of King David, used here to synchronize Greek and Hebrew chronologies.</note>, roughly fourteen hundred and fifty years before the birth of Christ—was set on fire and burned by Phlegra <note>Likely referring to the Phlegyans, a mythical tribe noted in Greek lore for attacking and burning the temple at Delphi.</note>; others say it was destroyed by thunder and an earthquake. It could also be that **Delphus**, the son of Celemon, or as some say the grandson of the Cretan Castalius (born to his daughter Thyia), gave himself out to be the son of Apollo. Later, he established the settlement around the temple and named it after himself. As his power increased, he declared and established this temple in honor of his father.

The **fourth temple** was built by the two master builders **Trophonius and Agamedes**, about whom we have spoken in the appropriate place, including the reward they received for it. This temple also did not stand for an exceedingly long time, as it was also burned during the time of **Servius Tullius**, the king of Rome.

Now, the city of **Delphi** is situated on a hill, at the very top of which stood the temple, with the city built all around it. Its perimeter took up about half a mile; from a greater distance, it appeared to be roughly one small mile. There lies a very fine, fertile plain, suitable for all kinds of grain and fruit. This spot is located exactly in the middle of the Greek lands, which is why some have called it the **navel of the earth** <note>The *Omphalos*, a stone monument representing the center of the world.</note>. **Pindar** <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet from Thebes.</note> brought forth the little myth that two eagles were sent out by **Jove** <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note>, one from the sunset and the other from the sunrise, and they met at the same point in flight. For that reason, a golden navel with beautiful decorations and two eagles once stood in the temple.

It is also said that the son of Deucalion, **Amphictyon**, King of Athens, built a council house there and established it so that in the pressing business of the common Greek lands—which were thereafter bound together—they should offer common sacrifices at designated festivals. They were also to maintain public spectacles at the common expense. Every province or city was to send its ambassadors and messengers, who were then called the **Amphictyons**. The allies were as follows: the **Ionians** (where the Quiscer <note>This may refer to a contemporary 16th-century name for a group under Ottoman/Turkish rule.</note> now live in Turkey), the **Dolopes**, **Thessalians**, **Aeaners**, **Magnetes**, **Malians**, **Phthiotians**, **Dorians**, **Phocians**, **Locrians**, and **Phocidians**. Later, the **Macedonians** also entered the council, while the Phocians and Lacedaemonians were removed. By the command of **Augustus**, the Malians and Nicopolitans were finally added. Thus, the Nicopolitans took the place of the Dolopes; the Macedonians and Thessalians each gave two councilors for their province. The Boeotians, Phocians, and Delphians each gave two men per province; the Dorians, Locrians, and those of Negroponte <note>Euboea.</note> each gave one man per province. The Ozolians gave one man. Thereafter, each of the aforementioned places gave one, so that in the time of **Hadrian**, there were thirty councilors of the Amphictyons.

The first to attack this city and temple was a lord from the island of **Negrepont** <note>The medieval name for Euboea.</note> named **Python**, who was a son of Crius. He was present at the very beginning; he plundered the city and the foundation. Since the Delphians were too weak to resist him, they complained of the tyrant's arrogance to **Apollo**. As the scoundrel was retreating into his camp, he and his band fell and died at that spot; thereafter, the place and the plot of land were named Python. This is where the myth comes from, regarding how Apollo slew a dragon called **Python**, and that is indeed the origin of the name. And this very event might perhaps be considered the first burning of the temple.

**Tochinolicasti** <note>Likely a corruption of a local place name.</note> is now a spot in Stymphalus, which was once called **Gorthynium**, where **Phlegyas**—the father of **Ixion** and a son of **Mars**—ruled. He was a reckless man; when he heard that his daughter had been dishonored by Apollo, he immediately set out and burned the second temple. Because of this, Apollo cast him into the **Underworld** <note>original: "hell"; referring to Tartarus in Greek mythology.</note> and had him chained there, such that a great stone constantly hangs over his head, the fall of which he must always fear. This may be the source of the second fire. However, some believe that Phlegyas represents the "fire" and "fiery spirit" of tyrants who raise themselves above all reason, from which height they are ultimately cast down to the ground. Then, once their conscience and knowledge begin to strike them, they first realize what a burden, danger, and misery lies upon their necks and over their heads, for which they must live in constant fear.

And although few write of it, some say that **Pyrrhus**, the son of **Achilles**, after returning home from Troy, practiced great piracy upon the sea and also plundered this temple—perhaps out of poverty, or perhaps out of arrogance. Ultimately, he was killed by Apollo or his priest **Macareus**. If anyone argues that this was the temple built by **Trophonius**, they will find no resistance from me; for about a hundred years before, Trophonius had established it. It is true that this same temple was also burned later, around the time of the **Jewish Captivity** <note>Referring to the Babylonian Exile (6th century BCE), used as a chronological marker.</note>, near its end. When these efforts did not succeed, they contracted with the **Amphictyons** <note>A religious league of Greek tribes that served as guardians of the Delphi sanctuary.</note> to rebuild the temple at Delphi that had burned. The Amphictyons agreed on a sum of money to give them; in return, the Alcmaeonids were to build the temple according to the given design and the agreed-upon decoration. An agreement was reached. The Alcmaeonids, who were previously wealthy and capable as builders, had the temple prepared by **Spintharus**, a master builder from **Corinth**, in such a way that where common stone had been contracted, the building was executed with beautiful **marble**—especially at the front entrance—and was much more costly and decorative than promised. Through such building, they earned the gratitude and great favor of all Greece. Now, this temple came into such high reverence that all the world sent and gave their gifts, indeed entire treasuries, there; this continued until the time of **Christ**, when it ceased to be visited or to provide any further answers. **Croesus**, the King in **Lydia**, gave to this temple several gifts—namely, seventeen gold tablets which cost twenty-four thousand **crowns** <note>The "crown" (Krone) was a common gold coin in the author's time, used here to provide a contemporary sense of value.</note>. A lion cost six thousand crowns; alongside it were two mighty large bowls, one of gold and one of silver, of which the gold one was worth five thousand one hundred crowns, while the silver one held nearly twenty-eight **fuder** <term>fuder: a large historical unit of liquid measure, roughly equivalent to a heavy wagon-load or a large tun of wine</term> of wine. Furthermore, there were two silver wine-casks and two casting-vessels, one gold and one silver. Besides other gifts, there were cast images of silver, along with several necklaces, belts, and borders of precious stones that his wife had worn; some estimate the value of what **Croesus** gave in gold and silver at eight million and four **tons of gold** <note>A "ton of gold" was a figurative expression for a vast sum, often 100,000 guilders.</note>.

When, some fifty or sixty years later, the captains of **Xerxes**, the Persian King, fell upon **Greece**, and a detachment of those people approached **Delphi** to plunder these and other treasures, the Delphians asked whether they should hide or bury such goods. The priestess gave them the answer that they should let them be; for **Apollo** was strong enough to rescue his own property. The Delphians let the matter rest; each looked to his own defense, hid his own belongings, and fled wherever he could, so that no more than sixty men, along with the priestess, remained in the city. The Persians arrived and occupied the **Temple of Minerva** <note>Referring to the Temple of Athena Pronaia.</note>, which stood in the valley before the Temple of Apollo, toward which they pressed. But from the mountains that lay above the temple, great rocks fell and split apart, crushing the robbers; thunder, lightning, hail, and bolts of fire put them to flight, so that the sixty men pursued them and slew a great portion of the enemies. 

Besides these gifts, there was a bronze ox of the **Corcyreans** <note>People of Corfu.</note>. This very wealth made the **Germans** or **Galatians** <note>Referring to the Celts/Gauls who invaded Greece in 279 BC.</note> under King **Brennus** quite eager, about a hundred years after the Persians had attacked the temple. Therefore, Brennus, with the consent of all the Galatians, prepared to overrun the Greeks. He knew of their wealth, both in the cities and in the religious foundations. He brought together one hundred and fifty thousand infantry, and twenty thousand four hundred **young lords** <note>noble cavalrymen or knights.</note>, each of whom was on horseback, yet accompanied by two servants who were also mounted and ready to spring into the saddle if needed. If the lord were wounded or stabbed, the servant would mount, or would carry the wounded man out of the battle. Thus, these lords were called the **Three-marr-men** or **Three-hitched** <term>Trimarcisia: a Celtic cavalry system where each rider was supported by two reserves</term>. # Of Pagan Gods

Since the Hungarians, Thracians, and Thessalians allowed their hair to grow long and shaggy <note>The author uses "haar glassen/ragtend" to describe a wild or unkempt appearance, often associated in early modern texts with "barbaric" warriors.</note>, they gathered themselves to resist the enemy. They brought forth about twenty thousand on foot and five hundred on horse, and thus came to clash with the enemy. They skirmished and killed many; however, they only succeeded in provoking the **Germans** <note>Though the author uses "Teütschen" (Germans), the historical event described is the Gallic invasion of Greece in 279 BC led by the Celtic chieftain Brennus.</note> into such a rage that they behaved with great brutality. They stabbed everyone who possessed life wherever they could gain the upper hand. They razed and plundered **Aetolia**, burned the cities and temples, and also forced a free passage through the mountain passes of **Mount Parnassus**, opening the narrow defiles so that Brennus could march directly upon **Delphi**. The citizens fled toward the temple, where the priestess promised them the help of **Apollo**. Whoever was able among the **Greeks** also marched there, for **Brennus** had divided his army. **Brennus** pressed on strongly, and the **Greeks** trotted after, harassing them as much as they could. As he now neared the temple, the earth and the camp began to tremble; a truly terrifying storm with hail, lightning, and thunder broke out. It came to a tempest of strikes, which cost many a man his life; the reinforcement did its best and held its ground well. At night, a great cold set in, followed by rain and snow, so that the **Germans**, who had no fire, could not easily help themselves. The mountain ridges collapsed, driving large boulders and stones into the camp, whereby the soldiers suffered great damage. Thus, ten, twenty, or thirty were struck down at once.

Now **Justinus** <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian who epitomized the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note> says that the temple is surrounded by precipices and rocks. People live therein as if in houses, and the city along with the temple has no wall, except for the steep rocks that surround them. Therefore, when a clamor and shouting arises from the people, it echoes in the ravines and creates such a resonance that one believes thunder and lightning are present; additionally, it shakes and loosens the stones so that they tumble down. Because of this, the ignorant are so greatly terrified, as if it were a punishment and special plague from **God** standing against them. Then, by day, the **Greeks** attacked them from the front and rear. Despite all this misfortune, while **Brennus** was still upright, a brave resistance was maintained; but when he was severely wounded and could not oversee all matters, things began to fail. Indeed, a panic entered the camp so that they all fled, as if a great army of knights were chasing them. They recognized neither friend nor foe and stabbed one another. At that same time, the entire countryside rose up and fell upon the enemy. But since their number was too great to be entirely restrained, the **Greeks** cut off all provisions for the remainder. Through this, hunger and the "rogue" <term>schelm: here referring to a pestilence or plague that follows famine</term> overcame the **Germans**. They say **Brennus** lost thirty-two thousand men there, between the initial battles, the storms, and the famine. **Brennus** took his own life when he saw that he had led out and led astray so many of his people in vain. After his death, they were all killed and wiped out by the **Greeks**, so that not a single one (as **Pausanias** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> believes) returned home. 

Yet there are those who say that the treasure and gold from this temple—valued at ninety times a hundred thousand **crowns**—made its way out to **Toulouse**. When they had done this, and later the Roman captain **Quintus Cepio** fished the gold out of the lake, the "rogue" <note>the plague</note> came behind him and his troop and strangled them all miserably. Therefore, when the Phocians occupied the field of the Cirrheans, which was dedicated to the foundation, they were fined a sum of money. If they paid it, they would be safe; if not, they and all their dominion were to be dedicated and banned <note>original: "verpannet," meaning placed under a religious curse or placed under a ban of outlawry</note> to Apollo. This matter seemed too burdensome for them, and they found a captain named Philomelus, who wished to be a leader; he plundered the temple and hired foreign mercenaries with that same money, so that he would be strong enough against the Amphictyons <note>The Amphictyonic League was an ancient religious association of Greek tribes formed to protect the temple of Apollo</note>, who would take up the matter. The Thebans were the first who withdrew from the affair and often clashed with the temple-robbers; they prevailed, and, as time allowed, they eventually put the Phocians to flight. Philomelus threw himself down from a cliff. Then a captain was raised up afterward named Onemarchus; he was considered a fool <note>original: "dūppel," a simpleton</note>, and the soldiers said he had led them astray, for which they had to suffer a misfortune <note>original: "schnapp," meaning a sudden blow or setback</note>; they shot him themselves. In his place, they elected Phayllus, who died miserably and soon. His son Phalecus became captain and commander; he had stolen from the treasure and had to flee; he was killed in Crete while besieging a city.

When the war had lasted ten years, Philip, the Macedonian King, also entered the game and came to march against the temple-robbers. However, when the Phocians wanted to build a fortress near the temple, they were overrun by the Boeotians, caught, and defeated—indeed, hunted all the way into the temple, which they themselves had desecrated. Yet they believed they should have sanctuary within it; this resulted in their end, for they burned in the temple, which was set on fire by someone unknown. Their cities and territory were razed; their legal standing in the Amphictyonic court was taken from them and granted to the Macedonians.

The Phocians are said to have robbed more than seventy-two million in gold from this temple. That is called "devouring church property," but it is also called "vomiting it back up" in return. This temple had a wide outer court, and after that a walkway <note>original: "Dhan," likely referring to a track or path within the sacred precinct</note>, and in front of the porch stood many kinds of statues. From this, it can be understood that Nero alone took five hundred bronze statues of gods and men from there. Next is the sacrificial altar, which is very large; then the chapel, which is built in a circle with beautiful columns, upon which hang several golden shields <note>original: "tartschen," small round shields or bucklers</note> that the Athenians offered after the Persian victory. In the porch of the temple are written the sayings of the ancient wise men; at the innermost part is an altar of Apollo, upon which he stands made of clear, cast gold. Few people are allowed to go to that place.

In front of the temple was a white rock upon which they said Herophile the Sibyl <note>The Sibyl was a woman in antiquity believed to possess prophetic powers</note> had stood and prophesied; also long before her, another Sibyl. Herophile, however, lived somewhat before the Trojan War; she calls herself Diana's sister, a daughter, and a wife of Apollo, and says she was born of an immortal mother.

When one comes back out of the court, one reaches the theater; there, every five years, the spectacles called the Pythian Games were held, in the same manner and form as the Olympic Games. These games were established in the times of Eurylochides the Thessalian and the leader in the Council of the Amphictyons, when the war against the Cirrheans was ended and victory was won. For the Cirrheans, whom I called Asprobitians and mentioned above, had withdrawn and taken by force some goods from Apollo and his foundation. Therefore, the Amphictyons did not want to let such a thing go unpunished and took counsel with Solon <note>Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker and one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>...

They brought forth about twenty thousand on foot and five hundred on horse, thus coming to encounter the enemy. They skirmished and killed many, but they first provoked the Germans <note>The author uses "Teutschen" (Germans) to describe the Gauls/Celts under Brennus, a common identification in early modern German historiography</note> into a rage, so that they dealt roughly, stabbing everything that had life wherever they could become masters. They razed and plundered Aetolia, burned the cities and temples, and also had to allow the march of Brennus to pass freely and open the narrow passes of the mountains, so that he moved directly upon Delphi. The citizens fled toward the temple; the priests promised them the help of Apollo. Whoever was able among the Greeks also marched there, for Brennus had divided his company. Brennus pressed on strongly; the Greeks followed behind, harassing them as much as they could. 

As he now neared the temple, the ground and the camp began to tremble; a most gruesome storm with hail and lightning, thunder and the like, presented itself. It came to storming and striking; the temple-keepers <note>original: "Koster," likely referring to the sacristans or guardians of the temple</note> played the man; the reinforcements did their best and held their ground well. At night a great cold set in, then rain and snow, so that the Germans—who had no fire—could not help themselves well. The mountains cracked and drove great boulders and stones into the camp, whereby the soldiers met with great harm, so that ten, twenty, or thirty were destroyed at once. 

Now Justinus <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian who epitomized the works of Pompeius Trogus</note> says that the temple is surrounded by cliffs and rocks. Therein the people dwell as if in houses, and the city along with the temple has no wall, except for the steep rocks that surround them. For this reason, when a clamor and cry is raised by the people, it echoes in the ravines and the resonance gives such a roar that one believes thunder and lightning are present; moreover, it shatters and loosens the stones so that they run down, from which the ignorant are so highly terrified, as if it were a punishment and special plague from God which stood against them. 

From behind and in front, the Greeks then fell upon them by day. In all this misfortune, while Brennus was still upright, a brave resistance was made; but when he was hard wounded and could not look to all matters, things began to fail. Indeed, a terror <note>This refers to "Panic" fear, traditionally attributed to the god Pan at Delphi</note> came into the camp so that they all fled from there, as if a great troop of horsemen were hunting them. They knew neither friend nor foe and stabbed one another. At that same time, the entire countryside was up in arms and fell upon the enemy. But as the number of the enemy was too great to be entirely subdued, the Greeks allowed no food to reach the survivors. Thereby hunger and <term>schelm</term> <note>original: "schelm," here referring to a pestilence or "murrain" affecting the troops</note> overcame the Germans. They say Brennus lost thirty-two thousand there in the first fighting, the storming, and in the distress of hunger. Brennus brought death upon himself when he saw that he had led out and misled so many of his people in vain. After his death, they were all killed and wiped out by the Greeks, so that not one (as Pausanias <note>Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD</note> believes) returned home. 

Yet there are those who say that the treasure and gold from this temple, worth nearly nine million crowns, came out to Toulouse; and as this city was constantly plagued thereafter with the pestilence or boils so that there would be no end to the dying, it was shown to them that as long as they did not cast the church-robbery <note>The "Gold of Toulouse" (Aurum Tolosanum) was legendary for bringing misfortune to its possessors</note> into the lake, they could not recover. When they had done that, and afterward the Roman captain Quintus Cepio fished the gold out of the lake, the <term>schelm</term> <note>The plague or curse</note> came upon him and his company and strangled them all miserably. <header>### The Third Book</header>

punishments, breaches of the land-peace, fines, and crimes of the cities and lands were assigned to this foundation <note>The "foundation" refers to the sacred precinct and treasury of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note>. Therefore, when the Phocians occupied the Cirrhean field, which was dedicated to the foundation, they were fined a sum of money; if they paid it, they would remain in safety; if not, they and all their dominion were to be dedicated and banned to Apollo. This matter proved too heavy for them; they found a captain named Philomelus, who wished to be their leader. He plundered the temple and hired foreign mercenaries with that same money, so that he might be strong enough against the Amphictyons <note>The Amphictyonic League was an ancient religious association of Greek tribes that protected the Delphic sanctuary</note>, who were the ones taking up the dispute. The Thebans were the first to involve themselves in the matter; they often clashed with the temple-robbers, prevailing over them. As time went on, they once put the Phocians to flight, and Philomelus threw himself off a cliff. Then a captain was raised up after him named Onemarchus; he was considered a fool <note>original: "dǔppel"</note>, and the soldiers said he had led them astray, for which they had to suffer a blow; they shot him themselves. In his place, they elected Phayllus, who died miserably and soon. His son Phalecus became captain and marched forth; because he had stolen from the treasure, he had to flee, and was killed in Crete while besieging a city. 

When the war had lasted ten years, Philip, the Macedonian king, also entered the game and came to march against the temple-robbers. But when the Phocians wished to build a fortress near the temple, they were attacked by the Boeotians, caught, and beaten—indeed, hunted right into the temple which they themselves had desecrated. Yet they expected to have sanctuary within it, which turned out for them in such a way that they were burned in the temple, which was set on fire by person or persons unknown. Their cities and province were razed, and their right to sit in the Amphictyonic court was taken from them and granted to the Macedonians. The Phocians are said to have robbed more than seventy-two million in gold from this temple. This is called "devouring church property," but it is also called "vomiting it back up again." 

This temple had a wide courtyard, and according to that layout, many types of statues stood in a plan and before the groves; it can be gathered from this that Nero alone took five hundred bronze statues of gods and men from there. Next is the sacrificial altar, which is quite large, and then the chapel, which is built in a circle with beautiful columns; upon it hang several golden bucklers which the Athenians offered after the Persian victory. In the vestibule of the temple, the sayings of the ancient sages are written. In the innermost part, there is an altar of Apollo, upon which he stands made of pure cast gold; few people are allowed to go there. In front of the temple was a white rock, upon which they say the Sibyl Herophile stood and prophesied; another Sibyl also stood there long before her. Herophile lived somewhat before the Trojan War; she called herself Diana's sister, a daughter, and a wife of Apollo, and said she was born of an immortal mother. 

If one then leaves the courtyard again, one comes to the theater; there, every five years, the spectacles called the Pythian Games were held, in the same manner and form as the Olympic Games. These games were established in the time of Eurilochides the Thessalian, the head of the Council of the Amphictyons, when the war against the Cirrheans had ended in victory. For the Cirrheans—whom I named Asprobitj above—had withdrawn some goods from Apollo and his foundation and taken them by force. Therefore, the Amphictyons would not let such things rest and consulted with Solon <note>Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker and one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Delphic sanctuary, moving from the military conflicts of the Sacred Wars to the establishment and organization of the Pythian Games. It bridges the previous discussion of the Phocian War with the cultural and religious traditions that defined the site of Delphi.</meta>

<header>->Of Pagan Gods<-</header>

It was decided that the city and territory of the Cirrheans should be consecrated to the God <note>Apollo</note>. They besieged them and took away their water; when that would not suffice, they poisoned the streams that flowed into the city. They drank from them and all became sick, so that the city was easily stormed and captured. From that same place, a harbor for the Delphians was made. At first, it was decreed that every nine years the festival should be held and a sum of money given to the victor; but later, every five years, a laurel wreath was established as the reward of thanks. All kinds of poetry were read there, and the speakers or poets came together; whoever wrote the best and most pleasing work in praise of Apollo or on another chosen subject was crowned. For just as the harp <note>original: "harpff"; likely referring to the ancient lyre or kithara</note> given to Apollo is lovely, they wished to show through this contest that it was a lovely thing to practice such arts and skills. Thus the crowning of poets began and has remained until our own times. Other athletic games were held, just as in the Olympic Games, and were rewarded in the same manner, though with a different kind of wreath.

When all the world comes to the theater early in the morning, the heralds walk before the Amphictyons <note>The council of representatives from the Greek tribes who oversaw the sanctuary</note>, shouting. Those who are prepared should step forward. Then one comes forth and shows himself in the weapons and armor in which he intends to do his best. If he finds his equal, it is well; if no one wishes to contend with him, the Amphictyons bid him step down, but they give him no thanks <note>i.e., no prize or recognition for an uncontested victory</note>. If he is not satisfied, he demands that the heralds offer a challenge to anyone who is fresh to come and try him; if he finds an opponent, the contest <note>original: "schimpff"; historically meaning a sporting contest or jesting battle</note> begins. When the race is run, the priestess <note>original: "pfāffin"</note> must stand at the goal in her finery, holding a palm branch in her right hand and a lit torch in her left; likewise with the running and other events.

I will not be led astray by those who say that Diomedes established these games when he returned home without harm or shipwreck from the Trojan War. For whether it was this man or the former, it matters little, unless you wish to calculate the time: Diomedes lived some six hundred years before this Eurylochus. It may be that the games lapsed in the intervening time and were thus renewed. Others bring forward that the games are even a hundred or more years older than Diomedes, because Chrysothemis and his son Philammon won the prize for their singing and poetry in the time of Ilus the Trojan. Thamyris also competed there; Orpheus and Musaeus thought themselves too proud to compare their poetry there. However, the poets had to be able to sing their written poems themselves and strike the harp <note>kithara</note> or draw the bow on the violin <note>original: "geygen"; the author uses contemporary 16th-century instrument names for ancient Greek ones</note>. For this reason, Hesiod was at one time not admitted, because he could not sing or play the strings. But since Ptolemy son of Lagus <note>Ptholemeus Lagi</note> won the prize with two racing horses in the sixty-ninth Pythian games—which happened nearly in the one hundred and ninth Olympiad—then Eurylochus may well have renewed them in the forty-first Olympiad. At that time, the wonder occurred with Arion, whom the dolphin rescued from danger; and Solon must have been in his prime at nearly the same time. It also seems to me certain that they were always held in the year before the start of an Olympiad—that is, in the third year of every Olympiad—and just as those were held in summer, these were held at the beginning of spring, with a shining splendor.

Now, regarding this idolatry <note>Götzendienst</note>, it was always in the beginning, even long ago...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Delphic Oracle, specifically detailing the methods of prophecy, the history of the priestesses, and the eventual decline and plundering of the site under the Romans and later Christian emperors. <header>### The Third Book</header>

A young woman was traditionally used <note>as the Pythia, or priestess of Apollo</note> because she was considered somewhat purer and more secretive. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says that the Sibyl or prophetess in Delphi was possessed by the spirit in two ways: either through a thin, fiery breath that emerged from the chasm, or when she sat upon her tripod chair, which was consecrated for that purpose. When she opened herself to receive the spirit, it surrounded her and ignited her completely, like a fiery glow. Sometimes flames of fire burst out from the cavern, making her appear entirely radiant; at other times, she sat alone upon the vessel, appearing possessed and driven to frenzy. Thus, the Sibyl was overtaken by the spirit in various ways; it would seize her suddenly, yet it remained distinct from her, being something other than fire or breath. It had no fixed seat of its own, nor a place where anything natural or artificial could fully grasp it.

However, eventually, a man from Thessaly named Echecrates fell in love with a priestess, kidnapped her, and violated her. Because of this, a law was established that a fifty-year-old woman should be appointed to the office, though she was still dressed as a young woman. From this story, perhaps, Heliodorus <note>An ancient Greek novelist</note> took his never-sufficiently-praised poem of *Theagenes and Chariclea*, which he wrote in ten books. It is said he chose to resign from his wealthy bishopric in Tricca, Thessaly, rather than destroy his work. I have translated this work into German for the amusement and instruction of those who value passionate and righteous marital loyalty and love, and I intend to publish it in time.

When the priestess had no duties, she occupied herself with hunting; the young women were also free to leave the service and marry if they wished. As for who this Apollo was, how and by what means he prophesied, and how each of his answers was received, we shall explain in the *Book of the Oracles of the Idols*. However, the oracle began to decline early on. By the time of Cicero, Pompey, Appius Claudius, Censorinus, and Strabo, it had already become a paltry affair. While Augustus was still alive, people stopped giving to the sanctuary and instead began taking from it. Nero plundered it entirely; furthermore, he had several people slaughtered and thrown into the chasm from which the speaking spirit emerged. He gave the Cirrhean fields to his soldiers and moved the poetic and athletic contests to Olympus. Finally, in the time of Constantine, the priestess abandoned the site because there were no more sacrifices. Her tripod chair and the statues were carried off to the Hippodrome <note>original: "Reßplatz"; the arena for chariot racing</note> in Constantinople. All the gold and silver images were melted down, and the bronze ones were set up in the city to be mocked; those made of stone or wood were otherwise destroyed.

## Triopius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; At Triopium.

Triopius, the father of Erysichthon, built a city in Caria and named it Triopium after himself, because it had three corners and outlooks. Although Diodorus believes it was a promontory situated opposite Crete in Cnidus—which might now be, and indeed must be, Capo Chrio—the three cities in Rhodes (Ialyssus, Camirus, and Lindus, of which more is said elsewhere), the island of Cos (now called Lago), Cnidus, Chios, and Halicarnassus <note>Called Messî in our times</note>, along with their allies and subjects who called themselves Dorians, held their federal council and temple there. Perhaps Triopius, as a grandson of Apollo, established it for his grandfather. These cities would not admit anyone else into their league and union; they used a distinct dialect of the Greek language that differed from the others. In the athletic games they established in honor of Apollo, they allowed no...

### ->Ismenius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Ismenian.<-

Thebes—sometimes called Stibes—located in Boeotia, had seven famous gates named Proetis, Neita, Cranea, Hypsista, Ogygia, Homole, and Electra, as it is told. There was the Proetus Gate (named after a citizen who lived there), the String-Gate, the Skull-Gate, the Upper-Gate, the King’s Gate, the Homole Gate, and the Copper Gate. Right at the right hand of this last gate, there was a hill consecrated to Apollo. This hill, as well as the Apollo there, was called Ismenius because the River Ismenius flows past it. On the hill stands the temple, containing a statue of Apollo carved out of cedar wood <note>Original: "Jeder," likely meaning "Zeder" or cedar</note> by Canachus the Sicyonian.

A young noble boy who is healthy, handsome, and strong is elected annually as the priest. He walks about continually wearing a small laurel wreath <term>Daphnophorus <note>Greek for "laurel-bearer"</note></term>. Some who have served as priests for the year gift a three-footed vessel <note>a tripod</note> to the god as a memorial of their service, though they do not all do so—only those who are wealthy enough. It is said that Hercules was once a <term>Daphnophorus</term> priest in this temple, and his stepfather Amphitryon gifted a stool there that is very old; the inscription upon it is written in Cadmeian letters <note>An ancient form of the Greek alphabet attributed to the founder Cadmus</note>. Also in this temple was a golden shield and a golden hand-bow with golden arrows, which Croesus, the King of Lydia, gifted to Amphiaraus <note>A legendary seer and hero</note>; the quiver and spear were of the same craftsmanship.

### ->Ptoos. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; He of Mount Ptoos.<-

Located five miles from Thebes (or Stibes), on the three-peaked Mount Ptoos above Lake Copais, lay a city called Acrephia. About three-quarters of a mile from there was the temple of this Apollo, which had a great reputation and far-reaching fame among the ancients because the answers given there were so very truthful. Ptoos was said to be the son of Athamas and Themisto, and he gave his name to this mountain and the temple to Apollo. Mardonius the Persian <note>A leading Persian military commander during the Persian Wars</note>, while he was stationed in Thessaly and wished to know the outcome of his affairs, sent messengers to various places, including this one. He sent a clever man named the Mouse <note>Original: "Maus," referring to the Greek name Mys</note>. Because Mardonius wanted the answer to be kept secret, the messenger was not only admitted to the priestess but was also given two men to listen to what she told him. When he entered the temple, the priestess gave an answer that neither he nor the observers understood; however, when he wrote it down, Mardonius was able to understand what was said to him, for she had spoken in his own recognizable language <note>The oracle reportedly spoke in a "barbarian" tongue, likely Carian, which the messenger understood but the local Greeks did not</note>.

There is another tradition that Apollo received his name from "terror" <note>The author likely connects "Apollo" with the Greek "apollyon," meaning destroyer, or the German "schräcken" (fright)</note>, because when he and his sister were born to Latona, Juno sent a wild

<header># The Second Book.</header>

## Cerdoon. The Profiteer.

Because the priests of this God <note>Apollo</note> occasionally allowed themselves to be bribed for the sake of time and money, and spoke only what people wished to hear, this name was bestowed upon the God. Demosthenes, as a wise and prominent man, noted this clearly when Philip, King of the Macedonians, intended to suppress Greece. At that time, the priestess promised Philip everything he desired; indeed, she gave favorable and beneficial answers on his behalf to others as well. Therefore, Demosthenes said she "favored Philip" and flattered him, indicating this with the word *philippizein* <note>original Greek: φιλιππίζειν; meaning to speak or act in the interest of Philip of Macedon</note>.

## Patroon. The Fatherly.

The ancients also called Apollo *Patroon* <note>from "Patroos," meaning ancestral or paternal</note>, because he possesses his designs and power like a father; that is, the Sun has the power to give and help bring all things forth. However, Plato believes that Ion—who was born of Apollo and came to Athens—honored and gave this name to his father. Aristophanes, on the other hand, claims he was called this because the Greeks accepted him, along with Jupiter, as gods before all others. It was also then that he wed Creusa, the daughter of Erechtheus, from whom Ion was born, who gave the Ionians their name.

In Athens, at the Ceramicus <note>a quarter of Athens, originally the potters' district</note>, he had a chapel and a statue made by Euphranor <note>a famous Greek sculptor and painter</note>.

## Nomius. Shepherd / Lawgiver / Singer.

Since the Sun faithfully nourishes and pastures everything it creates, just like a shepherd, he became known as the Shepherd <note>Nomius</note>. Additionally, some give him this name because of song, as he is the leader, guide, and lord of the Muses. Furthermore, there was a law <note>The author puns on "Nomos," which in Greek means both "law" and "musical mode"</note> for playing the flute, in which one always perceives the power of Apollo in the tuning. There were five parts to be played and tuned: *Pera*, *Cataceleusmus*, *Jambus*, *Spondeus*, and *Catachoreusis*, which are said to have been taken from the struggle with the dragon <note>The Python</note>. 

*Pera* is the Counsel <note>original: "Ratſchlag"</note>, where he decided whether he might win anything from the dragon or if it would be his end. With the *Cataceleusmus*, he provoked the dragon. In the *Jambus* <note>The Iambic part</note>, one hears the dragon whirring and snapping its teeth. In the *Spondeus*, he lets up, and the matter becomes somewhat softer, as if the battle were won. In the *Catachoreusis*, everything comes together with a strong voice, very joyful and exulting in the victory. 

I almost believe that those in the Alpine regions—specifically in Switzerland today—resemble this music quite a bit with their little songs, such as when the maiden drives the brown bull along. For in those songs, the duty, nature, and manner of both the shepherd and the bull are expressed through the music. Truly, nothing is missed in that little song to show how a faithful shepherd should diligently watch his cattle, so that they know his voice and run to him—just as a good beast must be natured—just as bravely as one could recognize the struggle of Apollo in those musical tones. You will find other such songs elsewhere, such as "The Battle" <note>likely referring to famous 16th-century descriptive "Battle" compositions that imitated the sounds of war</note>...
