Agasicles of Messene performed best on one occasion, but he took his tripod home with him by force, whereas everyone else had always dedicated theirs to Apollo. To avenge this insult, the other five cities expelled the entire city of Halicarnassus from their community.

## Ismenius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Ismenian.

Thebes <note>original: "Stibes," a medieval variation of the name</note>, situated in Boeotia, had seven famous gates. Their names were Proetis, Neita, Cranea, Hypsista, Ogygia, Homole, and Electra, as it is said. The Proetian gate was named after a citizen who lived there; then the Cord-gate, the Skull-gate, the Upper-gate, the King-gate, the Homoloian-gate, and the Copper-gate. Directly to the right hand of this last gate, there was a hill dedicated to Apollo, and that same hill, along with the Apollo there, was called Ismenius, for the river Ismenius flows past it. Upon the hill is the temple, and inside the temple is an image of Apollo carved from cedar by Canachus the Sicyonian <note>a famous sculptor from Sicyon active around 500 BCE</note>.

A young, noble boy who is healthy, beautiful, and strong was chosen annually as the priest. He walks about continually wearing a small laurel wreath. Some who have been priests for a year dedicate a three-footed vessel <note>another reference to a tripod</note> with handles to the God as a memorial; however, they do not all do this, but only as each one is wealthy enough. Hercules is said to have been the *Daphnephorus*—that is, the priest <note>original: "Daphnophorus," literally "Laurel-bearer"</note>—in this temple, and his stepfather Amphitryon dedicated a chair there which is very old, and the inscription upon it is written in Cadmean letters <note>an ancient form of the Greek alphabet attributed to the legendary founder Cadmus</note>. Also in this temple were a golden shield, a golden bow with golden arrows, which Croesus, the King of the Lydians, gave to Amphiaraus; likewise, there were the quiver and spear.

## Ptoos. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; He on Mount Ptoos.

About five miles from Thebes, on the triple-peaked Mount Ptoos above Lake Copais, lay a city called Acraephia. About three-quarters of a mile from there was the temple of this Apollo, who had a great reputation and far-famed renown among the ancients because the answers given there were so entirely truthful. Ptoos, the son of Athamas and Themisto, is said to have been the one who gave his name to this mountain and the temple to Apollo. When Mardonius the Persian lay in Thessaly and wished to know the outcome of his affairs, he sent messengers to various places and also there—a man named "the Mouse" <note>original: "Maus"; historically known as Mys, a messenger sent by the Persian general Mardonius</note>, a quick-witted person. Because he wished to receive the answer in private, he was not only admitted to the priestess, but two men were given to him to record what she said to him. When he entered the temple, the priestess gave him an answer that neither he nor the observers understood; but when he had written it down, Mardonius was able to understand what was said to him from it, for it was spoken in his own native language.

Otherwise, there is another conjecture that Apollo receives this name from "terror" <note>likely a reference to the Greek word *ptoein*, to terrify or scare away</note>; for when he and his sister were born of Latona, Juno sent a wild

# Cerdoon. The Greedy.
<note>original: "Gwhinsüchtiger"; referring to Apollo as a seeker of profit or gain</note>

Because the priests of this god sometimes allowed themselves to be bribed for money and spoke what people wanted to hear, this name was bestowed upon the god. Demosthenes, as a wise and prominent man, noticed this clearly when Philip, the King of the Macedonians, intended to suppress Greece; at that time, the priestess promised Philip everything he desired, and indeed gave favorable and helpful answers to others on his behalf. Therefore, Demosthenes said she was "Philippizing" <note>original: "φιλιππίζειν"; a term coined by Demosthenes to describe the Delphic Oracle's bias toward King Philip II of Macedon</note> and flattering him, indicating this with that very word.

# Patroon. Fatherly.
<note>original: "Vätterlich"</note>

The ancients also called Apollo "Patroon," because he holds his designs and power like a father; that is, the Sun's power of prayer and help brings forth all things. However, Plato believes that Ion, who was born of Apollo and came to Athens, gave and honored his father with this name. Aristophanes, on the other hand, claims he was called this because the Greeks, together with Jupiter, accepted them as gods before all others; it was there that he also married Creusa, the daughter of Erechtheus, from whom Ion was born, who gave the Ionians their name.

In Athens, at the Ceramicus <note>original: "Ceramico"; the potters' quarter of ancient Athens</note>, he had a chapel and a statue made by Euphranor <note>a famous Greek sculptor and painter of the 4th century BCE</note>.

# Nomius. Shepherd, Lawgiver, Singer.

Since the Sun faithfully nourishes and grazes all that it brings forth, just like a shepherd, he became known as the Shepherd. Some also give him this name because of his singing, as he is the leader, guide, and lord of the Muses. Additionally, he had a law <note>original: "gsatz"; here referring to the 'Nomos,' a traditional musical composition</note> for piping on the flutes, where one can always perceive the power of Apollo through the melody. There were five parts to be played and tuned: Pera, Catacelussimas, Iambus, Spondee, and Catochoreusis, which are said to be taken from the struggle with the dragon <note>the Python of Delphi</note>.

*Pera* is the "Counsel," where he decided whether he might win anything from the dragon or whether he should stand his ground. With the *Catacelussimus*, he provokes the dragon. In the *Iambic* part, one hears the dragon snarling and snapping its teeth. In the *Spondee*, he lets up, and the matter becomes somewhat gentler, as if the battle were won. In the *Catochoreusis*, everything comes together with a strong voice, quite joyfully and exulting in the victory.

I almost believe that those in the Alpine mountains—specifically in Switzerland—to this day compare not a little to this song with their little ditty, where the girl drives the brown steer along; for in that very song, the nature and manner of both the shepherd and the bull are expressed. Truly, no less care is taken in that little song to show how a faithful shepherd should diligently tend his cattle so that they know him by his voice and run to him, just as good cattle must be trained—as a brave man was able to make known by playing the struggle of Apollo. Thus you find other songs, such as the battle...

...at Pavia / the march of the Bernese in Savoy / there / the foot-soldier’s step / the riding of the horses / the thunder of the guns / and also every / stab / blow / pressure / can be perceived through non-alphabetical voices <note>original: "vnbüchstablichen stimmen"; likely referring to instrumental music or sounds that convey meaning without words, such as a battle piece</note>.

There were three sons of Neptune: Steropes, Brontes, and Arges <note>The name Steropes means "Lightning," Brontes means "Thunder," and Arges means "Brightness"</note>, whom Neptune begot from Amphitrite. These had only one round eye in their forehead and no other. These same were given to Vulcan on the island of Lipara <note>One of the Aeolian Islands near Sicily, associated with Vulcan’s forge</note> so that they might help him forge the thunderbolts that Jupiter used. But when Aesculapius, the son of Apollo and Coronis, brought a dead man back to life with medicine, Jupiter shot him dead with a bolt. In retaliation, Apollo executed these three Cyclopes, or **Round-eyes** (because they had forged the bolt), with his arrows to avenge his son. For this, Apollo was sentenced <note>original: "erkant"; legally judged</note> to be sold as a servant and become a mortal man instead of a god, serving as a shepherd for King Admetus of Thessaly for seven years. Thus the name remained with him. 

However, some give this little tale a different color and say he was called the Lawgiver; that he was a son of Jupiter and a king among the Arcadians who established, invented, and set up new laws and strict commands. Because of this, his subjects drove him out of the land because he was far too harsh and stern. He then fled to Thessaly to Admetus, who gave him a lordship by the water of Amphrysus.

Those who wish to speak of this in natural terms say that the arts among the Greeks are called "the Rounds" or *Cyclides*, and the experience of them is called *Cyclopedia* <note>original: "Cyclopedian"; referring to the "circle of learning"</note>. From this come these clever fellows who are called the sons of Neptune, because they were skillful and took almost everything serving human weaponry from the fishes: such as armor from the scales of the same, their combat from fish-bones, and building ships from sea-snails with their spiral passages, etc. Thus they are attributed to Amphitrite because of the din and clatter that echoes in such workshops. As Vulcan’s servants, they worked the iron through fire; and since fire constantly surges up at Lipara, Apollo—or the Sun—is the cause of all healing herbs and roots. Therefore, the physician Aesculapius is his son, who was lost in the mountains while diligently searching for roots and never found again, from which the delusion arose that he had been burned by a thunderbolt. 

Because those who work in fire are so dried out and exhausted of natural warmth and spirit by its heat that they pass away prematurely—to which the Sun also contributes much—it was said that Apollo had killed them. Thus heat and cold, dryness and moisture, are strongly opposed to each other, even if this is not always perceived. Therefore, Neptune and Apollo cannot be at one; thus he <note>Apollo/the Sun</note> must serve mankind through the seven planets and bring forth, prevent, and watch over all growing things.

On the island of Rhodes, in the city of Camirus, he was honored under the name *Epimelios* <note>original: "Epimelio"; Protector of the flock</note>, *Opilio*, or **Shepherd**. He was called *Pimnius* on the island of Mayo, which is now called Mykonos; his temple stood by the salt mines on the western side <note>original: "vff Nidergang"; at the sunset/west</note> of the island, called the **Shepherd’s Temple**. On Lesbos, in the island now called Mytilene, he had a temple under the name *Napeos*, which you might translate as the **Forest Shepherd**.

### The Third Book. Pythius, the Dragon-Slayer.
<meta>Signature: p iiij</meta>
<meta>Catchword: The</meta>

Enough has been said of this Apollo in the section on Delphi regarding how the dragon was destroyed, how the priestess received her name, and so forth. However, I wish to include the words of **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching</note> here as well. He says (he speaks) that this priestess, **Pythia**, was a woman who sat upon a three-legged stool <note>The famous Delphic tripod</note>; she rent her clothes and allowed the evil spirit to enter her through her lower parts. Thereby she became possessed and insane; then, with disheveled hair, she raved about, foaming at the mouth, and spoke without knowing what she said herself.

But that no God was present there is also stated by **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD), a Greek philosopher and priest at Delphi, who sought naturalistic or daemonic explanations for the oracles</note>; for these **ventriloquists** <term>Bauchlüler: literally "belly-howlers," referring to those who seem to speak from their stomachs, often associated with demonic possession or deception</term> were first called **Eurycleers** <note>After Eurycles of Athens, a famous 5th-century BC ventriloquist</note>, and afterwards were called **Pythia** or **Pythonesses**. For, says Plutarch, should God mix himself into the use and limbs of humans, he would diminish his respect and glory and lessen his high majesty.

However, the fact that the evil spirit—no matter how unclean the place may be—does not despise it, being himself the most impure of all, has also been proven in our own times. For in **Rovigo**, between **Padua** and **Ferrara**, some twenty years ago, something unusual occurred: there was a woman named **Jacoba** who lived there, from whose belly a small, grumbling voice of evil, unclean spirits was heard. Indeed, many of the powerful and wealthy, who were eager to know something of future or secret matters, often summoned this woman. They stripped her naked so that there would be no deception; then, when they called to "**Little Curly-Hair**" <note>original: "Cincinatulo"; a diminutive of the Latin 'cincinnatus,' meaning curly-haired</note> (for so the evil spirit wished to be named, and he responded quite readily to this name) and questioned him, even about entirely hidden and secret things that had happened or were at hand, he often revealed wonderful things. He spoke them out clearly; but whenever he was asked about future things, he always told great lies. Or, to cover up and disguise his ignorance, he would let out a voice and a rumbling that could not be understood. If you desire a witness to this, look to **Ludovicus Coelius** <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), also known as Coelius Rhodiginus, a scholar from Rovigo who recorded this event in his 'Antiquae Lectiones'</note> in the tenth chapter of his eighth book, who heard and saw it himself.

Because this **Pythian Apollo** was held by the heathens to be a god of prophecy—or rather of lies and truth—I wish to show you various kinds of that same divination, along with their names, which the ancients practiced, consuming their curiosity, their bodies, their lives, and indeed the salvation of their souls therein. And while I am at it, I will set out a small table for you—partly from **Caspar Peucer** <note>Caspar Peucer (1525–1602), a German scholar and physician who wrote a famous treatise on divination</note> and partly searched out from others—in which you may find what are righteous, Divine prophecies permitted in the Scriptures and also allowed by Law; whereas, on the other hand, you will find what **Devilish arts** or inventions have been patched in,

->which are to be avoided.<-

# Concerning Pagan Gods

Prophecy <term>Weyſſagung: from the German "weissagen" (to predict or divine), here defined as foresight of future events</term> is in itself a knowledge or perception of future things that are yet to come. You may divide this into four kinds:

<image-desc>A complex hierarchical diagram using large decorative brackets to categorize types of prophecy. The text is arranged into clusters branching from left to right.</image-desc>

Those given by the **Holy Spirit**, which may be proven by Scripture, such as:
> **Prophecy** of the Prophets: good shall be rewarded, evil punished.
> Christ’s **Predictions** of the destruction of Jerusalem.
> **Warnings** of the Apostles regarding false prophets.
> **Indications** of the martyrs and confessors, such as **Agabus** <note>original: "Agabis"; a prophet mentioned in Acts 11:28 who predicted a great famine</note> and the daughters of **Philip**, concerning the famine.
> **Raising** of the dead.
> **Healing** of the sick.
> **Enlightening** of the blind.
> **Miracles** in many things.

**Natural** and **Artificial** [prophecy] is divided into:

> The **significations** that come from natural causes; these are also of two kinds:
>> **Conjectures** that things might be and happen so. *Consumption <note>original: "Schwind ſucht"; tuberculosis or a wasting disease</note> causes the hair to fall out.*
>> **Appearances**, or when it looks as though it might be so. *If the new Moon rises dark, it is likely to rain.*

> The **effects** that flow from the causes recounted above, and which leave an impression on original things, as they are assigned and attached to them; these are also of four kinds:
>> **That which must be.** *The sun goes down and it will be night.*
>> **What nature provides of itself.** *A good rain in May is followed by the growth of leaves and grass.*
>> **Free will.** *He who likes to read will become learned.*
>> **Fortune or chance.** *A rogue fellow <note>original: "loſer kundt"</note> becomes king when the other dies.*

**Devilish**, [attained] through strange visitations <note>original: "gſüch"</note>, to obtain power, honor, or goods. *

**Peasant Practice** <note>original: "Paurn practick"; folk wisdom or weather lore</note> such as: *If it rains on St. Medard’s Day <note>June 8th</note>, it will bring forty days of rain,* and the like.

# Of Heathen Gods

<image-desc>A hierarchical diagram of divination methods, using large curly braces to group sub-categories under major thematic headings (marked VII and VIII in the margin).</image-desc>

<margin>
**VII**
The superstition of flight or the interpretation of omens is of four kinds; Forbidden.
</margin>

* **Regarding flight**
    * **Ornithoscopy** <note>original: "Orneotoscopia"</note> / From the flight of birds, they derived their meanings.
    * **Cledonomancy** <note>original: "Cledoniismos"</note> / From the trapping and the cries of birds, they determined their fate.
    * **Tripudium** <note>The "dance" of the sacred chickens</note>. The hopping of chickens. Based on how the birds behaved while feeding in the morning, the Romans decided how they themselves should rule and give counsel.
* **Encounters on the path**
    * If someone, upon first going out, encounters something—foxes, hares, wolves, etc.—and it runs across their path.
    * Stumbling, tripping, falling, hearing laughter or weeping, etc.
* **Ominous signs** <note>original: "Argwilligs," implying things that cause suspicion or ill-will</note>
    * **Oecoscopy** <note>original: "Oecoscopia"</note>. Seeing something unusual in the home, such as a black dog running inside.
    * Spilling salt, oil, vinegar <note>original: "ischen"</note>, wine, drink, or water during a meal.
    * Spilling food, speaking of fire while at the table, or a dog howling.
    * Lifting the table because someone sneezes, or hearing the wooden beams creak.
* **Dreadful signs of the body**
    * **Palmic omens** <note>original: "Palmiran"</note>, such as the twitching of the eyes.
    * Ringing in the ears, etc.
    * Tingling sensations <note>original: "Statgen"</note>, etc.

---

-> Regarding thunder in the sky: how, when, and where it strikes, and with what lightning, clap, etc. <-

<margin>
**VIII**
Lot-casting is of three kinds
</margin>

* **Civically permitted**
    * Regarding inheritance. Certain customs: using beans, small stones, or making little slips of paper; drawing, cutting, etc.
    * Regarding public offices. The Venetians use gold and silver balls.
    * Regarding military leadership. In some places, they draw small slips of paper <note>original: "zädelin"</note>.

* **Divine lots**, found in Holy Scripture in the book of Joshua, among the Apostles, etc.

* **For profit or knowing the future**; Forbidden:
    * **Cleromancy** <note>original: "Cleromantia"</note>. Placing items in a pot to draw them out.
    * **Palomancy** <note>original: "Palomantia"</note>. Throwers of marked tokens; those who prophesy based on what lies on top.
    * **Astragalomancy** <note>original: "Astragolomantia"</note>. Roller of knucklebones <note>ancestor to modern dice</note>, who seek profit and foreknowledge through them.
    * **Praenestine lots** <note>original: "Prænestinæ"</note>. "Quarrel-irons" <note>original: "Zanckeyfen"</note>, where a person is told their fortune based on what symbols come together.
    * **Antian lots** <note>original: "Antianæ"</note>. Pythagoras's sieve-shakers <note>original: "Rätterfchē"</note>, from which many names were drawn.
    * **Aponian lots** <note>original: "Aponi"</note>. Golden dice thrown into a well; observing what shows on top.
    * **Geomancy** <note>original: "Geomantia"</note>. Earth-drawers. These people could perform divinations by making lines or marks in the soil.
    * **Onomancy** <note>original: "Onomantia"</note>. Interpreters of names; those who calculate good or bad luck based on a person's name.
    * **Arithmancy** <note>original: "Arithmātia"</note>. Number-seers, who calculate good or evil from numerical values.
    * **Tephromancy** <note>original: "Tephromantia"</note>. Ash-diviners; those who knew what fortune was hidden in the ashes.
    * **Botanomancy** <note>original: "Botaniomantia"</note>. Sage-shakers; they derived fortunes from the leaves.
    * **Sycomancy** <note>original: "Sycomantia"</note>. Fig-leaf praisers; they knew how to weave a tale <note>original: "geschwät̄," chatter or gossip</note> from these.
    * **Ceromancy** <note>original: "Ceromantia"</note>. Wax-readers; they let wax drip into water and then tell the "truth."
    * **Stichomancy** <note>original: "Stichomantia"</note>. Verse-seekers; they sought answers in the books of Virgil, taking the first verse they happened to open to.

# The Third Book

<margin>
**IX**
Natural effects are of two kinds. Namely:
</margin>

- **Natural, orderly, usual, and customary things in simple matters.**
    - **Astrology and making practice <note>Predictions or prognostications</note> from it.**
        - **General Rules** <note>original: "Catholicon"</note>
            - > The effects of the changing constellations throughout the year, and the effects of the air in specific lands. Choosing the right day to do this or that.
        - **Birth Charts.** <note>original: "Genethliacon"</note> Casting a birth chart to see what shall befall the newborn.
    - **The effects of the four elements**
        - **Pyromancy** <note>original: "Pyromantia"</note> / Comets, the igniting of fire in the heavens, and the shining of the stars.
        - **Aeroscopy** <note>original: "Aëroscopia"</note> / The movement of the air.
        - **Hydroscopy** <note>original: "Hydatoscopia"</note> / The flow and rushing of water.
        - **Geoscopy** <note>original: "Geoscopia"</note> / The dryness or moisture of the earth according to its season.

---

- **Mixed things which are usually natural, yet not perfect**
    - Comets, vaporous flames, and running fires that move at night <note>Likely referring to will-o'-the-wisps or ignis fatuus</note>.
    - The violence of the winds.
    - The rising and drying up of waters; the fury of the sea.
    - Earthquakes <note>original: "Erdpidem"</note> and the like.

<margin>
In these matters, one should leave the power and guidance to God, and not become entirely attached to them.
</margin>

- **Perfect things**
    - **In Man**
        - **Physiognomy.** <note>original: "Physiognomia"</note> Judging a person by the appearance of their face and its parts.
        - **Metoposcopy.** <note>original: "Metoposcopia"</note> Knowing the wrinkles of the forehead and prophesying from them.
        - **Chiromancy.** <note>original: "Chiromantia"</note> Palm-reading; giving counsel according to the lines in the hands.
        - **Semiotics.** <note>original: "Semiotica"</note> What may be discerned from the healthy or sickly signs of the body, with the advice of physicians.
        - **Oneiropology.** <note>original: "Oneiropologia"</note> Interpreters of dreams, who are able to explain what dreams mean.
    - **In animals.** The changing nature of animals, such as when they stay within their dens or when they go out, etc.
    - **In plants.** Their strange changes, which at times are good and at times evil, etc.
    - **In ores.** The colors and the powers of ores and metals.
    - **In flowers.** The changing of their colors; the ripening of fruits and flowers.
    - **In the heavens.** The equality of day and night, their shortening and lengthening, and the weather's increase of power in all saps <note>Referring to the vital fluids in plants and living creatures influenced by the seasons</note>.

---

- **Unnatural, unusual, abominable, contrary to nature, and cruel.**
    - **Monsters.** <note>original: "Monstra"</note> Deformities in children.
    - **Portents.** <note>original: "Ostenta"</note> Appearances in the air, such as the sight of war in the sky.
    - **Prodigies.** <note>original: "Prodigia"</note> Rain of blood or grain.
    - **Phantasms.** <note>original: "Phasmata"</note> Mocking spirits <note>literally "spirit-monkeys," referring to deceptive or spectral apparitions that mimic reality</note>.

# Of Heathen Gods.

Thus you have here in a summary with what great diligence the ancients laid [this] upon their own misdeeds <note>original: "vnthů" - likely referring to folly or wrongful acts</note>. For as Favorinus <note>Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–160 AD) was a Roman sophist and philosopher who argued against astrology and oracles.</note> says: If it is the case that they had people who could announce or know things to come, and they then predicted something to the one asking, then the speech must have been either good or evil. If they promised something good, and the matter failed, then the person hoped in vain and was thus more miserable than before; for while he waits for his luck and consoles himself with the hope of it, he consumes the bloom of all the joy he would have had if the lucky event had happened to him unexpectedly. If they then predict something evil, and lie, then the person grieves in vain and makes his misery greater with useless fear. If, however, some evil is truly to befall someone, he is plagued in his heart and mind before the misfortune actually occurs. I also cannot omit adding the delightful little tale here, which Celio Calcagnino <note>original: "Cölius Calcagninus," an Italian humanist and polymath (1479–1541).</note>, that worthy man, wrote regarding this fantasy and soothsaying, to this effect: Maiden Curiosity <note>original: "Junckfraw Fürwitz"</note> had long ago allowed herself to be persuaded by Master Wonder <note>original: "Junckher Wunder"</note>, who toyed with her until she bore a daughter by him, named Sorcery <note>original: "Zauberey"</note>. Now, both parents feared Lady Truth <note>original: "fraw Warheit"</note> (with whom Curiosity and Wonder were always in constant strife and deadly war, yet could never withstand her), lest she might by chance happen upon the little daughter Sorcery and wring her neck. Therefore, they gave the child to two cousins, Lady Shamelessness <note>original: "fraw Vnuerschampte"</note> and Lady Fear <note>original: "fraw Forcht"</note>, two sisters, to guard the child. These two, not trusting themselves, hid the child in the lap of a great and famous mistress named Incomprehensibility <note>original: "Vnbegreifflichkeit"</note>, and commanded her that she should raise and instruct the child in a stealthy manner through delusions and ghostly tricks. Now, as this little daughter came into her own, she soon stole away and ran to a fortress called Fool’s Castle <note>original: "Narreburg"</note>; there she found shelter, was made pregnant, and gave birth to a daughter who was named Easy-Belief <note>original: "Glaubleichts" – referring to credulity</note>. No sooner was she grown than she began to support her own mother, who otherwise would have had to die of hunger.

Now back to our Apollo, whose Pythian festivals were held not in one but in several places, such as at Megara and Sicyon. Thus, some claim a Dragon guarded this chasm where the prophecy of Apollo was, and from this the name Pythian remained with him. Some divide Delphi and Python into two cities that are six miles apart from each other; some say it was a single city. There is also the legend that a Dragon surrounded the cradle when Latona bore the children, after Juno had long hunted her. This signifies, as some would have it, that after the first separation of the unformed world—when everything has now gained its appearance, but the earth was still somewhat moist with water, and the air had grown strong in warmth, and thus the fire heated the same even more—the two lights of Day and Night grew. The Sun, because of its fiery heat, was drawn upward; the Moon, being somewhat moister and colder, did not stay so far in the heights, but remained further down in the winds. Thus, the air, taken for Juno, begrudged Latona (the Earth) the birth of the two lights with its malice. But that the mists would not cease until the Sun became powerful is indicated by what the Dragon signifies. It is also said he is named Pythius because that little word refers to "asking" <note>original: "fragen" – likely referring to the Greek 'pythesthai'</note>; some say from "rotting" <note>original: "fäulen" – referring to the Greek 'pythein'</note>, which the excessive Sun brings; some want the city of Pytho to have been before the temple, from which the name then comes. ### The Third Book.

...was called the city of Delphi; first Mape <note>This may be a transcription error in the original for an obscure name or a variant of "Manteia."</note>, then Perroessa, then Crissa, and finally Pytho and Delphi. That little phrase which is held in such high regard in the mouths of all the learned and in all the worlds: **Know thyself.** They say that Phemonois the priestess <note>The first priestess of Apollo at Delphi, credited with inventing hexameter verse.</note> wrote this down by the command of Apollo. Others wish to have it that Panathea, the daughter of Delphus, wrote it; indeed, that Apollo himself gave it as an answer to Chilon when he asked what was most useful to man. However, many attribute it to Bias, others to Thales, but the most prominent attribute it to Chilon. At Hermione—where Damalia <note>Modern-day Ermioni in the Peloponnese (the Morea).</note> is now in the Morea—there was a temple of Apollo, called *Pythaeus*, for Pythaeus the son of Apollo is said to have first ruled there and established the temple. At Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note> in the marketplace, he also had a temple and an image, and a festival game which they called the *Gymnopaedia* <note>original: "Gymno Peidicaim"</note>, which they held quite strictly and seriously, where the youth performed beautiful leaps and dances. At Thornax, not far from Lacedaemon, he also had an image which Croesus honored by decorating it with much gold. At Asine near Napoli in Romania <note>Napoli di Romania was the medieval name for Nauplion, Greece.</note>, he also had a temple there. At Olympus, where the games of Jove are held, he also has his altar on the grounds; at Athens, an image. At Megara, his likeness also stood. On Mount Lyceum in Arcadia, he had his temple. By the waters of Patras, where once were Aegyra and Pellene (now Tarso), he has a beautiful temple with a marble sacrificial altar. At Samos and at Tegea, there were also temples consecrated to him.

# Concerning Pagan Deities.

...this name, and the glory of the Sun is above all things. The sacrifice, however, was held with this custom: those who led the hundred head of cattle they intended to sacrifice were dressed in long white linen garments, girded about; however, the arm and breast on the right side were bare. In their hands, they carried a sharp axe, cutting on both sides. The oxen almost all had to be black, with straight horns, and they bore those same horns gilded, adorned with little wreaths of various flowers. You will find more in the *Book of Sacrifices*. Likewise also under the entry for Juno. You should also note that in former times a coin was circulated and struck in Athens called "the ox." It was worth roughly fourteen kreuzer <note>A small silver coin common in Central Europe.</note>, and just as we say a hundred guilders, a hundred pounds, a hundred shillings, or a hundred blafferts <note>original: "plaphart" – a silver coin used in Switzerland and Southern Germany.</note>, so they said **Hecatombeum** <note>A "Hecatomb" originally referred to a sacrifice of 100 oxen.</note> when they wanted to name a hundred oxen. From this came the saying: "Hecatombean weapons," as if one were to say the armor is worth a hundred oxen in other currency. From this also comes the proverb: **An ox sits upon his tongue.** This is used when one wants to indicate that someone speaks for the sake of money, or alternatively, does not speak what would benefit the common good because he fears he might be punished for it. And it seems to me, as it did to Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist who wrote extensively on ancient coinage.</note>, that in these times one finds many who carry an ox on their tongue, a sheep on their forehead, a fox in their bosom, and a wolf in their heart.

## Mithras, Mithras, Mitrios, Sol. The Sun.

**Mithras**, who is the Sun among the Persians and also their primary god, was worshipped in a cave. His image had a lion's head, was dressed in the Persian fashion with a curved saber and a royal miter <note>original: "Künigs Inseln" – referring to an infula or ceremonial headband/miter.</note>, and held a steer by the horns as it struggled. This signifies that the Sun, the foremost in the heavens, has the Lion for its zodiac sign, and just as the lion excels among the beasts, so does the Sun excel among the stars. It also indicates that the Moon receives its light from the Sun when it becomes full and faces the Sun; yet the Sun would take all its shine away if it did not set. For this reason, Mithras is worshipped in a cave.

**Zoroaster** is said to have been the first to consecrate a cave to this Mithras, in a completely green place by a spring. Thus it was held thereafter, wherever Mithras was honored, that his shrine should be in a cave, to show that Mithras enlightened and brought forth the world—which was nothing but darkness—through his power. Inside, he also marked out and described the course of the stars, placing the altar of Mithras where day and night are equal <note>The equinox.</note>. For this reason, he carries a curved sword like a ram's horn, because that animal belongs to Mars. He also rides upon an ox, because the ox is exceptionally potent and fertile, to show how Mithras is a Lord of all emerging fruits.

**Origen** says that in this hole or cave, Zoroaster made two circles or spheres: one for the fixed stars, the other for the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>. Through these circles, he made a path for the souls in the form of a ladder or stairs, which has seven gates and entrances: the first of lead, the second of tin, the third of bronze, the fourth of iron, the fifth of stamped leather, the sixth of silver, the seventh <note>The original text mistakenly says "eight."</note> of gold. These indicate that **Saturn** is quite slow and melancholy, **Venus** is glitteringly beautiful yet soft...

<header>The Third Book.</header>

Jupiter is quite firm and rigid; Mercury is nimble for all manner of trade, agreeable, cheerful, and eloquent; Mars, however, is turbulent; the Moon is visible though not entirely bright; and the Sun is most radiant of all.

Whoever wished to become a priest in this temple <note>Referring to the temple or "cave" of Mithras.</note> had first to endure twelve indignities shown to him, such as blows, harsh words, cold, heat, and the like; indeed, these were so severe that his life was often at stake.

The kings of the Persians honored him highly, like Tiridates <note>Tiridates I of Armenia, who famously acknowledged Mithras when visiting Nero.</note>; they swore by his name, as Cyrus testifies. He was honored not only in Persia but also in Crete (or Candia), in Alexandria (now called Scandaria), and likewise in Rome; these caves Gracchus the Prefect destroyed, while Commodus otherwise defiled them. George, a persecutor of Athanasius and an Arian bishop in Alexandria—a great mortal enemy of idolatry—received the temple of Mithras (which had fallen into ruin in Alexandria) as a gift from Emperor Constantius. He had it cleaned out, and there he found a cave <note>original: "hůlin" — a small cave or hollow, referring to the Mithraeum, which was typically underground.</note> which lay full of signs and magical apparatus that the Greeks had used. When this came to light, the Christians mocked it and made sport of it, exposing the "foolish work" of the unbelieving Greeks and holding up to their faces the items they had dealt with. This "little worm" <note>An idiomatic way of saying this rankled or "got under the skin" of the pagans.</note> stung the pagans' noses; however, they remained silent until Julian became Emperor. Then they dared to stir; they fell upon the Christians, beat them to death, and even crucified some to mock our believers. They took Bishop George, already dead, and bound him upon a camel; they pelted him with dung, dragged him through the city until he fell to ashes, and the rest they burned.

## Philesius. The Kisser.

Because the radiance of the Sun is so lovely, and we hold it in special honor at its rising as if with kisses, he has received this name <note>Derived from the Greek "philein," to love or kiss.</note>. Canachus made his image and placed it in the temple of the *Didymaean* or "Twin" mentioned above; and at his festival, there was a game where the young children kissed one another for a prize to see who could do it best; from this, the name perhaps grew. The story concerning Branchus <note>A youth loved by Apollo who founded the oracle at Didyma.</note> we shall tell in its proper place.

## Smintheus. The Mouse-Killer.

The Cretans have a mouse called *Smynthas*; therefore, it is said that at one time there was a negligent priest who skipped and let pass the festivals and customs of Apollo. Consequently, the field mice came in swarms and entirely ruined and devoured the fruit upon the field belonging to the priest. Crinis the priest, and the peasant who worked the land, were greatly distressed; then, in the morning, a message was given to the peasant by Apollo: he should tell the priest to keep the festival properly and be diligent, then there would be an end to the damage. When the priest did his duty, Apollo shot all the mice to death. Others put forward this version: There were certain people called Teucrians who traveled from Crete; they were told they should settle wherever the "earth-born" should oppose them. When they came to the place where the promontory of Our Lady <note>A Christianized reference to a location near Troy; likely Hamaxitus.</note> now stands near Troy (at that time called Hamaxitus), and they had made camp, a swarm of mice came in the night and gnawed all their weapons and whatever other leather gear they had. For this reason, they remained there and built dwellings on the mountain lying nearest by, which they named Ida after the mountain in Crete. the sculptor from Paros <note>original: "Parien"</note> made a statue there, and a mouse lies beneath its feet. Thus, there are many mice around the temple which one is not permitted to kill; they must be given food from the public treasury, and they have their little burrows <note>original: "hülinen"</note> near the altar. The Sibyl named Herophile is said to have been a priestess for a long time in this temple and also died there; her tomb is said to be in the inner sanctuary <note>original: "Dhan"</note> of this Apollo, with an inscription that indicates as much.

Otherwise, Apollo was honored under this name in many and various places, so much so that not only were temples erected to him, but towns and regions were named after him. Such as at Paradiso, which was once called Parium, on the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> channel, and on the island of Rhodes. Also at Paron, where a statue stands on a rock or flat plateau made of beautiful marble, still undamaged. Likewise in Tenedos and many other places. ### Pasparius — Particular to the Parians.

Phavorinus <note>A 16th-century scholar and bishop, or perhaps referencing the ancient philosopher Favorinus.</note> says that the people of Pergamum and Paros had a dedicated foundation that was shared between them for their exclusive use, and no one else had any part in it; hence the name was given to him.

### Sauroctonos — Lizard-Slayer.

Praxiteles <note>One of the most famous sculptors of ancient Greece.</note> sculpted an Apollo who lurks for a lizard, poised and ready to shoot it. From this, he received this name.

### Horus — Orus.

The Egyptians gave this name to Apollo as the Sun; the twenty-four divisions that make up day and night were named the *Hore* after him, which we call the Hours. The four seasons of the year are also called *Hore* by some. Diodorus Siculus makes mention of this Horus in several places, as you may read. Furthermore, Plutarch argues that there are two Horuses: the elder, who is blind and called Aruerin <note>Haroeris</note>, born on the second day when the world was not yet perfect but only beginning to take shape. The other Horus was honored in Coptos in Egypt, where he had a specific but small site; his image is there, holding the reproductive organs of Typhon <note>original: "gpurt glider Typhonis" — referring to the myth of the conflict between Horus and Set/Typhon.</note> in one hand.

When the Egyptians wished to represent the Sun in this Horus, they shaved his head on the left side and left the hair on the right. This signifies that the Sun does not hide itself in any part of nature. The shaved part, however, indicates how the Sun, though it has set, shall and must return—just as the hair grows back after being shaved. Similarly, the shortening of the days would, in time, stretch and lengthen again like the regrowing hair.

His priests were also shaved and carried similar reproductive symbols in their hands; they jumped up and down and smeared their faces with fine wheat dough. They then plunged it into a boiling cauldron of water and gave the scrapings from their faces to the superstitious people; these were said to be good and healthy for many things, etc. You will find the written signs of Horus in a special place following this.

<header>The Third Book</header>

near Scyllaeum <note>original: "Schilli," a promontory in the Argolid</note>, not far from there, on a rock along the road toward Damalis <note>original: "Damalia," likely refers to the promontory near Chalcedon</note>, there was a temple of this Apollo. Because that rock was somewhat flat and broad, this Apollo received his name from it. Although some believe a tree stood there called the Plane Tree <note>original: "Platanus"</note>. The "Hard" Jupiter <note>Likely referring to *Jupiter Lapis*, the "Jupiter of the Stone"</note> once had an altar there; it was also sometimes called Thesti.

## Thearius.

In Troezen <note>An ancient Greek city in the Peloponnese</note>, there stood a very old temple, the like of which was hardly found in Greece. It was built by Pittheus <note>The mythical king of Troezen and grandfather of Theseus</note>. The statue was donated by Auliscus, and much later another statue was erected and made there by Hermion, a sculptor in Troezen. Out of love for this god, the Pythian games <note>One of the four Panhellenic Games of Ancient Greece</note> are said to have been established by Diomedes. This temple also had many ornaments and statues inside, which are not necessary to mention here.

## Myricæus.

On the island of Lesbos, which is now called Mytilene <note>original: "Meterelin"</note>, there was also a city of this name, Lesbos, where Apollo was honored. He carried a branch of Myrica <term>Myrica: The Tamarisk shrub, anciently associated with prophecy and Apollo's cult.</term> in his hand, from which his name was derived. This plant, Myrica, is a very old shrub that has long been known. Some take it for heather <note>original: "Heiden"</note> or small Tamarisk. Nicander says in his *Theriaca* <note>original: "Triacks," a poem on venomous creatures</note> that Apollo commanded all his priests to hold such a small branch in their hands when they prophesy. Therefore, he calls the shrub the "holy, consecrated magic wood." The Scythians also told the truth <note>performed divination</note> with similar sticks. Apollo also appeared to many in their sleep with this small branch in his hand.

## Mirenensis. 
->At Bircena.<-

Myra <note>original: "Mirea," an ancient town in Lycia</note> was once a city in Asia, now called Bircena <note>Likely referring to a site near the Lycian coast</note> on the Vriquiqui <note>Perhaps referring to the Eurymedon or a local gulf</note> waters. There, Apollo had a temple where the priest threw the leftover chopped meat from the sacrifice into the sea. Then the fish swam up like guests and consumed it.

## Amicleus. 
->At Amyclae.<-

Not far from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> was a city called Amyclae <note>original: "Amicle"</note>, surrounded entirely by fruitful trees and cultivated fields. There stood the temple of Apollo, along with a foundation of others that could match or even surpass all those in this region. The Lacedaemonians and Athenians once erected a treaty inscribed in stone there regarding their alliance. At one time, the Lacedaemonians wanted to gild this statue of Apollo but could not obtain enough gold in Greece. When they asked the god what to do, they were answered that they should write to King Croesus <note>The famously wealthy king of Lydia</note>. They say that Hyacinthus, the son of Amyclas <note>original: "Amycle"</note> and Diomede, was so dear to Apollo that he spent all his time playing with him. Once, when they were throwing a stone <note>the discus</note> together, the boy ran under the throw, and Apollo thus struck him to death. Therefore, his grave is still in this temple. At that same time, gold was so expensive and in such short supply that Hiero <note>original: "Hieron"</note>, the most prominent king in all his realm of Sicily, Italy, and Greece, could not afford enough gold to make the tripod <note>original: "dreyfüſſigen ſtül"</note> that he had promised to Apollo...

# Of Heathen Gods

<note>This section concludes the description of Apollo Smintheus.</note> the sculptor from Paros made a statue for that place, under whose feet a mouse lies. Thus, there are many mice around the temple which one is not permitted to kill; they must be given food from the common sacks, and they have their little holes near the altar. The Sibyl named Herophile is said to have long been a priestess in this temple, and she also died there; for her grave is said to be in the inner sanctuary <note>original: "Dhan," referring to the *Adyton* or the most sacred inner chamber of a Greek temple</note> of this Apollo, with an inscription that indicates as much.

Otherwise, Apollo has been honored under this name in many and various places, so much so that they have not only erected temples to him but also established villages and regions named after him. Such as at Paradiso, which was once called Parium, on the Propontis canal; and on the island of Rhodes. Also at Paron, which stands on a cliff or flat rock made of beautiful, unblemished marble. Likewise in Tenedos, and many other places. Similarly in the city of Chrysa, and also near Larissa.

### Pasparius. <margin>Special to the Parians.</margin>

Favorinus says that the people of Pergamum and Paros had a foundation <note>original: "Stifft," likely referring to a shared sacred precinct or priesthood</note> that was held in common for their own use, and no one else had any part in it; from this, he received his name.

### Sauroctonos. <margin>The Lizard-Slayer.</margin>

Praxiteles fashioned an Apollo who lurks after a lizard <note>original: "Heidochse," an archaic term for a lizard or salamander</note>, aiming his bow at it, intending to shoot it. From this, he also takes this name.

### Horus. <margin>Orus.</margin>

The Egyptians gave this name to Apollo as the Sun, from which the twenty-four divisions that make day and night were named the *Horae*, which we call the hours. The four seasons of the year are also called *Horae* by some. Diodorus Siculus makes mention of this Horus in several places; you may read of it there. Otherwise, Plutarch maintains that there are two Horuses: one who is the elder and blind, called Aruerin <note>original: "Aruerin," referring to Haroeris or Horus the Elder</note>, who was born on the second day when the world was not yet complete, having only been conceived as a form of something yet to be. The other Horus was honored in Coptos in Egypt, where he had a special, though small, village; his image is there, which held the birth-organs of Typhon <note>original: "gpurt glider Typhonis"</note> in one hand.

When the Egyptians wished to represent the Sun in this Horus, they shaved his head on the left side, but on the right, they let his hair remain. This signifies that the Sun does not hide itself in any parts of nature. The shaved part, however, shows how the Sun, even when it has set, shall and must return, just as the hair that is shaved off grows back; likewise, the shortening of the days would, with time, stretch and lengthen again like the regrowing hair.

His priests were also shaven and carried similar birth-signs in their hands; they jumped up and down and smeared their faces with semolina dough, then thrust it into a boiling cauldron of water. They then gave this to the superstitious who scraped it from their faces, claiming it was good and healthy for many things, etc. You will find the written hieroglyphs <note>original: "schrifftliche waarzeichē"</note> of Horus in a separate place following hereafter.

# Of Pagan Gods

...could afford to make out of gold. Also, whatever the Romans wished to dedicate to the Gods in gold, they had to melt down almost all of it from women's jewelry <note>original: "Kleynottern" — small pieces of jewelry, trinkets, or precious ornaments</note>.

### Cytinus. Pomegranate blossom.

Pomegranates drop a blossom which is called Cytinum <note>The calyx or flower of the pomegranate tree</note>; now, Apollo had a temple on Mount Rescyntbo in Thrace, of which mention is also made in connection with Juno, perhaps because so many of these fruits grow there.

### Cymnius.

There was a family and guild in Athens of this name who always produced the priests of Apollo, and they were also called the Cynny.

### Daphnæus, Laurel-bearer.

In Antioch, King Antiochus Epiphanes (some say his father Seleucus) built a temple to this Apollo; he even intended to rival the temple of Jupiter on Olympus with its design and unspared expense. Before the temple was a very beautiful grove or forest with cypresses and other trees, along with shrubs and herbs that remained green and bloomed throughout the year, giving a pleasant scent and being lovely to behold. It was also so thick that it provided great shade; beautiful springs, sources, and little brooks ran through it, which murmured sweetly, and when the wind blew through them, they made a most blessed sound. It is said that Daphne, the daughter of Ladon, fled from Arcadia into this wood from Apollo, who was pursuing her, and that she was there transformed into a laurel tree. However, otherwise, there was a base form of worship there; harlots and scoundrels commonly gathered there. Near the temple was a spring called Castalio <note>The Castalian Spring of Antioch, named after the more famous one at Delphi</note>, which was held to have the same power as the one at Delphi to grant the power of prophecy. The Emperor Hadrian blocked up its source because it was said that once it was revealed to him that if he crowned himself with laurel leaves and bathed therein, he would understand the secrets of the soothsayers; and once he had done this himself, he did not want anyone else to follow his example, so he destroyed the spring. Gallus, the Roman ruler <note>Caesar Gallus, who governed the East under Constantius II</note>, removed the idolatry from that forest, erected a Christian church, and had the body of the martyr Babylas <note>Saint Babylas of Antioch, a 3rd-century bishop and martyr</note> buried there. Immediately, the priests and their idols would and could no longer give any answers. But when Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan Roman emperor, who attempted to suppress Christianity</note> later wanted to reopen and restore the temple, it was burned by hellish fire <note>Likely referring to a lightning strike, which Christians interpreted as divine wrath</note>, so that not one stone remained that was not turned to ash and filth. The pagans blamed the Christians; the Christians attributed it to the vengeance of God. Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman historian</note> says a learned man named Asclepiades came to Julian and found him in the temple; and as he always carried with him a small tablet or figure of the Great Heavenly Goddess, he placed that same image at the feet of Apollo and lit some small candles before it; at midnight, when no one else was present, these caught fire and ignited others, so that everything was turned to ash.

### Daphnates, Daphnopolea.

The Syracusans in Sicily, who are now called the Saragossians <note>Modern Syracuse/Siracusa</note>, honored him under this name.

# The Third Book

### Corypæus, Oropœus, Pæon:

There is a dispute as to whether Nicander in his *Theriaca* <note>original: "Driackẽ", referring to Nicander of Colophon’s ancient Greek poem on venomous animals and their cures</note> (for the students of his poetry argue over which city they should name him after) mentions him; it is certain that at Sycaminum, which was once called Oropus, there was a magnificent temple of Apollo, though I find nothing so certain regarding the name Corypæus. For at Oropus, Apollo was held in great esteem by many followers and was named Paeon <term>Paeon: A title meaning "the healer," often used for gods of medicine</term>, which is why Nicander invoked him appropriately regarding his medical works.

### Carinos. At the Hook.

At Megara, there was a small fiery pillar <note>original: "fewrp feylerlin", likely referring to a pyramid-shaped monument or altar</note> dedicated to this Apollo near the water gate.

### Hylata. At Hylata.

In Cyprus, there was a city called Hyle, in which Apollo was worshipped and from which he received this name.

### Tembrus. At Tembria.

Much like the previous surname, Apollo receives this one from the city of Tembria located in Cyprus, where he then had his temple and worship.

### Tegyreius. Of Tegyra.

Some say that in this city of Tegyra, which was situated in Boeotia, this Apollo had a temple. Plutarch says it was destroyed and half-collapsed when the priesthood <note>original: "pfaffenwerck", referring to the temple establishment and its clergy</note> that was there was destroyed and burned by the Medes <note>The Persians</note>. Mount Delos is not far from there, at the foot of which two fragrant and wondrous springs bubble up; one was called the Palm and the other the Olive Tree. It is also said that Apollo was born there.

### Boedromius. Battle-hastener.

The Athenians worshipped Apollo under this surname because when the Athenians fell into disagreement among themselves, Ion the Eleusinian came to the aid of his allies in great haste. And when the matter was concluded, the Athenians named Apollo after the din and the shouting <note>original: "getümmel vnnd gschrey", referencing the Greek *boē*, a shout, and *dromos*, a running</note> and built him a chapel. Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> believes the name was given to Apollo when Xanthus came to the aid of the Athenians in great haste when Eumolpus, the son of Neptune, attacked them. Plutarch attributes it to Theseus, when he defeated the Amazons, after which the month we call June <note>original: "Brachmonat", the month for breaking or fallowing the soil</note> is called Boedromion by them, and their festival is held at that same time. At Thebes, there was also a statue of this Apollo.

### Metagitnius.

The month we call May is called Metagitnion by the Greeks, and they worship the God under this surname. <note>In the Attic calendar, Metagitnion actually corresponds to the period of August/September, though the author correlates it to May.</note>

### Abæus.

This is a village in Phocis; it had a temple there where answers were given to those who inquired, long before the pilgrimage to Delphi had arisen.

# Of Heathen Gods.

This temple was established by Abas, the son of Lynceus and Hypermestra. The Persians burned it down, but on account of the temple’s importance, the Romans granted the citizens their freedom. The Emperor Hadrian built another temple there, in which the ancient statues were placed. Before this, the Thebans and the Phocians, who had fled into the temple, also burned the old structure once after the time of the Medes <note>original: "Mediern", referring to the Persians</note>.

## Hyperinoides, Hyperion. ->Over-runner.<-

Because the Sun has its course above us, it received this name, although there are some who have written a poem stating that the Sun is the son of Hyperion, a Titan or Giant; read Diodorus regarding this.

## Phaesinbrotos. ->Help to Mankind.<-

Because the Sun is helpful to mankind with its light, the poets call it by this name <note>From the Greek *phaesimbrotos*, meaning "bringing light to mortals"</note>.

## Epitropios. ->At Epitropia.<-

Dionysius of Halicarnassus says that the Dorians in Asia built a temple to Apollo in Epitropium, where they gathered at appointed hours and days together with their wives and children. These were days for markets and sacrifices, and they also held competitive games. After the end of the festival, if one city had a dispute <note>original: "span"</note> with another, there were judges appointed on the spot to decide the matter. Furthermore, if there was anything to be resolved against a foreign enemy, or anything concerning rest and peace, it was also handled there.

## Episcopus, Musagetes. ->Overseer.<-

Because the poets say that Apollo presides over the Muses and takes his leisure with them, he has these names; the first because he keeps a watch over them, and the other because he leads the tone and the ringing of all the heavenly spheres. However, this name is also attributed to the Sun. This Apollo had a statue in Athens and also on Olympus.

## Metelineus, Malloes.

Near Mytilene, though outside the city—which Mytilene was the island in Caria <note>The author likely means Lesbos; Mytilene is its capital</note>—the Mytileneans held an annual festival where young and old went to observe the holy day. For this reason, the Athenians once intended to ambush them in the temple, but they were warned.

## Maleaticus or Melates, Maleates.
->The one at Malvasia.<-

The promontory of Malea in Morea <note>The Peloponnese</note>, which is now called Cape Mallo near the city of Malvasia—which was once named Epidaurus—is well known to all who use the sea. A king of the Tyrrhenians named Maleus stayed there in ancient times; from this, Apollo now receives the name because he also had a temple there. Likewise, he has a temple in Lacedaemonia <note>Sparta</note>.

## Hemerodromos. ->Day-runner.<-

Because the Sun runs the circuit of the world by day, he is named thus.

## Bel.

Those in Aglar, which was once called Aquileia, in Friuli <note>A region in North-Eastern Italy</note>. When Maximinus the tyrant <note>referring to Maximinus Thrax, a Roman Emperor known for his cruelty</note> [attacked] these...

<header>The Third Book.</header>

...besieged this city, a soldier said he had seen that Bel <note>An ancient Mesopotamian deity</note> (whom he took for Apollo) himself fighting for the city in the sky; for he was held there with special, great reverence.

### Hecabeletes, Hecabolos, Hecatebolos.
->The Far-Shooter.<-

Because he reaches every nook and corner of the world with his rays—which are then understood in place of arrows—he is thus named, especially during the highest length of day <note>referring to the summer solstice</note>. Some say he is named so because his power and might reach so far.

### Hecaergos. **The Far-Working.**

Pindar <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet</note> gives him this name along with others, because his influence and action are powerful in all lands and accomplish so much.

### Eurypharetras. **Wide-Quivered.**

Apollo is attributed with carrying a quiver with many arrows; therefore the poets have also given him this surname.

### Hecaton. **Far-Shining.**

Phonutus <note>likely the Stoic philosopher Cornutus</note> believes he has this name because his rays reach from afar and so widely. Others say that because he sometimes brings the pestilence with excessive heat, and the people then so faithfully call upon him to help, this name was given to him. And Strabo <note>A Greek geographer</note> says that all the islands together—of which there are about twenty in the <term>strait</term> <note>original: "Mehöt"</note> from <term>Mytilene</term> to <term>Tenedos</term>—were called <term>Hecatonnesi</term> <note>literally "Islands of the Far-Shooter"</note>, after Apollo whom they honored with many names.

### Pagasæus. **At Pagasa.**

Cape Werlich, or the promontory of Verlico, which was once called <term>Magnesium</term>, has a city <term>Iolco</term>, from which the first ship of the Argonauts set out, not far from Mount <term>Pelion</term>. Some say it happened and the ship was built at <term>Pagasa</term>, which is now called <term>Armico</term>, and that <term>Apollo</term> had a temple there; the city was thus named after the many springs <note>derived from the Greek *pege*, meaning fountain or spring</note> found there.

### Anax. **King.**

The little word <term>Anax</term> comes from its meaning, which is to take care, provide help and counsel; and all gods who are called kings—except for <term>Jupiter</term>—have this name; but he [Jupiter] is called <term>Basileus</term> <note>original: "Basileus", meaning King or Monarch</note>. Thus this name is also not unjustly applied to the Sun.

### Clarius. **At Claros.**

The <term>Colophonians</term> in <term>Ionia</term> had a spot called <term>Claros</term>, where <term>Apollo</term> had a sanctuary <note>original: "stifft"</note> which, besides the sanctuary at <term>Ephesus</term>, was the most beautiful in <term>Asia</term>. There was a beautiful shrine by the temple, along with a forest of ash trees. <term>Xerxes</term> <note>The Persian King</note> also had this temple burned down; however, it was first built by <term>Manto</term>, a daughter of <term>Tiresias</term>, whom <term>Rhacius</term>, the prince of that land, took as his wife. This place is now located in <term>Anatolia</term> <note>original: "Natolien"</note> in the governorship of <term>Chios</term> <note>original: "Quisco"</note> and is called the High Forest, or <term>Altobosco</term>.

<meta>catchword: Diccus</meta>

In this temple, if someone desired an answer <note>from the oracle</note>, they would call for a citizen from Miletus, or from other families in the land specifically designated for this purpose, who could neither read nor write. This person would go into the crypt of the temple to a spring and drink from it; he would then speak in beautiful verses what Apollo’s meaning was, which immediately revealed the concerns of every petitioner without them having spoken a word first. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> possessed a bronze <note>original: "öhrin"</note> image of this Apollo.

They say that the two prophets Calchas and Mopsus met at this temple after the destruction of Troy and made a wager as to which of them was the most certain in his art. Calchas asked Mopsus to guess how many figs were on the tree that stood nearby; Mopsus guessed correctly. In return, Mopsus tasked Calchas to say how many piglets the pregnant sow <note>original: "schweins mütter"</note> carried; Calchas failed in his guess and died of grief. Nicander is said to have been a priest of this Apollo by virtue of his lineage and descent. At Tegea, he was very highly honored; his image there was gilded in a beautiful temple in a high place with an annual dedication festival. During one such festival, when they were once attacked by the Lacedaemonians, they defeated the enemy through trickery. In Corinth, he has a bronze statue.

## Epibaterios. The Helper.

Diomedes is said to have built a temple at Troezen near the Scyllaean promontory after the Trojan War, dedicated to this Apollo in the sanctuary of Hippolytus, who lies buried there, provided with priests and singers. Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> says he is called *Epibaterios* <note>meaning "The Disembarker"</note> from the act of landing <note>original: "Außgang"</note>; others say the name comes from "helping up" or "assisting," because Diomedes was helped out of the fury of the sea, or helped onto the land.

## Thyrxæus.

In the straits <note>original: "güessen," likely referring to the Bosphorus</note> near Constantinople lie the islands that were once called Cyaneas or Symplegades <note>The "Clashing Rocks" of Greek myth</note>, and are now called Pagonare; there Apollo had a temple of this name, and by it was a spring in which one could see the thing one wished to ask about.

## Thyræus. The Door-keeper.

To this Apollo many altars were erected in various places in the land of Greece, placed before the doors to indicate that this God had power over the exit and entrance.

## Prostaterius. The One Before the Door.

He was also honored with this surname because he stood outside the gates. However, Pausanias says that not far from the marketplace at Megara, there was a temple of Apollo the Protector <note>original: "Vorsteer"</note> on the road, in which stood a very magnificent and costly image made by Praxiteles <note>One of the most renowned sculptors of ancient Greece</note>.

## Derradiotes, Diradiotes. The Friend of the Ridge.

At Argos, in the temple of the Pythian Apollo, stood a bronze image called *Dicadioten* <note>likely a variation of Diradiotes</note>, because that place was once called Diras; and there one received answers from a priestess who must not have relations with any man. Every month at night she sacrifices a little lamb; she drinks its blood, and then the spirit of prophecy comes upon her.

<header>The Third Book.</header>

## Dicæus, Dircæus. The Just.
<note>original: "Grecht"</note>

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman natural historian</note> reports that the sculptor Leontius created an image of Apollo with his harp, as well as one depicting him shooting the dragon <note>referring to the Python</note> down with his arrows. This same statue was called "Dicæus" <note>from the Greek 'dikaios,' meaning just or righteous</note> because a citizen of Thebes, when the city was conquered by Alexander the Great, hid his money in the lap of this statue and later found it there untouched. And just as the earth is called "just" because it faithfully returns what is planted in it, so this name also remained with Apollo.

## Lithesius. He of the Rock.

In Malea, or on the promontory of Malea, there was a rock or small headland upon which stood a temple of Apollo; from this, he retained this surname.

## Geruntios, Gerunthrios.

In Thrace, by the river Hebrus (which is now called the Valiza), the Aenianians had a temple consecrated under the name of Apollo. Elsewhere, in the territory of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> at Geronthrae, Apollo also had a temple in the castle, the head of whose statue was made of ivory.

## Telchinius.

This Apollo was worshiped on the island of Rhodes; and because Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> writes about it and mentions of the Telchines <note>mythical original inhabitants of Rhodes, known as skilled metalworkers</note> occur in other places, I will leave the matter here.

## Carneus, Craneus.

The Dorians, and above all the Lacedaemonians, held Apollo in high honor under this name. The reason, however, was a priest named Carius, who was a very gifted soothsayer. But when he was later stabbed to death by Hippotes, the son of Phylas, a plague <note>original: "der schelm," literally 'the rogue' or 'the misery'</note> entered the Dorian camp; Hippotes fled, and they established propitiatory sacrifices for this priest. Others claim that Carneus was a son of Jupiter and Europa, raised by Apollo and Diana, and for that reason, he later erected a temple to Apollo. They also celebrated games—a festival which the Lacedaemonians held for nine days with the attendance of all Greeks—where they lived in tents as if at war. There were nine such tents, and in each tent, several men were chosen from the tribes and appointed to prepare what was necessary for the games. In the theater at Sicyon, the inner part was consecrated to this Apollo. No one was permitted to enter there except for the priests. This Apollo has a statue in the Thierlin forest <note>likely a Germanization of a Greek place name, possibly the grove of Carnasium</note> not far from Messene; likewise at Sicyon, which is now called Vasilica. Also a temple at Sparta, and one at Cnocodion. Another then by Pharae. At Leuctra and Oetylus, and in other places as well.

## Mystes. Priest.

The Lydians had a statue and a temple in the city of Daldis consecrated to Apollo; from this, he received this surname.

## Genitor. The Begetter.

At Delos, Apollo had an altar that was consecrated to him, and there

# Of Pagan Gods

## Acersecomes. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Unshorn.

Because Apollo is a joyful god who brings no sorrow (for the dear Sun gladdens everything), this name was given to him <note>from the Greek 'akersikomes', meaning having long or uncut hair</note>; otherwise, in times of mourning, it was the custom to cut and shear off the hair.

## Euthresites.

Euthresis was a village near the Thespians; Apollo had a very magnificent temple there, which Zethus and Amphion <note>twin sons of Zeus in Greek mythology, famous for building the walls of Thebes</note> had built.

## Acrephius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Of Acrephnia.

Acrephius, a son of Apollo, established this city near Mount Ptous and erected a temple to his father, from which this name originates.

## Halæus. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Of the Salt-works.

Whether the monastery at Cassino, in the Duchy of Benevento, be it or not, I will not argue; for Philoctetes <note>a hero of the Trojan War</note>, wandering for a long time after being driven from Meliboea, came to the regions of the Calabrians and there erected a temple in honor of Apollo. Now, although the same is not specified as being far from Crotone, this very place—in land still uninhabited—was not far from it; one otherwise reads little of the temple except that which might fit here.

## Actius, Actiacus, Actæus, Epactius.

Where Preveza now stands on the gulf <note>original: "giessen"</note>, which was once called the waters of the Ambracians, a small headland extends into the sea; that was Actium, now called Capo Figo. At this same place, Augustus defeated Antony; and just in our own times, the Pope, the Emperor, and the Venetians hemmed in Barbarossa <note>Hayreddin Barbarossa, the famed Ottoman admiral</note>, the Turkish commander, there, and with two hundred and fifty <note>original: "dritthalb hūdert"</note> sails blocked his exit from the gulf; but afterwards, on the twenty-seventh of September <note>original: "Herbstmonat"</note> in the year 1538, they let him flee from there without any penalty. It is said that the first mariners of the ship *Argo* built an altar to Apollo there with stones gathered from the sea and consecrated a festival upon it, to be held once every five years, in the same manner as at Olympia. And when the customary ox is sacrificed there at the start of the games, which the Leucadians brought there, the flies would gorge themselves on the blood and never appear throughout the games. Augustus greatly adorned this temple after he emerged victorious. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> held the presidency and administration of the games. Beside the racetrack, there was also a pleasant forest.

## Theoxenius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Hospitable.

In Pellene in Achaia, which is now Tarso, is the temple of this Apollo, a brazen image; there was also a game at a festival where the victor received certain silver treasures. These games are said to have been established by Castor and Pollux when they heard that Hercules had been taken up into the number of the gods; some claim the best prize was a *chlena* <note>a thick, woolen Greek cloak</note>, a quilted winter cloak.

<header>The Third Book.</header>

## Hylius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; At Hysiae.

Just as at Claros <note>a Greek city famous for its oracle of Apollo</note>, there is said to have been a spring in the temple of Apollo in the small town of Hysiae, from which the priestess drank and then prophesied.

## Phaeton.

At times this name is used for the Sun itself, and at other times for Phaeton, the son of the Sun <note>original: "son Solis"</note>, as seen in Homer where Phaeton (the Sun) is called upon as the one who sees and illuminates all things, taken as a witness by Agamemnon when he desired to reconcile with Achilles <note>referring to Agamemnon’s oath in the Iliad</note>.

## Parrhisius.

On Mount Lycaeus in Arcadia, toward the sunrise, this Apollo had a temple. Below in the marketplace, they slaughtered and sacrificed to Apollo with the surname "The Helper" <note>likely referring to Apollo Epicurius, 'the helper' in times of plague</note>, of which mention was made before; but they carried the sacrifice into this temple with a great noise. They burned the shields and the haunches <note>term: "storzen" — the thick part of a leg or hindquarters of an animal</note>, and the rest they feasted upon together.

## Agyieus, Agyiates. Lord of the Ways. Lord of the Streets.

In alleys, streets, and ways, this Apollo is honored, from which he derives his name, because he made them bright through his light and kept them dry. They say that in Tegea there was a temple of this Apollo that was established in this manner: After Apollo and Diana <note>Artemis</note> were born, they traveled through the land and punished all those who had not welcomed or had persecuted their mother Latona while she was pregnant. When they came to Tegea, Scephrus, the son of Tegeates, stepped toward them and whispered something in Apollo's ear. The other son of Tegeates, Limon, thinking his <margin>*</margin> brother was saying something against him to Apollo, stabbed him to death. Diana, being enraged, shot Limon dead. Thus, Tegeates and Maera immediately erected a temple and sacrificed to Apollo under this name <note>Agyieus</note> because it happened upon the street or alleyway. At Acharnae, there was also a temple to this god; otherwise, he had several pillars and altars erected in other places as well.

## Pataræus.

In Briquien, which is roughly called Lycia, lies the city of Patara. There was a foundation of Apollo there which rivaled the one at Delphi in wealth and popularity. It was said that during the six winter months, Apollo kept house and allowed himself to be found at Patara, spending the summer in Delphi. This temple originated as follows (as was also mentioned somewhat under "Apollo Lycius"): There was a young maiden named Salacia from Ophionia who was tasked by her father to carry a gift to the Lycian temple. Within a small box <note>original: "lädlin"</note> were some strings, a bow and arrow, and several cakes. On the way, the maiden grew tired, sat down, and lay by the seashore to rest. She fell asleep, and the wind cast the box into the sea. When the girl awoke and did not find her little box, she wept and took it very poorly, returning home. However, the box was washed up on a point of land that jutted into the sea. It was found by someone who saw clearly that it belonged to Apollo. Thus, he sacrificed to Apollo and burned it. A temple was then built at that same place, and a city grew there, for in their language "Patara" signifies a chest or a small box.
