# Concerning Heathen Gods

...was not slaughtered; only at appointed times did one perform certain prayers there.

## Acersecomes. Unshorn.

Because Apollo is a joyful god who brings no mourning (for the dear Sun gladdens all things), this name was given to him; otherwise, in times of sorrow, it was the custom to cut and shave off the hair.

## Euthresites.

Euthresis was a small village near Thespiae; Apollo has a very magnificent temple there, which Zethus and Amphion <note>the legendary twin brothers who built the walls of Thebes</note> had built.

## Acrephius. At Acrephnia.

Acrephius, a son of Apollo <note>original: "Apollinis"</note>, established this city by Mount Ptous and erected a temple to his father, from which this name comes.

## Halæus. At Halae.

Whether this is the monastery at Cassino in the Duchy of Benevento or not, I will not dispute; for Philoctetes, after wandering long when driven out of Meliboea, came to the regions of the Calabrians and erected a temple there to honor Apollo. Now although the same is not located far from Croton, this place was in a still uninhabited land not far from there; one also reads little of the temple otherwise, except for the one that might fit here.

## Actius, Actiacus, Actæus, Epactius.

That which is now called Preveza on the Gulf of Arta, which was once called the Ambracian bay, is a small headland extending into the sea; that was Actium, now called Capo Figo. At this same place, Augustus defeated Antony, and only in our times, the Pope, Emperor, and Venetians cornered Barbarossa <note>Hayreddin Barbarossa, the famous Ottoman admiral</note> or the Turkish captain there, and with two hundred and fifty <note>original: "dritthalb hundert" — literally "three-half hundred" or 250</note> sails blocked the exit of the gulf for him; but afterward, on the twenty-seventh of September <note>original: "Herbstmonat"</note> in the year 1538, let him escape without any penalty. It is said that the first shipmates of the ship Argo <note>the Argonauts</note> built an altar to Apollo there with stones gathered from the sea and consecrated a festival to be held every five years, in the same manner as in Olympia. And when the customary ox is sacrificed there at the beginning of the games, which the Leucadians brought there, the flies would gorge themselves on that blood and, because of the games, never appeared there again. Augustus greatly adorned this temple after he was victorious. The Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> held the presidency and management of the games. There was also a pleasant forest next to the racetrack.

## Theoxenius. Hospitable.

In Pellene in Achaia, which is now Tarso, there is a temple of this Apollo with a bronze statue <note>original: "öhrin bild"</note>; there was also a game at a festival where the victor received certain silver treasures. These games are said to have been established by Castor and Pollux when they heard that Hercules had been taken up into the number of the Gods; some say the best prize was a <term>Chlaena</term> <note>a heavy, quilted winter cloak often awarded as a prize in ancient Greek games</note>.

<header>The Third Book.</header>

## Hylsius. At Hysa.

Just as at Claros, so too in the temple of Apollo in the small town of Hysa, there is said to have been a spring from which the priestess drank, after which she prophesied.

## Phaeton.

At times, this name is taken for the Sun itself, and at other times for Phaeton the son of Sol <note>original: "Solis" — the Roman Sun god</note>, as seen there in Homer, where Phaeton is called upon as the one who sees and illuminates all things, and is taken as a witness by Agamemnon when he desires to be reconciled with Achilles.

## Parrhisius.

Upon Mount Lyceum in Arcadia toward the sunrise, this Apollo had a temple; below at the marketplace, they slaughtered and offered sacrifices to Apollo with the surname "the Helper" <note>This refers to Apollo Epicurius</note>, of which mention was made before; but they carried the sacrifice into this temple with great pomp. The shields and staves they burned; the remainder they feasted upon together.

## Agyieus, Agylates. Lord of the Ways. Lord of the Streets.

At alleys, streets, and roads, this Apollo is honored; from this he takes his name, because he made the same bright through his light and through dryness. They say that at Tegea there was a temple of this Apollo, which was established thus: when Apollo and Diana were born, they later traveled about the land punishing all those who had not received or had persecuted their mother Latona while she was pregnant. And when they came toward Tegea, Scephnus, the son of Tegeates, stepped out to meet them and whispered something into Apollo's ear. <margin>*</margin> The other son of Tegeates, Lemon, believing his brother was saying something against him to Apollo, stabbed him to death. Diana, being enraged, shot Lemon to death. Thus the people of Tegea and Maera immediately erected a temple and offered sacrifices to Apollo under this name because it occurred on the street or alley. In Acharnae, there was also a temple to this god; otherwise, he also had several erected columns and altars in other places.

## Pataraeus.

In Lycia <note>original: "Brixien" — likely a misspelling or archaic reference to the Lycian region</note>, lies the city of Patara. There was a foundation of Apollo there which, in wealth and attendance, compared to the one at Delphi. It was arranged that for the six months of winter, Apollo would keep house and be found at Patara, and in the summer at Delphi. This temple arose in the following way, as some mention was also made regarding the Lycian Apollo. There was a young daughter named Salacia from Ophionia who was meant to carry certain gifts, given to her by her father, into the Lycian temple. All of this was locked in a small casket; there were several strings <note>likely for a musical instrument like a lyre</note>, a bow and arrow, and also several sacrificial cakes. The maiden became tired on the way, grew faint, and lay down on the shores of the sea to rest. She fell asleep, and the wind blew the casket into the sea. When the girl awoke and did not find her casket, she wept and took it very hard and went home. However, the casket was washed up at the point that extended into the sea and was found by one who saw well that it belonged to Apollo. Thus he offered it to Apollo and burned it; thereafter, a temple was built at that same place, and a city also grew there; for in their language, Patara signifies a small chest or casket.

# Of Pagan Gods
## Ecbasius, Embasius: The Embarker and the Disembarker.

The shipmates of the ship *Argo* <note>The Argonauts, legendary heroes of Greek myth</note>, as they were about to board and set sail, received an omen that they would be able to return home healthy and without harm if they first offered a sacrifice to Apollo. This they did as they were about to board, erecting an altar upon the shore where they performed their offering. Once they had reached the sea and arrived at Cyzicus—which is now the promontory of Spica—the inhabitants persuaded them to come ashore; and upon disembarking, they sacrificed once again to **Apollo the Disembarker** <note>original: "Apollini dem Außsteiger," referring to his Greek epithet Ecbasius</note>.

## Comæus, or Cumæus.

At Sanchis in Turcomania—once called Seleucia in Mesopotamia, situated on the Tigris river in the region of Erchef, which King Seleucus Nicanor (or Nicator) of Syria built—Apollo was honored under the name **Chomei**. This place possessed a right of sanctuary where criminals could seek refuge. Avidius Cassius, the general of the Roman Emperor Verus, conquered and plundered this city, even though he and all his troops had been received there as friends. Among other things, he took the statue of Apollo from there and had it brought to Rome to the Temple of the Palatine Apollo. It is said this booty did not bring him luck: for a soldier brought a small box from there, believing it contained much gold, and opened it. Out of it came such a poisoned air that not only Persia, but Rome and the entire world as far as the Rhine river was poisoned, and the plague carried off people everywhere <note>This refers to the "Antonine Plague" (165–180 AD), which ancient writers blamed on the opening of a tomb or casket in the temple of Apollo at Seleucia</note>.

Augustine says that the Cumaean Apollo wept when the Romans waged war against Aristonicus and the Achaeans. This continued for four days in a row, wherefore they wished to throw the statue into the sea. However, the soothsayers said that Apollo wept on behalf of the city of Cuma in Italy, showing that those among whom he dwelt would suffer great hardship. Without doubt, he speaks here of the Cumaean Apollo who is in the *Terra di Lavoro* <note>original: "Terraio Lauoro," a historical region of southern Italy</note> not far from Naples, where an old ruined church still stands. As for the people of Cuma in Asia—now called Castri, between Foglia and Griyona—I do not know if they had a temple of Apollo other than the one at Gryneium, of which we shall speak later. This Cuma in Italy was built by Hippocles and Megasthenes from Crete—others say by the Locrians. It is true that Livy says there is a temple of Apollo at Dicraeome <note>original: "Dicra Come"</note>, by which he perhaps means Castri; judge for yourself, though I do not know how the Romans could have intended to throw the weeping statue into the sea if it had been in Asia and not in Italy.

## Themenites, Themites, Themistes,
### Thesmotes, Temintes, Temeates, Themanites.

Though there are so many names that might rhyme as one, the cause is the lack of diligence among the ancients, as one reading is found in Cicero and another elsewhere. But Marius Aretius says that at the amphitheater now called "Paradise" in Zaragoza, there once stood the most beautiful and largest statue of Apollo, who was called **Themistes**. However, I read it as **Teneates**; for as Strabo says, Archias the Corinthian, coming from the village of Tenea...

<header>The Third Book.</header>
<sig>t ij Part</sig>

...he led many people from the village to occupy the city of Syracuse; thus it is easy to believe that since Apollo had a temple at that same place, those who were led into foreign lands—following their practice of idolatry—also established a temple in their new residence.

## Gergithius.

Apollo was honored under this name in a village called Gergis near Troy; from this same village came the Trojan Sibyl <note>A legendary prophetess of the ancient world</note>. The Gergithians also struck this Sibyl upon their coins, alongside the Sphinx.

## Cous.

Lango—which in ancient times was the island of Cos, the homeland of Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note>—also possessed a temple of Apollo along with a sacred grove. Publius Turulius had this grove cut down to build ships, for which he was later put to death by Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor</note>.

## Hiacinthides.

It was mentioned previously how Hyacinthus was so beloved by Apollo; from this come the festivals at Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, which is why this name remained associated with him.

## Thymbræus, Thymbracus.

In the wide, beautiful fields around Troy, there was a place called Thymbra, named after the water <note>The river Thymbris</note> that flows through it. This stream flows into the Scamander, and the heath there was called Thymbra because so many hyssop plants <note>original: "Garten Isopis"</note> grew there. There stood an ancient and precious temple of Apollo of which Homer says that Aeneas was healed there when Diomedes wounded him. Some name him thus because he "stills the rain."

## Tyrbenos.

What this name signifies is not entirely clear; Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Alexandrian grammarian and lexicographer</note> provides an unusual interpretation of it. Perhaps it comes from the fact that *tyrbē* <note>original: τυρβη</note> among the Eleans signifies the "air," and the Sun constantly follows its course through the air.

<margin>The Releaser.</margin>
## Aphetor.

Because Apollo gave answers and revealed secrets, and also visibly shoots out his "streams"—which are his arrows—this became his surname <note>derived from the Greek *aphetos*, meaning "released" or "set free"</note>. Otherwise, *Apheti* are those consecrated to God, and one might call a sacrificial yearling <note>original: "Thengi färlin"</note> an *Apheton*.

## Euholmos.

Some claim that the tripods or three-legged stools of Apollo were called *Holmi*; it was believed that whoever fell asleep upon them would be granted the power of prophecy. From this, Apollo also received this surname.

<margin>The one of Gryneum.</margin>
## Grynæus.

Strabo says that Gryneum is a village of the Myrinaeans which possesses a very ancient and precious temple made of white marble. Others claim that near Clazomenae (now called Stolaro) there was a grove called Grynaeus in which the temple stood; this forest was exceedingly beautifully adorned with wild, cultivated, fruitful, and fragrant shrubs.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

### Parnopius. Locust-hunter / Gnat-hunter.

In the citadel at Athens, there was a temple containing a bronze image of Apollo cast by Phidias <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BC</note>. They said it was erected to him because he once drove away the locusts <note>original: "schnacken," which can mean gnats or locusts; the author clarifies with "Hewschreckenjäger" (locust-hunter)</note> that had caused great damage to the land. This may have happened because the floodwaters usually leave moisture behind, from which the gnats grow until the sun dries them up. Strabo says that the Aeolians in Asia call *Parnopion* a mouse, but the Boeotians call it a locust; therefore, they offer sacrifices to him.

### Philalexander. Alexander's Friend.

When Alexander besieged the city of Tyre, there was an image that the Carthaginians had brought and consecrated from Syracuse in Sicily to Tyre (from whence they had originated). It appeared to a man in a dream that he should reveal how Apollo no longer wished to remain in the city. Because of this, the Tyrians made a golden chain and foot-rings, and they placed them on the image, shackling it to the altar of Hercules as if he were meant to hold him there. When Alexander conquered the city, he broke the bonds, freed him, and called him Philalexander <note>Greek: "Friend of Alexander"</note>.

### Argyrotoxus. He with the Silver Bow.

The sun runs just like an arch above us; therefore, that semi-circle is very beautiful, and the arrows with which he shoots are the beams of light—as has often been said—from which this naming comes.

### Toxophorus, Arciteneus. Bow-bearer.

These are surnames given to him by the poets in many places, both in Greek and in Latin poems.

### Chrysocomes, Auricomos. Golden-haired. Chrysocomes,
### Crinitus, Chrysaor.

These are also names derived from the luster, shine, and beams of the sun. For just as gold glitters or a polished sword shines, so too is his brilliance shimmering.

### Leschecorius, Leschenorios. He at the Gossip-Corner.

I do not wish to argue with anyone here, but although Phornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> and others attribute this name to him because people used to gather together in the sunshine to conduct their business or learn new rumors, I would rather believe another explanation. Since in Delphi and many other places in Greece—even in the time of Homer—there were certain houses and places where people met daily to handle serious matters or to hear news, perhaps Apollo was depicted there through paintings or other images, whereby this name was granted to him.

### Orchestes, Choropæos. Lead-singer / Leaper.

This is what Pindarus, Homerus, Orpheus, and other poets call him.

### Phyxius. The Banisher.

Those who were banished and wandered in misery offered sacrifices to this Apollo. Some believe there was a spot on the island of Lango <note>modern-day Cos</note> called Phyxia, named after the flight of Hercules, and that Apollo took the name from there.

### Napæus.

On the island of Metelin <note>Lesbos</note> there was a city called Nape, where Apollo was honored as a shepherd.

### Telmissius.

...[founded] a city called Telmissus, built by Telmissus who came from the Muscovites <note>original: "Moscouiten"; the author here follows an archaic tradition linking the Telmissians of Lycia to legendary origins in the north</note>, together with a temple of Apollo. However, some say this Telmissus was a son of Apollo and Themistone, the daughter of Zaby, a king in Muscovy. These descendants of Telmissus became great and highly esteemed people through their gift of prophecy, so much so that Croesus <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia</note> sent to them to consult about his war. These same people, when they took the island of Termissa near Sicily, were given the name Galeotae <note>original: "Gallinater"; a reference to the Galeotae, a family of diviners</note> because of their prophecies, just as the others were called Telmissians; likewise, they were called Satyrisci. It is also written that in Telmissus, everyone—young and old, woman and man—could perform some measure of prophecy. The Syracusans fashioned the spring of Telmissus into a human form, specifically that of a young boy whom they loved dearly and who shared the same name as the spring; they depicted him in that likeness for this reason.

### Euthryptos.
### The Dainty / The Gourmand.

In Athens, dainty cakes and other sweets were offered to this Apollo, from which he received this name.

### Thornax.

A mountain in the territory of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> where Apollo had a temple; he was given this surname after that place.

### Prosopius.
### The Watchful.

The Athenians have several pleasant mountains around the city, and also stone quarries; upon one of these, they had an altar dedicated to this Apollo.

### Decatephoros.
### The Tithe-Bearer.

At Megara, this Apollo was honored with this name; his image was crafted from ebony <note>original: "Nebenholtz," likely a variation of *Ebenholz* (ebony)</note>.

### Larissenus.

Sigella was once the highly famous city of Ephesus in the province of Caria, now called Quistian <note>likely a corruption of a contemporary Turkish name</note>. Near it is Larissa, a small spot on Mount Tmolus, situated in a field and plain through which the river Caystrus flows; there stood a temple of this Apollo, from which he received the surname.

### Polio.
### The Gray-haired.

In Thebes <note>original: "Stibes or Thebe"</note>, there was a temple consecrated to this Apollo. There, they sacrificed to him the nearest yoked ox that could be seized from its labor. This practice arose because once, when someone had sent for his ox, those who were supposed to bring it took too long; he quickly took the one he had standing at the wagon, and from this, the custom was born.

### Amazonius.

Not far from the promontory of Malea in the Lacedaemonian mountains, the Amazon women stopped their march near the small town of Pyrrhichus and erected a wooden image to Apollo.

### Stobæus.

This Apollo was honored at Abae in Phocis, of which mention was made previously.

### Tilphosius.

Not far from Talandi <note>likely Atalanti</note> in Morea <note>The Peloponnese</note> there was a mountain called Tilphosius...

Apollo is also said to have had a temple there.

### Phyllæus.

At the stream of Vollo, which was located in Achaea, there was a city called Phylo, from which the name of the stream comes. Apollo had a temple there, and thus the surname has remained with him.

### Tarrhæus. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Tarrheus.

In Candia <note>The island of Crete</note> there was a city called Tharra; there was also a city of this name in Lydia which the Cretans built at Mount Caucasus. However, Apollo received this surname from the city in Candia.

### Selirantius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Selinunter.

In the city of Selinunte, on the island of Negropont <note>The medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea</note>, Apollo had a temple and there delivered oracles. However, the Hellopians took the statue from that place and brought it to Istria, whereby that place gained a magnificent status and a great influx of people.

### Salganeus.

In Boeotia <note>A region in central Greece</note>, there was a city built by Salganius, located opposite Negropont. He also had his temple there, and took his name from that place.

### Musagetes. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Leader of the Muses.

This name has been mentioned before, but he is called so because he represents the unity that belongs to divine action and to the harmony <note>original: "z samen stimung"</note> of all things in the world. For this reason, he leads the nine Muses; through the two numbers, one and nine, the entire course of the heavens is completed and held together.

### Marmarinus

Salamis (sometimes called Budoris), a city in Negropont at the promontory now called Capo Mantello—formerly known as the "Little Lion’s Head"—has a beautiful stone quarry where marble is broken. A temple was also located there, from which the surname was given to Apollo since it was consecrated to him.

### Aleuromantis. <note>original: "Aleueomantis"; refers to Aleuromancy or divination by flour</note>

As has been said, in what way sorcery was practiced at times, and how he is given a final name for soothsaying: because of the flour cakes and barley that were offered to Apollo, after which his answer was heard, he has kept this name.

### Tragius. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; At Tragea.

On the island of Naxia (which is Naxos), there was a city called Tragea where Apollo was worshipped.

### Ixius.

Ixis was a little valley on the island of Rhodes in which Apollo had a temple; from this, the name is derived.

<header>The Third Book.</header>

## Lathræus.
This Apollo, according to the accounts of Strabo <note>A famous Greek geographer and historian from the 1st century BC</note>, had a temple in the Duchy of Acarnania <note>A region in western Greece</note> near the city of Calydon by the lake.

## Styracites.
Scyration was a mountain in Crete <note>original: "Cadien"</note> where Apollo was worshipped.

## Ilæus.
The Apollo at Troy also held this name.

## Aegleos.
The island of Anaphe is located not far from Crete; it is now called Anafi <note>original: "Namphio"</note>. Measuring about six miles in length and breadth, it tolerates no snakes at all; if one of these venomous worms enters, it barely touches the ground before it is dead. Within it was the city of Aeglete on a mountain, which has now been torn down because of sea-pirates <note>original: "Möyrauber"</note>. Apollo was worshipped there, from which he received this surname. Mention was made previously of Anapheus and Phanaeus.

## Mantois. &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; **Soothsayer.**
He has this name from his prophesying.

## Dynasta. &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; **Landgrave.**
The "Counts" <note>German: *Grafen*</note> among us take their name from this: our dear ancestors, the Germans, always held old age in honor, expecting much wit and reason from it, and they considered those with gray hair <note>The author provides a folk etymology, connecting the title *Graf* (Count) with the word *Grau* (gray hair/old age)</note> worthy of ruling cities and lands. Such governors were then called Counts, and those who had an entire province to administer were called Landgraves, Margraves, etc. This was the *Dynastæ* <note>Greek for "ruler" or "power"</note> among the Greeks, a name which the Romans <note>original: "Latiner"</note> also kept and used; however, it meant nothing other than a governor <note>original: "Vogt"</note> who did not inherit the position but oversaw such dominion as an appointed official.

## Cataon.
In the province of Anatolia <note>original: "Anaduole," referring to modern-day Turkey</note>, which roughly borders Cappadocia and Armenia, there was a region called Cataonia <note>original: "Cataonum"</note>, which is now approximately around Keve <note>original: "Cobeck"</note>. There, the entire province had a common temple in which they worshipped Apollo. From that place, this name was given to him.

## Cillæus.
The province of Cilicia is now called Karamania <note>A historical region in southern Asia Minor</note>; it has a temple of Apollo at a place called Cilla. There was also one of this name in Anatolia near the Landreniti, who were once called Adamiteni; likewise near Thebes.

## Cirrhæus.
The rock or the cleft that lies above the temple at Delphi was called Cyrrha. From this, Apollo also received his name.

## Elius or Helius.
Because the sun waters <note>Likely referring to the sun's role in drawing up moisture or vapors</note>, she <note>In the German language, the sun is a feminine noun</note> has this name.

<header>On Pagan Gods.</header>

## Cyrus, Talos, Samasa, Saos, Oetosyros.

The Persians called the Sun Cyrus; the Arabians Talos and Samasa; the Babylonians Saos; and the Scythians Oetosyros.

## Erisatheus, Enaurus.

Apollo was named thus in Attica, as well as Enaurus, from the coolness of the morning <note>original: "morgēs Kühle"</note>.

## Casius.

When people wished to hold a jesting play <term>Schimpffspil: a lighthearted, satirical, or comedic performance</term> with proverbs, those who intended to hold it would set up an altar to Apollo Casius.

## Astypalæus.

The island of Stampalia—which was called Astypalea by the ancients and is very rich in fish—also honored Apollo. Likewise, in Lango <note>The modern island of Kos</note> on the island formerly called Cos, there was a city of the same name in which Apollo was also worshipped.

## Odrysseus.

The water of Odryssa flows through the regions of the province of Asia, now called Bursa <note>original: "Bursia," likely referring to the city in modern-day Turkey</note>. On this same water was situated a temple dedicated to Apollo, from which he received this surname.

## Seirius.

Archilochus <note>A Greek lyric poet from the 7th century BC</note> calls him "the Little Dog," after the constellation that rises in August and is called the Dog [Sirius], so that it refers to the Sun when it is at its hottest.

## Euryalus.

Because the sun shines in all places and everywhere, Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian of the 5th century AD who compiled a famous lexicon of rare Greek words</note> named him thus.

## Zotæates.

Zotæa is a city located in Arcadia where Apollo was worshipped. Likewise, in the city of Argos, he also had a temple under this name.

## Zotelyftes.

In Corinth, he was worshipped under this name.

## Terelimion, Eresios.

These surnames were given to Apollo by Hesychius.

## Thyos, Thoaxus.

The Milesians <note>Inhabitants of Miletus, an ancient Greek city in Ionia</note> named him thus.

## Dionysiodotos.

In Phlya <note>An ancient deme or district in Attica</note>, an altar was erected to this Apollo as a gift from Bacchus <note>Dionysiodotos literally translates from Greek as "given by Dionysus"</note>.

## Thermius.

Some call him Thermius, and Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer</note> says he had an altar in Olympia <note>original: "inn Olympus"</note>.

## Sciallius.

Because the sun constantly changes its course and draws near to us toward midday, this name was given to it.

<header>The Third [Chapter]</header>

# Sosianus

In Seleucia there is an image of Apollo, <unclear>carved</unclear> and sculpted by Sosianus. This Seleucia is now called Soldino <note>original: "Soldino," a contemporary reference to the port of Seleucia Pieria</note>.

# Aperco

This is what Apollo is named by the Romans, because he gave words <note>This refers to his role as a giver of oracles</note>.

<margin>Heliopolita</margin>
At Heliopolis in Egypt <note>The "City of the Sun"</note>, there is an image of the Sun, or Apollo, completely <unclear>undecorated</unclear> and holding a whip like a charioteer. When this image was carried about, the [priests] had to take the head [of the litter] upon themselves after fasting for a long time. The image did not only give [vocal] answers, but if someone brought a sealed letter and asked about its contents, it would give an answer. Trajan, the Emperor, wished to test this before he went to war; he stayed at Rome while he sent a letter secured with his imperial seal. The image sent him back a blank paper. Then he sent another one, asking if he would return to Rome after the war. In response, the image had the treasures of the temple brought, wrapped in a cloth, and sent to Rome. This signified that he would return to Rome as a dead man <note>Macrobius recounts this legend, where the "treasures" or "tokens" symbolized the remains of the deceased Emperor being returned for burial</note>.

The Sun was also called [Adad] by the Assyrians, for the image was also fashioned by them to show that the [earth] is under its power; it has lions at its feet.

# Prasius

At Prasiae near Napoli <note>likely Prasiae in Attica, though the text says "Romanien," perhaps referring to the lands of the Eastern Roman Empire</note> there was a temple of Apollo. The first fruits came there annually in this manner: the [Hyperboreans] sent them to the Issedones; they then delivered them to the Scythians; the Scythians brought them to Sinope; and from there they were passed along until they reached Prasiae.

# Pyrois, Eous, Aethon

These are the four horses of the Sun. Each is named for its fiery power: the first from fire, the second from the dawn, the third from its course [speed], and the fourth from [its burning heat].

# Xanthus, Aethops

Some give him only these two horses.

# Erythraeus, Acteon, Lampas

Yet others give him four different names: the first from the Redness of morning, the second from Radiance, the third from Shining. This is because he shows himself as red in the morning when rising, then appears as a bright light, and at midday when he is at his highest, he appears [as a lamp].

<header>Concerning Heathen Gods.</header>

# Cyrus, Talos, Samasa, Saos, Oetosyros.

The Persians named the Sun Cyrus; the Arabs, Talos and Samasa; the Babylonians, Saos; and the Scythians, Oetosyros. <note>These regional names reflect the ancient practice of "interpretatio graeca," where foreign deities were identified with Greek gods—in this case, Apollo as the Sun.</note>

# Erifatheus, Enaurus.

Apollo was called by this name in Attica; he was also called Enaurus, from the coolness of the morning.

# Casius.

When a satirical play <note>original: "Schimpffspil," a humorous or mocking performance or contest of wits</note> involving proverbs was to be held, those who intended to host it would set up an altar to Apollo Casius.

# Astypalæus.

The island of Stampalia <note>modern Astypalaia</note>, which was called Astypalea by the ancients and is very rich in fish, also honored Apollo. Similarly, on the island of Lango <note>modern Kos</note>, which was once called Cos, there was a city of the same name in which Apollo was also honored.

# Odrysseus.

The river Odryssa flows through the region of Asia now called Bursa <note>original: "Bursia," likely referring to Prusa/Bursa in modern Turkey</note>. A temple dedicated to Apollo was situated by this same river, from which he received this surname.

# Seirius.

Archilochus calls him the "Little Dog" <note>original: "Hündlin"</note> after the star that rises in August and is called the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note>, so that the name refers to the Sun when it is at its hottest.

# Euryalus.

Because the Sun shines in all places and everywhere, Hesychius gave him this name. <note>The name implies "Wide-shining" or "Broad-stepping."</note>

# Zotæates.

Zotæa is a city located in Arcadia where Apollo was honored. Likewise, in the city of Argos, he also had a temple under this name.

# Zotelyftes.

He was honored under this name in Corinth.

# Terelimion, Erefios.

These surnames were given to Apollo by Hesychius.

# Thyos, Thoaxus.

This is what the people of Miletus called him.

# Dionysiodotos.

At Phlya, an altar was erected to this Apollo as a gift from Bacchus. <note>The name translates to "Given by Dionysus."</note>

# Thermius.

Some call him Thermius, and Pausanias says that he had an altar in Olympia.

# Sciallius.

This name was given to the Sun because it constantly changes its course and approaches us toward the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally "midday," used here as a cardinal direction</note>.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Apollo’s titles and associations, moving from regional names to descriptions of famous statues, oracular wonders, and the symbolic horses that pull the chariot of the Sun.</meta>

# The Third Book.

## Sofianus.

In Seleucia, there stood a statue of Apollo made of cedar wood and carved by Sosianus; it was later brought to Rome. This Seleucia is now called Soldino <note>likely referring to Seleucia Pieria in modern Turkey</note> and lies opposite Cyprus.

## Aperca.

Apollo was thus named by the Romans because he gave answers under an open curtain. <note>The name "Aperca" is likely derived from the Latin *aperire*, meaning "to open."</note>

## Heliopolitanus.

In Heliopolis in Egypt—which was formerly Thebes—there stood a statue of Apollo, or the Sun, entirely beardless. In its right hand, it cracked a whip like a charioteer; in the left, however, it held a thunderbolt. <note>Historical writers often conflated the "City of the Sun" (Heliopolis) with the great city of Thebes.</note> When the statue was carried about, princes and lords with shaven heads had to carry it upon their shoulders; they were required to fast and abstain for a long time beforehand, and they had to follow wherever the statue wished to go. The statue gave answers not only to those who were present, but if someone sent a sealed letter there, he would find the answer to his question within that same letter.

When the Emperor Trajan wished to lead a war against the Parthians, he was cautious while in Rome, fearing there might be some deceit. Therefore, he sent a letter secured with the Imperial seal, in which nothing was written. In response, the statue sent him back a blank page, exactly as much as he had sent. Because of this, the Emperor sent a second letter with this question: whether he would return to Rome after the end of the war. Then the idol <note>original: "Götz," a term often used by 16th-century writers for pagan statues</note> had a precious vine brought from among the offerings <note>original: "Eleynoctern," likely a corruption of the Greek *anathemata*, meaning temple gifts</note> of the temple, broke it in two, and sent it to Rome wrapped in a cloth. This later signified that Trajan would return to Rome dead [in pieces].

## Adad.

The Sun was also called Adad by the Assyrians, which signifies "The Only One." The statue is depicted with rays shooting down from it to show that the power of the Sun penetrates the earth; at its feet, it has lions.

## Prasius. At Prasiae.

At Prasiae near Napoli in Romania <note>Referring to Nauplia in the Peloponnese, Greece, which was sometimes called "Napoli di Romania" in the Renaissance</note>, now called Cyparissia, there was once a temple of Apollo. The first fruits came there annually from the land of the Hyperboreans, or Muscovy <note>The author identifies the mythical northern Hyperboreans with contemporary Russia</note>, in this manner: The Hyperboreans sent them to the Arimaspians; these forwarded them to the Issedonians; from there they came into Scythia; the Scythians brought them to Sinope; those of Sinope shipped them through Greece so that they arrived at Prasiae.

## Pyrois, Eous, Aethon, Phlegon.

These are the four horses attributed to the Sun. The first is named for its fiery power; the second for the dawn; the third for its course; the fourth for its rays.

## Xanthus, Aethon.

Some attribute only these two horses to him: Xanthus, of a yellow color, [and Aethon].

## Erythraeus, Acteon, Lampos, Philogaeus.

Others give him four different ones with other names: the first for the redness, the second for the glow, the third for the shimmering, the fourth for the setting. This is because in the morning, before the rising, the breaking Sun shows a redness; afterwards, as it emerges, it gives a bearable glow; around noon, when it is at its highest, it shimmers; and in the evening, it sinks away and the earth hides it.

<summary>This page describes various cult statues of Apollo, including the oracular "Heliopolitan" statue that predicted Emperor Trajan's death, and lists the traditional names and symbolic meanings of the horses of the Sun's chariot.</summary>

# Of Heathen Gods

The Greeks have, according to the number of their letters, twenty-four verses, where each has its beginning according to the order of the Alphabet; and the words of each verse are begun with that very same order, encompassing only the titles of honor of the God. And although translating them into English with the same order <note>The author refers to the "acrostic" nature of these verses, where every word in a line would start with the same letter.</note> would take much time and effort, which I cannot afford at this moment, I did not wish to omit such epithets in my haste, but have set them down here.

# Of Heathen Gods
<meta>catchword: Of</meta>

The Greeks have twenty-four verses according to the number of their letters, where each has its beginning according to the order of the Alphabet. And although the words of each verse do not start with that same order, they contain solely the honorary titles of the God. While it would take much time and effort to translate them into German in that same order—which I cannot spare at this moment—I did not want to omit these surnames in my haste, but rather set them down here.

# Of the Heathen Gods

According to the number of their letters, the Greeks have twenty-four verses, where each verse begins according to the order of the Alphabet. Although the words within each verse do not strictly follow that same sequence, they encompass only the titles of honor belonging to the God. While it would take a great deal of time and leisure to translate these into English <note>original: "uertteütſchen" (into German)</note> while maintaining that same alphabetical order—which I currently lack—I did not wish to omit such surnames in my haste, but have instead set them down here.

# Of the Pagan Gods /
## and their supposed power for which they were worshipped among the ancients.
### The Fourth Book.

Since in the previous three books, a very extensive report has been given regarding the ancients' groping and blinded opinions of God, as well as of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, Juno, Apollo, and Sol <note>The Sun</note>, the powers attributed to them, and the epithets <term>zünamen</term> <note>Literally "surnames," referring to the specific titles or cult names given to gods based on their functions or locations.</note> they obtained for that reason—not that there is not more to be found or added—it seems to me that so much can still be learned from them that, had it been known before, this work of mine might well have been spared. Now I wish to pick out and write down what may be found worthy of record concerning Diana, who is otherwise also called Luna <note>The Moon</note> and sometimes Hecate, and first begin with what the opinion of the learned is regarding her name, from whence it was given to her, and then proceed to her epithets.

## Diana and Luna.

<image-desc>Two woodcut illustrations side-by-side. The left image shows a hunting scene with several female figures; one in the foreground holds a bow and arrow, while in the background, ships sail on a body of water near a coastal city. The right image depicts a goddess figure, possibly Hecate, standing among various monstrous creatures, including multi-headed beasts; she wears a crown of foliage and holds a spear and a circular object (shield or mirror).</image-desc>

It is said that she was first called Dana, from which the letter D was later added; for Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar and writer known for his works on antiquities.</note> interprets Jana as Luna <note>original: "Janam Lunam"; Varro suggested "Jana" was an archaic form of "Diana" and the feminine counterpart to Janus.</note>, indeed claiming them to be the same thing. Others derive the name from Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, as if she were his daughter, and for that reason she shares part of his name. One also finds those who call her Deviana <note>Likely from the Latin *devia*, meaning "out of the way" or "wandering," referring to her role in the wilderness or as the moon.</note>,

# Of the Pagan Gods

...wandering as the straying one <note>German: *Irrsam*</note> who stalks the wild game here and there in the mountains. She is also depicted dressed in a deer skin, with a chain hanging from her neck, holding a torch or lamp in one hand and two dragons in the other. Sometimes she has wings on her shoulders, leading a lion with one hand and a panther with the other. Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman statesman and philosopher</note> mentions three of them: the first is the daughter of Jupiter and Proserpina; the second was fathered by Jupiter upon Latona; the third he calls the daughter of Opis and Glauce.

In Rome, after King Ancus <note>Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of Rome</note> had conquered many surrounding spots—such as Tellenae and Politorium <note>original: *Tenen Politarium*</note>—and included the Aventine Hill within the city, he settled the captured peasants there. He commanded them to build a temple to Diana, for Ancus had brought to Rome the image of Diana that Orestes had consecrated at Aricia <note>Referring to the famous cult of Diana Nemorensis at Lake Nemi</note>, modeled after the Scythian Diana, after he conquered that city. This temple stood where the Church of Saint Sabina is now. The freedoms and laws given to these new inhabitants were carved into the bronze pedestal or base <note>original: *öhrin stock*</note> upon which the image of Diana stood. On the Caelian Hill, where Saint John is now outside the city wall, a temple was also consecrated to her. In the time of Augustus, Lucius Cornificius also erected a chapel to Diana; there were also other images of Diana in the Temple of Apollo, in the Theater <note>original: *Schaw vnd spil hauß*</note> of Marcellus, and in other places. The slaves' holiday <note>original: *knecht feyer*; also known as the Nemoralia</note> in Rome on the thirteenth of August was held in this temple of the Aventine Diana, because Servius Tullius, who is said to have finished building the temple, was born to an enslaved woman. There the beautiful ox horn was hung, as was the custom in other places. This stag horn <note>The text uses "Hirzenghürn" (stag horn), though the legend typically refers to the Sabine Ox</note> is said to have come from the following: A beautiful ox was bred in the Sabine region by a man named Antronius Coratius. It was prophesied that whoever sacrificed this ox in the temple of Diana would gain dominion over Italy. Antronius intended to sacrifice it in Rome, but King Servius warned his priest. The priest told Antronius that he must first wash and bathe in running water; before he could return from the Tiber, the King had already sacrificed the ox and hung up the horns.

## Artemis. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Pure <note>original: *Reyn*</note>.

First, she is called Artemis by the Greeks because of her purity and modest conduct, as well as her virginal intent; furthermore, she keeps such a diligent watch over virtue that she remains untouched by any union with men. Strabo <note>Greek geographer and historian</note> believes she is so named because she makes one entirely agile and valiant in strength, as well as healthy, as Phornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, Stoic philosopher</note> suggests. Otherwise, if one considers the nature of the Moon alongside Macrobius <note>Roman provincial and author of the *Saturnalia*</note>, she is so named because she "penetrates the air."

## Bendis, Bubatos. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Fearless <note>original: *Vnerschrocken*</note>.

The Thracians called Diana by these names, as Strabo, Hesychius, and Phanorinus relate; likewise, the Athenians held a festival which they called the Bendidia.

### Angelus.

The Tarentines <note>The people of Taras/Taranto</note> honored Diana under this name, as Hesychius writes.

## Zaretis, Arsiloche, Orsiloche.

The Persians gave her these titles. In Tartary <note>A historical region in North and Central Asia</note>, in the area formerly known as Taurica where she was called Orsiloche, she had a temple on the island where Caffa <note>Modern-day Feodosia in Crimea</note> now lies. When foreign people arrived there, the inhabitants sacrificed such pilgrims to this goddess; for this reason, a far-reaching and terrible rumor spread regarding this temple.

## Asteroarche.

The Africans who lived around Carthage named her with this title <note>meaning "Ruler of the Stars"</note>. It is said that the Emperor Commodus Heliogabalus took her image into his chamber as his bride when he married her <note>This refers to the historical event where Elagabalus brought the cult of Caelestis from Carthage to Rome</note>. This same image was first erected by Dido when she built the citadel at Carthage; she was highly honored by all Africans, who also called her Urania <note>The "Heavenly One"</note> and placed her in the position of a male deity.

## Ado.

Under this name, the Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia famous for astronomy</note> worshipped her as the Moon.

## Iracunda. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Wrathful.

The ancients believed that Diana made people wrathful. This is perhaps because we see that some consider epilepsy <note>original: *Hirnschweynen*</note> to be "moon-sickness" <note>lunacy</note>. Therefore, if someone acted irrationally or with grim fury, they said that Diana had possessed him.

## Luna.

The Moon <note>original: *Mon*</note> takes its name from *Luna* among the Latins because of its shining, and specifically because it shines only at night, ignited by the light of another <note>the sun</note>. For this same reason, the Greeks gave her a name based on this "new light."

## Selaphoras, Phosphoros, Nychia,
->Nyctipolos.<-

These names mean a brilliance, a light-bringing nightly power, and a star that shines by night, which is what the Moon is in itself. Among the ancients, the Moon was sometimes esteemed as a woman and sometimes as a man, as can be found in the writings of Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> and Eusebius, and which Orpheus does not keep secret. Among the people of Carrhae <note>original: *Carenern*</note> (but Carrhae in Mesopotamia is now called Orpha <note>modern-day Şanlıurfa, Turkey</note>) there was a temple. An altar to the light-bringing Diana also existed in Phlius and Myrrhinus. At Messene, she had a beautiful marble image of the Moon-god. If a man called upon this deity as a woman, he was destined to be mastered by women <note>The text suggests he would be called "Master She" and women would be his master</note>. However, if one worshipped the deity in a masculine form, he would not be outwitted by women. It was near this temple that the Emperor Caracalla was stabbed to death.

## Dilonechos. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Two-Shining.

This goddess—whom we previously called Bendis and spoke more of regarding her festival held at Athens—is also worshipped under this name. As the poet Cratinus reports, she is so named because she has two lights: one from herself and one from the sun.

others of which Xenophon makes mention, as well as Titus Livius in his thirty-eighth book, and likewise Strabo, who says that the Athenians adopted their festivals from the Thracians; for this Bendis <note>A Thracian goddess of the moon and the hunt, similar to Diana</note> had a temple in Thrace, in the region now called Romania <note>Referring to Rumelia or the Balkan territories of the former Eastern Roman Empire</note>, situated beneath a high mountain not far from Ipsala and Enez <note>original: "Chipsala und Essamiclo"</note>, formerly known as Lysimachia.

### Cybeca.

Some also address Diana with this surname.

### Hecate.

Diana—or the Moon under the same name—was also called Hecate, because she casts her beams and light far and wide; and although this name otherwise signifies "a hundred," and is sometimes used to indicate an infinite number, it is not ill-suited as a title for her or the Moon, since Jupiter granted her so much power that her influence works upon all the stars <note>original: "gstirn"</note>, which are indeed innumerable. In Ephesus, before the temple of Diana, stood a statue of Hecate made of such glistering stone or marble that no one could look upon it long without injury or blinding of the eyes.

### Perseis.

It is said Hecate was a daughter of Perseus and Asteria, or as others say, of Jupiter and Asteria; yet she has retained this name from Perseus, though some were quite willing to forget it, as she was also said to be the wife of Perseus.

### Monogenes. <note>original: "Eingeborn"</note> The Only-Begotten.

The Only-Begotten; for as it is written, Jupiter impregnated Asteria and afterwards gave her to Perseus as a wife, with whom he fathered this single daughter.

### Daduchos, Chthonia, Phylaca. <note>Greek titles meaning Torch-bearer, Of the Earth, and Guardian</note>

Jupiter is said to have raised this daughter Hecate with Ceres; she was a heroine in her whole body, and he later sent her into the earth to seek Persephone <note>The daughter of Ceres/Demeter abducted to the underworld</note>.

### Prothyraea. <note>original: "Prothyrea"</note> She Before the Door.

Jupiter is said to have fathered this Hecate with Aeolus, and when the mother became afraid, she cast the child away from her and left it lying in an alley or on a street. The shepherds of Pheres, a king's father, found the little daughter and raised her among them; for this reason, she was later honored as a goddess outside of doors and gates. Previously, the Athenians had a temple for her in Eleusis. Likewise, there was an image of her at Argos and at Sicyon, which had come from Thessaly into Pherae, and from there to Argos. At Sicyon, which is now called Vasilika, she has a beautiful temple along with a theater <note>original: "Spilhauß"</note> and a marble bust.

### The Poison-Bearer. <note>original: "Giftköcherin"</note>

The Sun is said to have had two sons in Scythia, one of whom was Perseus. He ruled in Tartary and fathered this Hecate, who, as a strong and wild woman, roamed the mountains and the hunt every day. She discovered poisonous, deadly herbs, as well as those useful for all illnesses. Regarding this, you may also consult Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note>.

## Triformis, Trigemina. Triple-natured. <note>original: "Dreykünig"</note>

It is said the Moon has three aspects and shapes; that is, she sometimes appears with horns <note>the crescent moon</note>, sometimes she is full and round, and sometimes half.

## Epipyrgidia, Triprosopon, Triceps. <note>Names meaning "Upon the Tower," "Three-faced," and "Three-headed"</note>

->**Trimorphos, Tristocephalos.**<- <note>original: "Three-formed, Three-headed"</note>

Some call her the Three-headed for the reason that she is painted with a human head in the middle, having a horse’s head on the right and a dog’s head on the left. She was most highly honored at Lagina <note>original: "Legnia"</note> on the island, where they held an annual church-consecration and festival for her.

## Triglanthyna, Triglinos.

The ancients had an image of Diana which they called Trigla; by this, they wished to indicate that the Moon gives birth three times in a year, and that the Moon begins to shine on the third day after receiving her light <note>referring to the three days after the new moon</note>.

## Cynophagon. Dog-Eater. <note>original: "Hundsfresserin"</note>

On the island of Samothrace <note>original: "Samandraca"</note> there was a cave in which dogs were sacrificed to Diana; from this she takes her surname. This sacrifice was performed because, as a huntress, she also makes men go mad like dogs.

## Aphratos, Zea, Hypolampeiras.

As the "Shining One" or "Bringer of Food," she was honored in Miletus, which is now called Milas <note>original: "Melasso"</note>. In Athens she was called Zea, and elsewhere Aphracta. Thus she was highly honored at Lagina in Caria, in the region of the Stratoniceans—unusually so—where the people of Yatağan <note>original: "Erizeler"</note> now dwell, where there was a temple and an annual festival.

## Brimo. The Terrible One. <note>original: "Die Erschockenlich"</note>

The crew of the first ship, the *Argo*, sacrificed to her under this name, as she was meant to be a protector and help for their undertaken business and dangerous voyage; yet they called her the Cruel and Terrible, for it is said of her that she arranged the nightly phantoms that frighten people, as if threatening them.

## Noctivaga, Nyctipolos. Night-wandering. <note>original: "Nachtwandlend"</note>

Apollonius gives her this name.

## Curotrophos. Mistress of Discipline / Nurturer. <note>original: "Zuchtmeisterin / Erdfröwlin"</note>

Apollonius also says that the crew of the ship honored Hecate by these names; and the "Mistress of Discipline" or "Rearer of Boys" had a temple at Koroni in the Morea <note>the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note>.

## Titanis. <note>The Titaness</note>

It is held that Latona was born of a Titan, therefore this title was given to her, because Diana is a daughter of Latona.

## Agrotera. The Rustic. <note>original: "Die Bäwrisch"</note>

In Athens, Diana had a temple under this name in which her image carried a bow; and the legend was that as soon as Diana had come from Delos—

# On Heathen Gods

First, she made her way toward Athens and devoted herself to the hunt there. Thus, an altar to this Diana was erected before the town hall at Olympus; at Aegyra, which is now called Scolocastri <note>the medieval name for the ancient city of Aigira in Greece</note>, she had a temple by the harbor.
Likewise, at Megara, Alcathous built a temple to this Diana because Enippus killed the Cithaeronian lion there, having done so with the help of this Diana and her brother Apollo.

## Terophones, Teroctonos, Philotheros, Ecebolos. <note>These Greek names mean "Beast-slayer," "Wild-killer," "Lover of the Hunt," and "Far-shooter"</note>

Because she is regarded as a huntress, the poets call her the Slayer of Wild Beasts, the Lover of the Wild, the Scorcher of the Wild, and the Shooter of the Wild.

## Hippomelathia. Brown-Maid. <note>original: "Braunmetz"; this name likely relates to Diana's "dark" or "black" aspect or her association with horses</note>

This is what Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian</note> calls her.

## Euporia. <note>Meaning "The Abundant" or "Ease of Passage"</note>

According to Hesychius, she is said to have had this surname on the island of Rhodes.

## Anaitis, Anætis.

Calmadara <note>a regional name for the site</note>, situated where Zela <note>now Zile in modern Turkey</note> once was in the province of Anatolia (which was once called Armenia Minor), has a rock in a plain that is very broad and flat on top. The Sacae <note>original: "Sarceer," an ancient nomadic Scythian people</note> made this rock even larger by throwing up earthworks, surrounded it with walls, and consecrated a temple there to Diana Anaitis <note>the Persian goddess Anahita, often syncretized with Diana</note> along with other gods. The very first golden statue ever made was the one of Diana erected there. Lucullus, even though he had already devastated and plundered the kingdom of Tigranes, left this temple untouched. However, when Mark Antony marched against the Parthians, the temple was desecrated; yet the church-robber was struck blind and lame, and finally died most miserably of disease.

## Parthenicees. Virgin. <note>original: "Junckfraw"</note>

Some believe that Mount Parthenion in Arcadia, where Diana had a temple, brought her this surname; or else that the Parthenius water <note>a river</note>, which flows through the city of Amastris <note>original: "Amatriata"</note> and where Diana hunts, gave her this name.

## Phærea.

Pherae, the city in Thessaly that is now called Jemfar <note>likely Yenishehir</note>, possessed the image of Diana which was previously mentioned as having been brought to Argos. Otherwise, sufficient mention of this has already been made before.

## Ecbateria. <note>A name meaning "Of the Disembarking," given to gods who protect those coming ashore</note>

The island of Siphnos <note>original: "Siphno"</note>, which we have also mentioned elsewhere, honored Diana under this surname.

## Derrhiatis. At the Cliffs. <note>original: "Zů Scherrn"</note>

On Mount Taygetus, where Calamata <note>Kalamata</note> in Morea <note>the Peloponnese</note> now stands, there was once a village called Derrhi. There, Diana had a statue under the open sky.

# The Fourth Book.

## Daphnea. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; At Hypsus.

Hypsus was a small village located not far from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, which was dedicated to this Diana along with Aesculapius <note>the god of medicine</note>.

## Chesia. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; At Chesio.

A small town in Ionia, according to some; others write it was a promontory at Samos, where Diana was honored and thus received this name.

## Lucina. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Midwife.

Much has been said regarding this in the section on Juno, which you may look for in its proper place; however, Cicero <note>the Roman statesman and philosopher</note> says this: Luna <note>the Moon</note>, who has her name from shining <note>original Latin: "lucere"</note>, is the one otherwise called Lucina <note>original: "Lucina," the goddess who brings children to the light</note>. Just as the Greeks call her Diana and Luciferam <note>original: "Luciferam," the light-bringer</note>—the shining one—so pregnant women among us call upon Juno under this name. And because the Moon, with her moisture, dissolves and makes things loose, and because the necessity of childbirth requires that the wrinkles and all the curves of a pregnant woman's body expand and become loose, this office of "Lucina" has been attached to Diana.

## Omniuaga. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The All-Wanderer.

Furthermore, Cicero says Diana was also called Omniuaga <note>original: "Omnivaga," meaning "wandering everywhere"</note>, she who roams through all things. This is not because of her hunting, but because she is counted among the seven wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, and by wandering about, she makes the night like day with her light. She is, however, called upon at birth so that the fruit in the mother's womb—sometimes in seven, sometimes in nine months—might be ripened and brought into the world. From this comes that famous jest: on the night when Alexander the Great was born, the temple of Diana at Ephesus burned down. Timaeus <note>a Greek historian</note> said it was no wonder, for Diana had gone to Olympias <note>Alexander's mother</note> to serve as a midwife, and had left her temple and its lights unattended because her presence was so urgently needed by the Queen.

## Ilithyia.

At Athens, a temple was built to this Diana, of whom it is said that she came from the Muscovites <note>The author likely identifies the legendary "Hyperboreans" of the North with the Muscovites of Russia</note> to Delos in the form of a wolf to help Latona <note>Leto, the mother of Apollo and Diana</note> in her labor pains as Ilithyia <note>original: "Ilithyia," the Greek goddess of childbirth</note>. For without the knowledge of Juno, the other goddesses had sent Iris (the Rainbow) to summon Ilithyia to help Latona, who had been lying in the pains of labor for nine days. Therefore, the people of Delos hold a festival for Ilithyia and sing certain songs that their poet Olenes had composed. Diodorus, Pindarus, and Hesiod say she is not Diana, but rather that she was a daughter of Juno, and that the midwife was Eleutho; however, there is no place to mention that here.

## Lochia.

Lochia <note>original: "Lochia," from the Greek word for childbirth or the state of a woman in labor</note> is the name given to the afterbirth; from this, Diana also retained this surname.

Aeron is a mountain near the Argives; from this, Melampus <note>a legendary healer and prophet</note>, when he was curing Proetus's <note>the King of Argos</note> daugh-

## Coryphea. She of the Hilltop.

Near Corinth, in the village of Epidaurus—now called Aesculapio <note>named for Asclepius, the god of healing</note>—near the Leginer springs, Diana had a temple situated on the hilltop <note>original Greek: "koryphe," meaning summit</note> of a mountain, from which this name has remained with her.

## Episcopos. Overseer.

In Elis, she had a temple which was called Aristarchum. A man named Sambycus plundered it, but because of this, he miserably wasted away from disease.

## Dictynna, Aphea. The Chosen One.

The Cretans <note>original: "Candioten"</note> called Diana by this name, while those of Aegina called her Aphea, meaning "The Chosen One." Diodorus <note>the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus</note> mentions this in his fifth book, chapter 5. Phornutus <note>the philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus</note> believes she has this name because her power and influence penetrate everything that grows out of the earth. Not far from Cape Pagu in Morea <note>the Peloponnese peninsula</note> lay a village called Hypsus, where she had a temple and an annual festival. Similarly, in Amphissa in Phocis, she has a beautiful image and temple made of black stone or marble—like that of the Aeginetans—where the statue in the temple is clothed.

## Orthias.

There was a place in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> called Limnae, where a temple was erected to Diana under the aforementioned name. Some say it was established by Orestes and Iphigenia, who had stolen the statue and brought it from Cappadocia <note>likely referring to the land of the Taurians</note>. Now, it had once been commanded that men should be sacrificed there, or at the very least, that the altar of this Diana should be sprinkled with human blood. For a long time, lots were drawn to see which youth must be sacrificed annually, until Lycurgus the lawgiver changed this sacrifice to a punishment with rods. Instead of death, the young boys had to strike one another with rods <note>a ritual known as the diamastigosis</note> within the circle or ring near the altar, so that the altar became bloody with human blood. The priestess always stood by the boys as they struck one another, holding the image of the goddess in her hand. This statue was light by nature, but if the boys spared one another because of their handsome bodies, or if for some other reason—such as high birth—they did not strike bravely, the statue became so heavy in the priestess's hands that she was about to fall down under its weight. The image, it seems, insisted on having blood.

## Lygodesma. The Birch-Bound.

This statue is said to have been found in a birch thicket, and as the birch grew upward, the statue was lifted with it; for this reason, she kept the name <note>original: "Lygodesma," though typically referring to willow or withes (lygos) in Greek, the author identifies it here with birch</note>.

## Brauronia.

In Athens, Diana had a temple and a statue. The master craftsman of the statue was Praxiteles. The name comes from the village of Brauron; they say it is the same statue that we mentioned in the account of Diana Orthia.

### Trivia, Triformis. <note>original Latin: "Trivia" means "of the three ways" and "Triformis" means "three-formed"</note>

Some believe she received this name because her chapels were located at the crossroads <note>places where three paths meet</note>; others say it is because she possesses influence and power in the heavens, on the earth, and under the earth. Phornutus <note>the Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus</note> gives her the name because she transforms herself three times in her cycle: that is, when the moon is full, when it is dark, and when it rises with horns as a crescent; more regarding this is indicated under the name Hecate.

### Euhodia. Mistress of the Way.

On a path that is constantly trodden by travelers, no fruit can be produced; and Diana, as a perpetual virgin, is also unfruitful, and thus she received this name <note>Greek: "Euhodia" refers to a good journey or one who guides the way</note>.

### Leucophryne. Pale-browed.

Cape Ortliche, or the promontory now called Walich, was once Magnesia, where Diana was highly honored under this name. Likewise, the sons of Themistocles <note>the famous Athenian general</note> erected a statue to this Diana in Athens and gave her this name, for it was said that Diana had pale eyebrows <note>original Greek: "Leucophryne" means "white-browed"</note>.

### Saronis. She of the Oak Forest.

Troezen—which was once called Aphrodisia, Possidonia, Apollonia, and Saronia—had a gulf that is now called the Leginer Gulf, over which Saron once ruled. This same Saron built a temple for Diana by the sea. While he was once hunting and pursuing a stag, he fell into the sea along with the stag; he followed it some distance into the water until he drowned. The sea was thereafter named after him <note>the Saronic Gulf</note>. His body, which was cast up near the grove of the goddess, was buried there. Some say that in ancient times an oak was called *Saro*, and because there was a large forest of oaks at that same gulf where the temple stood, Diana was given this name.

### Laphria.

Laphrius, a son of Castalius at Calydon, once erected a statue to Diana there, and from this, the surname has remained with her. Truly, some say that Diana was angry for a long time with Oeneus <note>the OCR reads "Deneum," a likely typo for Oeneus, king of Calydon</note>, who ruled at Calydon, and when her anger relented, this name grew for her. Her statue was fashioned in a fine hunting style, made of ivory and gold by Menaechmus and Soidas, citizens of Lepanto <note>original: "Lepantho," also known as Naupactus</note>. But when the people of Patras stood by Augustus in the war against Antony, Calydon was destroyed by Augustus and this statue was handed over to the Patrensians, who held it in great honor with beautiful annual festivals and celebrations.

### Ephesia, Prothothronia. <note>original Greek: "Prothothronia" means "of the first throne"</note>

Croesus, a man of the land, and Ephesus—the son of the river-god Cayster <note>the OCR reads "son Jstri," likely referring to the Cayster or Ister</note>—are said to have built the city and the temple of this goddess, although it is also attributed to the Amazons, saying they established the foundation. It may well be that they renewed the statue with fine booty and high gifts, advancing and improving the foundation. This temple has always been considered among the highest and among the wonders of

...counted among the wonders of the world / indeed, held in high esteem / as much for its size / as for the costly nature of the statue and the magnificence of the goddess / and also because of the formidable protection maintained within the city. Ctesiphon—or as some would have it, Cersiphon, and others Archiphron—is said to have been the master builder who first constructed the temple. This same temple is said to have been set on fire and burned by Herostratus, a man driven by idle curiosity, on the very night that Alexander the Great was born. His reason was this: being utterly ambitious / and having it in his mind to commit a deed / that would be spoken of for all eternity / and since he could not achieve this through good means / he committed this villainous act and set the temple on fire. The Council indeed forbade / anyone from ever mentioning his name / and did not record it, but in vain / for it became known nonetheless. Afterward, the common inhabitants of Asia / for two hundred and twenty years / worked to rebuild the temple / raising it at communal expense. Its length was four hundred and twenty-five feet <note>original: "schüh", literally "shoes"</note> / the width two hundred and twenty. It had one hundred and twenty-seven columns / each of which was erected at the expense of a particular king. Each column was sixty feet high / thirty-six were carved with reliefs / one was made by the master builder Scopas / and provided at his own expense. The women also contributed their costly adornments and many jewels to it. Alexander wanted to have it completed at his own expense, provided he was granted the title <note>meaning the dedicatory inscription on the building</note> / but the Asians would not permit this. Some say Herostratus burned this work / and that Cheremocrates rebuilt it anew / I will not dispute this. This temple possessed a right of sanctuary <note>a "freedom" or zone where criminals were safe from arrest</note> / which Alexander extended to the distance of a gunshot <note>original: "büchsenschütz"; while historically a bowshot, the 16th-century author uses the contemporary term for a firearm's range</note> from the temple. Mithridates defined it as far as one could shoot with a bow. Mark Antony also granted a portion of the city to this zone. Augustus, however, did not want to have a den of murderers / and abolished the sanctuary.

Some claim Dinocrates <note>the architect of Alexandria</note> completed the temple in Alexandria in Egypt. The stairs by which one climbed to the very top of this temple / are said to have been made from a single grapevine / found in Cyprus / for they grow exceptionally large there. Memnon the Persian captain plundered this temple / but Alexander later devoted a great treasure to it. The temple has a marble walkway / in which stood the altar and the image of Diana Prothethronie <note>Greek: "Prothronia," meaning "she of the first throne" or "seated before the temple"</note>, which is to say, she in the bronze chair.

## Of the Seven Wonders of the World.

And since I mentioned before / that this temple is counted among the seven wonders of the world / I will here set down what was said by the ancients regarding the seven wonders. The first was the Wall of Babylon / which encompassed twelve miles in circumference / was two hundred feet high / and fifty feet wide. Each foot / was three inches longer than the Roman foot. And through this wall, the Euphrates flowed in and out at two places. It was made without lime / using only bitumen and baked stones <note>bricks</note>. These stones, however, were made from the mud / excavated while digging the city's moat / the bitumen was boiled so / that it was poured over the stones / and over crushed reeds. The battlements stood opposite one another with gates / and it also had battlements facing toward and away from the city / so that wagons could easily turn around upon them.

### Caryatis &emsp;&emsp; The one at Caryae.

Right at the beginning of the border or boundaries of the Laconians, Diana had a temple at the place called Caryae, along with a statue that stood under the open sky. In her time, when Xerxes invaded Greece and everyone fled from this land, the young women had hidden themselves. But according to custom, at the church-dedication festival <note>The author uses the Christianized term "Kirchweyche" to describe a pagan festival day.</note> of this Diana, no daughters were present to leap and dance. Therefore, the shepherds gathered together, held the festival, and performed a little dance according to their own singing; from this, the style of Bucolic <term>pastoral poetry<note>Poetry depicting the lives of shepherds or rural life, most famously associated with Virgil and Theocritus.</note></term> is said to still survive.

### Lye &emsp;&emsp; The Spleen-Healer.

Jana <note>An archaic name for Diana, sometimes viewed as the female counterpart to Janus.</note> was honored under this name among the Sicilians because she healed many people suffering from spleen ailments. Titus Livius mentions Luna <note>The personification of the Moon, often identified with Diana.</note> in the fifty-fifth book; one might look to see if it corresponds with this.

### Tauræa &emsp;&emsp; The one at Cassa.

When the Greeks gathered at Aulis, Agamemnon accidentally shot a stag belonging to Diana, for which she was enraged, as you may read in the history of Dictys of Crete near the beginning.

### Thoantis &emsp;&emsp; Thoantea.

When Agamemnon’s daughter, Iphigenia, was delivered to King Thoas in Tartary <note>The author uses "Tartary" to refer to the ancient land of the Taurians (Crimea).</note>, she became a priestess in the temple of Diana. And when she was required to slaughter and sacrifice humans there, she recognized her brother Orestes, who had been brought there as a sacrifice along with his companion Pylades, seeking atonement for a murder. Eventually, the matter reached the point where they killed Thoas, stole the statue of Diana, and carried it away.

### Fascelis &emsp;&emsp; The one in the Bundles.

Jana is so named because Orestes thrust the stolen statue into a bundle of wood <note>The name "Fascelis" comes from the Greek "phaskelos," meaning a bundle or faggot of sticks.</note> and thus brought it to Reggio in Italy. However, because the Romans would not endure such gruesome sacrifices, the statue was taken from there to Lacedaemonia [Sparta], where, as heard before, the "ring-hitting" <note>This likely refers to the ritual scourging of youths at the altar of Diana Orthia in Sparta, which the author describes using contemporary tournament language.</note> was established in place of the morning sacrifice. ### The one at Ariccia.

<margin>Aricina <note>Latin: "The Arician."</note></margin>
Ariccia <note>Original: "Rizza."</note>, which still keeps its name today, is situated about a mile from Nemi (which is now Genzano). There, the grove <note>Original: "Dhan," likely a corruption of "Hain" (grove) or a reference to Diana's sanctuary.</note>—which is now called Artemis—was once consecrated to Diana. There, a person who was wandering as a fugitive would be captured. Many of the same kind of companions stood around him; the poor soul had a knife in his hand, and every one who stood around him had one too. Whichever of them killed him first became the priest; whoever he could slay, he did not spare. Every year on the thirteenth of August, people ran out from Rome into this valley with torches and held a festival for the goddess.

### Mycanæa.

Not far from Fanari in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, Mycenae was located. There Iphigenia was born—she whom they wished to sacrifice to the goddess, but who later became her priestess and, together with her brother, brought the statue into Greece. From this, Diana has the name Mycanæa.

### Scythica.

Tartary lies in Scythia, and Caffa <note>Modern Feodosia in Crimea.</note> has always been counted among the Scythians; for this reason, she also has this name <note>The "Scythian Diana," often associated with human sacrifice.</note>.

### Iphigenia.

Pausanias says that at Hermione (which is now Santa Maria in the Morea), there was a chapel to Diana under this name; Diodorus also makes mention of this.

## Munythia.

At Athens there was a place that received its name from King Munychius, who had his court there. He also established a temple to Diana there with a floor plan <note>Original: "Plan," likely referring to the layout or precinct.</note> in which a bear lived that was consecrated to the goddess. However, the bear was shot dead, which enraged Diana. She sent a pestilence or plague <note>Original: "Keyber oder gepräſten."</note> into the city, with the sign that it would not cease unless someone willingly sacrificed his daughter. A man named Eubarus requested that the priesthood be given to him and his heirs as a hereditary right; if this were granted, he would sacrifice his daughter, which then occurred. From this arose the custom where the young girls who later carried the annual offering were called "The Bears" <note>This refers to the "Brauronia" ritual where young Athenian girls acted as bears, "arktoi."</note>.

->Alphaea Alphiaea.<-

Alpheus is said to have wooed Diana, but when he saw that it was all in vain, he intended to take the goddess by force. When Diana and her ladies perceived that Alpheus wanted to have them by violence, they smeared and stained all their faces exactly alike with mud, so that no one could be recognized from the others. Thus, Alpheus had to depart again without achieving his purpose, and for this she was honored at Letrinoi <note>Original: "Lethun."</note> in Greece.

->Elaphibolia Elaphiaea.<-

Because Diana hunts, shoots, and pursues stags <note>Original: "Hirzen."</note> in this manner, she received this name <note>From the Greek "elaphos," meaning stag.</note>. The Phocians honored her under this name because, when they were attacked and besieged by the Thessalians, they built a great woodpile upon the advice of Daiphantus. They packed it with materials that catch fire easily, intending to burn their wives, children, and all their goods if they should fail in their sally against the enemy. However, they remained victorious, and so they vowed to celebrate a festival to this Diana annually.

->Theroctona.<-

She is also called this on account of her hunting: "The Killer of Wild Beasts" <note>From the Greek "ther" (wild beast) and "kteino" (to kill).</note>.

->Cnagia<-

At Sparta there was a lord named Cnageus. He went to war against the Aphidnaeans, was taken prisoner of war, and was sold in Crete <note>Original: "Candien," the Venetian name for Crete.</note>, where he was a servant at the temple of Diana. Later he escaped and stole the statue, returning home with it along with a nun <note>Original: "Nonne," meaning a priestess or consecrated woman.</note> whom he had abducted from the convent; for this reason, Diana was given this name.

->Triclaria<-

In Ionia, the inhabitants of Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis honored this Diana; there, humans were also slaughtered and sacrificed.

->Pitho.<-

When Hypermestra was to go to court with her father, she sought the counsel of Diana <note>The catchword at the bottom of the page indicates the sentence continues: "...counsel of Diana."</note>
