# Icaria.

The island of Icaria <note>An island in the Aegean Sea.</note> was once entirely fertile; it also produced many animals: hares, roe deer, and similar game in great numbers. However, no one was permitted to hunt there without the command of this goddess, under threat of punishment; furthermore, if hunters hunted without the knowledge of the priests, they would catch nothing.

### Didyma: The Twin.

Because she was born in one birth with Apollo from Latona <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Leto.</note>, she was called "the Twin" by Pindar <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet.</note>.

### Pantodrophos.

In Corone in Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, this Diana was honored as the one who kept watch over young children, seeing how they were nourished and raised.

### Pellenea: She of Tarsus.

Pellene, the city in Achaea (now called Tarsus) <note>This likely refers to a local name or a historical confusion by the author; Pellene was a prominent city in the Peloponnese.</note>, had a temple and an image of Diana in the act of shooting. Once, when the image was moved by its priest, it turned its face so hideously that no one dared look upon it anymore. Indeed, not only did the people feel a great dread of it, but even the trees standing opposite it bore no more fruit at the proper time. And once, when the priest carried the image out against the enemies, they all took to flight. 

However, Plutarch writes that when the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans.</note> captured and plundered the city, one of them placed his helmet upon every young woman he captured. One captive named Epigethis—the prisoner of a warrior named Epilectarchos—waited in the temple at the exit. Just then, Aratus <note>A Greek statesman and general.</note> came to storm the city. As the rumor spread, the Lacedaemonians, being few in number, did not know what they should do. In that moment, Epigethis ran beneath the church door; the sun shone upon her, so that the citizens marveled at the radiance and height. The enemies, however, were terrified, believing it was the goddess Diana herself. Thus, the citizens took heart to resist the enemy, and the enemy was moved to flee.

### Hemeresia: The Restorer of Sanity.

At a spot in Arcadia where Melampus <note>A legendary soothsayer and healer.</note> lived, the daughters of Proetus <note>The Proetides, who were cursed with madness.</note> came running in a state of insanity. He cured them there with incantations <note>Original: "bschuůr er sie mit zaubereyen," implying ritual healing or exorcism.</note> so that they were found healthy again in the temple of Diana. From this, she was called "the Restorer of Sanity" <note>Original: "Witzmachend," meaning to return one's wits or reason.</note> or the "Soother," who knows how to help those with confused minds regain their reason.

### Polythysamia: The Well-Trimmed.

Some call Diana by this name because she is depicted in garments that are well-trimmed <note>Original: "geprämbt," referring to decorative borders or fringes.</note>. Others believe she has the name because she is heard from afar by the baying of her dogs, or because she was sacrificed to in many places.

### Eucleia: The Noble.

In Eusdiles <note>Likely a corruption of a town name in Boeotia.</note> in Boeotia, Diana was honored under this name. She had her temple and an image there made by the master craftsman Scopas <note>A famous Greek sculptor and architect.</note>. Likewise, she had her image at Locri; some esteemed her there as a daughter of Hercules and Myrtus. She was said to have remained a virgin forever; for this reason, grooms and brides offered sacrifices to her before they came together.

<header>Concerning Pagan Gods</header>

### Callistes: The Fairest <note>original: "Die hüpfehest" (likely a dialect variant of "Hübscheste"). From the Greek *Kalliste*, meaning most beautiful.</note>

In Krounoi in Arcadia <note>A region in the central Peloponnese of Greece.</note>, a temple of this Diana stood upon a hill, as mentioned by the poet Pamphos in his verse.

### Astrataea: She who Leads Away <note>original: "Abfüeverin" (Abführerin). From the Greek *Astrateia*, meaning "she who stops the expedition."</note>

It is recorded that near Apollo the Amazonian, where those women <note>The Amazons, a tribe of female warriors.</note> arrived and ceased their further march into Greece with their army, Diana also had a temple established nearby at Pyrrhichos. She was given this name as if she had halted the procession.

### Issoria Limnea: She of the Marsh

In Teuthrone, which is now called Cholokina, there was a temple of Diana under this name; she also had an annual festival held for her there. At Lacedaemon <note>The region around Sparta.</note>, she also had a temple of this name; she was nicknamed *Limnaea* <note>Meaning "of the lake" or "of the marsh."</note>.

### Philomeirax: Friend of Youths

In Elis, where the Olympic Games are held, there is a street by the wrestling grounds called the Silent Street, or *Siope*. Upon that street, Diana had a temple under this ancient name, as she was the one who oversaw the exercise of the young men.

### Cordax: The Dancer

Not far from Pisa in Elea, there stood a temple where the companions of Pelops <note>A legendary king of Mycenae.</note> always brought their offerings with jumping and dancing, so that this name remained with the goddess.

### Pyronia: Bringer of Fire

In the Crathis mountains, situated in Arcadia, there was a temple to Diana from which fire was always fetched whenever the Lernean sacrifices were held.

### Cedreatis

Orchomenus in Arcadia, a beautiful spot, possessed a large and beautiful image of Diana made from cedar wood <note>original: "Jederholz" (Zederholz).</note>, from which her name was derived.

### Heurippa: Finder of Horses

They say that Ulysses <note>Odysseus.</note> lost his horses and came into the region of Pheneus <note>original: "Pherea".</note> where he found them. Thus, he built a temple to Diana, drove the horses there to pasture, and prescribed a law for the shepherds on how they should graze and keep the horses.

### Hymnia: The Singer

Anchisia is a mountain that separates the Orchomenians and Mantineans; upon it stood a temple of this Diana. Two priests dwell there, a woman and a man, who must not only abstain from marital acts but also fast constantly, never bathe, and never enter the houses of common people. She also has a yearly festival there.

### Aethyopia: The Moorish Woman

In Lydia, there was a small territory called Ethiopion where Diana was honored, as Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer.</note> claims; from that place, she took her name. Some name her so because of her fiery radiance; others because she is also Hecate <note>A goddess of magic and the night.</note> and uses torches.

### Persia: The Persian

The Persians honor Diana greatly and highly; and specifically beyond the Euphrates, she had her own cattle without any shepherds; but they had no

In Castabala in Caramania <note>A region in modern-day southern Turkey.</note>, not far from Ayas, which was once Caesarea, this Diana had a church or temple where her priestesses <note>original: "Nonnen" (nuns). ->Phyllida: The Leaf-Blessed<- <note>From the Greek *Phyllis*, relating to foliage or leaves.</note>

->Pergaea, Pergasia<-

->Elymaitis<-

In the innermost part of Persia, toward the rising sun, right at the border of the whole land, is the region of Elymais; there was a temple of Diana which Antiochus Epiphanes <note>A Seleucid king who reigned from 175–164 BCE.</note> wished to plunder. # On the Pagan Gods

The Eretrians <note>People of Eretria, an ancient Greek city on the island of Euboea.</note> occupied this spot where the temple of Diana was located, which was erected by Amarynthus the hunter.

->Crefsia Crefsica<-

Callimachus and Diodorus <note>Likely Callimachus of Cyrene and Diodorus Siculus, classical authors.</note> name her after the place where she was also worshiped.

->Lysizona: The Girdle-Looser<- <note>From the Greek *Lysizonos*, an epithet of Artemis as the patron of childbirth.</note>

Those women bearing their first child loosened their girdles and offered them to this Diana; for this reason, Diana also had a temple under this name in Athens. Some say it was the custom that after the bridegroom untied the bride's girdle, it was offered to Diana.

->Cnacalysia<-

Caphyrae was a spot in Arcadia <note>A region in the central Peloponnese.</note> that had a small mountain called Cnacalus; there, a temple and annual church festival <note>original: "Kirchwiche" (consecration festival). The author uses contemporary Christian terminology to describe ancient pagan rites.</note> were dedicated to Diana.

->Condyleatis<-

Not far from there was a place and grove called Condylea, where honor was shown to Diana.

->Aparchomene: The Hanged One<- <note>original: "Aparchomena Die Erhänckt." From the Greek *apanchomene*, meaning "strangled" or "hanged."</note>

Diana, who was worshiped at Condylea, received this name because some young boys were playing mischievously by the temple on the mountain and, without any bad intention, found a necklace or rope; they slipped it around the neck of the statue and said Diana was hanged. The people of Caphyrae, enraged by the act, stoned the children to death. A plague <note>original: "der schelm" (the rogue/mischief), here meaning a pestilence or divine punishment.</note> came upon them, and their women no longer gave birth. When Apollo was consulted, he replied that the plague would not cease until the innocent children were buried. This was done, and Diana kept the name.

->Sciatis: She of Scia<-

Scia was a spot not far from Liodorio where Diana had a temple built by Aristodemus the tyrant.

->Angita<-

There is a river of this name flowing not far from the town of Pangaeum, where a temple to Diana was built; from this, she kept the name.

->Hegemacha or Hegemone: The Leader or Combatant<-

Cacesium, not far from the aforementioned spot, had a road leading toward Lycosura; along the way, Diana had her temple under this name. Aristomelidas, a tyrant of the Orchomenians, was stabbed because he had violated a maiden from Tegea. He fled to Tegea, and as if Diana had led him there, he built her a temple.

The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> had a training and drill school for running, where there was a chapel under the name Hegemache, which was also attributed to Diana.

# Book Four

<note>original: "x" — this is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in order.</note>

...temple where Telecles, the King of the Spartans, was stabbed. At Basilica, which was once Sicyon, she also had her chapel. In Patras, however, it is said that Preugenes—after he conquered Lacedaemonia and Argos—took away this image of Diana, assisted by a very faithful servant. That same image was kept for a time at Mersoe <note>Likely referring to a local site or a corruption of a known ancient city, possibly Meroë or a Greek equivalent.</note>, from whence it came. The statue of this goddess stood in Tegea, made of ebony, quite beautiful and large.

Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD).</note> writes of this Diana as follows: how the Lacedaemonians and Messenians quarreled over this sanctuary before Tiberius and the Senate at Rome, debating which city should oversee it. For the Lacedaemonians said it stood on their ground and soil and was founded by their ancestors; they sought to prove this with their city records and several hymns <note>original: "kirchen gsängen" (church songs). The author uses Christian-era terminology to describe ancient Greek religious songs.</note>. They admitted it was true that King Philip of Macedon had taken it from them in war, but after the death of Caesar, Mark Antony had awarded it back to them. The Messenians, in contrast, argued that the descendants of Hercules <note>Referring to the "Heracleidae," the legendary Return of the Heracleidae to the Peloponnese.</note>, in the division of the landscape, had assigned this temple to their king, as the inscriptions carved in marble and bronze could testify. Furthermore, more evidence could be found on their side in the writings of the poets. They argued Philip had acted by right of law rather than just force; likewise, Antigonus and Lucius Mummius had awarded the sanctuary to them. The Milesians, acting as arbitrators in a godly settlement, had also returned the sanctuary to them, which Attidius Gemianus, the most recent governor in Achaia, had confirmed. Thus, after a long quarrel, the sanctuary remained with the Messenians.

### Lycaotis.

On Mount Maenalus in Arcadia, there was once a city called Lycoa, and in that same city was a temple of Diana, along with a bronze statue, from which her name is derived.

->Chitene<-

The ancients were accustomed to hanging up the small clothes of children—which they had outgrown in their early years—to this goddess; from this, she received her name, although some believe it refers to a type of song and dance.

->Geneatis: The One of Genoë<- <note>original: "Die Weynheymerin." The author appears to be creating a German folk-etymological equivalent or referencing a specific local naming convention.</note>

Genoë was a city in Argia <note>The region around the city of Argos.</note>, and because she was worshiped there, Diana received this name. It is said that Proetus erected a temple and a statue to her there.

->Stymphalia: The One at Wusstí<- <note>original: "Die zů Wusstí." The author identifies the ancient Stymphalia with a contemporary name, likely "Wusstí."</note>

The city of Stymphalia, located in what is now Wusstí in Arcadia, had a famous name in ancient times because there is a lake, spring, or pool nearby where man-eating birds lived. Hercules shot these dead or drove them away, as is mentioned by Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note>. From this spring, however, the Emperor Hadrian led water into the city of Corinth; the spring provides a lake or pool, though a small one, and also a stream in the winter time that is very thin and mostly disappears, only to bubble up again in the region of Argos, where it takes the name Erasinus.

# Of Pagan Gods

In that same place stood a very old temple, within which was a wooden image of the Goddess that was almost entirely gilded. High above in the vaulted ceiling, birds were placed, carved from wood and covered in plaster. There also stood several maidens carved from white marble; from the waist down, they had the legs and claws of birds. <note>These are likely descriptions of the Stymphalian birds and the Sirens, associated with the sanctuary of Artemis Stymphalia.</note> It happened at one time that the abyss where this spring sinks into the earth became blocked, so that it had no more outlet or drain; consequently, the flood inundated the land for two miles. Now, a hunter was chasing a stag and pursued it so closely that they both ran into the marshes or floodwaters. The stag hit the sinkhole and fell in, and the hunter followed after him. In this way, the drain was opened up again, and the flood subsided. Because of this, the people of Stymphalus thereafter observed the feast and festival of the Goddess more strictly than before, for they believed it had happened to them because they had been negligent in their service to the idol.

### Colanis

At Myrrhinus <note>original: "Myrrhumusten." This refers to an ancient Attic deme; the author's reference to "Napoli in Romanien" likely means Nauplia in Greece.</note>, not far from Nauplia in Greece, a king named Colenus ruled before the time of Cecrops. He was a son of Mercury and built a temple to Diana. Some, however, maintain that her name comes from the sacrifice used there—namely, from the billy goats without horns, which are called *Motten*. <note>The author is attempting to explain the epithet "Colainis" through a local term for hornless goats.</note>

### Coloena

Around the city of Sardis in Lydia, there is a region that has a lake, first called Gygaean and later called Colo, in the fields of Hermus and Cayster. A temple of Diana stood there in high regard, at whose festival monkeys jumped and danced. <note>This likely refers to the "Coloenian" dancers, though the German text specifically says "Affen" (monkeys), possibly a contemporary misunderstanding of ancient ritual costumes or a textual corruption.</note>

### Opis

Apollo and Diana were raised by three little daughters from Muscovy <note>original: "Moscovien." In classical mythology, these are the Hyperborean maidens. Early modern writers often identified the legendary "Hyperboreans" of the north with Russia or Muscovy.</note>, one of whom was named Opis, from whom she received this name. She was highly honored among the Lacedaemonians.

### Coccoca

In Olympia, Diana was honored by this name and also had an altar there.

### Elusia, Lusia

The Ephesians called Diana by these names, as Hesychius <note>A Greek grammarian of the 5th or 6th century AD who compiled a famous lexicon.</note> reports.

### Chia (The one at Chios)

In the island now called Chios by the Genoese <note>The Republic of Genoa ruled Chios from 1346 to 1566.</note>, there stood her image, crafted by the sons of Anthermus, who were citizens there. The face was so fashioned that, because of the height at which it stood, it appeared entirely sorrowful to one entering, but entirely joyful to one leaving.

### Neleida

Neleus had a son who was very powerful and named Phrygius. He was at Miletus, and when a quarrel arose between the citizens, Phrygius went to Myus with his followers, so that there was little peace between these cities. However, while Phrygius was staying there for some time, he fell in love with a maiden named Pieria. She would not yield to him unless he first made peace with the other citizens. Thus, a settlement was negotiated, peace was struck, and it was established as a perpetual memorial that the daughters and maidens from both cities should annually visit this temple, which had been erected and endowed by Neleus.

<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

# Priapnia.

Not far from Spigia, where Cyzicus once lay, was a city named Priapus. There stood a temple of Diana which Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus (120–63 BC), a great enemy of Rome.</note> plundered; for this reason, it is believed that the King never had good fortune afterward. Lucullus, however, achieved a great victory there because of this.

->Delphinia.<-

Just as we have spoken regarding Apollo of this name, the same applies to this Diana in that place; you may look for it there. <note>The author suggests looking back at the entry for "Apollo Delphinius."</note>

->Astyrena.<-

Astyra was a village located in the territory of the Trojans, where Diana had a grove. However, some believe it was a temple at Astura, by the sea not far from Rome, in the village of the same name where Cicero was murdered. It was there that the noble Prince Conradin <note>Conradin (1252–1268), the last legitimate male heir of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, was captured at Astura after the Battle of Tagliacozzo.</note> was sold and betrayed, and thus the House of Swabia was utterly extinguished. We shall give a full account of this in the book of our Emperors.

->Bubastis.<-

The Egyptians in the city of Bubastus—which is now Azioch—held an annual assembly to honor Diana. There they made offerings in her temple; I know not what exactly, yet it seems to me they honored her with a cat. For "Bubaston" signifies as much as a cat. <note>The Egyptian goddess Bastet was indeed associated with cats and later identified by the Greeks with Artemis/Diana.</note>

->Panagra, The Pilgrim.<-

Those who run through every land and are constantly wandering about were signified by this proverb: they called her the "Roving Diana" who runs through all things. Perhaps this is because the power of the Moon <note>The author identifies Diana with the Moon, following common Renaissance mythography.</note> has its effect in all lands and upon all things that grow therein.

->Eleia.<-

In Arcadia there was a village—though some attribute it to the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> because of the Alpheius river, while others place it in a marsh—the same was called Helos, where Diana had a temple. The Arcadians had their priests at that same foundation. Otherwise, in Elis near Olympia, there is a temple which Sambicus plundered, for which it is said he died a wretched death.

->Sotera, The Savior.<-

Theseus is said to have erected an image of this goddess at Troezen after he overcame Asterion <note>The Minotaur.</note>, the son of Minos. Furthermore, he built a very magnificent temple to her and gave her this name because not only was the victory difficult for him due to the strength of Asterion, but it was also quite a heavy task to escape the Labyrinth without the help of the gods; for this reason, he attributed his escape to Diana, as she had been his helper.

At Megara she also had a temple and an image, which was erected for this reason: when Mardonius the Persian invaded the land, the Persians lost their way. They came into a narrow pass between the mountains at night, and as happens in times of distress, they saw what they stood near—stumps or rocks—and believed them to be the local people. Therefore, they shot arrows at them. Wherever they hit, it crunched, so they believed from the noise that these were people; thus they emptied their quivers. The locals, guided by Diana, fell upon the enemies who now had no more ammunition.

## Eleuthera &emsp; &emsp; The Free One.

The Lycians honored her under this name. <note>From the Greek "Eleutheria," signifying liberty.</note>

## Sarpedonia.

Not far from Candeloro in Carmania, which was once Cilicia / is a promontory named Sarpedon / where Diana herself had a temple / in which soothsayers lived / who were possessed by the spirit.

## Orthosia. <note>original: "Orthofia"</note>

Orthosia is a mountain in Arcadia / there she received the name from the temple which Diana had erected there.

## Magnesia &emsp; &emsp; The one of Magnesia.

Because Diana had a temple erected in that same city, this name remained hers.

## Chryselakatos &emsp; &emsp; The one with the golden spindle <note>original: "Chrysolæcate"</note>

Homer and other poets give her the name "the one with the golden bridle or spindle."

## Chrysenia.

Gold is used by the poets to mean lovely and elegant / for which reason sometimes Venus is called the Golden One / also everything that one considers exceedingly beautiful / and cannot express / one calls golden. Just as we Germans also name that which is dear to us. Thus we say: "Oh, my golden mother." Likewise, whatever one wished to highly praise in the goddesses was called golden.

## Cercera.

This statue of Diana was carried away from Greece to Persia by Xerxes / but Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> had it brought back to Greece to its place / namely to the island of Jero / which was once called Leros / where much aloe was made and found. There was a mountain called Cerceteus / where this Diana has a temple. This island is forty miles long and wide / perfect in everything that a human needs to live.

## Meroessa.

The Merustians lived in Sicily not far from Syracuse <note>original: "Serragosa"</note> / they had a small territory / in which was Diana's temple. Some believe she was also worshiped on the island of Meroë in Egypt / likewise there was a Meroë not far from Daphne by Antioch / whether she was worshiped in those places remains to be further sought.

## Gazoria.

Gazora was a city in Macedonia / there Diana had a temple / and was worshiped there, from which the name remained with her.

-># The Fourth Book.<-
->L iij<-

### Hippica: The Equestrian.
She was called "the Equestrian" <note>original: "Reysig," referring to one mounted on horseback.</note> by Pindar, and we have already made mention of this in the section regarding the "She with the Golden Spindle" <note>original: "Xhaßhämerin," referring to the epithet *Chryselakatos*.</note> or the one with the golden bridle; therefore, it is unnecessary to report further on it here.

### Aristobula: Of Good Counsel.
Themistocles <note>A famous Athenian general and statesman.</note> had fallen into great disfavor with the people. When his affairs were in a difficult state, he built a magnificent temple to this Minerva <note>Athena</note>, intending it for "Minerva of Good Counsel" <note>Aristobula means "best in counsel."</note>. He did this so that she might instill a good will toward him in the people; but it was in vain. For because of this very act, the common man became even more unfavorable toward him than before, believing it had been done by him so that he might more easily sneak into power and authority with such splendor. Whatever the case may be, it is the opinion of some that the hatred grew because he set up his own statue in Minerva's temple, which stood until the time of Trajan. Because of this, the people fell into suspicion, as if he were seeking his own glory and wished to be seen as the one by whose counsel and plans Greece had been preserved.

### Scylluntia.
Strabo mentions her and says that she had a temple at Scyllus, which was quite famous above others for its endowment and high prestige. Xenophon built this temple when he marched into Persia with Cyrus, the Persian king, leading several thousand Greeks with him against the will of the Athenians. For this reason, he was banned from the city and the land; his grave and dwelling were also there.

### Gerenia.
Gerenia, which is now Botonia in Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, also had a temple to this Diana, from which she received the name.

### Aria.
In the region of the Laconians, there was a spot called Marius, which was quite watery and full of springs. There she had a temple in which many springs arise, and from that place, she has this name.

### She of Lepanto.
Naupactus, which is now called Lepanto, had a very magnificent foundation made of snow-white marble, from which she takes her name; the statue stands in a pose as if it were shooting.

### Theutidis.
In Arcadia, there was once a place called Theutis. The name came to them from Theutis, the captain who led those same countrymen in the Trojan War. However, when he came into a quarrel with Agamemnon, he wished to turn back. But Minerva appeared in the form of Opis, son of Melas, so that he should continue the march. He became enraged and stabbed her in the hip with his spear and returned home with his men. There the goddess appeared to him thus wounded; he died of fright. A famine <note>original: "theüwre," literally a "dearth" or high cost of living due to crop failure.</note> came upon the land. At Dodona, the people were instructed how they should appease the goddess: they made an image for her that had the hip bound with red silk.

### Eurimones.
At Neospiti, which was once called Phigalia, there was a temple of this Diana <note>specifically Eurynome</note>, which was a female figure above and a fish below; she was bound by a golden chain. The temple was opened only once a year on a specific day; otherwise, it remained closed forever.

### Capuana and Camerina.
In Italy, near Capua and also at Camerina, Diana had her temples, and these names of hers come from those places. So much for Diana and Luna.

# Luna, which stands for the Month and is counted among the seven wandering stars.
## How the astrologers write of her regarding births and weather, along with certain powers.

<margin>
The Moon, as it is said, influences the birth of mankind as well as other matters according to her position, as follows.
</margin>

<margin>On the days.</margin> Monday

<margin>In the hours of the days</margin>
* Saturday: 7th hour.
* Sunday: 4th, 11th hours.
* Monday: 1st, 8th hours.
> **The child born in this hour** — Commerce and shipping are his pleasure; truthful, yet physically crooked or misshapen; a round face; well-proportioned yet pale.

* Tuesday: 5th, 12th hours.
* Wednesday: 2nd, 9th hours.
> **In these hours it is good to begin** — Hot-tempered; refuses to be subject to anyone; turns gray early; truthful, envious, prone to anger, sickly, weak, dies young.

* Thursday: 6th hour.
* Friday: 3rd, 10th hours.
> **In these hours to depart** — To buy livestock or meat; to begin construction; to use cunning; to build waterworks <note>irrigation or mills</note>.

<margin>If the Moon is the ruler</margin> To undertake long-term projects; to lend money; to purge the head or take medicine; to stable or purchase sheep.

<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

# Mercury.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the god Mercury (Hermes) standing in a landscape. He is depicted as a young man wearing a wide-brimmed winged hat (petasos) and winged sandals (talaria). He holds a caduceus (staff entwined with two snakes) in his right hand and plays a small flute or pipe with his left. At his feet are a rooster (cock) and a goat (buck). In the background, there is a building or temple nestled among trees and hills.</image-desc>

Mercury <note>original: "Medcurrius." The text suggests a folk etymology derived from *medius* (middle) and *currere* (to run), implying he is an "inter-runner."</note> was first so named by the Latins as the "inter-runner" who runs between all things and, through his words, acts as a mediator for mankind. For this reason, this god was designated as a guide for both speech and for commerce <note>original: "kauffmanschatz," referring to trade or merchandise</note>. Cicero recounts five versions of him: The father of the first was Caelus <note>The Sky</note> and the mother was Dies <note>Day</note>. The second was born of Valens and Phoronis; he is also called Trophonius. The third had Jupiter and Maia as parents. The fourth was begotten of the Nile; the Egyptians are not permitted to speak his name. The fifth is honored by the Pheneatae <note>People of Pheneus in Arcadia</note>; he is said to have invented silver, killed Argus, and showed the Egyptians their letters and writing. Otherwise, they say there are two more: one begotten of Liber <note>Bacchus/Dionysus</note> and Proserpina, the other of Jupiter and Cyllene.

This Mercury is credited with being a messenger and a herald of commerce and eloquence—an indicator of that which we have in our minds and express through speech. Therefore, he is the son of Jupiter <note>representing the mind or spirit</note> and Maia <note>representing wisdom or cleverness</note>, because speech should proceed from the mind and wit and be well-weighed beforehand.

He is painted as a youth because speech does not grow old. Generally, he was depicted as a square stone <term>Herm: a pillar-statue with a head, used as a boundary marker</term> for the reason that true speech stands firm and substantial. For this same reason, he is not overly adorned, colored, or painted, but has sharp eyes and narrow shoulders. However, because this Mercury is also counted among the seven wandering <term>planets: in the ancient sense, which included the Sun and Moon</term>, he is by nature hot and dry; he also takes on the nature of whatever companions he finds. Therefore, he is painted with a broad hat on his head to show that he is not affected by rain and is also seldom seen by people following the sun. For this reason, small wings are attached to his head and feet, because he mingles so quickly with the nature of the other stars. He holds the rods <note>the Caduceus or herald’s staff</note> in his hand to indicate that his influence makes life orderly and well-proportioned, and that he directs all his actions well. As for his ability to put people to sleep and wake them with these rods, or to make souls spring up from death, this comes from the belief of some that reason <note>original: "vernunfft"</note> enters the child in the mother's womb in the sixth month, and this sixth month is dedicated to Mercury.

Some also give him wings because speech penetrates all the air, and merchants traverse all lands for the sake of profit.

The rooster is painted at his feet so that the learned may wake at an early hour; likewise, merchants should not oversleep. The goat signifies that in labor, diligence, and the skill of shepherds, the gifts of this god are also somewhat helpful.

The Alchemists call him <term>quicksilver: or liquid mercury</term> because of his speed.

<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

# Mercury.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the god Mercury in a landscape. He is depicted as a young man with wings on his hat (petasos) and heels, holding a caduceus (herald's staff) in his left hand and playing a vertical flute or pipe with his right. At his feet are a rooster on the left and a ram or goat on the right. The scene is set in a landscape with trees and distant hills.</image-desc>

Mercury was first given this name by the Latins as the "intermediary" <note>original: "vnderlauffer," meaning one who runs between</note> who arranges all things and, through his words, acts as a mediator among men. For this reason, this god was designated as a guide for both speech and for commerce <note>original: "Kauffmanschatz"</note>. Cicero recounts five of them: The father of the first was Caelus <note>original: "Celus," meaning Heaven</note> and the mother was Dies <note>Day</note>. The second was born of Valens and Phoronis; he is also called Trophonius. The third had Jupiter and Maia as parents. The fourth was begotten from the Nile; the Egyptians are not permitted to speak his name. The fifth is worshipped by the Pheneatians; he is said to have discovered silver, killed Argus, and showed letters and writing to the Egyptians. Otherwise, they say there are two more: one begotten of Liber and Proserpina, and the other of Jupiter and Cyllene.

To this Mercury is attributed the role of being a messenger and herald of commerce and eloquence, and the indicator of that which we have in our minds, which we express through speech. Therefore, he is the son of Jupiter and Maia, because speech should proceed from the mind and wit, and should be well-weighed beforehand.

He is painted as a youth because speech does not grow old; and commonly he was depicted in square stones <note>A reference to "Herms," which were pillars topped with the god's head</note> for the sake of showing that true speech stands firm and solid. For this reason, he is also not overly adorned, colored, or painted; he has sharp eyes and narrow shoulders. Because this Mercury is also counted among the seven wandering planets, and is by nature hot and dry—taking on the character of whichever companion he finds—he is depicted with a broad hat on his head to show that he is not affected by rain, and is also seldom seen by people as he follows the sun. For this reason, small wings are attached to his head and feet, because he mingles so quickly with the nature of other stars. He holds the wand <note>The <term>caduceus</term>, a staff entwined with two snakes</note> in his hand to show that such attachments are moderate and well-distributed to the body, and that he directs all his workings well. That he uses it to put people to sleep or wake them, or to make souls leap up from death, comes from the belief of some that in the sixth month the fetus in the mother's womb receives its reason, and this sixth month is dedicated to Mercury.

Some also give him wings because speech penetrates through all the air, and because merchants roam through all lands for the sake of profit.

The rooster is painted at his feet to show that the learned stay awake during the fire-time <note>The hours of candlelight or early morning</note>, and likewise the merchants should not sleep through anything; the goat signifies that even in labor, diligence, and the skill of shepherds, the gifts of this god are somewhat helpful.

The alchemists call him quicksilver <note>original: "quecksilber"</note> on account of his speed,

<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

## Mercury.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Roman god Mercury (Hermes) standing in a landscape. He is depicted as a youth with winged heels and a winged petasos (hat). He holds a caduceus (a winged staff with two entwined snakes) in his right hand and gestures with his left. In the background, there is a building or ruin and rolling hills.</image-desc>

Mercury was first given this name by the Latins <note>original: "Latinern"</note> as the messenger <note>original: "vnderläuffer," literally "one who runs under/between"</note> who ran between all things and, with his words, served as a mediator for mankind. For this reason, this god was assigned as a guide for both speech and for commerce. Cicero <note>original: "Cicerone"</note> recounts five such figures: the father of the first was Caelus <note>original: "Celus," Sky</note> and the mother was Dies <note>Day</note>. The second was born of Valens and Phoronis, whom one also calls Trophonius. The third had Jove and Maia as parents. The fourth was begotten from the Nile; the Egyptians are not permitted to speak his name. The fifth is worshipped by the Pheneatae; he is said to have discovered silver, "Arguments" <note>logic or reasoning</note>, or to have shown the Egyptians letters and writing. Others say there are two: one born of Liber <note>Bacchus</note> and Proserpina, and the other of Jove and Cyllene.

To this Mercury is attributed the role of being a messenger and indicator of commerce and eloquence—representing that which we have in our minds and express through speech. For this reason, he is the son of Jupiter and Maia, because speech should proceed from the mind and wit and should likewise be well-weighed beforehand.

He is painted as a youth for the reason that speech does not age; and commonly he was depicted in square stones <note>This refers to "herms," which were square stone pillars topped with a head</note> for the sake of showing that true speech stands firm and solid. For this reason, he is also not excessively decorated, colored, or painted; he has sharp eyes and narrow shoulders. However, since this Mercury is otherwise counted among the seven wandering planets <note>The classical "planets" included the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, he is by nature hot and dry; just as he finds his companions, so he conducts himself. Therefore, a broad hat has been painted on his head to indicate that he is not subject to rain, and he can also seldom be seen by people because he follows the sun. For this reason, small wings are attached to his head and feet, because he mingles so quickly with the natures of other stars. He holds a rod <note>the caduceus</note> in his hand to indicate that his influence brings the body into moderation and good order, and also carries out all his effects well. The fact that he puts people to sleep or wakes them with this same rod, or causes souls to spring up from death, comes from what some believe: that in the sixth month in the mother's womb, reason comes to the child, and this sixth month is dedicated to Mercury.

Some also give him wings because speech penetrates all the air, and merchants roam through all lands for the sake of profit.

The rooster is painted at his feet so that the learned may wake at an early hour; likewise, merchants should not oversleep. The goat signifies that the gifts of this god are also somewhat helpful in the labor, diligence, and skill of shepherds.

The Alchemists call him quicksilver <note>original: "quecksilber," mercury</note> because of his swiftness.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Mercury’s various epithets and geographic associations, specifically focusing on his temples in Rome and his origins on Mount Cyllene, as well as the symbolic meaning of his staff.</meta>

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

The number five was dedicated to him, and sometimes the number four.
Where the Fish Market now stands in Rome and the Church of Saint Angelo <note>Sant' Angelo in Pescheria</note>, there once stood a temple of Mercury. It was erected in the fifteenth year after the expulsion of the Kings <note>The transition from the Roman Monarchy to the Republic, traditionally dated to 509 BCE</note> and was consecrated by Marcus Laetorius <note>original: "Marcum Lectorium"</note>. He also had a statue in the Temple of Concord that was carved by Pisicrates. Near the gate of Saint Sebastian—which was once called the Porta Capena—he had a consecrated grove where a small stream flowed called the *Aqua Mercurii* <note>The Water of Mercury</note>. Those who were guilty of perjury would wash themselves there, believing the water would wash away their sin; they would sprinkle one another with the water using a laurel branch while calling upon Mercury.

## Cyllius Cyllenius, He of Mount Cyllene.

In Arcadia there lay a mountain called Cyllene where he is said to have been raised. There are three springs there in which he was always bathed by water nymphs, for which reason those springs are dedicated to him. He has a temple there and a statue about eight feet tall made of Thya wood <note>A precious, fragrant wood from North Africa, often called citron-wood</note>, which grows in the deserts of Egypt. It was used for the paneling of temples because of its durability; it is much like what we call burl wood <note>original: "Maser"</note>, which is constantly in use.

Some believe the lower eyelids are called *kyllous* <note>original: κυλλοὺς; usually meaning "crooked" or "bent"</note> and that the name was given to him because Mercury induces sleep. The statue of Mercury that the Cyllenians honored stood there with a stiff, masculine member <note>An "ithyphallic" statue, common in ancient boundary markers</note>. Otherwise, those born with stumps for arms are called *kylloi*; yet because Mercury accomplishes all things through speech without the use of hands, they gave him this name and depicted him as quite adorned but without the extension of arms. Some also say a woman named Cyllene raised him and gave him the name.

->Arcas.<-

Some poets among the Latins call him Arcas—such as Statius, Martial, and others—after the region in which he was born <note>Arcadia</note>. Furthermore, the Arcadians erected a statue of him in the Olympic precinct which featured a ram under his wings <note>or "under his arms/shoulders"</note>, a hat upon his head, and he wore a robe and cloak, so that this statue was more famous than others.

## Caducifer, the Staff-Bearer.

Rocca del Papa <note>original: "Bapstsburg," literally "Pope's Castle"</note>, which was anciently called Algidum and is located two miles from Rome, is now surrounded by a forest called the Woods of Aglier. On that same hill there was once a Temple of Mercury where his image, cast in bronze, stood and was honored by orators and merchants.
Macrobius writes that his staff, the *Caduceus*—or "Staff of Office"—draws something of its nature from the Sun. Around this staff wind two snakes, a male and a female, which meet in a knot at the top, touching their mouths together as if they were kissing; their tails extend down to the handle of the staff. All of this points to the meaning of the incarnation <note>The process of a soul taking on a physical body</note>, for which four things are necessary: Spirit, Fortune, Love, and Necessity. The Spirit that gives life is the Sun; fortune and how

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the symbolic properties of Mercury’s staff (the caduceus) and transitions into his identification with the Sun (Apollo), his role as a herald, and his various epithets derived from Greek geography and mythology.</meta>

<header>The Fourth Book</header>

...whatever happens to a person, it comes from the Moon, which is signified by the two snakes; through the joining of their mouths, however, Love is signified. At the knot <note>original: "Knopff"; referring to the knot or knob on the caduceus, but also punning on the "knot" of a problem</note> lies Necessity <note>original: "Not"; often used to mean distress or unavoidable fate</note>.

And while I am on the subject, I will relate the opinion of those who believe Mercury is one and the same as the Sun, Apollo. The reason is that many peoples call the star <note>meaning the planet</note> of Mercury "Apollo," and because Apollo is the leader of the Muses, while Mercury provides them with speech. For this reason, his image is also painted with fins or wings, which signifies the speed of the Sun; indeed, the mind <note>original: "gmüt"</note> is the fastest thing in man, and he takes his name from this; yet the Sun is what brings mind and spirit <note>original: "gmüt und mhut"</note> to man. Furthermore, his images are commonly only four-sided columns <note>These are "herms," ancient boundary markers or sacred pillars</note>, from which nothing protrudes but the head and an upright, stiff masculine member, to signify that the Sun is the head and procreator of all living things in the world. Its power does not lie in the divided works of the limbs, but alone in the mind, which has its seat in the head. The four sides signify the four corners of the world, where all the radiance of the Sun reaches, and it encompasses the year in four parts with its luster and air.

### Ceryx, the Herald <note>original: "Ceryx Herold"; from the Greek κῆρυξ (kerux), meaning a messenger or town crier</note>.

It is an old legend that Mercury is the runner and messenger who makes known all the will of the gods to men; from this comes the office of the Heralds, to proclaim peace and to carry their staff as a sign of peace. Some say that accordingly Mercury and Apollo came into conflict because Mercury had stolen some of Apollo's oxen; then they came to an agreement that Mercury should give the fiddle <note>original: "Geygen"; the author uses the contemporary term for a stringed instrument to refer to Mercury's invention of the lyre</note> to Apollo for the offense. In return, Apollo gave him a rod which he carried safely in his hand. When Mercury came to Arcadia, he found two snakes biting one another; he threw the rod between them, and they were reconciled. From this, his rod was called the "peace-staff," which signifies nothing else than that the poison of war is stilled and removed by peaceful, good words.

Some compare the staff with the snakes to Dialectic <term>Dialectic: the branch of philosophy or logic that investigates truth through the exchange of opposing arguments</term>, which teaches one to decide what is right or wrong through "tangled knots" <note>likely referring to complex logical syllogisms</note>.

### God’s Messenger.

One recognizes the commands and orders of God through the address and graceful presentation of orators; for this reason, Mercury was called a messenger of God.

### Chrysorapis, He with the Golden Rod.

We have spoken before of how beautiful and lovely his little staff or rod is; just as through gold, the rod—and everything else that is renowned—is signified.

### Acacesius.

Acacesium was a city in Arcadia where the image of Mercury stood, carved from stone; he also had a temple in Londario. However, the name comes from Acacus, who is said to have raised Mercury. Others give him this name because he was given speech not to incite or perform evil, nor to suppress the good, but for the help, protection, and advancement of all that is good.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of names and epithets associated with Mercury (Hermes), following the previous discussion of his identification with the Sun and his role as a herald. It shifts from general attributes to specific titles used in antiquity and their symbolic or historical meanings.</meta>

<header>Of the Heathen Gods</header>

**Stilbon. The Shining One.** <note>original: "Stilbon. Der Scheinend." From the Greek στίλβων, meaning "the gleaming one," often used for the planet Mercury.</note> According to the writings of Cicero, he was given this name because of his star and its particular brilliance.

**Alevolus. The Excluded.** <note>original: "Alevolus. Der Verbünstig." Likely a corruption or specific variation of a Latin/Greek epithet. "Verbünstig" suggests someone banned from a guild or society.</note> The image of Mercury was called this because, among the ancients, no one was permitted to have it within his shop or stall.

**Tetragonos. The Four-Square.** <note>original: "Tetragonos. Der Vierecket." From the Greek τετράγωνος.</note> His likeness was fashioned as a four-cornered pillar without hands or feet; for the square stands more firmly than other pillar-work, which signifies that an upright man's <note>original: "Bidermand"</note> speech should be "yes, yes" and "no, no," and that every man should remain firm in his words. Likewise, the upright reproductive member <note>original: "vffrecht geburtglid"</note> upon him signifies that just as that member cannot produce fruit if it remains eternally rigid <note>original: "vorstarrend"</note>, so too does a false, stiff speech achieve nothing. It was also the custom that old men had their Mercuries painted with beards and upright members, whereas the young men had theirs fashioned without beards and with hanging organs; this was an indication that speech in the elderly is somewhat firmer and more upright than in the young.

The Athenians had many such images, and they were the first to fashion them in this way. One night, these were all at once overturned, or else beheaded and mutilated <note>original: "gmutzt"; likely referring to the historical "Mutilation of the Herms" in 415 BCE</note>, yet it was never rightly discovered who had done it, though suspicion fell upon Alcibiades. For this reason, those responsible were denounced as "Herm-breakers" <note>original: "Hermocopide"; from the Greek Ἑρμοκοπίδαι</note>, and a great bounty was placed upon them for anyone who could identify them.

The Athenians gave out these images to those who had committed some great deed or honorable act, as jewels and memorials of their integrity. Sometimes such a pillar was placed before a house, and sometimes in an open public square. Consequently, at that time, the city stood in great anxiety and feared that Alcibiades—with a following of supporters—had undertaken to stir up this alarm in order to root out all the nobility, to diminish their previously honored deeds, and to exalt himself alone.

**Tricephalos. The Three-Headed.** <note>original: "Tricephalos. Der Dreyköpffend." From the Greek τρικέφαλος.</note> This name was given to him because Mercury has power in the heavens, on the earth, and in the water; or because speech and art reveal the character of nature, how good customs are maintained, and how much is accomplished through speech. It was also the custom in former times to place this three-headed image at crossroads and to write upon it where each road led.

->**Amyetos. Amystos. The Ignorant.**<-
<note>original: "Amyetos. Amystos. Der Vnwiſſend." From the Greek ἀμύητος, meaning "uninitiated" or "ignorant of the mysteries."</note>

**In Athens**, this Mercury had a temple in the citadel <note>original: "schloß"; referring to the Acropolis</note>, and he was given this name as a clever jest, since surely no one is more eloquent or knowledgeable in all things than Mercury himself. From this comes the practice of sometimes scolding a simple boy who is, in truth, quite cunning and clever, by calling him by this name.

->**Argiphontes. Argephontes.**<-
<note>original: "Argiphontes. Argephontes." The "Slayer of Argus."</note>

**Io, the daughter of Inachus**, was seduced by Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, who transformed her into a cow to hide her from Juno. Juno then gave her to a herdsman named Argus to be guarded. This Argus was covered with eyes all over his body. By the command of Jupiter, Mercury slew him and struck off his head.

<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

Since the meaning shows that the heaven is full of stars, as if they were shining eyes, so "Argus" is a little word that takes its name from speed and brightness—just as the heaven is bright and very swift in its rotation. The earth, however, is symbolized by an ox or cattle, which is enclosed and protected by the heaven. Now, if Mercury is understood in the place of the Sun, it appears that he kills this Argus with his brilliance and high radiance when, bringing the day, he darkens the stars. Phornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus (c. 20 – 60 AD), a Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology.</note> believes he is called Argephontes <note>original: "Argephontes," traditionally translated as "Slayer of Argus," but also interpreted as "brightly shining."</note>, as one who makes all things glitter like silver. Others speak of "true speech," calling them "words." There are those who believe his star runs swiftly and shines more than others, which is where his name comes from.

## Harpedophoros ->The Sabre-Bearer.<-

The sword or the curved sabre with which he killed Argus was called *Harpe* <note>original: "Harpe," a Greek term for a sickle or curved sword.</note>, and from this, that name remained with him.

->Prophyleus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Cunning &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Strophyleus<- <note>original: "Prophyleus... Strophyleus." These likely refer to Hermes Propylaios (Before the Gate) and Strophaios (He of the Door-hinge), referring to his role as a guardian and a cunning god of transitions.</note>

Because he was so skilled, quick, and swift in merchant dealings, usury, exchange, and finance, some gave him this name; he was otherwise called Propyleus and was placed before gates to ward off thieves. Socrates, the wise man, carved his image, which stood at the castle gate <note>Likely referring to the Propylaea, the gateway to the Acropolis.</note> in Athens.

->Thoth. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Thauthus, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Thautus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Theuth &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Thoyth.<-

The Alexandrians called him by this name, after which the autumn month—which is the first among the Egyptians—was also named. To him, the Ibis bird was dedicated, as Horus reports. He was also credited with inventing numbering, calculation, measurement, astronomy, dice, board games, and writing.

->Hesus.<-

Our ancestors, the Germans, honored Mercury—as Tacitus writes—under the name Teutates, while those in France or Gaul called him Esus. The Germans and Gauls considered him an inventor of all arts, a guide for paths and roads, and a director of all trade, business, and commerce; they erected several images to him. In Spain, this Teutates was also honored, such as at New Carthage, of which mention is made by Titus Livius <note>Livy, the Roman historian.</note>. Consult Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> if you wish to know more about the Egyptian Mercury.

->Agoreos &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The one in the Market.<- <note>original: "Agoreos. Der vff dem Märckt." From the Greek "Agoraios," referring to the marketplace (agora).</note>

Although Mercury was honored by many under this name, he was held in especially high regard in Athens, for his image stood there in the Painted Porch <note>original: "vorschorpf Pecile," referring to the Stoa Poikile, a famous painted portico in the Athenian Agora.</note>. In Sicyon and Sparta, there were likenesses of him in the public squares.

In Pharae, a city of the Achaeans, there was a very wide and large market; in the middle of its square stood a bearded image of Mercury. It was dedicated by Simulo of Messenia; it was made of stone, squared at the base on the ground, and not particularly large. Before the image stood a fire-kettle; there, people sought answers, and those who wished for an answer came to the image in the evening. Beside the fire-pan, there were several oil lamps on leaden chains; the questioner would light these and put incense therein, place a groschen <note>original: "groschen," a contemporary German coin used here to translate an ancient small coin like the obol.</note> on the left corner of the image, and listen closely to it, or whisper into its

...thought <note>original: "ohten," likely the conclusion of "bedachten" (considered or thought).</note> about what he wanted to ask, then ran from the square, plugged his ears with his fingers, and as soon as he left the marketplace, he took his hands away; the first voice he heard, he took as an answer.
There was also a fountain or water trough on the square, dedicated to Mercury, for the reason mentioned regarding Rome <note>Mercury was associated with a sacred spring near the Porta Capena in Rome, where merchants sprinkled themselves for luck.</note>.

### Agonius, the Leader of the Struggle.

Pindar and other poets call him by this name <note>original: "Agonius," from the Greek *agon*, meaning a struggle, contest, or athletic competition.</note>, ascribing to him that he should be called upon by those entering into combat, as well as by those who desire some gain. He had a statue standing at the racetrack in Olympia.

### Quaestor animarum, the Appraiser of Souls.

The ancients ascribed to Mercury power and might both above and below the earth; he brought souls to human bodies, which are formed of earth and water. Those that remained pure and were purified through penance, he led to heaven; the others he accompanied to hell, according to the teaching of Pythagoras. <note>This is a Latinized title for Mercury's role as "Psychopompos," the guide of souls.</note>

### Chthonius, the Earthly or the Infernal.

Some call him the Earthly, others the Infernal—that is, the one under the earth <note>original: "Chthonius," from the Greek *chthonos*, meaning the earth or the soil, often referring to the underworld.</note>. It was also the custom that the Argives <note>The people of Argos, a city in the Peloponnese.</note> sacrificed to this Mercury on the thirtieth day after they had carried out a corpse; for they believed that just as the earth received the dead bodies, so Mercury received the souls.

### Chriophoras, the Ram-Bearer.

The people of Tanagra, which is now Talandi in Boeotia, were at one time greatly afflicted with the plague. Then Mercury was supposedly seen carrying a young ram or lamb <note>original: "Widerlin," a diminutive for a ram.</note> around the city wall, because of which the dying ceased. Therefore, his image was carved by an old master craftsman, showing him carrying a ram on his shoulders. And the custom has remained with them that on that same festival, a ram is always carried around by the most handsome youth to be found in the city.

### Promachus, the Front-Line Champion.

When the Eretrians from Negroponte <note>Negroponte was the medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea.</note> once attacked this city of Talandi unawares, the citizens saw that Mercury marched before the troops <note>original: "zeüg," meaning a military force or array.</note> they had sent against the enemy, fell upon the ships, and chased them into flight. He fought so bravely for the Talandrians <note>original: "Calander," likely a typo for Talandrians.</note> that they erected a statue and temple for him. They say the reason he bore such great love for this city was that he was raised there in a sanctuary <note>original: "Phan," referring to a *fanum* or sacred precinct.</note> near this temple.

### Pronaus.

The Greeks called the middle part of the church or temple a "ship" <note>The "ship" refers to the *nave*, from the Latin *navis*. The author is using contemporary church architecture to explain ancient Greek temples.</note>, for they were commonly built so that they have a raised chamber in the front called the choir. From there to the end, there is a long building, very high, where on each side upon several columns, a vault is attached to the side walls of the entire structure, which is never as high or as wide as the middle part. Now, the statue of Mercury at Isthmus was placed before the middle part <note>original: "Pronaus," meaning "before the temple (nave)."</note> of the Temple of Apollo, which is where he gets this name.

<summary>This page details several titles of Mercury/Hermes, including his roles as an athletic patron, a guide of souls, a protector against plague in Tanagra, and a military champion, as well as the architectural origin of the name Pronaus.</summary>

The Fourth Book.
y ij
<meta>catchword: Neger</meta>

## Nonacriates
<note>This title refers to Mercury's association with Nonacris, a town in Arcadia.</note>

Nonacris was a small town in Arcadia; there, a spring source dripped from a rock that was very high and craggy. These drops fell upon a large rock below, corroding right through it, so that the water flowed into the stream called Chiatis <note>original: "Chiatis," likely referring to the Crathis river.</note>. Now, livestock and people die from this water if they drink it; this was first noticed by the goats that climbed upon those rocks and drank from it. Its coldness splits gold, silver, lead, tin, ore, and all metals, as well as all glass, crystal, alabaster, earthenware, and in short, every vessel in which it is placed. Iron, horn, and bone cannot hold it; it rots or bursts them. Thus, even gold, which otherwise repels and overcomes all poison, must succumb to this water. This happens not without the special counsel of God, who wishes to show that often even the most famous things must succumb to the lowliest. As it happens, this water can only be kept in a donkey’s horn <note>The legend of the River Styx claimed its water was so corrosive only a hoof or horn of a mule or donkey could contain it.</note>, as I will describe more extensively in my description of that animal; for I intend to prepare a "Book of Animals," which I hope to complete, God willing. Now, Alexander the Great is said to have drunk from this water when he was poisoned. In that same place, Mercury was also honored as "the threefold."

### Dactoro. Messenger of Decisions.
<note>original: "Dactoro," likely a corruption of the Greek *Diaktoros*, meaning the Messenger or Guide. "Schidbott" is an archaic German term for a mediator.</note>

Because Mercury is eloquent, possesses a good voice, and is very skilled in negotiation—and because speech opens our minds and thoughts to others—the ancients named him thus. For this reason, in sacrifices, the tongue was dedicated and offered to him.

### Poligius, Polygius.

In Troezen, there stood a statue of Mercury to which Hercules offered a club. He had fashioned this club from a wild olive tree and had accomplished many deeds with it; this club is said to have afterward turned green and even brought forth fruit.

### Camillus the Servant. Casmilus.

The Tuscans <note>The Etruscans.</note> called Mercury "Camillus," meaning a servant, although he was first called "Casmilus." Later, because "Camillus" was easier to pronounce, he received that name. At weddings or bridal processions, the table servants were called *Camilli*. This name was also given to the noble boys who still had both father and mother and were required to serve the priests at the altar during high festivals. This was because Mercury was the common servant of the high gods and was named accordingly.

### Melostoos. The Guardian or Shepherd.
<note>original: "Meloſtoos," likely from the Greek *melo-ssōos*, meaning "savior of flocks."</note>

Homer calls him by this name and credits him with caring for and guarding all the herds of livestock dedicated to the gods.

### Eriounios. The Profit-Seeker.
<note>original: "Erioynias," a version of *Eriounios*, a common Homeric epithet for Hermes meaning "the luck-bringer" or "ready-helper," though here interpreted through the lens of trade and "gain" (Ghwinſüger).</note>

Aristophanes calls him by this name, and Phormutus calls him so as well, for the reason that he is a household protector—strong and powerful—just as speech can hold the honor of an entire household together.

### Enhodios, Hodios. He of the Way.
<note>original: "Enhodios," from the Greek for "on the road."</note>

As has been said, his statue was placed as a marker on the roads. At Paros on the island, he was honored under the name "Euhodos" <note>original: "Euhodos," meaning "of the good journey."</note>, as the one who should grant a fortunate voyage or journey.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

## Hegemonios. The Guide.
<note>original: "Hegemonios" (Greek: ἡγεμόνιος), meaning "leading" or "guiding."</note>

Homer cites him as the one who was to provide Priam with safe conduct to Achilles <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, where Hermes guides King Priam through the Greek camp.</note>. Phornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher who interpreted myths as allegories for natural or moral forces.</note> says the name arises from the fact that one should have him—that is, speech or reason—as a guide for instruction in all things.

## Empolæus. The Merchant.
<note>original: "Empolæus" (Greek: ἐμπολαῖος), from *empolaō*, to trade.</note>

He holds this name because he stands by merchants when they offer goods, and when they buy and sell.

## Cerdous. The Profitable.
<note>original: "Cerdous" (Greek: κερδῷος), associated with *kerdos*, meaning gain or profit.</note>

Regarding this, it is said that whoever seeks profit makes use of this god; hence the name was given to him.

## Cleptes. The Thief.
<note>original: "Cleptes" (Greek: κλέπτης).</note>

Precisely because speech <note>The author uses the German "die red" (speech/reason) as a translation of the Greek *Logos*, a common Renaissance interpretation of Hermes.</note> steals and takes away a person’s heart by creeping in secretly—leading and guiding people according to its own will—he also bears this name. Although a tale also exists that Mercury began his first masterpiece with theft, stealing the oxen of Apollo.

## Dolios. The Deceiver.
<note>original: "Dolios" (Greek: δόλιος), meaning crafty or deceitful.</note>

Furthermore, one credits Mercury with being the first to invent sorcery and similar arts, which is why this name remained with him, signifying the deceit practiced by such artists. In Tarsus, and perhaps in Pellene <note>The text mentions "Pellenen," likely referring to the city in Achaia famous for its temple of Hermes.</note>, this Mercury had a temple where there was great grace and indulgence; his image was decorated, and he had a beard and a sun-hat <term>petasos</term> <note>A broad-brimmed hat typically worn by travelers and messengers in antiquity.</note> upon his head.

## Nomius. The Lawgiver.
<note>original: "Nomius" (Greek: νόμιος), which can refer to either *nomos* (law) or *nomos* (pasture/herding).</note>

Speech indicates what is to be done and what is not to be done; hence this name comes to him. However, some argue the name comes from the livestock he protects, for which he is also called the God of Shepherds, as Hesiod describes him.

## Parammon. The Sandy.
<note>original: "Parammon" (Greek: παράμμων), associated with the Oracle of Ammon in the Libyan desert.</note>

While he was honored under this name in Egypt and those same deserts, he also had his image and offerings at Elis in Olympia.

## Sphenopagon. The Pointed-Beard.
<note>original: "Sphenopagon" (Greek: σφηνοπώγων), meaning wedge-shaped beard.</note>

When Mercury is depicted with a beard, it is made long, yet braided and pointed at the tip, just as our own braggarts <note>original: "eysenbeysser," literally "iron-biters"—a slang term for swaggering soldiers or mercenaries.</note> still wear them today.

## Ales. Alipes. The Wing-Footed.

He received this name from the little wings that are painted upon his feet.

## Atlantides.

He was called by this name after his grandfather Atlas, the father of Maia.

## Maiugena.

The poets also frequently call him by this name after his mother, Maia.

## Charidotes. Giver of Grace.
<note>original: "Charidotes" (Greek: χαριδότης), meaning giver of joy or grace.</note>

Those on the island of Samos who wished to carry out robberies, plundering, theft, and similar matters offered sacrifices to this Mercury, whose temple was among them. Yet they do this in memory of a time when they were attacked by enemies,

Driven away, they fled to the island of Mykonos <note>original: "Micone." An island in the Cyclades near Delos.</note>, which is about thirty miles long and wide, situated near Delos. It possessed strong castles, fortresses, and cities, of which some buildings still remain. There they found a great many wild goats, but almost all the people there were bald <note>In antiquity, the inhabitants of Mykonos were proverbially known for their hairlessness, a detail noted by writers such as Pliny the Elder and Strabo.</note>. Now, they remained on this island for ten years by means of piracy; and when the enemy believed they no longer had any regard for their fatherland, they surprised them unawares and resettled themselves in their old home. They gave Mercury this name <note>referring to the title below</note> as the one who had shown them grace and help in returning to their seat.

->Psithyristes: The Tale-Bearer.<-
<note>original: "Psithyristes" (Greek: ψιθυριστής), meaning "the whisperer" or "the murmurer."</note>

In Athens, this Mercury was honored, as Demosthenes reports.

->Galeancon: The Stumpy-Armed.<-
<note>original: "Galeancon" (Greek: γαλεάγκων), literally "weasel-armed," a term for those with shortened or deformed forearms.</note>

It was said before that those born with stumpy arms are so named; however, the Egyptians honored him under this name. You may easily conclude the reason for this from the ancient writings.

->Phædros, the Joyful; Agetor, the Leader.<-
<note>original: "Phædros" (Greek: φαιδρός, bright/beaming) and "Agetor" (Greek: ἀγήτωρ, leader).</note>

Some call this one the Joyful, others the Miraculous; he had a temple at Londario <note>Possibly a corruption of a Greek site such as Lyncus or Lyncestis.</note>, along with a festival called the Agetoria.

->Leucas.<-
<note>original: "Leucas" (Greek: λευκός), meaning "white."</note>

In Boeotia he was honored under this name, perhaps because his image was carved from white marble.

->Cynosurius.<-
<note>original: "Cynosurius" (Greek: κυνόσουρος), meaning "dog’s tail," but here referring to a location in Arcadia.</note>

Cynosurius was a son of Mercury who built a fortress upon a hill in Arcadia and erected a temple to his father in that same place.

->Alychmius.<-

At Alychme this Mercury was honored, from which place the name comes to him.

->Ennius.<-

On the island of Chios, Mercury was held in high regard under this name.

->Epithalamites: The Wedding-God.<-
<note>original: "Epithalamites" (Greek: ἐπιθαλαμίτης), derived from the bridal chamber or wedding song.</note>

In the islands of Negroponte <note>The medieval and Renaissance name for the Greek island of Euboea.</note>, this Mercury had his temple, statue, and festival.

->Epactius: The One on the Shore.<-
<note>original: "Epactius" (Greek: ἐπάκτιος), from "akte," meaning the coast or shore.</note>

On the island of Samos, this Mercury was also held in honor.

->Epitermios: The Boundary-Marker.<-
<note>original: "Epitermios" (Greek: ἐπιτέρμιος), meaning "at the borders."</note>

Perhaps this image of Mercury was erected at ends or boundaries where great domains were divided, and thus he kept the name <note>Mercury, as Hermes, was the god of boundaries; his "herms" (pillars with his head) were used to mark territories and roads.</note>.

->Eucelos and Dyscolos.<-
<note>original: "Eukolos" (Greek: εὔκολος, easy-going/kind) and "Dyscolos" (Greek: δύσκολος, difficult/grumpy).</note>

Some call him the friendly, tame, and kind; others call him the ill-tempered, wild, and disobedient.

->Logios: The Orator.<-
<note>original: "Logios" (Greek: λόγιος), from "logos," meaning speech, reason, or eloquence.</note>

Since they attributed the power of speech to him, they also honored him with this title.

->Pedachorus.<-
<note>original: "Pædacoros." Likely a reference to Mercury as a "leader of the dance" or youth.</note>

Among the Metapontines—a city located in Apulia, of which not a shoe’s breadth remains today; it was situated in a valley not far from Policoro <note>original: "Pelicore."</note>—this Mercury was highly honored.

->Phlyesius and Candaulas.<-

Historians and poets mention these names in various places, which they titled after cities and people where and by whom they were previously honored.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

# Woden.
<note>original: "Vuoda." This refers to Woden or Odin, the chief god of the Germanic peoples.</note>

Paul the Deacon <note>Paulus Diaconus (c. 720–799), a Benedictine monk and historian of the Lombards.</note> says the Lombards held Mercury in high regard under this name.

### Perseus.

Some say Mercury's father was Perseus <note>In standard Greek mythology, Perseus is a son of Zeus, and Mercury (Hermes) is his half-brother; the author here notes a variant genealogy.</note>, from which he took his name; whether this is correct is not necessary to investigate here.

### Anubis.

The Egyptians depicted Mercury with a dog's head; sometimes the head was black, sometimes gold-colored. In his left hand he carried his wand of sleep <note>The Caduceus, which Mercury used to bring sleep or wakefulness.</note>, and in his right a green palm branch. Since the dog excels other animals in its sense of smell, and Mercury investigates all things with his speed, they wished to signify this underlying reason through that image. Above all, he was called Anubis <note>The Egyptian god of the dead, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes as "Hermanubis."</note> when his influence was seen to be used in heavenly and superior matters.

### Hermanubis.

When Mercury allowed his light and power to work in earthly things, or things beneath the earth, he was signified by this name. For this reason, a red rooster was sacrificed to him, whereas a white one was dedicated to Anubis. The reason for this is that heavenly, upper things are all light and bright, while the lower ones are different and of many colors, such as red.

### Trypho &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Trophonius.
<note>original: "Tryfchon" and "Trophon."</note>

Whether Cicero's words are correctly placed—and perhaps "Trophonius" <note>Trophonius was a Greek hero/god with a famous oracle in a cave.</note> was set instead of "Chthonius" <note>meaning "of the earth."</note>—is a matter for another work. Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio, whose "Genealogia Deorum Gentilium" was a primary source for Renaissance mythography.</note> calls him Trypho because of the spinning wheel and his swiftness, as he lets himself be easily changed—a trait which also belongs to merchants who, wherever they go, must adopt the customs of those with whom they deal.

### Trismegistus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Thrice-Great.

Although this Mercury was not placed among the number of the gods but was esteemed as a wise naturalist, he is often associated with Mercury under this name. You should know that he lived before Pharaoh <note>Renaissance scholars often dated Hermes Trismegistus to the time of Moses or earlier.</note> and was called "Thrice-Great" because he wrote such high and true words concerning the Holy Trinity—namely, that within three Persons there is one Godhead of the Lord. His words are these:

> There was a light that understood, or had understanding, before that which had
> understanding; and there was ever and always a mind of the mind thus enlightened;
> also, there was nothing other than unity, together with the spirit that encloses or
> contains all things. Outside of this, there was neither God nor angel nor any other
> essential being; for he was Lord of all things, and Father, and God. All was under
> him, for his Word is perfect, constant, fruitful, a master craftsman that fell into a
> fruitful, generative nature; also, the water that was fruitful and produced animals
> made the water. Further he says:
> You wise work of the great God, O Heaven, I adjure you. You, the voice of the
> Father, which he brought forth at the very first when he established the world, I
> also adjure; I call upon you through the only-begotten Word, through the Father
> who contains all things, be merciful to me.

This little book of Mercury <note>The "Corpus Hermeticum," a collection of philosophical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> I translated into German <note>original: "verteütscht."</note> approximately twelve years ago; I believe it may still be found in the possession of Master Georg Frölich.
