# Of Pagan Gods

## Wodan <note>original: "Vuoda." This refers to the Germanic god Wodan or Odin, whom the Romans and medieval writers frequently identified with Mercury due to their shared roles as guides of souls and masters of wisdom.</note>.

Paulus Diaconus <note>An 8th-century Benedictine monk and historian known for his history of the Lombards.</note> says the Lombards <note>original: "Langbarter." A Germanic people who ruled most of the Italian Peninsula from 568 to 774.</note> held Mercury in high honor under this name.

->Perseus.<-

Some say Mercury's father was Perseus <note>A legendary hero in Greek mythology; the author notes this genealogy is debated.</note>, from whom he received the name; whether this is correct is not necessary to settle here.

->Anubis.<-

The Egyptians painted Mercury with a dog’s head; sometimes the head was black, sometimes gold-colored. In his left hand he carried his wand of sleep <note>The caduceus, used to guide souls or bring sleep.</note>, and in his right, a green palm branch. Because the dog is foremost among other animals in its sense of smell, and Mercury investigates all things with his speed, they wished to signify this through that symbolic foundation. Furthermore, he was first called Anubis when his appearance and influence were seen in heavenly and higher matters.

->Hermanubis.<-

When Mercury let his appearance and power work in earthly things, or things that were beneath the earth, he was signified by this name <note>A syncretic deity combining Hermes and Anubis, representing the transition between the world of the living and the dead.</note>. For this reason, a red rooster was sacrificed to him, whereas a white one was dedicated to Anubis. The reason is that heavenly, upper things are all light and bright, while the lower things are different and of many colors, such as red.

->Tryphon and Trophonius <note>original: "Tryschon & Trophon." Likely referring to Tychon, a god of chance, and Trophonius, an oracular hero.</note>.<-

Whether Cicero's words <note>Likely referring to Cicero’s "De Natura Deorum."</note> were correctly set down, and whether "Trophonius" was perhaps placed instead of "Chthonios" <note>Greek for "of the earth/underworld."</note>, is a matter for another work. Vocatius <note>Possibly a reference to a classical or Renaissance commentator.</note> calls him Trypho because of his "wheel-like" nature and swiftness, for he allows himself to be easily changed. This also pertains to merchants, who, wherever they go, must adopt the customs of those with whom they must trade.

->Trismegistus, the Thrice-Great <note>original: "Trissmegistus / Der Dreymal groß."</note>.<-

Although this Mercury was not placed among the number of the gods, but was instead esteemed as a wise man and a student of nature, he is often cited under the name of Mercury. You should know that he lived before Pharaoh and was called "Thrice-Great" because he wrote such high and true words concerning the Holy Trinity—namely, that in three Persons there is one Godhead of the Heart. These are his words:

> There was a light that understood, or had understanding, before that which has understanding; and there was ever and always a mind <note>original: "gmüet." In this context, it refers to "Nous" or Divine Intellect.</note> of the mind that is thus enlightened. Also, there was nothing other than this unity, together with the spirit that encloses or encompasses all things. Outside of this, there was neither God nor Angel, nor any other essential being, for He was the Lord of all things, and Father, and God; everything was beneath Him. For His Word is perfect, constant, fruitful, a master-builder that fell into a fruitful, procreative nature; also the water, which was thus fruitful and animal-producing, made the water. He says further:
> You, the wise work of the great God—O Heaven—I adjure you! You, the Voice of the Father, which He brought forth first of all when He established the world, I also adjure you! I call upon you through the only-begotten Word, through the Father who contains all things: be merciful to me.

I translated this little book of Mercury <note>Referring to the *Hermetica* or the *Poimandres*.</note> into German roughly twelve years ago; I believe it is still to be found with Master Jörgen Frölich.

# The Fourth Book.
<note>Signature: y iiij</note>

...former Town Clerk of the most highly renowned city of Augsburg, a true lover of all arts, my particularly favorable Lord.

**A**epytus. At Tegea <note>An ancient city in Arcadia, Greece.</note>, this Mercury had a temple and received his surname from it.

**E**pimelius. At Corone in Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, this Mercury had a statue in the marketplace; from this, he received the name.

**I**nterpreter <note>original: "Dolmetsch."</note>. He has always and forever been regarded as an interpreter and messenger of the gods, because he reveals their will and opinions to humanity. This perhaps comes from the fact that those born under the influence of Mercury <note>A reference to astrological belief that being born under this planet grants eloquence and intellect.</note> are credited with a particularly high expertise in spiritual and worldly matters, and thus this name was given to him.

**P**lutodotos, Giver of Wealth <note>From the Greek "Ploutodotēs," meaning "giver of riches."</note>. Faunus, a son of Picus (the son of Jupiter), is said to be called Mercury by the Greeks. He is said to have come to Candia <note>The island of Crete.</note> himself, and there discovered the ore-works and gold veins; he also showed others and taught them how to work and deal with them. The Dicteans <note>The inhabitants of the region around Mount Dicte in Crete.</note> were the first who learned this art from him, and soon after they intended to kill him out of envy. When he noticed this, he stole away in secret and fled to Egypt. There, he showed himself in a golden piece of cloth or a garment that glistened in the sunlight. As soon as the Egyptians saw this, they believed he was a god and fell down before him to worship him. Now, as he also taught them how to handle ore and gold, as well as what belonged to mining and where to find it, and they perceived some profit and wealth from it, they erected a statue for him and counted him among the gods because of his benevolence.

->So much concerning Mercury<-

# ->Mercury, as he is counted as one of and among the seven wandering stars <note>In traditional astronomy, the "seven wandering stars" are the planets: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, as the stargazers write of him, concerning birth, weather, and several of his powers.<-

<margin>In this hour you may begin.</margin>
- Trading and exchanging money. Carrying out errands and messages, riding, demanding money, writing letters, calculating, planting, setting trees, starting construction, putting children in school, learning the arts, putting on fine clothes, and riding dapple-gray horses.

<margin>Beware in this hour.</margin>
- Of women, buying inherited goods, hiring servants, swapping houses, or releasing someone from prison.

---

<margin>Length of Life</margin>
- A very good influence gives 76 years.

- A bad influence gives 20 years, or 20 months, 20 days, and 20 hours.

<margin>If he is the ruling lord.</margin>
- **Actions.**
    - His cycle lasts 10 years and 9 months.
    - With the Moon: Writing, calculating, acquiring ecclesiastical livings <note>original: "pfründe," referring to a church office that provides an income</note>, buying, selling, and trading.
    - With the Moon: Teaching others, putting children in school, buying, selling, trading, and dealing with debt.
    - With the Moon: Calculating debts, sending messengers, and the same as above.
    - With the Moon: Dealing with writing, merchant's treasures, seeking livings, and putting children in school.
- **Year.**
    - Thus, he has the first 28 days as a good time for merchants and artists to have good governance.
- **Lands.**
    - Greece, Crete <note>original: "Candien"</note>, Achaia, Coele-Syria, Orchomenus, Hyrcania, Armenia, Cyrene, Marmarica, and Egypt. He makes the people there high-minded, learned, cowardly, and pleasure-seeking.

---

- To Jupiter, he gives 12 months.
- To Mars, he gives 15 months.
- To the Sun, he gives 19 months.
- To Venus, he gives 8 months.
- To the Moon, he gives 25 months.

- Jupiter. Venus. You will find these in their respective places.

<margin>In the signs.</margin>

- From the common people: Forgers of letters, punished for it with prison, fire, or other penalties; inconsistent, gossiping, persecution, anxiety, worry, and idleness.

- **Taurus /** Wandering children, singers, gluttons, drunkards, lazy, slow, idle, cunning, secretive and sullen; ending in anxiety and much misfortune.
- **Gemini /** Sharp-witted, artistic, inclined to evil, quarreling and bickering, from which comes shame, disgrace, anxiety, distress, poverty, and begging.

<margin>In the houses of heaven <note>The Twelve Houses are divisions of the sky in a birth chart, each governing a different area of life like wealth or health.</note>.</margin>
- **I** Scholars, Doctors, Clergy, those experienced in Holy Scripture, orators, and advocates. High at the courts of princes, honorable, pious, and Treasurers. occasionally they suffer a setback.
- **II** Disregarded, evil-minded, unlearned, mad, poor, practicing usury, or perhaps merchants; sometimes artists who think they know something; sometimes it brings a blow.
- **III** High priests, clergy, doctors, those who know the heavens, who discover much themselves; sheltered and blessed in their deeds. Great-minded, members of the high council, governors, and lords of the land.
- **IV** Clever and sharp-witted, receivers of the common purse <note>tax collectors or treasurers</note>, secret artists, advocates, fiscal officers, tower guards, goldsmiths, doctors, and fencers.
- **V** Treasure diggers, those who keep house well, treasurers and managers of others' goods; sometimes those with a little property who check everything, land surveyors, and stargazers.
- **VI** Through eloquence and trade, they win great wealth; sometimes they are interpreters, fishermen, bird-catchers, sculptors, or even evildoers, thieves, and criminals. Masters of the court, judges, officials, and governors.
- **VII** Unchaste, cowardly, visiting prostitutes, standing by loose people; tavern keepers, panderers, those who die soon, narrow-chested, fugitives, chased into misery. Rich wives.
- **VIII** Lazy, sluggish, those who undertake nothing, evil fools, hard of hearing; they find inheritance by chance, otherwise having enough luck but with a miserable body.
- **IX** Quarrelsome people, restless, who want to know much but understand nothing; evil yet persistent; priests, soothsayers, stargazers, etc. Godless and [haters of] churches.
- **X** Famous for wonderful deeds, governors, mayors, faithful, pious, and wise. Or a miserable death, wandering, or being cast into the water.
- **XI** Artists to whom much is entrusted. (Scribes, law-breakers, sorcerers; sometimes they suffer [misfortune].
- **XII** Governors and officials in the common interest, yet with danger to their lives; learned people, merchants, helpful to others, powerful but secretive <note>original: "duckelmausser"</note> people who [do] evil.

---

<margin>In these signs.</margin>
His effect is greatest in Gemini and Virgo.
In Pisces, he is at his weakest.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Minerva (Athena) from the previous page, moving from a list of her epithets to a detailed description of her origins, various historical accounts of her identity, and the allegorical meaning behind her traditional symbols.</meta>

<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

## Minerva.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the goddess Minerva. She is depicted as a warrior wearing classical armor, a helmet with a crest, and a long cloak. She holds a tall spear in her right hand and a shield in her left. To the left of her feet sits an owl (symbol of wisdom), and to the right is an olive tree. In the background, a building with a gabled roof and arched doorway is visible.</image-desc>

The Latins name her Minerva because she is accustomed to warn <note>original: "ermanen," suggesting an etymological link to the Latin "monere," to warn or advise</note>, or because she is a guide to the fine arts; for this goddess has always been regarded as a wise woman, skilled in both peace and war. For this reason, she was also painted in armor, as if she were threatening, and thus called *Minans armis* <note>Latin: "threatening with weapons"</note>. The Greeks call her Athena, as one who never sucked at a breast but was born fully grown from the head of her father, Jupiter; also, that through her special wisdom, she foresees all things as they shall happen in the future. Because of this, she is always free and subject to no one. There are also some who take her for the Moon, some for the highest part of the air, and many for Memory.

All artists, craftsmen, and those who deal with writing have honored the goddess as the inventor of all subtle works. Cicero writes that there were five of her: the first, the mother of Apollo. The second, born of the Nile, whom the Sais in Egypt held in high regard. The third, who was enclosed in the head of Jupiter. The fourth, whom Jupiter fathered from the daughter of Oceanus named Polyphe; the Arcadians call her Coryphasia. She is said to have invented four-horse chariots. The fifth was the daughter of Pallas, who slew her father when he intended to violate her.

Arnobius also counts five, saying the first bore Apollo by Vulcan; the second was the daughter of the Nile. The third he gives as a daughter of Saturn, who first invented armor. The fourth, Coryphasia at Messene. The fifth, the daughter of Pallas, and so on.

One paints this Minerva indeed dressed in armor, grim-faced and predatory, with arched eyes that are entirely cat-grey <note>A translation of the Greek "glaukopis," describing eyes that are flashing or greyish-blue like an owl’s or a cat’s</note>, with a long spear, a crystal shield, with a helmet upon her head, and a long cloak over the armor, with a little owl standing at her feet together with an olive tree.

Now, that she was born thus without a mother from the head and brain of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> signifies that all wisdom comes from the unfathomable, unrevealed foresight and wit of God, which earthly nature—that is, Jupiter’s wife Juno—cannot give or bear. That she remained a virgin forever and brought forth no fruit or child signifies that true Divine Wisdom involves itself with no earthly or mortal stain, but always remains in its purity and light; thus it remains perfect, and does not seek that which is temporal, for its profit and fruit are for the eternal judgment.

The beautiful, subtle little veil that some give to her signifies how the speech of a wise man is flowery, adorned, and somewhat gracious. The little owl <term>kåuzlin</term><note>An owl, specifically a little owl (Athene noctua), which became the symbol of wisdom because it can see in the dark.</note> signifies that the wise man is not given to sleep and laziness, but rather wakes at the time when others are sleeping, and handles the matters which he...

<meta>catchword: ...must handle</meta>

<summary>This page describes the origins and iconography of Minerva, goddess of wisdom, detailing different mythological versions of her birth and her various historical identities according to Cicero and Arnobius. It concludes with an allegorical interpretation of her virginity, her birth from Jupiter's head, and her symbols like the owl and the veil.</summary>
<keywords>Minerva, Athena, Jupiter, wisdom, armor, owl, olive tree, Cicero, Arnobius, Juno, allegory, mythology</keywords>

--- Page 272 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the goddess Minerva, specifically interpreting the allegorical meaning of her traditional warrior’s attire and symbols, followed by the origins of her name "Pallas" and the history of the sacred "Palladium" statue.</meta>

<header>Of the Heathen Gods</header>

...act according to their senses. Her armor signifies that the wise man resists internal and external temptations and, with the counsel of reason, withstands evil. Her predatory face <note>Likely referring to the Gorgon Medusa on her breastplate, intended to strike fear or represent gravity.</note> is meant to show that the prudent person does not cast their eyes upon lust, but rather turns and focuses them on serious matters. The long spear signifies that the wise man perceives and recognizes much of the future—that which is yet to come—from the current course of events; therefore, he knows well how to ward off whatever might befall him from afar. The crystalline shield <note>Often a reference to the Aegis, sometimes described in medieval and Renaissance texts as being made of crystal or polished stone to reflect truth.</note> means nothing other than the steadfastness with which the wise man outlasts the enemy, spies out their actions, knows himself, and understands moderation. What Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> writes of her is unnecessary to report here. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> considers her to be the power of the Sun, which makes human beings ingenious. Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet.</note> gives her a mother whom he calls Prudence <note>original: "fürſichtigkeit," referring to the goddess Metis</note>, who, as soon as she was swallowed by Juno <note>The text likely means Jupiter here, following the common myth, though the OCR says Juno.</note>, gave birth to her fruit—with which she was pregnant—out of Jupiter's brain.

Sometimes her image is painted sitting, with a rooster upon her helmet, an owl beside her, and the head of Medusa along with a small olive tree on her shield. This tree, like wisdom, is eternally green. Since the rooster is a watchful, brave animal in its nature, and the owl represents old age, it signifies that the counsel of the wise brings profit for many years. Some believe that because she is designated a goddess of war, no war can be successfully waged without wit <note>meaning intelligence or strategy</note>; but since the olive tree is a sign of peace, it is given to her to understand that one takes war in hand only so that one may be able to have peace.

**Pallas.** Some give her this name because she killed a giant named Pallas. Others say she sprang from the Lake or pool called Palla. Others say the name rhymes with a Greek word <note>original: "pallein," meaning to brandish or shake a spear</note> that means to shake a spear or to leap and press forward in war. Then some come with a vague account <note>original: "ſtempeney," an archaic term for a confused story or fragment</note> that she killed her father Pallas, who wished to violate her. Some also say that Pallas, the son of Lycaon, raised her, from which the name remained with her.

Regarding the image of Minerva that is called the **Palladium**, there are many tales. Some claim that Jupiter gave it to Dardanus and showed him thereby that the city which kept this image in secret and did not allow it to be taken away would have dominion and prominence in the world. Dardanus thus kept it in the fortress of Troy in a completely hidden place; however, he had a duplicate made which he set up publicly in the temple. This duplicate was taken from the temple by night by Ulysses and Diomedes, acting as scouts. But Aeneas snatched the true one during the city's misery and brought it with him to Italy; it was thereafter kept in Rome in the Temple of Vesta until Constantine the Great took it to Constantinople and buried it there in a secret place. In Athens, however, a place was called "Palladium" for this reason: when Diomedes had stolen the Palladium from the temple and Troy was now destroyed, he sailed back home. He landed by night in Attica, and not knowing whether they were in the land of friends or enemies, his men began to take booty, rob, and burn. Demophoon <note>A legendary King of Athens and son of Theseus.</note> set out, also thinking they were enemies, and gathered his people in haste. He gave battle to Diomedes, killed many of the Argives <note>Greeks from Argos</note>, and took the loot from them along with the Palladium, which he hid and placed in a certain spot. Because of this, he was later brought to court for having accidentally killed an Athenian.

<meta>Continuity from previous page: This page continues the description of the Palladium (the sacred statue of Minerva/Athena) and moves into a detailed explanation of her epithets "Parthenos" and "Tritonia," blending classical mythology with early modern interpretations.</meta>

# The Fourth Book

The statue is said to have been four and a half feet <note>original: "fünffthealb schůch"</note> tall, holding a spear in its right hand and in the left a spindle with thread wound upon it—or it is said to have carried a distaff. It was a unique object that fell from heaven; Diomedes, by the command of the priests <note>original: "pfaffen," here referring to pagan priests or oracles</note>, had to return it during his illness if he wished to become healthy again.

**Parthenos.** The Virgin. In the city of Athens, within the citadel or fortress <note>the Acropolis</note>, this Minerva was greatly honored with the splendor of a temple and churchly pomp, which Pericles established. When the temple was finished, Pericles climbed to the very top of the peak and fell down; Minerva then appeared to him in his sleep and showed him the herb that is thought to be "Peter’s herb" <note>likely *Parietaria* or pellitory-of-the-wall; historically, this refers to the "Parthenium" plant</note>, and with this herb, he was healed.

**Tritonia.** A watercourse that occasionally surged during storms was located in Boeotia; it created a lake called Triton. When the lake grew large, it flowed toward the Southern Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>, where it had its outlet. At that same place, Minerva is said to have been raised, and her name is said to have come from there. The Pheneatians in Arcadia also had a temple dedicated to her. Caps <note>possibly referring to the Gulf of Gabès</note> was once where the river Triton was in Africa, where the province of Zeugitana is now; a city was located there which was also called by the name Tacape. Not far from there lies a lake, the name of which was Tritonis, now called Palupalla. From this, some give Minerva that surname. However, they give the lake its name because Jason, having been blown off course by the wind along with his shipmates, came into Africa and specifically into this lake. When the violence of the sea subsided and Jason sought the exit—not knowing where he should go out again—a "sea-piper" <note>a merman or sea-god</note> named Triton appeared to him. He told Jason that if he would give him the tripod <note>original: "dreyfüssigen stůl," a three-legged sacrificial seat</note> that he intended to carry to Delphi, he would learn the way out from him; Jason agreed to this. 

Pallas, however, as an inventor of many crafts and arts, was raised by this lake and also used flutes or trumpets <note>original: "bausannen"</note> for her amusement. One time while piping, she saw her puffed-up cheeks reflected in the water; she threw the pipes away from her into the lake, saying it was hideous for a woman’s image to be so puffed up. From this event, her name is also derived.

Some say she is so named because she shared three gifts with mankind: Right Counsel, Just Judgment, and Doing What is Fair. Others say she is taken to represent the air, which changes three times a year—being cool, cold, and hot—or that she represents the moon, which begins to appear on the third day after it is new.

There is said to have been another Tritonia in Thessaly; however, Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> places the Alipherians in Arcadia. They had a bronze statue <note>original: "öhrin bild"</note>, a temple, and a spring which they called Triton, from which all the previous stories were told—how she was raised among them, etc. The statue was large, beautiful, and well-made, and it had an annual festival. Otherwise, it is said that Minerva was a daughter of Neptune and Tritonis, a nymph <note>original: "feettlen," a term for a female spirit or sometimes an older woman</note> in Libya; but when she angered her father Neptune, Jupiter adopted her as his own child. On her feast day or temple consecration, the virgins would gather together and fight one another with stones and clubs. Whichever one was wounded was no longer considered a pure virgin; the one who won the prize <note>original: "den danck erholt"</note> was led around the lake in a small chariot while songs were sung to her, and the other virgins gave her gifts.

# Concerning Heathen Gods

<margin>Tritogeneia. <note>Greek: "Triton-born"</note></margin> For the reasons already mentioned, she also received this name; however, some add that she is called this because she is cruel and terrifying to behold, and bold in war, making her enemies fearful.

<margin>Tritone. The Tireless. <note>original: "Die vnuerschliffen," meaning unpolished or unworn, here implying one who does not tire</note></margin> Because she was entirely undaunted and quite swift in all labor and art, this name was given to her; she was also called Tritogonia <note>three-angled</note> because of the three corners drawn according to a straightedge to make a "true foot" <note>likely a reference to geometry or architectural precision</note>.

<margin>Strateia. The Warlike. Aretia.</margin> Soldiers took great comfort in her; she was also held to be a leader and instructor in wars started for the sake of justice, which is why she was called by these names. In Athens, she had an altar that Mars erected for her when he killed Halirrhothius <note>original: "Alirrhotiū"</note> and was brought to justice for it, but was found innocent. Likewise, it is said that Orestes was brought to trial there on account of his mother; and from the spoils that the Athenians took from the Persians at Marathon, they also erected a temple to her. This temple was at Plataea, and the statue within was made of wood, gilded, though the face, fingers, and toes were of marble. In size, it was equal to the statue of this same Minerva in their citadel, which was erected from bronze taken from those same spoils.

<margin>Hippia. The Equestrian. <note>original: "Ippia Die Reysig," referring to one who rides or travels on horseback</note></margin> Because Minerva was the first to prepare racing chariots, she is named thus, and several statues of her in mid-run were erected, such as at the Olympic playing field in Athens. For this reason, she was also called "The Horse-Tamer" by Phurnutus <note>Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note>. Pausanias says that her statue stood in the citadel at Sparta, and that she received the name from being a chariot driver in the War of the Giants <note>original: "Riesenkrieg"</note> against Enceladus.

<margin>Polias. Sthenias. The Strong, The Civic.</margin> At Troezen, there was a temple to this Minerva; for when she came into a dispute with Neptune <note>original: "Neptuno"</note> over which of the two should possess that region, Jupiter delivered the judgment that the city and land should belong to both of them. There was likewise a temple of this Minerva at Trachis; because she would not abide by Jupiter’s judgment unless she were given the surname mentioned above. Neptune, however, wanted to be called "The King" in return, to which she agreed.

There was a temple of Polias at Tegea; the priest <note>original: "Pfaff"</note> entered it only once a year. There, Minerva is said to have promised Cepheus, the son of Aleus, that Tegea would never be conquered; as a token of this, she also gave him some of Medusa’s hair to keep in the temple. This temple was called the "Protection of the City." In the fortress at Athens was her image; coins were struck with Neptune’s trident or three-pronged spear on one side, and the face of Minerva stamped on the other. In the temple was a lamp that never went out, and a small convent <note>original: "Nonnen clösterlin," an early modern interpretation of the Parthenon's later use as a church/cloisters</note> that Ictinus built and founded; the Palladium was also kept within it. In Erythrae or Rocho in Negroponte <note>the island of Euboea</note>, she had a temple, and within it a large wooden statue sitting upon a magnificent throne, carrying a filled spindle in both hands, with the celestial sphere upon its head.

# The Fourth Book.

They believe she was called the **Grey-eyed** <note>original: "Grawaugẽde," likely referring to the Greek "Glaukopis"</note> because the owlets <note>original: "Kåutzlin"</note> that are dedicated to her also have grey eyes. Diodorus also makes mention of this. Gellius believes she received the name from her staring, fierce appearance.

<margin>Caesia, Coelia, Yellow. The Gold-haired.</margin> Among the Romans, she was called *Caesia* <note>originally: "Cessiagnant"</note> for *Coelia*, which signifies the color of the sky, says Gellius; he says she was the same one whom the Greeks called *Glaucopis*. And because she had beautiful gold-colored hair, the name was given to her.

<margin>Gorgopos. The Grim-faced.</margin> Because Minerva has such a gruesome, staring face, this name was bestowed upon her.

<margin>Poliochos. City-Protector.</margin> The fortress of the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> was once considered the highest-situated; in that same place, Tyndarus began to build a temple. When he died before its completion, his sons undertook to finish it; when they also died during the work, the Lacedaemonians completed it a long time afterward. They placed a bronze <note>original: "ôhrin," meaning brazen</note> image within and gave her this name. Emperor Vitellius called his massive serving platter, because of its great weight, the "Shield of Minerva the City-Protector."

<margin>Chalkioikos. She in the Bronze House.</margin> They named the previously mentioned goddess with this name as well, perhaps for the reason that her chapel in the temple was made entirely of bronze; yet some believe she is called *Chalcidia* because those driven out of Negropont <note>the island of Euboea</note>, which was called Chalcis, built that same temple for her. Our Lady over Minerva <note>the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva</note>, where the Dominican friars <note>original: "Prediger můnch"</note> are in Rome, was once a temple of Minerva, of which a sign is still present: namely, the tablet in which the deeds of Pompey are described. For he built that very temple to Minerva from the loot and booty of the Roman enemies whom he had conquered. So that you may recognize the deeds of this noble man from his monument, I will record their contents from Pliny; you will find it in the twenty-sixth chapter of the seventh book of his *Natural History*.

<margin>Gnaeus Pompeius the Great.</margin> A commander of the Roman soldiers, who in thirty years of warfare, from those he scattered, hunted, put to flight, captured, and killed, took two million and eighty-three thousand men. Of ships, he sank and captured about eight hundred forty-six. He took one thousand five hundred thirty-eight cities and towns. From the Sea of Azov <note>original: "Zabackischẽ," referring to the Palus Maeotis</note> to the Red Sea, he brought almost all lordships under the yoke, for which he is rightly praised, and he built this temple to Minerva.

<margin>Hellotis. She of the Marsh.</margin> Not far from Marathon in Attica is a marsh called *Helos*; Minerva has a temple there, from which, according to some, the name comes. Others claim she is so named because she was the first to capture and bridle Pegasus, the winged horse of Bellerophon. Finally, some say the Dorians, together with the allies in Morea <note>the Peloponnese</note> who came to their aid, captured and set fire to Corinth; there, two sisters, Eurytio and Hellotis, fled into the temple of Pallas and burned to death piteously. Immediately afterward, a plague <note>original: "schelm"</note> followed, and it was decreed that one should appease the souls of the burned women; whereupon the temple of Minerva was built and a competition <note>the Hellotia games</note> was established.

## Concerning the Heathen Gods
<meta>catchword: Ophthal-</meta>

By this lake there also once stood a city called Helos. When the whole province of Morea <note>the Peloponnese peninsula</note> first became subject to the Spartans, this city held citizenship and equal rights to all offices. The councilors were called Helots, as Helos was considered the oldest city. Consequently, they no longer wished to be under the Spartans, became rebellious, and were overtaken by other allies, subdued, and sold into eternal servitude. Their city was destroyed; therefore, all slaves and sold persons among the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> are called Helots. Plutarch also says that at one time five thousand Spartans marched against the Persians, each taking seven Helots with him. Now, it is unlikely that Minerva takes her name from this city; it is more credible that the name comes from *Hellotis*, one of the aforementioned burnt maidens. For this reason, these games were held in Corinth, and the youths competing there had to run carrying a vessel <note>original: "amplen," likely a lamp</note> or a torch that was lit; the prize went only to the one who first reached the goal with his torch still burning; otherwise, it counted for nothing.

**Coryphagene.** <note>Greek: "Head-born"</note> When it is said how Jupiter wished to give birth to her and was in pain, Vulcan grabbed a bronze axe and split open his brain; from there Minerva leaped out and shouted so that heaven and earth were terrified. This is interpreted to mean that, apart from God, wisdom comes from no one else. Furthermore, wisdom cannot take hold of a child or youth without a schoolmaster, or else he must endure great toil and labor until he learns something. Thus, Vulcan is a hardworking god, or the fire which—restless and active—drives out sweat until it teaches man something. In short, there can be no idleness here, but rather a special diligence from the teacher. But once this wit is born, she cries out so that heaven and earth echo with it; this is nothing other than wisdom shouting for piety, fear of God, justice, and the like—which sounds dreadful to the world, but rings beautifully and sweetly all the way to heaven. Thus, this name remained with Minerva.

**Coryphasia.** The one in Ionia. The promontory near Modon, where the city of Pylos—now called Ionia—once stood, was named Coryphasium. Now, Pylos lies approximately two and a half miles from Modon; it was built by Pylus, the son of Cleon, along with a temple, and from this the name of Minerva arose. Arnobius believes Coryphe <note>Greek for "the Peak" or "Head"</note> was her mother, from whom she takes the name; or perhaps she appeared first on this promontory carrying a glittering shield for her father Jupiter, which caused terror among those living nearby.

**Cyndia.** The one at Lindos. On the island of Rhodes there is a city called Lindos, about which Diodorus writes regarding how Minerva was honored there; you may look into his work. Strabo says the Danaïdes <note>the fifty daughters of Danaus</note> built a very costly temple to Minerva at Lindos.

**Capania** or **Pania.** At Argos, in the wrestling school <note>original: "kampffschůl"</note> of Cyllabarus (for a son of Sthenelus named Cyllabarus built it), there was an image of Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva</note> which they called by this name, either after Capaneus, who is buried not far from there, or else named after the wagons which the Thessalians called *Capania*.

# The Fourth Book.

**Ophthalmitis** <note>original: "Ophthalmitis/ Optiletis"</note> / **The Eye-Healer.** Lycurgus <note>the legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> had prescribed a law for the Spartans with which he intended to do away with all drunkenness. This was initially quite vexing to the wealthy; therefore, they stirred up a riot against him, from which he had to flee into a temple. However, a youth named Alcander hurried after him aggressively, and as Lycurgus turned around, the youth struck him in the eye and knocked it out. When Lycurgus turned back toward the citizens, looking so wretched and fouled with blood, the citizens felt a sense of remorse that they had treated their lawmaker so poorly. They handed Alcander, who had struck out his eye, over to him. But Lycurgus did not harm him; instead, he raised him to be a brave and valiant man. He built a temple to Minerva, praying that she should stand by him so that he would not also lose his other eye.

**Oxydercus.** **The Sharp-Sighted.** When Diomedes <note>a Greek hero</note> came to fight before Troy, the goddess removed the mist from before his eyes <note>an event described in Homer’s Iliad</note>; for this reason, he later built a temple to her under this name at Corinth.

**Cyparissia.** **The one at Nico.** Esapo <note>likely Asopus</note> is a city located in Laconia, sometimes called Asapo; it has a fortress within it containing a temple of Pallas <note>Minerva</note>. Likewise, not far from there lay a city and suburb called Cyparissus, where the city of Nico now stands and where the mountain of the "Conellen-heads" is located; she was also worshipped there, which is where her name originated.

**Alea.** The entire province of Morea <note>the Peloponnese peninsula</note> honored this Minerva with special devotion. For the city of Alea was built by a man named Aleus, the son of Apheidas <note>original: "Alephidantis"</note>, who erected several temples and first established one to Minerva there. In Tegea, however, there was a very old temple of this Minerva which burned down; the citizens rebuilt a beautiful one of marble from the public treasury through the master-builder Scopas <note>a famous Greek sculptor and architect</note>. In this same temple, the shackles or chains were later hung up which the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> had brought with them when they invaded Tegea, intending to bind the Tegeans, but were instead defeated in battle and had to leave them behind. Likewise, the bronze horse-manger of Mardonius <note>a Persian general</note> was kept there. During the Theban war, the Arcadians held and fortified this temple as a stronghold against the enemy.

In Mantinea, there was also a temple of this Minerva containing her image. Furthermore, the Emperor Augustus carried away the image of this Minerva from Tegea and placed it in the main market in Rome; it was made entirely of ivory. Endius the sculptor <note>an early Greek artist</note> had fashioned it. In this temple was the skin of the Calydonian Boar <note>a monstrous creature from Greek myth</note>, and a young boy served as priest there until he reached manhood. Not far from Therapne, she also has a temple; I believe it is the one mentioned by Xenophon.

**Alea.** The poet Statius mentions her often. Strabo, in my opinion, writes that this was the most prominent one. For his words are: Tegea still exists in some form, and therein is the temple of the Elean Minerva or Pallas.

**Meter.** **The Mother.** Hercules and his followers invaded Elea, and their allies came to their aid. The women of Elis, having lost so many men in the defeat by Hercules that the land was nearly emptied of men, entreated Minerva that she should grant them the grace that as soon as one...

# Concerning Heathen Gods

At this lake <note>likely referring to the marshy regions of Laconia mentioned on the previous page</note> there also once stood a city called **Helos**. When the entire province of Morea <note>the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note> first swore its duty to the Spartans, this city held the rights of citizenship and could hold all offices with equal dignity. Their councilors were called **Helots**, as Helos was considered the oldest city. Because of this, they became proud and no longer wished to be under the Spartans. They became rebellious and were eventually conquered by other allies, subdued, and sold into eternal servitude. Their city was torn down, and for this reason, all servants and sold persons among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> are called Helots. Plutarch also says that at one time, five thousand Spartans marched out against the Persians, and each one took seven Helots with him. Now, it may not be that Minerva takes her name from this city; it is more believable that the name comes to her from the *Heloti*, the aforementioned "burned maidens." The reason for this is that in Corinth, these games were held where the youths who competed had to run, carrying a vessel that was set on fire, or a torch. He who reached the goal first with his burning torch won the prize; otherwise, it counted for nothing.

<margin>Coryphagene.</margin>
**Coryphagene.** <note>original: "Coryphagene," from the Greek for "head-born"</note> Then they say how Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> wished to give birth and was in great pain. Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> grabbed an iron axe and split his skull open, from which Minerva leaped out and screamed so loudly that heaven and earth were terrified. This is interpreted to mean that, outside of God, wisdom comes from no one else. However, a child or youth cannot grasp this wisdom without a schoolmaster, or he must endure great toil and labor until he learns something. For this reason, Vulcan is a "working god"—or he represents fire, which is restless and active, drawing out sweat until it teaches a person something. In short, there can be no idleness here, and a teacher must show special diligence. But once this wit <note>intelligence or wisdom</note> is born, it cries out so that heaven and earth ring with it. This is nothing else than wisdom crying out for piety, fear of God, justice, and the like; such things seem harsh to the world, but they ring beautifully and pleasantly in heaven. Thus, this name remained with Minerva.

<margin>Coryphasia. The one at Zonichia.</margin>
**Coryphasia. The one at Zonichia.** The promontory near Modona <note>modern Methoni</note>, where the city of Pylos—now called Zonichia—once stood, was called Coryphasium. Now, Pylos lies about two and a half miles from Modona. This city was built by Pylus, the son of Cleson, along with a temple, and from this, the name of Minerva grew. Arnobius <note>an early Christian apologist</note> believes that Coryphe was her mother, and she took the name from her; or perhaps she appeared on this promontory first, carrying a shining shield before her father Jupiter, which terrified those living nearby.

<margin>Cyndia. The one at Lindos.</margin>
**Cyndia. The one at Lindos.** On the island of Rhodes, there is a city called Lindos. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> writes of how Minerva was honored there; you may look it up. Strabo says the Danaids <note>the fifty daughters of Danaus</note> built a very costly temple to Minerva at Lindos.

<margin>Capania/Pania.</margin>
**Capania / Pania.** At Argos, in the wrestling school <note>gymnasium</note> of Cyllabaris—for a son of Sthenelus named Cyllabarus built it—there was an image of Pallas <note>Minerva</note> which they called by this name. It was either named after Capaneus <note>one of the "Seven against Thebes"</note>, who is buried not far from there, or else named after the wagons which the Thessalians called *Capania*.

### The Fourth Book

**Ophthalmitis** / **Optiletis**. The Eye-Comforter. <note>original: "Augentrost," likely referring to Athena Ophthalmitis, the "eye-seer" or "protector of sight."</note>
Lycurgus <note>the legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> had prescribed a law for the Spartans with which he intended to stop all their gluttony and drunkenness. This was at first entirely vexing to the wealthy, which is why they raised a riot against him. He was forced to flee into a temple, but a youth named Alcander chased after him fiercely. As Lycurgus turned around, Alcander struck him in one eye and knocked it out. When Lycurgus turned back toward the citizens, looking so wretched and covered in blood, the citizens felt a great remorse that they had treated their lawgiver so poorly. They handed Alcander over to him—the one who had struck out his eye—but Lycurgus did not harm him. Instead, he raised him to be a brave and valiant man. Lycurgus then built a temple to Minerva, praying that she should stand by him so that he would not lose his other eye as well.

**Oxydercus.** The Sharp-Seeing. <note>original: "Oxydercus," from the Greek *oxyderkes*, meaning sharp-sighted.</note> When Diomedes <note>a hero of the Trojan War</note> went to fight before Troy, the goddess removed the mist from before his eyes. Because of this, he later built a temple to her under this name in Corinth.

**Cyparissia.** The one at Nico. Esapo is a city located in Laconia, once called Asapo. It has a fortress within which there is a temple of Pallas. Likewise, not far from there lay a city and promontory named Cyparissus, where the city of Nico now stands and where the mountain is called the "Little Heads of Conellen." She was also honored there, which is where her name came from.

**Alea.** The entire province of Morea <note>the Peloponnese</note> together held this Minerva in special honor. The city of Alea was built by a son of Alephidantis named Aleus, who established several temples there, and primarily one to Minerva. In Tegea, however, there was a very old temple of this Minerva. When it burned down, the citizens, using their common funds, had a beautiful marble temple erected by Scopas the master builder <note>a famous Greek sculptor and architect</note>. In this same temple, the foot-irons or shackles were later hung up which the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> had brought with them when they invaded Tegea, intending to bind the Tegeans. However, having been defeated in the battle, they were forced to leave them behind. Likewise, the iron horse-mangers of Mardonius <note>a Persian general during the Persian Wars</note> were kept there. In the Theban War, the Arcadians held this temple as a fortress against the enemy and fortified it.

In Mantinea, there was also a temple of this Minerva containing her image. The Emperor Augustus later carried away the image of this Minerva from Tegea and placed it in the main market in Rome; it was made entirely of ivory. Endius the sculptor had crafted it. In this temple was also the hide of the Calydonian Boar, and a young boy served as priest there until he reached manhood. Not far from Therapne, she also has a temple; it is said to be the one that Xenophon mentions.

**Alea.** The poet Statius mentions her often. Strabo, in my opinion, writes that this was the most prominent one. For his words are: Tegea is still somewhat significant, and there stands the temple of the Alean Minerva or Pallas.

**Meter.** The Mother. Hercules, along with his followers, had invaded Elea. Their allies came to their aid, but they were defeated by Hercules. # Of the Pagan Gods

...placed with a man, she became pregnant immediately. She assists women <note>likely in the context of childbirth or fertility</note>, and for this reason, they established a temple for her there called "Bady" <note>original: "Bady," possibly a corruption of a Greek local epithet</note> for the same purpose.

**Telchinia**, the Enchantress. Certain Cretans who practiced sorcery were expelled from the island and came to Rhodes. They did not have a place there for long either; they were called the Telchines. Some of them came to Teumessus in Boeotia and built a temple to Minerva there, but they did not place any statue within it.

**Budea Boacmia**, Tamer of Oxen. Budeus, a Magnesian, built a temple to Minerva; a similar one was also in Phrygia (now Anatolia), from which she is said to have taken the name. Some say she received the name because Minerva, through her wisdom, devised how agriculture should be conducted using oxen.

**Echea**, the one at Tremiti. Apulia <note>original: "Puglia"</note>, the region in Italy, is the place where she was called Daunia, after Daunus, the father-in-law of Diomedes. This Diomedes—who ruled in Achaia before the Trojan War, where Romania <note>here referring to the Byzantine or former Roman territories in the East</note> is now—was a son of Tydeus and Deiphile. After the destruction of Troy, he was tossed to and fro upon the sea with his company, for his wife Aegiale had committed adultery in the meantime; therefore, he did not wish to return home and set out for Italy. When the women in his ships arrived at these islands near Apulia—now called "Our Lady of Tremiti"—they set the ships on fire so that they could sail no further and instead had to seek out a place to dwell. There are six of these islands, among which Tremiti is the largest; it is now inhabited by the regular lords of the Order of Saint Augustine and is very strongly fortified and well-built as a bulwark against the Turks and other attacks. On the other islands, they keep their cattle, dairy farms, and sheep folds. There, Diomedes built a temple to Minerva, where the monastery now stands. It breeds many geese, which were once called the "Birds of Diomedes"; it was said of them that they showed much kindness to the Greeks by flying and serving them, but they attacked and pecked at foreigners to harm them. The weapons of Diomedes were also said to have hung there in the time of Aristotle, and it is said the birds behaved as mentioned before.

**Panacheia**, Common to the Achaeans. At Patras, in the portico of the temple of Diana Laphria <note>original: "Diane Laphrie," referring to Artemis</note>, there is a chapel of Minerva containing an image made of gold and ivory. The Achaeans maintained the temple and the image at their collective expense.

**Pallenis**. When the tyrant and despot Pisistratus was driven from Athens for the second time and attempted to return with the help of others, the Athenians marched against him to negotiate in a temple dedicated to the Pallenian Minerva, located between the city and Marathon. He came from the island of Negroponte <note>Euboea</note>, from Eretria (now called Rocho), where this Minerva previously had a temple; perhaps the former temple between Marathon and Sethin <note>an old name for Athens</note> or Athens took its name from this one.

**Chalimitis**, the Bridler of Minerva. She was so named because she was helpful to Bellerophon in many things, and especially with the bridling of Pegasus. Her statue was made of wood, except for the bare limbs, which were of white marble <note>this describes an "acrolithic" statue, where only the exposed flesh was stone</note>.

# The Fourth Book

**Scirias: Scirrhada.** At Dodona <note>an ancient sanctuary in Epirus known for its oracle</note>, there was a priest named Scirus. He built a temple to Minerva at Phalerum <note>the ancient port of Athens</note>. This priest died while the people of Eleusis were fighting against Erechtheus <note>a legendary king of Athens</note>, and he was buried by the stream Scirus. Later, that same place became the site of the public brothel, a place for masks and scoundrels in Athens.

**Apaturia.** Seductress or Procuress. Near Phanar <note>possibly referring to a lighthouse or coastal point</note>, there are crags or rocks in the sea like islands. In one of these was the grave of Sphaerus, the charioteer of Pelops. Aethra was persuaded by Minerva to offer sacrifices to him there. When she arrived, Neptune <note>Poseidon</note> violated her. Because of this, she built a temple to Minerva, and ever since, the maidens or brides at Troezen or Phanar have had to give their belts to this Minerva.

**Hygeia.** The Healer. This Minerva has an altar in the stone quarries of Athens, and also in the citadel <note>the Acropolis</note>. In the citadel, Pericles erected a bronze <note>original: "öltin bild," likely meaning bronze (from 'olte' or 'erzen') or an oil-treated statue</note> image of her after his architect nearly fell to his death; when the man recovered, Pericles dedicated this monument. At Pallen, not far from Tegea, she also has a temple built by Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>.

**Lias.** About ten miles from Skopje, which is now the capital of Macedonia, there is a place called Lidasagni, formerly known as Daulia. There stood a temple and a very ancient statue of this Minerva, erected by the Greeks during the Trojan War. Within it were dogs that were completely hostile toward strangers who entered, but were entirely affectionate and fawning toward the Greeks.

**Singa. Siga. Sais.** They say that Cadmus came from the city of Thebes in Egypt, and when he arrived in Boeotia, he erected an altar and an image to Minerva there. She was called "The Stayer" <note>original: "Ställering," one who brings to a halt</note>, which in Egyptian is called *Siga*, after the city otherwise known as Sais.

**Crastia. Cratesia.** On a hill called Crastius, the Sybarites built a temple to this Minerva, not far from where "Our Lady of Patyro" <note>the Abbey of Santa Maria del Patire</note> now stands in Calabria by the river Crathis. The city of Sybaris was once so powerful that it could put three hundred thousand men into the field, but they were so entirely devoted to pleasure that when one person invited another to a feast, they always announced it to the guests a full year in advance. This was done so that both the host and the guest could prepare themselves sufficiently. They devoted themselves to pastimes, dancing, jumping, and so on, to such an extent that even their animals and horses had to dance for them. This led them into great distress. The cause was an invasion by the Crotoniates; when the attackers began to play trumpets and pipes, the Sybarite horses thought it was music for a dance and began to hop and prance. In the midst of this, the Crotoniates slaughtered them. For this reason, I read in Herodotus the name "Cratesia" and not "Crastia," which comes from the river where the temple stood.

**Aphrya.** The Taker of Spoils. Lycophron calls her by this name because she was accustomed to being weighed down with the plunder of wars.

**Pyletis.** She of the Gates. Her image was frequently painted on the gates of houses, cities, and all settlements as a sign that wisdom should be practiced within those houses and towns. From this, she received her name.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

**AEthyia** The Diver / **Endarthyia**. The Diver, or the bird that one calls a little diver <note>original: "Daucherlin," likely a gull or cormorant</note>, swims with great daring and is also quite white; for this reason, this name was given to **Minerva**, as some claim. But others say it refers to a cliff in the sea, located not far from **Megara**, which was called "The Little Diver," and she was named after it. Others bring forth a fable of how **Minerva** transformed herself into a diving bird and, having hidden **Cecrops** <note>a legendary king of Athens</note> under her wings, carried him to **Megara**. The statue of this **Minerva** in **Megara** is made of wood and gilded, but where she is bare, the hands and feet are made entirely of ivory. Her temple is also located there.

**Ergane** / **Ergatis** / **Eriene**. Instructress of women's work. This **Minerva** first held this name in **Athens** because she directs the business and labor of women. In **Lacedaemonia** <note>Sparta</note>, she also has a temple, as she does in **Samos**.

**Salpinga** / The Trumpeter <note>original: "Sackpfeifferin," literally "bagpiper," but the Greek 'Salpinga' refers to the salpinx, a straight trumpet</note>. In **Argos**, a temple was built by **Hegeleos**, the son of **Tyrrhenus** and grandson of **Hercules** and **Omphale**. He taught the **Dorians** much about the trumpet <note>original: "Sackpfeiffen"</note>, and therefore named the temple of **Minerva** which he built as a memorial to this.

**Gigantophontida.** Slayer of Giants. The first humans born from the earth were once very stubborn and bloodthirsty, murdering one another; they knew nothing of court or law. The gods, who were wise people and upheld justice, had to set themselves against these senseless fools <note>original: "unbsinten tropffen"</note> until, with friendly persuasion and great skill, they brought them to a good end and peace. Sometimes they had to seize the rough, foolish churls by their hoods <note>original: "auff die hauben greyffen," a metaphor for discipline or physical correction</note> until they renewed the people and brought them to a good way of life. For this reason, nearly all the great gods received this name, as did **Minerva**.

**Victrix** The Victress. In **Athens**, **Minerva** was held in bronze <note>original: "ehern"</note> under this name. Her image was without wings; in her right hand she carried a pomegranate, and in her left a helmet. In **Spain**, **Cato** also erected a temple to this **Minerva** at great expense, placing a bronze statue within it at the place where he finished the war with his enemies.

**Alipherea.** In **Arcadia**, there was a city called **Aliphera** which had a citadel on a high rock, along with a bronze statue that surpassed all other images of **Minerva** in beauty and size. **Hypatodorus** <note>OCR reads "Decatodorus"</note> and **Sostratus** made the statue; this is also mentioned in the accounts of **Tritonia**.

**Itonia.** Not far from Koroni in the **Morea** <note>the Peloponnese</note>, there was a temple of this **Minerva** into which King **Antiochus** had his likeness placed. Furthermore, there was a city in **Thessaly** called **Itona**, where **Itonus**, a son of **Amphictyon**, also built a temple to this **Minerva**, not far from **Itome** <note>OCR: "Jemsar"</note> and **Larissa**. There, King **Pyrrhus** hung up the shields of the **Germans** <note>original: "Teütschen," likely referring to the Galatian Celts whom Pyrrhus defeated</note> and **Gauls** which he had captured in battle. It is also said that in **Macedonia** there was a city called **Itonia** with a temple to this **Minerva**, where **Autonous**, the son of **Hercules**, once ruled.

**Ithomia.** **Ithome** is a city also located in **Thessaly** where there was an ancient chapel and statue of this **Minerva**; from this she receives her name.

<summary>This page details several epithets of Minerva (Athena), describing her as a patron of women's work, a slayer of giants who brought order to early humanity, and a goddess of victory associated with specific temples in Greece and Spain.</summary>

# The Fourth Book.

**Zosteria.** <note>original: "Zosteria," from the Greek 'zoster,' meaning belt or girdle, used here in the context of buckling on armor.</note> **Amphitryon**, the stepfather of **Hercules**, when he wished to fight against the **Euboeans** <note>original: "Negroponter," the medieval name for the Greek island of Euboea</note> and was putting on his armor, had two wooden columns erected in **Thebes** that were both dedicated to **Minerva**. Because **Zosteria** signifies the putting on of armor, this name is said to have remained with her. This **Minerva** is also said to have been worshipped in **Locris**, across from **Euboea**.

**Thallophoros.** The Branch-Bearer. **Xenophon** mentions this **Minerva** when **Critobulus** says to **Socrates**: Beauty is to be gathered in every age—in the child, the youth, the mature man, the adult, and also in the old. This is shown by the fact that at the festival of this **Minerva**, those who must carry the olive branches are all chosen elders, and they are chosen because they are handsome men.

**Alalcomenes.** **Alalcomenes** was a son of **Hercules** who had a city in **Boeotia**, as well as a temple and altar built according to his name, from which her name is derived.

**Agelea. Alalceis.** **Phornutus** <note>a Stoic philosopher, also known as Cornutus</note> believes she is helpful and does the best for the people, so she has this name; she also drives the nations and gathers the spoils of war.

**Alcides.** The **Macedonians** worshipped this **Minerva** highly. When King **Perseus** marched toward **Catium** (which is now **Bligitza**), he sacrificed to her with great splendor, as **Livy** indicates, so that she might assist him in the war against the **Romans**.

**Aculeana.** **Quintus Lutatius Catulus** built a temple to **Minerva** in **Rome** below the **Capitoline Hill**, from which she takes this name.

**Musica.** The Singer. **Demetrius** the Master Craftsman made an image of **Minerva** with such artistic skill that the snakes on her shield and on the **Gorgon's** head made a sound whenever a harp was played nearby; from this, she was called the Singer.

**Capta.** The Captive. A temple was erected to this **Minerva** on the **Caelian Hill** in **Rome**. She received the name because she was brought to **Rome** from **Falerii** (now **Montefiascone**) along with other captives when that city was conquered. **Ovid** believes the word comes from *Caput*, which signifies a "Head" <note>original: "Caput hãr / das ein Haupt bedeütet"</note>, for this reason: the head is the seat of reason and wit, and since **Minerva** is a goddess of skill, or perhaps because she was born from her father's head. Otherwise, there was also a place by this temple where thieves and those whose lives were forfeit were executed, where the custom was to strike off the head; from this, she might also have had the name. Also, because "to take" and "to catch" can well be signified by the little word *Capere* <note>original: "Capere," Latin: to take, seize, or capture</note>.

**Nerine. Neriene.** **Porphyrio** shows in his commentary on **Horace** why **Minerva** is so named: namely, that she fought with **Mars** for her virginity and prevailed. Therefore, neither in March nor in May—the months in which they fought one another—will the **Romans** join together women or men <note>meaning they avoided weddings in these months</note>.

**Oleria.** **Olerus** was a city in **Crete** <note>original: "Candie," the old Venetian name for Crete</note>, where **Minerva** was worshipped with church pomp and holidays, from which her name comes to her.

# Of Heathen Gods

**Anemotis.** The Windy One. **Modon** <note>modern Methoni</note> in **Morea** <note>the Peloponnese</note> was continually plagued and devastated by evil winds. Therefore, **Diomedes** built a temple to **Minerva** there, established an altar and an image for her, and offered sacrifices. Through this, these rough winds were stilled. Near the temple flowed a spring with pitch mixed into the water.

**Cydonia.** In **Candia** <note>the island of Crete</note> there was a city called **Cydon**, which is now called the capital and **Candia** <note>likely referring to modern Chania</note>; it gave its name to the whole island. **Elymenus**, a descendant of **Hercules**, came to that region and built a temple to **Minerva**, naming it after his homeland.

**Acria.** She of the Peak. At **Argos**, this **Minerva**, along with **Juno**, **Venus**, and **Diana**, had a temple at the highest point in the city’s citadel; from this location, they were given that name.

**Colocasia.** At **Sicyon** (now **Chiarenza**), **Minerva** had a temple under this name. This may have originated because the husks or pods of the **Egyptian bean** <note>the *Colocasia* or lotus</note> were so large that drinking vessels and helmets were made from them. **Minerva**, however, is constantly depicted wearing a small helmet. **Epopeus** built her a temple that was quite magnificent and large, but thunder struck it once, so that it burst apart entirely, right down to the altar, which remained standing for a long time afterward.

**Epyrgirites.** Tower-Guardian. **Hesychius** <note>an Alexandrian grammarian</note> writes that **Minerva** was honored at **Polystilo**; likewise at **Corinth**, where she had a slender statue <note>original: "dhünbild"</note>.

**Atrytone.** The Unwearied. **Phornutus** <note>the Stoic philosopher Cornutus</note> believes she possesses this name because she is invincible in wars and can neither be defeated nor wounded.

**Paionia.** The Physician. At **Athens**, in the **Theater** <note>original: "Spilhauß," literally 'play-house'</note>, there stood an image of this **Minerva**, most beautifully crafted; likewise at **Sucamino**, which in ancient times was called **Dropus**, she also had her altar.

**Asia.** Very near the small peak of **Pagus** <note>near modern Izmir</note>, once called **Gythium**, there lay a spot anciently called **Las**. There **Castor** and **Pollux** erected a temple to this **Minerva** when they arrived home safe and sound from their voyage to **Colchis**. For in **Colchis**—which is in **Greater Armenia**, now called **Turkomania**—there was a city now named **Calpuert**, where **Minerva** was also honored.

**Hippolaitis.** At the promontory of **Taenarum**, now **Cape Matapan** <note>original: "Caput Maino"</note>, there once lay a small town called **Hippola**, where **Minerva** had a temple named after the place.

**Promachorma.** Around **Corinth**, where there are many currents, there is a harbor called **Amporthmos**. This harbor had several reefs and rocks like islands, and within it was a temple to **Minerva** as the **Protector of the Anchorage** <note>from the Greek *Promachorma*, signifying a goddess who guards the harbor</note>, as she provides safety and space in these harbors.

**Celeuthis.** The Advocatess. When **Ulysses** <note>Odysseus</note> returned home and fought against the **Suitors** <note>original: "Hoffbüler"</note>, and **Minerva** gave him her assistance, he erected an image and temple to this **Minerva** at **Lacedaemonia** <note>Sparta</note>.

**Agorea.** She of the Market. The **Lacedaemonians**, just as they did for many other gods, also had a temple to **Minerva** in the marketplace.

-># The Fourth Book.<-

**Nedusia.** A small stream flowed through **Laconia** <note>a region in the Peloponnese, home to Sparta</note> called **Nedo**; upon it lay a city, **Peassa**, where a magnificent temple stood, built by **Nestor** upon his return from **Troy**.

**Ambulia.** The **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans</note> also had an altar in **Lacedaemon** dedicated to this **Minerva** <note>original: "Mineruen"</note>; you may find more information regarding this under **Jupiter Ambulius** <note>Zeus Ambulios, the "god of delay" or "prolonger," often associated with safe travel</note>.

**Paria. Parea. Pania.** Likewise, there was at **Sparta**, on the road used when one wished to go into **Arcadia**, a beautiful statue of this **Minerva** under the open sky. In **Argos**, however, on the exercise ground <note>original: "yeb platz," likely the gymnasium</note>, stood a statue of **Minerva** which was called **Pania**.

**Axiopoena.** The Avenger <note>original: "Die Rächerin"</note>. In another place it is mentioned what **Hercules** did with **Hippocoon**; as a memorial of this, **Hercules** erected a temple to **Minerva** in **Lacedaemon**.

**Cyristis.** Not far from **Aleppo** in **Syria** lay a city, **Cyristis** <note>Cyrrhus</note>, after which an entire province was named; it had a temple dedicated to **Minerva**, from which this name is derived.

**Sotera.** The Savior <note>original: "Die Heylandin"</note>. A medicine used to hunt out poison <note>an antidote</note>, as found in the works of **Galen** and others, was given this name. Also, **Ulysses**, when he returned from **Troy**, erected a temple to her on **Mount Boreion** <note>original: "Borco"</note>, not far from **Leontarium** <note>original: "Londario"</note>. To this place, the captured **Lacedaemonians** who had been held in leg irons brought their rings and chains and hung them up once they were set free.

**Sunia.** **Attica** has a very prominent headland <note>original: "vor bůrg"</note> that was once called **Sunium**, but is now called **Capo Colonne** (or the "Cape of Columns") <note>original: "Säul kőpfflin"</note>; upon its highest peak stood a temple consecrated to **Minerva**, from which she received this name.

**Leistis.** The Robber <note>original: "Die Räuberin"</note>. Because the state and the land are governed with wisdom and foresight, the name was given to **Minerva** as the "Wise One" who also brings good order to domestic affairs. However, **Cornutus** <note>original: "Phornutus," a Stoic philosopher</note> believes that since she is a goddess of war, she takes her name from robbing and plundering.

**Aedon.** The Nightingale <note>original: "Die Nachtgall"</note>. The **Pamphylians** gave **Minerva** this name, as **Favorinus** and **Hesychius** write, yet they do not record the reason why.

**Narcea.** At **Pisa** <note>near Olympia</note> there was once a woman named **Physcoa**, who bore a son by **Bacchus** named **Narceus**. He was a brave man who brought much land under his rule and built a temple to **Minerva**.

**Arsenothemis.** Man’s Wrath <note>original: "Manns zorn"</note>. Because **Minerva** does not display a flighty, feminine anger, but rather a persistent, manly fury in her actions, she was designated by this name.

**Aranea.** Near **Elateia**, this **Minerva** <note>likely Athene Cranaia</note> has her temple upon a very steep mountain; it had many small houses for priests in the forecourt. Only young, beardless boys served the foundation; their office lasted for five years and no longer. Her image was painted on a shield, just as in **Athens**, showing her armed for battle.

<header>-># Concerning Heathen Gods<-</header>

**Dymea. Larissea.** Not far from **Patras**, about four miles away by the **Canigriza** stream <note>modern-day Glaukos river</note>, which was once called the **Olenus**, there lay a city called **Dyme**. There stood a temple of **Minerva**, from which she received this name. This city was destroyed by the **Romans** under **Flamininus** <note>Titus Quinctius Flamininus, a Roman general</note>; there flowed a small stream called the **Larissus**, where she also had a temple that gave her yet another name.

**Coresia.** In **Candia** <note>Crete</note>, this **Minerva** is said to have been honored on **Mount Cozion**.

**Graule. Aglaura.** She was given this name because of the agricultural work <note>original: "pawrs werck," referring to farming or husbandry</note> which this **Minerva** promoted in several places and taught to the people.

**Lemnia.** In **Athens** there was a statue of **Minerva** which **Pericles** had made at his own expense; it was very beautiful and highly esteemed, a work of **Phidias**, which he allowed to be called **Lemnia**.

**Allydonia.** The temple of this **Minerva** was held in such high honor that if a person had forfeited their life <note>been sentenced to death</note> through fraud <note>original: "bscheysserey"</note> or had received a physical punishment <note>original: "gele straaff"</note>, they would be cleared of all punishment if they could escape and run to this temple or statue into freedom <note>sanctuary</note>.

**Itica Onga.** In **Thebes** there was a gate called the **Old Gate**, or the **Onca Gate**; a temple of **Minerva** stood right there, from which she took the name. For there was once a city in **Phoenicia** after which **Cadmus**, the builder of **Thebes**, named the gate. Now, this **Thebes** is located in **Boeotia**, in the place called **Haliartus** <note>original: "Ediles," likely a corruption of Haliartus</note>. The one located in **Phocis**, however, is now called **Zitouni** <note>modern Lamia</note>. The third **Thebes** lies in **Egypt** and retains its name.

**Aracinthis.** This was a name for **Minerva** that came to her from the mountain located in **Boeotia** called **Aracinthus**.

**Styris.** In **Phocis** <note>the text says Phoenicia, but Styris is in Phocis</note> there was a city of this name, from which her name is derived, as **Stephanus** <note>Stephanus of Byzantium</note> says.

**Assessia.** In **Anatolia** <note>original: "Natolia"</note> there once lay a city called **Assessus**; there **Minerva** had a temple which King **Alyattes** <note>King of Lydia</note> burned down.

**Itonogenes.** The In-born <note>original: "Die eingeporn," likely referring to the Itonian Minerva</note>. **Catullus** gives her this name, saying she was honored on **Mount Itonus**.

## Gorgona.

The **Greeks** and **Latins** say much regarding the head of the **Gorgon**, which they paint upon the shield of **Minerva** with a gaping mouth and full of snakes instead of hair. Now, I wish to describe this little tale and its significance somewhat more extensively. About twelve miles from **Genoa**, and as far from **Corsica**, very near the island of **Elba**, lies this island of **Gorgona** where these **Gorgons** are said to have ruled. There were three of them, all maidens: the first was **Medusa**, the second **Stheno**, and the third **Euryale**. They were daughters of **Phorcys**, the King of **Sardinia** and **Corsica**. These three are said to have had only one eye, which they lent to one another. Now, **Phorcys** is otherwise called a sea monster <note>original: "mörwunder"</note>, a son of **Neptune**; which sea monster, when it opens its maw, gives off such a lovely scent or smell that all the fish in the—

<header>### The Fourth Book</header>

...to swim toward him, and thus enter into the throat, so that he might satisfy his hunger. Therefore, because these three daughters were so very beautiful and graceful—from which they received the name **Gorgons** <note>The name "Gorgon" is derived from the Greek *gorgos*, meaning "dreadful." Here, the author links it to their captivating beauty.</note>—they brought many young men to love with their beauty, many of whom became obsessed with them. That they are said to have had only **one eye**, however, signifies that they looked so much alike that one could hardly be distinguished from the other. And because their beauty was so overwhelming that everyone who looked upon them was stunned and ignited with love, it was said that they turned people into stone with their gaze.

Now the most beautiful among them, **Medusa**, was defiled by **Neptune** in the temple of **Minerva**. This angered the goddess, who wished to take revenge; she transformed **Medusa’s** hair into nothing but snakes, so that she who was previously the most beautiful became the most hideous. By this beautiful, gold-colored hair, some wish to understand the great wealth that this **Medusa** possessed. **Neptune**, however, represents another lord who pursued this wealth and sailed to the island before she could collect her thoughts and find help in the temple of **Minerva**—that is, in the council—on how to resist the enemy. When she was then robbed of her goods, snakes grew upon her head; that is, she fell into anguish, worry, and despondency, grieving bitterly over her lost property.

It may well be that he who thus attacked her was **Perseus**, of whom it is said that, with the help of **Minerva**, he came to the other three daughters of **Phorcus**, who were named **Memphides**, **Ennyo**, and **Dino**. These, as soon as they were born, looked like old women and had but a single eye and a single tooth, which objects they lent to one another as needed. **Perseus** took both of these from the three; when they begged him to return them, he said he would, provided they gave him the wings, the pouch, and the **Cap of Invisibility** <term>Nebelkappe: literally a "mist-cap," a common folkloric item in German tales used here to describe the Helm of Hades</term> which they possessed, so that he might fly and be invisible, and also carry provisions with him on a long journey. All three items were given to him.

He flew to the island of the **Gorgons**, who, as some claim, could also fly and had boar's tusks. Among them, only **Medusa** was mortal; and because she had such a terrible head, he wished to have it so that he might turn his enemies into stone. Now, he had a **crystalline shield** which he held before him; she, however, could not see him because of the **Cap of Invisibility**. Thus, with the help of **Minerva**, who guided his hand, he struck off her head. This signifies nothing other than that **Perseus** took the wings, the cap, and the pouches—meaning he arrived unexpectedly, well-equipped, with a ship that came very swiftly to the island—using skill to wrest all her dominion from her. The **crystalline shield** is the **prudence** and **caution** with which a warlord should be gifted; this comes to him from **Minerva**. For wit or wisdom also sees and considers future things that may come to pass. 

This temple of **Minerva** was in **Argos**, where **Medusa's** head is said to have been kept. It is said that her father was named **Phorcus**, who ruled near **Lake Triton** in **Africa**; after his death, she held the power and devoted herself to hunting and warring. **Perseus**, however, had set out with an army from **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note> to wage war against her, and by night he killed her through a ruse. When he saw how very beautiful she was the next morning, he cut off her head and placed it in this temple to show it to the **Greeks** as a trophy and a monument of his glory.

There are some who tell the matter differently. Namely, that in **Africa** there are also wild forest-people, among whom there was once a woman...
