<header># Of the Pagan Gods</header>

...female figure at Lake Triton; having pursued the hunt, she took a liking to that countryside, for which reason she plagued the local people for so long until **Perseus** came to their aid, slew her, and honored **Minerva** for the deed, etc. **Phornutus** <note>original: "Phornutus"; likely referring to the Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus.</note> says that the image of the **Gorgon** on the shield of **Minerva** sticks out its tongue to signify that speech is the most precious thing in man.

**Alossos, Protector of the People.** <note>original: "Leüthschutz"; a translation of a Greek epithet signifying a defender of the common folk.</note> This name is given to her by **Phornutus** and **Theocritus**, because the common people are well-commended to her care.

**Assea.** At **Malvasia** <note>Now known as Monemvasia.</note> in **Morea**, there was a castle or fortress where this temple of **Minerva** was located.

**Laurobolia.** The island of **Andros** has at times been called **Caunus**, **Antandrus**, **Lasia**, **Monacria**, **Hydrusa**, and **Epagria**; now it is still called **Andros**. It lies opposite **Negropont** <note>The island of Euboea.</note> and was possessed by **Andrus**, the son of **Anius**, who built a temple therein, from which **Minerva** received this name; for his father **Anius** had given him an ox, which he was to sacrifice at the place where he first settled. He then came to this island and sacrificed it to her.

**Callutia.** A body of water not far from **Ionia**, which flows into the sea and was once called **Scylluntis**, now **Laguardo**. There stood a temple of this **Minerva**, which was counted among the most exquisite works in **Greece**.

**Sais.** **Sais** was a city in **Egypt**, where **Minerva** was honored under the name of **Isis** <note>original: "Isidis".</note>. Before the temple stood a **Sphinx**, which is a beast with a maidenly face and breasts, wings instead of arms, bird's feet, and a dragon's tail, to signify that the secrets of the gods are not easily understood.

**Sicyonia, She of Chiarenza.** **Epopeus** built a temple in **Chiarenza**, which was once called **Sicyon**; it was quite beautiful, yet it was burned by a bolt of lightning.

**Auxiliaris, The Helpful.** **Cassius Brutus** is said to have been besieged and died of hunger in a temple of **Minerva the Helpful**.

**Pronaea.** <note>From the Greek "Pronaia," meaning "before the temple."</note> Regarding this, you may take what was written of the choirs in **Apollo**, just as it stands under **Mercury Pronaos**; for in the same way she was honored at **Ismenion** <note>A sanctuary in Thebes.</note> and also in that same place, as well as at **Delphi**.

**Pronoia.** <note>Greek for "Providence" or "Foresight."</note> This name comes to her from wisdom and foresight, which **Phornutus** says the ancients attributed to her, and they also erected many temples to her.

**Magarsia.** In **Karaman** <note>original: "Caramanien"; the region of Cilicia in modern-day Turkey.</note>, which was once **Cilicia**, there lay a city called **Mallus**, now called **Malo**; not far from there was a beautiful tomb on the plain of **Magarsa**, in which **Mopsus** and **Amphilochus**, the two soothsayers, died and were buried while fighting for sovereignty. A magnificent temple to **Minerva** had previously been built there by these two. **Alexander the Great** sacrificed there with great solemnity.

**Mygisia.** In **Caria**, in the province now called **Quisco** in **Anatolia**, there also lay a city called **Mygisia**, in which a temple gave this name to **Minerva**.

# The Fourth Book

**Alcimacha.** <note>Greek: *Alkimacha*, meaning "strong in battle."</note> **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon.</note> gives her this name on account of her bravery in strife and war.

**Stathmia.** She of the Station. This name has many meanings, such as a station, a harbor or landing place, a camp, a stable, a scale, and more. Since **Hesychius** <note>A Greek grammarian of Alexandria.</note> does not report from whence he named her so, I would gladly offer my own opinion if it were of any value. Since the goddess was honored as a warrior in many places, she might have been depicted and called upon in military camps.

**Parapeplemene.** The Enwrapped. **Pollux** <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> gives her this name, which he gathered from barber shops. <note>original: "Balbierheüsern"</note>

**Oricentera.** The Spear-User. **Phornutus** <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher.</note> calls her this because she is depicted with a spear, with which she fights in skirmishes.

**Opechyn.** Strong-Armed. This name is given to her on account of her strength and brave nature, primarily by the poets.

**Neith, Ephestia, Bombylia, Agripha, Epanißia, Menalis, Ellefye.** In **Egypt**, she was called **Neith**, and many other names are given to her by the **Greeks** and **Latins**, the reasons for which the writers remain silent.

**Alaitis.** The **Lydians** honored **Minerva** under this name, and the **Medes** carried that same image away.

**Cnagia.** You will also find this name under **Diana**, where we spoke of **Cnageus**; for it is one and the same matter.

**Clitoria. Coria.** Very near to **Wüssi**, perhaps **Stymphalia**, lies a mountain belonging to the people of **Clitoria** called **Corius**, upon which there is a temple dedicated to **Minerva**. <note>The word "der" appears to be split across the end of a line and the beginning of a short final line in the original print: "dē" and "er".</note>

**Lacia.** At **Athens**, on the road toward **Eleusis** which is now called **Antimilio**, there was a district <note>German: "Dhan"; referring to a Deme, a local division of ancient Attica.</note> belonging to the hero **Lacius**, in which there was a temple of **Minerva**; from this, she took her name.

**Athena.** The highest and most common sanctuary in **Athens** was dedicated to **Diana** <note>The author likely means Athena, or refers to the sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia on the Acropolis; however, the subsequent description of the "fallen" image and the lamp clearly refers to the Erechtheion and the statue of Athena Polias.</note>; and although almost every guild there had its own particular god, they were all inclined and obligated to offer sacrifices in this temple and to this goddess. For the image of **Minerva** which was then in this sanctuary is said to have fallen from heaven before the citizenry had ever assembled or come together from the countryside to the place where the city now stands. In her temple was a lampstand or candelabra so artfully made that oil was placed in it only on the evening of the church dedication festival, yet it burned throughout the entire year, unquenchable; one never had to tend to it. The wick was made of **Carpasian flax** <note>A type of asbestos known in antiquity as "linen of Carpasia," which was fireproof.</note>, which cannot be consumed by fire. Atop the lampstand stood a bronze **Phoenix**, which caught the smoke from the burning oil so that the church did not become sooty. **Callimachus** <note>A famous Greek sculptor and architect of the late 5th century BC.</note> made this lampstand with singular skill. Before the temple stood an **Olive Tree**, which is said to have been the first olive branch in all of **Attica**, from which all other olive trees later descended. **Minerva** is said to have planted it first; and when it was burned during the **Persian War**, it put forth new shoots three feet high on the very next day. Other adornments which were undoubtedly in such a highly praised city, in the highest sanctuary (especially among the **Greeks**, where such idol-worship was always performed and maintained in the most lavish manner), allow one to easily perceive how great a treasure it was worth, seeing as the city was named after her.

<summary>This page lists various epithets and local titles for Minerva (Athena) across the ancient world, culminating in a description of her primary sanctuary in Athens, featuring the miraculous eternal lamp of Callimachus and the sacred olive tree.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page concludes the discussion of Minerva (Athena), specifically her contest with Neptune (Poseidon) over the naming of Athens, and transitions into Book Five, which begins an extensive catalog of the names and attributes of the war god Mars.</meta>

Of this goddess, it is said that she quarreled with Neptune regarding which of them should have the city or the assembly of citizens named after them. The dispute was brought before the gods, and the decision was thus: whichever of them struck the earth and produced the most useful thing from their blow should be the one to give their name to the city. Neptune struck with his trident <note>original: "gährn"</note> upon it, and from that came a horse. Minerva struck the ground with her spear <note>original: "glänen"</note>, and an olive tree sprouted forth; thus, hers was judged to be the best. 

This signifies nothing other than the fact that since this city—a stronghold of Greece—was situated by the sea and on fertile soil, a quarrel arose in both places between the sailors and the farmers or craftsmen as to which brought more benefit to the city. For by the speed of the horse, seafaring may be understood; and by the olive tree, the richness and cultivation of the soil. Thus, the land was regarded by some as far superior to the sea in terms of peace, security, and abundance. However, it is not necessary to elaborate here on how this was decided with great reason.

**Armipotens.** <note>Latin: "Powerful in arms."</note> **Armisona.** <note>Latin: "Resounding in arms."</note> Virgil and Cicero gave her these names because she rings out in her armor, in which she appears entirely brave and powerful.

# The Fifth Book.
## Mars.

Varro believes that Mars is so named because he stands before men in war and leads them, or that the Sabines in the Duchy of Spoleto first honored him and called him "Mamers" before his cult came to Rome. Cicero calls him "Mavors" because he *Magna Vortet*, that is, he "overturns great things" or executes important matters. The Greeks call him "Ares," derived from a word <note>original: "phornuto," likely a corruption of the Greek *phono*, to kill</note> meaning "the murderer" or "the rebel." Otherwise, the two small words *agas* and *apus* <note>Greek-derived terms used in early modern etymology</note> signify harm and slaying; Plato gives him a name derived from that which is "unshakeable" <note>original: "Abhörbar," likely referring to the Greek *arratos*</note>.

Regarding the birth of this Mars, some say that Juno was indignant because her husband Jupiter, without the help of any woman, gave birth to Minerva from his brain. She, however, was barren; therefore, she wished to go to Oceanus to seek counsel on how she might also bear something. But when she sat down, exhausted, by Flora, the housewife and spouse of Zephyrus, she was asked by her where she was going and what she intended. Juno recounted the matter to her and gave her her oath never to reveal it if she would give her advice and help so that she might come to fruit. Flora showed her a flower in Olenus—which is now called Canigritza <note>A medieval name for the Greek region of Olenus</note>—which, if she smelled it, would cause her to conceive immediately without a man. Thus, Juno gave birth to Mars.

However, the reason the ancients did not want to say that Mars was born of Jupiter is that Mars is so predatory, murderous, reckless, and cruel; by contrast, Jupiter is entirely mild and kind. They did not want it to be said that he had fathered a son who was so completely ill-bred. But if one takes Juno to represent the Earth, then he is rightly her son, for the sake of which—to rule over it—everyone fights, all bloodshed is prepared, and cities and lands are torn apart, overrun, and plundered.

Some say Jupiter fathered him with Enyo <note>A goddess of war and destruction</note>, because Jupiter also sometimes directs the animals to fight with one another, and has given strength and manhood in battle to humans, especially to the male. To this, he adds a reckless, raging, and wild spirit of anger, which is Enyo. That he is said to have been born in Thrace is because those people were all considered crude, wild, and warlike.

He was painted with the face of a robber, sitting upon a traveling wagon <note>a war chariot</note> clad in armor, with other weapons around him. He had a helmet on, a sword at his side, and a whip in his hand. The wagon was led by spirited horses; before him trotted a wolf, which carried a sheep in its mouth. Homer gives him two horses for the wagon and calls them "Deimos" and "Phobos" <note>original: "Dimon und phobon"</note>, which signifies fear and terror. Others say he has four, all of which strike fire out of their nostrils, born of Boreas <note>the North Wind</note> and the Erinyes <note>the Furies</note>. Their names are Aethon, Phlogius, Conabos <note>original: "Combas"</note>, and Phobos.

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

**Phobos.** <note>original: "Phobos," Greek for "Fear," often personified as the son or companion of Mars</note> He is also associated with the jay or the jackdaw, which is a crested bird. Among all other nations, the Romans held Mars in the greatest honor, as he was the father of Romulus and Remus, the founders of that city, and thus the source of their lineage. Now, let us consider his surnames.

**Communis.** The Common One. Both the Latins and the Greeks named him thus. This is because in war he is helpful to both sides, speaking to them, driving and inciting them, so that his instigation finds a place in all quarters.

**Pater.** The Father, or <term>Marspiter</term> <note>A contraction of "Mars Pater," meaning Mars the Father</note>. Because Mars was considered by the Romans to be the father of Romulus and Remus, and thus the origin of the city—and since almost all the gods were called "fathers"—this name was also given to Mars.

**Gradivus.** The Advancer. <note>original: "fürttrucker," one who pushes forward</note> This name was given to him because of his manliness, with which he protected and advanced the city. Just as in battles the one who gains the "push" <note>original: "truck," meaning momentum or pressure</note> usually prevails, it was attributed to Mars that his strength always held the forward momentum. Therefore, a temple was erected to him under this name outside the city gate, on the Appian Way. There, his statue "sweated" <note>In antiquity, a sweating statue was considered a dire omen</note> during the time when Cnaeus Servilius and Flaminius were Consuls <note>original: "Burgermeyster," literally 'mayors,' used here to translate the Roman office of Consul</note>.

Some also wish to derive this name from the little tale we mentioned above—how he sprang from a grass flower—which is why a small wreath of grass was given to those who conducted themselves well in battle. Others believe it is not a Latin word but a Thracian one, meaning a warrior, much like how we say in German, an "upright youth."

**Quirinus.** The Spear-bearer. Mars was called this by the Sabines, for they called a spear "Quirin," which they dedicated to this god. As one who kept a diligent watch over the welfare of the city, a temple was built for him within the city at the place where the church of Saint Vitalis now stands, on the Viminal, or Osier Hill.

**Mamers.** The Oscans <note>An ancient people of southern Italy</note> called him "Mamertem," as did the Sabines. From this name, the city of Messina in Sicily also received its name. For at one time, during a great mortality in all of Abruzzo, there was a great army and a prince of the land named Asthemius Aetius. He called the country folk together and said that Apollo had appeared to him in a dream and told him that if they wished to be free of the plague, they should perform a <term>Sacred Spring</term> <note>original: "verbannt glentz," a translation of the Latin *Ver Sacrum*, a ritual vow to sacrifice or exile the offspring of a particular year</note>. That is, they should vow that whatever was born in the next spring, they would sacrifice to Mars. This they did, making the vow. When the same plague returned to them twenty years later, they asked Apollo what should be done. He answered that the vow had never been fulfilled; for although all other animals had been sacrificed to Mars, the children born at that time had not been given up, and therefore they could no longer be tolerated in the land.

So, all those children willingly departed from the land and came into

## The Fifth Book.

In **Sicily**, they came to the aid of a people who were at war with the **Tauromenians**. After achieving victory, they were accepted into the community by them. They then cast lots to determine what the city they were building in that place should be named; it so happened that they drew the lot of **Mars**, and for that reason, they named the city **Mamertina**. <note>The Mamertines were mercenaries who famously seized the city of Messana (modern Messina).</note>

**Syluestris.** The Woodman. <note>original: "Syluestris"</note> **Marcus Cato** offers sacrifices to this Mars and describes them in his books on agriculture, saying: "O Father Mars, I call upon you and pray that you be favorable to me, and also gracious toward my household and my business. For this reason, I have ordered the sacrifice of the swine, sheep, and bull <term>Suovetaurilia</term> <note>A traditional Roman triple-sacrifice of a pig (sus), sheep (ovis), and bull (taurus)</note> to be led around my house, courtyard, and field." Shortly thereafter, he says: "To Mars the Woodman, vow a particular sacrifice for every head of cattle."

**Salisubulus.** The Leaper. <note>original: "Der Hopper"</note> This name was given to him because of the rhythmic stepping and leaping performed to the beat of drums during wartime. <note>This refers to the Salii, the "leaping priests" of Mars who danced through the streets of Rome.</note>

**Allosprofallos.** Now for this one, then for that one. <note>original Greek: αλλοπρόσαλλος, meaning "fickle" or "leaning first to one side, then the other"</note> In war, events are very strange, and no one can propose anything certain; for this reason, **Homer** calls him the companion or assistant now of this side, now of that side.

**Caecus.** The Blind One. This is because wartime affairs are often—and indeed most frequently—conducted at night and in fog; therefore they call him the blind one, just as the night is dark.

**Thurius.** The Charging One. The Greeks have a small word, **thorein** <note>original: "θορέιν," meaning to leap or rush forth</note>, which signifies to run at someone with violence and impetuosity; from this, he received this name.

**Marmessus.** The Warlike. This word carries the weight of saying that Mars is a supervisor of war, and all those who make use of war may be called **Marmessos** or "the Martials," because they are birds of misfortune who see more unrest than peace.

**Enyalius.** In **Olympia**, there was an image of Mars on horseback in full armor, and he had **Venus** with him. He was called **Enyalius**, after **Enyo**, whom some call his mother and others his sister. <note>Enyo was a Greek goddess of war, often acting as a companion to Ares/Mars.</note>

**Ultor.** The Avenger. The Emperor **Augustus**, during the war he waged in Macedonia against the murderers of his stepfather <note>Augustus was actually the grand-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar.</note>, vowed a temple to Mars if he would help him avenge this murder. There now stands **Saint Martin’s Church** <note>In the 16th century, the ruins of the Temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus were associated with local churches.</note>; that temple is said to have been of the most costly and beautiful construction, decorated with all kinds of sculpted weapons, as some ancient carvings are still present there to be seen. Some believe that because the temple stood in the square or market of Augustus—which is called the **Forum**—the statue which is called **Marforius** (as in *Mars Fori*, Mars of the Forum) is still present and is the very one from which the temple took its name. This does not closely resemble the truth based on the appearance of the statue, for you have heard previously how that was shaped in the section on **Jupiter the Baker**. In that temple, they held council over matters concerning war, and it was there that the generals, when they rode back into the city, had to hang the tokens of their deeds.

**Bisultor.** Twice the Avenger. **Crassus**, together with his son, was slain by the **Parthians**; the tokens, banners, and other belongings of the Romans remained with the enemy...

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

...so that a mighty army was not lost on the battlefield. Now, the **Parthians** <note>A powerful empire in the East (modern-day Iran) that was a major rival to Rome.</note> returned the standards <note>The military flags or "eagles" of the Roman legions.</note> to **Augustus**; he hung them up in this temple and called **Mars** by this name <note>The name "Ultor," meaning the Avenger.</note> to show that he had received a twofold protection and vengeance from this Mars. However, whether they were hung in this temple or in the **Capitol**, where he also had a chapel, is a matter of some doubt.

**Tyrannus. The Tyrant.** **Homer** gives him this name, saying: "You overwhelming, impetuous Tyrant," undoubtedly because in war there is no mercy, and everything goes toward destruction and turmoil.

**Rex. The King.** There was an Athenian general named **Timotheus** who performed many magnificent deeds against the **Persians** and **Asians**; he always called upon **Mars** by this name, which has remained with him.

**Alpheneus. The Bountiful.** <note>original: "Alpheneus," likely a variation of Apheius, meaning "the sender" or "bountiful."</note> **Tegea** in **Arcadia** has a small hill called **Cresium**, where **Europa**, the daughter of **Cepheus**, was said to have been made pregnant by **Mars**. She died during the birth, yet the child **Aeropus** suckled from her even after she was dead. This was brought about by Mars, who made it possible for the deceased woman to still provide milk. For this reason, he was called "The Bountiful."

**Theritas. The Wild.** **Thero** is said to have raised Mars, and from this woman he received the name; some say that he first had an image under this name in **Colchis**, which **Castor and Pollux** <note>The twin heroes of Greek mythology known as the Dioscuri.</note> brought back with them to **Greece**. Others say, however, that the name comes from his grimness and wild nature, as soldiers are generally as grim and predatory as wild beasts. It is said the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> honored the one we just called **Enyalius** with this name.

**Gynacothean. Women's Help.** <note>original: "Gynacothean," from the Greek "Gynaecothoenas," meaning "he who feasts the women."</note> **Marpessa**, a citizen of **Tegea** in **Arcadia**, once gathered all the women in the city and the countryside to march against the **Lacedaemonians**, who intended to ambush them and who had a captain named **Charillus**. These women lay in wait, and when the men on both sides began to clash, the women unexpectedly rushed forth, overran the enemy, and captured the commander. Thus, they established a festival and holiday for this Mars, which the men were not permitted to attend, nor could they partake in the sacrifice. They also erected a pillar of this name in the open market at **Tegea** to remember that Mars had helped them perform an exceptionally brave deed. Marpessa's spear and armor were hung in the temple of **Minerva**.

**Hesus.** In the section on **Mercury**, mention was made of how the **Gauls** honored **Hesus** as a god; some consider him to be Mercury, others Mars.

**Odrysius / Geticus / Thratius.** In the regions where **Bulgaria** is now, near where the **Danube** flows into the sea, these peoples once lived: the **Odrysae**, the **Getae**, and the **Thracians**. They honored this god highly and commonly. I do not know if the name might be derived from being "defiant" <note>original: "trazlich," implying a bold or stubborn warrior.</note>, for a reckless soldier is a defiant thing.

<header>The Fifth Book.</header>

->**Belliger / Bellipotens / Hoplochares / Armiger / Armipotens.**<-
->**The Waging of War / Mighty in War / Armor-bearer / Powerful in Arms.**<-

He holds all these names among the poets because he enters into war with will, spirit, weapons, and armor, and therein shows himself to be entirely joyful and brave.

**Coricolos. Cerythaix.** <note>original: "Korythaix," meaning "shaking the helmet-crest."</note> **The Helmet-shaker.** This is because Mars was depicted with a beautiful helmet ornament, or because men consider him fresh and brave in war. For those who are fresh and bold commonly show their high spirits by shaking their heads; thus **Homer** gave him this name.

**Olos. The Destructive.** War never creates anything good; therefore, he has received this name not without cause.

**Oletor. The Oppressor.** <note>original: "Oletor," likely a variation of "Oletros," meaning destroyer or bane.</note> What is more burdensome to a poor man than when war and unrest take the upper hand? Then all welfare is shattered, which is indicated by this name.

**Obrimothymos. Obrimos. Ombrimos.** All these words indicate and signify a powerful, high-spirited heart, such as he must possess who wishes to wage war.

**Sanguineus. Aemochares.** <note>original: "Haimochares," meaning "rejoicing in blood."</note> **Blood-thirsty.** **Homer** says that Mars has a joy in shedding blood, and wherever he may bring it about, he is given this name by him and other poets as well.

**Androphonos. Killer of Men.** **Orpheus** says he rejoices in the blood that rushes from the people whom these man-slayers kill.

**Pheraspis. Chalcaspis. He with the bronze shield.** **Homer** describes him as a shield-bearer, specifically one carrying a bronze shield; therefore he has this name. He also calls him **Chalcoristes** <note>original: "Chalkoristes," meaning armed with bronze.</note> because his armor is made of bronze.

**Briepios. Brisarmatos. The Clamorous.** From the sound and clatter of his weapons, armor, and gear, as well as from the rolling of his chariot, the poets have invented this name for him, so that he might be heard from afar.

**Chrysopelex. The Golden Helmet.** Some wish to interpret this word as meaning either a golden whip or a golden helmet carried by Mars.

**Brotoligos. Miephonos.** <note>original: "Brotoloigos" (bane of mortals) and "Miaiphonos" (blood-stained).</note> **Slayer of Mortals.** The donkey babbles "Myahan, Myahan" <note>An onomatopoeia for a donkey's braying.</note>; for this reason, that animal is slaughtered and sacrificed to Mars. This reflects the nature of Mars in his shouting, showing how he gladly strangles people and consumes them in war.

**Tichesipletes.** <note>original: "Teichisipletes," meaning "wall-stormer."</note> **Wall-breaker.** They call him this because of the storming of fortifications, which is almost the roughest work in warfare.

**Adamastos. The Unconquerable.** Because he can never be defeated or subdued in either war or peace, they give him this name.

**Craterochyr. Strong-handed.** <note>original: "Kraterocheir," from kratos (strength) and cheir (hand).</note> The hands are often understood to represent the deed itself; since Mars is so powerful in his actions, it is said he uses his hands and has a mighty fist. From this comes our proverb <note>The author likely refers to a German proverb about a "strong hand" or "mighty fist" signifying military force.</note>.

# On the Heathen Gods
<meta>catchword: who therein</meta>

I would not dip my hands in such base matters. Likewise: To set a hand to. To go at it with a hand. <note>These phrases appear to be idiomatic expressions for taking action or involving oneself in a task.</note>

---

**Agathenes Hypermegethes.** <note>original: "Hypermegethes," a Greek term for "exceedingly great."</note> This name is given to him on account of his particular and hard stiffness.

**Oristhenes. The Pike-Bearer.** <note>original: "Langtknecht," literally a "long servant," a term used here for a pikeman or a Landsknecht mercenary.</note> If someone steps forward with a pike in such a way that the pike wobbles, or if he carries it in a masterly and brave manner, everyone says, "That is a free Swiss Confederate," and "Let that man be a bold soldier," and the like. Thus, according to the old legends, Mars also knew how to carry his pike well, from which he received this name. For a pike and the length of fabric for four pairs of trousers are nearly equal in their measure.

**Rinofaros / The Wolf-Pelt.** <note>original: "Rhinopharos," meaning one who wears a hide or skin.</note> It is a common custom now—and one can observe from this name that it is an ancient custom—that those who were or are "iron-biters" <note>a term for fierce, hardened soldiers</note> and men of war, almost intentionally chose how to disguise themselves so that people would think them devils, as they would like to be seen. Hence, this one clothes himself in an elk-hide, which is not entirely out of place, as it may serve as armor if it is of good quality. That one wears a bear-skin or wolf-pelt, which is not unhelpful against rain, lice, or fleas, but rather can serve well in the cold, day and night, in place of both clothing and a bed. But for what purpose the twelve pairs of trousers or woolen sacks that people hang from their backsides in our times might be useful to men of war, I cannot know. However, I find that throughout time, the most lightly and decently clothed soldier is able to be the most agile. For armor, and then this clattering finery, as much as it weighs, so much does it hinder one in their position and in the handling of weapons, and it creates a deformed shape upon a person. I would also like to hear who had ever praised an image where such a large appendage <note>likely referring to the exaggerated codpieces or slashed "puff and slash" fashion of the 16th century</note> and, above the knees, a stump or block tattered with rinds stood, upon which a decorated body rested, seen in painting or carving. But may it be lamented to God, because the loyalty, faith, and manliness of our dear ancestors have been cast into oblivion; what wonder is it then that we no longer know which clothing truly adorns us?

**Hippius / The Mounted Soldier.** <note>original: "Der Reißig," referring to a mounted trooper or traveler-at-arms.</note> It was indicated above how Mars is a man of war, for which reason he is also called "The Mounted Soldier," and as was said under the name **Enyalius**, he had his image-symbol in the Olympic games.

**Ares.** In Athens, there was a street where a courthouse stood, which was called the **Areopagus** <note>meaning "Hill of Ares"</note>. There, it is said, Mars was first summoned before a court and had to answer for the homicide he committed against **Alirrhothius**, for that man had raped Mars' daughter, **Alcippe**. At that same court, the platforms upon which the advocates stood were made of silver. There were two: the one upon which the accuser spoke was called the **Stone of Insult**; the one upon which the accused gave his answer was called the **Stone of Impudence**. This authority had no end nor limit; every year, several new court lords were chosen for them from among the **Thesmothetae** <note>law-givers or magistrates</note>, who were men who first, before they were appointed to the city court, had to demonstrate that they had lived their lives as honorable men. They also had to stand and offer to give an account and answer to everyone—from the lowest to the highest—if there were anyone who thought they knew of some claim or misconduct against them. Once they had sat on the city court for a time and one was chosen to be an **Areopagite**, a proclamation was made: "This man or that man, who conducted his affairs thus, and sat upon the City Court, has been chosen as an Areopagite; if there be anyone...

## The Fifth Book.

...who therein knew of any hindrance, let the same step forward and declare it. If someone then came who could prove that such an elected **Councilor** <note>original: "Ratßherr"</note> was worth even a pin’s weight <note>original: "gluffen wherdt"; an idiom meaning even the slightest bit of corruption or worthlessness</note> in embezzling from the common good, or if he had wasted even a farthing’s worth <note>original: "hellers wherdt"; a heller was a small German copper coin of very low value</note> of the city’s money, or was otherwise burdened with the vices of shady dealings <note>original: "finantz tryben," referring here to usury or unethical financial maneuvering</note> in buying and selling, or was ungenerous, greedy, and the like, the elected man could not take the position. Also, to ensure no one could sneak in—since it was the custom to place a little wreath upon them—they did not need to be crowned in secret; it had to happen in the open square before the entire **Community**.

Their office was to weigh all serious matters concerning the common welfare, and also what was done not out of sudden anger in a moment of haste, but out of evil intent—such as brewing poison to give to people, crippling them, bewitching them, robbery, arson, homicide, wounding, treason, and acting against the fatherland.

When they sat in judgment, the accuser had to swear an oath and confirm it. If he used deceit there, he prayed to the gods that he and his entire household and lineage be rooted out. He stood between a **Boar, Ram, and Bull** <note>The sacrifice of these three specific animals was a ritual used to seal the most solemn of ancient oaths.</note>, which were slaughtered <note>original: "gmözigt," a term for ritual butchery or slaughter</note> on the appointed day by persons specifically ordained for that purpose on the named square, and thus sacrificed for the oath. If the accused wished to clear and defend himself, he had to take the same oath. If not, he could flee after hearing the accusation, and no one would chase after him; if he escaped after the verdict, they let it be. Nevertheless, they would hold his property as they saw fit. This Council or court was so high in dignity and wisdom that their judgment was never appealed or revoked. Their secrecy was so absolute that a proverb arose from it. But here, because time permits no further delay, enough has been said of **Mars** <note>original: "Marte"</note>, as we now set down his **Planetary Table** <note>original: "Planeten tafel"; a mathematical magic square used in Renaissance astrology to represent the power and influence of the planet Mars.</note>.

# Of Heathen Gods

I would not "thrust my hands into my bosom" <note>An idiom meaning to be idle or lazy.</note>. Likewise: to set one's hand to work. To go at it nimbly.

**Egasthenes Hypermegethes.** <note>Greek: *Hypermegethes* means "extraordinarily large."</note> He is given this name because of a particular fineness and a hard stiffness.

**Aristhenes. Long-Servant.** <note>original: "Langknecht." Likely a play on *Landsknecht*, the famous German mercenary infantry.</note> When someone marches behind a pike in such a way that the pike wobbles, or carries it in a masterly and brave fashion, everyone says: "That is a free Confederate! Let him be a *Latzknecht* <note>original: "Latzknecht"; likely a local or mocking variant of *Landsknecht*, perhaps referring to the "Latz" or codpiece/bib of the uniform.</note> for me," and the like. Thus, according to the old tales, the pike of **Mars** suited him well, and from this, his name was derived. For the pike and the lance are "four pairs of trousers made of the same cloth" <note>An idiom meaning they are essentially the same thing.</note>.

**Rhinotaros, The Wolf-Pelt.** It is a common practice now—and one can observe from this name that it is an ancient custom—that those who were or are "iron-biters" <note>original: "eysen beysser"; a term for fierce, grizzled soldiers or swashbucklers.</note> and men of war, knew well in what manner they should disguise themselves so that they might be regarded as devils, just as they would like to be. Therefore, one dresses in an elk skin <note>original: "ellends haut"; elk or moose hide was often used for "buff coats" because of its thickness and durability against blades.</note>, which is not entirely out of place, as it serves as a substitute for armor where it is of good quality. Another wears a bear skin or a wolf-pelt, which are not unhelpful against rain, lice, and fleas; rather, in the cold, they may serve as both clothing and bed, day and night. But what use the twelve pairs of trousers or "wool-sacks" that people hang from their backsides in our times <note>A critique of the "plunderhosen"—the oversized, puffy breeches fashionable in the 16th century.</note> might be to soldiers, I cannot know. However, I find that throughout time, the most simply and honorably dressed soldier is likely to be the most agile. For just as armor and this decorative jingling <note>original: "glämper"</note> are heavy, so too do they hinder one’s posture and the handling of weapons, appearing as an unformed shape upon a person. I would also like to hear who would have ever believed an image—painted or carved—that showed such large thighs, and above the knees a stump or block tattered with bark, upon which an adorned body stood. But God be lamented, since the loyalty, faith, and manhood of our dear ancestors have been forgotten, what wonder is it then that we do not know which clothing truly graces us?

**Hippius** The Mounted One. <note>original: "Der Reißig." From *Hippos*, Greek for horse.</note> It was indicated above how **Mars** was a man of war, for which reason he is called "The Mounted One," and how it is said in **Enyalios** that he had his statue in **Olympia**.

**Arex.** <note>Refers to Ares/Mars.</note> In **Athens**, there was an alley where a courthouse stood called the **Areopagus** <note>Mars' Hill.</note>. There, it is said, **Mars** was first summoned before a court and had to answer for the homicide he committed against **Halirrhothios** <note>original: "Alirzhotio"</note>; for that same man had raped **Mars'** daughter, **Alcippe**. At that same court, there were the places where the advocates stood, which were made of silver. There were two: the one upon which the accuser spoke was called the Stone of Reproach <note>original: "Schmachstein"</note>; the one upon which the accused gave his answer was called the Stone of Impudence <note>original: "vnverschampten Küßling"; *Küßling* refers to a large stone or boulder.</note>. This authority had no end nor limit to its number; every year, several new judges were chosen for them from the **Thesmothetae** <note>original: "Theßmothetern"; the six junior archons in Athens who functioned as "law-givers."</note>. These were men who, before they were placed on the city court, had to demonstrate that they had lived their lives as honorable people. They also had to stand and offer to give an account and answer to everyone—from the least to the greatest—if there were anyone who believed they had a claim or knew of any misconduct regarding them. When they had sat on the city court for a time and one of them was elected as an **Areopagite**, a public announcement was made: "This person or that, who has conducted his affairs in such a manner while sitting on the city court, has been elected as an **Areopagite**; if there be anyone..."

# The Fifth Book.

If anyone knew of any hindrance regarding an elected official, he should step forward and point it out. If someone appeared who could prove that such an elected **Councilor** <term>Ratßherr: a member of the city council or senate, expected to be of the highest moral standing</term> was "worth a pin" <note>original: "einicher gluffen wherdt"; an idiom meaning someone of no value or prone to petty theft.</note>, had embezzled from public goods, or had "drunk away" even a **heller's** <note>A heller was one of the smallest denominations of currency; to waste even this much of the city's money was a disqualifying offense.</note> worth of the city's wealth, or was otherwise burdened by the vices of usury, harshness, greed, or the like, the elected man could not take office. To ensure that no one could sneak into the position, it was the custom to crown them with a **small wreath**. However, they were never crowned in private; it had to be done in an open place before the entire **Assembly**.

Their office was to weigh all difficult matters concerning the common good, as well as crimes committed not out of a sudden "flying fit of rage," but out of evil intent—such as the brewing of poison, crippling people, enchanting them through sorcery, robbery, arson, murder, wounding, treason, and acting against the fatherland.

When they sat in judgment, the accuser had to swear an oath to confirm his testimony. If he acted with deceit <note>original: "gfaar"; meaning malice or perjury.</note>, he called upon the gods to ensure that he and his entire household and lineage be rooted out. He stood between a **Boar**, a **Ram**, and a **Bull**, which were slaughtered on designated days by specially appointed persons in a named place, and thus sacrificed for the oath. If the accused wished to clear and defend himself, he had to take a similar oath. If not, he was permitted to flee after hearing the accusation; no one would pursue him. If he escaped after the verdict was given, they let it be; nevertheless, they maintained their own judgment on the matter. This Council or court was so esteemed for its bravery and wisdom that no one ever appealed or revoked their verdict. Their secrecy was so absolute that a proverb arose from it. # Mars, as he is counted as one among the seven wandering stars; as the Astrologers

->write of him—regarding births, weather, and several other powers.<-

---

<language>German</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>

<margin>
**Mars, as they say, governs the birth of man and other matters according to his position as follows.**
</margin>

<margin>
On days:
- Tuesday
- Saturday [hours] 3, 10
- Sunday 7
- Monday 4, 11
- Tuesday 1, 8
- Wednesday 5, 12
- Thursday 2, 9
- Friday 6

On hours of the day:
- Saturday 3, 10
- Sunday 7
- Monday 4, 11
- Tuesday 1, 8
- Wednesday 5, 12
- Thursday 2, 9
- Friday 6

On hours of the night:
- Saturday 5, 12
- Sunday 2, 9
- Monday 6
- Tuesday 3, 10
- Wednesday 7
- Thursday 4, 11
- Friday 1, 8
</margin>

<insert>
**Physical Appearance:** Goat-like, wide and open mouth, broad teeth, red hair, sharp face, curly head, a squinting face.

**A child born in this hour would be:** A maker of misfortune, who never rejoices unless a land is falling. He boasts of evil, likes to lie, a robber, an arsonist, a murderer, and an ungracious violator of women.

**In these hours it is good to begin:** Purchasing war equipment, red cloth, putting on armor and other weapons, and marching against the enemy.

**In these hours avoid:** Forming alliances or partnerships. Using medicine, bloodletting, marrying, traveling across fields, or beginning any other creative work.

**These hours are almost the same as those above.**
</insert>

<margin>
Lifespan:
- Very good: he gives sixty-six years.
- Average: he gives forty years and six months.
- Bad: fifteen years, or fifteen months, or fifteen days.
- Thus his cycle <note>the time it takes to complete a full planetary influence period</note> is ten years and nine months.
</margin>

<insert>
Mars keeps 15 months for himself: This increases the influence of the birth in anxiety and distress.
To **Saturn** he gives 45 months: making one lazy, accomplishing nothing, stingy, and a wretched wretch in everything.
To **Jupiter** he gives 12 months: Such as luck, salvation, gain, offices, health, and plenty of wealth.
To the **Sun** he gives 19 months: uprising, misery, distress, blindness, sickness, danger, and damage.
To **Venus** he gives eight months: luck, shame, and courtship, adultery, with danger and capital punishment.
To **Mercury** he gives 20 months: false letters, theft, and their punishment.
To the **Moon** he gives 25 months: Misery, exile, suffering, anxiety, distress, poverty, and a wretched death.
</insert>

<margin>
Mars is Lord <note>ruler of the year</note> for the first 26 days.
</margin>

> **In Aries:** Great winds, storms, eye pain, little rain in Trine <note>an astrological aspect of 120 degrees</note>. Otherwise cheap prices, rain, dying, earthquakes, war, and uprising.
> **In Leo:** War, quarrels, death of neighbors, good sailing weather, yet cattle plague <note>original: "Feib," likely "Keib" meaning carrion or disease</note> among the livestock.
> **In Sagittarius:** War in the West, little wine, dying, bad trade, coughs, eye pain, worms in children <note>original: "hunds würm"</note>, cold, little rain, expensive fruit, rare diseases, hay; murderers have good luck, sudden death; toward midnight good air, toward noon luck in merchantry.
> **In Taurus:** Wind, hail, thunder, coughs, death of women and cattle, war, blindness.
> **In Virgo:** Cheap prices, eye pain, war, dying.
> **In Capricorn:** Great heavy unrest and war, good pasture, much snow, death of great lords, the French disease <note>syphilis</note>, wicked war, great misfortune.
> **In Gemini:** Summer, coughs, great drought, war, murderers, gnats in the ears, hatred toward priests, the rich, and the learned.
> **In Libra:** Wind, dying, rain, wine and pasture become expensive, misfortune for merchants.
> **In Aquarius:** Great misery, much snow, cold, high prices, beetles, locusts, vermin, caterpillars.
> **In Cancer:** Tempestuous seas, sicknesses, high taxes, cattle dying, accidents for farmers, lust.
> **In Scorpio:** Cold, fog, darkness, high prices, murder, sicknesses, merchant’s luck accompanied by anxiety.
> **In Pisces:** Destruction of power, great fishing, high prices, thunder, hail, eye pain.
> **Sun in Conjunction with the Moon:** <note>The text uses planetary symbols to denote aspects with Mars</note> A stern, brave builder, settles all quarrels.
> **Moon in Conjunction with the Moon:** Shameful with the enemy; quarrels with kings, princes, and noblemen. Buy riding horses and anything that is red; otherwise, light the fire for alchemy.
> **Moon in Sextile with the Moon:** Stay away from the nobility; also, do not burn anything in alchemy.
> **Moon in Square with the Moon:** Occupy yourself with soldiers and trade; buy cattle; use alchemy.
> **Moon in Trine with the Moon:** Form no friendship, courtship, nor war; do not hire any servant.

<margin>
Concerning the actions to be done or avoided.
</margin>

<margin>
Countries: England, France, Germany, Russia, Judea, Syria, Cappadocia, Morocco. It makes people wild, warlike, strong, predatory, and amorous.
</margin>

---

<margin>
**When he joins with other planets and provides aid**
</margin>

- **Saturn.** You will find information about this under Saturn.
- **Jupiter.** Look under Jupiter.
- **Sun.** Death of the father, great labor and suffering, disadvantage from weapons and fire regarding property, fickle-minded. **Trine (△):** Great high power, generals, mighty lords of the land, and captains. **Conjunction (☌):** A bad end, a wretched life, blindness, confused senses. Tearing apart and dismemberment of the body through uprising, being persecuted both in life and after death. **Opposition (☍):** Wretched death, unforeseen accident, eye damage, begging, poverty, etc.
- **Venus.** Quarrels in courtship and with women, disadvantage, damage. Great whoring. **Trine (△):** Daily gain, a lucky marriage. Wealthy and proud. Many wives. **Square (□):** Great misfortune from women, unchaste people, yet quiet. **Opposition (☍):** And dealings with wife and children.
- **Mercury.** A liar, skillful, wise, clever, busy, therefore pleasant to people, loved by parents, a thief, cunning. **Trine (△):** Whatever begins here is lucky; great wealth and skill with writing and counsel. **Square (□):** All his plans go backward, bad reputation, creates bad company, deniable, in prison, predatory, thievish, insolent, financial deceit. A terrible end. **Opposition (☍):** Evil forger, guilty, shameless, lacking honor, cheated, deceiving, false, lustful.
- **Moon.** Surrounded by the sword or otherwise pitiful, mother’s anxiety and suffering, overburdened by friendship. **Trine (△):** Lucky in all doing and not doing; great power, yet constantly sick. **Square (□):** Mother soon a widow, or other great misfortune, possessed by an evil spirit, anxiety, distress, poverty, in death and life. A wicked wife who is proud, pretty, and wasteful. **Opposition (☍):** They die almost at birth, remain without a wife. A wretched death. Fit for the gallows.

---

<margin>
**In these signs he has his strengths.**
</margin>

> **Aries.** Thief, shouter, cunning, a maker of quarrels, brawler, captains, sheriffs, always in armor. Low-born fighters <note>original: "Bilberzlen"</note> who always strut about like braggarts and sword-eaters.
> **Taurus.** Joyful, insolent, a glutton to whom everything is equal, associated with manslaughter, not very handsome, yet joking; produces honorable, brave men who achieve wealth and honor.
> **Gemini.** Soldiers who are skillful and active, yet deliberate; they accomplish more with skill than with force. High at courts, but leaves one shamed and injured in body, entirely poor.
> **Cancer.** Mounted soldiers, riders, archers, holding military offices, quite misshapen. Skillful with wounds and other such medicines, sorcerers, poison-mixers.
> **Leo.** Mighty, manly, brave, quite skillful on horse and foot, misshapen in face, much headache, cautious.
> **Virgo.** Entirely misshapen, furious with anger which they hide. Bold, insolent man-slayers who wager everything. Leaves one likely blind, lame, poor, and despised.
> **Libra.** No handsome people; they give themselves over to pleasure first: joy in weapons and shooting. Soon has misfortune, yet finally a quiet, pleasurable life until the end.
> **Scorpio.** Mighty, powerful, brave, superior to the enemy, of high fame, who guard their property wisely. At first poor, envious, hated, doing evil, subject to soldiers, fools for women whom they love and quarrel with.
> **Sagittarius.** Weak, womanish, insolent, lazy wretches, small gentle minds; yet they soon become brave and bold, calling themselves busy; they are feared for their powerful business in honor and taking. In order, they yield to no one's power, settling marriages with fairness.
> **Capricorn.** Kingly companions, noble, powerful. Victorious and held in high honor, achieving things another would only dare to think of. But they love pious persons.
> **Aquarius.** Evil-minded, faithless, perjurers, rogues, quarrelsome, misshapen, fickle, airy, murderers or judges, rioters. Their mind is set on horses and war equipment. Blindness, thievery, and finally a life without any freedom.
> **Pisces.** Jugglers who live in excess, low-born lovers, soothsayers and similar companions who are wonderful and therefore held in high regard. Manslayers, evil boys who intend to deceive everyone.

---

<margin>
**In these houses of the heavens**
</margin>

- **I.** Wasteful, spending more than is earned. Cruel, great, powerful lords in war and peace, whom all the world fears because of their grim spirit. They hate wife and child; they are cunning, bold, insane, inconstant, wandering. In the end, their splendor, greed, and lordship vanish; misery is their reward.
- **II.** Great misfortune, accident to the body, weak, naked, often wounded by cattle, shot, struck, badly frozen, captured, sold, beaten, foundlings, fighters, fencers, soldiers, etc.
- **III.** Honor achieved with difficulty, often loses other property, bad conscience, enemy of the whole world. Gain from the public purse along with high offices; nobility before his friends; bailiff, judge, governor, tax collector.
- **IV.** Soldiers, industrious, struggling for honor, master sawyers, lackeys, runners; parents die soon, and the family seat disappears; many wounds; widowhood; one son or none. Wicked wife, lunacy <note>original: "Mõsucht," literally moon-sickness</note>, full of devils, etc.
- **V.** Great honor, wealth, and fame among princes, lords, and the common people; beautiful of form; always abroad; in many dangers, where good comes to them. Yet always a servant, judge, counselor, or juror; finally an unforeseen accident, exile, often trembling, misery, anxiety, distress, imprisonment, no child.
- **VI.** Much evil, finds harm for his children, now luck then misfortune, limping, haughty, all kinds of diseases.
- **VII.** Exceedingly great evil, innumerable dangers, industrious people, murderers, villains, traitors, torturers, executioners, unforeseen wretched death, quartering, falling to death, imprisonment, stocks, blocks; perishing in collapsing buildings, being murdered, drowning in shipwreck, burning; he will also take up robbing and burning; will kill wife and child.
- **VIII.** Robbery of all goods, exile, misery, imprisonment, eyes gouged out, great anxiety and distress, want, fought and murdered through cunning, ambush, or fighting; before all the world he drowns, is suffocated, falls from a cliff; stripped of power and splendor; given death, or the blow.
- **IX.** Long life, honor, luck, all great offices, captaincy, judge of capital crimes <note>original: "Plürichter"</note>, with dangerous travels. Learned speakers, yet blasphemers, godless, perjury, sorcerers.
- **X.** Great lords over life and death, guild masters, princes, captains, emperors, kings, high command in wars, governors who ruin land and people, establishing new things; yet they do not live long, some die a cruel death abroad, leaving their power behind; none take it up; perish in misfortune; have few or no children at all.
- **XI.** Much good, increasing wealth, favor of the people, great offices, power over life and death.
- **XII.** Great sicknesses, treacherous health that causes him harm, brings him dishonor; those he oppresses bring him into danger; he is driven to kill himself or creates a wretched death; he causes all the misfortune in the world, makes things unfruitful.

---

<margin>
**In these signs**
</margin>

- Aquarius, Pisces, Taurus: His light is a glow.
- Taurus, Gemini, Cancer: His shine decreases.
- Leo, Virgo, Libra: His shine darkens.
- Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn: His shine increases.
- Aries and Virgo: His shine is entirely unlucky and wicked.

<insert>
If Mars is in his course as follows, it signifies:
- Conjunction <note>☌</note> or Opposition <note>☍</> in the Sun's signs: drought, little rain, cloudbursts, thunder with damage.
- Conjunction or Opposition with Venus: Rain.
- Conjunction or Opposition with Mercury: Wicked drought; in "wet" signs <note>Water signs</note>, rain and much wind.
</insert>

# Venus.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration shows the goddess Venus standing in a four-wheeled chariot being pulled across a landscape by two birds (possibly swans or doves). Venus is depicted nude, wearing a crown of leaves, and holding a sphere or apple in her right hand and a small flower in her left. The background features a body of water with a sailing ship and a coastline with trees.</image-desc>

The Greeks called her Aphrodite <note>original: "aphodite"</note>, and all the heathens regarded her as a goddess of procreation and pleasure, as well as of beautiful form. The Latins said her name [Venus] came from the fact that she "comes to all things," or that all things come about through her <note>A traditional medieval etymology linking *Venus* to the Latin *venire*, meaning "to come."</note>. Regarding the story that a fiery seed grew from heaven and fell into the sea, from which foam Venus was born: this is meant to signify that the joining of heat and moisture gives life to all that is born. Cicero recounts four of her. One born of Heaven and Day. The second from the aforementioned foam, who is said to have sired Cupid <note>original: "Cupidinem"</note> with Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>. The third is a daughter of Jupiter <note>original: "Jovis"</note> and Dione, and the wife of Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcani"</note>. The fourth he calls Astarte <note>original: "Astartem"</note>, sired by Syria <note>original: "Syro"</note> and Tyre <note>original: "Syren"</note>.

Sometimes she was painted as a young maiden arriving from the sea on a sea-shell—these people called her Andymionem. Sometimes she was in the form of a woman carrying a shell in her hand, crowned with roses and flowers; beside her stood the <term>Graces: "Holdfåligkeyten," the personifications of charm, beauty, and creativity</term>, Cupid and Anteros, Mercury, and Peitho <note>original: "Pitho," the goddess of persuasion</note>. Sometimes she traveled upon a small chariot pulled by doves, because the dove is a pure, chaste, and—in its pairing—quite lovely and passionate animal. Others have her pulled by swans. Sometimes she stands upon a sea snail <note>likely referring to a nautilus or tortoise shell</note> as a sign that a woman and housekeeper should stay at home and be still, or that young maidens require protection.

In Magdeburg, Saxony, a temple to this goddess is said to have stood, where she was depicted thus: Naked, she rode along upon a little chariot; her head was crowned with myrtle; upon her breast she wore a burning torch; in her right hand the sphere of the world; in her left three golden apples. The Graces, with their hands wound together, brought her gifts. The chariot was pulled by two swans and two doves.

The myrtle tree was attributed to her because it grows willingly around the sea and is naturally helpful for courtship or love. Roses were attributed to her because they are so fit for wreaths and also inspire love with their scent.

Phosphorus the Morning Star <note>original: "Phosphorus Morgenstern"</note>. Hesperus the Evening Star <note>original: "Hesperus der Abendstern"</note>. She is called the Morning Star or "Light-bringer" because that star is assigned to her, shining more brightly than all others.

Alitta. Mitra. Urania the Heavenly <note>original: "Urania die Himblisch"</note>. Alilat. The story that the procreative organs <note>original: "gpär zeůg oder schellen," literally "procreative gear or bells"</note> were cut from Saturn by Jove and thrown into the sea was intended by the ancients to signify how heavenly love—which is pure and clear—is entirely distinct from worldly love or courtship. Therefore, they gave her this name [Urania], and the Syrians built her the first sacrificial temples and church decorations. At Athens, she also had a temple. Likewise in Cyprus, at Paphos <note>original: "Baffo"</note>, and at Ascalon in
<meta>Palestina/</meta>

# The Fifth Book.
## Venus.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration with a decorative frame depicting the goddess Venus. She is shown nude and crowned, seated in a small four-wheeled chariot that is pulled by two birds (doves or swans) across a body of water toward a distant shore. In her left hand, she holds a circular mirror, and in her right, a sprig of flowers or fruit. The background shows rolling hills, a small boat on the water, and a bright sky.</image-desc>

The Greeks called her Aphrodite <note>original: "Appodite"</note>, and all the heathens regarded her as a goddess of procreation and pleasure, as well as of beautiful form. The Latins said her name [Venus] came from the fact that she "comes" <note>An etymological play on the Latin "venire" (to come).</note> to all things, or that all things come forth through her. However, the story that a fiery seed grew out of the heavens and fell into the sea—from which foam Venus was born—is meant to signify that the joining of heat and moisture gives life to the born. Cicero <note>A famous Roman statesman and writer.</note> counts four of them: One born from Heaven and Day. The second from the aforementioned foam, who is said to have fathered Cupid with Mercury.

The third is said to be a daughter of Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis"</note> and Dione, and the wife of Vulcan. The fourth he calls Astarte, born of Syro and Syren.

Sometimes she was painted like a young daughter coming out of the sea upon a sea-shell; they called her Anadyomene <note>original: "Andymionem"; this refers to the "Venus Anadyomene" or "Venus Rising from the Sea."</note>. Sometimes she was in the form of a woman carrying a shell in her hand, crowned with roses and flowers; beside her stood the Graces <note>original: "Holdsáligkeyten"</note>, Cupid and Anteros, Mercury, and Peitho <note>original: "Pitho," the goddess of persuasion.</note>. Sometimes she traveled in a small wagon pulled by doves, because the dove is a pure, chaste, and, in its mating, a very lovely and fervent animal. Others have her led by swans. Sometimes she stands upon a sea-snail <note>likely a conch shell</note> as a sign that a woman and housewife should always be at home and quiet, or that virgins require protection.

In Magdeburg, Saxony, a temple of this goddess is said to have stood, designed in this way: she traveled there naked upon a small cart; her head was crowned with myrtle; upon her breast she wore a burning torch; in her right hand she held the globe of the world, and in her left, three golden apples. After her came the Graces with intertwined hands, bringing her gifts; the cart was pulled by two swans and two doves.

The myrtle tree was attributed to her because it likes to grow around the sea and is naturally helpful for wooing or love. Roses were attributed to her because they are so fit for small crowns and also create love with their scent.

Phosphorus, the Morning Star. Hesperus, the Evening Star. She is called the Morning Star, or light-bringer, because the star assigned to her is so bright above all others.

Alylitta. Mitra. Urania, the Heavenly One. Alilat. That the generative organs or testicles <note>original: "gpår zeůg oder schellen"</note> were cut off from Saturn by Jupiter <note>original: "Joue"</note> and thrown into the sea was intended by the ancients to signify how heavenly love—which is pure and clear—is entirely and utterly distinct from worldly love or wooing. Therefore they gave her this name, and the Assyrians established the first sacrificial temples and church-buildings for her. In Athens, she also had a temple. Likewise in Cyprus, at Paphos <note>original: "Baffo"</note>, and at Ascalon in Palestine.

# Of the Heathen Gods

...Palestine; the image in Athens was made by *Phidias* <note>A renowned Greek sculptor, painter, and architect of the 5th century BC.</note>. The Egyptians in the village of *Schussa*, which belongs to the governorship of *Hermopolis* or *Beni Suef*, worship this *Venus* in the form of a cow, because this animal runs passionately to satisfy the desires of the bull. When the *Scythians* plundered the temple of this *Venus*, they were all afflicted with the flux <note>original: "Monsluß"; likely referring to the "feminine disease" described by Herodotus as a punishment for plundering the temple of Aphrodite Urania at Ascalon.</note>, which their descendants inherited from them. The Arabians called her *Al-Lat* <note>original: "Alai Allat"</note>; the Assyrians *Mylitta*; the Persians *Mitra*. In the temple of this *Venus* in *Babylonia*, all women were required once in their lives to spend a day there, on which they had to have dealings with foreign men; she was also called *Zalambo* by the *Syrians*, and *Peribaso* by certain other peoples.

**Pandemus** <note>original: "Pandemus"; meaning "Of all the people" or "Common."</note>. **Of the Common Man.** So *Theocritus* <note>A Greek poet from Sicily.</note> named her, and yet she is the very same who was worshipped at *Elis* in *Olympia* under the name *Uranie* <note>original: "Vranie"; meaning "Heavenly."</note>. She also has an image made from the spoils captured at *Corfu* by the Romans, along with a temple. Not far from there was the image made of ivory and gold; with one foot she stood upon a snail <note>A symbol of domesticity and staying at home.</note>. Within the enclosure there was also an altar upon which *Venus* rode a goat; *Scopas* <note>A famous Greek sculptor and architect.</note> made that image, and she was also called "of the Common Man." In *Boeotia* she had an image that *Harmonia*, the wife of *Cadmus*, made from the wood that had once been *Cadmus’s* ship. *Solon* <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker.</note> also erected an image of her using the tax that the city collected from the common prostitutes.

**Verticordia. Apostrophia.** **The Turner.** Just like the previous two, *Harmonia* made an image of this one from the same wood. She was so named because she turns, or directs, the hearts of men away from evil and sin, and from impure desires, turning them toward the good. At *Megara* she had a temple, and likewise in Rome, before the *Pincian* gate (which was once called the *Colline Gate*). This was built for her when three Vestal Virgins <note>original: "Nonnen Veste"; refers to the priestesses of the goddess Vesta who took a vow of chastity.</note> were found to have been unchaste at once, which the Romans held to be a disastrous omen. Thus they honored this *Venus* with a prayer that she might turn the hearts of women from unchastity to shame. And when they dedicated the temple and image to her, she chose one hundred of the most noble women from among all the wives; these hundred then cast lots to choose ten; and those ten gave the honor of dedicating and consecrating the site to *Sulpicia*, the daughter of *Servius Paterculus* and wife of *Quintus Fulvius Flaccus*.

**Murtia. Myrtia. Murcea.** The Myrtle <note>original: "Myrtus"</note> was dedicated to her instead of the *Verbena* or vervain, and it was used for the oath when the Romans reconciled with the *Sabines*. She was later called *Murcea* as the one who is lustful and sluggish; whether it was truly her or another goddess is not a matter for long debate here.

**Astroarche. Dea Syria.** **Astarte. Theosphoros.** **Bringer of Day.** The *Sidonians* worshipped *Venus* under this name through the image of a star, using the name *Heosphoros* <note>original: "Heosphoros"; the Greek name for the Morning Star.</note> or bringer of day. Some called her the *Syrian* Goddess and said she awakened and brought forth all growing things. You will find much concerning the *Syrian* goddess in the writings of *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note>.

**Maitis.** *Agathius* says the *Persians* gave her this name, and *Strabo* indicates that in the city of *Zela* she had a festival which they called *Sacas*. But more of this is found under the section on *Diana*.

# The Fifth Book

<margin>Amathusia</margin>
Amathus was a city in Cyprus; from it, Venus—because she was worshipped there—received her name, and she also gave this name to the entire island. The city's name came from Amathus, the son of Hercules. There hung a necklace that Harmonia had worn and was called Eriphyle’s <note>In mythology, this necklace was cursed, bringing misfortune to all who owned it; Eriphyle was bribed with it to betray her husband.</note>; the woman had taken it as a gift and given it to her husband; the necklace was made of turquoise and set in gold.

<margin>Schonida</margin>
Schonida. Regarding the teeth <note>original: "zänẽ"; this may be a printer's error for "zämen" (taming) or "szene" (scenes), but the context refers to the plant squill.</note>, there is the sea-onion <note>the squill plant</note>; moreover, if one eats it, it makes one unchaste; also, an ointment is made from it with which common women <note>a period term for prostitutes</note> anointed themselves; from this, Venus took her name.

<margin>Dione</margin>
Dione, a water goddess in Dodona and mother of Venus, whom she conceived with Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, gave her daughter the name.

<margin>Pythionice</margin>
Pythionice. Harpalus, a provincial governor and courtier in Macedonia, a servant of Alexander the Great, had a mistress named Pythionice; after her death, he built a temple in place of a grave for her, which cost several tons of gold; in it he had inscribed <term>Aphrodite of Pythionice</term> <note>original Greek: "πυθιονικης αφροδιτης"</note>. This means Venus of Pythionice.

<margin>Cytherea / Cythereia / Cytheris / Cythera</margin>
Cytherea / Cythereia / Cytheris / Cythera. An island located about one mile from Malvasia <note>modern Monemvasia, Greece</note>; in ancient times it was called Sothera, Porphyris, and Cythera; now it is called Cerigo. It still has a castle named Cithara; it is twelve miles wide and long, very poorly inhabited at present, and full of wild donkeys. A stone is also found there which is quite useful against the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and stings; furthermore, it is very helpful to women in childbirth. There she has a highly famous temple, which is the oldest in all of Greece. Venus is said to have this name for another reason: from "covering" <note>German: "Verdeckẽ"</note>, because lovers wish to keep their love hidden among themselves and from others as much as they can, or because Venus wants such things to be concealed. Paris and Helen first enjoyed their love there.

<margin>Philomedea</margin>
Philomedea. The Gracious-Laughing One. Some say she has the name from her lovely laughter; others from the genitals <note>original: "gpärſchellen"; referring to the myth that she was born from the severed parts of Uranus</note> of Uranus, of which we spoke before.

<margin>Epitragia</margin>
Epitragia <note>meaning "Upon the Goat"</note>. On the sixth of March, a buck-goat is sacrificed to her in memory that Theseus, when he wished to sacrifice a goat to Venus while sailing to Crete <note>original: "Cadiẽ," likely referring to Candia/Crete</note>, the goat was transformed into a male goat <note>or perhaps a man</note> who then steered the ship. The Bed-mate. She has this name because she is serviceable in bed.

<margin>The Rogue / The Man-Slayer</margin>
The Rogue / The Man-Slayer. Lais was a very beautiful woman, so much so that in all of Thessaly, the young fellows and married men pursued her alone; because of this, some women, angered by jealousy, caught her and, in the temple of Venus where she had fled, stabbed her to death with wooden pins <note>likely weaving needles or hairpins</note>.

<margin>Glateſiz</margin>
Glateſiz <note>likely a rendering of "Kallipygos," meaning "Beautiful Buttocks"</note>. Some say she has the name because Venus had a round, smooth seat, which is considered beautiful in women. Others say that two village daughters argued over which had the prettiest backside; for that reason, they went out onto the road and met a youth, whom they chose as judge. He gave the prize to the elder and was inflamed with love for her; he went home and told the matter to his brother, who also wanted to see, and he fell in love with the other; so both took their respective girls in marriage. Thus both became rich and built a temple to Venus under this name.

<margin>The Proven</margin>
The Proven <note>or "The Trusted"</note>. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> honored her under this name,

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the various epithets and local cults of Venus. The previous page discussed titles like Amathusia, Schonida, and Dione; this page moves into specific legends associated with the Spartans, the Romans, and the famous sculptor Praxiteles.</meta>

<header>Of Pagan Gods</header>

...for when those same Messenians were besieged, they came out from the city with weapons in hand through their watch; they marched upon Lacedaemonia to plunder Sparta. There, the wives of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> drove them out of the city, pursuing those who fled. In the meantime, the Lacedaemonian men learned of the enemy's sortie and intended to march against the enemy; there they encountered their own wives and prepared to fight, believing them to be the Messenians. When the women realized this, they took off their armor and stood there naked. Then the Lacedaemonians fell into lust and, still armed, each mingled with the nearest woman; thus it happened that several maidens were defiled because it occurred at night. From these, the Parthenians <note>A class of Spartans born out of wedlock during the Messenian Wars</note> were fathered, and in memory of this Venus <note>original: "Venerj"</note>, a temple was built.

**B**earded, the Masculine. The Romans had an image of Venus that was bearded and carried a comb <note>original: "strål," likely a grooming tool or strigil</note>, for the reason that once the women were so inflamed with lust that their hair fell out, so that they no longer needed a comb. Now, the women were greatly ashamed of this misfortune and vowed great sacrifices to the Goddess; they also made the image bearded when they recovered, as a sign that she, like a man, had the power of procreation. Therefore, she was male above and female below.

**T**he Bearer <note>original: "Die Gebärerin," referring to Venus Genetrix</note>. Caesar dedicated a temple to her and built it; the image was made by Archesilaus, a housemate of Lucius Lucullus. To this image, Caesar offered a breastplate made of nothing but noble English gemstones, pearls, and others. Caesar vowed this temple when he intended to fight against Pompey on the Pharsalian fields.

**C**nidia / Dorida. Euploea. Praxiteles, the most famous stonemason who ever lived, loved a female figure named Phryne; in her likeness, he is said to have carved an image out of Parian marble in Cape Crio <note>Knidos</note>, which was naked, smiling, yet covering her private parts with her left hand. The temple where it stood had two doors, so that one could see her from the front and the back. A youth once fell so passionately in love with this image that he hid himself in the temple at night and left a mark of his debauchery in the marble. To see the beauty of this image, the most curious people from all over the world sailed there. When Praxiteles made two images of this Venus, and those on the island of Kos <note>original: "Lango"</note> bought the one that was draped and clothed from him, he offered the naked one to them even more dearly; although he had given them the first choice, the Cnidians took the one that the others did not want. King Nicomedes offered to pay an immeasurable sum of debt that the Cnidians owed far and wide if they would give him the image, but it could not be granted to him.

**S**icyonia. At Chiarenza <note>Sicyon</note> she had her temple; her image was seated, cast from gold by Canachus. In one hand she carried several poppy-heads, in the other an apple, and on her head a drinking vessel <note>likely a polos, a high cylindrical crown</note>. She had two priestesses, of whom the older, a woman, tended the temple inside, while the maiden tended it outside.

**C**olias. Not far from Athens, about half a mile long, is a suburb called Colias; there, the storm cast up and shattered the Medes <note>The Persians</note> when they plundered Athens and the surrounding area. Some say the name comes to her from an Attic youth named Colias, who was once captured by a pirate; then the master's daughter became fond of the youth and made him free and rich; this he [dedicated] to Ve-
