<header>### The Fifth Book</header>

**Alcopolis.** Alcamenes, a pupil of the sculptor Phidias, created a statue for this Venus; she received this name because she stood before the city <note>The name likely refers to Venus "of the citadel" or "by the city walls."</note>.

**She of the Gardens.** The Romans regarded this goddess as a protector of gardens, for the reason that she brought about growth; for sometimes Venus was used to represent herbs and plants, just as Ceres was used for bread and Neptune for fish. Therefore, the poet Naevius says under the name of the Cook:
> I have eaten Neptune,
> Ceres and Venus sat at the table before me.
> <note>original: "Neptunum hab ich vffgeffen / Ceres / d Venus / ehe ztisch gseffen." A poetic way of saying he ate fish, bread, and salad/greens.</note>
Even when the Festival of Must <note>The *Vinalia Rustica*, a wine festival</note> occurs (says Varro) on the 21st of August, it is the dedication day of the temple of Venus, and one entrusts to her the protection of the gardens; the gardeners also have their holiday on this day. Pausanias mentions her and speaks of her image at Megara, yet nothing is certain, so let it rest there.

**Praxis, the Active.** Under this name, she had a temple and an image made of ivory in Attica <note>original: "die Würckend." *Praxis* refers to Venus as the goddess of "Action" or "Success" in love.</note>.

**The Dark-Eyed.** One attributes beautiful black eyes to Venus, with lovely round brown eyebrows and lids; hence the poets write much about her under this name.

**The Victorious.** Hypermestra had a father named Danaus, who had forty-nine other daughters besides her; he gave these daughters to the sons of his brother (who likewise had exactly fifty sons) in marriage. But he secretly commanded them that each should kill and strangle her bridegroom at night when he was well-drunk. All obeyed him except Hypermestra; she helped her husband Lynceus to escape. The father brought his daughter to trial for her disobedience, but she was acquitted. Thereupon, she built a temple to Venus under this name in the Plane-tree forest by the waters of Pontinus; in Achaia, not far from Corinth, Juno also had a temple there.

**The Looking-Up.** Phaedra, who was inflamed with love for her stepson Hippolytus, wished to and did constantly look out upon the place where he exercised; afterward, a temple was built there, and the name was given to Venus in remembrance <note>original: "Die vfflügend." This refers to Venus *Epistrophia*, the one who "turns toward" or "looks back."</note>.

**Morpho.** On a small hill in Lacedaemonia <note>Sparta</note>, there was a very old temple; above the main floor of the same, there was still a chapel dedicated to this Venus. Her image sat with a covered head, and on her feet she had bands or iron chains, in order to show that the loyalty of wives should or would be completely firm and constant.

**The One at Migonium.** A village not far from Sparta had a temple from which Venus took this name, for the village was called Migonium. Paris is said to have established this temple there, and after the destruction of Troy, Menelaus is said to have established images of Thetis and Praxidice there.

**Symmachia, the Ally.** The Mantineans held this Venus in especially high honor, primarily because she had stood by the Romans in the war at Coronea and at Actium <note>original: "Mitstreiterin." *Symmachia* means "fellow-combatant" or "ally" in Greek.</note>.

**Byblia.** In Byblos in Syria, she had a temple; she was otherwise called the "Syrian Goddess."

**Elephantina.** In Egypt, there was a city called the City of Elephants <note>Elephantine</note>; there Venus was highly honored, for she was painted there most beautifully in the nude upon ivory <note>original: "helffantenbein," literally elephant bone</note> and inlaid with precious, noble stones

**Architis.** The Assyrians and Phoenicians held this goddess in high honor; she had an image on Mount Lebanon with a veiled head, and half of her face was tucked into her clothing; she stood there as if she were weeping, so says Hieronymus <note>Saint Jerome, a 4th-century church father and scholar</note>.
**Erycina.** In Sicily, there was a city situated on a mountain called Eryx (now called Saint Julian <note>Monte San Giuliano, today known as Erice</note>); from this same mountain and temple, this Venus is named, for Eryx, the son of Butes and Venus, built it there; Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> also says much about him. # The Fifth Book

**Nephthe. Athor. Senephthe. Se Nephthe.** The Egyptians worshiped her under these names. Some interpret the first word as "The Dead," "The Ending," or "The Victorious" <note>original: "die Tödteē, die Endend, die Sigend"</note>. The second name refers to the autumn month in their calendar called Athyr. During that month, her festival days were celebrated. Epiphanius <note>a 4th-century bishop and church father</note> attributes the remaining names to her.

**Epitymbia. Libitina, Lubentina, Lubentia.** Among the ancients, it was believed that this goddess assisted at birth as well as at death. For this reason, she had a temple in Rome, though it is not known exactly where. Young daughters would offer up their dolls <note>original: "docketē," meaning small dolls or playthings</note> to her there once they had outgrown childhood. She also had a shrine in Rome. It was also attributed to her that she watched over graves. Hence, there was a statue of her in Delphi under the name **Epitymbia** <note>Greek for "Upon the Grave"</note>.

**Basilis** (The Queen). In the game of chess <note>original: "schachzabel"</note>, the highest piece that overcame all others was called Venus; from this, she takes the name "The Royal."

**The Knightess.** Aeneas erected a statue of her on horseback; from this, she takes that name.

**Elimea.** In Persia, there is a region called Elymais where this Venus had a temple. The Roman envoy Popilius was sent there to forbid Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note> from waging war against the Ptolemies. When the King asked for time to consider his answer, Popilius drew a circle around the King with the staff he held in his hand and said, "You shall not step out of this ring until you say whether you will cease the war and be a friend to us Romans, or be our enemy." While Strabo attributes the plundering of this temple to Diana, you will find more on this name under the section for Diana.

**She of the Cape of the Cross.** The Pyrenean mountains separate France and Spain; not far from Perpignan, at the promontory called the "Little Head of the Cross" <note>likely Cape Creus</note>, this temple of Venus once stood.

**The Common Prostitute.** **Syca Auco**, which is now perhaps Abydos, located at the very front of the flow of the waters of Constantinople, was once overrun by enemies and brought under the yoke. It was later liberated through the help of several common prostitutes; therefore, the city gave her this name in remembrance. It may well be that this originates from the fact that certain peoples—such as those in Cyprus, Armenia, Assyria, Lydia, the Augilae in Barbary, and in Calicut—would betroth their daughters to this goddess and make them common <note>public prostitutes</note> before they were married. The Locrians also once vowed to do this if they were successful in war. In this, one perceives the vows and promises of those who are uninstructed in the faith. Valerius Maximus reports that something similar occurred in Africa at Syca in the second book of his examples.

**The Friend / The Paramour.** On Samos, this Venus had a temple, and the reason for this could be understood in two ways: either that Venus helps whores and knaves come together, or that she sometimes establishes friendship among honorable people.

**Idalia. Acidalia.** There was a forest in Cyprus called Idalium where Venus was worshiped, and she took her name from there. Similarly, there was a spring in Orchomenus called Acidalia, from which her other name comes. However, some say the name might be translated as "Thrusting Care Away" <note>original: "die Sorg ein ſtoſſend"</note>, for the reason that a paramour brings care.

**Architis.** The Assyrians and Phoenicians held this goddess in high honor; she had an image on Mount Lebanon with a veiled head. Half of her face was tucked into her clothing; she stood there as if she were weeping, according to Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus," the 4th-century scholar and Bible translator</note>.

**Erycina.** In Sicily, there was a city situated on a mountain called Eryx (now called Saint Julian). This Venus is named after that same mountain and temple; for Eryx, the son of Butes and Venus, built it there. Diodorus [Siculus] also says much about him. Fabius Maximus built a temple for her in Rome, following the advice of the Sibylline prophecy. Similarly, Lucius Portius vowed and established another by the Pincian Gate during the Ligurian War <note>original: "Genneser Krieg," likely referring to the wars in the region of Genoa</note> in the year when Aquileia received a Roman garrison. Plutarch and others say this Argynnus ran into the sea—which was stormy and raging—to spite Diana, because Diana had been moved to anger against him because he shot a stag she loved. Thus he drowned as a result of the goddess's revenge.

Her image was in long clothes, holding a victory branch <note>original: "Sigengelen," a palm or branch of victory</note> in her hand and a mirror in her left.

Scotia.** This name is used because humans mingle in love at night—not during the day like wild beasts—but rather in the night, which is somewhat black <note>The Greek "Skotia" means dark or shadowy</note>. The Corinthians worshiped her under this name in a grove <note>original: "Dhan," likely a variant of "Hain"</note> of cypresses before the city. Similarly, she had her temples in Thespis and in Egypt.

**Epicreontis.** A wanderer named Devicreon <note>likely a corruption of Epicreon</note> came to the island of Samos and made the women on that same island—who were so very shameless and lustful—pious with certain blessings and magic; thus this name was attributed to Venus. Some say this man was a steersman on a ship who once sailed to Cyprus for trade; when he was about to load for departure, Venus warned him that he should put nothing but drinking water in the ship. When he did so, such great heat and stillness came upon the sea that he and others could not sail, and almost everyone nearly died of thirst. Because he had water while the others had none, he gained great wealth from it, and afterward he erected an image to the goddess under that name.

**Erynthia / Zerineha / Zereres.** It is mentioned in the section on Hecate how there was a cave in the province of Thrace where she was worshiped along with Venus; you may search for it there.

**Ladogenes.** Because Venus is said to have been born by a water called Ladon in Arcadia, she has this name.

# The Fifth Book.

**Nephthe. Athoz. Senephthe. Se Nephthe.** The Egyptians honored her under these names. Some interpret the first word as "the dead," "those ending," or "the victors." The second name refers to the autumn month among them, called Athyr <note>The Egyptian month corresponding roughly to October/November</note>; it was during this month that the feast days of Venus were held. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note> attributes the remaining names to her.

**Epitymbia. Libitina, Lubentina, Lubentia.** It was believed among the ancients that this goddess assisted both at birth and at the time of passing. For this reason, she had a temple in Rome, though it is known by what rites it was governed: young daughters, when they grew out of childhood, offered up their dolls <note>original: "docketẽ," referring to the practice of girls dedicating childhood toys to a goddess upon reaching marriageable age</note> there. She also had a shrine in Rome. It was also attributed to her that she watched over graves. Hence, in Delphi, there is an image of her under the name **Epitymbia** <note>Greek for "she upon the tombs"</note>.

**Basilis.** She of the chessboard <note>original: "Schachzabel," an old term for chess or a similar board game</note>. In chess, the highest piece that overcame everything was Venus; hence she received this name.

**The Knightess.** Aeneas erected an image of her on horseback; hence she has the name <note>original: "Die Ritterin," reflecting Venus Equestris</note>.

**Elimea.** In Persia, there is a region called Elymais where this Venus had a temple. Popilius was sent there by the Romans to forbid Antiochus from continuing the war against the Ptolemies. When the King asked for time to consider his answer, Popilius drew a circle around the King with the rod he held in his hand and said, "You shall not step out of this ring until you say whether you will cease this war and be a friend to us Romans, or be our enemy." Regarding how Antiochus plundered this temple—which Strabo attributes to Diana—you will find more under the entry for Diana of the same name.

**She of the Runtzial.** The Pyrenean mountains separate France and Spain; there, not far from Perpignan at the promontory called "Cross-head" <note>original: "Creütz köppflin," likely referring to Cap de Creus</note>, this temple of Venus once stood.

**The Common Harlot.** Syca Auco—which is now perhaps Abydos <note>original: "Abidus"</note>, located at the very front of the flow of the Golden Horn <note>original: "Constantinopolitaner güessen"</note>—was once overrun by enemies and brought under their yoke. It was liberated again through the efforts of several common harlots; therefore, the city gave Venus this name in remembrance. This name might also have arisen because certain peoples—such as those in Cyprus, Armenia, Assyria, Lydia, the Augilae in Barbary, and in Calicut—betrothed their daughters to this goddess and made them common <note>A reference to ritual temple prostitution</note> before they were married. The Locrians also once vowed to do the same when they were hard-pressed in war. In this, one perceives the vows and promises of those who are unlearned in faith. Valerius Maximus reports that a similar thing occurred in Africa at Syca, in the second book of his examples.

**The Friend, the Lover.** On Samos, this Venus had a temple. The reason for this name might be understood in two ways: either that Venus helps harlots and rogues come together, or that she occasionally establishes friendship among honorable people.

**Idalia. Acidalia.** There was a forest in Cyprus called Idalia where Venus was worshiped, and she took her name from it. Likewise, there was a spring in Orchomenos called Acidalia, from which her other name comes. However, some say the name might be derived from a word for "care" or "sorrow" <note>original: "sorg"</note>, for the reason that lovers bring much care upon themselves.

<margin>Golgia.</margin> **Golgia** was a city in Cyprus where she was honored.

<margin>Pontia. The Sea-kin. Soligena/Limeneia.</margin> **Pontia** <note>Greek for "of the sea"</note>. **The Sea-kin**. **Soligena** <note>Latin for "Sun-born"</note> / **Limeneia** <note>Greek for "of the harbor"</note>. Since she was born—as it is said—from the sea (which in Latin is called *mare*, from which "sea-kin" is derived), she possessed these names. Maidens and widows who wished to marry offered sacrifices to her so that she might provide them with a good husband. In Lepanto <note>Modern Naupactus, Greece</note>, she has a temple in a cave.

<margin>Cypris. Cypria.</margin> The island of **Cyprus** is such a womanish, cowardly, and soft land that even the bravest men who arrive there fall somewhat into lust and weakness. All manner of unchastity was practiced there before the Venetian rule; indeed, it was a notorious island for all kinds of debauchery due to the natural temperament of its air. It is said that the trade of flesh <note>Refers to ritual or commercial prostitution</note> involving women originated there and was considered no disgrace, as young daughters earned their dowries with the work of their hands. Thus, this island specifically gave its name to Venus <note>original: "Cypris" or "Cypria"</note>.

<margin>The Bald One.</margin> When the **Germans** <note>Likely referring to the Cimbri or Teutones</note> and **Gauls** took Rome in the three hundred and sixtieth year after its founding, and only the Capitoline Hill remained standing, those in the garrison no longer had any sinews for their bows or ropes for their slings. The women swore an oath and allowed sinews to be made from their long hair; therefore, a temple was later erected to this Venus and given this name <note>original: "Die Glatzend," referring to *Venus Calva* (The Bald Venus)</note>.

<margin>Entirely Golden/ Golden/ Silver-footed.</margin> **Entirely Golden, Golden, Silver-footed**. The poets attribute to her golden-yellow hair and beautiful shins to signify her value and the lovely appearance of gold and silver.

<margin>Paphia.</margin> **Paphia**. After the destruction of Troy, **Agapenor** was cast into Cyprus by a storm upon the water; he came to Paphos and built a temple to Venus there. This Agapenor was a grandson of Lycurgus and a son of Ancaeus; his daughter Laodice erected a temple to her at Tegea. Some say **Aerias** built this temple for Venus. Tacitus says **Uranus** erected it and **Cinyras** consecrated it. The goddess herself, having been born from the sea, is said to have sought her resting place there. Her image was not a human figure, but rather a crude pillar that was pointed at the top like a needle <note>The famous conical baetyl of Paphos</note>. Some, like Phornutus <note>Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note>, give her names based on the weak, wavering words of lovers—though these words are sometimes so hollow that they even deceive wise people.

<margin>Acrea/ Ascrea.</margin> **Acrea / Ascrea**. On the island of Cyprus, there was also a city called Carpasia, near which was a promontory named Acreum; upon it stood a temple of Venus into which no woman was permitted to enter. At Troezen, Ascrea also has a temple.

<margin>Apaturia (The Deceptive).</margin> **Apaturia (The Deceptive)**. In Muscovy <note>Used here to refer to the region of Scythia/modern Russia</note>, where Apatrinica is now (once called Phanagoria), Venus had a truly magnificent temple. The reason for this is told in a somewhat mocking way: The giants wished to violate Venus; she called upon **Hercules** and made a bargain with the giants, saying she would submit to each of them one after the other. Hercules waited for them at the appointed spot and killed them. From this, a festival or feast day arose, which also commemorates the day in Athens when the son of King Cotys of Thrace was accepted as a citizen. This feast lasts four days. First, on the eve, the feast-companions came together, paid their dues, and had a meal. On the second day, they sacrificed to **Jupiter** the Companion and to **Pallas**. On the third day, they took young boys and daughters into the brotherhood. On the fourth day, they held the after-feast. This festival is said to have had its origin from...

For when the Athenians came into conflict over the village of Oenoe <note>original: "Coͤlents," referring to the border town of Oenoe</note>, which the Boeotians wished to hold, a man named Xanthus stepped forward on behalf of the Boeotians and offered a duel to the Athenian King, Thymoetes. As they arrived upon the battlefield, Melanthus cried out to Xanthus amidst the fighting—though I know not how justly—"You do well to prepare yourself, for there is a helper standing behind you who is ready to leap to your aid!" Xanthus turned around to see who this person might be, and in that moment, Melanthus struck him dead. For this reason, the duel was called the "Overcoming" or "The Deception" <note>This refers to the origin of the festival *Apaturia*, from the Greek *apate*, meaning deceit</note>.

<margin>Melinea Castania.</margin> **The Brown** or **Chestnut-colored One**; this is what Lycophron <note>A Greek poet</note> calls her.

<margin>Cluacina.</margin> **The Purifier**. *Cluere* among the Latins means as much as "to fight" or "to cleanse" among us. At the place where the Sabines and Romans fought, until the women intervened with their pleas and ran between them, the men laid down their weapons; there, the Romans built a temple to her. It stood not far from the main market <note>the Roman Forum</note> in Rome.

<margin>Anadyomene.</margin> **The One Rising from the Sea**. In the chapel of Caesar, Augustus hung a painted image of Venus under this name in honor of his father <note>his adoptive father, Julius Caesar</note>. This painting, when it began to rot slightly at the bottom, no painter was skillful enough to restore. Because the panel was eventually ruined by age, Nero had it replaced with a painting by Dorotheus, a famous artist.

<margin>Mechanites.</margin> **The Artful One**. Or **The Ingenious**. She was given this name because of the various strange gestures and behaviors that lovers use in their romance, as if she were equipped for every kind of strategy.

<margin>
Adikos / Baiotis / Eleymon / Erientes / Enthion / Antheris / Endoso / Epicoon / Milites / Erototrophos.
</margin> In Libya, she is called **The Unjust One** <note>original: "Adikos"</note>. Among the Syracusans in Syracuse, she is **The Pounded** <note>original: "Baiotis," perhaps a reference to treading or crushing</note>. She is **The Sleeping** or **The Recumbent** <note>original: "Erientes"</note>. In Chalcedon, she is **The Burning Heat** <note>original: "Enthion"</note>. Elsewhere, she is **The Lovely** <note>original: "Antheris"</note>. In Cyprus, she is **The Painted** <note>original: "Endoso"</note>. In Knossos, she is **The Horse** <note>original: "Epicoon"</note>. In Carthage, she is **The Judge** <note>original: "Milites," likely a confusion with "Virgo Coelestis" or a judicial title</note>. She is also called **The Sweet** and **The Love-breeder** <note>original: "Erototrophos"</note>.

<margin>The Hospitable.</margin> **Momemphitica**. In Egypt, Helen of Troy established a temple for her when she was a guest of Proteus <note>original: "Protho"</note>. Similarly, she was honored in the form of a cow around the region of Caycus.

<margin>Aeneis frugi / Fruta.</margin> She also held these names among the Romans as the **Mother of Aeneas**, **The Domestic**, and **The Overseer**. In the place where the Church of Saint Barbara now stands in Rome, she once had a temple.

<margin>Eleusinia.</margin> Not far from Turgeta, she also had a temple where Hercules was healed by Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note> after he had been wounded.

<margin>Ononia Olympia.</margin> In Sparta, she had a temple and a very ancient statue where mothers would offer sacrifices when they married off their daughters.

<margin>Nympha.</margin> In Troezen, Theseus built a temple to Venus under this name because Helen had been given to him. On the island of Delos, there was once a statue of Venus whose hand had been broken off by old age; it was square at the base. This statue was made by Daedalus, given to Ariadne, and carried away by Theseus. He eventually gave it to Apollo and set it up so that the image would not constantly renew his painful memories. In Patras, there were two chapels to Venus: in one, there was a statue that fishermen had found in a net while fishing; the other was made of wood, except for the face, feet, and hands, which were of marble. In Lemnos, Pelops made a statue of her from myrtle wood, which he had promised when he wished to race for the hand of Hippodamia. There are others in Aegio and various places that would take long to recount, but it is unnecessary.

# Of Heathen Gods

<margin>Golgia.</margin> **Golgia.** Golga was a city in Cyprus where she was worshipped. <note>Golgi was an ancient city in Cyprus famous for its temple of Aphrodite.</note>

<margin>Pontia.</margin> **Pontia.** The Sea-born <note>original: "Mhörnerwhante," a dialect variant for "born from the sea"</note>, Soligena <note>Latin: "Sun-born"</note>, and Limeneta <note>Greek: "Of the Harbor"</note>. Because she was born (as they say) from the sea (which is called *mare* in Latin), she held these names. Virgins and widows who wished to marry offered sacrifices to her so that she might grant them a good husband. At Lepanto <note>Naupactus in Greece</note>, she has a temple located in a grotto.

<margin>Cypris.</margin> **Cypris.** Cypria. The island of Cyprus is such a womanish, lazy, and soft land that even the bravest men who go there fall somewhat into lust and weakness. All manner of impurity occurred there before the rule of the Venetians <note>The Republic of Venice ruled Cyprus from 1489 to 1571</note>; indeed, it was a notorious island for every kind of debauchery due to the natural climate. It is said that the trade of women's flesh originated there and was not considered a shame, provided that young daughters accustomed themselves to it before they were married. Thus, this island especially gave its name to Venus.

<margin>The Bald One.</margin> **The Bald One.** <note>original: "Die Glatzend," referring to *Venus Calva*</note> When the Germans and Gauls took Rome in the three hundred and sixtieth year of its building, and only the Capitol remained standing, the garrison had no more sinews for their bows and no ropes for their slings. The women took it upon themselves to let their long hair be cut to make sinews; therefore, a temple was later erected to this Venus and this name was given to her.

<margin>Entirely Golden.</margin> **Entirely Golden / Golden / Silver-footed.** The poets grant her golden-yellow hair and beautiful curls to indicate her nature through the preciousness and lovely shine of gold and silver.

<margin>Paphia.</margin> **Paphia.** After the destruction of Troy, Agapenor was tossed by a storm upon the waters into Cyprus and came to Paphos, where he built a temple to Venus. This Agapenor was a grandson of Lycurgus and a son of Ancaeus; his daughter Laodice erected a temple to her at Tegea. Some say Aerias built this temple for Venus. Tacitus says Uranus erected it and Cinara dedicated it. The goddess herself, when she was born from the sea, is said to have sought her resting place there. Her image was not a human figure, but rather a rough pillar that was pointed at the top like a needle. <note>This refers to the famous "aniconic" (non-human shaped) black stone worshipped at Paphos.</note> Some give her the name Phornutus <note>referring to the philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus</note> because of the weak and wavering words of lovers, though these words are sometimes so clear that they deceive even wise people.

<margin>Acrea.</margin> **Acrea / Ascrea.** On the island of Cyprus, there was also a city called Carpasia, near which was a promontory called Acreum. Upon it stood a temple of Venus into which no woman was permitted to enter. At Troezen, Ascrea also has a temple.

<margin>Apaturia.</margin> **Apaturia** or **The Adventurous.** <note>The name *Apaturia* actually stems from the Greek word for "deceit."</note> In Muscovy <note>referring to the region of the Black Sea/Azov</note>, where Phanagoria once stood, Venus had a very magnificent temple, the reason for which is told somewhat mockingly. The giants wished to rape Venus; she called upon Hercules and made a deal with the giants that she would submit to each of them one after another. Hercules waited for the appointed giants and killed them. From this, a festival or feast arose, which also commemorates the time in Athens when the son of King Sitalces of Thrace was accepted as a citizen. This festival lasted four days. First, on the eve, the members of the festival came together, drank, and had a meal; on the second day, they sacrificed to Jupiter the Companion and Pallas; on the third day, they took small boys and girls into the brotherhood; on the fourth day, they held the post-festival. This festival is also said to have originated from that event.

## The Fifth Book.

...had, which they called the Deception or the Cheat of the Companions <note>original: "Abenteütrig oder Bscheiß den gsellē." This refers to the festival of Apaturia, from the Greek *apate*, meaning "deceit."</note>. For when the Athenians came into conflict over the spot called Colenis, which the Boeotians also wanted, Xanthus stepped forward on behalf of the Boeotians and challenged the Athenian king, Thymoetes, to a duel. The King, believing Xanthus was of unequal standing and birth to himself, refused the combat. Then a Messenian named Melanthus stepped forward and accepted the challenge. As they came onto the battlefield, Melanthus said to Xanthus during the heat of the fight—I know not how fairly—"You have it easy, for there is a helper behind you who is jumping to your aid." Xanthus turned around to see who this might be, and in that moment, Melanthus struck him dead. Therefore, this combat was called the "Deception of the Comrade."

<margin>Melinea Castania. Lycophron calls her the Brown and Chestnut-colored one.</margin> **Cluacina.** <term>Cluere</term> <note>original: "Cluere," a Latin root usually meaning "to cleanse" or "to be famed," but here the author links it to conflict.</note> among the Latins means the same as "to fight" among us; at the place where the Sabines and Romans fought, until through the intercession of the women and their running between them, they laid down their weapons, the Romans built a temple to her. It stood not far from the main market <note>The Roman Forum</note> in Rome.

<margin>Anadyomene.</margin> <note>Greek: "Rising from the sea."</note> In the Chapel of Caesar, Augustus hung a painted image of Venus under this name in honor of his father [Julius Caesar]. When this painting became somewhat decayed at the bottom, no painter was skillful enough to restore it. The panel also perished from age; Nero had another painted and hung in its place, which was made by Dorotheus, a famous painter.

<margin>Mechanites. Of all kinds. Because of the strange gestures that lovers use in their passion, this name is given to her, as if she were prepared for every business.</margin> <note>Greek: *Mechanitis*, meaning "The Contriver" or "The Deviser."</note> **Adikos** <note>Greek: "The Unjust"</note>, **Baiotis**, **Eleymon** <note>Greek: "The Merciful"</note>, **Erientes**, **Enchion**, **Antherio**, **Endoso**, **Epicoon**, **Milites** <note>Latin: "The Soldierly"</note>, **Erototrophos** <note>Greek: "Nourisher of Loves"</note>. In Libya she is called the Unjust; among the Syracusans in Syracuse, the "Thrusting One"; those who sleep or lie; the "Burning-Heat" at Chalcedon; elsewhere the "Lovely One"; in Cyprus the "Anointed One"; at Knossos the "Horse"; at Carthage the "Judge," and the "Sweet One." Also, the "Mother of Love."

<margin>The Hospitable. Momphitica.</margin> In Egypt, Helen erected a temple to her when she was a guest of Proteus. Likewise, she was honored in the form of a cow around the Caicus river.

<margin>Meneis Frugi, Fruta.</margin> She also held these names among the Romans, as the mother of Aeneas, the "Domestic" and "Fruit-bearer" <note>original: "häußlich vnnd Obserin," from *frugi* (useful/thrifty) and *fruta* (fruit/produce).</note>. Where St. Barbara’s Church now stands in Rome, she also had a temple.

<margin>Eleusinia.</margin> Not far from Thyreatis <note>OCR: "Turgeta"</note>, she also had a temple where Hercules was healed by Aesculapius after being wounded.

<margin>Inonia Olympia.</margin> At Sparta, she had a temple and a very old image where mothers offer sacrifices when they marry off their daughters.

<margin>Nympha.</margin> <note>Greek: "The Bride."</note> At Troezen, Theseus built a temple to Venus under this name because Helen had become his. In Delos, there was once an image of Venus whose hand was broken off from age; at the bottom, by the feet, it was square. Daedalus made this same image and gave it to Ariadne, and Theseus carried it away with him, gave it as a portion to Apollo, and set it up so that the image would not constantly renew his memory <note>meaning his painful memory of Ariadne after he abandoned her.</note>. At Patras, there were two chapels to Venus: in one, an image that fishermen found in a net while fishing. The other was made of wood, except that the face, feet, and hands were of marble. At Lemnos, Pelops made an image of her from myrtle, which he had vowed when he wished to race for Hippodamia. Also at Aegium and other places, which would take long to recount and are yet unnecessary.

# Of Pagan Gods

<margin>Golgia.</margin> Golgia was a city in Cyprus where she was worshipped.

<margin>Pontia.</margin> Pontia, "The Marine One." Also *Soligena* <note>original: "Soligena," likely meaning sun-born or sea-born</note> and *Limenea* <note>meaning "of the harbor"</note>. Since she was born from the sea (which in Latin is called *mare*), as they say, she held these names. Virgins and widows who wished to marry, praying that she might grant them a good husband, offered sacrifices to her. At Lepanto, she has a temple inside a cave.

<margin>Cypris.</margin> Cypris. Cypria. The island of Cyprus is such a womanish, lush <note>original: "feyg," literally "fig," a metaphor for softness or over-ripeness</note>, and soft land that even the most valiant men who arrive there fall somewhat into lust and weakness. All manner of unchastity occurred there before the Venetian rule; indeed, it was a notorious island for all kinds of debauchery due to its natural climate. It is said that the trade of women's bodies began there and was not considered a shame, where young daughters would earn their dowries with the work of their hands. Thus, this island specifically gave its name to Venus.

<margin>The Bald One.</margin> The Bald One <note>original: "Die Glatzend"</note>. When the Germans and Gauls took Rome in the three hundred and sixtieth year of its founding, and only the Capitol remained standing, those in the garrison had no more sinews left for their bows and no rope for their slings. The women stepped forward and allowed sinews to be made from their long hair; because of this, a temple was later erected to this Venus and the name was given.

<margin>All Golden, Golden, Silver-footed.</margin> All Golden, Golden, Silver-footed. The poets attribute golden-yellow hair and beautiful legs to her, indicating this through the costly and lovely appearance of gold and silver.

<margin>Paphia.</margin> Paphia. After the destruction of Troy, Agapenor was cast onto Cyprus by a storm at sea. He came to Paphos and built a temple to Venus there. This Agapenor was a grandson of Lycurgus and a son of Ancaeus; his daughter Laodice erected a temple to her at Tegea. Some say Aerias built this temple for Venus. Tacitus says Uranus established it and Cinaras consecrated it. The goddess herself, when she was born from the sea, chose her resting place there. Her image was not a human figure, but a crude pillar that was pointed like a needle <note>referring to the famous conical black stone or baetyl worshipped at Paphos</note>. Some, like Phurnutus <note>original: "Phornutus," the Stoic philosopher Cornutus</note>, give her this name because of the weak, wavering words of suitors, though these words are sometimes so clear that they even overcome wise people.

<margin>Acrea, Ascrea.</margin> Acrea, Ascrea. On the island of Cyprus there was also a city called Carpacia, near which was a promontory named Acreum. Upon it was a temple of Venus into which no woman was permitted to enter. At Troezen, Ascrea also has a temple.

<margin>Apaturia.</margin> Apaturia, the Deceptive One <note>original: "Abenteurig," here used in the sense of a trickster</note>. In Muscovy <note>referring to the region of the Cimmerian Bosphorus</note>, where Mapattrinica—once called Phanagoria—now stands, Venus had a magnificent temple. The reason for this is told in a somewhat mocking way: the Giants wanted to rape Venus, so she called upon Hercules. She made a bargain with the Giants, saying she would submit to each one, one after the other. Hercules waited for the appointed ones and killed them. For this reason, a festival or holiday arose, on which it is also remembered that at Athens, the son of King Sitalces of Thrace was accepted as a citizen. This festival lasted four days. First, on the eve, the festival companions came together, drank, and had a meal; on the second day, they sacrificed to Jupiter the Companion and to Pallas; on the third day, they took young boys and girls into the brotherhood; on the fourth day, they held the after-celebration. This festival is also said to have had its origin from this event.

# The Fifth Book.

<note>This section explains the origin of the *Apaturia* festival, which translates to "The Deception."</note> This name arose because they called the event the "Trick" or the "Deception" <note>original: "Abenteütrig oder Bscheiß"</note> among the companions. For when the Athenians were in a dispute over the village of Oenoe <note>original: "Colents"</note>, which the Boeotians also claimed, Xanthus stepped forward on behalf of the Boeotians and challenged the Athenian King, Thymoetes, to a duel. The King, believing Xanthus to be of unequal status and lineage to himself, refused the combat. Then a Messenian named Melanthus stepped forward and accepted the duel. As they arrived on the battlefield, Melanthus shouted to Xanthus—I know not by what right—"You have it easy, for there is a helper standing behind you who is about to leap upon me!" Xanthus turned around to see who it might be, and in that moment, Melanthus struck him dead. Because he had so thoroughly tricked his companion, this combat was named after the "Deception."

**Melinea Castania.** Lycophron <note>a Greek poet</note> calls her the "Chestnut-brown One" <note>original: "Braun vñ Kastenfarb"</note>.

**C**luacina. To the Latins, *cluere* <note>original: "Cluere," meaning to cleanse or to fight</note> is the same as "to strive" among us. At the place where the Sabines and Romans fought, and where through the intercession of the women—who ran between them—the dispute was settled, the Romans built her a temple. It stood not far from the main market in Rome.

**A**nadyomene <note>meaning "Rising from the Sea"</note>. In the Chapel of Caesar, Augustus hung a portrait of Venus under this name, dedicated to his father. This painting was slightly damaged at the bottom, and no painter was deemed skilled enough to repair it. Because the panel had also decayed due to age, Nero had it replaced with a painting by Dorotheus, a famous artist.

**A**echanites <note>likely *Amechania*, the Resourceful or Irresistible</note>. On account of all kinds of strange gestures that lovers use in their romance, this name was given to her, as if she were prepared for every kind of business.

**D**ikos, Baiotis, Eleymon, Erientes, Enchion, Antheris, Endoso, Epicoon, Milites, Erototrophos. In Libya, she is called "The Unjust One" <note>original: "Die Vngreche"</note>; among the Syracusans in Syracuse, "The Cast-out One" <note>original: "die gstoße"</note> who sleeps or lies down; "The Lustful One" <note>original: "Die Brunhizig"</note> at Chalcedon; and elsewhere "The Lovely One" <note>original: "die Lieblich"</note>. In Cyprus, she is "The Anointed One" <note>original: "die angstrichẽ"</note>; at Knossos, "The Horse" <note>original: "die Roß"</note>; at Carthage, "The Judge" <note>original: "die Richterin"</note> or "The Feet" <note>original: "die fůeß"</note>. Likewise, "The Love-bringer" <note>original: "die liebzeügerin"</note>.

**T**he Hospitable One. Momemphita. In Egypt, Helen erected a temple to her when she was a guest of Proteus. Similarly, she was worshipped in the form of a cow around the Caycus River.

**A**eneis frugi, Fruta <note>The Fruitful or Domestic</note>. She also held these names among the Romans as the Mother of Aeneas, the Domestic and Provider. Where the Church of St. Barbara now stands in Rome, she also once had a temple.

**E**leusinia. Not far from Turgeta, she had a temple where Hercules was healed by Aesculapius <note>the god of medicine</note> after being wounded.

**D**uonia Olympia. In Sparta, she had a temple and a very ancient statue where mothers would offer sacrifices when they married off their daughters.

**N**ympha <note>The Bride</note>. At Troezen, Theseus built a temple to Venus under this name because Helen had been given to him. In Delos, there was once a statue of Venus whose hand had broken off from old age; at the bottom of the feet, it was square. This statue was made by Daedalus, given to Ariadne, and carried away by Theseus. He dedicated it to Apollo and set it up there so that the sight of the statue would not constantly renew his memories <note>of Ariadne</note>. At Patras, there were two chapels to Venus: in one, a statue that fishermen had found in a net while fishing; the other was made of wood, except that the face, feet, and hands were of marble. At Lemnos, Pelops made a statue of her out of myrtle, which he had promised when he wished to race for Hippodamia. In Aegium and other places, there are more, but it would take too long to recount and is unnecessary.

V: Things go according to their wishes, high priests, many benefices <note>church appointments providing income</note>.
VI: Unhappy marriage, those who mistreat [others] in birth, otherwise...
VII: Fortunate old age, late wives, notorious for harlotry before...
VIII: Late or not very good wife, little good, driven by a great burden...
IX: Null, forest, wooden-shoe bridges, those whom the devil constantly rides <note>a phrase for being plagued by bad luck or impulses</note>.

XI: Unbearable <note>or perhaps sterile</note>, those who hang onto loose women <note>original: "schlepsack," a derogatory term for a low-status woman or harlot</note>, gracious, pretty.
XII: Anxiety because of women, whom they take from the common house <note>original: "gmeine hauß," meaning a brothel</note>.

# Calculated among the seven wandering stars as the stargazers say thereon

Regarding weather and various other powers:

**Lifespan**
- Good: 81 years <note>In ancient astrology, 81 years is considered the "Greatest Year" or maximum natural lifespan associated with Venus.</note>
- Average: 45 years, 6 months
- Bad: 8 years or 5 months and [some] hours.

**Time**
- Its own specific cycle lasts 10 years and 9 months.

**Planetary Influences:**
- It holds for eight months: Luck and joy in marriage.
- With Saturn, she gives 30 months: Strife in marriage, separation by death.
- With Jupiter, she gives 7 months: A joyful time but bad rumors.
- With Mars, she gives 15 months: Fear, distress, adultery, and other burdens.
- With the Sun, she gives 8 months: Separates a marriage with danger to life.
- With Mercury, she gives 20 months: Profit, joy, and pleasure.
- With the Moon, she gives 30 months: Secret fear and great misery.

**The Year**
- On her own, she provides a good, quiet, and peaceful year; however, expect some earthquakes and misfortune where she has "bad companions" <note>This refers to Venus forming difficult aspects with "malefic" planets like Saturn or Mars.</note>.

**Zodiac Signs:**
- Aries signifies rain.
- Taurus: Abundance and feuds.
- Gemini: Abundance and a good year.
- Cancer: Good air and peace.
- Leo: A good year, yet cattle will die.
- Virgo: Peace and pleasure.
- Libra: Abundance and peace.
- Scorpio: Quiet years.
- Sagittarius: Good air, abundance, and peace.
- Capricorn: Wet weather and a cold winter.
- Aquarius: Abundance and a good year.
- Pisces: Little wine, otherwise a good year.

**Actions**
- Venus with the Moon in <term>Trine (△)</term> <note>An aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, usually considered very harmonious.</note>: Taking a wife, wooing, sexual intercourse, and hiring servants.
- Venus with the Moon in <term>Sextile (✶)</term> <note>A harmonious 60-degree aspect.</note>: Marrying, wooing, dressing in beautiful clothes, and addressing the nobility.
- Venus with the Moon in <term>Square (□)</term> <note>A challenging 90-degree aspect.</note>: Marrying as mentioned above.
- Venus with the Moon in <term>Conjunction (☌)</term> <note>When two planets are in the same position.</note>: Marrying, styling one's hair, and as mentioned above.

# Vulcan.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting Vulcan at his forge. Vulcan is shown as a bearded man wearing a simple tunic and a soft cap, standing by a stone anvil. He holds a piece of metal on the anvil with tongs and raises a large hammer in his right hand. In the background, a furnace with glowing embers is visible. To the left, a large peacock (associated with Juno) stands watching the scene.</image-desc>

By the Greeks, he is called **Hephaestus** <note>original: "Ephestios"</note> and regarded as the god of radiance or light. The Latins have sometimes called him **Vulcan** <note>original: "Volcanum"</note> due to the fury of the fire. It is said that Juno conceived him from the wind without a man; he is also said to have been misshapen, cast out of heaven immediately, raised by apes, and afterwards became a blacksmith on the island of **Lemnos**. Some say he is the son of Jupiter, begotten with Juno. And while Jupiter is sometimes taken for the true elemental fire, and Juno for the other [element, the air] which is ignited from that same fire in the sky, he is **Vulcan**—that is, the fire found in wood and kindling, coming from them. That he is limping and crooked signifies that fire—manifesting through the clouds in lightning, thunder, and the like—does not descend straight down but divides itself into flames, now high, then low, just like a limping gait. That he was raised by apes is taken from the nature and character of that animal: because they wish to imitate everything humans do and attempt various things, just as fire brings all kinds of artistic works into being. And because the islands of **Lemnos** (or **Stalimene** <note>original: "Scalimene"</note>, as they are called now) are constantly plagued by thunder and lightning, it was said he fell there. That he represents the blacksmith of the gods means that almost all artistic works must pass through fire. His workshop is therefore on the islands of **Lipari** <note>original: "Lypara"</note> and **Vulcano**, because a constant sulfurous, burning steam rises there.

Cicero counts several **Vulcans**: the first was born of **Caelum** <note>original: "Cölum," meaning the Heavens</note>, whose children were **Apollo** and **Minerva**. The second was begotten by the **Nile**; he was called **Opas** <note>original: "Opas," an Egyptian name for Ptah</note> by the Egyptians, and was kept as a protector. The third they call a son of **Jupiter** and **Juno**, this very same blacksmith. The fourth had **Menalius** for a father, a king of the **Vulcanian** islands. Regarding this **Vulcan**, you also have information in the writings of **Diodorus**.

# The Fifth Book.

His image has a **blue hat** on, to signify that the true fire is in the heavens; which, when it strikes down here and cannot remain without a fuel source, is then "limping" <note>This refers to the mythological lameness of Vulcan, interpreted here as fire being less "perfect" or stable on earth than in the celestial realm.</note>.

Many wives are attributed to him: **Maia**, **Majesty** <note>original: "Majestatem"</note>, **Venus**, and one of the **Graces** <note>original: "hold sälikeyten"</note>. All of this may be because there were many "Vulcans" <note>Referring to the historical theory that several figures were merged into one god</note>, and perhaps for that reason it was said that everything made with such skill should be called graceful, Venereal <note>associated with beauty</note>, majestic, and delightful.

**Ennius** <note>An early Roman poet</note>. Because Vulcan was taken to represent the air from which the lightning or thunderbolts come, it is said that because of his misshapenness—as mentioned above—he was thrust out of heaven and thrown down into **Lemnos**, from which he takes this name <note>Lemnius</note>. From this island comes **Sealed Earth** <note>original: "Terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay used since antiquity</note> which is sold in the **Apothecary** (I must use some foreign words here against my will) which stops bleeding and drives away poison. More on this in another place.

**Mulciber, the Iron-drawer**. So named because he, as a learned craftsman, taught how one should make iron soft and malleable.

**Of Etna** <note>original: "Ethneus"</note>. In Sicily, where the mountain **Mongibello** <note>The local Sicilian name for Mount Etna</note> stands, which either steams or rumbles. There, Vulcan had a temple surrounded by a grove of fruitful trees; in the middle of the temple was an inextinguishable fire. Certain dogs guarded this temple and no one else; whoever went in there having confessed and done penance with devotion—as the saying goes—the dogs did nothing to him, but fawned upon him. However, they would sense an impure, wicked rogue and tear him apart. This mountain, **Etna**, has frequently cast out entire flowing streams of fire or ignited sulfur, such as at the time when the Greeks first invaded this island, under the consulship of **Fulvius Flaccus** and **Quintus Calpurnius Piso**, one hundred and thirty years before the birth of Christ. In the time of **Augustus**, it made itself terrifyingly known. Scarcely nine years after that, it happened again. Three years after that, it did such great damage that the Romans waived the taxes for the people of **Catania** <note>original: "Catinensern"</note> for ten years. In the year 254, and again in 1165, always in the month of **February** <note>original: "Hornung"</note>, it erupted cruelly. Afterward, in the year 1329 after the birth of Christ, it erupted four times and overflowed like a spring. Just recently, seventeen years ago—two years after I, **Johann Herold**, returned home from Sicily—it did unspeakably great damage, entirely burning several villages, and covering and darkening all of Sicily and **Calabria** with ash, stench, and smoke.

**Powerful in Fire**. Because some attribute to him the invention of fire, or even that he is fire itself, but for **Jupiter** he forges the lightning bolts; thus he received this name. Also, three smith-servants were given to him: **Brontes**, **Steropes**, and **Pyracmon**, of whom mention was made in the section on **Apollo**. I also well believe that these names come from certain places situated around this mountain, of which **Brontes** is still present.

**Ptah** <note>original: "Phebas," likely a corruption of "Phthas," the Egyptian deity associated with Vulcan</note>. The Egyptians honored him under this name, and it may perhaps be the one whom **Cicero** called **Opas** (unless his books have been corrupted by poor copying).

**Kloos**. The **Dorians** gave him this name, as **Hesychius** <note>A Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> reports.

# Vulcan.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Vulcan working in a smithy. He is shown bearded, wearing a hat, and striking an object on an anvil with a hammer. A brick forge with fire is visible behind him.</image-desc>

By the Greeks, he is called **Hephaestus** <note>original: "Epheſtios"</note> and is regarded as the god of shine or light. The Romans <note>original: "Latiner"</note> sometimes called him **Vulcan**, from the wildness and violence of fire. It is said that **Juno** conceived him from the wind without a husband; he was also said to be misshapen and was cast out of heaven immediately. He was raised by apes <note>A unique mythological variation; typically, he is raised by sea-nymphs. The author explains the "ape" connection as a metaphor for mimicry below.</note> and later became a smith on the island of **Lemnos**. Some say he is the son of **Jupiter**, fathered with Juno. 

But because Jupiter is sometimes taken to represent the true elemental fire and Juno represents the air, it is said that Vulcan—that is, the fire found in wood and flint—comes from them when they ignite within the atmosphere. The fact that he is limping and crooked signifies that when fire descends from the clouds in the form of lightning and thunder, it does not fall straight. Instead, as it divides into flames, it flickers now high, then low, just like a limping man walks. 

The story that he was raised by apes is derived from the nature and character of that animal, which wishes to mimic everything humans do; fire, similarly, "imitates" or undertakes many kinds of work, bringing all sorts of things into being. And because the islands of Lemnos (or **Stalimene**, as they are now called) were constantly plagued by thunder and lightning, it was said that he fell to earth there. That he is known as the smith of the gods signifies that almost all skillful works must pass through the fire. His workshop is therefore placed on the islands of **Lipari** and **Vulcano**, because a sulfurous, burning steam constantly rises from them.

**Cicero** counts several different "Vulcans": the first was born of **Caelum** <note>The Sky</note>, and his children were **Apollo** and **Minerva**. The second was fathered by the **Nile**; he was called **Opas** <note>A reference to the Egyptian Ptah</note> and was honored by the Egyptians as a protector. The third, they say, is the son of Jupiter and Juno—this is the smith himself. The fourth had **Menalium** as his father, who was a king of the Vulcan Islands. You may also find information regarding Vulcan in the writings of **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note>.

<header>The Fifth Book</header>

His image has a blue hat on, to signify that the true fire is in heaven; which, if it strikes down and cannot remain without tools, it is limping. <note>The author interprets Vulcan's limp as a metaphor for celestial fire (lightning) needing physical materials to continue burning on earth.</note>

Many wives are given to him: **Maia**, **Majesty** <note>original: "Maiestatem"</note>, **Venus**, and one of the **Graces** <note>original: "hold fälikeyten"</note>. All this may be because there were many "Vulcans" <note>Ancient mythographers often suggested there were multiple figures who shared the same name across different eras</note>, and perhaps it is said for this reason: that everything made so artistically is called lovely, Venus-like, majestic, and delightful.

**Ennius** <note>original: "Emnius"</note>. Because Vulcan is taken in place of the air from which the lightning bolt or thunder-arrow comes, it is said—because of his deformity as mentioned above—that he was pushed out of heaven and thrown down into Lemnos; from this he has this name. From this island comes **Sealed Earth** <note>original: "Terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay used since antiquity</note> which is sold in the apothecary (I must use several foreign words here against my will) which stops blood and drives away poison. Of this, more in another place.

**Volciber** or **Iron-drawer**. Because he, as a master artist, taught how one should make iron soft and pliable.

**Of Etna** <note>original: "Aethneus"</note>. In Sicily, where the mountain **Mongibello** <note>The local Sicilian name for Mount Etna</note> stands, which either smokes or rumbles; there Vulcan had a temple, surrounded by a grove <note>original: "Dhan"</note> of fruitful trees; in the middle of the temple was an unquenchable fire. Certain dogs guarded this temple and no one else; whoever went in and had confessed and done penance with devotion (as they say), the dogs did nothing to him, but flattered him; but when they felt the presence of impure, evil rogues, they tore them apart. This mountain, **Etna**, has many times cast out flowing streams of fire or ignited sulfur; as at the time when the Greeks first invaded this island, under the consulship <note>original: "Burgermeysterthumb"</note> of Fulvius Flaccus and Q. Calpurnius Piso, one hundred and thirty years before the birth of Christ. In the time of Augustus, it made itself dreadfully noticed. Scarcely nine years after that, it happened again. Three years after that, it did such great damage that the Romans remitted the taxes of the people of Catania <note>original: "Catinensern"</note> for ten years. In the year 254; also in the year 1165, always in **February** <note>original: "Hornung"</note>, it erupted cruelly; thereafter in the year of our Lord 1329, it made four eruptions and overflowed like a spring. Most recently, seventeen years ago—two years after I, **Johann Herold**, returned home from Sicily—it did unspeakably great damage, completely burning several villages, and covering and darkening all of Sicily and **Calabria** with ash, stench, and smoke.

**Powerful over Fire**. Because some credit him with the invention of fire—even fire itself—but since he forges the lightning bolts for Jupiter, he received this name. Also, three smith-assistants were given to him: **Brontes**, **Steropes**, and **Pyracmon**, of whom mention was made under the section on Apollo. I also believe that these names come from certain places situated around this mountain, of which **Brontes** is still present.

**Phthas**. The Egyptians worshiped him under this name, and it may perhaps be the one who was called **Opas** by **Cicero** (if his books have not been corrupted by poor copying).

**Eloos**. The **Dorians** gave him this name, as **Hesychius** reports.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Vulcan's various epithets and his mythological deeds, specifically focusing on his lameness, his role in the creation of Pandora, and his interactions with other gods like Juno, Bacchus, Venus, and Mars.</meta>

<header>Of Heathen Gods</header>

**Stilt-foot**, **Slow-foot** <note>original: *Tardipes*</note>. **Lame** <note>original: *Claudus*</note>. **Limp-leg**, **Stilt-foot**, **Shuffler**, and similar names he has because of his fallen hip and uneven gait, although some call him **the one who hops on both legs** <note>original: *ἀμφιγυήeis* (amphiguēeis)</note>.

**Famous-minded**, **Famous-artisan** <note>original: *Clytometes*, *Clytotechnes*</note>. **Strong-handed**, **Art-judge** <note>original: *Craterocheir*, *Technodictos*</note>. The poets in their poems give Vulcan these names for the sake of his noble art, which shows itself in manifold ways in the work of fire; for they also say that he and **Minerva** <note>The goddess of wisdom and craftsmanship</note> taught the people, who previously lived in huts, how to build houses; therefore he is called the **Noble Artist**, or **Noble Master-Workman**, **Mighty of Fist**, and **Judge of Works**. This Vulcan is said to have made **Lady Algaab**, whom they call **Pandora**, which woman was beyond measure beautiful in form, gesture, speech, and all things. When Jupiter sent her into the world, he gave her a box in which all misery was locked. When she offered said box to **Prometheus**, he would not accept it, and also forbade his brother **Epimetheus** from taking any gift from her when he was not at home; but curiosity <note>original: *für witz*</note> overcame his command. Epimetheus, in the absence of his brother, took the box and opened it to see what was inside; thus all misery and all plagues rushed out. He could hardly get the lid back on, so that only **Hope** remained within. This is given to be understood as: in human life, there is nothing that does not have its joy and sorrow, and hope alone sustains the rest.

In **Rome**, at the **Flaminian Racecourse**, he has his temple, where also the dogs were sextons as they were at **Etna** <note>Ancient sources mention that dogs guarded the temple of Vulcan on Mount Etna, being friendly to the pious but driving away the wicked</note>; his festival was on the twentieth of the **Month of Fallow** <note>original: *Brachmonadt*; an old Germanic name for June</note>. In **Athens**, he was painted thus: because **Juno** had thrown him from heaven, he forged a seat that had hidden clamps to ensnare whoever sat in it. He gave it to Juno; she could no longer get off it once she had sat in it. All the gods were unable to persuade him in heaven to release her, except for **Bacchus**, who was on good terms with him; he filled him full of wine and brought him to the point that he freed her. This signifies that wine opens all secrets. He also has a chapel in Athens with an altar; in **Olympus** also an altar; in **Lacedaemonia** <note>The region of Sparta</note> an image showing him freeing his mother. The **Scepter of Agamemnon** was made by Vulcan and was honored at **Chaeronea**. The poem that **Venus** endured the unshapeliness of her husband Vulcan, yet broke the marriage with **Mars**; Vulcan, when he noticed this, caught both in the act with a wonderfully made net or yarn; this signifies that adultery brings many, and indeed the greatest, shames. It has certainly several other meanings, such as that in war, a boldness and power should be won and maintained, yet with some friendliness and loveliness; also other natural things, which I omit here for the sake of brevity.

<header>The Fifth Book.</header>

# Vesta.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the goddess Vesta. She stands within a round-topped frame, holding a cornucopia filled with fruits and greenery in her right hand and a leafy branch or staff in her left. A hilly landscape with trees is visible in the background.</image-desc>

This goddess was honored and held in very high esteem by the ancients, sometimes representing the Earth and sometimes representing Fire. Some give her this name because she "stands fast" <note>The author is connecting the name Vesta to the German word *stehen* or Latin *stare*, meaning to stand</note>. Some say she adorns or clothes the ground with flowers, herbs, fruits, and roots. Plato calls the world the house of the gods, and Vesta is the one who stands unmoving within it—that is, the Earth.

Those who take her to be Fire do so because fire and its power keep all things in the world firm, and they generate and bring all things forth.

**The Virgin** <note>original: *Virgo*</note>. She is also called the Virgin because she brings nothing forth on her own. The reason is that fire is in constant motion and cannot produce anything by itself; but when something else is added to it, then it is productive. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, an ancient Greek historian</note> also mentions her; you may look him up there. Some say she is the daughter of **Saturn**; others say she is the wife of **Uranus**; and some give her to **Janus** as a wife.

<margin>Abith, Norchia, Labithi <note>Etruscan names for deities associated with Vesta or fate</note></margin>
The Tyrrhenians <note>Another name for the Etruscans of ancient Italy</note> honored her under these names, as did the Scythians. It is said she is the first and the last to be born of herself. This comes from the fact that everything on earth comes from the earth and must finally become earth again.

<margin>Fire.</margin>
The Romans kept a fire constantly burning and unextinguished; the Athenians did the same in the **Prytaneion** <note>The seat of government in ancient Greek cities where the holy fire of the state was kept</note>. In the temple at **Delphi**, it was not permitted for the fire to go out. The Persians constantly carried it before their king. These fires, if they should happen to go out, had to be relighted only by the sun, and were honored in the name of Vesta.

<margin>Counselor.</margin>
Her chapel or altar was almost always located in the town halls; for this reason, she received this name.

<margin>Threcia.</margin>
Hesychius <note>A Greek grammarian</note> calls her by this name but does not explain the reason why. In Athens and Oropus (which is now called Sucamino), Vesta had her image; in Hermione (now called Santa Maria), she had a temple in which there was no image, but only a fire-altar.

The **Nuns of Vesta** <note>original: *Nonnen Veste*. The author uses the contemporary term "nuns" to describe the Vestal Virgins</note> were held in high honor and regarded with great majesty by the Romans. Their convent lay on the Palatine Hill not far from the Capitol, where our **Lady of Grace** <note>original: *de Gratia*. Referring to the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie</note> now stands. The chapel of Vesta was round; by day, everyone was allowed to enter, but by night, no male person was permitted. There was no image there, only the fire, as was said before. At first, King **Numa** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome</note> ordained four of them: **Gegania**, **Verenia**, **Canuleia**, and **Tarpeia**. Later, when the city was divided into six tribes, each tribe wanted to have one, so two more were added. With time and power, the number grew until it reached twenty. Their superior was the **High Priestess** <note>original: *Bischouin*, literally "female bishop"</note>, who was the highest among them. The High Priest chose them; they had to be from a noble, free lineage, of entirely good reputation, chaste and pure, and modest girls. He took them from their fathers by force—oh, with such reluctance the fathers had to let them go—unless the father was himself a Bishop or Priest...

soothsayer. If a father has more than three sons but does not have the same number of daughters, she could also be chosen; likewise if her sister was already a nun <note>The text uses the term *Non*, anachronistically applying the Christian term "nun" to the Vestal Virgins</note>. She could not be under six years of age, nor over ten; she must still have both father and mother. When the Bishop <note>original: *Bischoff*; referring here to the Pontifex Maximus or High Priest</note> received her, he did not call her by her own name, but called her **Amata** <note>original: *Amatā*; Latin for "Beloved"</note>, for the first Vestal nun is said to have been so named. These women had to guard the fire of **Vesta**, taking turns day and night, washing and tending to it so that it would not be extinguished. They had to remain perpetual virgins and pure, for which reason they were held in such high honor that they were regarded as holy relics. Whatever they said or commanded to be done, no court, law, guild, or mayor dared to oppose. As soon as she became a nun, her father and mother no longer had any power over her; she could manage her own property and bequeath it to whomever she wished without any authorities or guardians, though they inherited nothing unless it was specifically bequeathed. The High Priestess among them was permitted to give testimony in court, and her word carried as much weight as a man's. If an uprising or misunderstanding arose among the citizens, they were the ones who could walk through unharmed to intervene and propose a settlement or peace. If something was done amiss, they were used to plead for mercy from the authorities. If anyone wished to keep something secret—such as a legacy or a last will—that he did not want opened until a certain time, it was deposited with them. No one could even leave the vestibule <note>original: *vorschopff*</note> without the church servants walking before them with small staffs. If one became ill, or had to go out for business, many of the noblest and most pious women were assigned to her to accompany her through the streets. The Mayor, the City Governor, the Magistrate, and all lords of office or command—indeed the entire Council—gave way to them in the street. If they encountered a man who had committed a capital crime and was being led to his execution, he could no longer be put to death. If an enslaved man who had been purchased ran away and was caught before leaving the city, these nuns could petition for him to be set free. If someone intended to do wrong or deny justice to another, they could intervene with the judge and the authorities, and pass judgment themselves; no one was allowed to appeal it, nor do or arrange anything against it.

For thirty years she had to remain a virgin and was bound to this service for that length of time. For the first ten years, she learned what the mysteries consisted of. For the next ten years, she performed those same duties. For the last ten years, she taught the young ones and guided them. After these years had passed, she could request another religious office, marry, have children, or remain there and complete her service as a nun. The city paid them a salary and provided for them.

If they let the fire go out, the whole city was in great sorrow and held it to be a bad omen that would bring great misfortune. The High Priest announced it to the people; all shops were closed, a holiday was observed, and no work was done until the fire was lit anew. The nun who had been asleep or had let it go out was scourged by the High Priest until she bled, in a secret, hidden place. In their presence, no one dared to do or say anything shameful, whether through gestures or words. Once a year, the one chosen by lot went to the Choir-King <note>original: *Chor Küng*; likely a reference to the Rex Sacrorum</note> and the High Priest, reminding and exhorting him to take diligent care that everything pertaining to the service of the gods <note>original: *Gößendienst*</note> was fulfilled. Up to this point, it was a good thing to be a nun. But if one committed harlotry <note>original: *hůret*; referring here to a breach of the vow of chastity</note>, the priests were the ones who judged her; no one else was allowed to lay a hand on her. The man who committed the act was scourged to death in the open market. She, however, was led to a place called the Scoundrel’s Field <note>original: *Schelmē platz*; historically the *Campus Sceleratus*</note>. There, a deep hole was dug, with steps leading down like a staircase. At the bottom, a small bed or couch was prepared; a lamp burned there, and they placed some bread, a little milk, a vessel of water, and a jar of oil. The transgressor was deconsecrated; they stripped her of her veil and nun’s clothing and placed her on a funeral bier with wailing...

## Neptune.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the Roman god Neptune (Poseidon) as a bearded, muscular man holding a trident. From "darkening" and "beclouding" (for moisture covers the earth with vapor) is how this god is said to have received his name <note>The author is following an old etymological theory linking *Neptunus* to *nubes* (clouds) or *obnubere* (to veil/cover)</note>. And since his name in Greek is **Poseidon**, some believe he reminds people that the first humans drank only water <note>original: *vttel wasser*; "eitel wasser" or pure water</note>...

## Neptunus.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the Roman sea god Neptune. He is shown as a bearded man holding a trident, seated in a shell-like chariot that is being pulled through turbulent waves by two hippocamps (mythical sea horses). In the background, other figures, including a siren or mermaid, are visible in the water.</image-desc>

This god is said to take his name from "darkening" and "mistiness" (for moisture covers the earth with haze). As Varro and Arnobius <note>early Christian and Roman scholars who wrote on the nature of the gods</note> say; Cicero maintains that Neptune "stuffs" <note>original: *stopffe*; a folk etymology linking *Neptunus* to *nabre* or *nāre*, to swim or flow</note> the ground with his feet, and from this he has his name. Socrates claims it is because the sea is an obstacle, so that one cannot travel around the floor of the earth on foot, thus he is called Posydeumon, meaning "foot-band." <note>A Greek etymological pun: *Poseidon* interpreted as *pous* (foot) and *desmos* (bond or shackle)</note> And because his name is Poseidona in Greek, some believe he reminds people that the first humans were mere water

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Neptune’s various epithets and their mythological origins. It follows a list of titles introduced on the previous page, detailing his association with the element of water, his connection to bulls and horses, and specific geographical cult sites in Greece and Rome.</meta>

# Of the Heathen Gods

...drank water. Fulgentius <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Latin mythographer from the late 5th century</note> considers him to be the third element—water—and his name is derived from the fact that one may see oneself in it as if in a mirror. The trident <note>original: *Gehrn*; literally a spear or wedge, here used for the three-pronged spear of Neptune</note> was given to him because water has three powers: it softens, it drenches, and it generates.

**The Liquid.** He is called "the Flowing One" by the poets, or "the Softener," because of his fluid nature.

**The Second Jupiter.** Because Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto are three brothers, and in the division of the world Jupiter received the Heavens, Neptune the Sea, and Pluto the Underworld to rule, he is called the "second" or "other" Jupiter. **The King.** Regarding this, you have the reference in the section on Pallas <note>Athena</note>, who is called "the Civic One."

**Trident-bearer**, *Orsotrieras*, *Aglaotrienas*. Fishermen use these tridents to catch large fish, and since Neptune was regarded as their helper, he was called the **Trident-bearer** based on the meaning described above.

**Trident-mighty, Trident-raging, Trident-proud**, *Mycecas*. This name was given to him from the "bellowing" of the sea, which rumbles so violently in a storm that it sounds almost like an ox.

*Taurocranos, Tauros, Tauretos, Taureos, Tauriceps.* <note>Latin and Greek terms for "Bull-headed" or "Bull-like"</note> Typically, brown bulls were sacrificed to him; and as mentioned before, since the sea rumbles or bellows like an ox, these names were given to him: **The Bull**, **Bull-head**.

*Onchestius.* Not far from Orchomenos was the city of Onchestus, named after the son of Neptune; there, a temple, statue, and shrine <note>original: *Phan*; from the Latin *fanum*, a consecrated place</note> were built for Neptune, from which he received this name.

**The Inundator.** Neptune and Juno quarreled over the land of the Argives. Inachus, a chosen judge, awarded it to Juno. Neptune, enraged, flooded the land. Juno entreated him to let the flood recede; for this reason, the Argives dedicated a temple to him.

*Tenarius, Asphalius.* The promontory in Laconia, Taenarus, is now called "The Little Head" or *Castro Maino* <note>Cape Matapan in Greece</note>; the ancients believed it was a passage and entrance into Hell. There, Neptune has a temple under the name *Asphalius* <note>original: *Asphali*; from the Greek *Asphaleios*, meaning "The Securer" or "Protector from falling"</note>. The temple is like a small cave, and his statue stands prominently outside. At one time, the Helots <note>original: *Heloter*; the serf class of Sparta</note> of the Lacedaemonians fled there for sanctuary; the Spartans strangled them all there, for which they were regarded as godless; whenever a great murder occurred, it was compared to this event.

**Sea King, Prince of the Sea.** In many places, the poets call him such, as the one who holds power over the water.

*Tenedius.* *Diphiusa, Hydrusa, Erusa, Tenos* were names for the island that is now called Tinos; it has a small town but a magnificent, large temple in a shrine outside the city, which was a site of great pilgrimage. The island is about eight miles wide and long, with a populated village in the center; toward the east and west, there are strong towers at the harbors or landing places.

*Elytius, Elymnius, Eresius, Mesopontius.* On the island of Euboea (or *Negropont*) as well as on Lesbos (which is now Mytilene), Neptune was worshipped and received these names from the cities in which he had statues and temples, as written by Stephanus, Hesychius, and Callimachus <note>ancient Greek scholars and poets</note>.

**Consus, Of the Horses, The Knight, The Councilor.** When Romulus arranged the racetrack, he found an altar of an unknown god under the earth, which he dedicated to **Consus**...
