### The Fifth Book

**Consus**, because he was said to give good counsel <note>original: *Conso*; an ancient Italian deity often identified with Neptune as *Neptunus Consus*</note>. It was intended that this same altar be called "The Knight Neptune," and the altar was kept hidden at all times except when tournaments were held. They called his festival the **Consualia**. On that day, horses were allowed to rest, and wreaths were placed upon the heads of mules. Likewise, they enacted the story of what had happened when Romulus took the daughters of the Sabines by force. Near St. Anastasia in Rome, a chapel was recently fully excavated which is believed to have belonged to Neptune; for on its walls, various sea-monsters <note>original: *Mőrschnãckẽ*; literally "sea-snails," but likely referring to grotesque sea creatures or Tritons in relief carvings</note> were carved and depicted, and in the vaulting above was a crested eagle, otherwise white but with a red head—a portent signifying war and wisdom, or *Consum* <note>meaning "counsel" or "purpose"</note>.

**Hippius the Equestrian**. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> makes mention that Neptune invented riding and the armor for cavalry horses. This Neptune had a temple, an altar, and a gift at the Academy in Athens. He had an altar at the racing stables in Olympia, and likewise on the peak of Methydrium in Arcadia. He also had a temple near Mantinea on a mountain called Thales; whoever entered it was unexpectedly sprayed with water and blinded, and died shortly thereafter if he broke the stretched thread that Agamedes and Trophonius <note>famous legendary architects</note> had placed there, for they had been the master builders there. Thus, it was ultimately forbidden for anyone to look inside. It is said that in Thessaly there was a place called Petra, where Neptune is said to have struck the ground with his trident <note>original: *Ghern*</note>, and from there the horse Scyphius is said to have sprung. Some say that in Illyria, they threw three horses into the sea every ninth year to honor Neptune. Phornutus <note>Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> believes he has these names because one travels as swiftly by ship as by horse. Ulysses also erected a statue to this Neptune at Pheneos.

**Utelaris the Protector, Asphalion**. Mention was made before of Taenarum; however, Strabo <note>a Greek geographer</note> further says that when the Rhodians were masters of the sea, they built a temple between Thera and Therasia—now called Santorini <note>original: *S. Erini*</note>—on the two islands. At Patras, near the coast, they also erected a temple and a statue to him. Sometimes he is called **Asphalion**, "The Stabilizer of the Earth" <note>original: *Erduestner*</note>.

**Neosichthous, Seisichthous, Enosigetes, Tinactorogetes**. All these names mean an **Earth-shaker**, mover, and shatterer. This is the opposite of the previous title, whereby one may perceive that the heathens often attributed two different types of power to a single god.

**Isthmius**. Enough was said regarding the Corinthian Isthmus under the section on Jupiter; for there, between two arms of the sea, was such a narrow passage that ships were pulled from one water into the other, just as is done at Lizzafusina near Venice <note>original: *Lucafusina*</note>. There, Neptune had a very famous temple in a damp forest. There too, as at Olympia, festival games called the **Isthmia** were held every fifth year. For when Athamas, the son of Aeolus, a madman <note>original: *wittling*</note>, took Ino the daughter of Cadmus as his wife, he fathered Learchus and Melicertes by her. Juno became very angry and made Athamas insane, whereupon he killed his son Learchus. Ino fled from the madman with the child Melicertes and threw herself off a cliff into the sea. Neptune took pity on them both; he made Ino a sea-goddess and called her **Leucothea**, and made Melicertes a sea-god and called him **Palaemon**. Having joined with other sea-nymphs, they came at one time to Sisyphus, the King in Corinth, and told him he should establish this festival for Melicertes. Thus, they were held at night—

# On Pagan Gods

<note>This section refers to the Isthmian Games</note> first prepared as a funeral rite. Now, these games had ceased for a time because the robberies were so great that no one could travel to them, until **Theseus** killed the highwayman **Procrustes**; then they were renewed. Thereafter, until the time of **Cypselus**, the Lord of Corinth, they were strictly kept in order, but he allowed them to lapse. After his death, approximately three hundred and thirty years before Christ, the Corinthians renewed them with such great cost and such great splendor that it became the most precious festival in Greece. Indeed, it was so strictly maintained that for a hundred and eighty years—up until the time that **Lucius Mummius** <note>The Roman general who destroyed Corinth in 146 BC</note> besieged, captured, and burned the city—nothing was overlooked. Even when the Corinthians could no longer afford the cost and were completely ruined, they handed over the rights to the games, along with all the equipment and preparations, to their nearest neighbors, the **Sicyonians**, so that these games would not be abandoned. The Athenians also had a magnificent seat of honor at these games, as wide as a spread-out ship’s sail. At first, a small wreath of celery <note>original: *Epffich*; wild celery was the traditional prize before being replaced by pine</note> was given, and later one made of pine or stone pine trees; otherwise, everything proceeded in the same manner as in the **Olympic**, **Pythian**, and **Nemean** games, about which enough has been said in their proper places. At the time when they held these games, it was usually around autumn, when, because of the many people who gathered together, villainy <note>or "pestilence," referring to the diseases that spread in crowded summer/autumn heat</note> and sickness often arose.

**Samius** <note>The Samian</note>. The one at Samos, or **Samicus**. **Lepreum** was not far from Olympus, where he was worshiped. At Olympus stood a statue of a beardless youth, with one foot crossed over the other, leaning with both arms upon a spear; they dressed him in a linen shirt, a woolen tunic, and a silk cloak, but otherwise he was made of bronze. He was also worshiped on the island of **Samos**, as he stood there by the landing place and had a temple, for which reason he was called "The One on the Shore."

**The Stonebreaker** <note>original: *Steinbrecher*; a translation of the Greek epithet *Petraios*</note>. The Thessalians named him thus; they said that he had broken through the mountains near the groves of **Tempe** and brought it about that the water, which previously had ruined and flooded the land with its overflow, was made to flow through.

**Heliconius**. **Helike**, the city in **Achaia** (which is now called **Morea**), was located about a mile from the sea; there the citizens had a temple of Neptune. When at one time the Ionians fled there as if to a sanctuary, and the people of Helike drove them out, Neptune became enraged and sent an earthquake that utterly destroyed the city. He had a festival there called the **Panionia**.

**Nysireus**. It is believed that **Nisyros** is a broken-off piece of the island of **Cos** or **Lango**; it is now called Nisaro and is nearly round. There Neptune had a temple which, in its territory, encompassed two miles. Many millstones are made there. It has five villages: **Mandrakion**, **Pali**, **Panagia**, **Nikeia**, and **Argos**; between these lies a burning mountain <note>a volcano</note>, near which are salt pits. It has warm baths and a forest; if one places the sick inside it, they become healthy within a few days. It is said that Neptune pursued a giant named **Polybotes**, and when the giant escaped him, Neptune struck off a piece of the island of Cos with his trident <note>original: *gehren*; a spear or fork</note> and threw it at the giant, hitting him. Thus, that piece became the giant’s grave and an island itself.

**Phytalinus** <note>or **Phytalmios**</note>. The Nourisher of Plants. The **Troezenians** became aware of how the land was occasionally flooded by the outflow of the sea, whereby...

**The Savior.** <note>original: *Soter*</note> When the Greeks heard how King Xerxes had suffered great damage and shipwreck with his war fleet upon the sea, they built a temple to Jupiter and also to Neptune in those same places, each under the name of "the Savior."

**The Hidden One.** <note>original: *Camerling*</note> Because the temple of Neptune at Lacedemon <note>Sparta</note> stood so surrounded by a grove of plane trees that one could not see it until one arrived there, it was named thus.

**Aegeus.** This one was honored in Negropont <note>the island of Euboea</note> in a city called Aegis; he is named after this place.

**Encheius.** At Cenchreae, at the shipyard of the Corinthians, Neptune has a temple which gave him this name.

**Erechtheus.** This one had a temple in Athens containing a spring; it would bubble up and become turbulent whenever the south wind blew, but otherwise, it was quite still and motionless.

**The Blue-Maned One.** <note>original: *Er mit wasserplawen Mänin*</note> Orpheus gives him this name in the sacrificial hymns.

**The Earth-shaker.** <note>original: *Euchos / Der Erdschüteler*</note> At Corinth, Neptune has a bronze statue; under his feet lay a dolphin that gave water. At Gythio he also has his statue; at Aegio a bronze statue and temple. At Antycira (which is now Suola), his temple was of the most beautiful sort, made of marble on the outside and fully decorated with mosaics inside; his statue was bronze, standing with one foot on a dolphin; with one hand he supported himself on his hip, and in the other, he carried his three-pronged spear <note>the trident</note>. # Ceres

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the goddess Ceres seated on a throne under a decorative canopy. She wears a crown composed of stalks of grain. In her right hand, she holds a dolphin, and in her left, she holds a bird, identified in the text as a dove. She is flanked by ornate floral decorations or cornucopias.</image-desc>

The Latins named Ceres after the springing of fruit <note>original: *fruchtspringen*; the author suggests an etymology linking Ceres to the "growth" (crescere) of crops.</note>. She was first called Ceres; the Greeks called her the Giver and Earth-mother <note>Demeter</note>. In her honor, because she was held to be a giver of grain, the ancients fasted to signify that without her help, one must suffer hunger. She was sometimes depicted as you see her sketched here; however, in Elaios in Arcadia, she had an image made of unburnable wood <note>original: *vnentpreñlichẽ holz*</note> that sat upon a stone, resembling a woman—except for the head, which was a horse's head. In one hand she carried a dolphin, in the other a dove. She was crowned with dragons' heads and also other heads of wild beasts. What the meaning of this may be, I have found nothing certain.

<margin>Now at Castrogiovanni. Enna, the city in Sicily, is now called Castrogiovanni; it once had an image of Ceres that was so divine that anyone seeing it believed it was a divine image, not made by human hands. It is of that same—</margin>

### The Fifth Book.

...some remains of the temple are still present; there, as in other places, Verres <note>Gaius Verres was a Roman governor of Sicily infamous for plundering local temples and artworks.</note> carried out his robberies.

**The one at Catania.** Catania is a city in Sicily near Mount Etna; there was a temple there which no man was permitted to enter; only women served there as priestesses and ministers.

**The Golden-yellow.** <note>original: *Laua* (Flava) and *Cloes Euchloes*</note>. This name was given to her because of the ripe grain, which produces golden-yellow kernels; among the Greeks, she was also greatly honored as the one who makes the grain sprout.

**Hermionian.** Hermione—as has been frequently mentioned, now called "Our Lady" in the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>—is where she had a temple, from which she kept this name.

**Pampanos.** Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian and lexicographer.</note> writes that she was worshiped under this name in the city of Heraclea.

**Anaxidora.** The **Fruit-bringer**; <note>The text lists several Greek epithets here: *Zeidoros* (Grain-giver), *Diodoros* (Gift of Zeus), *Pheresbios* (Life-bringing), and *Carpophora* (Fruit-bearer).</note> She had her temple at Tegea, and likewise at Phoica (which was once Phlius); she was worshiped under this name because, by showing the fruits she had taught them to cultivate, she brought or gave fruit and life to mankind.

**The All-nourishing.** Hesiod, who in his poem on the origin of the gods <note>The *Theogony*.</note> says that she nourishes all things through the invention of farming.

**Prostasia, the Presiding One.** In the Piraeus <note>The port city of Athens.</note> she was honored by this name; no woman was allowed to go there; she had a beautiful image there.

**Pelasgian.** She took this name from Pelasgus, the son of Dryops, because he built a temple for her when he received Ceres as a guest and learned from her how to farm the fields.

**Gracious Lady, Queen.** She was called "Gracious Lady" for the reason that she preserved life with her discovery <note>Agriculture</note>, for which reason she is also called the Queen.

**The one in the Moss.** At Loundaria she has a temple in the moss <note>meaning a marsh or swampy area</note> about a quarter-mile from the city; no man was permitted to enter there either.

**The Beer-drinker.** After Ceres lost her daughter <note>Proserpina/Persephone</note>, she no longer wished to drink wine, but drank beer wherever she went. When she once stayed with Metaneira, the wife of Hippothoon, and refused to be cheerful, a servant girl named Iambe devised a humorous, mocking poem and sang it before Ceres to refresh her; from this, it is said that **Iambic poetry** <term>Iambic poetry: a metrical form of poetry historically associated with satire and mockery</term> originated.

**Caberia.** Near Thebes in Boeotia (now called Siles), this Ceres had a temple and grove where no one was allowed to enter except those in the order or brotherhood of Ceres.

**Syritis.** Syris was a city located in Phocis; she had a temple there and took the name from it.

**Milesian.** At Miletus she also had a temple; when the soldiers of Alexander the Great captured it and wished to plunder it, they were blinded by a fire that struck out against them, as Lactantius <note>An early Christian author who often recorded pagan myths.</note> writes.

**Rharian.** Around Eleusis there is a field that takes its name from Rharios, the father of Triptolemus; the first grain is said to have been sown there. Ceres took this surname from that place.

**Pylagora Amphictyonis.** At the pass <note>original: *Claus*</note> near the hot springs not far from Delphi, which was once called Thermopylae, there was a village called Pyles; there the Amphictyons <note>An ancient religious association of Greek tribes.</note> met twice a year for the god...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the surnames and epithets of the goddess Ceres (Demeter), focusing on her associations with seasonal rituals, her search for her daughter Proserpina, and her role as the founder of civil law and domestic order.</meta>

# Of Heathen Gods

...spring and at the beginning of autumn; these were the sessions held at Pylae <note>Pylae, also known as Thermopylae, was the site of the Amphictyonic League meetings in ancient Greece.</note>. The first thing the Amphictyons <note>Members of a religious league of Greek tribes.</note> did was to offer a sacrifice to Ceres. And because the one who recorded the day was called **Pylagoras**, Ceres was also called by that name. She was also named after the **Rhaitoi** <note>original: "Rhätten." Likely referring to the Rhaitoi, sacred salt-water streams near Eleusis dedicated to Demeter and Persephone.</note> in that regard.

**Literia.** <note>original: *Lyteria*, meaning "The Deliverer."</note> This name is also mentioned in connection with Jupiter, because together with him, during a great famine, she warned the millers so that the flour would not be taken from them.

**The Torch-bearer.** It is said that Pluto kidnapped Ceres’s daughter Proserpina near Enna in Sicily. There, Ceres lit an inextinguishable torch and searched for her throughout the whole world. Some wish to interpret Proserpina as the **Moon**, which waxes from below, and she is said to be led away by Pluto when she is eclipsed under the earth. Others take her to represent the **grain**, which cannot grow when the weather is unfavorable, and it remains still under the power of Pluto when it does not sprout. Then Ceres—who represents the **farmer**—runs about, laments, and seeks her daughter until Jupiter—representing **good weather** and a fertile year—helps her again.

**The Bearer of Ears. The Bearer of Poppies.** Because Ceres is given a wreath of ears of grain and a small bundle of oil-poppies, she bears these names.

**Chea, the Sorrowful or Anxious.** <note>original: *Achea*, from the Greek *achos*, meaning grief or pain.</note> Because she searched for her daughter in such great and high sorrow, she was called "The Anxious One." The Gephyreans <note>An ancient family or clan in Athens.</note> who moved to Athens built a temple to her under this name.

**Pipolla, Epicyclia, Luanassa, Epotis, Epopis.** <note>Various Greek epithets emphasizing her roles: *Luanassa* (Mistress of the Harvest), *Epopis* (The Overseer).</note> As a good housekeeper, counselor, and citizen—a noble, brave leader and a prudent queen—she was honored under these names.

**Onalosia, the Bin-filler. Alos. Alloa.** <note>original: *Analoia* or *Alóa*.</note> Because she gives grain and abundance in great riches, she has this name. Therefore, the country folk held a festival for her, from which, without doubt, the traditions of the sickle-benches and flail-hangings <note>Traditional German harvest celebrations involving farm tools.</note> originate.

**Opnia, Leimena.** Because the grain fields, all their fruits, and even the fields, pastures, and meadows are dedicated to her, she is given these names.

**Sito, Simalida, Megaloarti, Megalomazi. The Baker.** <note>From the Greek *Sitos* (grain) and *Megaloartos* (of the great bread).</note> Because she teaches people how to deal with grain, flour, bread, and fruit, Hesychius, Athenaeus, and others have given her these names. Under these names, she had several statues in places where they baked beautiful, large loaves of bread, cakes, pretzels, rings, and rolls.

**The Wool-bearer.** <note>original: *Malophoros*.</note> In Megara, it is said that the first herds were raised, and she was honored there as the one who had shown them such a profitable trade.

**Mea.** <note>original: *Maia*, meaning "Nurse" or "Mother."</note> Just as a nurse nourishes children, she is called "The Nurse" because she brought forth everything necessary for human nourishment.

**The Lawgiver, or Thesmophoria.** As soon as it was discovered how to farm grain—which Ceres introduced—the people, who previously lived without law or discipline, joined together and established a civil society. For this reason, she is called "The Lawgiver." The Egyptians attributed this same role to **Isis**, about which you can read much in Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note>. She was called **Thesmophoria** and had a festival in Athens with special spiritual rituals; there, the women had to fast and sleep on leaves strewn on the ground, so that their wantonness <note>original: *geylheyt*.</note> would pass.

# The Fifth Book

<margin>Hermesia.</margin> Not far from Hermione, by the sea, lay a temple dedicated to this Ceres.

<margin>Chthonia.</margin> Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who discussed pagan deities in *The City of God*.</note> believes that because she is sometimes taken for the Earth itself, she is named thus, as if one were to say "the Earthly One." Furthermore, almost all other gods assigned as overseers of earthly things are called "Chthonic." At Hermione, she had her temple, along with a festival and games where one was given a small wreath of autumn flowers—though I would sooner believe they were the "gold-flowers" <note>original: "Goldplūmen," likely marigolds or similar yellow harvest flowers.</note> that appear during the harvest.

<margin>Mysia.</margin> A man from Argos built a temple to Ceres from Pallene or Tarsus; he was named Mysus. This name might come from the word meaning "satiety" <note>original: "Ersättigūg"</note> because she satisfies all things with her fruits.

<margin>Erinnys.</margin> Some believe that when the gods are angry and punish the world with famine, she is the one who carries out their command and wrath like one enraged and insane, bringing forth nothing.

<margin>Lusia / The Bather.</margin> Near Thelpusa <note>An ancient city in Arcadia.</note>, a body of water flows called the Ladon; there, Ceres once bathed and purified herself. A temple was built there to preserve her name.

<margin>The Black One.</margin> Near Neospiti <note>Likely referring to the cave at Mount Elaius.</note> there was a grove; there, Ceres is said to have dressed in black mourning clothes, wept for her daughter, and hidden herself so that she could not be found for a long time. However, the Arcadians built a sanctuary in her honor.

<margin>Eleusinia.</margin> About four or five miles from Athens is the village of Eleusis, though the citizens there eventually moved into the city itself. Triptolemus <note>A figure in Greek mythology who was taught the art of agriculture by Demeter.</note> held dominion there; he was the first to discover, by Ceres' instruction, barley and other grains, as well as how to prepare and cultivate them. He also sent this knowledge throughout the world. He established a great sanctuary for "Ceres of the Ears," which was kept entirely secret and hidden, and organized sacred processions, of which more shall be said in its proper place. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> also mentions these things.

<margin>Chamyna / Chamina.</margin> Chaminus, a very wealthy citizen of Pisa near Olympus, rose up against the lord of Elis named Pantaleon. He was strangled, and from his confiscated property, a temple was built to Ceres; hence her name.

<margin>Patrensis / Of Patras.</margin> At Patras, Ceres had a temple in which there was a spring. The priest would dip a mirror into it and then tell those asking—who were sent there on behalf of the sick—whether the ill person would recover or die in their bed.

<margin>Africana.</margin> In Barbary <note>A historical term for the Maghreb/North Africa.</note>, Ceres was highly revered, especially by widows who, like nuns, left father, mother, and child to dedicate themselves to her service, no longer allowing their children to come before them. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage.</note> makes mention of this.

<margin>Lybissa.</margin> In Argos, there was a place called the Libyan field, dedicated to Ceres, because grain was first brought there from Libya by Ceres; thus she received the name.

...left her. For this reason—that her daughter was snatched away from her, and she no longer had either husband or child—she was named thus by the poets.

<margin>Mycalessia</margin>
In Boeotia, there was a city named Mycalessus, where Ceres had a temple. The legend regarding this place was that Hercules opened and closed it every night. The first fruits were offered there, so that everything else might ripen well and last for a long time.

<margin>Archedonta</margin>
In Carthage, she shared a temple with Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine</note> to signify that she provides nourishment for mankind and that the two <note>bread and wine</note> should never be separated from one another.

In Rome, Ceres had a temple outside the Pincian Gate. This was because one should enter her temple with nothing but devotion and a pure heart; one should only go there when intending to offer a sacrifice. Otherwise, where churches stand within the cities, everyone runs through them without any devotion. Aside from this, there was a chapel dedicated to her at the place now called the *Scola Greca* <note>The "Greek School," associated today with the Church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin in Rome</note>.

The poppy heads <term>original: "Magſat"; poppy seeds/heads</term> which she carries in her hand signify the roundness of the earth. Just as the poppy head is uneven, so too is the earth covered in mountains, valleys, hollows, and trees, as the inner part of the poppy shows. The seeds, so manifold and innumerable, signify the many different fruits that are produced from the earth.

# Janus.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Roman god Janus. He is depicted with two bearded faces looking in opposite directions. He wears classical armor with a short tunic and sandals. In his right hand, he holds a large ornate key, and in his left hand, he holds a staff or wand. He stands on a stone courtyard with a masonry wall and a curtain or foliage in the background.</image-desc>

Now that we have mentioned the "Superior Gods," of whom there are twelve—or fourteen if one includes the Sun and Moon, who are contained within Apollo and Diana—we wish, as far as time permits, to describe the most prominent of the remaining six, beginning first with Janus.

This is reckoned to be the first and oldest god of Italy; indeed, some want him to have been a king there. There are those who believe him to be Noah <note>In the Renaissance, Janus was often identified with the biblical Noah because both "saw" two worlds: Janus looking forward and backward, and Noah seeing the world before and after the Great Flood</note>. Some value him as the year, others as the world itself. Many call him Camesen <note>Camesus, an early mythical king of Latium</note>.

# The Sixth Book.
<meta>Signature: dd iij</meta>
<meta>Catchword: Note</meta>

Those who take him to represent the year depict him with two, or sometimes four faces. Two represent Summer and Winter, or the exit and entrance of the year; those who give him four also represent the four seasons of the year, while his fingers represent the number of days. They place twelve altars beneath his feet to signify the twelve months, and give him two keys so that he might close the past year and open the one to come.

**Bifornis <note>Latin: "Two-formed"</note>. Geminus <note>Latin: "The Twin"</note>.** Some suggest that he may have known two languages: his own, and the one he learned in Italy. Or that, as a wise man, he held both the past and the future well in his memory.

The temple of this Janus stood opposite the Capitol <note>The Capitoline Hill, the religious and political center of ancient Rome</note>, serving as an ornament in the middle of the marketplace. His chapel was made entirely of bronze and was so large that the statue of Janus, which was five feet tall, could stand within it. On all sides it had bronze doors; these were closed in times of peace, but whenever war began, they stood open. The statue had only two faces, which is why he was called the *Geminus*. The tradition of closing and opening this temple comes from a legend: when the Sabines <note>An ancient Italic people</note> came to fight the Romans over their daughters <note>Referring to the "Rape of the Sabine Women"</note> and overran the city, the Romans tried to strike the door shut, but it would repeatedly open itself. As the Romans fled and the Sabines tried to push through the gate, a great stream of boiling water <term>original: "südtegs wasser"</term> erupted from the chapel of Janus and flowed against the enemies, burning and drowning them in the whirlpool. Therefore, in times of war, the temple was opened to signify that this God should have room to come to their aid. It has been closed only three times: first, in the time of Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome</note>; the second time, after the conclusion of the Second Punic War <note>original: "Carthaginensischer krieg"</note>; and the third time, at the time of the Birth of Christ.

**Quadrifrons <note>Latin: "Four-fronted"</note>.** It is said that Saturn brought Janus out of Oenotria <note>original: "Oenotrion"; an ancient name for Italy meaning "land of vines"</note> and taught him and his brothers how to plant grapevines. When the peasants first drank of the wine, they became intoxicated; some fell and some slept, and upon waking, they believed they had been poisoned. For this reason, they struck Janus dead. In grief, his four daughters hanged themselves. Then his spirit <term>original: "schelm"; here referring to the ghost or shade of the deceased</term> came among the Latins and told them that if they wished to be free of this burden of guilt, they should appease Saturn on Janus's behalf. Thus, Lutatius Catullus erected a chapel to Saturn on the Tarpeian Hill, placing within it a four-headed statue of Janus to commemorate his daughters. Others say that because he looks toward the four corners of the world, he has four faces.

**Key-bearer. Closer. Opener.** As previously mentioned, because he closes the year at one end and opens it at the other, these names and the keys are attributed to him.

**Consuvius <note>Derived from the Latin "conserere," meaning to sow or join together</note>.** He bears this name because, through time and the years, he joins together the procreation of the human race.

**Quirinus.** This name was given to him because he was considered powerful in wars.

**Matutinus <note>Related to the morning or the dawn</note>.** Because he is a lord of the days, this name was given to him by those addressing the days.

**Father. Forefather <note>original: "Ervatter"</note>.** As the most ancient of beings and the father of the other gods who followed him, he held this name.

**Sanqus. Septimianus.** This is what the Sabines called him. He also received his name from the Septimiana gate, which still retains that name today.

Note also that the ceremonial triumphal arches <term>original: "schwyböge"</term> that are erected—whether of wood, stone, or other material—which are meant to stand for a short or long time to receive Emperors and Kings upon their entry, are called *Jani*. Of this there is still an old monument of marble in Rome, which they call the House of Boethius; however, this is named incorrectly, for it is actually the Temple of Janus.

## Genius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Genius. The winged figure, dressed in a short tunic and boots, stands before a rectangular altar. In his right hand, he holds a shallow dish (patera) and pours a liquid offering onto the altar. In his left arm, he cradles a large cornucopia (horn of plenty) filled with fruits and agricultural products.</image-desc>

Saint Augustine <note>A significant early Christian theologian (354–430 AD) who often wrote about Roman paganism to contrast it with Christianity</note> maintains that this deity was appointed and held power, according to the opinion of the Heathens, over all growing things. Others say that there was not just one alone, but rather that every person, every place, and every species had its own [Genius]; this compares very closely to what we Christians say: that everyone has their own Good and Evil Angel. His image was sometimes as you see it here, and sometimes as I saw it on a coin <term>original: "Münz"</term> held by the respected Mr. Heinrich Petri, a master printer in Basel. On that coin he was naked, before him an altar upon which he pours wine from his dish; in his left hand he carried the full horn of plenty <term>original: "Obßhorn"</term>. On one side of the coin the letters stood thus: FL. VAL. CONSTANTINVS NOB. C. <note>Refers to Flavius Valerius Constantinus Nobilibissimus Caesar, or Constantine the Great</note>. On the other side: GENIO POPVLI ROMANI <note>Latin: "To the Genius of the Roman People"</note>. Near the image on the right side was the letter N, and below at the feet were the letters P. L. C. He wore beautiful boots and a clean cloth draped from one arm to the other, covering his private parts.

## Saturnus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Saturn. An elderly, bearded man is depicted outdoors in a landscape with a mountain. He is largely nude, with a cloth draped over one shoulder and around his midsection, and wears a soft cap. He holds a large curved sickle in his right hand and a small object in his left.</image-desc>

This one is presented as a son of Caelus <note>Heaven</note> and Hecate, and is otherwise called Uranus. He was the first king of the Aborigines <note>The mythological first inhabitants of Italy, not to be confused with modern usage of the term</note>—that is, the original inhabitants of Italy—who were so entirely just and pious that under his rule no one suffered anything evil or servile, and all things were held in common. In memory of this, during the festival of Saturn <note>The Saturnalia</note>, which occurred around Shrovetide <note>original: "faßnacht"; the author compares the Roman festival to the pre-Lenten carnival</note>, the servants sat at the table with their masters. The sickle signifies that he was the first to teach agriculture.

## Saturnus.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of Saturn as an elderly, bearded man, mostly naked with a cloth draped over his shoulder. He holds a large, curved scythe in his right hand and holds a small child in his left hand, which he is depicted eating. He stands in a simple landscape within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

He is said to be a son of Caelus <note>the Sky</note> and Hecate, and is otherwise called Coelum Uranum <note>Uranus</note>. He was the first King of the Aborigines—that is, the original inhabitants of Italy—and was so entirely just and pious that during his reign no one suffered any evil or lived in servitude; all things were held in common. In memory of this, during the festival of Saturn <note>the Saturnalia</note>, which occurred around Carnival, the servants sat at the table with their masters. The sickle signifies that he was the first to teach the cultivation of the fields.

# The Fifth Book.

In Saxony, at Harzburg <note>The author uses "Hartenburg"; this refers to the Harzburg fortress where the idol Krodo was famously located</note>, there was an image that they called (as Albertus Krantz <note>A 15th-century German historian</note> writes) **Krodo**. Some say it was **Saturn**, though that does not seem right to me. The image stood upon a fish and looked like an old man; he held a wheel in one hand to indicate the unity of the common people, and in the other a jug, signifying an abundance of all things. Charlemagne overthrew it.

**Chronos.** He was so named as a "father of time"; otherwise, the name **Saturnus** is meant to signify that he takes his name from sowing <note>original: "saatt"</note>, or that he was satisfied by its harvest, having grown old. As some say, he drew the people to himself by satisfying them with grain and food.

**Scythe-bearer.** Because time strikes down or cuts all things like a scythe, it is placed in his hand. That he swallows his children and gives them back again <note>A reference to the myth of Cronus devouring his offspring</note> is meant to show that with time, all things grow, come forth, pass away, and perish.

**Sterculius.** He was called the **Dunger of Fields** because he was the first to show how one should manure the fields.

**Vitisator.** He was called the **Vine-planter** because he was the first to show how they should be dug, planted, and trained, as was previously mentioned regarding **Janus**.

**Myantos, Megasthenes, Garenarches, Ancylometes.** <note>These are transliterated Greek epithets for Saturn/Cronus</note> Orpheus gives him all these names; he calls him the **Unpolluted** <note>original: "Vnuermäligsten," likely a translation of *Amyantos*</note> because in his time no wickedness had any progress; the **Strong and Powerful One** who led a strong, good, and stable rule in peace, and thereby, as a prince of generation, brought forth much in people, cattle, and all things. Also, through his great age, many things changed, for time takes some things away and puts others in their place.

A coin is found where on one side is a two-faced bust with the inscription **IANVS**, and on the other a sea or lake, upon which in a small boat is a naked male figure, wearing nothing but a broad hat and a cloth draped over his shoulders, stretching his arm upward with a scythe toward a star shining above him.

In Athens he had a temple, as well as a very ancient one at Olympus, not far from Londario; on Mount Cronius <note>original: "Crono"</note> they sacrificed to him annually when the day and night were equal in the spring <note>the vernal equinox</note>.

In Rome he had many temples and chapels, of which some landmarks still remain, such as **Santa Maria in Portico** <note>original: "im vorschöpff"</note>, **San Salvatore at the Scales** <note>original: "ann der wag," likely referring to San Salvatore in Statera</note> near the Capitol, where now, in place of the temple, there are several taverns and shops, and at **San Adriano**. In this temple lay the guild books, which were called "Elephantine" <note>original: "helfantische," referring to the *Libri Elephantini* or ivory books</note> because of their size, in which were recorded all the citizens found in the thirty-five tribes <note>original: "zünffte"</note> of the city. Likewise, the accounts of the common income and expenditures were kept there.

The Carthaginians and Cyrenians also honored Saturn highly, but they sacrificed humans to him. Of the names in other places.

# Pluto.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the god Pluto seated on a throne within an ornate architectural frame. He holds a long scepter in his right hand. At the base of the throne, the three-headed dog Cerberus is lying down. The scene is framed by classical pillars and decorative motifs.</image-desc>

Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher</note> says this god was assigned and dedicated all the powers and types of earthly things, since from the earth all things come and to the earth they return.

**Ditis the Rich.** For the reason just mentioned, he is said to be called "the Rich." However, Quintilian <note>a Roman rhetorician</note> turns it around, saying he is named thus in mockery <note>original: "gspött," referring to the rhetorical device of antiphrasis, calling something by its opposite</note>, because as a god of the departed soul-shadows, he possesses nothing.

**Infernus Jupiter.** He was called the **Hellish Jupiter** <note>original: "Infernus Jupiter"</note> because of the division of the world, of which mention was made in the section on Neptune <note>referring to the myth where Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto divided the heavens, seas, and underworld between them</note>.

**Hades the Dark, Aidoneus.** Because his kingdom, where the souls travel down to Hell, is entirely dark, fleeting <note>original: "eylẽd," which could mean swift or wretched/exiled</note>, miserable, and sad, he has this name.

**Agathylus. Agesilaus. Agelastos.** Some call him *Agelastos*, meaning "the laughterless," because there is no laughter <note>original: "keins lachens"</note> for those who fall to his lot. Others believe he is called *Agesilaus* because of the great multitude <note>original: "mãnge"</note> of the dead over whom he rules. Otherwise, *Agathylus* signifies that he brings an end to the pleasures, goods, and joys of this time.

**Axiocerses. Arimanes.** The Cabiri <note>mysterious deities of Samothrace</note> and the Persians—according to the tales of Apollonius of Rhodes and Hesychius—name him thus.

**Leptynes. Good Counsel. Clymenus.** Orpheus and Nicander call him **Good Counsel** <note>original: "Gůtrhat"</note> because he does good for humanity and counsels them, releasing them from many kinds of worry and anxiety through death by calling them to himself. He is called *Leptynis* because he turns dead bodies into shadows and thin air <note>original: "dün," meaning thin or vaporous</note>.

**Chthonius. Isodetes.** The name *Chthonius* <note>meaning "of the earth"</note> has been shown often before; the other name, *Isodetes*, comes from the fact that death (taken here as Pluto) opens the door through which all the world must go.

# The Sixth Book.

**Orcus. Uragus. Norchius.** <note>original: "Orcus. Vragus. Norchius." Names for the ruler of the dead</note> Hell is named thus because he, as a lord of it, carries the name; likewise, the perjurers <note>those who swear false oaths</note> belong almost entirely to him, which is why the name is directed toward them.

**Summanus.** In Rome, this god had an image in the temple of the "Best and Greatest" Jupiter; thunder struck its head away so that it could never be found, until the soothsayers pointed it out in the Tiber River. Among the ancients, he was held as the one who thundered at night, and he was highly honored in Rome before the temple of Jupiter was even built. From this history, it likely comes that people refer to the thunderbolt as "hellish fire."

**Soranus.** Where Abruzzo and once Sora were located—which Emperor Frederick II destroyed—there was a hill containing a small cave. From this cave came a vapor that killed those standing around it; there, Pluto was worshipped.

**Polydectes. Postulio. Polydegnion. Polyarchos.** <note>These Greek titles refer to Pluto as "The Receiver of Many," "The Demander," "The Host of Many," and "The Ruler of Many"</note> As he is a great lord who demands much if one wishes to obtain his grace, these names were given to him.

**Februus. Stygius. Quietalis.** He is named thus because he purifies <note>term: "Februus" relates to the Roman purification rituals, the *Februa*, from which the month February takes its name</note> after death, or because one washes the corpse, helping the dead to reach rest from worldly affairs, and because he rules over the "Stygian" <note>hellish</note> waters.

**Ruler of the Depths. Vedius. Veiouis. Leader of Erebus.** <note>original: "Vector Profundi. Vedius. Veiouis. Dux Herebi."</note> Why he is called Vedius or Veiouis was explained in the section on Jupiter; thus, the poets have called him a ruler of Hell, the Depths, and Erebus <note>the primordial darkness of the underworld</note>.

**Serapis. Osiris.** Some name and hold him to be these Egyptian gods. Enough of this is written in Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note>. Yet I will record here the answer he gave to a King of Egypt to describe the nature of God, as Heraclides Ponticus describes it:

->In the beginning, God, Word, and Spirit are one thing,<-
->All three bring forth one Life and Essence.<-

## Pluto.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting Pluto seated on a throne inside a vaulted stone structure. He wears a crown and holds a long scepter. At his feet lies Cerberus, the three-headed dog. In the background, through an archway, figures are visible in a cavernous landscape.</image-desc>

Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), a Roman statesman and philosopher</note> says that to this god were once attributed and dedicated all the powers and types of earthly things, for indeed everything comes from the earth and returns to the earth again.

**Ditis the Wealthy.** For the same reason just mentioned, he is said to be called "the Rich"; however, Quintilian <note>A Roman rhetorician</note> refutes this in a jest, saying he is called so because, as a god of the departed soul-shadows, he possesses nothing at all.

**Hellish Jupiter.** He was called the "Hellish Jupiter" because of the division of the world, of which mention was made in the section on Neptune <note>referring to the myth where Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto divided the sky, sea, and underworld between them</note>.

**Hades the Dark, Aidoneus.** He has this name because his kingdom—where the souls travel down to Hell—is entirely dark, swift, miserable, and mournful.

**Agathylus. Agesilaus. Agelastos.** Some call him *Agelastos*, meaning that there is no laughing for those who fall to his lot; others believe he is called *Agesilaus* because of the great multitude <note>term: "Agesilaus" is derived from the Greek words for "leading the people"</note> of the dead over whom he rules. Furthermore, *Agathylus* signifies that he brings an end to the pleasures, goods, and joys of this life.

**Axiocerses. Ahriman.** The Cabiri and the Persians <note>Ahriman is the spirit of evil and darkness in Persian Zoroastrianism</note>, according to the accounts of Apollonius Rhodius and Hesychius, call him by these names.

**Leptynes. Good Counsel. Clymenus.** Orpheus and Nicander <note>Ancient Greek poets</note> call him thus because he does good for men and counsels them, releasing them from many kinds of worry and anxiety through death by calling them to himself. He is called *Leptynis* because he makes the dead bodies thin and shadow-like.

**Chthonic. Isodetes.** The name *Chthonic* <note>meaning "of the earth"</note> has been indicated often before; the other name comes from the idea that death—taken here to be Pluto—opens the door through which all the world must pass.

<header>The sixth book.</header>

**Orcus. Uragus <note>original: "Vragus"</note>. Norchius.** The underworld is so named because he, as its lord, bears that name; thus, perjurers <note>those who break their oaths</note> are especially subject to him, which is why the name refers to that place.

**Summanus.** In Rome, this god had a statue in the temple of the Best and Greatest Jupiter. A thunderbolt struck off its head, which could not be found until the soothsayers <note>diviners who interpreted signs from nature</note> pointed it out in the Tiber River. Among the ancients, he was considered the one who thundered at night, and he was highly honored in Rome even before the temple of Jupiter was built. From this, it may well follow that people still refer to the thunderbolt as "hellish fire."

**Soranus.** In the region now called Abruzzo, where Sora once stood (which Emperor Frederick II destroyed), there was a hill with a small hole from which a vapor emerged that killed those standing nearby. There, Pluto was worshiped.

**Polydectes <note>original: "Polydetes"</note>. Postulio. Polydegmon <note>original: "Polydaginon"</note>. Polyarches <note>original: "Polydarchos"</note>.** He received these names as a great lord who demands much <note>Polydectes means "receiver of many"</note> if one wishes to have his grace.

**Februus. Stygius. Quietalis.** He is so named because he purifies after death <note>the month of February is derived from "februare," to purify</note>, or because one washes the corpse to help the dead find rest from worldly affairs. He also rules over the waters of the Styx.

**Rector of the Deep <note>original: "Rector Profundi"</note>. Vedius. Vejovis. Leader of Erebus <note>original: "Dux Herebi"</note>.** Regarding why he is called Vedius or Vejovis, it is discussed under Jupiter; the poets called him a ruler of Hell, the Deep, and of Erebus <note>a region of the underworld representing darkness</note>.

**Serapis. Osiris.** Some name and consider him to be these gods. Enough on this may be found in Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note>. However, I wish to write here the answer he gave to a King of Egypt to reveal God, as Heraclides Ponticus describes:

->In the beginning, God, Word, and Spirit are one thing,<-
->All three bring forth one Life and Essence.<-
<note>This "oracle of Serapis" was often cited by Renaissance writers to suggest that even ancient pagans had a mysterious intuition of the Christian Trinity.</note>

# Bacchus.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicts Bacchus as a youth riding a tiger through a landscape. He is accompanied by two attendants; one leads the tiger, while the other behind him plays a flute and carries a jug and a platter of food. Mountains and a city are visible in the background.</image-desc>

This one is called Dionysus by the Greeks, about whom you can find an abundance in Diodorus <note>referring to Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> in the fourth and fifth books.

**Liber / Liberator / Eleutherius <note>The Free One</note>.** Because those drunk on wine speak much and freely, he is said to have this name; also because it then frees the mind from all worries, or because boys who lose their youth <note>original: "magthumb," referring to the transition from childhood to adulthood</note> (as Augustine says) are freed of their seed. For this reason, he was set up in temples sometimes as a male figure and sometimes as a female figure with the name **Libera** <note>The Free Lady</note>. Some understood these figures to be Venus <note>goddess of love</note> or Ceres <note>goddess of agriculture</note>. In Lavinium, he also had a temple and festival; his sacrifices were mocked by Augustine <note>referring to St. Augustine’s "City of God," where he critiques pagan rituals</note>.

**Thioneus. Semeleius. Dithyrambus.** Of these you also have information at length in Diodorus.

**Meliastes. Meonius. Ligyrens. Lysius.** Near Mantinea there was a spring called Meliastes; certain peoples in Lydia were called Maeonians; in Thrace were the Ligyrians; and at Thebes and Corinth, he was honored under the name **Lysius** <note>The Releaser</note>. For he was called **Lyceus** and **Lysius** because often through drunkenness discord arises and the friendship of men is dissolved, or perhaps because there is then a free, unburdened mind in people.

**Maronius. Cephalenus. Cressius. Methymneus.** The people of Methymna once found the head of Dionysus while fishing, from which the name comes to him; likewise, he buried Ariadne near the temple consecrated to him at Argos, and because she was a Cretan <note>original: "Cressin" or "Candiotin"</note>, he has the name from that.

**Melanegis <note>Of the Black Goatskin</note>.** In the [festival of] Venus Apaturia, it is said of the struggle between two fighters, that the one in black stood behind the back of Xanthus...

<summary>This page lists numerous epithets for the god Bacchus and explains the mythological and linguistic origins of names such as Liber, Lysius, and Methymneus. It focuses on Bacchus's role as a "releaser" of the mind and his various cult locations across the ancient world.</summary>
<keywords>Bacchus, Dionysus, Liber, Eleutherius, Diodorus Siculus, Augustine, Greek mythology, epithets, wine, Methymna, Ariadne</keywords>

<header>The sixth book.</header>

...the name was given to Bacchus, for in memory of him a temple was established there.

**AEsymnetes <note>original: "AEsymnetes", Greek for "Arbitrator" or "Ruler"</note>.** Eurypylus, a son of Evaemon, received in the loot of Troy a small chest that Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> had given to Dardanus and Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> had forged; however, whoever opened it improperly was destined to go mad. In that same chest lay Dionysus or Bacchus. Eurypylus built a temple for him after he was found again, and established a festival and sacrifice for him.

**Hygiates <note>original: "Hygiates", the Healer</note>. Soter <note>original: "Soter", the Savior</note>.** What is more wholesome than wine if it is drunk in moderation? On the contrary, the Greeks gave him this name because when they landed in Mysia, they were badly beaten by Telephus; if they had not set out wine to make his men drunk, they would have been entirely driven away.

**Morchos. Morichus.** The Musty One. His festival was performed with dances, which is why he had the name **Enorches** <note>original: "Enorches", meaning "The Dancer" or "In-the-testicles", though the author here connects it to festive movement</note>; because he makes things musty and soiled in autumn when the wine is drawn off <note>referring to the "must" or sediment of new wine</note>, he is called Morichus.

**Problastus <note>original: "Problastus", the Germinator or Sprouter</note>.** A covering is made for him with vine shoots; hence he has the name.

**Erebinthius <note>original: "Erebinthius", associated with the chickpea or perhaps a grain-based drink</note>.** Where one makes a drink from grain or malt instead of wine—sometimes with barley or wheat, in one place different from another—from this he received the name.

**Sycites <note>original: "Sycites", of the Fig Tree</note>.** Those on the island of Naxos made statues of him, some from vine wood, some from fig wood; they said he was the first to discover how to plant vines and likewise figs.

**Sabazius. Nyeus.** Diodorus also makes mention of him, and the general opinion is that his name also comes from dancing—and as they say, "to go shalatzen" <note>original: "Schalatzen gon", an old dialect term for wandering or reveling</note>, an Italian-derived word used by curious folk.

**Iacchus.** This name was given to him because of the shouting and cheering that drunkards do.

**Oinos <note>original: "Oinos", Wine</note>. Theoïnos <note>original: "Theoïnos", Wine-God</note>.** From wine—because he is considered a god of it and its inventor—he has these names.

**Enoles. Manicos.** Because wine makes one insane, he was so named. <note>The author connects "Enoles" and "Manicos" to the Greek words for madness and frenzy.</note>

**Eraphiotes. Eribromos. Eribremetes.** The quarrelsome, raging, furious, much-shouting, and more of the same; he has such names from the nature of wild people.

**Bygenes <note>original: "Bygenes", likely meaning "Ox-born"</note>.** Because he is depicted with horns—the reasons for which Diodorus reports—he is called the Son of the Ox.

**Dusarcos. Dyalus.** Thus the Nabataeans and Vossians named him. <note>original: "Dusarcos" refers to Dushara, a Nabataean deity identified with Dionysus.</note>

**Taurophagus <note>original: "Taurophagus", the Bull-Eater</note>.** Because the bull is a stormy <note>violent</note> beast—as wine-guzzlers often are—he has this name.

**Nebon.** He had no beard, which is why he was given this name.

**Lampteres <note>original: "Lampteres", of the Torches</note>. Phausterius <note>original: "Phausterius", the Enlightener</note>.** At Pellene he had a temple where his festival was held at night with torches; from their glow the name remained with him.

**Cratophorus <note>original: "Cratophorus", the Bearer of Strength</note>.** Unwatered wine was so named and considered precious; therefore, this god was held in very high regard under this name at Phigalia.

# Of Pagan Gods

**Mitrephorus <note>original: "Mitrephorus", meaning "Miter-bearer" or "Headband-wearer"</note>.** Because those who are so full of wine wrap their heads—since those full of lethargy suffer from headaches—he was given this name.

**Biformis <note>original: "Biformis", meaning "Two-formed"</note> / Aethyopis.** Diodorus attributes the first name to him because he is of two-fold shape. Anacreon and Hesychius call him "the Maple" <note>This may refer to the wood used for early cult statues or a specific botanical association</note>.

**Phleona <note>original: "Phleona", from the Greek word for "to teem" or "to overflow"</note>.** Because the grapevines at times, and generally, are heavily laden, he received this name from that very fullness.

**Orthos / Rectus / The Upright.** The fullness that comes when one drinks strong wine undiluted with water brings paralysis and a shrinking of the limbs. Bacchus taught Amphictyon <note>A legendary king of Athens</note> to mix it with water so that it clears the others <note>likely meaning it clears the head or the ill effects</note>; thus people remained "upright" while drinking the same. For this reason, he was honored and named so.

**Eubulos <note>original: "Eubulos", meaning "Good Counselor"</note>.** Orpheus says he is "good counsel," and that drinking wine in moderation strengthens the reason; for this reason, he gives him the name.

**Callydonius <note>original: "Callydonius", the Calydonian</note>.** He was honored in Calydon. His priest, Coresus, loved Callirrhoe; she would not listen to him, and the citizens went completely mad. They came to their senses again when they agreed that Callirrhoe should be sacrificed, or another person who would willingly stand in her place. She found no one else, so the priest himself stood forth and was sacrificed <note>original: "gmödzig", likely a variation of "gemetzelt" or "gemordet," meaning slaughtered or killed in sacrifice</note>; for he had prayed to Bacchus for the citizens' madness to end.

**Eyon. Euan. Bachepea. Babactes. Jobacchus. Bromios. Eleleus. Bacres.** All these names he received from the shouting and cheering of the drunken crowd who praised him with loud noise.

**Bassareus.** This name was given to him because of the fox skin <note>original: "fuchsbeltz"; a "bassara" was a long Thracian garment made of fox skins</note> that he is said to have worn.

**Stigena. Pytigenes <note>likely "Pyrogenes", meaning "Fire-born"</note>.** Because wine is of a hot and fiery nature and ignites a person, this is his name.

**Agreus / Paredros <note>original: "Paredros", meaning "Companion" or "Assessor"</note>. Chonius.** Pindar gives him as a companion to Ceres <note>Demeter, the goddess of the harvest</note> and also calls him by this name, as does Hesychius.

**Sodotes <note>original: "Sodotes", the "Giver of Companions"</note>.** Where this name comes from, you have it from Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>; it may perhaps be here because wine brings many people together as companions.

**Limnies. Edonius. Gorgyieus. Elygeus.** He was honored at Limnae in Attica, from which he took the name. And because a people in Thrace called the Edonians held this Bacchus in high honor, he was also called the Edonian. Likewise, he was named in Samos after two spots called Gorgyia and Elygen.

**Asares. Ma.** Ma is said to have been a wet-nurse to Bacchus when Jupiter fathered him by Semele. When she was asked by Juno what child she was carrying, she said "Areos" <note>Ares/Mars</note>. That is, a son of Mars.

**Antheus / Areus / Melpomenes / Cuseus / Dialicus / Comus / Mesadeus / Colonatas.** Pausanias says that the people of Patrae, as well as the Athenians, honored him under these names, such as: The Blooming, The Warlike, The Singing, and The Ivy-crowned (because ivy was first seen in Attica). Likewise, he was called "of the Colonatans" after the spot so named in Laconia. Furthermore, as Hesychius says, "The Reveler" was also honored under the names mentioned above.

<meta>This page concludes the list of epithets for the god Bacchus and introduces the goddess Tellus (Earth), detailing her various names and associations with fertility and the natural world. It continues the catalog of pagan deities from the previous page.</meta>

<header>The Sixth Book.</header>

**Nyctelius.** Because his celebrations and festivals were held almost entirely at night <note>original: "znachts", referring to the Greek 'nyx' for night</note>, he was given this name.

**The Winged.** Bacchus lifts up man just as wings lift a bird, making him more nimble than he otherwise is; from this, his name is derived.

**Pryseus. Oreus.** He has these names from the mountains in which he is said to have been raised, and also from the promontory in Mytilene called Brysa.

**Imadius.** The Chians sacrificed to Bacchus with gruesome customs, for they tore a human being apart for him in a piteous manner, as Eusebius <note>A Roman historian and Christian polemicist</note> says.

**Salaminius.** The Athenians had a ship <note>the 'Salaminia', a sacred state trireme</note> that they never used except in the direst need; therefore, Aristophanes <note>The Greek playwright, particularly in his comedy 'The Frogs'</note> wishes Bacchus had never entered it, as he is one not fit for war.

**Lymites. Lebenus.** He is called "The Nursling" <note>original: "Wiegenkindlin", literally 'little cradle-child'</note> by Hesychius, who also calls him Lebenus.

**Protalt. Myobarbarus.** Thus the Arcadians called him, regarding him as the one who kept watch over betrothals and alliances confirmed by oath. Cyriacus of Ancona <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar and traveler</note> gives him the other name, as one who constantly mingled among foreign peoples.

The Church of Saint Constance <note>Santa Costanza</note> in Rome was once a Temple of Bacchus on the Via Nomentana; some images were recently found there, the depictions of which are widely circulated. So much for Bacchus.

# Tellus.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration. A goddess, representing Tellus/Cybele, wears a turreted crown and sits in a four-wheeled chariot pulled by two lions. She holds a floral scepter or branch. The background depicts a landscape with trees and a building on a hill. In the foreground, there are flowering plants and two large birds, possibly peacocks or cranes. The image is placed to the left of the following text block.</image-desc>

Tellus is distinguished from the word *Terra* in that the former refers to the goddess, while the latter refers to the earth itself. Some believe she is named so because she is rubbed or trodden upon by feet <note>A traditional etymology linking 'Terra' to the Latin 'tero', to rub or wear down</note>. Some take her for Juno, others for Ceres; some for Vesta, others give her the name Hecate or Proserpina, because the earth is accustomed to return the fruit a hundredfold compared to the seed.

**Aia. Great Mother <note>original: "Magna Mater"</note>.** She is sometimes called Maia, the Great Mother, because she brings forth and nourishes all the world like a mother, and at death, she willingly receives them back into her womb.

**Good Goddess <note>original: "Bona Dea"</note>.** She is the cause of good food and fruits, for which reason she has this name.

**Anna.** Because she is favorable and generous to the livestock with good pasture, she has this name.

**Ops.** From her helpfulness, as she is helpful and conducive to us in life.

### Of Pagan Gods

**Fatua.** The Mute <note>original: "Die Stum"</note>. A witless woman; [she represents] children in the mother’s womb who cannot yet speak nor have any understanding.

**Medea.** She is held to be so chaste and pure that she is said to have never left her chamber; no man is said to have ever known or seen her.

**The Infinite.** <note>original: "Ie Vnendlich"</note> Because the earth is a circle <note>meaning a sphere or cycle</note> which has neither beginning nor end, this gave her that name; for this reason, Plutarch <note>The Greek historian and philosopher</note> also says she is "the enclosed one."

**Pales.** She takes her name from the fodder <note>original: "füter"</note> that grows from the earth for the livestock.

**The Mother.** Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author</note> writes of her thus: "Even to this one alone, who is yet the greatest part of nature, we rightly grant the honor of a mother as she deserves; for as soon as we are born, she receives us, sustains us, feeds us, and when one is separated from other natural states, she takes us up again and covers us <note>a reference to burial in the earth</note>."

This goddess was depicted on a wagon because the earth is surrounded by air and rotates like a wheel, which the wheels on the wagon signify. The lions that lead her signify maternal loyalty which overcomes all, for she endures everything to sustain us. The servants who run alongside the wagon with bare swords signify that every honorable man <note>original: "biderman"</note> should fight for his fatherland. The crown of towers shows the cities that the earth supports. The round drum signifies the circle and roundness of the world or the ground, upon which there is a constant sound and commotion with struggling and laboring. The roosters <note>original: "hanen"</note> signify her priests, who were called *Galli* <note>a pun on the Latin 'gallus' meaning both 'rooster' and 'a Gaul' or priest of Cybele</note>; they were insane and lewd. In Rome, she was honored in the round temple of Our Lady <note>likely referring to the Pantheon, which was consecrated as Santa Maria Rotonda</note>, where her stone head with two fish is still built into the wall of the temple. In Augsburg, she is said to have had her temple on the Isenberg. Likewise, the city’s coat of arms <note>referring to the 'Zirbelnuss' or pinecone of Augsburg</note> is said to have its origin there, but that will be discussed in another place.

In Rome, at Saint Peter in Chains <note>San Pietro in Vincoli</note>, her temple once stood, which Titus Sempronius vowed to build. Cicero had his image within it; some write that it is the Church of Saint Pantaleon. We shall let that be.

Now, friendly dear reader, take this in good part, for time could bear no more. Through your friendly goodwill, you shall incite me to further work that will be even more pleasing to you.

## Concerning the first beginning of the world and of humanity
### Chapter 1.

The highly learned and preeminent men, who have written the truth concerning Nature and the most certain facts in history, bring forward two types of opinions regarding the first beginning of human procreation. Some wish to claim the world was never born <note>The author uses "born" (erporn) here to mean "created" or "brought into existence."</note> and is also indestructible; thus, the human race has been eternal from time immemorial, having never had a beginning or origin. Others believe the world was born or created, and must eventually perish <note>original: "wider zü grundt ghen," meaning to return to the ground or be destroyed.</note>, so that humans also have a temporal beginning.

For in the beginning of all things, heaven and earth were of one form, and the natures of both were mixed together. But when the physical bodies <note>referring to the elements of matter</note> separated, the world took on such an order and form as it is now seen to be. The air took on a strong motion, and the fire, because of its lightness, rose into the heights. For the same reason, the sun and the moon, together with the other stars, were brought into their courses. The re- <note>original: "Die ver-"; the catchword "mischte" suggests the next page continues with a discussion of the "mixed" or "remaining" elements.</note>

# Of the Beginning and the Originators of Diverse Things.

## The Second Chapter.

The Egyptians maintain that the first humans were created among them. They conclude this based on the fertility and goodness of the land, as well as the Nile River, which by its own nature produces many things and abundantly nourishes what it brings forth. For it produces a reed, the root of which—along with the clover and beans that grow beside it, and another herb they call Erseum—feeds the people along with many other things. They also conclude this from the fact that animals were first produced among them, noting that even to this day, at certain times near the city of Thebes, many large mice grow <note>The ancient author is referring to the theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise directly from mud.</note>; many people are astonished when they see that the front part of the chest down to the front feet moves and lives, while the hind part is not yet formed or even begun. Therefore, they say this is a certain sign that mankind originated among the Egyptians, for it is heard of nowhere else in the world that animals are produced in such a manner as in Egypt.

Dionysius says that Isis is Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture; the author is identifying the Egyptian goddess Isis with her Roman equivalent.</note>, whom Osiris took as his wife; they ruled together and discovered many benefits for the human race. Through their skill, they put an end to the deadly conflicts that occurred among men over food. For Isis discovered wheat and barley, which were previously unknown to mankind and grew wild among other grasses without any cultivation.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a woman (Isis) on the left holding a long staff, and a man (Osiris) on the right guiding a yoked ox through a field of grain. In the background are stylized plants and hills.</image-desc>

When Osiris became aware of this and saw how useful it was for food, he instructed the people so that they all might make use of it, both for the sake of the sweetness they perceived in it, and because they saw it as a means to put aside the grim and cruel deadly strife. They also say that this is still the sign that Isis discovered the grain: that according to ancient tradition and law, it is still the custom today that those who harvest select a sheaf of the finest ears, which they offer up to the Goddess with invocations, giving Isis great praise for her discovery. In some cities, when they walk in procession with Isis, they carry wheat and barley before her in memory of her discovering them.

Isis is also credited with having first established laws, so that fairness and justice might be done for everyone, and that willful lawlessness might be stopped through the fear of punishment. From this also comes the fact that the Greeks call Isis the Lawgiver <note>original: "Gsatzgeberin"; likely a translation of the Greek title *Thesmophoros*.</note>, as she who first devised the laws. There is also a legend that the city of Thebes in Egypt was built in the time of Isis and was named the Hundred-Gated City <note>Homer famously described Egyptian Thebes as having a hundred gates, distinguishing it from the seven-gated city of Thebes in Greece.</note> after her. Some of the later historians say that Thebes is named the city of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>. For not only the foreigners but even the Egyptian priests themselves do not know for certain who built that city. There are many who write that Thebes was not built in the time of Osiris, but long afterward by a king. However, we will speak of that later in another place.

Isis and Osiris erected a magnificent temple to their parents, Jove and Juno, which was wonderful in its size and decoration. Also, two golden chapels <note>shrines</note>: the larger consecrated to the celestial Jupiter, the smaller to the lesser Jupiter the King, who was their father and called Ammon <note>Amun or Ammon, the chief Egyptian deity, whom the Greeks and Romans identified with Zeus/Jupiter.</note>. Indeed, they also erected small golden churches for many other gods mentioned by us above, assigning to each his own honor and priests. Wherever anyone invented some art that appeared useful for life and human welfare, he was held in high and good regard by the two, Osiris and Isis. For they soon found themselves...

In Thebes <note>The ancient capital of Egypt</note>, the gold and bronze smiths were established, from which weapons were made to destroy wild animals and tools were fashioned to cultivate the earth. They say also that he discovered wine and taught others the planting and cultivation of vines. Furthermore, he honored **Mercury** <note>Hermes</note> above all men because of his new inventions, which were so beneficial to humanity. For Mercury was the first to teach how to put words into an orderly arrangement and gave names to many things. He invented the letters <note>writing</note> and established the duties and ceremonies by which the gods should be honored. He was the first to observe the course of the stars <note>astronomy</note>, introduced arithmetic, provided part of the medicine for the body, and invented a musical instrument with three strings, devised according to the three seasons of the year: he created three tones—a sharp one representing summer, a deep one for winter, and a soft, middle tone for spring. In addition, he taught the interpretation of languages, for which reason he was called by them <term>Ermēs</term> <note>From the Greek 'hermeneus,' meaning interpreter or translator.</note>; indeed, those historians who lived in the time of Osiris acknowledge that they heard all such things from Mercury and recorded them from him. He was a constant counselor to Osiris, whose advice was always followed. They also maintain that Mercury, and not Minerva <note>Athena</note>, invented the cultivation of the olive, even though the Greeks attribute it to her alone.

Afterward, they write that Osiris, as a brave and glory-seeking man, gathered a great host of people in order to travel through the world with an army to teach people in all places how to plant wine, wheat, and barley, and how to raise livestock for their benefit. He believed that if he could bring people from such a coarse, beast-like existence into a civil and moral life, he would afterward be granted immortal honor (which he indeed achieved). For not only the ancients, but also those who came after him, held the discoverers of crops to be the highest gods. They also say that when Osiris had established the Egyptian Kingdom, he entrusted the entire administration to **Isis**, his wife, giving her Mercury as a counselor—

For this reason, these two animals are highly honored among the Egyptians, and the two sons are held as gods in the form of these same animals. Osiris also took **Pan** with him, whom the Egyptians honor not simply, but in many ways. xi
# The First Book.
<meta>catchword: rim be</meta>

Having traveled the circle of the world, he planted beneficial fruits to sustain mankind. In regions where the land was not suited for the vine <note>grapes for wine</note>, he taught the people to brew **beer** from barley; this drink was not much inferior to wine in either its aroma or its strength. When he returned to Egypt, he brought with him precious gifts that people from all over had presented to him in his honor. Because of his many good deeds, he earned an immortal name and was held to be a heavenly God after his death—a transition from man to divinity that was, without doubt, well-deserved. Immediately following this, **Isis** and **Mercury** <note>The god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes/Mercury</note> established offices and solemn church rites for him, as they would for the highest of gods, and they devised many things to ensure he was held in high esteem. Egyptian historians describe how **Osiris**, after reigning long and justly in Egypt, was murdered and slain by his brother **Typhon**, who was a godless and evil man. The murderers (of whom twenty-six had conspired together) each cut off a piece of his body. **Typhon** did this so that these prominent and powerful men would be more faithful to him, as they would all share in the same guilt and punishment, and would thus help him protect and hold the kingdom more firmly.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration depicts a fortified city under siege. In the foreground, four large cannons (bombards) mounted on wooden carriages are positioned on hills. Soldiers are active around the artillery, with one figure appearing to load a cannon. The city in the background is enclosed by stone walls with multiple towers and gabled buildings visible within. Several flags or banners with various designs fly from the city towers and from poles near the cannons. The landscape includes rolling hills and a few smaller buildings outside the city gates.</image-desc>

But things turned out poorly for them, for **Isis**, with the help of her son named **Horus**, took revenge for the death of her brother and husband. She violently destroyed **Typhon** and all those who were guilty of Osiris’s death and ruled over them with power. This was not achieved without battle, however; the conflict took place in **Arabia** near a body of water at the place called the Hamlet of **Antaeus** (so named because **Hercules** had previously slain **Antaeus** there). After winning the battle, **Isis** did not wish for her husband to have one specific, known grave, but rather that he should be honored by everyone in all places. For this reason, she had all the pieces of her husband brought to her. She preserved them with noble spices and wax, and after she had recovered all the limbs and parts—except for the genitals <note>original: "vßerhalb der gmächten"; in many myths, the phallus was lost in the Nile and eaten by fish</note>—she had each piece filled out and fashioned into the likeness and form of her husband. She then summoned all the priests in Egypt and gave each temple an image of her husband. She told each group of priests in secret that she was entrusting the entire body of **Osiris** to them, and she took an oath from them that they would never reveal where they had buried **Osiris**.
