## Of Diodorus Siculus

...should have buried him, and also that they should honor him in their churches as a god, assigning to him whatever animal they wished, under whose form they would perform divine services for him. She also requested that they do the same with her own body after her death. To ensure she obtained this from the priests more quickly, she established that the **priests'** stipends be maintained from a third of the income of Egypt, so that they might carry out the <term>religious worship</term> <note>original: "Gözendienst"; here referring to the ritualized cult of a deity</note> with great abundance. The priests, mindful of the good Osiris had once shown them and enticed by the rich endowment of Isis, performed everything that Isis had requested. Therefore, there is still a dispute in all the temples as to whether Osiris rests with them. Furthermore, whatever animal each temple first assigned to him, they still hold in honor; and when that animal dies, they mourn Osiris anew.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a structure with four rectangular compartments, each containing vertical lines and a small square or opening at the base, potentially representing tombs or a sanctuary enclosure.</image-desc>

They also sacrifice to Osiris two consecrated oxen, one of which is called **Apis** and the other **Memphis** <note>likely referring to the Mnevis bull of Heliopolis, though the text associates it with the city of Memphis</note>, and these are held as gods by all Egyptians. For they say that this animal was entirely helpful to those who discovered grain and was very well-suited for farming. They also say that **Isis** swore to Osiris that if he should pass away, she would take no other man after him; and just as she followed him in his reign, no one ever ruled more kindly or honorably. After her death, she also attained immortal honors and was buried at **Memphis**, at the site of <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The Egyptian god Ptah, whom the Greeks and Romans identified with Hephaestus/Vulcan</note> where her grave is still shown at this time. Some believe the bodies of these gods do not lie there, but rather in the mountain of **Athon** in Egypt, near an island called the **Gates of the Nile** <note>The island of Philae, a major center for the cult of Isis</note> which is consecrated to them. There they also show several markers and the tomb built for Osiris, which has long been honored by the Egyptian priests. They fill three hundred and sixty buckets with milk every day for their religious service and begin a lamentation, calling upon the gods. For this reason, no one dares to sail to the island. Among the **Thebans**, where the oldest city is located, the highest vow and oath is taken by Osiris, who "hovers in the air." Since all the body parts were buried by Isis as previously mentioned—except for the **genitals** (which none of the murderers under Typhon would take, and so he threw them into the water)—Isis had them searched for and found. She buried them with no less honor than she had given the other pieces and also arranged for an image of that part to be honored as a god with office and church splendor, giving that god a special, magnificent name. For this reason, the Greeks, when they observe the festivals of the **Orgia** or **Dionysus** (the customs of which they brought out of Egypt), also specially honor this part of the body and include it in their church mysteries as the **Phallon** <note>original: "Phallon"; refers to the Phallus carried in Dionysian processions</note>. Some claim that from the time of Osiris and Isis until **Alexander the Great** (who built a city in Egypt after his own name), more than ten thousand years passed; others claim it was a little less than twenty-three thousand years. Those who say that Osiris was born in **Thebes** in **Boeotia** to **Jupiter** and **Semele** are mistaken; for when **Orpheus**, who was a particularly good friend of the Thebans and highly honored by them, traveled to Egypt and...

#### The First Book.

...withdrew and learned the religious services there; he then returned to the Thebans. Even the Greeks themselves say this and claim he gave them the origin and account of these religious services. There, the people, out of misunderstanding, gladly accepted such a <term>cult</term> <note>original: "götzendiēst"; referring here to the ritualized worship of a deity, which the 16th-century translator labels with a term implying idolatry</note>, except that they later thought this god had been born among them. 

However, as to the claim that **Orpheus** is so ancient that he brought this cult and the evidence of this god's antiquity into Greece, they suggest that **Cadmus** was born in Egyptian Thebes and later, in Greece, among many children, fathered a daughter named **Semele**. She was later secretly seduced by someone, whereupon in the seventh month she bore a small child who looked like and was named after **Osiris**. But perhaps this was against the gods, or nature was too weak; at any rate, the child soon died. Cadmus was greatly troubled by this, but received an answer that he should celebrate a festival for his ancestor. He then gilded that same child and established a cult for him, so that people would take him for Osiris. He also traced the child’s lineage back to **Jupiter**, so that he might attribute Osiris's deeds to the child and defend the shame of his daughter being seduced. 

From this it comes that the Greeks believed Osiris was fathered by Jupiter through Semele, the daughter of Cadmus. Thus Orpheus (after he had learned Egyptian theology, returned to Greece, was highly honored by all Greeks, and was well-received by the Thebans for his lovely poetry) applied the lineage of the ancient Osiris to this young one for the sake of the Thebans. He thus established a new cult, from which the fable then grew that people claim **Dionysus** was born of Semele and Jove <note>original: "Joue", the Latin ablative for Jupiter</note>. Out of misunderstanding and through the influence of Orpheus, the people in Greece set him up as a god. Afterward, they gave credit to the poets' tales, which they cry out in the plays, and thus calculated the lineage of this god. 

The Egyptians claim all heroes and gods as their own countrymen and say the Greeks are a remnant of them, a people sent out who inhabited those places. For **Hercules**, who was a born Egyptian, conquered a great part of the world with his boldness and—as the Greeks themselves testify—erected a pillar in **Libya**. It is also undeniable that Hercules fought with the gods against the **Giants**. Now,

# Of Diodorus Siculus

...beasts and their armor. Now, they say this **Hercules** was born of **Jupiter**, ignoring his mother; for he whose mother was **Alcmena** lived over a thousand years later, and was originally called **Alcaeus** <note>original: "Alcesus"; the birth-name of the Greek Heracles</note>, only later taking the surname of Hercules. He did this because he wished to equal the deeds of the ancient Hercules as much as possible, and he did not earn his honor and name through the "envy of **Juno**," as **Matris** <note>original: "Onitres"; likely a corruption of Matris of Thebes, an author who wrote about Hercules</note> says. Furthermore, the praise given to Hercules for slaying all the monsters and beasts of the world applies more to the ancient one than to the one the Greeks speak of, who lived around the time of **Acasis**. Additionally, during the latter's time, men were already quite civilized, all the fields were cultivated, and there were cities and communities of people everywhere. Yet in ancient times—especially in **Egypt** (where there are many deserts and many fearsome beasts)—the wild animals caused great damage. Hercules took pity on this, his fatherland, and destroyed the wild game so that the earth could be inhabited by people; thus he attained divine honor from them.

Furthermore, the Greeks imagine that **Perseus** was born in Egypt, and that **Isis** is the one who, under the shepherd **Argus**, was transformed into a cow <note>The author is identifying Isis with the Greek figure Io</note>; but all of this is a fictional story about the gods. Some call Isis **Ceres**, some **Thesmophoros** <note>original: "Thessmophoram"; a title meaning 'Law-Bringer'</note>, some **Luna** (the Moon), and some call her **Juno**. Some give her other names. Similarly, **Osiris** also has many names. One calls him **Serapis**, another **Dionysus**, this one calls him **Pluto**, that one **Ammon**, this one **Jupiter**, and even **Pan**. Many argue that the one the Greeks call Pluto is actually Serapis.

Furthermore, the Egyptians say that Isis discovered many kinds of medicine for illnesses, and that she now, as a goddess, occupies herself with the welfare and health of humanity. She is pleased when people cultivate the earth well and show her honor. Indeed, she often appears visibly in sleep to those she deems worthy of her help, demonstrating her power by showing them the remedies by which they may regain their health. Moreover, there are certain visible works proving that people become healthy through her help, and these are no fictional tales as among the Greeks; for wherever in the world the goddess is honored, the public help for the sick is felt. She appears to the sick in their sleep and tells them what they should use for their health, and even when the doctors have despaired of someone, if the sick person does what the goddess commands in the sleep, he becomes healthy. Likewise, if someone is blind, lame, or otherwise injured in a limb and calls upon the goddess, they say he becomes healthy.

They also say she discovered a medicine with which she makes people immortal; for when her son **Horus** <note>original: "Orus"</note> was secretly murdered by the **Giants** and thrown into the water, she found him and not only brought him back from death and suffocation but also made him immortal. He is the last god who reigned after the death of his father Osiris. Some say Horus is otherwise called **Apollo**, who learned medicine and prophecy from his mother Isis; therefore, by foretelling future things and providing healing medicines, he has done much good for humanity.

## The calculation of time according to the Egyptians’
->presentation and opinion.<-

The Egyptians count from the reign of King Sol <note>original: "Sol"; the Sun god, Ra</note>, who ruled over them, until Great Alexander came to Asia, about one thousand and twenty years. And they say besides that the ancient gods ruled for more than twelve hundred years, and those who followed for less than three hundred. And because such a large number is unbelievable, some argue—since the sun's path was not yet known to the ancients—that the year was calculated according to the moon's path. Therefore, because a year lasted only thirty days, it would be quite possible that some lived twelve hundred years. For even now, when the year is twelve months long, some are found who live more than a hundred years.

Thus they also defend those who lived for three hundred years. They say that these same ones, because of the unequal division of time, considered the spring <note>original: "Glentz"; an archaic German term for spring</note> as a year, it being four months long. Likewise the summer, and then the winter also. From this it comes that the Greeks took a part of the year for a whole year, from which then arose the inequality of time and disagreement among the writers. 

Furthermore, the Egyptians say that some people in the time of Isis were large of body, whom the Greeks call Giants, but the Egyptians call "wonder-beasts" <note>original: "wundthier"</note>. These same ones were slain by Osiris, and some believe that they sprang from the earth, just as it first produced the animals. Some claim that those who surpassed other people in physical strength and performed somewhat braver deeds were afterward called Heroes or Giants, who, according to many reports, were all killed together when they opposed Jove <note>original: "Jouem"; Jupiter or Zeus</note> and Osiris. 

The Egyptians also have a law that exists nowhere else in the world; it allows a brother to take his sister in marriage. They perhaps took this from the example of Isis, who had her brother Osiris in marriage; after him, by her oath, she wedded no other, after they had ruled in all justice and shown much good to mankind. Therefore, even today, more honor is shown to all queens in Egypt than to the king himself. It is also said that among the common people, the woman is the master; indeed, that in the marriage contract, the man promises that he will be obedient to the wife. 

It is also not hidden from me that the burial of these gods is said to be in Nysa, which lies in Arabia, as some write. From this, Dionysius is called "of Nysa" <note>original: "Nyseus"</note>. They also say that a pillar was erected there for each of them, and their memorial was written therein in Egyptian letters. The writing on the pillar of Isis reads as follows:

> I am Isis, the Queen of Egypt,
> spouse of Osiris.
> Well-taught by Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; identifying the god Thoth with Hermes/Mercury</note>,
> Let my law remain undisturbed by everyone.
> I first discovered the fruit that nourishes;
> King Horus <note>original: "Orus"</note> is my child.
> I illuminate many lands with my light,
> and am called the Dog-star <note>original: "Hund"; referring to Sirius</note> among the constellations.

## What customs the Athenians have in common with the Egyptians.

There were several Egyptians who became leaders of the Athenians, namely **Dipetes** <note>likely a corruption of "Cecrops," who was called *diphues* (of two natures) in Greek</note>, a father of **Mnestheus** <note>original: "Mnesthei"; a king of Athens mentioned in the Iliad</note>, who was also famous in the Trojan War. This Dipetes, an Egyptian, became a citizen of Athens and later became a king there.
It is said he had two natures; from this, it was fabled that he arranged his rule according to the customs of the Greeks and the Egyptians, which in part resemble human nature and in part share something of the disposition of wild creatures <note>This refers to the myth of Cecrops being half-man and half-serpent</note>. They also say that **Erichthonius** <note>original: "Erichteus"</note>, the King of the Athenians, was also an Egyptian, which they confirm by this: when the entire world, almost everywhere except Egypt, was afflicted by heat, resulting in a great shortage of crops and people, they say Erichthonius brought much grain from Egypt to Athens because he was related to them. Because of such a good deed, he was made king by them. As soon as he came to power, he prescribed to them the offices used in Egypt and the religious services, such as how they should behave toward the goddess **Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture</note>, whom they call **Eleusina** <note>referring to the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>. Indeed, that same goddess lived at that time and, in the midst of the drought, brought much grain to Athens and taught them how to sow and farm wheat. Thus, the Athenians themselves admit that in the time of Erichthonius, when all fruit had withered, the goddess Ceres helped them with corn, and they established her divine service based on what they had learned from the Egyptians. Furthermore, the priests they call **Eumolpides** <note>the hereditary priests of the Eleusinian Mysteries</note> and the **Pastophori** <note>a class of Egyptian priests who carried the sacred images</note> also come from the Egyptian priests. Along with this, they say that among all the Greek heralds, only the Athenian swears by the goddess **Isis**, and they are also entirely similar to the Egyptians in appearance and customs. Now, all of this is spoken more with boastfulness than with truth. And one must rightfully doubt how it could be that such a magnificent city should have arisen from foreigners. Yet the Egyptians say that the number of lands they occupied was due to the power of their kings and the large population of their people whom they sent here and there throughout the world. But since nothing certain is written of this anywhere, we have considered it useless to report much further on the matter and will let it remain as the Egyptian priests claim,

## Description of the geography of Egypt and the nature of the Nile. Chapter 3.

Because Egypt is so well protected by Nature itself, and indeed far surpasses other kingdoms in its pleasantness, it is evident that it is situated entirely in the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally "Noon," the traditional German term for the southern cardinal direction</note>. From the West <note>original: "Niedergang," literally "the setting [sun]"</note>, it borders the deserts and a portion of wooded Libya, which extend quite far; due to the lack of water and its infertility, as well as the danger, these areas are impassable and unsuitable for traveling into Egypt. From the South, it is hemmed in by the course or the cataracts <note>original: "strudel," referring to the rapids or whirlpools of the Nile</note> of the Nile and its adjacent mountains. Additionally, it lies separated from the Troglodytes <note>literally "cave-dwellers," an ancient term for tribes living along the Red Sea coast</note> and the outer Ethiopians <note>original: "Möhrn"; here referring to the peoples of the Upper Nile region</note> by about one hundred and thirty...

twenty-eight miles across, one cannot easily cross the water there by ship. It must be a powerful King who wishes to travel there by land, and he must be very well supplied with fodder. From the East <note>original: "auffgang," literally "the rising [sun]"</note>, however, it is bordered by the Nile and a vast desert called the Barathrum <note>From the Greek word for a pit or abyss; here referring to the dangerous terrain near the Delta's edge</note>. Between Syria and Egypt, there lies a marsh called Serbonis <note>The Serbonian Bog, a lake in Egypt known in antiquity for its treacherous shifting sands</note>; it is not wide, but nearly five miles long. Those who are not knowledgeable about the path fall into great danger there, which they do not expect. For in that narrow passage, great heaps of sand lie all around; the wind sometimes blows these so thickly into the water that one believes it to be solid ground. One cannot clearly see where the water or the earth begins. Many have perished there by following the sand with all their military equipment; as soon as they stepped upon the sand, thinking it was land, they fell through it into the water. Swallowed up by these holes, they could not swim back out, for they were covered by sand and there was no hope of rescue, as they could not use their strength while sinking deeper into the sand and mud, and ships could not come to their aid. Therefore, that same place is called Hell or "The Maw."

Now, so much for the three directions that surround Egypt. The fourth side, toward the North <note>original: "Mitnacht," literally "midnight," the traditional German term for the northern cardinal direction</note>, is enclosed by a stormy sea that one can hardly navigate. From Paraetonium <note>An ancient port city in Libya</note> in Libya to Joppa <note>Modern-day Jaffa in Israel</note>, which is a bay in Syria—and from there to Pharos <note>The island of the Great Lighthouse of Alexandria</note>, a good one hundred and twenty-five miles—there is no harbor where one may safely land. Furthermore, the sea overflows the border back and forth, and it is not well known to sailors. Thus it often happens that when they wish to flee the dangers of the sea and seek a safe bay on land, they are instead thrown into an overflow of water that never recedes, nor does it swell, so they can move neither backward nor forward. Sometimes, because they cannot see the land they are approaching—for it is very flat—they are cast into the swamps and deserts. Thus, Egypt is well protected on all four sides.

The land stretches out in length; the coastal border is fifty miles long, and toward the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally "noon"</note> it measures more than forty miles. In the number of its people, it once surpassed all other lands, and it still yields to no other country in terms of its multitude. In their books, one finds that in ancient times there were up to eighteen thousand famous and notable spots and cities. In the time of Ptolemy Lagi <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt</note>, three thousand were recognized, and in our own time, the number is no less. It is said that some seven million people once lived there. Even now, there are no fewer than three million inhabitants. This is also the reason why, as history records, the ancient Kings of Egypt were able to erect such wondrous buildings <note>original: "gepeüw"</note> as monuments to their rule using such vast crowds of people. But we shall write more diligently of this later. Now, let us describe the wonders of the Nile’s nature, the regions through which it flows, its properties, and its situation. Its origin is in the South; its course is toward the North. It rises in the furthest parts of Ethiopia, and because of the great heat, one cannot reach its source through the deserts. # Diodorus Siculus

...it runs through many lands, twisting strangely; now toward the East <note>original: "auffgang," the rising sun</note> into Arabia, then toward the West <note>original: "nidergang," the setting sun</note> into Libya. Its course from the mountains of the Ethiopians down to the sea covers nearly three hundred and forty miles, including all its bends. Among the many large floodplain-islands <note>original: "Awen" (Auen), referring to fertile riverside meadows or islands formed by river branches</note> that it creates in Egypt, Meroe is the most famous; there, the river is somewhat less than half a mile wide. At the lower part of its course, it is more narrow and divided into two branches: one arm, which runs into Libya, is swallowed up by the wilderness, the desert, and the sandy vastness; the other, which extends toward Arabia, runs into large lakes and marshes. It is roughly a quarter-mile wide, sometimes less, and does not run straight but winds strangely—sometimes toward the North <note>original: "mitnacht," literally "midnight"</note>, then toward the West, then toward the East, and at times even back toward its source in the South <note>original: "mittag," literally "midday"</note>. # The First Book.

... hundred floodplain-islands <note>original: "awen" (Auen), fertile riverside meadows or islands</note> in the Nile. In some of these, as they say, the Athiorni dwell, and millet is produced there. Some are inhabited only by poisonous serpents <note>original: "würmen," often used historically for any creeping reptile or snake</note>; others by people with dog’s heads <note>a reference to the mythical Cynocephali, commonly described in ancient travelogues</note> and various wild beasts, so that one may not easily enter them. In Egypt, the Nile divides into many branches and forms the shape of a Greek Delta. It also becomes deeper because it pours itself into the sea there through seven branches. The first branch runs toward the East <note>original: "Orient"</note> and is called the Pelusian; the second branch the Pfamnitic; the third is called the Mendesium. After these are the Phaeniticum, the Sebeniticum, and the Bolbitinum; the last is called the Canopicum, though it is named the Herculeum by some. 

Some inlets into the sea are man-made, which one should not fail to mention. At each of these inlets, a city is built, so that from both banks of the water, one must enter the city across bridges, which are well-staffed with guards. From the Pelusian inlet, there is a man-made canal <note>original: "graben," literally a trench or ditch</note> that goes all the way into the Red Sea and the Arabian river. This same canal was begun by Necho, the son of Psammetichus; later, Darius, the King of Persia, undertook to finish it, yet he desisted from it due to the warnings of some who persuaded him that if he completed the work, the entire land of Egypt—which lay lower than the Red Sea—would be drowned. 

Nevertheless, Ptolemy the Second <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note> finished this canal, although he began digging it in a more convenient place and arranged it so skillfully that, whenever he wished to sail through, he could open it and then close it again. For this reason, the canal was called the Ptolemaic. Also, at the end of this canal, a city is built called Arsinoe. 

The floodplain-island called Delta is shaped like the island of Sicily; on two sides it is nineteen miles long, and it expands gradually so that where it borders the sea, it encompasses nearly thirty-three miles. It is divided by many man-made trenches. It has the most fruitful fields in all of Egypt, for it is surrounded by water, moistened by it annually, and covered with silt <note>original: "lätten," referring to the fertile alluvial mud</note>. Furthermore, the inhabitants are very diligent in farming and water the land at times by means of a machine which, because of its shape, is called "the screw" <note>the Archimedean screw</note>, and was invented by Archimedes of Syracuse; because of this, the land bears fruit in great abundance and fullness. 

Thus the Nile flows softly and gently, carrying much and various silt; it overflows in the low-lying places, making the region fruitful and good. Many kinds of roots grow therein with pleasant scents, and various fruits and herbs that serve not only as food for the poor but also as medicine for the sick. Beyond that, the poor can nourish themselves well on the many "Nile-cresses" <note>likely referring to the edible lotus or water lily</note> it bears, from which they make bread to sustain life; it also bears Egyptian beans <note>original: "faygbonen," likely the seeds of the Nelumbo nucifera</note> in abundance for food.

Thus, in a short time, without much effort, cost, or harm, they bring in a great harvest, whereas elsewhere one must expend great effort and massive cost on farming. The Egyptians alone have almost no labor or cost, yet they possess fertile soil. Their vineyards likewise are moistened in this way and produce wine in abundance.

[The land is] protected by ditches; therefore, when the Nile overflows, it appears just as if they were the islands called the Cyclades. <note>The Cyclades are a group of Greek islands in the Aegean Sea, arranged in a circle.</note> Any wild animals remaining in Egypt that do not reach high ground are all drowned when the river overflows, unless they manage to reach the mountains. Through this, they have also learned to recognize immediately at the start of the rising water whether it will be a fertile or an unfertile year. The reason why the water overflows in this way is hidden, and has brought much doubt among natural philosophers as well as historians, resulting in many different opinions. Therefore, we wish to speak a little about this here, yet in such a way that it is not too much for a history book, and yet ensuring that what everyone desires to know is not skipped over.

# The First Book

Whichever Greek it may have been, they were never able to reach Ethiopia, or even the mountains of Egypt, because of the great danger and hardship involved. The very first among all the Greeks was Ptolemy <note>Likely referring to Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who sent explorations into Ethiopia.</note>, who marched into Ethiopia with an army and diligently investigated the nature of that land. Therefore, ignorance of these distant places gave the ancients an occasion to write fables.

Regarding the source of the Nile: up to this time, there is no one who has written of it having seen it themselves, or having heard of another who saw it. For this reason, men have relied upon conjecture and opinion. The Egyptian priests write that the beginning of the Nile comes from the Ocean Sea, which surrounds the entire earth. However, they bring forth no certain proof for this; rather, they wish to confirm uncertain things with "certain" reasons, and through faith, they present as credible that which requires a great deal of belief. Among the Troglodytes <note>An ancient term for "cave-dwellers."</note> there is a people called the Volgios, who live in the hollows of the mountains because of the heat; they say that in their land there is a plain that is very watery and full of springs that flow together, from which (they believe) the Nile is formed. Now, those who live in the region of Meroë <note>An ancient city on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan.</note> are much closer to that place and should know it better; yet the origin of the water is so unknown to them that they call it *Asopos* <note>original: "ἄσοπος"</note>, which is to say, the "dark source," as if it springs forth out of darkness. It is also not hidden from me what Herodotus writes (who says the Nile flows through Libya toward the East and then turns through that same land toward the West). Among other things, he writes how the Nasamonians <note>An ancient Berber tribe of southeastern Libya.</note> diligently sought the source of the Nile and claimed that it springs from a lake near them and then flows through Ethiopia. Yet, as it now appears, one cannot well believe these Libyans according to Herodotus, for they say nothing certain. Let this be enough regarding the source and its course; now we wish to write about its growth and its flooding.

Thales, who is counted among the Seven Sages <note>Thales of Miletus, often considered the first Greek philosopher.</note>, says that the Nile floods when the East winds blow; for then it cannot flow into the sea because the sea swells and pushes the water back, from which the inundation of Egypt—which is a flat land—follows. Even if this seems to have some likeness to the truth, it may still be easily rejected as false. The reason is that if this were true, all waters would swell at that time, which does not happen; therefore, one must seek a truer cause. Anaxagoras <note>The OCR reads "Anavagoras." Anaxagoras was a Pre-Socratic philosopher.</note>, the master of nature, indicates that the reason the Nile grows is that the snow then melts in Ethiopia; his pupil Euripides is also of this opinion and writes the same. But this cannot be so, for everyone knows well that because of the great heat in Ethiopia, no snow can fall; and especially around the entire Nile, there is almost no winter or cold weather. And even if one were to admit that snow falls in Ethiopia, it still could not be the cause of the Nile overflowing; for every water that flows from snow brings mist and cold air with it, but the Nile alone has neither mist nor [cold] air. And Herodotus says the Nile is the same water flowing out as it is when it follows its natural course, but that this is the cause: In winter, the sun is more inclined toward Libya and draws the water of the Nile to itself; therefore, the Nile becomes unnaturally smaller. But in summer, the sun moves toward the North <note>original: "Mitnacht," literally midnight, a traditional term for the North.</note>; therefore the waters become smaller in Greece and elsewhere. For this reason, it is not to be wondered at...

### Diodorus Siculus

...that the Nile rises in the summer and becomes smaller in the winter in Egypt. If this were true, then the other waters in Libya <note>In antiquity, "Libya" often referred to the entire African continent known to the Greeks, excluding Egypt.</note> would also have to decrease during the winter; but since this does not happen at all, it is found that Herodotus is mistaken here. In the land of Greece, the waters do not become larger in winter because the sun is further from them, but rather from the heavy rains that occur constantly. Democritus of Abdera <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher best known for his atomic theory.</note> blames the northern snows and not the southern snows, as Anaxagoras and Euripides claim. He says: In the north, the snow piles up greatly and freezes together; but in the summertime when it melts, moisture and vapors rise, and then large mists and clouds are formed from them. These same clouds are driven by the annual winds <note>original: "Ostwinden" (East winds), though referring to the Etesian winds which blow from the north/northeast.</note> onto the highest mountains (such as those in Ethiopia) and turned to rain, which water then increases the Nile at that very time. This opinion is also easily dismissed if you take note of what time these winds blow. The Nile begins to rise when the sun is at its highest point and turns back <note>Referring to the summer solstice.</note> on the seventeenth of June, even though these winds are not blowing then; and it decreases only at the autumn equinox, when these winds have long since ceased. Now, where the causes of the writers' opinions are debated, one should praise the searching diligence and skill of the writer, but one must not immediately give him credit. For I will not mention here that these winds, as is obvious, blow no less from the West than from the North. For neither the Northeast nor other North winds, but the South winds—those coming from the West and the southern side—are those called the annual winds. To say that such a thing happens on the Ethiopian mountains is not only to be rejected, but is entirely unbelievable. But then comes Ephorus and brings something new, yet incredible. He says: The land of Egypt is nothing other than mud cast up by the Nile, which is by nature thin and full of cracks. He claims there are also many large hollows in that same soil, which in winter suck up all the water, and in summer they pour it out again like sweat, thus watering the land. Now, this man shows with his writing not only that he does not know the nature and situation of Egypt, but also that he has never heard from those who provide certain accounts of Egypt. For if the Nile becomes large in Egypt itself, it would not overflow above Egypt, where it runs through mountains and rocks; yet it also overflows in Ethiopia, a hundred and fifty miles' journey before it comes to Egypt, just as it does in Egypt. And even if the Nile lay lower than Egypt, the hollows in the mud of which he speaks could never suck up so much water, especially since the water constantly washes a thin layer of soil over them. Furthermore, it is impossible that the mud, which according to his word lies above the Nile, could carry so much water as it afterwards pours out, for the hollows would have to float above the water. If the Nile were higher than the mud, it would be impossible for the water to run upward out of the compressed hollow places; and who would ever believe that a thin soil, as he describes it, could provide so much water that this river could cause all of Egypt to "sweat"? I will not mention that one can see that in a thin, cast-up soil, so much water could never remain, but would seep out on its own. For the river Meander <note>A river in Asia Minor, famous for its winding path (the origin of the word "meander").</note> has carried much earth to Asia and cast it up, where it was later found

### The First Book.

...there is nothing quite like it when compared with the Nile. Similarly, the river Achelus <note>A major river in western Greece.</note> in Acarnania, and the Cephisus in Boeotia—which flows past the Phocians—have deposited so much silt and soil that one can certainly build and live upon that land; however, neither of them experiences such a seasonal overflow. From this, one may clearly perceive that Ephorus <note>A Greek historian (c. 400–330 BC) often criticized by later scholars for historical inaccuracies.</note> was in error; indeed, one need not look for much truth in his writings, for he has recorded little that is worthy of belief.

Certain people in Memphis <note>The ancient capital of Egypt.</note> have offered reasons that one cannot easily refute, yet also cannot easily believe. They divide the world into three parts: one which we inhabit, another located directly opposite us, and a third which they say is uninhabitable due to the heat. If the Nile were to rise during the winter season, it would have to originate in our region, for that is precisely when it rains the most here. However, since it rises in the summer, it is a sign that it has its source in the region opposite us <note>The "Antipodes," or the southern hemisphere.</note>; for in that land, it is winter when it is summer for us, and for that reason, the river becomes so large at that time. They argue that no one can reach its source because it flows out of that opposite region through the uninhabited zone. They also believe that the nature of the heat gives the Nile its flavor, which is why this water is so sweet and superior to other rivers.

But this opinion is quickly refuted. It is equally impossible for water originating in the region opposite us to rise and flow "upwards" toward us <note>The author is struggling with the concept of a spherical earth and how gravity/flow works between hemispheres.</note>. Although the earth is entirely round, and even if they wished to suppress the truth with these arguments of theirs, nature simply does not permit it. They only place wildernesses and uninhabited places between us to embellish their opinion and protect their claims, so that certain knowledge cannot be used against them. It would be only right that if someone offers something as a certainty, he should have certain knowledge of it—or at least remain consistent in the opinion he initially allows, so that his presentation holds together. Furthermore, if the Nile alone among all waters flows to us from the opposite part of the world, other rivers would necessarily have to behave in the same way. 

As for their claim that heat is the cause of the water being so sweet, that has no foundation at all. If heat made this water sweet and "cooked" it, then no fish or other creatures found therein could grow; for water that has its natural properties taken away by fire is barren and produces nothing. Since the Nile is of an entirely different nature, it is found that the cause of its rising is none of those which they have proposed.

Inopides of Chios <note>A Greek mathematician and astronomer; often spelled Oenopides.</note> writes that the waters within the earth are quite cool in the summer and warm in the winter. This can be seen openly in wells, which are coldest during the greatest heat and warmest during the peak of the cold. Therefore, he claims it happens that the Nile is small and drawn together in winter because the internal heat of the earth then "sips up" or absorbs the moisture. In the summer, the earth—having been כך moistened—no longer draws more water to itself even if it does not rain, which allows the Nile to easily increase in volume. To this, one could answer that there are many waters in Libya <note>The ancient Greek term for the African continent.</note> that are similar to the Nile in their flow into the sea and their currents, yet they behave differently; for those same rivers grow large in winter and small in summer. Thus, the matter must not have been understood in this way. Agatharchides of Cnidus <note>A Greek historian and geographer who correctly identified that the Nile's flood was caused by seasonal rains in the Ethiopian highlands.</note> has come closest to guessing the truth of the matter.

## Of Diodorus Siculus
<note>original: "Diodori Siculi"</note>

He himself <note>Refers to Agatharchides of Cnidus, a Greek historian and geographer.</note> says that every year in the mountains of Ethiopia, from the time when the sun is at its highest <note>The summer solstice.</note> until the autumn equinox, there is a steady and unceasing rain. Therefore, it is no wonder that the Nile is small in winter, as it has no more water than what its springs provide, yet in summer it may swell from the influx of rain. Even if this man has hit upon the truth, we should not omit our own opinion here. We see many things that seem unnatural to us, the causes of which cannot be fully experienced or known. Good evidence for this is found in the things that happen in Asia; for there are certain mountains in Scythia <note>An ancient region in central Eurasia.</note> that nearly touch Mount Caucasus, which every year after the end of winter are covered in snow for many days in succession. On the borders of India that lie toward the North, great hailstorms occur at certain times every year, so terrible that it is unbelievable to describe. By the river Hydaspes <note>Now known as the Jhelum River in India and Pakistan.</note>, it always rains for some time at the beginning of summer, and then several days later in Ethiopia. Thus, I shall not miss the mark if I say that the steady rain in the neighboring Ethiopian mountains causes the water to rise, especially since those who live there give testimony of the great rains. 

Now, if it seems unnatural to someone what is written of the Nile—because he does not perceive the same in our own waters—he should not reject this as untrue. For when the South wind blows among us, it brings rain, whereas in Ethiopia it brings fair weather. Likewise, the North winds are very harsh in Europe, but in Ethiopia they are mild. Now, so that we do not overstate the matter, let this much be said regarding the flooding of the Nile. # Of Diodorus the Sicilian and
## renowned historian: regarding the history

### of all the world and the glorious reigns. Book Two.

## Of the first beginning of the world and of mankind. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A large, ornate decorative drop cap letter "D" featuring intricate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

This book has been divided into two parts due to its great size. In the first part, we provided the preface and overview of the entire work: the initial origin of the world and all things, the Gods, and the cities said to have been built in their names. Likewise, we described the first origin of mankind and the earliest way of life; the honors paid to the immortals; and the temples <note>original: "Kirchen"; the translator uses the contemporary word for "churches" to describe ancient temples.</note> first established among the Egyptians and others. We also described the geography of Egypt and the various opinions held by scholars concerning the Nile—why it overflows and what the naturalists <term>naturalists: those who study the physical world and its laws</term> and historians say about it, highlighting their conflicting views. This current book, as with the previous one, shall proceed to recount the deeds of the ancient Egyptian kings up until Amasis <note>Amasis II (reigned 570–526 BC), a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty.</note>, beginning first with the lifestyle of the Egyptians. 

The ancient Egyptians first lived upon herbs and water-roots, which they found to be good and pleasant to the taste. Above all, they ate the herb *Agristim* <note>Likely referring to a type of marsh grass or clover (Agrostis), valued for its sweetness.</note>, which was quite sweet and beneficial to both cattle and people. In memory of its usefulness, they still harvest it and offer this herb to the Gods, believing that man is a creature made of clay and moisture. They conclude this because of man's simple origin—being entirely natural—and because he requires more moist than dry food. 

Afterward, they say, the Egyptians lived on fish, which the Nile provided in great abundance as the waters receded. Then they began to hunt wild animals, using their skins for clothing. They built houses out of reeds—a practice shepherds still use today—and held no other buildings in such high regard. After much time had passed with such food and lifestyle, they began to seek out other fruits, among which was bread made from lotus <note>original: "Lotho"</note> or millet <note>original: "Milkreß"</note>. Some attribute this discovery to Isis; others give credit to Menas <note>original: "Mene"; likely Menes, the legendary first pharaoh of Egypt.</note>, a king who reigned long before her. Their priests say that Mercury <note>The Roman name used here for the Egyptian god Thoth, often associated with wisdom and invention.</note> was the inventor of the fine arts, and that the kings discovered whatever else was useful for life and its preservation. For this reason, among the ancients, power was not inherited; instead, whoever discovered something beneficial for mankind and was most useful was elevated to the rank of King—either by public acclaim...

It has a circumference of nearly four German miles <note>The original Greek text specifies 150 stadia, roughly 17–18 miles. The city is well-protected and well-situated, for the Nile itself, with its outflow toward the south, has a great embankment raised up, serving as a dam against the rushing water and against enemies should they wish to overrun the city. In other places, it is surrounded by a man-made embankment with water-filled moats, and then a special trench into which the floodwaters flow in their season, providing double protection. The first founder took advantage of this location and prepared it in such a manner that almost all kings thereafter left Thebes and lived there, building their palaces and royal courts within it. ...Son <note>The text refers back to a previous lineage</note> he begat, after whom the whole land was named; for his name was Egyptus. This same man ruled in a friendly and just manner and was an exceedingly excellent man in all things. Because he was so agreeable to everyone, he left his name to the land, which everyone gladly accepted. After his death, his twelfth son, named Myris <note>Historically known as Moeris</note>, held power. He built the northern portico <note>German: vorschopff, an architectural forecourt or vestibule</note> of the palace at Memphis in such a manner that this same building surpasses all the wonders of the earth. About a quarter-mile above the city, he dug a lake that brings wondrous benefits, and whose size is almost unbelievable to report; for it is nearly forty miles in circumference and fifty cubits <note>original: eln (ells)</note> deep in some places. Thus, when one considers the great, excessive construction, the foresight of the king, and the benefit that arose for the land of Egypt, one cannot praise this king enough. For the Nile does not always rise equally, and as it rises, so the land gives fruit. Therefore, if it rises too much, this pit was made so that the silt <note>original: lett (clay or mud)</note> it carries does not overflow the land but remains in this pit. Or if it flows out too little, so that the soil does not dry out and be less fertile. For when it pours out too little water, one can drain the lake and thereby moisten the land. The trench that goes from the Nile into the lake is two miles long and one acre <note>original: Juchart, a historical unit of land area representing what a yoke of oxen could plow in a day</note> wide. Through these trenches, one may direct the water into the lake or out of it; one could open or shut it to water the land as desired after the Nile had flowed out, yet not without great cost, for it always costs up to thirty thousand crowns to close or open it. This lake has remained for the great benefit of the Egyptians until our times and has kept the name Myris from its builder. In the middle of the lake, the king left a place where he established his tomb, which stands upon two pyramid-shaped columns <note>original: feur spitz seüln, literally "fire-pointed columns," a term used for pyramids or obelisks</note>, one stadium <note>A classical unit of length, roughly 185 meters</note> high. One column was erected for him and the other for his consort; upon these stood two stone statues, each sitting on a throne <note>original: künstül</note> which he had raised because he wished thereby to create an eternal memorial for himself. The tax collected from the fish of the lake he bequeathed to his wife for her finery. It brought in six hundred crowns every day. Twenty-two kinds of fish are said to have been heard of in this lake. Among them were such mighty catches that there were enough salted fish to export to foreign lands, with plenty left over. Now after this Myris, his seventh son ruled: Sesostris <note>Historically identified with Senusret I or III, or Ramses II</note>, who surpassed all kings before him in honor, dignity, and glorious deeds. Not only did the Egyptian priests write much about this king, and even made songs about him, but many Greeks also remembered him, though inconsistently; therefore, we wish to describe what is found that is still worthy of memory and closest to the truth. ### Diodorus Siculus

...that they were accustomed to toil; none were allowed to eat unless they had first run four and a half miles <note>original: "fünffthalb meyl"—a German mile in the 16th century was roughly 4.6 modern miles, making this a grueling 20-mile run</note>. Thus, they all became brave and strong youths. At his father’s command, Sesostris marched with them into Arabia, where no Egyptian king had ever gone before. There he also became accustomed to cold, hunger, and thirst, so that he and his men soon traversed and conquered all of Arabia, which had previously been a land of free and independent people. From there, he pushed further into Libya and, while still a young man, brought a large portion of that region under his control.

When his father Myris passed away and he came to the kingdom, he was emboldened by his past deeds and set his mind upon the mastery of the whole world. Some say his daughter, named Athyrtia, directed him toward this goal, for she was a very wise and sensible person who persuaded her father that, with the army raised alongside him, he could easily bring the world under his power. Others say she was a prophetess <note>original: "warssagerin"</note> who could see and tell of future things by the stars and through sacrifices. There is also a legend that when Sesostris was born to Myris, a dream came to the father showing that his newborn son should rule the entire world. This caused him to have all Egyptian children born on the same day raised alongside his son and kept in royal discipline, so that his son would be more capable of acquiring such great power.

When Sesostris reached manhood and became aware of this prophecy, he took heart and gathered a great army <note>original: "Heerzeiig"</note>. So that his undertaking might proceed more easily, he made all Egyptians his friends. He did this so the soldiers would be more obedient to their captains and more willing to face life or death with their leaders, and so the citizens would remain loyal while he was away in foreign lands without ceasing. He left no one unrewarded: to some he gave money, to others landed estates, and some who were punishable he set free. He gave kind words to everyone and treated them well. There were a great many who were deeply in debt; for these, he satisfied the creditors. If anyone had acted against the King, he was forgiven. He also divided all of Egypt into thirty-six districts, which are called *Ezicht* <note>original: "Ezicht"—this refers to the "Nomes," the traditional administrative divisions of ancient Egypt</note>. To each district, he gave its own magistrate <note>original: "schultheyß"</note> and also its own collectors, who demanded the King’s rents and taxes; in return, they oversaw what was useful and necessary for that district. He chose his army from the strongest men to carry out his plan. On foot, he had six hundred thousand men; of cavalry <note>original: "reysiger"</note>, twenty-four thousand; and eight thousand and twenty war chariots. [They loved] one another like brothers and were all heartily loyal to the king. To all of them, he granted fertile fields so that they would have their sustenance and suffer no want, enabling them to devote themselves better to the art of war. When he was well-prepared, he first attacked the Ethiopians, who lived toward the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally midday, but used geographically to mean South</note>, and conquered them, forcing them to pay an annual tribute of gold, ebony wood <note>original: "hebenum"</note>, and ivory.

He brought all of Asia under his rule by waging war on land; he conquered not only the lands that Alexander the Great later subdued, but he even went further than Alexander ever reached. For Sesostris crossed the river Ganges into Cambaya <note>likely Khambhat in modern-day India</note> and traversed all of Media and the land called Serica <note>original: "Seruon," likely referring to the land of the Seres, or China</note> as far as the Ocean sea.

Likewise, he conquered the Scythians, who live by the Tanais <note>original: "Teysa," referring to the Don River, which ancient geographers considered the border between Europe and Asia</note>, where Europe and Asia divide. He left a great multitude of Egyptians there, from whom the Colchians <note>an ancient people on the eastern coast of the Black Sea</note> are descended; evidence of this is that the children there are circumcised, as is the custom among the Jews, who also came from the Egyptians. He also conquered the remaining parts of Asia; most of the Cyclades islands in the Archipelago <note>the Aegean Sea</note> fell under his yoke, and from there he marched into Thrace.

When he had moved into Europe, his army suffered great distress from a lack of fodder and food, as well as the harshness of the land. Therefore, he did not wish to go further, but everywhere he had won a victory, he erected monuments <note>original: "sig zeichen," victory signs or stelae</note> inscribed with Egyptian script (which is called the sacred script <note>hieroglyphics</note>), stating: "This land was overcome and conquered by Sesostris, the King of all ruling Kings."

Wherever a people had stood against him and fought manfully, he had a male member <note>a phallus, symbolizing bravery</note> carved into their pillar; but to those who surrendered fearfully without a fight, he set up a monument inscribed with female private parts. By this, he intended to show which nations had proven braver and more excellent than the others. In several places, he erected pillars where his likeness was made, showing the age he was when he waged these wars; the likeness held a bow and arrow more than four cubits <note>original: "Elnbogen," an ancient measurement roughly the length of a forearm</note> long. He treated the conquered peoples well, and when he had completed this expedition in nine years, he ceased his warring and commanded all lands to honor him once a year with their gifts. Darius was not at all angry at this, but instead rejoiced that the priest had spoken the truth to him, giving him only this answer: that if life were granted to him, he would strive to act in such a way that he should not be esteemed less than Sesostris. He (the priest), however, should compare his age against the age of Sesostris and weigh them; then he would find that high-mindedness and virtue were not lacking in him. After the death of Sesostris, his son ruled, who bore his father's name, but he had no regard for doing anything magnificent. <meta>This page continues the history of the Egyptian kings following the reign of Sesostris. It details the reign of his son (historically known as Pheron), the tyranny of Amasis, the conquest by the Ethiopian king Actisanes, and the construction of the Labyrinth by King Moeris.</meta>

In anger and scorn, he <note>This refers to Pheron, the son of Sesostris, who according to legend was struck blind for his hubris against the river</note> shot arrows into the river Nile. Because of this, he called upon the help of the gods and offered them costly sacrifices, believing he could thus appease them, but it helped him not at all. Only ten years later was it announced to him that he should reconcile with the god honored at Thebes and find a woman there who had never been unfaithful to her husband; by her, he would receive his sight again. He began with his own consort and examined a great number of women, but in vain. At last, a gardener's wife was found who restored his sight with her gaze. As soon as he could see, he took her in marriage; all the others he locked in a chamber and burned. For this reason, he was thereafter called "the Destroyer." Afterward, he showed himself thankful toward the god at Thebes as he had been commanded, and erected two pillars from a single stone, each twelve feet <note>original: "schüch," literally "shoes," a historical measurement roughly equal to a foot</note> wide and one hundred and fifty feet high. After this king, many ruled who performed nothing worthy of memory. At last, the kingdom came to Amasis, who was a great tyrant and committed such outrages as none had ever done before; he killed many against the law and robbed others of their property; toward everyone, he was proud and frivolous. Because no one could protect themselves from this insolence and tyranny (for lack of opportunity), his arrogant power was tolerated until Actisanes, the king of Ethiopia <note>original: "Mhornland," literally "Land of the Moors"</note>, invaded the land. Then secret envy broke out in all places, and many defected from Amasis, so that he was soon captured, and Egypt fell into the hands of the Ethiopian. Actisanes did not boast of his victory; he behaved kindly toward the Egyptians and maintained good justice. He suppressed murderers and insolent people with a special court. He did not kill them, nor did he leave them unpunished; rather, when they were convicted, he summoned them before him in crowds, cut off only their noses, and drove them to the furthest edge of the desert. There he built them a city located between Arabia and Egypt, not far from the sea, in a very suitable place, which was then called Rhinocolura <note>From the Greek words for "nose" and "cut off"</note> and is now called Faramida. The entire ground there is salty; moreover, in the city, there is only a single bitter spring. Now, the king had banished them there so that they would not lead the pious people of neighboring nations astray, and so that one could recognize what sort of fellows they were; yet he let them seek their sustenance in the desert with great toil and labor, so that their insolence might be subdued. Their first food was made by making nets out of reeds and stretching them out many furlongs <note>original: "stadia," a Greek unit of distance</note> wide, with which they caught many birds that lived there for the sake of the fish.

There are another three pyramids which measure two juchart on all sides. In their artistry and materials, they are equal to the others in everything except for their size. It is said these three kings built them for their wives; it is also said they surpass all other wonderous works of Egypt in cost and material—indeed, it is said more of the master builder’s skill was applied to these than to any others, which is why they are more famous. For whatever praiseworthy things the master builders added, they did so out of free artistry, whereas the great costs the kings expended were the sweat and labor of the common man. But as to who actually ordered them built, the Egyptians themselves do not know, nor does anyone describe it with certainty. Some claim, as we have written, that the aforementioned kings built the three large pyramids; others say that Armeus built the larger, Amasus the middle, and Masus the smaller. Furthermore, some claim that one is the tomb of a famous courtesan named Rhodopis, and that certain princes who were her lovers erected such a monument to her.

After Mycerinus, Bocchorus <note>a ruler of the 24th Dynasty</note> became king, who surpassed all previous kings in bodily strength and also in reason. After his death, a long time having passed, Sabacus <note>the Nubian Pharaoh Shabaka</note> ruled, an Ethiopian who was praised for his piety and generosity more than the previous kings. A good sign of his character <note>original: "dapparkeit"</note> is the piety and love he bore for the good, and also his skillful and practical mitigation of the punishments which, by right of law, were laid upon the wicked. Those condemned to death he did not execute; instead, he made them perform all the public works in the cities, though they had to wear chains on their feet. Whoever had work to be done used these men, and the king gave their wages to the community. From that money, they constructed canals and embankments that were useful to the land. In this way, he softened the harshness of punishment and the useless cruelty...

Through his judgments, he served the common good. His piety and his well-bred life since youth may be understood from his dream. The god who is worshiped in Thebes <note>referring to Amun-Ra</note> appeared to him and said that he would not be able to rule Egypt happily or for long unless he killed all the priests in Egypt and trampled their corpses along with his servants. This dream came to him often, so he called all the priests in Egypt together, presented his dream to them, and spoke: He did not wish to stay in Egypt to kill anyone, but would much rather remain pure and free of all vice, renouncing the Egyptian kingdom—even dying—rather than ruling with such cruel slaughter. Therefore, he immediately left the kingdom of Egypt and returned to Ethiopia. The Egyptians remained for two years without a king, through which a great uprising grew and civil wars arose; for this reason, they chose twelve princes from the most honorable men to rule the entire kingdom. They gathered together in Memphis <term>Memphis: referred to in the text as "Meßer," likely a variant of the Arabic name Misr</term> and ruled harmoniously in total peace for fifteen years. They also desired that, just as they had ruled well and harmoniously in life and were held in high regard, they should also lie together after their deaths and be honored with a single tomb.

They then undertook to build such a work that it would surpass the buildings of all previous kings. For this purpose, they chose a site located near a lake in Libya <note>In ancient geography, Libya often referred to the region of North Africa west of the Nile</note>, by the water that flows into Lake Moeris <note>original: "See Miridem"</note>. The roof was made of a single stone, carved with vaults and decorated with various figures which recounted the lives, establishments, and histories of all the kings, the temples, and the events of Egypt. Indeed, this building was begun with such great expense and such magnificent labor that it would easily have surpassed all the tombs of the previous kings if the construction had been completed while the twelve were still living together in unity. # The Second Book

Then Psammetichus took the most beautiful of the eleven golden bowls, which a priest had brought out by mistake, and offered a sacrifice to the God. When his fellow rulers became aware of this, they did not wish to kill him, but instead banished him from the government to the marshes by the sea, either because of the oracle’s warning or out of pure envy. But Psammetichus hired soldiers from Arabia, Caria, and Ionia <note>Caria and Ionia were regions in what is now modern-day Turkey, known for providing skilled Greek mercenaries</note>, and fought a battle against his colleagues near the city of Memphis <term>Memphis: The German text uses "Meßher," a corruption of the Arabic "Misr"</term>. He was victorious in this battle; some of the other rulers were stabbed to death, while the rest fled into Libya and surrendered their majesty. After achieving this victory and winning the royal dignity, he had a beautiful vault or portico built for the God at Memphis, facing the sunrise. Around the temple, he erected twelve statues in place of columns, each of which was eighteen feet high. To the foreign soldiers he had hired, he gave honorable gifts over and above their wages; to the others, he distributed the territory located on the banks of Damietta by lot, which much later King Amasis <note>original: "Amasus"</note> brought back under the control of the people of Memphis.

Now that Psammetichus had bestowed honors upon these foreign soldiers, he relied upon them and treated them generously. However, when he marched with a host into Syria, he gave the foreigners the place of honor and the lead, positioning them on the right wing, while placing the Egyptians on the left side. The Egyptians considered this such a grave insult that more than two hundred thousand of them revolted against the king and marched into Ethiopia to dwell there. Upon this, the king sent his captains to them, instructing them to dissuade the men from this act as mildly as possible. When these messengers achieved nothing, he hurried after them himself by ship, for they were traveling along the Nile, and he caught up with them just at the Egyptian border as they were about to cross over. There he begged them to abandon their undertaking and to remember their gods, their fathers, their wives, and their children. At this, they all cried out at once, struck their weapons together, and answered: they were also soldiers and well-armed, and for that reason, they could easily win a new fatherland. Furthermore, they lifted up their clothes and showed their male members, shouting that they would not lack for wives and children as long as they were well-equipped <note>This is a famous historical anecdote where the deserting soldiers suggest their virility ensures they can start new families elsewhere</note>. With this answer, they showed contempt for those things which other men value most highly, and they marched into Ethiopia. Finding the land there most fertile, they immediately occupied everything they captured. 

Their departure greatly troubled Psammetichus; he returned to his kingdom, established customs and taxes, and formed friendships with the Athenians and other Greeks, setting up new alliances. He showed himself quite friendly toward the foreigners who sailed to Egypt and did much good for them. Above all, he loved the Greeks; he sent his children to them to learn their language and arts. He is the first of all the Egyptian kings to have invited foreigners to bring their commerce into his land and to allow them to travel within it with safe conduct. For in the times of the previous kings, no one came to Egypt by ship from foreign lands; anyone who arrived there was either killed or thrown into prison and slavery. This cruelty, which occurred most of all under Busiris <note>Busiris was a legendary Egyptian king said to sacrifice all foreigners who entered his country</note>, gave the Greeks cause to compose myths about him. After Psammetichus, in the fourth generation, Apries <note>original: "Aprieus"</note> ruled for twenty-two years. He attacked Cyprus and Phoenicia by water and land with war, and when he had captured Sidon in Phoenicia by force, he subdued the remaining cities located in that land and sailed from there with a mighty fleet into Cyprus.

They were not at all frightened by the dangerous journey to Egypt; and among those who traveled to Egypt with such great desire were the oldest: Orpheus, Homer, and later Pythagoras of Samos, and the lawgiver Solon <note>original: "Solo"</note>. The Egyptians write that the movement of the stars, calculation, and many other arts were invented by them. Also, the best laws originated from them, which can be inferred from the fact that for nearly three thousand seven hundred years, only native-born kings held power in Egypt. Egypt is also better provided for than other lands on earth, which could not be the case if there were not very good customs and the best laws—indeed, if they were not well-taught in all the arts. -># The Second Book.<-

[be] revealed. ¶ First, the kings in Egypt did not rule according to their own whim, like the kings of other nations who consider whatever they decide to be the law; rather, these kings had their income and daily conduct governed by the law. No one served them at court who was a bought or born slave; instead, only the sons of the priests <note>original: "pfaffen" - while this is a Christian term for clergy, the author uses it here to describe the Egyptian priestly class</note> and the most noble, all of whom were over twenty years of age and more learned in the arts than others, served them. This was so that the king, in the presence of these brave people who were around him day and night, would not dare to do anything improper. For powerful lords are seldom evil unless they have servants who help them in all their whims.

Day and night, the king had his scheduled hours during which he was to do each thing. He had to rise early and read through the complaints of all the burdened and similar writings, giving answers to them regarding what was to be done and how to act therein, so that every matter would receive its proper time. After this, he bathed with the most noble men. Having then put on costly clothes, he went and sacrificed to the gods. Then the priests came and stood around the sacrificing king, crying out with a clear voice so that all the people heard: "Health, peace, and all good things shall be granted to the law-loving king through the mercy of the gods."

Then they recounted to the people the king's particular virtues: how he was God-fearing <note>The translator uses "gotsforchtig," applying 16th-century religious vocabulary to describe ancient piety</note>, merciful to his subjects, faithful, not willful, chaste, just, magnanimous, truthful, generous, and entirely steadfast against all desires. They said he did not punish as harshly as the misdeeds of the subjects sometimes required, but in rewarding good, he was more generous than the good deed itself demanded. After they had spoken much good of the king, the priest cursed the <term>tyrants</term> <note>original: "Wüetterich" — a term for cruel, bloodthirsty, or arbitrary rulers</note>; and if something occurred that burdened the Egyptians, he said it was not the king's fault, but the fault of some of his advisors who had misdirected him.

After this, the high priest exhorted the king toward divine service, toward a good life and good morals, and pleaded with him not to let himself be led astray by evil counsel, but rather to take in hand that which served praise and virtue. Afterward, when the king had sacrificed an ox, the priest read to him the deeds and lives of several noble men as an example, so that he might keep himself similarly just and God-fearing in his reign.

Not only in matters of tribute and tax, nor in the courts alone, but even in walking, eating, bathing, and sleeping with the queen—in conducting his entire life—the king had to follow the law. He ate simple food, for nothing was served to him except calf and goose. He had a set measure of wine to drink, so that he could not overfill his belly with food and drink, nor could he get drunk. Indeed, his life was to be lived according to an order that looked as if the most proven physician, and not merely a lawgiver, had established such a regulation.

Therefore, it is truly marvelous that the kings of Egypt were bound to live not according to their own whim, but according to the laws, just like common men. It is even more to be wondered at that they were not allowed to amass money, nor to judge anyone out of anger or envy, nor to kill anyone unjustly out of pride; rather, without any resentment, they were subject to the law like common men and considered themselves blessed whenever they were obedient to the laws. They said themselves that those who ruled according to their own whim—even beyond what they knew of themselves—would often sin, either out of favor, hatred, or other things that affected them, whereby they would then fall into great danger. All this was avoided where one [followed] wisdom in...

# Of Diodorus Siculus

exercised power and lived according to the laws. Thus, these kings who ruled so justly earned the favor and submission of all Egyptians, so that in the entire realm, not only the priests but also the common people cared more for the welfare of the king than for themselves, their wives, or their children. As long as the kings remained within the discipline of these laws, they generally achieved a good end to their civic lives and brought many other lands under their rule. They amassed wealth, royal buildings, and mighty works, and adorned the cities with excessive gifts and ornaments. 

It is also clearly shown how beloved and highly honored the common people held their kings by what they demonstrated after their deaths. For as soon as one of the kings died, everyone mourned in common, tore their clothes, and closed the temples; all shops and trade were shut down and ceased. No wedding celebrations were held; for seventy-two days they covered their heads with mud <note>original: "koat" - filth or mud, used as a sign of extreme mourning</note>, girded themselves with linen around the chest, and men and women—about two or three hundred of them—ran around the city twice a day, renewing the lamentation. With composed songs, they sang of the deceased king's virtues. They ate no cooked food, nor any kind of meat; they drank no wine, set no tables, did not bathe, used no ointments, prepared no beds, and performed no marital acts <note>original: "eelich werck"</note>, but mourned the entire time just as if their own children had died. During this time, they prepared what belonged to the funeral. On the final day of mourning, they placed the body

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicts a funeral scene. A rectangular sarcophagus or bier is set on the ground. Above it hang two ornate oil lamps with flames. The background is simple line-work.</image-desc> 

took him in a bier and set him before the tomb. Then, before all the people (for everyone came and gathered there), they read what the king had done in his life. Anyone who had been burdened by him had the power to accuse the dead body. The priests stood around and praised the king's good deeds; if the people heard that he was being praised with the truth, they shouted and wailed; if not, and if too much was attributed to him, they protested with a great clamor. 

Thus it often happened that some kings did not enter their appointed burial place and did not receive their honor after death. This then compelled the other kings to live justly, so that they would not earn the eternal envy and hatred of the people after their death. Now, in this manner the ancient kings had to conduct themselves. 

The entire land of Egypt was divided into many parts, which they called prefectures <note>original: "Vogteyen" - referring to the Nomes or administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>, each of which had a magistrate <note>original: "Schultheyße"</note> who managed all affairs therein. The income of Egypt was also divided into three parts. The foundations of the priests claimed the first part; they held great prestige among the common people because they administered divine service and were learned people. Therefore, this third of the income was given to maintain the church ceremonies and to support the priests. For they deemed it good that the worship of God should not be neglected, and that the counselors and servants of the community should be well-provided for without lack of sustenance. The reason was that the priests were always at the forefront when something difficult occurred in which the king needed counsel; then they prophesied from their knowledge of the stars <note>original: "gstirns" - referring to astrology and astronomy</note> and sacrifices. Also, from their knowledge of the sacred scriptures (in which the lives of previous kings were recorded), they knew the

For it is not as it is with the Greeks, where in every temple there is but one priest or priestess; rather, they have many, who thereafter instruct their children in the same divine service and also raise them for that purpose. They are also free from all burdens <note>original: "beschwerden" – likely referring to taxes and compulsory labor</note> and are honored as the highest in rank after the King. The second part of the income is assigned to the King, from which he conducts war, maintains his splendor and royal estate, and rewards those who conduct themselves well. Thus, one does not need to fleece <note>original: "schinden" – literally to flay or skin</note> the common man for these things. The third part of the income is distributed to the military <note>original: "Kriegsvolck"</note> and other equipment necessary for war, so that through such payment, the "war-throats" <note>original: "kriegßgurglen" – a colorful term for soldiers or mercenaries</note> are all the more willing and ready for battle. For it was considered unjust that those who undertook to protect the fatherland in common should receive no benefit from the very land for which they fight. And a particular benefit also arises from this: that those who are well-paid can provide for themselves and are more inclined to bear children, so that the land becomes populous and has no need for foreign help; indeed, the children are thus raised by their fathers, old soldiers, and becoming accustomed to their innate paternal boldness and learning the laws of war, customs, and tactics, they become much better soldiers. Furthermore, the estate of the Egyptian land is divided into three parts: shepherds, farmers, and craftsmen. The farmers rent the fields for a very small fee from the priests, the king, or the soldiers; they remain there for their entire lives, attending without cease to the plowing of the fields. Consequently, the Egyptians are more knowledgeable of farming than any other people, and the reason for this is that through long habit and the instruction of their elders, they have learned it so well. They recognize better than anyone else the nature of every field, and when it ought to be sown and reaped. Additionally, they know which fruit lasts the longest and how it should be preserved. In this way, no one is cheated in their learning, nor does any civic hatred—which often occurs in government—hinder anyone; nor is anything else in the way to stop a man from being all the more devoted to his craft. # Diodorus Siculus
