### On the Punishment for Killing Children.

The fathers who killed their children were not put to death, but they were required to stand by the dead body for three days and three nights in a row, guarded by watchmen of the authorities. For they [the judges] considered it unjust that those who should give life to their children should be executed for taking that same life away again. It seemed to them sufficient that they should deter others through such long-lasting pain and the remorse for their deed (having committed it).

### On Parricide.

If someone killed their parents or brothers, they were judged miserably and cruelly; for after one limb after another was cut off, he was then burned alive on a pile of thorns. They regarded it as the most cruel vice for one to take the life of the person who had given them life. <note>original: "Blutmord" – literally "blood-murder," a term used here for the killing of close relatives, specifically parents.</note>

### Punishment of Pregnant Women.

Women who were sentenced to death and were pregnant were not executed before the birth; they thought it was wrong that the innocent should suffer with the guilty, or that two should be punished where only one had sinned. And that which has never done wrong should not have to pay for a person who willingly did evil. Moreover, it seemed to them that since the mother alone had sinned, it would be unjust for the child—who belonged not to her alone, but also to the father—to suffer with the mother. It would happen to them just like those judges who sometimes let the guilty go and kill the innocent.

### On Deserters.

If someone in a war fled from the ranks <note>original: "auß der ordnung" – literally "out of the order" or formation</note>, or was disobedient to the commanders, he was not killed for it but was proclaimed to be the most dishonorable of all. However, if he redeemed this through bravery and some bold deed, he was then held in the same regard as before. This law accustomed the people to fear such shame more than death, and gave it to be understood that the dead could no longer be of use to mankind. Also, those so dishonored were incited to many virtues in order to regain their honor.

### On Treason.

Whoever revealed a secret to the enemy had his tongue lost; it would be cut off from him.

## On the Forging of Coins and Documents.

Anyone who clipped the coins <note>The practice of "coin clipping" involved shaving small amounts of precious metal from the edges of coins to sell for profit.</note> or falsified the minting, made the weight too light, altered the identifying marks, wrote their own name upon them, or removed the official inscription, or produced forged letters, had both hands cut off. This was done so that the part of the body which had sinned would do penance throughout the person's entire life, and so that others, reminded by this misery, would guard themselves against similar misconduct. Furthermore, much harsher punishments were established for women if they committed any such offense.

## On the Defiling of Virgins.

Whoever defiled a free woman had his genitals cut off. The reason was that they said in one single act he had sinned threefold: against the law, by the destruction of good morals, and by the uncertainty of the children’s lineage <note>This refers to the "purity" of the bloodline and the legal confusion caused when a child's paternity is unknown.</note>.

## On Adultery.

Those caught in adultery, having entered into it willingly, were beaten with a thousand lashes of the whip. The woman had her nose cut off so that her face was disfigured; she was punished in the very place that made her most beautiful and had brought her into this desire. As for the laws established regarding the trade and commerce of people with one another, these were set down by Bochoris <note>Bocchoris, or Bakenranef, was an Egyptian Pharaoh of the 24th Dynasty, famous in later Greek tradition as a wise judge and lawgiver.</note>; they read as follows.

## On Disputed Debt.

Where someone lent money to another without a written contract, and the debtor refused to acknowledge the debt to the creditor, the creditor should then be paid by the debtor upon a sworn oath. For they held the oath to be a very holy thing and believed that since those who swear constantly retain less credibility, an honest man would swear but rarely so that he would not lose his honor. It was the lawgiver’s opinion that because all trust resided in being honorable, people should be drawn toward honesty through good customs, so that they might easily be believed. It also seemed unjust to him that a person who had lent money to another without requiring an oath should not be believed in his own cause if he were finally forced to swear to recover what was his.

## On Usury.

Usury <note>In this context, usury refers to any interest charged on a loan, not just excessive interest.</note>, even if established with written documents, was not allowed to be paid at a rate higher than double the principal sum. Furthermore, the usurer was permitted to claim only the debtor's property and not his body. They believed that property alone belonged to the debtor, but the body belonged to the common good for use in peace and war. For it seemed unjust to them that a soldier, who had braved every danger for the sake of the fatherland, should be placed in prison because of usury, or that the welfare of the common good should be subjected to the greed of a single individual. This law was also brought to the Athenians by Solon <note>Solon was a famous Athenian statesman and lawmaker.</note>, who called it <term>relief from burdens</term> <note>original: "σεισάχθειαν" (seisachtheia) – a set of laws instituted by Solon to rectify widespread serfdom and slavery that had run rampant in Athens due to debt.</note>, which mandated that citizens should not be imprisoned for the sake of usury. On this point, some of the Greeks complained, not without reason, against their own lawgivers who forbade the seizure of a plow or a...

## On Theft.

The Egyptians also had a unique law regarding thieves. Those who wished to steal had to write their names on a small scroll and give it to the priest who was the head <note>The High Priest or Chief Magistrate.</note>, and whatever was stolen had to be brought immediately to that priest. Whoever had been robbed would also go there, though he had to specify the time, day, and hour when he lost the item. In this way, the stolen property was easily found, and a fourth part was given to the thief. For the lawgiver believed that since theft could not be entirely prevented, it was better for a person to lose a quarter than the entire sum.

## On Marriage.

In marriage, the Egyptians do not have a single custom for everyone. The priests are not permitted to have more than one wife, but the commoners may have as many as they wish and are able to raise, believing such a law serves the increase of the population and the strengthening of the common good.

## On Illegitimate Children and the Upbringing of Other Children.

No one is considered to be of "dishonorable birth" <note>The German term "Banckharten" refers to children born out of wedlock, who in the translator's era would typically face severe social stigma.</note>, even if he were born of a maidservant. This is because they believe the father alone is the author of the child's human existence, while the mother provides only the place of birth and nourishment. For this reason, contrary to the custom of the Greeks, they call fruit-bearing trees "males," and the others which serve for fertilization "females." 

They raise children with such light and minimal cost that it is almost unbelievable; they take the roots of rushes <note>Specifically the papyrus plant.</note> and other stalks that grow in the marshes, boiling or roasting them in hot ashes, and sometimes giving them to the children raw. The children go about barefoot and naked, for the land is warm through and through. All the costs they spend on a child until he reaches manhood do not exceed two crowns <note>A "krone" or crown was a common European coin; the author uses it here to approximate the very low cost of living in ancient Egypt.</note>. For this reason, Egypt is more populous than other lands, and so many unbelievable and wonderful buildings have been erected there. 

The priests instruct their children both in the script which they call "holy" <note>Hieroglyphics.</note> and in other arts, especially in <term>geometry</term> <note>original: "vßmässung" (measuring out)</note> and calculation. This is because the Nile, with its annual flooding, creates new boundaries in the fields, which causes many disputes that cannot easily be settled without the art of measurement. Likewise, calculation is useful in the home and contributes much to the observation of the stars and measurement. 

The observation and tracking of the course of the Heavens is much more common and certain among the Egyptians than among others, for they have devoted themselves to it for a long time. They have applied great diligence to the proof of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>original: "Kreißgstierns"</note>, its configurations, and its risings, and what power each has over a person's birth—what good or evil it might bring—so that knowledge of these things might give them warning to avoid evil omens with good deeds. From this, they also investigate whether the years will be fruitful or barren, and what diseases or deaths might befall the livestock...

For they say that all illnesses come from an excess of food, and therefore the best medicine is that which prevents the beginning of the illness.

## On Physicians.

When they go to war or travel across the country, they are treated medically without having to pay anything for it. For the physicians receive their wages from the public treasury and their maintenance; they must help the sick according to the law, in the manner they find described in the books that their ancient physicians wrote and left behind. If someone follows these same books and yet cannot heal the sick person, he has committed no crime. However, if he heals someone with a different medicine than what is contained in the books, he must die, even if he helped the sick person. For the lawgiver believes that nothing better can be found for human illnesses than what was discovered through long observation by the best physicians.

## On the Animals that are Worshipped as 
## Gods by the Egyptians, and how they are Honored.

### Chapter 4.

The Egyptians honor certain animals so highly in their religious service that it is almost unbelievable; for they keep no moderation in this, showing great honor to them not only in life, but also in death. Specifically: the Cat, the Dog, the Hawk, the Nile Mouse <note>The ichneumon, a species of mongoose celebrated in Egypt for eating crocodile eggs.</note>, the Ibis <note>original: "Jb," a wading bird sacred to the god Thoth.</note>, the Wolf, the Crocodile, and many other animals. We will say a little about these animals and afterwards show why they are so honored. First, they assign to each animal they worship a place and territory that is sufficient for its maintenance and nourishment. Likewise, in times of sickness, they vow to bring their children there; they shave off the child's hair, encase it in gold and silver, pay a great price for it, and present it to the animal. The priests who tend to the animal show great diligence; they cut meat for the hawks and call them with a loud cry until they come and eat. To the cats and mice, they give bread in milk and fish from the Nile to eat, and they stroke and cherish them. To the other animals, they give food according to their nature. They are not ashamed

### Of Diodorus Siculus <note>original Latin: "Diodori Siculi"</note>

...publicly recognize these animals as their gods; rather, they desire to hold them in honor. They travel and go on pilgrimage from one city to another to visit them, and even while they are still far from them, they demonstrate with what great devotion they run toward them. When one of these animals dies, they wrap it in silk, raise a great lamentation <note>original: "gheil," a loud mourning cry or wailing</note> over it, beat their own breasts, take salt or brine and other noble ointments, and bury it, thus anointed, with great ceremony. If someone were to kill one of these animals out of malice, he is brought before the court and sentenced to death. But if anyone kills a **Cat** or an **Ibis** <note>original: "Ib"</note>, he must die immediately, for the common people rush together at once and kill him miserably. For this reason, everyone fears this so much that if they see one of the animals dying of its own accord, they begin to howl and shout while still far away, so that the blame does not fall upon them. 

And this superstition and mad undertaking has taken such a hold among them that even until the time of **Ptolemy** <note>Referring to Ptolemy XII Auletes, who reigned in the 1st century BCE and sought an alliance with Rome</note>, who united himself with the **Romans** and made a treaty with them, this was still in practice. For when he had made a treaty with the Romans and they were well received by him—which was very pleasing to the people, as everyone applied themselves to show the Romans love and kindness and to prevent all riots—it happened that one of the Roman soldiers, by accident, struck a **Cat** to death. Then the people ran to his dwelling, and they could be turned away neither by the command of the King (who sent his high officials to quiet them) nor by the fearful power of the Romans from putting the Roman to death. I, **Diodorus**, write this not from hearsay, but I saw it myself when I was traveling by ship in Egypt at that very time. 

All this might seem unbelievable to some, but one should not wonder so greatly at it, for what we write hereafter is even more marvelous. When a time of such terrible famine occurred in **Egypt** that people even ate one another, yet they did not touch these consecrated animals. Whenever a **Dog** is found dead in a house, the entire household shaves <note>original: "beschürt," referring to the ritual shaving of the head and body in mourning</note> their whole bodies and goes into mourning. Likewise, whatever grain, wine, or other things humans use to sustain life which are in that same house where the dog is found dead are never used but are thrown away. They also carry these same animals that die into the city for burial where they are honored, and often travel so far with them that they run out of food on the way and must suffer great need. 

It is easy to say that people worship the **Apis bull** <note>original: "Apim"</note> in **Memphis**, the **Mnevis bull** <note>original: "Mneuin"</note> in **Heliopolis**, a **Goat** in **Mendes** <note>original: "Midera"</note>, the **Crocodile** by Lake **Moeris** <note>original: "Miridis"</note>, and a **Lion** in the city of **Leontopolis** <note>original: "Leonta"</note>, and many other strange animals in many places; but it is difficult to describe such things as true to the unbelieving and the unlearned. Now, these animals are maintained with great diligence and at immense cost within the courtyards of the temples, and not by common people but by the most highly respected men. These men prepare and cook for them food made of fine white flour and milk in the best way, and they give them boiled and roasted geese every day. But those that live on flesh, these they feed with freshly caught birds; indeed, they were maintained with the highest diligence and greatest cost; they wash them in warm...

When one of them dies, they mourn no differently than if their own children had died, and they bury and inter them with exceeding heartfelt devotion. After the death of **Alexander the Great**, while **Ptolemy Lagus** <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt</note> ruled, the bull at **Memphis** died of old age. The man who had undertaken its care was so diligent in giving it a magnificent burial that, in addition to the money he had collected from offerings and spent of his own wealth, he borrowed fifty silver talents from **Ptolemy** to spend on the bull's funeral. Now we shall set forth and describe what we have seen regarding the worship of the bull called **Apis** <term>Apis: the sacred bull of ancient Memphis, considered a mediator between humans and the gods</term>. When he has died and been buried with great ceremony, there are priests chosen for the task who must travel to and fro until they find a calf that is identical to the previous one. Once it is found, the people's lamentation ends. Now the priests must seek him out and maintain him. As soon as he is found, he is first led to the city situated on the **Nile**, where he is fed for forty days; then he is placed in a ship with a golden cabin <note>original: "hobel," referring to a pavilion or structure on the boat</note> and well covered, and carried up the water to **Memphis** like a god, and placed in the **Chapel of Vulcan** <note>Referring to the Temple of Ptah; the Greeks and Romans identified the Egyptian Ptah with their god Vulcan/Hephaestus</note>. Afterward, they are never again permitted to look upon the bull. Now, they say the reason this bull is so honored is that the soul of **Osiris** entered into a bull, and always passes from that one into its successors of the same kind. Some say that after **Typhon** <note>The Greek name for Set, the god of chaos who murdered Osiris</note> had murdered **Osiris**, **Apis** gathered his limbs together and placed them in a carved wooden bull, which he covered with a white oxhide. From this, the city was also named **Busiris**. Many things that are invented are said of this **Apis**, which would take long to recount. But why such exceedingly great honor is shown to these animals by the **Egyptians** has perhaps brought about doubt and wonder. The priests have such matters in secret writings, as was said before, but many **Egyptians** point to three reasons. The first is quite doubtful and well worthy of noting the ancient simplicity therein. For they say: When the oldest gods were so few in number and the people very many, they feared the wantonness of men and transformed themselves into certain animals; thus they escaped the mischief and violence of humans. Afterward, however, when the world was brought under their rule, they—being thankful—established divine worship for the animals whose forms they had used for their own safety, and showed men how they should maintain them while living and bury them after death. The other reason is given by some ancient **Egyptians** as follows: In the first **Egyptian** wars, there was no military order among the inhabitants, for which reason they were often slain by their neighbors. Therefore, their captains devised a way to keep the people in order: each group followed after a sign set up in the shape of an animal—those which they now honor—so that everyone knew where he should remain and stand. # Of Diodorus Siculus
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

[...] had gained the victory and prevailed. Therefore, out of gratitude for the victory, they bestowed honor upon these animals, as if the victory had come from them, and they forbade the killing of any animal whose form had shown such kindness; on the contrary, it was commanded that they be specially honored. The third reason they argue is this: so much benefit comes from these animals that they are well worthy of being honored.

### Of the Divine Honor Shown to Oxen.

The cows, which bear the oxen used for plowing the fields, are not unsuited for honor; the sheep give birth twice a year and provide wool for many uses, as well as plenty of milk and cheese.

### Why Dogs are Gods.

The dog is useful for hunting and for guarding; for this reason, the god they called **Anubis** <note>original: "Anubim"</note> is painted with a dog's head, intended to show how he was the bodyguard of **Osiris** and **Isis**. Some say that when Isis searched for the body of Osiris, the dogs drove away wild beasts and people, guarding only the body of Osiris. Therefore, on the feast days of Isis, they lead several dogs ahead in the procession so that their gratitude may be shown.

### Why Cats are Held in High Regard.

They say that cats are good against the bites of venomous and other animals.

### The Nile Mouse and Its Honor.

The Nile mouse <note>This refers to the Ichneumon or Egyptian Mongoose</note> watches the crocodile and breaks its eggs; this brings safety to those traveling and trading on the waters of the Nile. Indeed, though it seems unbelievable for a beast, this little creature also kills the crocodile; for it coats itself in mud, and when the crocodile lies sleeping on the shore, it jumps suddenly through its throat down into its belly, gnaws through its entrails out of the body, and escapes unharmed while the beast <note>original: "wurms," here meaning a large reptile or monster</note> dies.

### Why the Ibis is Honored.

Among the birds, the **Ibis** <note>original: "Ib"</note> is beneficial; it eats and kills snakes, beetles, and other vermin.

### Of the Honor of the Hawk.

The hawk <note>Likely the falcon, traditionally associated with the god Horus</note> allows no scorpion to remain, and tolerates no horned snakes (or Cerastes), nor other creeping things that poison with their bite. Some believe the hawk is honored because they divine from its flight. Some say that in ancient times, a hawk brought a book written in dark brown letters to **Thebes**, and the priests—specifically those who record their books and secrets—still wear a hawk’s wing wound with a dark brown cord upon their heads.

### Why the Eagle is Honorable.

At **Thebes**, the eagle is honored because it is a royal bird and is dedicated to **Jupiter** <note>The author uses the Roman name Jupiter to refer to the Egyptian god Amun</note>.

# The Honor of the Goat.

They have worshiped the goat because **Priapus** <note>The Greek god of fertility and procreation</note> was held in high regard among the Greeks; for the member from which all the world originates is largest upon him, and this is honored by the Greeks and other nations as a cause of our human creation. The priests of Egypt must perform their first priestly duties at this same divine service.

## Why Satyrs are Honored.

They also say that **Pan** <note>original: "Pani"</note> and the **Satyrs** <note>original: "Satyri"</note> are honored by men for this reason, and they place certain images in the temples—fashioned like goats—so that they may obtain fertility, because that animal is very lusty. They worship the oxen **Apis** and **Mnevis** <note>original: "Apin vñ Mneuim"</note> as gods. Also, in honor of **Osiris**, as the one who discovered fruits and grain (to announce and celebrate an immortal memory thereof), they slaughter red oxen and sacrifice them to him. This signifies that **Typhon**, who murdered Osiris, was also red-complexioned. In ancient times, it was even grimmer: whenever a person with red hair was found, the kings, wishing to serve Osiris well, slaughtered the poor soul upon his grave. Consequently, very few red-haired people were later found in Egypt, though many foreigners who were red-haired were captured. From this, the Greek myth may have grown and a rumor spread about **Busiris** <note>A legendary Egyptian king said to have sacrificed all visitors to his country</note> that he killed pilgrims, though such things actually happened at the tomb of Osiris.

## Why the Wolf is Held in High Regard.

They say the wolves are honored among them because they are similar to dogs and run with them. There is also another reason, though it is much like a fable. They say that when **Isis** and her son **Horus** <note>original: "Orus"</note> were about to give battle to Typhon, Osiris rose from the dead in the form of a wolf and brought help to his kin. Therefore, because they overcame Typhon, they bestowed such honor upon the animal with whose help they achieved victory. Some claim that when the **Ethiopians** invaded Egypt, the wolves banded together and drove them back as far as the city called **Elephantine**. From this, that place is still called **Lycopolis** <note>original: "Lycopolis oder Wolffstatt," meaning Wolf-City</note>, and the animal is worshiped there.

## Why the Crocodile is Worshiped.

Now some wonder why, since the crocodile eats humans and causes much harm, it is nevertheless worshiped as a god by the law of the Egyptians. To this they say that not only the Nile, but also the crocodiles within it, are very useful to the land of Egypt. For the robbers in **Arabia** and **Libya** do not dare to cross the water to plunder the land for fear of the crocodiles. Furthermore, the historians provide another reason why the crocodiles were held so high. King **Mena** was once hunted by his own dogs and driven to Lake **Moeris** <note>original: "See Myris"</note>,

Each would throw the other’s deluded opinion and superstition in their face, whereby they would never again be in agreement. Others, however, bring forward another reason.

# What occurred regarding the deceased corpse and mourning
## among the Egyptians. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting the process of mummification or funerary preparation. A deceased person lies horizontally on a raised table or platform. Above the table are three suspended vessels or lamps. The scene is enclosed within a double-line border.</image-desc>

From the things described above, one might wonder; but it would seem a simple matter to him if he considered what wonders certain Egyptians perform when someone dies. Nearly every region has its own customs. Now, the common man conducts himself thus: When someone dies, his friends smear their heads with mud, and as long as the corpse is unburied, they go back and forth in the city; during this time they drink no wine, eat only the poorest food, and clothe themselves in the simplest manner. They make three kinds of graves: the most costly, the moderate, and the simple. The common man's most expensive burial costs up to six hundred crowns; the moderate costs about twenty crowns; the simplest costs somewhat less. The grave-diggers, who know how to handle the matter and have learned it from the ancients, tell the friends what the burial will cost. Depending on whether they wish to bury him at a high or low price, they prepare the grave accordingly. Then the friends come and bring the deceased; then the first man, whom they call the **<term>Gramaticus</term>** <note>original: "Gramaticum"; here referring to a ritual scribe who marked the body</note>, takes the body, lays it on the ground, and marks how far one should rip open the left side. After this, the "cutter" comes; he has a sharp Egyptian marble stone <note>likely a reference to obsidian or flint used for ritual incisions</note> and with it he slits the deceased's side as far as is customary and required. He then flees away, for immediately after the incision, the bystanders throw stones at him and curse him terribly; for they think themselves duty-bound to hate those who violate the dead body of their friend. Afterward come those whom they call **<term>Salitores</term>** <note>original: "Salitores"; meaning "the salters" or embalmers</note>; these same men are highly esteemed and held in great honor. One of them reaches into the opened body, pulls out the entrails and the heart; another washes the same with red wine and fragrant waters. Afterward, he washes the entire body and then smears it for thirty days in succession with cedar juice, myrrh, cinnamon, and other spices, which keep the body undecayed and sweet-smelling for a long time. Then they give the corpse back to its friends; they take it and keep it for a long time (so that even the eyelids and brows remain undisturbed for many years, just as if sleeping) at home in their house in a costly tomb, and some may see their ancestors through long generations inside as if sleeping, and take pleasure in them as if they were still alive. Before the corpse is buried, the friends summon everyone, even the Judges, for the day on which they wish to bury him; they call him by name and say he wishes to "cross the sea." Then the Judges come and sit on the other side of the sea in vaulted judicial chairs, usually about forty of them. Then those appointed to the task lead the ship across the sea; these same ones have their steersman and leader of the ship, whom they call **<term>Charon</term>** <note>original: "Caronē"; the mythical ferryman of the dead</note>. Hence some say that **Orpheus** took his servant, about whom we shall write something later—

taken. For since he <note>Referring to Orpheus, the legendary Greek musician mentioned on the previous page.</note> had seen such things among the Egyptians, he afterwards described it as if it took place in the underworld, just as he had seen it, though he also added some new elements of his own. Now, when the ship is thus on the lake, before the corpse is buried, anyone who wishes may bring a complaint against the dead. But if someone brings a complaint and it is found that he has unjustly accused the dead, he is severely punished. If, however, the complaint is found to be true, the judges decree that the deceased is unworthy of burial. If there is no accuser, or if the deceased was unjustly accused, the friends set aside their mourning and begin to recount and praise his virtues. They do not do as the Greeks do, who speak much of a person's ancestry (for the Egyptians consider all their citizens to be equally noble), but they begin from the childhood of the dead, recounting his upbringing and education; they then move to his adulthood, where they point out his piety <note>original: "Gottsforcht"</note>, justice, chastity, and other virtues. Then they call upon the gods of the underworld <note>referring to the deities who preside over the dead, such as Osiris</note>, praying that they might deign to place him among the blessed. At this prayer, all the people shout for joy and praise the deceased as one who shall dwell forever among the blessed. Then they bury the body at home in tombs prepared for that purpose; if they have not prepared one, they create a repository where they lay him against the strongest wall of their house. 

But if someone is forbidden from being buried because of his misdeeds or debts, they lay him unburied in a place at home until his descendants become wealthier and can satisfy the creditors regarding the debt and atone for the misdeeds; only then do they bury him magnificently. For the Egyptians consider it a great honor to bury their elders and friends magnificently. It also happens that one man may pledge the deceased body of his father to another as collateral; it is the highest shame if one allows such a body to remain unredeemed, and such a person is himself deprived of burial after his own death. One must truly wonder that the lawmakers of Egypt labored so greatly not only in those things pertaining to the maintenance of life, but also in how one should be served after death. For one clearly sees how they sought to find ways through which they might bring men to good morals. 

Even though the Greeks, through fabricated fables <note>original: "erdichten mårlinen"</note> and the writings of poets, present unbelievably great joy and rewards for the pious and terrifying punishment and pain for the wicked, they have nonetheless been unable to bring the world to good morals thereby; instead, they are only mocked and despised all the more by the wicked. The Egyptians, however, presented no fictions; rather, visible punishment was imposed upon the wicked, and visible praise followed for the pious. Both the good and the wicked are daily reminded of what reward their works will receive. Therefore, they have daily disposed themselves toward better behavior. And those should be considered the best laws which make people not rich, but honorable and wise. Therefore, we wish to speak of the Egyptian law-

<header>Of Diodorus Siculus</header>

laws—as if he did so by the command of their god (whom they call Mneues) <note>Mneues refers to Mnevis, the sacred bull of Heliopolis, whom the Egyptians regarded as an oracle of the sun god</note>—and these lawgivers did this either because they considered the laws to be a divine, wonderful, and exceedingly useful thing for mankind, or perhaps they believed that by invoking the fear of God, they might gain more prestige for their proposals, so that the common people would obey them better. The second lawgiver of Egypt is said to have been Sasychis, a very highly wise man. He is said to have attached everything pertaining to the service of God to the laws; he also invented the art of measurement <note>original: "vß messung"; referring to geometry, which the Greeks believed was invented in Egypt to redraw boundaries after the Nile floods</note> and showed the inhabitants the course of the stars. The third lawgiver is Sesostris; he attached everything that serves military order to the laws. The fourth they call Bocchoris, and they attribute to him the establishment of how one should conduct oneself toward others in commercial dealings; he is still highly regarded among the people for his skill. They say he was of a weak body and, more than all other kings, was driven by the pursuit of money. Amasis they count as the fifth lawgiver; they say he established everything belonging to the maintenance of the King and the payment of the councils throughout all Egypt. They say he was a very prudent man who loved justice and equity, and for that reason was elected King, though he was not of that royal lineage. When the people of Elis wanted to establish the Olympic games and sent their embassy to him to ask how they might organize them so that no unfairness would arise, he gave them this answer: that would happen only if no inhabitant of Elis took part in the games themselves. He also warned the tyrant of Samos, who was named Polycrates and with whom he had formed an alliance, that he should not rule so harshly but should live by equity; for he heard how he used too much arrogance toward his own citizens and also toward foreigners. But when such warnings could not prevail with Polycrates, he immediately renounced the alliance and wrote to him that since it was certain that Polycrates must soon rage himself to death and suffer greatly for it, he did not wish to experience any sorrow over his ally. The Greeks greatly marveled at such wisdom of the King, for just as he had written to Polycrates, so it happened to him shortly thereafter. The sixth lawgiver of Egypt, they say, was Darius, the father of Xerxes; for as he felt a displeasure at the godlessness that Cambyses before him had practiced in the kingdom, he lived in a friendly and God-fearing manner. He took great interest in the Egyptian priests and described for them a history and record of their divine services as contained in their holy books and written of the great deeds of the previous kings. He adopted that instruction for himself and conducted himself in such a manner that the Egyptians—a thing which had never happened to anyone else—called him a God while he was still living, and after his death, he attained all the honors that were customarily given to Egyptian kings according to the order. The aforementioned kings established the common laws with great honor and fame; however, they were significantly changed later after the Macedonians <note>referring to the conquest of Alexander the Great and the subsequent Ptolemaic dynasty</note> took over the kingdom.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Egyptian influence on Greek culture, moving from the lawgivers discussed on the previous page to the poets and philosophers who traveled to Egypt to study its wisdom and religious rites.</meta>

The poet Lycurgus the Spartan <note>A legendary lawgiver of Sparta who, according to tradition, modeled the Spartan constitution on Egyptian or Cretan systems</note>, Solon the Athenian, their countryman Plato, Pythagoras of Samos, Eudoxus, Democritus of Abdera, and Oenopides of Chios. Proof of their visits can still be seen today; for in some places statues have been erected to them, and in others, certain locations are named after them. All these men learned in Egypt those things for which they were later held in high regard in Greece. Thus, it is said that Orpheus brought from Egypt many of the hymns to the gods and other religious services, as well as the poetry concerning the Underworld. Likewise, the worship of Osiris in Egypt and that shown to Dionysus in Greece are one and the same thing. In the same way, Isis and Ceres <note>original: "Isidis vnd Cereris"; the Greek goddess of the harvest</note> are the same, though their names differ. It is also said that he <note>Orpheus</note> took the idea of the punishment of the damned and the Elysian Fields <note>the paradise for heroes in the afterlife</note> or the Limbo of the Ancients from Egyptian graves and brought them to Greece. Following these same customs, he invented the myth that Mercury is a guide of souls <note>original: "seelbleiter"; referring to the psychopomp who leads the dead to the afterlife</note>. For among the Egyptians, it was the custom when they processed with the god Apis <note>the sacred bull of Memphis</note> that one of the priests would cut something from the bull and throw it to a dog standing nearby. Since Orpheus brought all this from Egypt into Greece, Homer followed him in the twenty-fourth book of the travels of Ulysses <note>referring to the *Odyssey*</note>, describing it in his poem as he says:

The Egyptians call the Nile by its name "Oceanus"; the "Gates of the Sun" is their city of Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun," a major religious center</note>; the flowery meadow, however, is a poetic invention representing the place across the Acherusian Lake <note>original: "See Acherusie"</note>, which is located near Memphis, surrounded by green reeds and woods. Indeed, the graves of the Egyptians are almost all located in that same place, and the corpses of the dead are still carried across that lake even today, just as was heard before. Thus, this poem grew among the Greeks, and the ship in which the corpses are carried has many names; however, the Greeks say that a toll is given to the boatman, whom the Egyptians call Charon <note>original: "Charontē"</note>.

...taken, and they say this is why the temple of Hecate <note>the Greek goddess of magic and the underworld</note> is quite dark, and the gates of the "Forgetful Cocytus" <note>original: "vergãßnigen Croasti"; Cocytus was a river in the underworld, and this refers to the gates of forgetfulness or Lethe</note> are barred with iron. Furthermore, there is the Door of Truth, and beside it an image of Truth that has no head. They claim many such things are fables based on what takes place during Egyptian funerals. For in the city of Acanthos <note>original: "Achanta"</note>, which lies on the other side of the Nile toward Libya, about four miles from Memphis, there is a perforated vessel into which three hundred and sixty priests carry water from the Nile every day. At that same place, they also show a fable about a donkey at a wedding festival: one man has a long rope and continuously ties knots in it, while those following behind him untie them. 

They also say that Melampus <note>a legendary healer and prophet</note> brought the festivals of Dionysus <note>the god of wine and theater</note> from Egypt to the Greeks, and taught them about Saturn and the battle of the Titans against the gods, and after that, all the stories of the gods. They say that Daedalus <note>the master craftsman of Greek myth</note> modeled his Labyrinth after the Egyptian one, which is still standing today. They say this Egyptian labyrinth was built by Mendes, though some claim King Maron built it long before Saturn reigned. The number of columns the Egyptians erected long ago is exactly the same as those Daedalus made for the Greeks. It is certain that Daedalus built the Temple of Vulcan <note>the Roman name for the Greek Hephaestus; in Egypt, this was the god Ptah</note> in Memphis, which is the most beautiful of all. For this reason, a wooden statue of him—which he carved himself—was placed in the portico. Because of his artistic skill, the inhabitants even showed him divine honors, for on an island near Memphis, there is still a temple today dedicated to Daedalus.

<image-desc>Woodcut portrait in a square frame depicting a bearded man in profile facing right. He wears a laurel wreath on his head and classical robes fastened at the shoulder.</image-desc>

Many things indicate that Homer was in Egypt; primarily, when he describes the potion that Helen gives to Telemachus to drink, so that he might forget past sorrows. For that same drink which banishes grief—which he gives to Helen—was once made by Polydamna <note>original: "Polymneia"</note>, the wife of Thonis, in Thebes. Even now, only the women in Heliopolis make such a drink <note>The author notes that Thebes and Heliopolis are regarded here as the same city</note>, and it was invented by the ancients as a way to soothe pain and anger. Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> is called "the Golden" by the ancients, and there is still a field not far from Memphis dedicated to the "Golden Venus." 

What is written concerning the marriage of Jupiter and Juno, and their pilgrimage into Ethiopia, comes from the fact that every year the temple of Jove <note>Zeus/Amun</note> is carried across the water into Ethiopia or Libya and then back again, as if Jupiter were returning from Ethiopia. Likewise, Plato, Solon, and Lycurgus took many laws from the Egyptians and prescribed them for the common good of their own people. Similarly, Pythagoras drew much from the sacred books for his teachings on proportions and mathematics <note>original: "erteylung vnd Rechnung"</note>, and he learned how souls migrate from one body into another <note>the doctrine of reincarnation or metempsychosis</note>. They also believe that Democritus learned much about the stars during the five years he spent in Egypt. Oenopides <note>original: "Inopides"</note>, through the friendship he made with the priests and his practice in explaining the movements of the heavens, brought the knowledge of the sun’s path and the twelve signs of the zodiac, along with many other arts, back to Greece to his great honor and profit. Among the ancient stonemasons and sculptors, Telecles <note>original: "Theledeus"</note> and Theodorus, the son of Rhoecus, are held in high val-

highly valued they were, and these same men made the statue of the Pythian Apollo <note>original: "Piconische Appollonis"</note> in Samos; one half was made by Telecles, and the remaining part by Theodorus, who crafted his portion in Ephesus. It was so skillfully made that after it was assembled, it was judged by everyone to have been crafted by a single master. This art is unknown among the Greeks but is in use among the Egyptians; for they work by measurement and proportion alone, and not by sight. Thus, they assemble a single statue in a fixed, correct form from many parts. This is truly a wondrous thing: that many master craftsmen, in locations distant from one another, should make many pieces which all fit together with complete skill and precision. Indeed, some statues were made by twenty or forty masters, and of just as many pieces. A certain proof of this is the statue in Samos, which was divided into many pieces from the head down to the groin, and yet joined so freely together as if it had been made from one stone and by one master. There is also a statue made in Egypt that extends its hand and spreads its legs as if it were running. Now, enough of the Egyptians for now; now we shall speak of the Assyrians.

And he prepared quite lavishly everything that belonged to the construction of his intended city. He had no child of his own; therefore, he took the little daughter and raised her with all diligence as his own <note>original: "ann Kindtstatt auff," meaning adoption</note>. When the daughter reached marriageable age and was more beautiful than any other maiden, the king sent his governor <note>original: "vogt"</note> in Syria, Menon, at that time to settle accounts with the head shepherd Simma. While Menon was lodging with Simma, he fell in love with the maiden, took her as his wife, and brought her with him to Nineveh. By her, he fathered two sons, Japetes and Hydaspes. Semiramis was a prudent and very virtuous woman, so much so that her husband, who loved her beyond measure, did nothing without her counsel.

It then happened that Ninus, having completed the city, wished to wage war again against the Bactrians. The land, however, lay in the mountains and had dangerous narrow passes, and was well-manned by brave people. Since he had been unable to achieve anything before, he resolved to assemble a more powerful army than ever before. He gathered this from all his subject lands, so that he marched out with great power. Ctesias writes that he had seventy times one hundred thousand <note>7,000,000. Ancient historians often recorded vastly inflated numbers for these legendary armies.</note> on foot, and two hundred thousand on horse. Of scythed chariots <note>original: "geſichelte karren," war chariots with blades attached to the wheels</note>, there were slightly fewer than ten and a half thousand <note>original: "eylff halb tauſent"; literally "eleventh-half," meaning 10,500</note>. Such a multitude might perhaps astonish someone as to how it was brought together and seem to them quite unbelievable. But if one considers the size of Asia and its populousness, it will not seem so very unreasonable. One would also easily believe what we now write if one considers that Darius, when he fought against the Scythians, marched with eight hundred thousand men. Likewise, that Xerxes led an innumerable people into Greece.

If one wishes to consider what has occurred even within Europe itself, one will more easily give us credit. For from Syracuse, the single city in Sicily, Dionysius led one hundred and twenty thousand on foot, twelve thousand on horse, and of long three-rowed ships <note>triremes</note> and large galleys <note>original: "Krafeel"</note> of five oars <note>quinqueremes</note>, some four hundred from a single port. The Romans, a short time before Hannibal, when they considered that a great war would arise, summoned ten times one hundred thousand <note>one million</note> fighting men in Italy among their citizens and allies. Yet all of Italy is not to be compared to the smallest district in Asia. We have recounted this so that no one should judge the populousness of the ancients by the scarcity of the present.

Ninus divided this mighty host he had gathered against the mountainous land and narrow gorges of the Bactrians into many divisions. In Bactria, there are many cities that are large and magnificent, but the royal city is called Bactra, and it is much larger than the others, and also better fortified and defended with walls and castles. Their king was named Zoroaster; he gathered four hundred thousand men and met Ninus right at the border. He intentionally let some of the enemy fall into the land, whom he later ambushed, put to flight, and chased as far as the mountains, killing about one hundred thousand of them. fled home to guard his city. When Ninus had conquered the land, he marched against Bactra, which was very well protected by its location and other defenses. As the siege lasted a long time, Menon, the husband of Semiramis, longed for his wife; he could not be without her for long and sent for her. She, however, being a very wise woman who sought not only the things proper to a woman but also aimed for manly deeds, believed she had reached a time when she could show her high-mindedness and bravery, and she set out with pleasure on the long journey. She also put on and had a garment made for her that was designed so that no one could tell whether she was a woman or a man. When she arrived in Bactra, she surveyed the layout of the city and noted exactly where it might be scaled. She learned that the citadel <note>original: "schloß," here meaning a fortress or acropolis</note> was left unguarded because of its terrain, as everyone was occupied only with protecting the city where it lay on the plain. It was assumed that the citadel, situated among such steep cliffs, could not be won, and therefore they had no worries about that spot.

So she took good climbers who were accustomed to mountains and cliffs, scaled the mountain where it was steepest, and captured the uppermost part of the citadel or castle. To terrify those within, she made a great clamor and gave her people a signal that the castle was won. Those in the city, realizing the citadel was captured, were struck with fear; they abandoned the walls and fled as fast as they could. The Assyrians rushed in and conquered it.

### How Ninus took Semiramis
->as his wife. Chapter 3.<-

The city being won, Ninus marveled greatly at the bravery of Semiramis. He rewarded her honorably, and her beauty pleased him so well that he attempted to persuade her husband to give her to him as a wife; in exchange, he offered to give him his own daughter Sosame as a spouse. When Menon refused this, the King threatened to poke out his eyes. Menon was so terrified and distressed by this that he hanged himself out of sorrow. Thus Semiramis became the King's wife. The treasure and all the possessions of the Bactrians fell into the power of King Ninus. He then dismissed his army, provided for the conquered land with governors <note>original: "Vogtē"</note>, and returned home. There he fathered a son by Semiramis, whom he named Ninyas <note>original: "Ninū"</note>. Then Ninus died and left the kingdom to his wife. He was buried in royal fashion, and a tomb was erected for him that was nine <term>stadia</term> <note>A Greek unit of measurement; nine stadia is roughly one mile or 1.6 kilometers high—a clear historical exaggeration</note> high, as Ctesias writes, and ten stadia wide. And because the city lay on the plain by the Euphrates, this tomb towered over it so that from afar one would think it was a castle in the city, even though it was situated far from it. And some say it still stands.

They say that every day, a wall one stadium <term>stadium: An ancient Greek unit of length, approximately 600 feet.</term> long was built; therefore, it had as many stadia in its circumference as there are days in the year, which then amounted to nine miles. Their height, as Ctesias writes, was fifty paces; as some after him have written, fifty cubits <term>cubit: An ancient measurement based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 to 22 inches.</term>. The width was such that two wagons had enough space to pass side-by-side. There were two hundred and fifty <note>original: "dritthalbhundert," an archaic German expression meaning two and a half hundred</note> towers, the height and width of which were proportional to the size of such a circumference. And no one should wonder why there were no more towers in such a vast circumference; because many marshes lay around the city, they did not wish to spend money on defenses there, where the city was already naturally protected. Between the wall and the cluster of houses, there is an open space <term>zwinger: A buffer zone or clearance area between the city walls and the first row of buildings.</term> two jugera <note>original: "juchart," a measure of land area that could be plowed in a day</note> wide. When the walls had been completed within one year, she had a bridge built over the water where it was narrowest, yet it was still five stadia <term>stadium: an ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters</term> wide. It was constructed with great skill, with large stone pillars rising from the riverbed, spaced twelve feet <note>original: "schüch," literally "shoes"</note> apart from one another. She fastened the square stones together with iron clamps and sealed them with lead. The pillars were angled and pointed at the front so that the pressure of the water would break against them, allowing the bridge to better withstand the force of the water. The bridge was thirty feet wide; the timberwork was made of solid cedar, palm, and cypress of great size—indeed, the entire bridge was made such that it could well be compared to any of Semiramis's other great works. 

She also erected a wall on each bank of the river, one as high as the other outer wall, just as long, and of the same thickness as the previous ring-wall. Directly at both ends of the bridge, she built royal palaces that overlooked the entire city and served as two fortresses for the town. As the Euphrates flows toward the south, one castle faced the sunrise <note>the East</note> and the other toward the sunset <note>the West</note>, both sumptuously built. 

For the one toward the sunset had within its circuit seven-quarters of a mile <note>approximately 1.75 miles</note> of high and magnificent walls made of fired bricks. Inside, it had another inner wall <note>original: "zwinger"</note> one mile in circumference and three hundred stones thick; within this wall, all kinds of animals were depicted in their natural colors and forms, pressed into fired clay <term>bas-relief: a type of sculpture where shapes are carved to stand out slightly from a flat background</term>. Ctesias <note>a Greek physician and historian</note> writes that it was fifty paces high. The gate built into it was seventy paces high. 

Then there was a third wall, whose circumference was three and a half <note>original: "vierdehalb"</note> quarters of a mile, equal in height and thickness, but even more magnificent than the other circuit. In this wall and its towers, the forms and colors of all kinds of animals were again naturally carved. Additionally, one could see all sorts of hunts in which Semiramis sat upon a horse attacking a lioness, and her husband Ninus killing a lion with a spear. She also erected three gates, which were decorated with various types of bronze <note>original: "ärz"</note>. 

And this castle was made far more magnificent than the other that lay toward the sunrise, for that royal chamber was only three-quarters of a mile wide, surrounded by a wall of fired bricks, inside of which, instead of animals, bronze statues were erected of King Ninus,

In the middle of the city, she had a temple built to Jupiter, the magnificence of which cannot be precisely described because of the long passage of time. It is certain, however, that because of the height of the temple, the Chaldeans <term>Chaldeans: a people of Mesopotamia famous in antiquity as priests, astronomers, and astrologers</term> were able to accurately observe the course of the stars, both their rising and their setting. The statue of Opis sits upon a golden throne, and there stand two lions made of gold that reach to her knees; beside her are two silver dragons, each weighing thirty talents. These three statues had a common altar of pure gold, beautifully wrought by hand, forty feet long, twelve wide, and weighing fifty talents. All of this the Persian kings later took away. Likewise, the palaces and other beautiful buildings have partly fallen into ruin from age and have partly been destroyed by men. This garden was four jucharts <term>juchart: an ancient land measure, approximately the area a team of oxen could plow in one day</term> long on all sides; the entrance into it was made exactly like a mountain, with one level of the building always higher than the next, so that one could see far around oneself. Large vaults and spiral stairs were raised from the ground to support the weight, and were placed one upon another for support; and the foundation upon which the garden wall stood was seventy-five feet <note>original: "schůch," literally "shoes"</note> high and twelve feet thick. The wall around the garden was very expensively made, twenty-two feet thick. And the floor was laid upon it as follows: Stone columns, which were about sixteen feet long and six wide, were laid in place of beams along the length; across these, reeds were spread and bound together, and then double-baked bricks were laid upon them and well-plastered with gypsum. Upon these were placed plates of lead, so that the moisture could not reach the vaults. After that, channels were made through which the excess water could run out; also, so much earth was poured upon it that large trees could grow there, of whatever kind they might be, all quite pleasant to behold. Furthermore, the vaults that supported the garden were so light and bright that they were used for royal apartments. In addition, secret conduits <term>teüchel: wooden or clay pipes used for water transport</term> were laid, through which the water was led into the garden. Now, this garden was built long after the time of Semiramis. Semiramis did, however, build many other cities on the Euphrates and Tigris, in which the merchants who came from Media and Parthia <note>ancient regions corresponding to modern-day Iran</note> could trade and do business. In antiquity, this term often referred to the Persian Gulf or the Indian Ocean rather than the modern Red Sea</note>. Afterward, Semiramis had a stone prepared in the Armenian mountains, which was one hundred and fifty feet <note>original: "ander halb hundert schůch"</note> long and twenty-four thick; she brought it by many paths to the water, upon which she transported it to Babylonia and erected it by the busiest road. It is a wonderful thing to behold, and because of its shape was called the **Obelisk of the Stream**; it was also counted among the seven wonders of the world. And although there are many wonderful things in Babylonia, one may marvel no less at the pitch <note>original: "Bech," referring to bitumen</note>, of which there is so much. For it does not only flow out there in enough quantity for such great and mighty buildings, but such a great multitude of people dry it and use it for wood; they draw such a great heap of it daily from a spring, near which there is a great cavern of a strange sort. From this same cavern comes an evil, sulfurous stench, so that all who pass before it must die; the stench stifles the breath so that one can never recover it, but must die immediately. Above the water there is also a lake or puddle, not large, but it has this nature: if someone unknowingly passes before it and comes into the smoke that rises from it, it draws them so strongly to itself that they cannot retreat, falls in, and is pulled to the bottom and drowned, only then to be cast up again.

# How Semiramis traveled into Egypt and
## India. Chapter v.

After the city was fully built, Semiramis gathered an army together and marched against the Medes; and when she came to Mount Bastigano <note>likely Mount Behistun</note>, which is consecrated to Jupiter <note>original: "Juppiter," the Roman name for the king of the gods, here likely referring to a local deity identified with Zeus</note>, she struck her camp and built a passage at the foot of the mountain in the wide field, twelve stadia <term>stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</term> in circumference, and set up a spring therein, from which the garden could be watered. Beside the garden, she had a stone carved seventeen stadia high, and at the bottom, she had her own image depicted along with a hundred other figures who brought her gifts and offerings; she inscribed upon it in Syrian letters <note>likely referring to Old Persian cuneiform</note> that through the labor of the wondrously beautiful Semiramis, this stone was erected. When she had ascended the mound, which she had thrown up from the plain to be equal in height to the erected stone, she came to the city of Chaon, situated in Media; and seeing an exceedingly high rock in a wide field, they made another beautiful garden in the middle of it, with costly pleasure houses, from which she could view and oversee the garden and her entire host that lay below in the field. She also stayed at that same place for a good time, enjoying rest and her own spirit. She would take no other husband, fearing she would lose her rule; but when she had desire, she chose the handsome ones from the crowd; they had to fulfill her will, and their reward was death. Afterward, she turned toward Ecbatana, toward Mount Jarcieo; whoever wished to cross it had to climb many stadia high over great roughness and rocks; therefore, it came into her mind that she wished to begin work on this mountain that would never be forgotten, and also to shorten the way for herself. There she had the detours torn down, the hollows filled in, and made the road much lower and closer at great expense.

so that the same place is still called "Semiramis" after her today. Afterward, she marched toward Ecbatana, a city situated on a plain; there she built a magnificent fortress. Since the city had no springs anywhere nearby and suffered a great lack of water, she brought water into the city through tunnels and pipes <note>original: "teüchel"</note> at great expense, which was extremely useful. Not far from the city, about half a mile away, there is a mountain called Orontes, which is very high and steep to climb, for its height is three miles; on its other side lies a lake, from which a large stream flows. She diverted this water into the city by cutting through the base of the mountain. The trench was fifteen feet <note>original: "schūch"</note> wide and forty-five feet deep. When she had completed these works in Media, she traveled into Persia and other regions where she ruled, breaking and tearing down mountains and cliffs to make the lands traversable. On the plains, she threw up great mounds <note>original: "wääl," likely referring to tumuli or ramparts</note>, building tombs for her commanders as well as cities. She also had a custom, whenever she was in the field with her army, to have a high mound thrown up in the midst of the camp and pitch her tent upon it, so that she might overlook the entire camp. From this practice, it comes that many great structures are still seen today in Asia which are called the **Buildings of Semiramis**. 

Afterward, when she had traveled through all of Egypt and brought Libya under her control, she went to the oracle of Jupiter Ammon <note>A famous temple and oracle in the Libyan desert</note> to ask how she would die. She was answered that after her death, she would be worshipped as a goddess by many peoples of Asia, and that this would happen when her son Ninus sought her life. From there, she traveled into Ethiopia and brought many cities under her power, where she encountered many strange wonders. They say there is a square lake in Ethiopia, the circumference of which is one hundred and sixty feet; its water is blood-colored and has a lovely scent, and in taste it is just like old wine. It is said to be a marvel, for when one drinks it, people become so senseless that they speak all their secrets; however, this is not easily believed. 

The Ethiopians bury their dead very differently than other peoples. Herodotus <note>The famous Greek historian</note> writes that they salt the corpses, enclose them in glass, and set them upon pillars so that they remain visible to their kin forever. Ctesias of Cnidus <note>A Greek physician and historian</note> denies this, saying it is indeed true that they salt the dead, but they do not put them naked into the glass in such a way, for the heat would melt the bodies and cause them to decay. He says the rich make images of gold, the middle class of silver, and the poor of earth and clay; they enclose the dead within these and then encase them in glass, so that one can see the images through the glass just as if they were the dead themselves. Glass is very cheap in Ethiopia and much of it is made there, so that both the poor and the rich can afford it. But concerning the customs of the Ethiopians and what is worthy of memory among them, we will tell hereafter when we write specifically about them. 

When Semiramis had settled matters in Egypt and Ethiopia, she traveled into Asia to the Bactrian region with her army. Because she had kept such a large force together and had enjoyed a long peace, she was seized by ambition and devised a plan to begin a memorable and worthy war. She had heard how the Indians were very numerous and possessed such a magnificent land; therefore, she intended to invade them as an enemy. At that same time, Staurobates ruled in India; he had gathered a great force and had raised many elephants for war. Now India is, before all other lands, quite beautiful and fertile...

India has much water that moistens the land, because of which it yields fruit twice a year. In all places, there is an abundance of all fruits; there is never a shortage, and the harvest never fails. Also, there are countless **elephants** <note>original: "Helfanten," an archaic German form of Elefanten</note> there, which are large and strong, more so than the Libyan ones. Gold, silver, iron, bronze <note>original: "ärtz"</note>, precious stones, and other things that serve luxury and wealth are found there in great heaps. Such things made Semiramis all the more eager for war. As she considered how difficult a war it would be and what great equipment she would need, she commanded all the **governors** <note>original: "Landuögtē," provincial administrators</note> of her subjects to summon as many young men as possible who were fit for war. She ordered them to prepare good new weapons and train the men; the others she commanded to gather in **Bactria** <note>An ancient region in Central Asia, now part of Afghanistan and Uzbekistan</note> in three years, well-armed and well-provided. Meanwhile, she had ships built in Phoenicia, Cyprus, and other places situated by the sea where timber could be obtained. These ships were designed to be suitable for flowing waters, for the River Indus, which borders all of India, requires many ships to drive the enemy from the banks, to cut off their supplies, or to bring supplies to her friends. However, no timber grew near that water from which ships could be made, and Semiramis would have had to transport it over land from Bactria. Therefore, she devised a plan: when she saw that she was lacking in elephants and did not equal the Indians in that regard—and fearing that this might lead to her defeat—she thought of a trick to strike fear into the Indians, who believed that no elephants were to be found outside of

These she later filled with hay so that they looked exactly like real elephants. Inside each one, she placed a man upon a **camel** which carried the load. She also had these things made in secret places so that no news of it might ever reach the Indians, so that she might terrify them all the more unexpectedly when they suddenly caught sight of these beasts as if they were real elephants. When she had prepared herself for two years, they had to assemble in the third year in Bactria. The number of her forces, as **Ctesias** <note>Ctesias of Cnidus, a Greek physician and historian whose works are now largely lost</note> writes, was **three million** <note>original: "dreissig mal hundt tausent," or thirty times one hundred thousand</note> foot soldiers, five hundred thousand horsemen, and one hundred thousand chariots. There were also many men on camels with swords **four cubits** <note>original: "vier elnbogē." A cubit was roughly the length of a forearm, about 18–20 inches</note> long. She had two thousand ships, in which she carried the images of the elephants along with the horses. She also accustomed the horses not to shy away from the elephants. This same trick was used many years later by **Perseus**, the King of Macedonia, when he fought against the Romans who had Libyan elephants. But this helped neither that king nor Semiramis. When the King of India learned of and heard about the great equipment of Semiramis, he strove to be even stronger than she. In India, there grow in the waters and marshes such large reeds <note>likely bamboo; the text describes them as being so thick a man cannot put his arms around them</note> that no man can encircle them; thus, one may make good, strong ships out of them. Thereafter, he <note>King Staurobates of India</note> prepared a great armament with weaponry and summoned all of India, so that he brought together more people than were in Semiramis’s army. He hunted wild **elephants** <note>original: "Helfanten"</note> and trained them for war, so that he might strike fear into the enemy. When he had prepared everything necessary for war, he sent his embassy to meet Semiramis, rebuking her for her wantonness and ambition in invading him, since he had never done her any harm. He testified and swore by the gods that if he overcame her, he would crucify her. When Semiramis had read the letter, she laughed. She said one must use hands and not the mouth for the struggle, and thus she advanced as far as the Indus mountains. There she found the King’s naval fleet, well-prepared and waiting for the enemy. She led her own sailors against them, and there was a long and violent battle on both sides. In the end, the Indian fleet was defeated; a thousand of their ships were sunk and many people were captured.

Immediately, Semiramis built a bridge, well-fortified on both sides, so that she might bring her people across more conveniently. Whatever meadows were there and whatever cities lay along the water, she brought under her power. After the King’s ships were defeated, he acted as if he were fleeing and withdrew quite far back from the water to lure the enemy. Semiramis noticed this; she left a group of people by the bridge to guard it and marched toward the King. She had the fabricated **elephants** <note>the decoys made of camel hides mentioned on the previous page</note> brought to the front, so that the King’s scouts <note>original: "Kutschaffer"</note> might be struck with fear when they reported this to the army. However, the trick did not remain hidden for long. For some of Semiramis's train were captured, and they revealed the secret after they were interrogated and tortured by the Indians—who had been deeply terrified—to discover from where Semiramis's elephants had come.

When the two armies drew near to one another, the King sent his cavalry and chariots forward. Semiramis had the images of the elephants moved and pulled forward, at which the King’s horses were terrified. For although they were well-accustomed to real elephants, they could not endure the sight of these beasts nor the smell <note>original: "geschmack"</note> of the **camels**. They balked and ran backward, some breaking formation, so that in the beginning Semiramis prevailed. She followed the disorder with her elite troops at the forefront, fighting bravely as a commander, and drove the Indians into flight.

As the cavalry thus fled back to the infantry, Staurobates was not greatly dismayed, but instead moved the infantry forward with the real elephants. He held the first charge on the right side; sitting upon a massive elephant, he charged at the Queen, who by chance was also fighting at the very front of that same wing. The true elephants soon prevailed over the fabricated ones, and the battle became quite unequal. The King’s men hunted and struck many of the Assyrians to death; some were trampled by the elephants, some were gored by their tusks <note>original: "zänen," literally teeth</note>, and others were killed by their trunks <note>original: "schnabel," literally beaks</note>. 

As great heaps of the dead now lay here and there, a fear and terror came upon the Assyrians, so that none of them wished to stand any longer and they took to flight. Then the King struck Semiramis with an arrow in the arm, and afterward in the shoulder, but the wounds were not deep and gave the Queen little trouble. She leaped onto a horse and made her escape; it was a narrow thing that the elephant did not overtake her and lead to her capture. Thus, Semiramis exchanged prisoners, marched back into **Bactria**, and dismissed the majority of her troops. Afterward, she learned that her son **Ninyas**, through the help of a eunuch <note>original: "erschnittnen diener," literally a "cut servant," a common role in ancient courts</note>, had plotted against her life. She forgave him, just as **Jupiter Ammon** <note>an oracular god whose temple she had visited</note> had commanded her. And when she had commanded all the officials to obey her son Ninyas as king from that time forward, she vanished. According to the prophecy of the gods (as some claim), she was taken up among the gods. Others imagine that she was transformed into a **dove**, for when many doves entered the house, she flew away with them. For this reason, the Syrians worship the queen as a goddess in the form of a dove. Excluding the Indians, she ruled over all of Asia, as **Ctesias of Cnidus** <note>an ancient Greek physician and historian</note> writes. She lived sixty-two years, twenty of which she reigned alone.

## Concerning the successors in the kingdom of Semiramis
->and their rule. Chapter 6.<-

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'N' featuring floral scrolls and a seated figure.</image-desc>

After the death of Semiramis, when Ninus her son <note>often called Ninyas in historical texts to distinguish him from his father</note> came to the throne, he established peace with everyone. He did not follow in his mother's footsteps, but instead remained shut up in the royal palace his whole life. He wasted his days among women and eunuchs <term>verschnitten</term> <note>original: "verschnitten," meaning castrated male servants who often held high-status roles in ancient courts</note> in the pursuit of pleasure, and did not go out among the people. For in his opinion, a king was not blessed unless he was free from all care and labor, living constantly in revelry and enjoying himself. 

However, so that he might rule more securely, he chose new soldiers <term>Kriegßuolck</term> <note>literally "war-folk"</note> and new captains every year. These he stationed here and there in the cities as a garrison to strike fear into the people. The entire host had to gather before **Babylon**, and then he divided them up, giving each land one of his advisors as a captain. When the year was up, he sent for the previous soldiers and brought the captains home, appointing others in their place. Therefore, the citizens had to obey, for every city—just as if it were besieged by an enemy—had to live in fear of the soldiers that the King had placed over them. If any wished to be rebellious, they were punished in an instant. 

He believed that the annual rotation of the soldiers benefited him so that the cities, soldiers, and captains would not get to know each other well in such a short time, nor could they form such friendships that they might conspire together or league themselves against the King. For long wars make the masses stronger and the captains more experienced <note>original: "fürsichtiger," meaning more cautious or shrewd through experience</note>, from which great pretext and opportunity often arise to defect from the authorities. But since the foreigners did not know what kind of life the princes led, their wantonness remained hidden; they were regarded as an invisible god—indeed, no one was so bold as to wound them with even a single word. 

Now, this Ninus appointed captains, governors, stewards, judges, and other officials who administered all the provinces and the whole empire, while he enjoyed himself. In this way, thirty kings followed one another in the government until **Sardanapalus**, in whose time the Assyrian Empire—which, as **Ctesias** <note>a Greek physician and historian</note> writes in another book, then passed to the **Medes**—had been under the Assyrians for one thousand three hundred and sixty years. Regarding the names of these kings, or whether their lives—since they performed nothing worthy of memory—...

The Ethiopians burned his body and brought the bones home to his father Tithonus. They write that such things are recorded of Memnon in the Assyrian chronicles.

Arbaces gave his advice upon such news, which they all followed: that they should march against them with force and try whether they could bring the Bactrians to defect through kindness, or if not, drive them back with a pitched battle. Thus the captains of the Bactrians, and soon after the common men as well, were persuaded to join Arbaces. Sardanapalus knew nothing of this yet; he thought only of his previous life, which was merry, gave his army a costly feast with plenty of wine to drink, and made them of good cheer. 

This was reported to Arbaces by several spies and defectors from the King: how they were all drunk and mad, and that in the King's entire camp there was no watchfulness or concern. The reason was that his ancestors had received an answer and prophecy: the city of Nineveh <note>original: "Nina"</note> could never be conquered until the water became the city's enemy. He believed this would never happen. Therefore, he thought he was quite safe in the city, and that in time, people would come to rescue him.
