# The Third Book.

After the King had burned himself, they entered the city through the collapsed walls, and Arbaces was immediately dressed in royal robes, chosen as king, named as such, and promised obedience. Once he had accepted the kingdom, he immediately rewarded his allies and other princes well, according to their merit, and made them governors of the lands. Belesus—who had previously foretold to him that he would rule—reminded him of his promise and also obtained the governorship <term>of the Babylonians<gloss>The province of Babylonia</gloss></term>. Along with this, he desired the ashes (on the advice of a chamberlain who had revealed to him how much gold and silver had been burned therein with Sardanapalus). He claimed that while the outcome was still in doubt, he had made a vow that if the King were overcome, he would burn the royal palace along with the King and then carry the ashes with him to Babylon, placing them next to the temple in a structure built so high that it would serve as a sign to all those sailing upon the Euphrates and give them to understand that the Assyrian Empire was destroyed. Arbaces knew nothing of this trick, believing everything had perished with Sardanapalus and been turned to dust; he granted Belesus his desire. He declared the city free of all taxes, and Belesus, with ships prepared for the purpose, carried a great pile of gold and silver along with the ashes into Babylon. Later, when he was accused before the King for this reason, a court was appointed to judge him and investigate the matter. Now, the judges were all among those who had helped Arbaces conquer the kingdom. Out of contempt for the offense, they sentenced Belesus to death <note>original: "sein leben ab," literally to speak away his life</note>. But the King, who was a magnanimous man, wanted his reign to begin mildly and friendly; he forgave Belesus and let him keep the silver and gold, as much as he had brought away; indeed, he even let him remain in the governorship of Babylon. He said the good deeds Belesus had shown him were worth more than so much gold, and more significant than this misconduct. When news of this great goodness of the King spread, he earned favor and honor from everyone; he was deemed worthy to rule by many because he could so well spare those who had occasionally erred. Afterward, Arbaces allowed the citizens to take away their property, and he set upon the city, razed it to the ground, and carried the gold and silver—which had melted into many <term>talents<gloss>A large ancient unit of weight and value</gloss></term>—into the city of Ecbatana, which is located in Media. In this way, the Assyrian hegemony, which had reached the thirtieth generation after <term>Ninus<gloss>The mythical founder of Nineveh and the Assyrian Empire</gloss></term>, perished after fourteen hundred years. Now it seems proper to me, so that nothing worthy of memory be skipped over, that we write of those who are called Chaldeans among the Babylonians.

# Diodorus Siculus

...the Bactrians with a large army to aid King Sardanapalus in great haste, as they were not far from them. Arbaces <note>The Median general leading the rebellion</note> gave his counsel upon this news, which they all followed: that they should go against them with force and attempt to see if they might bring the Bactrians to defect through kindness, or if not, to drive them back with a pitched battle. Thus, the captains of the Bactrians were soon after persuaded—as were the common soldiers—to join Arbaces. Sardanapalus knew nothing of this yet, thinking only of his former life of joy; he gave his army a costly feast with enough wine to drink and made them of good cheer. 

This state of affairs was reported to Arbaces by several spies and defectors: how the men were "full and mad" <note>meaning heavily intoxicated</note> and that in the King's entire camp there was no watchfulness or care. Therefore, he rightly considered how they were sleepy from gluttony and drinking and lying at rest. He set out in the dead of night and fell upon their camp with ordered ranks. Because they were caught unaware and unready, they were easily scattered, struck down, and killed; those who were not stabbed fled into the city. 

When Arbaces had taken the King's camp, he appointed his wife's brother, named Salamenus, as a field commander, while he himself undertook to maintain the siege of the city. Arbaces advanced upon the enemy remaining in the field and won two battles against them. In the last of these, Salamenus was stabbed to death; the others were cut down in flight or driven into the river Euphrates <note>original: "wasser Euphraten"; Diodorus famously confuses the Tigris, where Nineveh sat, with the Euphrates</note>, where they drowned. Few of them escaped into the city. So great a bloodshed occurred at that time that the water became entirely blood-red. 

As Arbaces now besieged the King within the city, many lands defected to seek their freedom and joined Arbaces. When Sardanapalus saw the danger in which he stood, he sent his three sons and two daughters with a great treasure of gold and silver into Paphlagonia <note>An ancient region on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia</note> to his most trusted advisor, Cotto. He wrote letters to other lands that had not yet fallen away from him, exhorting them to help, with the intention of holding out during the siege. The reason for this was a prophecy given to his ancestors: that the city of Nineveh could never be captured until the water became the city's enemy. 

He believed this would never happen; therefore, he felt secure within the city and thought that in time, people would come to rescue him. Thus the enemy encamped around the city, which they could not scale because of the height of the walls. Furthermore, at that time there was no <term>gwärff<gloss>artillery or siege engines</term>, nor <term>katz<gloss>a "cat" or mobile protective gallery</term>, nor <term>bock<gloss>a battering ram</term> with which walls are now broken. The people in the city were provided long before with all the nourishment and fodder necessary for the maintenance of life through the King's foresight, so the siege did not trouble them at all. 

But after the enemy had lain before the city for two years, in the third year such great rains came that the water rose up and overthrew the walls of the city for more than half a mile. When the King saw this, he realized the time of the prophecy had arrived. So that he would not fall into the hands of the enemies, he prepared a fire in the royal palace, into which he threw gold, silver, and all his treasure, as well as his wife, his concubines, and his chamberlains. Then he set it on fire and jumped into the flames himself, burning to death with them. After the cry arose in the enemy's camp...

# The Third Book.

...they came. After the King had burned himself, they entered the city through the collapsed walls. Arbaces <note>The Median general who led the rebellion against the Assyrians</note> was immediately clothed in royal garments, elected as King, and everyone promised him their obedience. Having accepted the kingdom, he immediately bestowed gifts upon his allies and other princes according to their merit, and appointed them as governors of the lands. Belesus, who had previously prophesied that Arbaces would rule, reminded him of his promise; he thus obtained the governorship of the Babylonians. Additionally, he requested the ashes from the fire <note>referring to the funeral pyre of Sardanapalus</note> because a chamberlain had secretly informed him of how much gold and silver was burned within it. He pretended that while the outcome of the war was still in doubt, he had made a vow that if the King were defeated, he would carry the King's remains and the ashes to Babylon. He claimed he would place them near the temple in a high-built structure so that it would serve as a sign to all who sailed upon the Euphrates, making them understand that the Assyrian Empire was destroyed. Arbaces, knowing nothing of this trickery and believing that everything had been reduced to dust and powder with Sardanapalus, granted Belesus his request. He declared the city free of all taxes and allowed Belesus to transport a great heap of gold and silver—hidden among the ashes—to Babylon using prepared ships. Later, when the true reason was reported to the King, a court was established to judge him and investigate the matter. Now, the judges were all among those who had helped Arbaces conquer the kingdom. Due to his contemptible actions, they sentenced Belesus to death. But the King, who was a magnanimous man and wished his reign to begin with mercy and friendship, forgave Belesus and let him keep as much silver and gold as he had carried away. Indeed, he even allowed him to remain in the governorship of Babylon, saying that the good deeds Belesus had previously shown him were worth more than all that gold, and were more significant than this current wrongdoing. When this great goodness of the King was proclaimed, he won the favor and honor of everyone; he was considered worthy by many because he could so graciously spare even those who had gone astray. Afterward, Arbaces allowed the citizens to take their property away and then set upon the city, razing it to the ground. He carried the gold and silver—which had melted into many talents <note>An ancient unit of weight and value</note>—into the city of Ecbatana, located in Media. In this manner, the Assyrian hegemony, which had lasted for thirty generations since Ninus over a span of one thousand four hundred years, came to its end. Now it seems proper to me, so that nothing worthy of memory is skipped over, that we write concerning those who are called Chaldeans <note>A group famous in antiquity for their knowledge of astronomy and occult sciences</note> among the Babylonians.

...to ward off evil and acquire good, through which they are wise. Thus they are quite

inquiring after nothing else. For this reason, through long practice
and persistence, they are entirely learned and well-versed in the same.
Among the Greeks, only the old apply themselves to the study of nature, and
when they have spent a little time in it, they seek profit therein;
and it is not the custom among them for children to follow their fathers' arts,
but rather, according to their own will and desire, each gives himself to an art that
pleases him. However, the Chaldeans <note>An ancient Mesopotamian people renowned in antiquity for their mastery of astronomy and astrology.</note> always remain in the one art which they undertake.
But the Greeks, for the sake of profit, take up something new every day,
and are constantly at odds with one another in the most important matters,
confusing their disciples through such discord so that they do not know whom to
follow; thus they confuse them so that throughout their lives they do not know the right
way and wander in error. From this it comes that even when one of the most
learned gathers an opinion, they are inconsistent with one another, and he
discovers the greatest discord within. In contrast, the Chaldeans
say that the world is an eternal thing; it never had a beginning and will
never have an end. But that all things have their beauty and order in this way
is a divine arrangement. Likewise, all celestial things together
are not by chance, nor arranged by themselves, but are instead
carried out according to the will, certain purpose, and good pleasure of the gods.
Likewise, they have applied themselves for so long to the stars and their courses,
and have observed them for so long, that they can accurately tell men
what shall happen to them. Above all, they say that the five stars, which they
call the wandering stars <term>wandering stars: the planets, which move across the sky differently than the "fixed" stars of the constellations</term>, are quite effective and powerful in their influence,
especially the one called Saturn by the Greeks.
The most excellent, brightest, and most powerful in its effect
is the Sun; the other four they name as we do: Mars,
Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter. They also call them all together
Messengers <note>original: "Mercurios"</note> because, unlike other stars, they do not wander
around the heavens without a certain course, but have their movements at fixed times,
through which the will of the gods is announced, from their rising,
setting, and color—all of which those who understand can well perceive.
Likewise, from the winds, rain, heat, earthquakes, comets <note>original: "schwanzschein," literally "tail-shine"</note>, eclipses of the Sun
and Moon, portents of the earth, and many other signs, they know how to
teach people what good or evil shall befall them; and this is not
only for the common man, but also for high-ranking people, kings, princes,
and lords. Beneath the wandering stars, they say there are thirty more stars,
which they call the Counseling Gods; half of their course is downward,
the other half upward, to observe what occurs among the gods and men;
and every ten days they send one from among them upward and another downward,
as a messenger of the stars; such is their course,
which is assigned to them in an eternal cycle. They say there are twelve chief gods,
to each of whom they assign a month and a zodiac sign;
before these the Sun and Moon and all the wandering stars must run:
the Sun for one year, the Moon for one month, and the others each as long
as is fitting for their speed and time. They also say that the wandering stars

This loss was brought upon him by Persodes, who was a Persian, bold, intelligent, and highly renowned for other virtues. He was loved by the King above all others and was the chief among his counselors. However, the King angered him with a certain judgment; for this reason, he fled from the King with three thousand men on foot and thousands on horseback and joined the Cadusians. They welcomed him, and he married one of his daughters to the most prominent man among them. As he could no longer desire to return from his defection, he persuaded the Cadusians to claim their freedom. Thus, they appointed him as their leader because of his boldness. He gathered a great army of over two hundred thousand men and set up his camp on the borders of the Cadusians' land. He defeated Arceum the Mede (who marched against him with eight hundred thousand men) in a battle in which approximately fifty thousand Medes perished. Having driven the others out of the Cadusian lands, Persodes became King. He then marched into Media, devastated the entire land, and achieved great fame. When he had grown very old and lay on his deathbed, he cursed all his descendants who might cease the hatred between the Medes and the Cadusians. He also established a penalty and heavy punishment for anyone who made peace or an alliance between the two peoples—indeed, even if someone merely thought of peace, they were to be driven into exile, even if they were of his own lineage or a Cadusian. Therefore, the Cadusians remained enemies of the Medes forever after, refusing to be subjects to any Median king until the Persian Empire was established by Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Empire (reigned c. 550–530 BCE).</note>. After the death of Arceum, Artines ruled in Media for twenty-two years, and after him Artibanus for forty. During his reign, the Parthians <note>A nomadic people from the region of modern-day northeastern Iran.</note> revolted from the Medes and handed over their land and capital city to the Sacians <note>The Sacians (Sakas) were a group of Scythian horse-nomads of Central Asia.</note>. However, a treaty was finally made stating that the Parthians should again be subject to the Medes, and the Medes should make an alliance with the Sacians to help each other forever. At that time, Queen Zarina <note>A legendary Saka queen mentioned by Ctesias, known for her beauty and military leadership.</note> ruled over the Sacians. She was bold, always eager for war, and highly renowned above other women and the Sacians for her heroic deeds. In the land of the Sacians, there are very strong and bold women who dare to invade even the men with war—indeed, they sometimes gain more honor through it than even the boldest men. So was she, as they say: beautiful in form, wise in counsel, and of wonderful foresight. She attacked the neighboring peoples who had ruled over the Sacians and oppressed them with their pride, and she forced them to deal more graciously with her people. She built many cities, to which she gave better and more useful laws than others had provided. After her death, the people—being grateful for her virtue and kindness—built for her the most beautiful tomb that had ever existed among them. It was a triangular, elevated "fire-pillar" <note>This likely describes a pyramid-shaped monument or an obelisk.</note>; it measured three stadia <term>Stadion: an ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet (185 meters).</term> in width at each side and one stadium in height, tapering to a point at the top. ## Concerning the Indians and Their Neighbors
->the Scythians.<-

The situation of India is bounded on four sides: toward the east and south, it is enclosed by the sea; to the north, the Emodes mountains <note>The Emodes, or Hemodos, refers to the Himalayan mountain range.</note> separate it from the Scythians, who are called the Sacae. To the west, it is bordered by the river Indus, which is considered the greatest body of water after the Nile. They write that the distance from the borders of India in the east to the border in the west is eight hundred miles, and from north to south, it is about five hundred miles. Now, this great expanse of India lies entirely under the summer circle <note>This refers to the Tropic of Cancer, reflecting the ancient understanding of the sun's path.</note>. In many parts of the land, they say that if one sets a piece of wood upright, it casts no shadow from the sun. Likewise, at night, one sees no stars of the Great Bear <note>original: "Bärwagen"; the Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note>, and in the furthest parts of India, one cannot see the front part of it at all, for there the shadows lean toward the south. In India, there are many large mountains and various kinds of great trees; there are wide, beautiful fields that are fertile and pleasant. The land is everywhere divided by great waters that moisten the fields, so that it yields fruit twice every year. It produces many kinds of animals that are stronger and larger than in other places, both birds and others. There are many elephants, which are larger than those from Libya. They

The land is rich in fruits; it bears many and various kinds of ores, such as silver and gold in great abundance, and not a little iron, <term>bell metal</term> <note>original: "glockenspeyß"; a specific bronze alloy used for casting bells.</note>, and brass. Indeed, there is much else that serves for ornament, utility, and the maintenance of life, as well as being useful for war. Among other grains, much rice grows among the Indians, and otherwise a vegetable that they call <term>Bosphorum</term> <note>original: "Bosphorum"; likely a corruption of "bosmorum," a type of grain or millet mentioned by ancient historians like Diodorus.</note>, along with other foods that would be tedious to recount; this is made possible by the water that irrigates the fields continuously. For this reason, they say that there is never any famine or hunger in India. For where other people sow rice in the winter time, these people are already harvesting it. They do the same with the *Bosphorum*, the malt, sesame, and millet; when other people are sowing, they are harvesting. From this, such great abundance must exist among them, because the fruits grow of their own accord, especially those that grow as vegetables, such as certain roots that provide people with a very sweet meal; for the entire land receives a sweet moisture, both from the river and from the rain that comes annually in its time during the summer. One also finds roots that are roasted and are very sweet, especially the skins. Furthermore, the custom they observe in wars with one another contributes greatly to such fertility. For in other places, people ruin the landscape, devastate all fields and forests, and allow no one to work in the field in peace. But there, the <term>farmer</term> <note>original: "pawerßman"; refers to the peasantry or agricultural class.</note> is just as safe in war as in peace. Only the military folk fight with one another and kill each other; no one harms a hair on the farmer’s head, but each side regards him as a common servant. Thus, no one burns another's land or damages any tree. Beyond

The entire Indian people are divided into seven guilds <note>These "guilds" (zunfften) refer to the seven classes or castes of Indian society as described by ancient Greek historians.</note>.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting four scholars or "natural masters" in a study. The first are the Natural Masters <note>original: "Naturliche meister"; referring to the Brahmins or philosophers (Sophoi)</note>, who are few in number, yet are considered higher than other people and the most distinguished. They are free from all civic burdens; they serve no one and rule no one. From private individuals, they receive what is required for divine service and the preparation of the dead. They are honored as those beloved of God, who know what is happening among the gods, and are treated with many gifts and tokens of honor. In return, they are entirely useful to the lives of the Indians, for they gather annually at the beginning of the year and tell the people whether it will be a dry, wet, windy, or pestilent <note>original: "schelmig"; here referring to a year of disease or plague</note> year, and other things that are beneficial for them to know. For when the king and the people hear the future in this way, they know how to prepare themselves to strive for the better and to flee from the evil. But whichever of these naturalists fails with his prophecy has the punishment that he must henceforth remain eternally silent and never speak to the people again. The second guild is that of the Farmers; they are the most numerous. They do not take up war but are

otherwise free from all other work, attending only to their plowing of the fields. No enemy does them any harm, nor robs them; instead, the enemy believes the farmer works for him just as well as for

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing peasants in a field. One man on the left carries a large bundle on his back using a strap around his forehead. On the right, another man is bent over or working near a large conical structure, possibly a haystack or a simple shelter.</image-desc>

another, and therefore does not offend him. Thus, the farmers spend their lives in total safety, finding joy in their labor and cultivating enough fruit for the land. They live in the fields and keep house there with wives and children, never coming into the cities. To the King (for India is subject to several kings) they give tribute, which amounts to a fourth part of the crops; and no private person can possess any field without this tribute.

### The Third Book.

...whom they hunt, they make India—which is otherwise full of harmful wild beasts and birds that do great damage to the crops—safe. The fourth guild consists of

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a man standing in 16th-century attire, wearing a tunic, breeches, hose, and a soft hat.</image-desc>

the artisans. Among them, some are smiths for the needs of war, others for the tilling of the soil; some do this, others do that, whatever is useful and beneficial for mankind. These are not only free from all taxes, but the King also provides for their sustenance. The fifth guild consists of the warriors, who, next to the farmers, are the greatest in number. They are raised in the practice of war and all apply themselves to weaponry, using horses and elephants suitable for battle. And the King feeds them all. The sixth guild consists of the overseers <note>original: "pütel"; in this context, it refers to the inspectors or "Ephoroi" mentioned by ancient Greek sources who monitored the population</note>, who

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a hunter riding a long-necked animal, possibly a horse or a stylized camel, and aiming a bow and arrow upward at a winged serpent or dragon in the air.</image-desc>

learn of everything that happens in India and report it to the King or, if the King is not present, to the Councils. The seventh guild is that of the Public Councilors, of whom there are few; the most noble and wise among them are chosen to be the King's advisors. Counsel is sought from them in public affairs concerning the common good, or if something significant should occur. Commanders and other officials are chosen from their ranks. Now, the government of the Indians is divided in this way: no one may take a wife from a guild other than his own, nor may anyone change his trade. The warrior may not go to the fields to farm, and the craftsman may not apply himself to the profession of arms.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, grand building or palace with multiple gables, windows, and an arched entrance. A group of people in 16th-century dress is gathered in the foreground.</image-desc>

India has many large elephants, which are also very strong. This animal climbs just like horses and other four-footed animals, and not as some say, like a human <note>The author is refuting a common medieval myth that elephants had no knees and could not lie down or climb easily</note>. At the shortest, they give birth in the seventeenth month, and at the longest, in the eighteenth. They give birth to no more than one at a time, just like mares; they nurse the young for six years. They commonly live as long as an old man, but those that grow truly old live for two hundred years.

Princes are also appointed in India who must ensure that foreigners suffer no harm. If a foreigner becomes sick, the doctors appointed for that purpose must heal him. These same doctors also bury those who die, and their left-behind property is given to their nearest friends <note>meaning their next of kin</note>. The judges weigh all matters diligently and punish wrongdoing in an orderly fashion. So much for the Indians; now we wish to speak of the Scythians.

# Concerning the Scythians, Amazons,
## and Hyperboreans. Chapter 6.

The Scythians originally held only a very small territory, which they later—through their courage and prowess, and by subjugating many other regions—increased and greatly expanded with much profit and fame. At first, they lived in obscurity and were looked down upon due to their lowly and impoverished origins. However, once they acquired a warlike King who distinguished himself through military campaigns, they quickly expanded their rule. They conquered the mountain ranges as far as the Caucasus <note>original: "Caucaso"</note> mountains, the plains, all the lands as far as the Ocean, and the Maeotian Lake <note>the Sea of Azov; original: "Meotischen jez Zabaccer See"</note>. Later, they seized many other lands as far as the Tanais <note>the Don River; original: "Teys oder Tanaim"</note>.

The Scythians say that among them, a maiden was born from the earth who had a human form down to her navel, but was shaped like a serpent <note>original: "wurm"; likely referring to the mythological figure Echidna</note> below. She is said to have borne a son whom she named Scythes <note>original: "Scytham"</note>. He gave the name to the Scythians, for he was such a bold and magnificent man that he surpassed all who came before him in noble deeds. He also left children behind him, from whom two brave brothers were later born; one was named Palos <note>original: "Pluto"</note> and the other Napas <note>original: "Napis"</note>. Their lineage ruled over the people for a long time, and with their strength and skill, they conquered many lands beyond the Tanais, even as far as Thrace.

Afterward, they turned in the other direction and reached as far as the Nile in Egypt. They brought all the lands lying in between under their control, as far as the Eastern and Caspian Seas, and also the Maeotian Lake. Having thus increased in power, they had very brave Kings, some of whom were called Sakae <note>original: "Sace"</note>, others Massagetae <note>original: "Massagete"</note>, and others Arimaspi <note>original: "Arimaspe"</note>.

Under these Kings, several cities were settled from the conquered lands, two in particular: one consisting of Assyrians located between Paphlagonia and Pontus, and the other consisting of Medes on the Tanais River. These people were called Sarmatians <note>original: "Sauromathe"</note>. Many years later, these same people fell upon Scythia, having previously expanded their reach far and wide, leaving the land in several places entirely wasted and desolated <note>original: "edöfiget"</note> of livestock and people.

After the lineage of these princes passed away, it is said that women ruled in Scythia, who were powerful in both body and spirit. For in the land of Scythia, the wives of the King also take part in affairs and are just as brave as the men. With their bravery, these women not only frequently performed great and manly deeds within Scythia, but they also proved their high-mindedness abroad in foreign lands. For Cyrus, the King of the Persians, who invaded the Scythian borders with a great army, was defeated and slain in battle by a Scythian Queen, who captured and crucified him <note>Referring to Queen Tomyris; classical accounts vary on whether Cyrus was crucified or decapitated</note>. Likewise, the courage of the Amazons was so well known to everyone that they not only conquered neighboring lands but also brought many regions in Asia and Europe under their rule. And since we have begun to write about them, it seems to me not in vain to record that which is told of them, even though much of it is more fiction than truth—

...provides much to describe. By the Thermodon river <note>original: "Thermodonta"</note>, the race of the Amazons was first recognized. These same women dared to fight just as well as the men; in body, they were straighter and stronger. Their Queen assembled a whole army of women, trained them from the beginning, and practiced them in all knightly deeds. Afterward, she overran several neighboring lands with them and conquered them. From this, she attained great fame, expanded her realm, and bore a daughter whom she called a daughter of Mars <note>original: "Martis"</note>. 

The men all had to spin, sew, weave, and do other things that are appropriate for women among us. The women she practiced in the customs of war and taught them all knightly games. In order that this way of life should be maintained, she established a law: that all women should be instructed for war, and the men should take no other work in hand except that which was womanly. Whatever little boys were born to them, they crippled in their arms and feet so that they could not use them for war. For the little daughters, she burned the right breast so that it would bring them no hindrance in handling weapons <note>original: "gwhỏr"; here referring to the use of the bow or spear</note>, from which they also have the name of the Amazons <note>The name was traditionally interpreted in Greek as "a-mazos," meaning "without a breast."</note>. 

The Queen, who was praised by many for her wisdom and skill in war, built a city where the Thermodon river flows into the sea, and named it Themiscyra <note>original: "Themystram"</note>. She built therein a magnificent royal palace, and with her good leadership which she used in war, she first brought the surrounding peoples under her, as far as the Tanais <note>original: "Teyß"; the Don River</note>. 

And when she later died fighting manfully in a battle, her daughter succeeded to the realm, who followed her mother in everything—indeed, her deeds far surpassed her mother’s. She trained the young maidens from childhood in the hunt and instructed them in the order of war. She established several offices for the god Mars and the goddess Diana, which were called bull-festivals <note>original: "ταυροπόλια" (Tauropolia), festivals associated with the goddess Artemis/Diana</note>; she demonstrated how one should offer sacrifices to them. She later led an army across the Tanais <note>original: "Teyß"</note> and conquered all peoples as far as Thrace <note>original: "Thraciam"</note>. She returned home with great booty, built splendid temples to her gods, and with just and friendly rule she made all her subjects obedient and loyal. Afterward, she moved across the water to the other side and advanced into Asia, which she conquered as far as Syria. After her death, her closest kinswoman took her place, who governed the realm justly <unclear>regiret</unclear>, so that the Amazons came into great dignity and power. 

Long after, when their praise had resounded throughout the whole world, it is said that by order of Juno and Eurystheus, to Hercules the...

# Of Arabia, its situation, and
->certain other matters. Chapter VII.<-

Arabia lies between Syria and Egypt. It has various peoples, for as it is situated toward the East, it is inhabited by those Arabs called Nabataeans. There is a barren desert and waterless <note>original: "wässerig" - likely a typesetting error for "unwässerig" (waterless), as Diodorus describes this region as lacking surface water, leading to the use of hidden wells.</note> land; it bears fruit in few places. Therefore, they nourish themselves solely from booty and robbery which they daily wrest from the surrounding peoples; they are also good and invincible warriors. Those who have a lack of water dig hidden wells <note>original: "sod prunnen"</note> unknown to foreigners, which ensures they do not need to worry much about war; for if one wishes to pursue them, he finds no wells and cannot return without great labor. Thus these Arabs live entirely free and are invincible, never having been subjected to any kings, neither of the Assyrians, Medes, or Persians. Likewise, no Macedonian king ever overcame them, no matter how strongly he invaded the land. There is also in the land of the Nabataeans a rock <note>This refers to the ancient city of Petra, known for its defensive "Rock."</note> which is naturally

to cast out the pitch, it gives a sign twenty-two days beforehand; then around the lake there arises such a foul, great stench that it even takes the color from gold and ore <note>original: "ärtz"</note>, which returns to it afterwards from good air. From the stench and the hitz <gloss>heat</gloss> of this lake, the inhabitants become quite ill; it breeds many diseases and causes them to live only a short time. The land has many palms, for they are well-watered by the wells and rivers. In addition, it has a valley in which grows balsam, which grows in no other place in the world.

Such fragrance comes from the nature of the **sun**, so that in certain places, when digging, one finds certain **fragrant clods of earth**. It has so many **sheep** and other tame animals that many lands are supplied by them. There is no lack of **grain**, for the land produces all kinds. <header>Diodorus Siculus</header>

## Of Newly Discovered Islands in the Ocean

->situated toward the south. Chapter 8.<-

Regarding this island in the Ocean toward the South <note>original: "gegen Mittag," literally "toward midday," a common archaic term for the South</note> / we wish to show the cause / how and in what manner it was discovered / and what unbelievable things are said of it. A man named Iambulus <note>Iambulus is a legendary merchant-traveler mentioned by Diodorus; his "Island of the Sun" is considered one of the earliest utopian fictions in Western literature</note> / who was educated in the liberal arts in his youth / and after the death of his father / took up his father’s legacy / the trade of a merchant. As he traveled into Arabia / there to buy spices / highway robbers captured him / and he was made a shepherd along with one of his fellow servants. Afterward, he and his companion were captured again by certain Ethiopians / and led by them into the Ethiopian region / which lies by the sea, to be sacrificed (as foreigners) and to turn away the anger of the gods. For it was the custom in that same place from of old / as well as a command of the gods / given to them twenty generations or six hundred years ago (for a generation is counted as thirty years) that they should sacrifice foreign men / when they were punished by the gods / and wished to soften their anger. For this purpose, they had prepared a small boat / which two men could guide wherever they wished / and which was protected against the turbulence / or waves of the sea. Into this boat they put as much food / as was sufficient for two men for six months / then they placed the two inside / and told them: they should direct their voyage toward the South / so they would come, by the promise of the gods, to an island / wherein they might lead a blessed and good life / among hearty people. Also, their own fatherland would (provided they arrived safely at that same island) remain in rest and peace for another six hundred years. But if they turned back / and shunned the long voyage / they would, as godless / and wicked scoundrels, bring the whole land into misfortune. When they had thus persuaded the two men and sent them away / they kindled a great fire by the sea / sacrificed / and called upon the gods / that they might give the sailors good weather. Now in this way, the two were sent off / and when they had sailed for four months / and suffered great danger / they came to a round island / which was about sixty-three miles <note>likely German miles, which were significantly longer than modern miles</note> in circumference. As they approached the island / the inhabitants ran toward them / pulled the small boat onto the land / and others came also / wondering from whence the foreign people came / received them friendly / and shared with them what good things they had. These same people on the island / are like us neither in body nor in customs. But among themselves they all have one form. All are four cubits high / they are so flexible <note>original: "gläychnig," meaning supple or double-jointed</note> / that you may bend their bones back and forth wherever you wish. Their bodies are much swifter and stronger than ours. For when they grasp something in their hand / no one can tear it out of their hands / except for the head and eyebrows they have no hair at all / and are so very smooth / that one would not find a single tiny hair elsewhere on them. They have handsome limbs, beautiful and well-adorned. Their ear-holes are larger than ours / and they are also not like us in their tongues. For Nature has given them something special and ingenious / their tongue is divided from the bottom up in two / therefore they have so many kinds of voices / that they also freely mimic the song of birds.

There are seven islands, each as large as the other; they have one law, and one people inhabits them; they are also situated equally far from one another. They use their fruits moderately, although an abundance of everything grows among them. They use simple food, which is sufficient for their nourishment; they boil and roast meat, but they do not care for many-spiced and costly cooked dishes, holding them to be useless. The gods—especially the one who rules all things—they honor, as well as the Sun and other stars. They catch various fish and birds. Many fruitful trees also grow among them without any labor: olive trees and grapevines, from which they have heaps of fruit. Large worms, yet harmless, are on the island, such that they eat their meat because of its sweetness. Their clothes they make from wool and the soft hair of the animals <note>original: "thöter," an archaic term for beasts</note> that grow among them, and they dye them with purple snails, so that they are precious and beautiful. It is unbelievable how many kinds of animals are said to be among them. During the day they eat no more than once: one day fish, the next birds, the third cattle; sometimes only fruit or some other crop. They practice various exercises, and one always comes to the aid of the other. Some fish—this one or that one has the occupation that is convenient for their maintenance. Some (though the elderly are excluded) divide the necessary work among themselves and complete what is to be done. On feast days and high holy days, they sing songs of praise to the Gods, especially to the Sun, to whom they commend themselves and their island. The dead they bury on the shores of the sea, so that when the sea is turbulent, it might cast the sand upon them and cover them well. Their grain <note>original: "hor," likely referring to ears of corn or grain</note> from which they take their fruit, increases and decreases like the Moon. The warm springs and their water remain

Furthermore, they <note>the Ethiopians</note> claim that the first worship of God originated among them, along with the feast days, processions, ceremonies, and similar honors paid to the gods. Therefore, it appears as though, because of the piety and devotion of the Ethiopians, no worship or sacrifice is more pleasing to the Gods than that which they perform. This is attested to by the most ancient writings, particularly the testimony of Homer. They also say their piety has received this reward from the gods: that they have never been conquered by any foreign king, but have remained free throughout time, even though many various kings have attacked them with great armies. None has been able to seize the kingdom. Cambyses <note>the King of Persia</note> marched against the Ethiopians with a powerful force, but he lost his equipment there and barely escaped with his life. Semiramis <note>a legendary Queen of Assyria</note>, though she was widely renowned and feared for her great deeds and courage, also came into Ethiopia, yet she abandoned the venture, as she did not trust herself to achieve anything. Likewise, Hercules and Dionysus <note>Bacchus</note>, who otherwise traversed the whole world and conquered all that lay around Egypt, did not invade the Ethiopians—partly because they felt a dread of troubling such pious people, and partly because they did not believe they could gain anything from them. Furthermore, they give it to be understood that the Egyptians are descended from them and are their colonists, led into Egypt by Osiris <note>the Egyptian god of the afterlife and fertility</note>. This may well be the case, because in ancient times and in the very beginning, Egypt was part of the sea and not fit for habitation. # The Fourth Book

the furrow of the sea <note>The text refers to the seabed being filled by sediment. The previous page mentioned "the moisture of the earth," and here it describes how the Nile's silt filled the "furrow" or "trench" of the sea.</note> was so overwhelmed with it that over many years, a whole land grew out of it. This same thing may still be seen and understood today at the places where the Nile flows into the sea. For every year the land increases from the silt <term>lätten</term> <note>fine clay or mud</note> that the Nile carries out of Ethiopia, and the sea recedes. In this way, the entire land of Egypt has grown from the land of Ethiopia. 

Thus, those who came from Ethiopia into Egypt have kept many of their ancestors' laws, just as they are still held in Ethiopia. For the kings are honored as gods, one like the other; they also take great care with burials and use these and many other practices that come from the Ethiopian school. Likewise, the setting up of statues, and even the letters of the Egyptians, are all the art of the Ethiopians. Although the Egyptians have their own writing and letters which the common man also learns, the priests have a special script which they call the **sacred script** <note>hieroglyphics</note>; this same script is common among the Ethiopians, and the Egyptian priests learned it from their elders and have thus kept it in use. 

Furthermore, the priestly classes of both peoples have the same customs and order; for they strive with all purity and chastity to perform their divine offices, and they wear the same ornaments and cloaks. Likewise, the kings of both have similar royal scepters made in the shape of a plowshare. They also wear hats in both places with long tassels, which are wound in the middle with **asps** <note>original: "Nitzschlangen," likely referring to the uraeus or royal cobra found on Egyptian crowns</note>. This carries a certain meaning: that those who dare to rebel against the king are subject to death. Much else is said of their ancient origin and the colonies that were sent into Egypt, which is unnecessary to mention here. 

Now, however, so that nothing worthy of memory is left out of this history book of ours, we wish to make some mention here of the Ethiopian letters, which among the Egyptians are called the **sacred script**. This script or letters are fashioned in many different likenesses of animals. Likewise, some are like human limbs or certain tools used by craftsmen. For they do not describe their words through syllables and letters; instead, they only use certain pictures with which they create a memory for man. 

If they make a **hawk**, a **crocodile**, a **snake**, or a **human eye**, a **hand**, a **face**, or the like, it signifies that a matter was carried out swiftly, for the hawk <note>original: "Habich"</note> is almost the swiftest of all birds. If something regarding household management occurs, it is described with its own corresponding form. The **crocodile** signifies much evil; the **eye** signifies the preservation of justice and the protection of the entire body. The **right hand**, being held open, signifies liberality; the **left hand**, being closed, signifies greed and stinginess. Thus, the other limbs also each have their own meaning. Therefore, long-standing experience has acquired the knowledge so that they know immediately what each signifies. 

The laws of the Ethiopians have a great difference from the laws of other people, especially in that which serves for the election of kings.

## On the election of kings.

When they elect priests, they choose the most pious among them. Whichever one of them is then possessed by the spirit, so that he runs about like one who has gone mad, the people make that man their King. Immediately, the people fall to their knees before him and worship him as one who has been given to them as a God through the providence of the Gods.

## On the power of the rulers.

The king then lives according to the law and does nothing except what is the custom of the land; he rewards and punishes no one except as the laws direct. The custom is such that he brings no evildoer before a court; instead, if a man is condemned and has already forfeited his life, the king sends him a bailiff <term>büttel</term> <note>a court official or messenger</note> who carries a token announcing his death. Upon receiving such a message, the poor soul goes home and takes his own life in whatever manner he chooses.

## On banishment.

They also consider it unjust for anyone to be banished from the land, or for a man to flee because of such a sentence when his life is forfeit—as is the custom among the Greeks. They say that once, when a death-token was sent to a man, he attempted to flee and depart from the land. His mother then threw a girdle <note>a belt or cord</note> around his neck—against which he dared not resist—and she strangled him herself and cut his throat, so that he might not bring dishonor upon his family by his flight.

## On the death of the king.

Furthermore, it is a marvel beyond all others how the kings themselves are put to death. For the priests who are in the temple at Meroe <note>an ancient capital of the Kingdom of Kush, famous for its pyramids</note> and are held in high regard by everyone, send a message to the king whenever they see fit, commanding him to put himself to death. They proclaim this to him as the command of the Gods, which no mortal should resist. With such arguments, they persuade the king to willingly give himself to death according to ancient custom. In this regard, the ancient kings were all obedient to the priests; they were not subdued by weapons or force upon receiving such a command, but were conquered by superstition and put themselves to death.

This lasted until the time of Ptolemy II <note>original: "andern Ptolemei"; referring to the Greek ruler of Egypt from 283 to 246 BCE</note>, when Ergamenes ruled in Ethiopia. He was well-schooled in natural philosophy and the other arts of the Greeks and refused to follow this custom. Instead, he took a wise counsel for himself, as befits a king: he marched with his army into the golden temple of the Ethiopians, which is in the sacred place <note>original: "Auato"; likely referring to the *Abaton* or a forbidden sanctuary</note>, slew all the priests, abolished this custom entirely, and ruled thereafter according to his own good judgment.

# Of the King’s Counselors.

But the remarkable custom observed by the King’s advisors, as it is told, is still practiced among them. For as it has been written, the custom among the Ethiopians was that if the King should happen to suffer an injury to a limb, and that limb was damaged, all the members of the royal household <term>hoffgsind</term> <note>the courtiers and servants attending the monarch</note> would gladly injure themselves in that very same place. They held it to be a great shame if the King were to enter limping and they did not all limp as well. Indeed, they considered it only right—since one mourns the misfortunes of friends and rejoices in their good fortune—that friends should also share in the physical injuries of the body. Likewise, it is said that the King's dearest friends would voluntarily kill themselves when the King died, believing it to be the most honorable death and a true testament of friendship. For this reason, one cannot easily depose or assassinate a King of the Ethiopians, as he and his counselors are of one mind and look after their collective well-being. These laws are held by the Ethiopians who inhabit their capital city and island of Meroe <note>an ancient city-state on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan</note>, which borders Egypt. There are also other Ethiopian peoples, very populous, who live on both banks of the Nile and in its floodplains <term>Awen</term>, and they are the closest neighbors to the Arabians.

Their diet is neither human nor familiar to us; indeed, their customs are vastly different from our own. For protection, some use a shield covered in raw ox-hide and short spears. Others use fire-hardened, pointed stakes or wooden bows with arrows four cubits <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches, making these arrows about six feet long</note> in length. They shoot these at the enemy by bracing one foot against the bow for leverage. When they run out of arrows, they fight with the aforementioned wooden stakes. The women must also fight for a certain period of their lives. These people commonly wear a ring in their lips. They have no clothing; they go naked their entire lives and roast in the sun, never seeking shade unless they happen to come under trees or bushes. Some, to cover their shame, tie animal tails in front of themselves. Others use skins. Some weave a covering out of their own hair to hide half their bodies, for their sheep have no wool. Some eat grass that grows naturally in the water, whether it is flowing or still. Others eat the fruit of trees, using the leaves to cover themselves at midday because of the heat. Some sow Moly <note>original: "Molz"; likely referring to the mythical or medicinal herb "Moly"</note> and Lotus. Some eat the young roots of reeds. ### On the selection of the king.

When they choose priests, they select the most pious among them. Whichever of these is then possessed by a spirit—so that he runs about like those who go mad—that man the people make King. They immediately fall to their knees before him and worship him, as one who has been given to them as a God through the foresight of the Gods.

### On the power of the rulers.

From then on, he lives according to the law and does nothing except what is the custom of the land, rewarding or punishing no one except as the laws dictate. The custom is that he brings no criminal before a court; instead, if a man is condemned and has forfeited his life, the King sends him a messenger <term>büttel</term> <note>a court official or herald</note> who carries and displays a sign that announces his death. Upon receiving such a message, the poor soul goes home and takes his own life in whatever way he chooses.

### On banishment.

They also consider it unjust for anyone to be banished from the land, or for one to go into exile when he has forfeited his life, as was sometimes the custom among the Greeks. They say that once, when the death-token was sent to a man, he intended to flee and depart from the land. His mother then threw a girdle around his neck, against which he dared not resist, and she strangled him herself and cut his throat so that he would not bring dishonor by his flight.

### On the death of the king.

Furthermore, it is truly wondrous how the kings bring about their own deaths. For the priests who are in the temple at Meroe <note>the capital city of the Kingdom of Kush in modern-day Sudan</note>, and who are held in high regard by everyone, send a message to the King whenever they see fit, commanding him to put himself to death. They proclaim this to him as a command of the Gods, which no mortal should resist. With such talk and the like, they persuade the King to give himself willingly to death according to ancient custom. In this matter, the ancient Kings were all obedient to the priests; they were not forced by weapons or power at such a command, but were overcome by superstition and put themselves to death. This continued until the time of Ptolemy II <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the Greek Pharaoh of Egypt</note>, when Ergamenes <note>Arkamani I</note> ruled in Ethiopia. He was well-versed in the natural and other arts of the Greeks and refused to follow this custom. Instead, he took a wise course of action, as befits a king: he marched with his soldiers into the golden temple of the Ethiopians, which is in Anato <note>likely referring to Napata, the sacred city of the Kingdom of Kush</note>, slew all the priests, abolished this custom entirely, and ruled thereafter according to his own good judgment.

## Concerning the King's Councilors.

But the remarkable custom which the King's councilors <term>Räth</term> <note>These are the advisors or courtiers closest to the monarch.</note> practiced is, as they say, not yet abolished among them. For as it has been written, the custom among the Ethiopians was that whenever a limb was injured or struck on the King's person, the entire court household would willingly injure themselves in exactly the same place. There are also other Ethiopian peoples, quite numerous, who dwell on both banks of the Nile and in its floodplains <term>Awen</term> <note>The fertile meadows or marshy areas created by the river's overflow.</note> nearest to the Arabs.

To the gods who are in heaven, some of them say they are immortal and eter=

they showed to mankind, have attained immortal honor. Among those whom they ven=
erate first are Pan, Hercules, and Jupiter, as they were the ones who showed es=
pecially many good deeds to men. Some Ethiopians believe
there is no God at all; therefore, when the Sun rises, they flee into swamps
and puddled places and curse it. They also have various customs for
burying the dead. For some throw their dead into a body of water, holding that to
be the most precious grave; others enclose them in glass so that they
may be seen by their descendants and their ancestors are not forgotten;
still others place them in earthenware vessels and bury them near the temples,
and to swear by them is the greatest oath among them. The power over them
they give to the most pious, considering it a gift of fortune when someone
reaches the kingdom or is pious. Some give it to the shepherds who are diligent and
pious, as those who attend to their affairs with industriousness. Others
raise the wealthiest to be King, or the one who is best able to come to the aid
of the subjects. Some want a King from among the strongest and
bravest, holding that he is most worthy to rule who achieves
the most in war. The region of Ethiopia that lies along the Nile and toward Ly=
bia surpasses all others in beauty; for not only in everything that
man may enjoy, but also to escape the heat of the Sun, they have very
convenient, watery places. From this it follows that they are often invaded
by the Libyans and other Ethiopians and lead great wars. Further up,
they are overrun by elephants <term>Helfanten</term> <note>An archaic German term for elephants, likely derived from the Greek "elephas."</note> who follow the sweet and good pasture.
For there are great lakes in that same region, which the water creates with its over=
flow, in which grows various vegetation, many reeds, and herbs
that the elephants like to eat; for this reason, they then betake themselves
and remain there, so that they eat up the humans' food and force them
to retreat to other places. The reason is that elephants love watery places
and do not like to be in the middle of the land or in the drought, because there,
due to a lack of springs and water, little pasture grows; also because the peo=
ple, such as shepherds, dwell in their huts and believe that the land is
most useful to them far from the lakes. They also say that in some places
there are exceedingly large snakes in the deserts; these same creatures fight
with the elephants for the sake of the water. The struggle is as follows: the
snakes wind themselves around the elephant's feet and pull themselves
together in such a way that they heavily fell the exhausted animals because of their
great size; then many of them come together and eat it without danger,
for the fallen elephant cannot defend itself, nor can it get back up again.
When they do not have elephants, they have their pasture elsewhere and do not stay
in the open, but rather in dark, long valleys; they dwell in deep caves,
nor do they easily leave their advantage and nest. Thus does Nature
teach how every animal may protect itself. Now, so much for the
Ethiopians. Now we wish to recount who those are who have written the
like concerning the Egyptians and Ethiopians and brought such wondrous
things to light; for some of them—who were eager to write from hear-say
and to compose according to their own desire—are not much to be
believed.

Where Egypt borders Arabia and Ethiopia, there are certain places that yield ore; from this, gold is produced with great toil and expense. It is a black earth which has white veins and seams, appearing just like a white marble <note>original: "Marmel"</note> that shines from a great distance. The mine overseers <note>term: "Berguögt" (Bergvögte). High-ranking officials appointed by the crown to manage mining operations</note> maintain many ore-miners. All the evildoers who have angered the King of Egypt—those condemned to imprisonment or death, or those captured in wars—are sent there to this labor. In this way, they punish the criminals while simultaneously deriving great profit from them. There is a vast number of these people, all with fetters on their feet; they must work without ceasing, day and night. They are never permitted to rest, and they are so closely guarded that none of them can escape. This is because the guards who watch over them are from foreign lands and speak entirely different languages, so that the prisoners understand none of them. Thus, neither through pleas nor through friendship can they establish enough familiarity with one another for anyone to be helped. Now, gold is extracted from the hardest earth once it has been fired <note>referring to the process of "fire-setting," where rock is heated then cooled to make it brittle</note>. The softer rock is broken with iron tools; there are many thousands of workers.

They do not dig a straight or level path, but follow wherever the veins lead them. Because these paths are so crooked and impassable, they are completely dark; therefore, the miners carry lights upon their heads. They continue breaking and hacking off large pieces without pause, being treated poorly and beaten severely. # Of the Fish-eaters who border on the Troglo-
## dytes and Ethiopians, who are situated toward the South. Chapter 3.

We shall begin with those whom one calls Fish-eaters or <term>Ichthyophagi</term> <note>original: Ichthiophagos; from the Greek 'ichthys' (fish) and 'phagein' (to eat)</note>, who are located by the Arabian sea <note>original: Arabischen mhör; likely referring to the Red Sea or the Gulf of Aden</note>, also bordering southern Ethiopia toward the south wind and the <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>original: Trogloditer; literally 'cave-dwellers'</note>. These same people border the coast of Carmania and the Gedrosians, reaching as far as the Arabian bend, which stretches out far and has two outlets; one is at the end of <term>Arabia Felix</term> <note>original: Seligen Arabien; 'Happy Arabia,' a historical name for the southern Arabian Peninsula, particularly modern Yemen</note>, the other is at the Troglodyte border. In this enclosed land, these animalistic people spend their entire lives naked; women and children are held in common among them, and they lead a wild, beastly life. Because they have no desire for pleasure, they likewise know nothing of pain, even when they experience natural or physical injury. They also know of neither prosperity nor adversity. Their dwellings and caves are not far from the sea, in the promontories, where there are great wild valleys, deep caves, and narrow corners that are by nature impassable and crooked. Such places—as if Nature had created them for this purpose—they seal with stones wherever there is an entrance, and with this same masonry, they catch fish just as we do with fishing nets. For the sea flows in and out there every day around the third and ninth hours <note>This refers to the Roman system of counting hours from sunrise; approximately mid-morning and mid-afternoon</note>, and through its swelling, it completely covers the land and brings many various kinds of fish. These fish then dart back and forth across the land seeking their food, at which point the sea recedes again, so that they remain on dry land. Then the Fish-eaters run toward them in groups, making a great shout of joy because they have hunted such a good bounty. Women and children run to the small fish, while the strong men run to the <term>sea monsters</term> <note>original: Mhörwundern; literally 'sea wonders,' referring to whales or large marine creatures</note>, each catching the kind that they encounter. Now, the sea casts up not only scorpions,

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a large, scaly sea monster on a shore. The creature has prominent gills, a large eye, and a snout. Inside its open mouth, a small human figure is visible. To the right and slightly below the monster, another naked human figure stands with arms outstretched. The text of the page wraps around the right side of this illustration.</image-desc>

morays, dogfish, and similar small fish, but also <term>seals</term> <note>original: Mhörkälber; literally 'sea calves'</note> and many types of fish that cannot be easily named due to their strange forms. Now, they do not kill these sea monsters with any iron, but rather they have sharpened, pointed goat horns and sharpened stones.

For necessity instructs Nature, who is a mother of time, and adapts itself to that which usage requires. Now, when they have caught large and strange sea monsters, they lay them upon hot rocks that face the south and are thoroughly heated by the sun; they turn them and flip them until they are roasted all over. Then they take them by the tails and strike them against the rocks until the bones fall away, which they throw up

Then they take the flesh of the fish and pound it in a mortar, and add thistle seeds to it, which they consider a great delicacy. The reason is that they make this meat and seed into a dough, shaped just like a brick, bake it in the sun, and then feast upon it quite happily until they have had enough. They do not count how many pounds or pieces one eats; when he has satisfied his desire and hunger, he stops. Thus they have plenty of this food continually, as if they had granaries; for the sea is their plow and field. 

But when the sea runs out stormily, it sometimes overflows the nearby shore so that they cannot fish for several days. Then they gather large snails to satisfy their hunger, for these same snails taste just like the flat shellfish called <term>Ostreas</term> <note>original: Ostreas; Latin for oysters</note>. They break them open with large stones and eat the meat raw. But if the storm and the flooding last so long that they have even eaten all the snails, then the fish bones that they previously threw into a pile must suffer. They gnaw on the soft and tender ones; the hard and large ones they crush with stones and eat like dogs or cats. Thus they sustain themselves with bones and fish skeletons. 

They have a marvelous custom of eating fish flesh that no one would easily believe; for after they have caught their fish, they sit for four days together, singing and howling amongst each other in great joy. Then they couple with one another promiscuously, whichever woman a man happens to seize, so that he may impregnate her; otherwise, they have no care, for they need not worry about where they will find food. 

On the fifth day, they all go together to seek sweet springs and brooks where the shepherds drive their herds (for they run there with bleating and crying, just like the cattle and oxen that are driven to the watering hole). They carry their suckling children with them, raving and raging like the elders, rejoicing in seeking their nourishment. Their nature is not yet corrupted, and they consider it the greatest good to have stilled their hunger; they seek no other pleasure. When they reach the watering place, they drink until their bellies are so full they can hardly walk; they eat nothing that day and lie there just as if they were full of wine. On the sixth day, they go out again to catch fish. Thus they spend all their lives, and because of their simple life, they are seldom ill. However, they do not live as long as we do.

## Concerning the Fish-eaters who border the Troglodytes and Ethiopians who lie toward the South. Chapter 3.

We shall begin with those who are called Fish-eaters or <term>Ichthyophagi</term> <note>original: "ychthiophagos"; from the Greek 'ichthys' (fish) and 'phagein' (to eat)</note>, who live by the Arabian Sea, bordering southern Ethiopia toward the south wind and the <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>original: "Trogloditer"; literally 'hole-dwellers,' referring to people who lived in caves</note>. Their territory borders the coasts of Carmania and Gedrosia <note>ancient regions corresponding to modern-day Iran and Pakistan</note> and reaches as far as the Arabian Gulf, which stretches a long way and has two outlets; one is at the end of Arabia Felix <note>original: "Seligen Arabien"; Latin for 'Happy Arabia,' referring to the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note>, and the other is at the Troglodyte border. In this enclosed land, these bestial people go naked all their lives; wives and children are held in common among them, and they lead a wild, animalistic life. For just as they have no desire for luxury, they also know nothing of pain, even when they suffer natural or bodily harm. They also know nothing of good or ill fortune. Their dwellings and huts are not far from the sea, located in the foothills where there are large wild valleys, deep caves, and narrow corners that are naturally impassable and crooked. As if Nature herself had created these places for them, they block the entrances with stones wherever there is an opening, and with these same walls, they catch fish just as we do with fishing nets. For the sea there runs in and out every day around the third and ninth hours <note>referring to the Roman system of dividing daylight into twelve hours; the third hour is mid-morning, the ninth is mid-afternoon</note>, and through its swelling, it covers the land entirely and brings in many various kinds of fish. These fish then dart back and forth upon the land seeking their food, but then the sea recedes again, so that they remain on the dry land. Then the Fish-eaters run out in crowds, making a great cry of joy because they have hunted such a good bounty. Women and children run for the small fish, while the strong men go for the sea monsters; each person goes for what they can reach. Thus the sea casts up not only scorpions <note>likely referring to scorpionfish</note>,

# The Fourth Book.

Then they take the flesh of the fish and pound it in a mortar, mixing thistle seeds <note>original: "Distell saamen"</note> therein; this they consider a fine delicacy. For this reason, they make this flesh and seeds into a dough, shaped exactly like a brick, bake it in the sun, and then feast upon it right merrily until they have had enough. They care not how many pounds or pieces a man eats; when he has satisfied his desire and hunger, he stops. Thus they have enough of this food forever, as if they had granaries; the reason being that the sea <note>original: "mhör"; archaic German for sea</note> is their plow and field. However, when the sea runs wild, it sometimes overflows the nearby shore so that they cannot fish for several days; then they gather large snails, with which they satisfy their hunger, for these same snails taste just like the flat mussels that are called oysters <note>original: "Ostreas"; Latin for oysters</note>. These they crack open with large stones and eat the flesh raw. But if the storm and the overflow last so long that they have even devoured all the snails, they must endure the fish bones <note>original: "grädt"</note> which they had previously thrown into a heap. The soft and tender ones they gnaw; the hard and large ones they crush with stones and eat like dogs or cats. Thus they sustain themselves with the bones and remains. 

Regarding the eating of fish flesh, they have a wondrous custom that no one might easily believe. After they have caught their fish, they sit together for four days, singing and wailing among one another in great joy. Then they lie with one another indiscriminately—it matters not which woman a man seizes to make her pregnant—and otherwise they have no cares, for they need not worry about where they shall find their nourishment. On the fifth day, they all go together to seek fresh springs and streams, where the herdsmen drive their flocks (for they run there with bleating and shouting, just like the cattle and oxen do when they are driven to water). The children who are still nursing are carried along, raging and storming like the elders, rejoicing to seek their nourishment. Their nature is not yet corrupted, and they consider it the greatest good when they have stilled their hunger; otherwise, they seek no pleasure. When they come to the watering place, they drink until their bellies are so full that they can hardly walk; they eat nothing that same day and lie there as if they were full of wine. On the sixth day, they go out again to catch fish. Thus they consume all their lives, and because of their simple life, they are seldom sick. However, they do not live as long as we do.

# Of Diodorus Siculus <note>original: "Diodori Siculi"</note>

They are said to possess no emotion <note>original: "anmût"; refers here to passion, desire, or typical human reactivity</note>, for I do not write this alone, but testimony is given by the Egyptian merchants who sail there upon the Red Sea <note>original: "rhot mhôr"</note>. Ptolemy III <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes, a Greco-Egyptian king</note>, being desirous of capturing certain elephants of the same kind, sent one of his good favorites named Simian <note>historically Simias</note> to that place to scout the land. When he returned, as Agatharchides of Cnidus <note>a Greek historian and geographer</note> writes, he said that these Ethiopians, who live without emotion, do not drink by nature. They are neither amazed by the arrival of ships nor by the presence of strangers; they stand still when one looks at them, as if they had no understanding at all. Even if one draws a sword <note>original: "zuckt... vō leder"; literally "pulls from the leather"</note> and strikes one of them, he does not flee, nor does he flinch from the blows, no matter how one treats them or what insult, harm, or evil one shows them. Even when they are wounded, they do not move, and none among them seeks to avenge such a thing when it happens to another. Even if they see their wives and children struck down before them, they look on, yet they show neither anger nor pity; indeed, they endure all evil with a light spirit <note>original: "rhingē gemüt"</note>. They only look at those who strike them, and whatever is done to them, they merely shake their heads. Furthermore, it is said they cannot speak, but only beckon and point to indicate what they lack or what they want. And what is even more wondrous is that the seals <term>sea-calves<gloss>original: "Mhôrkalber"; seals were often called "sea-calves" in early modern texts</gloss></term> go about with them and wait with them for the fish-catch. They help one another build their huts; they raise their children in common; they are peaceful with one another; and they do no harm to any foreign living animal or man.

Now, such a life, however marvelous it is, has lasted among them for many ages; perhaps because necessity demanded it, or because long habit established it. They do not have dwellings like the first Fish-eaters; instead, they build their huts facing north <note>original: "mitnacht"; literally "midnight," the traditional term for the North</note>, where the air and shade protect them from the sun. For the places situated toward the south <note>original: "Mittag"; literally "midday," the traditional term for the South</note> are just like hot ovens, so that they cannot live there because of the heat. Those who live toward the north make their huts from the curved fish-bones of the great sea monsters <term>whales<gloss>original: "mhôrwundn"; literally "sea-wonders," referring to whales or massive sea creatures</gloss></term> which the sea casts up in great variety. They set these up on both sides, weave them together, and cover them with sea-weed to avoid the heat; thus Nature, which desires to protect itself, found this art among them out of necessity.

Item, they also have another kind of dwelling. There are many large trees that stand on the shore of the sea and hang over it; they are very thick with leaves and have a fruit just like chestnuts <note>original: "Costintzen"</note>. These they weave into one another so that they provide shade, and they have their dwellings thus both on land and in the water. They can escape the sun's heat through the shade of the trees, through the waves of the sea, and the air. 

Yet fourthly, they have another dwelling: over a long and eternal time, the sea, by casting up moss, other weeds, and refuse that grows in the sea, has piled up a great mound on the shore, which has hardened and grown together like a mountain. In this, they are able to dig long, deep hollows. From these they run out to catch fish when the sea recedes; when the tide comes in, they go inside and steam <note>likely meaning to dry or cure</note> what they have caught. Their dead they throw into the sea; in the turbulence of the sea, they cast them to the sea monsters. Some of the Fish-eaters live in places that cause many who attempt to scout the land to fall into doubt as to what kind of people they might be; for they live thus...
