### Of those who feed solely on
### Snails. Chapter V.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial N with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

Now we wish to speak of the snail-eaters. Not far from that land, there lie several islands in the Ocean Sea <note>original: "mhőr Oceano"</note>, many in number, small and insignificant, which bear neither wild nor tame fruit. And because they are situated so close to one another, no flood or storm of the sea reaches them; instead, the sea is forever in good rest, so that the snails <note>The description of these "snails" being as large as boats suggests the author is likely describing giant sea turtles or perhaps massive shellfish like the Giant Clam.</note> gather there in great numbers, nestling between the islands so that they may be more secure. At night they lie on the seabed and graze; by day they come out between the islands toward the sun, looking exactly like overturned fishing boats because of their size, which they have above all other sea snails. The inhabitants of the islands swim secretly beneath them and push them aside onto the land; or else they turn their bellies upward so that they cannot turn back or escape from them, tie a long rope to their tails, and pull them out while they are still swimming. When they have brought them onto the island, they then crack open <note>original: "knällen"; likely referring to the shells bursting or being pried open</note> in the sun and are soon roasted, after which the snail-eaters fall upon them and have their food therefrom. With the snail shells they accomplish much. They are their ships with which they sail to the mainland; they keep their water inside them; they cover their huts with them and use them instead of tents. Thus Nature has accomplished much with a single thing, for these snails serve them for food, as vessels for their water, for housing, and for shipping. Opposite these on the shore live certain peoples who lead a very undisciplined life. Their nourishment is also from the whales <term>wällfischen</term> that the sea casts out, which are sometimes so large that they feed the people sufficiently; at other times, when they are not caught, they bring such hunger upon them that they must eat the fish-bones and sea-crustaceans <note>original: "mhőrkressig"</note>. Now, this is as much as I find concerning the Ichthyophagi <note>original: "Ichtyophagis"; Greek for "fish-eaters"</note>. The shore situated toward Babylon is adjacent to a fruitful, cultivated land, and therein is a great multitude of fish, so that the inhabitants never lack for them; for all around the shore they stick pointed stakes, set closely together so that they look just like fishing nets. In these same fences there are many entrances which have little doors that go open and shut. When the sea flows in <note>the incoming tide</note>, it pushes them open with its flow; when it flows out <note>the outgoing tide</note>, it shuts them. Thus, every day many fish are saved by flowing in through the gates, which are then closed when the water recedes, and they remain lying on the dry land in such great quantity that one would think it was a heap of salted fish; the fish provide both nourishment and much profit. ### Diodorus Siculus

They are said to possess no sense of feeling; for I do not write this alone, but the Egyptian merchants who sail there across the sea bear witness to me. The third **Ptolemy** <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes, Pharaoh of Egypt (reigned 246–222 BCE).</note>, being desirous to capture some elephants of the same species, sent one of his good companions named **Simian** <note>original: "Simian"; likely Simmias, an explorer and officer under Ptolemy III.</note> there to scout the land. When he returned, as **Agatharchides of Cnidus** <note>A Greek historian and geographer from the 2nd century BCE; he is the primary source for Diodorus's descriptions of these regions.</note> writes, he said that these **Ethiopians** <note>In antiquity, "Ethiopia" referred generally to the regions of Africa south of Egypt.</note>, who live there without feeling, do not naturally drink water, nor are they amazed by the ships that come to them or by the presence of others. They stand still when one looks at them, as if they had no understanding at all. Even if someone draws a sword from its scabbard and strikes one of them, he does not flee, nor is he troubled by the blows, no matter how one treats them, or what shame, harm, or evil one shows them. Even if they are wounded, they do not move because of it, nor is there any among them who desires to avenge such a thing when it happens to another. And though they see their own wives and children struck down before them, they look upon it plainly, yet show neither anger nor pity; indeed, they endure all evil with a tranquil mind, only looking at those who strike them. Whatever one does to them, they merely shake their heads. Furthermore, it is said they cannot speak, but only beckon and point to what they lack or what they want. And what is even more wondrous is that the **seals** <note>original: "mhörkalber," literally "sea-calves."</note> go about with them and wait with them for the fish-catch. Their women help one another, they raise their children in common, and they are peaceful toward one another. They also do no harm to any foreign living animal or man. Now, such a life, however wondrous it may be, has endured among them for many ages, either because necessity demands it or because long habit has established it.

They do not have dwellings like the first **Fish-eaters**, but rather they set up their huts toward the **North** <note>original: "mitnacht," a common Early Modern German term for North, as the sun is never there at midnight.</note>, where the air and shade protect them from the sun; for the places situated toward the **South** <note>original: "Mittag," literally "Midday," meaning South.</note> are just like hot ovens, so that they cannot live there due to the heat. Those who live toward the North make their huts out of the curved **fish bones** <note>original: "Vischgrädē"; likely whale ribs.</note> of the great **sea monsters** <note>original: "mhörwundn"; referring to whales or other large marine mammals.</note> which the sea casts up in great variety. They set these up on both sides, weave them together, and cover them with seaweed to avoid the heat; and Nature, which desires to protect itself, found this art among them out of necessity.

Item: they also have another kind of housing. There are many large trees that stand on the shore of the sea and hang over into it; they are quite thick with leaves and have a fruit just like **quinces** <note>original: "Costintzen." The translator likely refers to quinces or perhaps chestnuts (Kastanien) to give readers a familiar comparison for the unidentified tropical fruit.</note>. They weave the branches into one another so that they create shade, and thus they have their dwelling both on land and in the water, and may escape the sun's heat through the shade of the trees, the waves of the sea, and the air.

Yet fourthly, they have another dwelling: over a long and eternal time, the sea has cast up a great pile of moss, weeds, and refuse that grows in the sea onto the shore, until it has become like a mountain, hardened and grown together, so that they can dig long, deep hollows into it. From these they run out to catch fish when the tide goes out; when the tide comes in, they hide inside and consume what they have caught. Those who have died they throw into the sea, offering them to the sea monsters when the sea is stormy. ## Of those who nourish themselves solely 
### upon snails. Chapter 5.

Now we shall speak of the snail-eaters. Not far from the land, there lie several islands in the Ocean Sea <note>original: "mhör Occeano"; a term used in the period to refer to the vast outer sea, here likely the Indian Ocean or Red Sea.</note>, many in number but small and insignificant. These islands bear neither wild nor cultivated fruits. Because they lie so close together, there is no flood or storm of the sea; instead, the water is always in good repose, so that the snails gather there in great numbers, crowding between the islands to remain safer. At night, they lie on the bottom and feed; by day, they emerge between the islands toward the sun. Because of their great size, they look exactly like overturned fishing skiffs <term>nachen</term><note>A small, flat-bottomed boat or skiff used for fishing.</note>, far exceeding other sea snails. The inhabitants swim out to them secretly and push them aside to the land; or else they turn their bellies upward so that they cannot turn back or escape, tie a long rope to their tails <note>In this context, this refers to the fleshy part of the mollusk's foot or body.</note>, and pull them out while swimming. Once they have brought them onto the island, they let them burst open in the sun and they are soon roasted. Then the snail-eaters fall upon them and have their meal. They achieve much with the snail shells: these are their ships in which they sail to the land, they keep their water in them, they cover their huts with them, and use them in place of tents. Thus, Nature has accomplished much with a single thing, for these snails serve them for food, as vessels for their water, for housing, and for sailing. Opposite these people on the shore, there live certain tribes who lead a very undisciplined life. Their nourishment also comes from whales that the sea washes up; because these are so large, they provide the people with enough food at times, but at other times, when none are caught, they suffer such hunger that they must eat the fish skeletons and sea crayfish. Now, this is as much as I find concerning the **Ichthyophagi** <term>Ichtyophagis</term><note>From the Greek for "fish-eaters."</note>. The coast situated toward **Babylon** is adjacent to a fertile, cultivated land where there is such a great multitude of fish that the inhabitants never lack for them. Along the shore, they stick sharp little stakes close together so that they look like fishing nets. In these same fences, there are many entrances with little doors that go open and shut. When the sea rushes in, it pushes them open with its flow; when it recedes, it shuts them. Thus, many fish pass through the gates every day with the incoming tide, and when the water recedes, they are locked in and remain lying on the dry ground in such great quantity that one would think they were a heap of salted fish. ## Of the root-eaters and other people who
### fight with wild beasts. Chapter 6.

Now we wish to turn ourselves to those Moors <note>original: "Mören"; a historical term used here to describe the dark-skinned peoples of Ethiopia.</note> who dwell in Ethiopia above Egypt/ by the water called Astopa <note>The Astapus River, now known as the Blue Nile.</note> and are called the Rhizophagi <note>original: "Rhizophagi"; Greek for "Root-eaters."</note>. They have nearby woods where they dig up the roots of reeds/ which they wash clean/ and pound with stones/ until they become soft/ and cling together/ out of which they afterwards make cakes/ shaped like broad bricks/ that a man may grasp with his hand/ and they bake them in the sun/ and eat them. They have this food alone/ which is quite sweet/ and they have plenty of it/ therefore they live in constant peace with one another/ yet they wage war with the lions. For when the air becomes heated in the summer/ the lions run out of the wilderness/ seeking the shade among them/ as well as to hunt smaller animals. Many Ethiopians are also torn apart by them/ when they emerge from the marshes/ for they have no weapons/ and are too weak for them. The lions would have long ago exterminated this people/ if nature had not provided them a singular assistance. Around the beginning of the Dog Days <term>Hundstag</term><note>The hottest period of the summer, historically associated with the rising of the "Dog Star," Sirius.</note>/ there comes a wondrous/ innumerable swarm of gnats/ though without wind/ the people flee into the marshes/ where they are not harmed/ but the gnats drive the lions out of the land with biting and humming. Bordering these are those/ who are called Hyliophagi <note>Greek for "Wood-eaters."</note> or Spermatophagi <note>Greek for "Seed-eaters."</note>/ who gather the fruits that fall from the trees in the summer time/ and they enjoy such food without labor/ but at other times/ they cut or pluck the grass/ which grows in shady places/ and nourish themselves upon it. Their wives and children travel with them to the flat lands/ climbing the trees and breaking off the shoots for food. They become so well-practiced in this climbing through habit/ that they swing from one branch to another/ and from one tree to another like birds/ and leap upon very thin branches without danger/ for if they should happen to slip with their feet/ they catch themselves with their hands/ perhaps on a branch/ and are able to prevent a fall because of their lightness (for they are very thin and light of body)/ and even if they do fall, the fall does not harm them because of their slenderness. Thus they fill their bellies with the shoots of the trees. They also go about naked/ and they have wives and children in common/ they wage war with one another over their dwellings/ their weapons are sticks/ and those who are overcome/ must serve the others. They generally die of hunger/ the cause being that they go blind/ and must lose the eyes/ with which they primarily seek their food/ the rest of their land is inhabited by those whom men call the Gymnetae <note>original: "Gymnetas"; from the Greek *gymnos*, meaning "naked ones."</note> of whom there are few/ and who are different in their ways and life. Their dwellings are forests/ which are quite rough/ with little water. They sleep at night in the trees/ for fear of wild beasts. When the day breaks/ they move toward the waters thus armed/ and hide themselves in the thickets. When the heat

# The Fourth Book.

When the heat begins, the **jackals** <note>original: "Drochsen"; likely referring to the jackal (Greek: *thoes*) or a similar wild canine.</note>, **tigers** <note>In the 16th century, "Tyger" was a general term for any large, predatory cat, often leopards or panthers in an African context.</note>, and other wild game draw near to the watering holes to drink and avoid the heat. They drink so much that they can barely move. Then the **Ethiopians** climb down from the trees, pierce them with sharpened, fire-hardened stakes, shoot at them, or throw stones at them. At times—though rarely—one of the hunters is killed by a beast; whatever is caught is divided and devoured. They also kill many animals through cunning and skill. Where there are no wild beasts that they can catch or kill, they take the hides of those they caught previously, scrape the hair off, dry them over the fire, divide them, and eat them. They teach small boys to shoot at a target, giving them no other food than what they have hit. Thus, hunger makes the most certain archers out of them. 

Those bordering this region, situated toward the West, fight with **elephants**. For these also dwell in forests that are very thick with trees; the hunters sit upon these trees and watch how the elephants move to and fro. Where there is a herd together, they let them pass, for they cannot overcome them. But if one travels alone, they are so bold that one man will undertake to attack the elephant. For when the elephant passes next to a tree, he who has hidden himself there jumps down quickly, catches the animal’s tail, and swings his feet onto the hindquarters. Thus braced, he takes a small axe, which he always carries with him and which is very sharp (he can also use it with one hand); with this, he cuts through the tendons in the elephant’s right leg. He uses his left hand to avoid the harm the beast might do to him, and as it attempts to injure him, he steers his light body to escape the animal. In this struggle, the lives of both are at stake; the danger of death for one lies in the life of the other.

[A woodcut illustration depicting a hunter attacking an elephant. The hunter is positioned behind the animal, gripping its tail and leaning against its hindquarters while using a small hand-axe to strike its rear leg. The elephant has large tusks and is set against a background of sparse trees and hills.]

For it often happens that after the elephant’s tendons are cut, it falls onto the injured or wounded side and drags the **Ethiopian** down with it, thus crushing him. Sometimes it runs with him against another tree or stone and crushes him. At times the elephant becomes enraged by the pain, and since it cannot defend itself against the enemy, it runs into the distance for so long until the **Moor** <note>original: "Mor"; a historical term used here to describe the dark-skinned peoples of Ethiopia.</note> cuts it down. Then the Ethiopians run to it in a crowd and hack pieces from the living animal, which they eat. 

There are others who dwell not far from these who catch these elephants without danger to themselves; for this animal has a very different nature than other animals have. It cannot lie down for lack of joints <note>This reflects a widespread classical and medieval misconception that elephants lacked knee joints and therefore could not stand up if they fell.</note>. Therefore, its habit is such that when it comes from the pasture and has eaten enough, it does not lie down, but leans against a tree to rest. During this, it soils and wears down the tree with its weight, so that the inhabitants soon become aware of where it stays at night. Thus they saw the tree at the bottom, yet not completely through, so that it...

In the evening, when the **elephant** <note>original: "Helfant"</note> is full, it creeps to its usual haunt and leans completely against the sawed-through tree, falling down together with the tree. It lies thus the whole night with its feet turned toward heaven, for it cannot right itself. In the morning, the **Ethiopians** come and kill the animal, then set up a small hut on that very spot until the beast is entirely consumed. Among these people are those who dwell toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang"; literally "the sunset," referring to the western horizon.</note>, called the **pug-nosed Ethiopians** <note>original: "kumpfnasende"; likely referring to the *Simi*, a tribe described by ancient geographers as having flat noses.</note>; those toward the South <note>original: "Mittag"; literally "midday," referring to the direction of the sun at noon.</note> are called **Ostrich-eaters**. 

For among them is a bird which is half-beast, and for that reason, it is called a **stag-bird** <note>original: "hirtzuogel"; a 16th-century German rendering of the Greek *strouthokamelos* (ostrich), which literally means "sparrow-camel." Here the translator compares it to a deer or stag due to its size and speed.</note>. It is a large bird, like a stag; it has a long neck, round and feathered sides, a small head, long and strong legs, and a cloven foot. Because of its weight, it cannot fly high, yet it runs beyond measure swiftly and quietly, especially when the wind is at its back and enters its wings, which it spreads out just like a sail on a ship. They throw stones as large as a fist behind them at the hunters. When the wind stops, they can no longer use their wings, and they soon become tired and are captured. Because there are so many of them, they are easily caught with various types of **snares** <note>original: "glädtwerck"; likely referring to nets or smooth-sliding traps.</note>. Thus, their meat is eaten, their skin is used for clothing, and they also make beds from their feathers. The **pug-nosed Ethiopians** cause them much grief.

They also defend themselves against them with their beaks; these same beaks, of which the inhabitants may possess many, are very useful to them because they are large and well-suited for cutting.

The Fourth Book.

# On a people who nourish themselves on locusts
->and perish in a wondrous way. Chapter VII.<-

Not far from these dwell the **Acridophagi** <note>original: "Acridophagi"; from the Greek *akris* (locust) and *phagein* (to eat). This group was a staple of ancient ethnographic writing.</note>, who border the desert; they are somewhat smaller than other people, with bodies that are excessively lean and black. During the season of the spring equinox, the **west winds** <note>original: "Westwhinnd"; referring to the Zephyrs.</note> blow an innumerable swarm of locusts to them; these are large in size and have a fearful, wretched color on their wings. The **Ethiopians** know at what time these locusts will arrive and from where they fly; therefore, they carry all sorts of wood and brushwood into a nearby valley that is several miles long. They mow down all the grass, and as the swarm draws near, they set fire to the wood. The locusts flying over it are so weakened by the smoke that they can no longer fly out of the valley; they fall down in heaps and provide enough food for the entire region. For they have much salt and salt these locusts down, which they consider a fine delicacy <note>original: "gůtter schleck"; a 16th-century term for a treat or dainty morsel.</note>. They sustain themselves on these locusts alone, for the reason that they neither keep nor raise any cattle, nor do they eat fish, as they dwell too far from the sea; thus they have no other nourishment except that which Nature provides them. They are of slight build and can run well, but those who grow very old do not exceed their fortieth year. They meet not only a wondrous but even an incredible end. For as old age approaches, winged lice <note>original: "fliegend läuß"; this refers to a historical medical condition known as phthiriasis or "louse-disease," often used in ancient texts to describe the gruesome death of tyrants or cursed peoples.</note> grow out of their bodies, which are not only strange but also terrifying to behold. These first devour their bellies, then the chest, and finally the entire body in every part. At first, when the disease takes hold, the skin bites as if he were becoming mangy, and he begins to scratch, so that the itching feels both pleasant and yet painful. Afterward, the lice crawl forth and pus is discharged; the pain and the horror of the disease become so great that the sufferer, with great lamentation and cries, tears himself apart everywhere with his nails. Then the worms fall out one after another in such great quantities that one would swear he were shaking them out of small canisters. Such a cruel death they must suffer, either because of their food or the air. Bordering these people is a vast land endowed with many kinds of fruit, yet it is desolate and uninhabited, so that no man

Of Diodorus Siculus

In **Media** <note>original: "Medien"; an ancient region in modern-day Iran.</note>, there were so many sparrows that they devoured all the seed that was sown, so that the people were forced to occupy another land. Those who are now called the **Actariotae** <note>original: "Actariotas"; likely referring to the Autariatae, an Illyrian tribe whose migration was famously attributed to a plague of frogs by ancient historians.</note> came to the land where they now live because they were driven out by frogs that once rained down upon their fatherland. Everyone well knows that among other deeds for which **Hercules** attained divine honor, it is counted that he drove away the harmful birds that lived in the **Stymphalian Lake** <note>original: "Stymphalischen see"; one of the Twelve Labors of Hercules, involving man-eating birds with metallic feathers.</note> and ruined the surrounding countryside. Several cities in **Libya** were abandoned for the reason that so many lions came and harassed them. I recount these examples only so that those who perhaps give little credit to writers when they write something that is not easily believable will not wonder so much. Thus we will return again to the record of our history. At the outermost

toward the **North** <note>original: "Mitternag"; literally 'midnight', the traditional German term for the North.</note>, there dwell people who are called **Cynamolgi** <note>original: "Cynamolgi"; from the Greek for "dog-milkers." Ancient ethnographies claimed they lived on the milk of large dogs.</note> by the Greeks and **Wild-folk** by others. These people have large, long beards and raise great packs of wild dogs for the protection of their lives. For from the longest day of the year until the middle of winter, an innumerable host of **Indian oxen** comes to them. The cause of this is not yet certain; it is not known whether they are fleeing other wild beasts that pursue them, or whether they are following food, or whether Nature—which has many wondrous inclinations unknown to man—drives them there. Since these people are too weak to face them alone, they protect themselves with dogs, which they use to hunt these oxen, catching many of them with their help. Some they eat fresh, and some they salt. In addition, they catch much other game with their dogs, which they eat. Those at the furthest **South** <note>original: "Mittags"; literally 'midday', the traditional German term for the South.</note>, though they have human form, live like wild beasts. But let enough be said of all these.

-># On the Troglodytes and others.<-

These **Troglodytes** <note>original: "Troglodyter"; from the Greek for "cave-dwellers." Diodorus describes them as a pastoralist group living along the Red Sea coast.</note> are called shepherds by the Greeks for the reason that they get all their nourishment from livestock. They have tribes and princes among them; except for the prince, no one has his own wife, but wives and children are held in common. If anyone [other than the prince] approaches a woman, the prince punishes him with a set fine. They cook their sheep in blood and milk in the sun, and that is their food during the times when it rains heavily and the wet east winds blow. All the strife they have among themselves arises over the meadows and reeds where each wishes to go once the pasture has been grazed down. Whatever old livestock is failing, becomes sick, or is about to die, they slaughter and live upon it. The elders do not give their children names of men or women...

...women names as we do; instead, they name them after sheep, rams, or cows. On the other hand, the elders are not named "father" and "mother," but after the livestock. It is said that they are provided for by the livestock, and not by a father or mother. The common people drink burdock juice; the princes and "big shots" <note>original: "grossen hansen"; a colloquial German term for people of high status or "bigwigs."</note> drink the juice from a flower, which is much like our weakest cider. They drive their herds continually with them and do not remain in one place, but dwell here and there. Their clothing is nothing but a small pelt, with which they cover their private parts. The **Troglodytes** <note>Ancient Greek term for "cave-dwellers," though here describing pastoralist tribes near the Red Sea.</note> all circumcise themselves like the **Egyptians**, except for those who, because of their gait, are called "the limpers." These live among the **Bastarnae** <note>A powerful tribal group in ancient Eastern Europe; their mention here alongside Ethiopians reflects the often-confused geography of early modern texts.</note> and are cut with a razor in their childhood so that they must limp.

Those among them called the **Megavares** have shields made of raw ox hides that are entirely round, and they carry a club studded with iron; some carry bows, and many carry spears. They have a very strange and ridiculous way of burying the dead: they bind the corpse with thistle vines, tying the feet and head together, and lay it on a small hill. They pelt it with stones until they have covered it, then they place a pair of goat horns upon the stone heap and depart with a laughing mouth.

They war with one another not out of envy or ambition, as the **Greeks** do, but for the sake of pasture. Their quarreling begins with stone-throwing; if one is then wounded, they reach for the bow, at which they are very skillful, and then it becomes a slaughter. Their wars are settled by the elderly women, who run safely and boldly between the fighters (for it would be a great crime if someone harmed a woman); immediately, their war is settled.

Those who, due to age, are infirm and can no longer follow the cattle, tie an ox tail around their own necks so that the ox may drag them to death. If, however, someone does not wish to kill himself in this way, and another had previously been requested to tie him up and help him end his misery, that person has performed a great act of kindness if he complies. Those who have the rot <note>original: "rütten"; likely referring to a wasting disease or glanders, often applied to livestock but here to human illness.</note> or other sicknesses are all put to death in this way. For they hold it to be the greatest evil when a person wishes to live who can do or perform nothing worthy of life. Therefore, one rarely sees a sick Troglodyte; they are all fresh and healthy, but none of them survives past sixty years.

But let enough be said of them here. If there is anyone who reads this writing of ours and will not give it credit because of these strange and wonderful things, let him consider the climate of the **Scythians** and Troglodytes compared to ours, and he will not be so offended by it. For it is unbelievable how different a climate we have compared to those mentioned here. In some places, the flowing waters freeze over so thoroughly from the great cold that loaded wagons and entire armies can travel and pull across the ice. Likewise, wine and all liquid things freeze so hard that one must chop them apart. And what is even more wonderful: sometimes the clothes a person is wearing fall off from the cold, the eyes become clouded, the fire loses some of its radiance, and the bronze statues <note>original: "ohrinen bilder"; likely a corruption of "erenen bilder" (bronze/brass images).</note> crack open. In those same places, because of thick mists, one can see neither lightning nor hear thunder. Nature works many such things—and many more wonderful ones—which are quite unbelievable to the ignorant, while the experienced do not doubt them. In **Egypt** and other regions of the Troglodytes, the sun...

...of stones <note>original: "stein/"; this catchword links to the previous page's description of burial mounds.</note> and finally place a goat’s horn on top.

Around noon it is so hot that those standing almost directly across from one another cannot see each other, which the thick air causes. They also cannot walk without shoes, for if they wander barefoot, their feet are immediately covered in blisters. If they are thirsty and do not drink immediately, they die in an instant, for the heat of the sun licks the moisture out of their bodies from that moment on. If one puts food into an earthen vessel, pours water over it, and sets it in the sun, it cooks immediately without any other fire. Yet, even though it goes poorly for the inhabitants and causes them pain, they do not leave that same land; instead, they love it above all others, believing they could live in no other country. So great a love of the <term>fatherland</term> <note>original: "vatterlāds"; here meaning one's place of birth or ancestral home.</note> is born into us by Nature, so that habit, begun in childhood, overcomes the harshness of the climate. 

Now, so many strange lands are not even contained within a vast distance; for from the **Maeotian Lake** <note>The Sea of Azov, north of the Black Sea, considered by ancients to be the edge of the frozen north.</note>, where many **Scythians** live in villages in the extreme cold, many have traveled in ten days as far as **Rhodes** with large merchant ships, and in four days from there to **Alexandria**. From there, they have sailed on the **Nile** in ten days into **Ethiopia**. Thus, one can sail from the coldest place in the world to the hottest in only twenty-four days. Therefore, since the climate changes so much over a distance that is not very great, it should not be a matter of much wonder that their lives, customs, appearance, and other things are so very different from ours.

...moderate. <note>original: "mässig sey"; a continuation from the previous page's description of a beast's temperament.</note> The animals that are called **Crocote** <note>original: "Crocote"; likely referring to the hyena or the mythical Crocotta, often described as a hybrid of a dog and a wolf</note> by the **Egyptians** are of the nature of dogs and wolves, though more vicious than either of these species. They have such strong teeth that they crush all bones and digest whatever they eat. Some claim that this animal makes a human voice, which does not seem like the truth to us. There is a great variety of serpents <note>original: "gewhürm"; literally 'vermin' or 'creatures', but here referring to reptiles and snakes</note> among them, and...

<image-desc>A woodcut of a slender, long-legged dog-like creature with a pointed snout, possibly a hyena or the "Crocote" described in the text, shown mid-leap towards the right.</image-desc>

...are found there in the deserts of unbelievable size. For some dare to say that one finds serpents a hundred cubits long <note>original: "hundt elnbogẽ"</note>. We, like others, not without reason doubt this. But they rhyme an even more unbelievable and wonderful thing with it, saying that because the land is entirely flat and the snakes are so large, when they are coiled in a circle, one might see a snake lying there and think it is a large hill. But little is to be held of this size. We, however, wish to write of the largest serpent that was ever seen, how it was captured and brought into **Alexandria**. **Ptolemy II** <note>original: "Der ander Prolemeus"; Ptolemy Philadelphus, known for his interest in zoology and exotic collections</note> had a desire to obtain **elephants** <note>original: "helfantẽ"</note> and other wonderful, wild, cruel, and strong animals. He gave great gifts and rewards to hunters so that they might bring him the most beautiful elephants and other beasts. Because of this, many animals unknown to the **Greeks** were brought for them to see.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a variety of serpents and scorpions. Several long, winding snakes are shown, some with dragon-like heads or ears. Two large scorpions are featured prominently in the center of the arrangement.</image-desc>

Now these huntsmen, when they saw the generosity of the King, resolved that they would bring one of the great snakes to Alexandria, however they might. And although it seemed a difficult matter to them, they swore together that they would undertake it; and so their plan prospered. Beside a small stream there lay a snake, about thirty cubits long—which makes ninety feet <note>original: "neünzig schůch"</note>—wound round and round upon itself. Whenever other animals or livestock went to the brook, it would snap up quickly, catching some with its teeth. Others it entangled with its tail and ate. Now, when the hunters saw that it was so long, and moreover bold by nature, they resolved to catch it with ropes and chains. They approached it bravely. But as they drew near and became aware of the fiery eyes and the hissing tongues, and heard it shaking and raising its scales, and saw it tear its gullet open, they lost their color and were quite terrified. Yet they cast [the nets] so...

<page-num>cxxxix</page-num>
<header>The Fourth Book.</header>

...they, trembling, [threw] the chain onto its tail. As soon as the creature felt this, it turned toward them with a great hissing <note>original: "pfeysen"; literally "piping" or "whistling," referring to the sound of a snake's hiss</note>, crushed the nearest man in its jaws, and swallowed him alive. Another, who fled and was already far away, it caught with its tail and squeezed to death. The others, seeing this, were terrified <note>original: "trostten sich gar bald"; used here perhaps ironically or to mean they "consoled" themselves quickly by realizing flight was their only option</note> and saved their lives through flight. 

Yet they would not cease from trying to capture the serpent, for the hope of profit overcame all fear. Thus, they resolved to succeed by cunning rather than by force. They first made a net out of large, strong ropes, fashioned like a massive fish trap <note>original: "hosferigen visch bären"; likely a type of hoop net or "weir" used for catching large fish</note>, large enough for the beast <note>original: "whurm"; literally "worm," but historically used for any creeping thing, including dragons and serpents</note> to fit inside. After this, they scouted the serpent’s nest and its various entrances and exits, noting the time of day when the snake went out to hunt <note>original: "weydt"; literally "pasture," referring to the animal's feeding grounds</note>. Then they blocked the opening of its nest with stones. Not far away in a valley, they created a wide entrance into a hole, mimicking its natural nest—as if rabbits <note>original: "kůllin"; likely "Kaninchen" or similar burrowing animals</note> lived within—and laid the net inside. 

When the serpent returned home from hunting, many men appeared with bows, slings, and trumpets <note>original: "busaunnen"; early brass instruments like sackbuts, used here to create a frightening noise</note>, and some were mounted on horses. However, having seen what happened before, none of them dared to approach the snake; instead, they shot and threw weapons from a distance. They blew the trumpets and raised a great clamor with the horses and many dogs they had brought, so that the serpent, frightened by the noise, fled toward its nest. Finding it blocked, the riders pursued it with a great clattering of hooves and the blaring of trumpets. Driven by the noise, the shouts of the hunters, and the barking of the dogs, the serpent grew cowed and sought flight toward the artificial hole. 

Once it had entered and fallen into the net, it writhed back and forth, hissing violently and tearing at the mesh with its teeth. Finally, they subdued it; they dragged it out in the net, struck it with heavy blows on its tail, and broke off its teeth until the pain eventually made the creature somewhat tamer. Thus they brought the serpent in the net to **Alexandria** and presented it to the king. All who saw it were struck with wonder, and those who only heard of it thought it unbelievable. 

Over time, as the serpent grew hungry and weak, it became so docile that everyone was amazed. **Ptolemy** rewarded the hunters and provided the snake with a fixed ration of food every day. Whenever foreigners visited him, he would show them the serpent as a great marvel. Since such a massive serpent had been publicly seen and captured, one may well believe the **Ethiopians** when they claim that the stories of their enormous snakes are not entirely fictional. For they say serpents are found there of such size that they consume not only oxen and similar large beasts, but are sometimes even large enough to challenge elephants. In the initial attack, the snake coils itself around the animal's legs so that the elephant cannot move; then, it creeps up toward the face and blinds the elephant with its fiery eyes, bringing it down to be devoured.

For this part of the world—much like Britain or other lands situated toward the North <note>original: "Mitternacht"; literally "midnight," the traditional German term for the North</note>—is known to few. We shall speak of the northern lands and of Britain when we describe the deeds of Caesar (who expanded the Roman Empire to those very places and made those unknown regions recognizable). The outlet of the Arabian Sea <note>The Red Sea</note> flows into the Southern Ocean; it is many miles long and borders the lands of the Arabians and the Troglodytes <note>term: Troglodytes; literally "cave-dwellers," an ancient Greek name for various ethnic groups living along the Red Sea coast</note>. This outlet is seventeen stadia <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; 17 stadia is roughly 2 miles</note> wide, and from the harbor called Panormus <note>original: "Panormus"; a Greek name meaning "all-sheltered" or "always fit for landing"</note> to the landing point situated opposite is as far as one may sail in a single day.

But near Mount Tirito, the sea is very wide, and one cannot see the opposite landing points; yet the further it stretches, the wider it gradually becomes until it reaches the landing or the outlet. Now, this curve of the sea has many large islands; it is narrow for sailing, and the sea rushes quickly in its ebb and flow. The Arabian Sea also possesses this quality: we shall describe last how one navigates within it and what wonders there are to tell. We shall begin at those shores on the right hand, extending to the desert where the Troglodytes dwell. As one travels up and down the coast from the city of Arsinoe, one finds in many places salt water running out of hard rocks into the sea. From there onward, across a wide field, is a green mountain <note>This likely refers to the "Emerald Mountain" or Mons Smaragdus, famous in antiquity for its gemstones</note> that immediately dazzles the eyes of those who look upon it. At the foot of the mountain lies a lake which is difficult to navigate and is called the Lake of Aphrodite. Three islands are located within it; two of them bear figs and plenty of olives. The third lacks trees but is full of guinea fowl <note>term: Meleagrides; birds named in Greek after the sisters of the hero Meleager, who were said to have been transformed into these birds while mourning him</note>. 

Afterward, one comes to a bend in the coast called Achatartus <note>likely "Akathartos Kolpos," meaning "the Foul Bay" or "Impure Gulf"</note>, where the sea has a narrow passage to sail into the sea lying opposite. It seems to me, however, that the reason why this island was cleared should by no means be skipped over. this. Furthermore, the inhabitants of the island are allowed no ships at all, so that none of them may steal the stones and sail away with them. Whatever vessel arrives there, out of fear of the king, makes as much haste as possible to sail away from the island again. Those who are in the garrison go on watch, divided into shifts; and whenever they see the stone glistening, they mark the spot, then dig it out during the day and hand it over to the lapidaries <note>original: "balliesreren"; stone-cutters or polishers</note>, who prepare it as it should be. The surrounding coast is mostly inhabited by the Troglodytes <note>term: Troglodytes; ancient Greek for "cave-dwellers"</note> and the Fish-eaters <note>term: Ichthyophagi; a group of people whose diet consisted almost entirely of fish</note>, who are all herdsmen. The land is entirely flat—it does not have even a small hill—and the sea is no more than three steps deep and entirely green in color. Some say the water is not like this of its own accord, but rather it is the fault of the vegetation <note>original: "gmüß"; seaweed or aquatic plants</note> with which it is filled. It is good for sailing and never stormy, and it is full of fish; however, the ships that carry elephants <note>The Ptolemaic kings of Egypt built specialized ships called "elephantago" to transport war elephants from Ethiopia</note> must endure great danger there because of their height and heavy load, for at night strong winds blow that drive them into the sand or sometimes onto rocks. If the water then enters the ship, or if they cannot drive the ship off the sand, they throw everything overboard into the sea except for the food—though at times it helps little, for there is no island, no land, nor any other ship where they might seek help. Because it is an uninhabited region where few people sail, it quickly comes to pass for them...

It also has a very deep sea, in which there are exceedingly large whales <note>original: "waldfisch"</note> that are harmless to humans, unless one accidentally falls into their fins. They cannot swim after the ships, for the sun blinds them. The furthest land of the Troglodytes <note>A term used by ancient writers to describe "cave-dwellers" in the regions south of Egypt</note> is enclosed by the mountains called the Pseuae.

The Fourth Book.

## Concerning the land of Phoenicia.
### Chapter 6.

The other mountain range, which lies opposite Arabia, is called Neptunum, named after the altar that Aristo the explorer <note>Aristo was a navigator sent by Ptolemy II Philadelphus to explore the Arabian coast.</note> erected to Neptune when he was sent by Ptolemy to scout Arabia along the Ocean. That same region, as it stretches along, is widely famous for its resources and is named Phoenicia <note>original: "Phoenicia"; this refers to the "Palm Grove" (Phoinikon) on the Red Sea coast, not the Mediterranean Phoenicia.</note> after the fruit of the palms, which bear much and sweet fruit. The surrounding area has little flowing or spring water, and where it lies toward the south, it is exceedingly hot; therefore, the barbarians have not unjustly dedicated and attributed this land—which lies endowed with all kinds of fruit amidst the desert—to the gods. For the many springs therein, and the little brooks—which are nothing more than cold meltwater from the snow—make the earth green and pleasant to look upon. There is also a temple there made of hard stone, built long ago, and inscribed with letters that no one can read.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, octagonal building with a prominent central dome. The structure features multiple tiers with arched openings or niches on the lower levels and decorative architectural detailing on the upper levels. It represents the temple described in the text.</image-desc>

In that same temple, there is always a woman and a man who perform the service of the idols throughout their lives, and they are considered blessed for dwelling in that same spot. At night they sleep in the trees, fearing the wild beasts; because near the promontory where the sea runs into Phoenicia, there is an island called the Island of Wild Beasts, so named because so many animals live there that many must wonder how so many can live together. Opposite and nearly adjacent to this island is a promontory of Arabian Palestine called Petra <note>Though Petra is famous as a city, the text here identifies a coastal landmark by this name.</note>; to this place the Gerrheans and Minaeans bring frankincense and other noble scents from Upper Arabia. The other regions are inhabited by the Mataneans, and bordering them are the Garindeans, who have possessed this land in the manner described. In Phoenicia, of which we just wrote, a festival was held in ancient times every five years, to which the neighbors traveled with fat camels to perform the sacrifice they called <gloss>hecatombs</gloss> <note>original: "ixatoubnas", a corruption of the Greek 'hekatombe', a sacrifice of a hundred oxen.</note> in the same temple to honor the gods. When returning home, they carried water with them, which was prepared to be good for curing all illnesses. The Maraneans also traveled to Phoenicia at one time to perform their sacrifice and fetch water; meanwhile, the Garindeans banded together and slaughtered those who had remained at home in the Maraneans' land. Afterward, they set an ambush and killed those who were returning home, so that not one survived. Thereafter they took over the desolate land, dividing the livestock, the fruit, the pastures, and the dwellings. This land has few neighboring lands, yet it is separated everywhere by mountains, from which much benefit arises for the inhabitants, beyond the pleasure of the place.

The Fourth Book.

## Of the Land of Phoenicia.
### Chapter VI.

The other mountain range, situated across from Arabia, is called Neptune, after the altar which Aristo the explorer <note>Aristo was a scout sent by the Greek-Egyptian King Ptolemy to map the Red Sea coast</note> erected to Neptune when he was sent by Ptolemy to scout Arabia around the Ocean. This same region, as it lies along its length, is widely famed for its usefulness, and is named Phoenicia <note>original: "Phoenicia"; in this context, the name refers to the "Palm Grove" (Phoinikon) on the Red Sea coast, rather than the Mediterranean nation</note> from the fruit of the palms which bear much sweet fruit. The surrounding area has little flowing or spring water, and where it lies toward the south, it is exceedingly hot; therefore, the barbarians have not unjustly consecrated and attributed this land—situated between the deserts and endowed with all manner of fruits—to the gods. For the many springs within it, and the little brooks that are no warmer than cold snow-water, make the earth green and pleasant to look upon. There is also there a temple built of hard stone in long-ago times, and written therein with letters that no one can read.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a polygonal, possibly octagonal, multi-storied domed building with arched windows and decorative tiers, topped by a small cupola.</image-desc>

In this same temple there is always a woman and a man who attend to the idol-service their whole lives; they are held to be blessed because they dwell in that same place. At night they sleep in the trees, fearing the wild beasts; the reason being, near the promontory where the sea runs into Phoenicia, there is an island called the Island of Wild Beasts, because so many animals dwell therein, at which everyone must marvel, how so many can dwell together. Opposite and near this island is a promontory of Arabian Palestine <note>likely referring to the Nabataean coast</note> called Petra, thither the Gerrhei and Minaeans bring frankincense and other noble scents from Upper Arabia. The other regions are inhabited by the Maranei, who are bordered by the Garindaei, who possessed this land in the manner described hereafter. 

In Phoenicia, of which we have just written, they held a festival every five years, to which the inhabitants came with fat camels to hold the sacrifice, which they called <term>Exasoubum</term> <note>a phonetic rendering of a local or Greek term for a grand ritual sacrifice, possibly related to a "hecatomb"</note> in that same temple to honor the gods. They then carried water back with them on their return home, which was prepared to be good for all illnesses. The Maranei also went at one time into Phoenicia to hold their sacrifice and fetch water; then the Garindaei banded together and, in the meantime, slaughtered those who had remained at home in the land of the Maranei. After that, they lay in ambush and killed those who were on their return journey, so that not one survived. Afterwards, they took over the desolate land, dividing the livestock, the fruits, the pastures, and the dwellings. This land has few harbors, yet it is divided throughout by mountains, from which, beyond the pleasure it provides, much benefit arises for the inhabitants.

# Of Diodorus Siculus

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a sailing ship struggling in a turbulent sea. Large, stylized waves curl around the vessel. To the right, a shore is visible with a small building or chapel. In the foreground of the water, serpentine sea monsters are shown among the waves.</image-desc>

...that the sea fills the ship with sand, and it is immediately thrown up with the sand like a whale. Then they cry out—though in vain—for help; yet they still have a hope that they might be rescued, for it often happens that the sea, in its ebbing and flowing, carries the ship back out to the high sea, as if some God had delivered them from such great danger. 

But if help does not come, the strong throw the weak into the sea so that their food might last longer. Yet in the end, they must perish much more miserably than those who were cast out; they surrender their spirit to Nature, from whom they received it, in an instant <note>original: "in eim hui"</note>, while those remaining prolong their lives in great anguish, merely drawing out their death, and after they have already suffered much, they too must eventually die. The ships are then covered over with sand and remain as their graves for a long time; and though the mast is high, it cannot easily be seen from a distance, so that no one can even feel pity for those who have died. But if the King becomes aware of such a tragedy, he commands that markers be set up to warn those sailing past. 

There is an old legend that those who live not far from the fish-eaters <note>The Ichthyophagi, or "Fish-Eaters," were ancient coastal peoples of the Red Sea</note>, in that same bend across from them, once saw a beautiful, green, dry land there and felt no more water; but a short time later, the sea returned through storms and surging tides and turned these waters into a swamp. Now, we have described this voyage from Ptolemaida <note>Ptolemais Theron, an ancient port on the Red Sea</note> to Mount Taurus in the book where we spoke of the elephant hunts of Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus established these ports to capture African elephants for use in war</note>. 

From Mount Taurus, there is a shore facing the east where, during the dog days <note>The hottest days of summer, typically July and August</note>, the shadow falls toward the south until the second hour—a thing which does not happen at all in our lands. Many rivers flow in this region from the mountains (which are called Psebas); it also has exceedingly large valleys that bear cinnamon <term>Zimat: Cinnamon</term>, sweet flag <term>Calmus: An aromatic marsh plant used in perfumes</term>, cardamom <term>Carodomomlin: Cardamom</term>, and very large palm trees, followed by various fruits that are bitter and unknown to us. 

In the middle of the country are many elephants, wild oxen, lions, and other beasts. One cannot easily sail there because of the many islands, which bear no cultivated fruit. Strange birds and eggs are found there which are wonderful to behold. The sea there is very deep, containing exceedingly large whales <note>original: "waldfisch"</note> which are harmless to humans unless one accidentally falls into their fins. They cannot swim after ships because the sun blinds them. The furthest land of the Troglodytes <note>The Troglodytae, or "Cave-dwellers," a group of people traditionally located by ancient geographers along the Red Sea coast</note> is enclosed by the mountains called Pseuaras.

# Of the land of Phoenicia.

## Chapter vi.

The other mountain range, which lies opposite Arabia, is called Neptunum, named after the altar that Aristo, the navigator, erected to Neptune <note>original: "Neptuno"</note> when he was sent by Ptolemy to explore Arabia along the Ocean. This same region, as it stretches out in length, is widely renowned for its usefulness; it is named Phoenicia after the fruit of the palm trees <note>The name "Phoenicia" here is derived from the Greek "phoinix," meaning date palm</note>, which bear abundant and sweet fruit. The surrounding area has little flowing or spring water, and where it lies toward the south, it is exceedingly hot. Therefore, the barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers generally to non-Greek or non-Roman local tribes</note> have not without reason consecrated and attributed this land—situated as it is between the deserts and gifted with all kinds of fruit—to the gods. For the many springs within it, and the little brooks that are no warmer than cold snow-water, make the earth green and pleasant to behold. There is also an ancient temple there built of hard

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration of a monumental octagonal temple built of stone blocks. It features three tiers: a wide base with arched niches, a narrower middle section with smaller arched openings, and a domed cupola on top. The architecture suggests a classical or near-eastern antiquity style.</image-desc>

stone, constructed long ago, and inscribed with letters that no one can read. Within this temple, there is always a woman and a man who perform the service to the idols throughout their lives; they are considered blessed for dwelling in that same place. At night, they sleep in the trees, fearing the wild beasts. Near the promontory where the sea runs into Phoenicia, there is an island called the Island of Wild Beasts, for the reason that so many animals live there; one must marvel at how many are able to live together there. Opposite and nearly touching this island is a promontory of Arabian Palestine called Petra, to which the Gerrhaeans and Minaeans bring frankincense and other noble scents from Upper Arabia. Other regions are inhabited by the Maranaei <note>OCR reads "Mataneis"</note>, who are bordered by the Garindaeans, who possessed this land in the manner described below. In Phoenicia, of which we first wrote, a festival was held in ancient times every five years, to which the inhabitants traveled with fat camels to perform the sacrifice which they call a <term>pleasing sacrifice</term> <note>original: "ἐναυθύμῳ" (enauthymo), likely referring to a sacrifice "in the mind" or "with good spirit"</note> in that same temple to honor the gods. When they returned home, they carried water with them, which was prepared to be good for all illnesses. Once, the Maranaei traveled to Phoenicia to hold their sacrifice and fetch water; during this time, the Garindaeans banded together and slaughtered those who had remained home in the land of the Maranaei. Afterward, they lay in wait and killed those who were returning home, so that not one survived. They then occupied the deserted land, dividing the livestock and the delights of the pastures and meadows. This land has few entrances, yet it is divided everywhere by mountains, from which—beyond the pleasure it provides—much benefit arises for the inhabitants.

# Of the Nabataeans.
### Chapter vii.

And from there, as one sails, one arrives in the Elanite region <note>The Gulf of Aqaba, named after the town of Elath</note>, where there are many villages of the Arabs who are called Nabataeans. They occupy a great part of the coast and also reach far into the interior; they dwell there in great numbers and are rich in livestock. In former times, these people led an honorable and upright life, being content with what their livestock provided them. However, later on, after they began to rob the Alexandrian merchants (much like the pirates of the Pontic region <note>The Black Sea area, notorious in antiquity for piracy</note>), they were attacked by a fleet of triremes <note>large warships with three banks of oars</note> and were promptly brought to an end. Following this is a fertile, well-watered land which, because of its many springs, produces "Median grass" <term>Alfalfa or Lucerne; a nutrient-rich forage plant</term> and tall wild-clover <note>original: "Mörkleins manns hoh," likely referring to the great height of the local flora</note>. There, because of the richness of the land, are found countless sheep, wild camels, stags, roe deer, and other such game that graze there.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a four-legged animal, possibly a bear or a hyena-like creature, depicted with a thick mane or ruff of fur around its neck. It stands in a rocky outdoor landscape near several leafy shrubs or small trees.</image-desc>

Because of the abundance of prey, lions also come in great numbers from the deserts, as well as tigers <note>In historical texts, "tigers" often referred to leopards or panthers</note> and wolves. Because of this, the shepherds must constantly fight to protect their herds; the fertility of the land brings its inhabitants into such danger. The reason for this is that when Nature gives humans a little good, she often mixes much evil into it. Along this plain lies an inlet of the sea which is about twelve and a half miles wide, wonderfully enclosed by nature with many large cliffs that create crooked and confusing exits. At the mouth of it lies a large, long rock that hinders entry or exit; ships can only pass over it when the tide comes in, or otherwise when they are driven over it by the wind during a storm. The inhabitants of the surrounding area are called Banizomene <note>Likely the Banu Zamman tribe</note> and they support themselves by hunting. Among them is a very highly esteemed temple, which the Arabs hold as sacred and magnificent beyond measure. Three islands lie not far from there which have many harbors; the first is uninhabited and contains many ancient walls and foundations,

Behind the islands, about twenty-five miles away, is the border of the sea, full of rough cliffs; the sea cannot be navigated there, for it has no landing place nor any spot where one may anchor, and all ships caught in a storm there must go to the bottom. A high mountain hangs over the sea, with rough and many hollows at the base, into which the waves of the stormy sea strike, making a roar as if it were thundering. Some waves strike the cliffs and run up them, producing a wondrous foam; some fall into the deep hollows with a great roar and tumult, so that sailors who come somewhat near perish from fright. These shores are inhabited by the Arabs called Thamudeni <note>original: "Thamüdenos"; an ancient Arabian civilization</note>. From there, there is another gulf of the sea with many islands that look just like the islands of the Echinades <note>original: "Echinasiæ"; a group of islands off the coast of Greece</note>. By the shores are great banks of black sand that spread out far. After that is a desert land with the very best harbors ever mentioned in writings, called Carmutha; for its harbor, situated under a rock facing the west wind, is not only pleasant to look upon, but also useful beyond others. Its entrance is two yokes wide <note>original: "Juchart"; a measurement of area, used here to describe the width of the channel</note>, large enough for two ships to stand within; it is quite still, for a mountain lies around it with a circumference of about two and a half miles. Additionally, a large stream flows into it, and in the middle is an island full of springs and well-suited for gardens. One compares it to the Carthaginian gulf which they call the Cothon <note>original: "Cothonum"; the famous circular inner harbor of ancient Carthage</note>, of whose usefulness we shall speak in another place. This landing place has many fish, which come from the sea into the sweet stream of the water because they love the food found in the fresh water. Those who sail around there see five mountains that stand well apart from each other and are shaped like the signal pillars <note>likely referring to Egyptian obelisks</note> of Egypt. Then one comes again into a gulf that is completely round and surrounded by promontories, in the middle of which stands a mountain like a long table, upon which three temples of magnificent construction are built. These are dedicated to the unknown gods of the Greeks, and much is sacrificed there daily by the inhabitants. The shore is rich in water, full of sweet little brooks, and there is a mountain with many kinds of trees called Gabinus. The Debae <note>original: "Debare"</note>, a people of the Arabs so named, live round about there. They use their camels for all their business; they fight upon them, carry all their burdens with them, drink their milk, eat their meat, and ride them to and fro. In the middle of this land there is a stream that carries gold in its sand, but they cannot extract any of it; they allow foreigners—though not everyone—to carry the sand away. Only those from Boeotia and the Peloponnese <note>regions of Greece</note> may carry such sand away; they permit this to them because of Hercules, for they say they have heard from their ancestors that Hercules showed them great kindness, and therefore they wish to repay that same kindness by allowing this removal of the gold. Not far from them live Arabs called the Alilaei <note>original: "Abileos"</note> and Gasandi <note>original: "Gasandos"</note>; the land is not so very hot as the surrounding areas, but has a gentle air, and thick, moist clouds that rain often, moistening the land at the usual times and making the summer fruitful. It is by nature a fertile soil, but the negligent people do not cultivate it. They dig gold without any cost; they do not need to smelt it, for it is pure in itself. Therefore they call it "unfired" <note>original: "Vngfeüret"; referring to native gold found in nuggets that does not require refining by fire</note> gold...

## Concerning the Sabeans
### Chapter 7

After these same people, one comes to the Carbi, and then to the Sabeans <note>The Sabaeans, an ancient South Arabian people of modern-day Yemen, famous for the Biblical Queen of Sheba</note>, whose land is the most populous in all of Arabia, called "Happy Arabia" <note>original: "die sälig Arabien"; historically known in Latin as *Arabia Felix*</note>. Their fruits are the most precious among us, and they also possess much livestock. Many noble, sweet-smelling herbs, roots, and trees grow here and there across the land, so that they surpass all other countries in this regard. For where they meet the sea, there grows Balsam and Cassia <note>An aromatic bark similar to cinnamon</note>; the latter, while fresh, greatly delights the eyes, though it dims the sight when it is old. In the middle of the country, there are pleasant forests containing trees of frankincense and myrrh, calamus <note>A sweet-smelling reed</note>, palms, and cinnamon, as well as other fragrant shoots. It is impossible to recount all the noble spices this region bears, so abundantly has Nature planted such fragrant growth there. It is truly a divine thing, impossible to describe, what a noble scent wafts from this land; for even when one is still far off at sea, this lovely aroma meets those who are sailing. When the sun shines, the winds carry this noble fragrance into all the surrounding lands; for this spice does not dissipate like it does in other places, nor does it grow stale, but has a much stronger and ever-fresh scent that overwhelms all one's strength. And this scent reaches far out into the sea, refreshing the sailors and keeping them healthy. Furthermore, this fragrance does not come from crushed spices or prepared, costly ointments, but is such a sweet-smelling air that wafts naturally from this land and its trees, so that those who smell it must say it is the Ambrosia <note>The food or fragrance of the Greek gods</note> of the gods of which the poets write; and they believe they could not rightly call it anything else.

Yet, Nature has not left such a magnificent gift unbittered, but has mixed much evil into it—as if she did so out of envy—to remind us that eternal prosperity in worldly things leads to the contempt of God. For in these fragrant forests there dwell many kinds of harmful snakes and vermin, red in color and a span long <note>About 9 inches</note>, which spring at people and give them a deadly bite, from which they later become ill and eventually die. The inhabitants also have a peculiar sickness; they die slowly over a long time, and when they see that their nature is completely exhausted, wasted away, and becoming so weak that they can hardly be revived, they burn pitch and goat hair. They smoke themselves with this so that the foul stench may neutralize the overwhelming power of the sweet scent. For no matter how good a thing may be, it brings neither benefit nor pleasure unless it is used in moderation; whoever takes too much of it without a mediator will suffer harm.

The capital city of this people is called Saba <note>The ancient city of Marib in modern Yemen</note>, situated upon a mountain. Their kings inherit the kingdom, wherein they experience both good and bad days. They consider themselves blessed because they rule over others and never have to give an account of their conduct; however, their great sorrow is that they may never leave the royal palace. If they appear publicly outside the royal court, they are stoned by the people, and this is done by the command of their gods. This people is not only more prosperous than all those...

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'N' featuring floral scrollwork and a bird (possibly a swan or goose) nestled within the letter's structure.</image-desc>After these same people, one comes to the Carbi, and then to the Sabeans, who are the most populous nation in all of Arabia, inhabiting what is called Arabia Felix <note>Latin: "Happy" or "Blessed" Arabia, so named by the ancients for its fertility and wealth compared to the surrounding desert</note>. In the middle of the country, there are pleasant forests containing frankincense and myrrh trees, calamus, palms, and cinnamon, as well as other fragrant shoots. This scent carries far out into the sea, refreshing the sailors and keeping them healthy. Yet nature has not left them such a magnificent gift without bitterness, but has mixed much evil into it, as if she did so out of envy—truly wishing only to warn us that eternal prosperity in temporal things brings a contempt for God. If they are seen coming out of the royal court in public, they are stoned by the people, and this is done at the command of their gods. All cornices and doors are made with golden or silver frames, inlaid and decorated with precious stones; for here silver shines, there one sees gold, and there precious stones stand out. Some are covered with ivory or other noble materials that men value highly. 

Now, they have enjoyed this prosperity for many ages, for among them, there was no greed or covetousness at all—vices which have brought so many of us into great distress. In their region, the sea is white <note>The "White Sea" likely refers to the "Erythraean Sea" or parts of the Indian Ocean; ancient writers often puzzled over the milky appearance of the water caused by coral reefs or bioluminescence</note>; and because this is quite contrary to nature, it has raised many questions throughout the world as to how it occurs. Not far from there lie many rich islands whose cities have no walls. The camels <note>original: "kāmbel". This is likely a traveler's myth or a misidentification of the oryx or another horned desert animal, as camels do not have horns.</note> all have white horns. And merchants of all kinds from all lands come out of necessity to Potana <note>The text ends at "Pota", but the vocabulary list confirms the full name as "Potana", likely an ancient trade port</note>...

Now we wish to speak of what happens in their heavens, which is well worth describing, starting with the Seven Stars <note>The Pleiades or perhaps the Big Dipper</note> or the Scales <note>likely referring to Libra</note> which make the sailors quite confused. Likewise, the sun has no dawn-glow or radiance, but instead begins to shine suddenly in the middle of the dark night. Therefore, one cannot say that there is daylight there before the sun arrives; they say it rises out of the sea <note>original: 'mhőr'</note> like glowing coals and casts its rays from afar. It is not round like it is with us, but oblong like a pillar, appearing larger at the top. It has no radiance or rays before the first hour, but is seen without shine, like a fire in the darkness. By the second hour, it becomes like a targe <note>a small, round shield</note> and gives off an exceedingly hot light, and in the evening when it wishes to go down, the opposite occurs; it is just as if a ball were ignited with new rays, which lasts for two hours, or as Agatharchides of Cnidus <note>a Greek historian and geographer</note> writes, three hours. At this time, the inhabitants have their pleasure, for the heat diminishes, and the West and Southeast winds blow as they do elsewhere; however, the South winds are unknown in Ethiopia and have no power. Among the Arabians and the Troglodytes <note>term: 'Troglodytes', a Greek name for 'cave-dwellers'</note>, these winds are so hot that they burn all the herbs and weaken those who do not flee into the shade. Therefore, the North wind is rightly considered the most noble, for it is cool in all places.

### Concerning the Peoples of Libya. Chapter 11.

Now we will turn to the Libyans who border Egypt and travel through their nearest lands. Four kinds of people inhabit Libya around Syene <note>modern Aswan</note>, bordering the Syrtes <note>two large gulfs on the coast of Libya</note> and other inland areas. Those toward the South wind are called Nasomones; toward the West are the Anochite. Between Egypt and Cyrene on the shores of the sea dwell the Marmarides. The fourth is a populous land, and the people are called Mace. Those who dwell by the Syrtes are the only ones who have a well-cultivated, fruitful land, and they tend to livestock, by which they nourish themselves very diligently. These two regions are ruled by kings; they lead a life that is not entirely wild and are not altogether unfriendly. The third group has no king, nor any laws...

## The Fourth Book.

...nourish themselves on the plunder which they capture in the desert without horses, and as soon as they have gained some booty, they trot back home. All the Libyans together have no houses; they dwell in the forests and eat nothing domesticated. They live like wild beasts off the hunt and cover themselves with goat skins, knowing no other clothing.

The grandees <note>original: 'grossen Hansen', a colloquial German term for powerful men or chieftains</note> have no city, but rather towers near the waters, in which they keep what they wish to store for nourishment. They swear in the common people every year to maintain obedience to the princes. Those who are obedient are treated as good friends; the rebellious are treated as murderers and persecuted. Their weaponry is suited to the land and their way of life. The land is entirely flat; they carry no swords or other weapons in war, only three small spears and several stones in a leather pouch. They fight with these; when they are attacked, they flee, seeking only to wound the enemy, and are well-practiced in running and accurate stone-throwing. To foreigners they are neither loyal nor friendly, keeping no faith with them. The region that borders Cyrene <note>An ancient Greek and later Roman city in present-day Libya</note> is flat, full of crops, wine, fruit, and rich in fish; it also has large, magnificent waters that serve the inhabitants well.

But the area lying toward the North, enclosed by the desert, is infertile, has no water, and looks just like the sea. The desert bordering it is vast, desolate, and dangerous to travel through. One finds no birds there, and besides gazelles <note>original: 'räch', likely referring to roe deer or desert gazelles</note> and oxen, no four-footed animals. In the midst are great heaps of sand, and the less fruit there is, the more harmful vermin are found, especially the horned snakes, which are called <term>Cerastos</term> <note>original: 'Cerastos'; referring to the Cerastes or horned viper</note>, whose bites are deadly. They are also sand-colored so that one cannot see them easily, and one thinks there is nothing but sand before him; therefore, one often steps on them and must die from it. They say that these snakes once crawled in great numbers into Egypt and laid waste to entire lands, for the people fled from them. On this shore and around the <term>Syrten</term> <note>original: 'Syrten'; referring to the Syrtis, two large gulfs on the coast of Libya known for dangerous sandbanks and shallows</note>, a most wonderful occurrence takes place. For sometimes, when it is windless and no air moves, various shapes of animals appear in the sky, some still and quiet, some moving, some fleeing, and others rushing after people. They are all so large and monstrous that they terrify those unaccustomed to such things and instill fear in them. Wherever one of these forms reaches a person, a cold breeze blows upon them; at this, the foreigners are terrified, but the inhabitants, being well-used to it, pay it no mind. And although it is a wonderful thing, almost unbelievable, the investigators of Nature <note>natural philosophers or early scientists</note> have undertaken to explain the causes and say: That in these lands almost no wind blows; if a wind does blow, it is very weak and quiet. Thus the air is still and motionless because there are no mountains, no valleys, no caves, nor large waters there; indeed, the whole region is infertile and releases no vapor from which wind could arise. Therefore, it happens that in this thick, stagnant air—just as with us in the clouds during summertime—many kinds of animals are seen, to which the air (moved by small, thin breezes) gives shape. Then, when the air is moved somewhat, they fall to the earth in the same form they had in the air, and when they fall upon someone, they cling to them.

But that one should move more than another is not to be attributed to the will or pleasure of the signs, for in a thing that has no life, there is...

# Of the Amazons and Gorgons. Chapter XV.

It remains for us to speak of the Amazons, who in ancient times, as some write, dwelt in Libya. Many argue that they were only those who ruled by the river Thermodon <note>original: "Thermodoonta"; a river in modern-day Turkey traditionally associated with the Amazons</note> and in Pontus. But they are mistaken, for the Libyan Amazons existed many years before those, of whom we read many things worthy of memory. Although we are not unaware that some will give no credit to this our writer. Now, that same people was destroyed long before the Trojan War, whereas those who lived by the Thermodon river only ruled long afterward. Thus, it is quite believable that the great deeds, which faded due to antiquity, obscured the previous Amazons, and people attributed such things to the newer ones because of their novelty—especially among those who were inexperienced at that time. Since, however, we read of these previous deeds in many poets and historians, we will also strive to bring their actions to light and take our beginning from Dionysius <note>Dionysius Scytobrachion, an ancient mythographer used as a source by Diodorus</note>, who described the stories of the seafarers, as well as of Bacchus and other heroes. If we wish to take an example from our own women, one sees that these women were quite brave and powerful. They occupied a land at the furthest edge of the earth toward the sunset <note>The West</note> and did not live like our women; for they have the custom that during the time of their maidenhood—to keep themselves pure—they employ themselves in military exercises until they are of age and have fulfilled the years they must wage war.
