### Of the Atlanteans and the Origin of the Gods from Coelus. Chapter 16.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'D' containing a landscape scene with figures.</image-desc>The Atlanteans, as has been heard, dwell near the Ocean in a fertile land; they are god-fearing and friendly toward foreigners, so that they have been praised above other peoples for these qualities. 
The race of the gods is said to have come from them, and the most distinguished poet of the Greeks <note>likely referring to Homer</note> bears witness to this. He calls Oceanus <note>original: "Oceanum"</note> a father of the gods, and Juno <note>original: "Junonem"</note> he calls Tethys <note>original: "Thetin"</note>, the mother of them all. They claim that Coelus <note>The Roman name for Uranus, the personification of the Sky</note> first reigned over them; and as they wandered here and there in the land, he urged them to form assemblies and build cities, and he moved and drew them from this wild, coarse way of life into a moral, civilized life. Likewise, he accustomed them to sow domestic fruits and other things that serve common human life well. He also held the greatest part of the world, especially the lands lying toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang," literally "the setting of the sun"</note> and the North <note>original: "Mitnacht," literally "midnight"</note>. Furthermore, he devoted himself to the stars and diligently investigated their courses, foretelling many future things to the people. The year, which was previously confused and which no one could account for, he described according to the course of the sun and the months according to the course of the moon, and he divided all the seasons of the year. From this, many who had not investigated the infinite course of the heavens marveled at his prophesying and believed he must be a partaker of a divine nature. Therefore, after his death, both for his proven good deeds and for his skill in the course of the heavens, he was honored and worshipped as a god. His name was given to him because he knew the rising and setting of all the stars so well; and because of the good deeds he showed his subjects, he was called an eternal one and a King of Kings. This Coelus fathered forty-five sons by many wives, seventeen of whom Titea bore him; to each he gave his own name, but he gave the mother's surname to them all <note>These children are the Titans</note>. Titea was a very wise woman who desired to help all people; therefore, after her death, she was regarded as a goddess and named Terra <note>The Roman name for Gaia, the personification of the Earth</note>. Coelus also fathered several daughters, of whom one was called Regina <note>A name meaning "Queen," often identified as Basileia</note> and the other Rhea, whom they call Pandora; they were the eldest and more famous than the others.

# Of the Great Mother’s Children

->The Sun and the Moon. <note>original: "Sol vnd Luna."</note><-

Basileia <note>Her name literally means "Queen" or "Royalty" in Greek</note>, who preceded Pandora in age, was furthermore excellent in wisdom and virtues. For the sake of her mother, she raised all her brothers, and for this reason, she was called the "Great Mother." When her father ascended to the gods after his death, she was accepted into the kingdom by the choice of her brothers while still a maiden, for she did not yet have a husband. Later, desiring to leave behind heirs who should rule, she took her brother Hyperion as a husband and bore two children with him, one of whom she named Sol <note>The Sun</note> and the other Luna <note>The Moon</note>. As many people marveled at these beautiful children and praised them for their intelligence, the brothers feared the kingdom would be snatched from them and pass to the lineage of Hyperion. They became enemies to the children and devised an evil deed: they murdered Hyperion and drowned the child Sol in the river Eridanus <note>A mythical river often identified by ancient writers with the Po River in Italy</note>. Luna loved her brother so much that she did not wish to live without him; she jumped from the roof and fell to her death. When this tragedy came to light, the mother searched for her son's body by the water. There she fell asleep, and in her sleep, it appeared to her that her son came to her and comforted her, adding a request that she should no longer mourn for her children, for the murderers would eventually suffer enough for their crime. He told her that he and his sister had, through the providence of God, attained immortality; for just as he had previously been called the "holy fire," he would hereafter be called the "Sun" by men, and his sister, who was previously named Mena <note>A Greek name for the moon</note>, would receive the name of the "Moon." 

When she awoke from her sleep and told many people of her sorrow and her dream, she offered divine sacrifices to her children. She lived immeasurably long, until at last she lost her mind. Beating the cymbals and small drums that had belonged to her little daughter, she ran about the land with great wailing and disheveled hair, so that everyone who saw her felt great pity. But when the people ran to her to quiet her, and she was already being held in the arms of some, a great rain arose, and with a clap of thunder, the queen vanished, at which the people marveled greatly. They gave the children the names of the Sun and the Moon and established the mother as a goddess, with an altar erected before which they stood. They beat the drums and cymbals, doing just as she had done, and offered her divine honor.

## Nature of the Goddess Cybele.

Some say this goddess's origin comes from Phrygia <note>An ancient kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey</note>. They say that Meones was a king in Libya and Phrygia and had Dyndimene as his wife. They bore a daughter together, but because they did not wish to raise her, they had her carried to a mountain called Cybelus to be food for wild beasts. But by the providence of God, leopards <note>original: "Pard"</note> and other wild beasts suckled her until a woman who tended cattle became aware of it. This woman marveled at the sight, took the child, and named her Cybele after the mountain. As she grew older, her beauty and reason increased, and she became very ingenious; for she is the one who invented the harmony of many pipes played together, as well as cymbals and small drums suitable for amusement and dance. ## Sol and Luna.

Basileia, who preceded Pandora in age, and was also excellent in reason and virtue, raised all her brothers out of love for her mother; for this reason, she was called the Great Mother <note>original: "Großmůter," meaning Grandmother or Great Mother, a title for the goddess Cybele</note>. And when her father, after his death, had departed to the gods, she was accepted into the kingdom by the election of her brothers while she was still a maiden, for she did not yet have a husband. Since she then desired to leave heirs behind her to rule, she took her brother Hyperion as a husband and bore him two children, one of whom she named Sol <note>the Sun</note> and the other Luna <note>the Moon</note>. As many people marveled at these beautiful children and praised them for their cleverness, the brothers <note>the Titans</note> feared that the kingdom would be snatched from them and pass to the lineage of Hyperion. They became enemies to the children and devised a wicked deed: they murdered Hyperion and drowned the child Sol in the river Eridanus <note>The river Po in Italy</note>. Luna loved her brother so dearly that she did not wish to live without him; she leaped from the roof and fell to her death. When this became known, the mother searched for her son’s body by the water; there she fell asleep. In her sleep, it seemed to her that her son came to her and comforted her, with an attached plea that she should no longer mourn for her children, for the murderers would yet suffer enough for it. He and his sister, however, had attained immortality through the providence of God. For as he was previously called the "holy fire," so would he hereafter be called the "Sun" by mankind, and his sister, who was previously named Mena, would receive the name of the "Moon." When she awoke from sleep and told many people of her grief and her dream, she offered divine sacrifices to her children and lived beyond measure until at last she lost her mind. She beat the cymbals and small drums of her little daughter and, with a great howling and disheveled hair, ran about the land so that everyone who saw her took pity on her. But when all the world ran to her to quiet her, and she was already held in the arms of some, a great rain arose, and in a clap of thunder, the queen vanished, at which the people marveled greatly. They gave the names of the Sun and the Moon to the children and established the mother as a goddess with an erected sacrificial altar before which they stood, beating the drums and cymbals, doing as she had done, and rendering her divine honor.

## Nature of the Goddess Cybele.

Some say this goddess’s origin comes from Phrygia; for they say Menoes was a king in Libya and Phrygia, and had as a wife Dindymene. They bore a daughter together, but for some reason, they did not wish to raise her, but instead had her carried to a mountain called Cybele to be food for wild beasts. But by the arrangement of God, leopards <note>original: "Pard"</note> and other wild animals suckled her until a woman who tended the livestock became aware of it. This woman marveled at the deed, took the child, and named her Cybele after the mountain. With age, beauty and reason increased in her, and she became very clever; for she is the one who invented the harmony of many flutes together, as well as cymbals and small drums suitable for jesting and dancing. Likewise, she was the first to show the medicine for young children and livestock. Because she...

## Of Saturn and the Dionysians.
### Chapter 17.

After the death of Hyperion, they say that the children of **Coelus** <note>Uranus or Sky</note> divided the kingdom among themselves. The two most prominent among them were named **Atlas** and **Saturn**. To Atlas, in the division, were given the lands situated on the shores of the Ocean; his subjects, as well as the highest mountain located by the Ocean, were named after him. They say he was a man highly experienced in the stars and was the first among men who dared to speak of the sphere of the heavens. Because he demonstrated this knowledge, he gave rise to the fable <note>original: "gedicht," meaning a poetic myth or story</note> which says he carries the heavens on his shoulders.

## Of King Hesperus.

He is said to have fathered many children, and among them all, one who attained great fame for his piety, his gentleness toward his subjects, and his justice, was named **Hesperus**. Once, when he had climbed to the peaks and summit of Mount Atlas to observe the stars, the winds suddenly swept him away so that he was never seen again. Because of this disappearance, his people bore great sorrow and, after his death, attributed to him the honor of an immortal hero; for the sake of his virtue, they gave his name to the **Evening Star**.

## Of the Daughters of Atlas.

Atlas also fathered seven daughters, to all of whom their father's name was given, so that they were called **Atlantides** <note>commonly known in Greek mythology as the Pleiades</note>, although each had her own name: such as **Maia**, **Electra**, **Taygete**, **Asterope**, **Merope**, **Alcyone**, and **Celaeno**. These, they say, were courted both by heroes and by the gods, and bore children who, for their virtue, were regarded as gods, heroes, and princes of the human race. For Maia conceived **Mercury** <note>Hermes</note> by **Jove** <note>Zeus/Jupiter</note>, who invented various arts; likewise, each of her sisters bore children who became prominent and famous men, raised whole nations, and built cities which were named after them.

## Of Saturn and Jupiter.

**Saturn**, however, the brother of Atlas, was a very cruel and unkind tyrant, entirely consumed by greed. He took his sister **Tithea** <note>likely referring to Titea or Theia, a Titaness</note> in marriage. From her was born **Jupiter**, who was later called **Olympus**. For there was also another Jupiter, a brother of **Coelus** <note>Sky/Uranus</note>, who ruled on the island of **Crete**; however, he was nowhere near as famous as this younger one. The reason being that the younger Jupiter brought the whole world under his authority, while the other ruled only a single island and fathered ten sons who were called the **Curetes** <note>The Curetes were legendary protectors of the infant Jupiter</note>. He named the island after his wife, **Idea**, and was also buried there after his death, just as the Cretans still show his grave to this day, of which we shall speak later.

Saturn was powerful in **Sicily**, **Libya**, and **Italy**, primarily in the lands situated toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang," the setting sun</note>. That was his finest kingdom; but in all places, he built strong castles and fortified cities so that he might rule as he pleased for a long time. For this reason, even now in Sicily and other western regions, the high castles are called **Saturnia**. 

**Jupiter**, his son, led a much different life than his father; he was gracious and friendly toward everyone, for which reason he was called "Father" by the people. Thus, partly through his father’s own fate and partly through the uprising of the common people—who rebelled against Saturn because they hated him—Jupiter was elevated to be King. But when he sought to restrain his father’s excesses too tightly, the father allied himself with the **Titans**, his brothers. Thinking he would thus be too strong for his son, Saturn attacked him but was defeated in battle, though through the son the Kingdom was ultimately preserved. 

Afterward, Jupiter traveled through the whole world and did much good for mankind. Because of his physical strength and skill, he soon brought the world under his rule. He applied all diligence to punish the willful and reckless wicked rogues, to uplift and reward the pious, and to promote the common good of all people. For this reason, after his death, he obtained the name **Jovis** <note>Jupiter/Jove; the text suggests an etymological link to "helping" or "welfare"</note>, because he had been the cause of the good conduct and welfare of humanity. By those to whom he had shown kindness, he was regarded as a god; they freely acknowledged him as a God and Lord, and as an eternal ruler of the entire world.

to signify wine through his name; 
one represents the divine nature 
and the other the human nature. 
They also called one more noble 
than the other, because the vine 
increases when planted in the 
earth, and later brings forth wine-grapes. In this way, wine would be born twice: first from the earth, through the growth of the vines, and then through the pressing of the grapes. Some even attribute a third birth to him, saying he came from **Jupiter** and **Ceres** <note>Jupiter represents the sky/rain, and Ceres the earth/grain</note>, and was torn apart and boiled by men, whereupon Ceres set his limbs back together and thus made him a youth again. All of this is applied to the nature of wine.

He is called the son of Jupiter and Ceres because the wine-vine grows from the earth and rain, bringing forth grapes from which wine is pressed. That he was "torn apart" by men is an allegory meaning that the vine-dressers harvest the grapes and then boil them so that the wine remains more potent and sweet. And because Ceres is regarded as the Earth, the saying that she made him alive again and brought his limbs together signifies that the earth, at a certain time in the autumn, gives the vine its fruit once more. That Ceres was called "Mother Earth" is attested by the ancient writers and poets, as well as **Orpheus** <note>the legendary musician and prophet</note>, who mentions it in the sacred rites <note>original: "kirchengeprāng," referring to the Dionysian or Orphic Mysteries</note>, of which those who do not understand such rites may not easily speak. 

Similarly, when some say he was born of **Semele** and that the earth was first called **Chion**, they also apply this to nature. For Semele signifies the reverence <note>original: "Erbar-keit"</note> with which the God is honored, while Chion signifies the sacrifices offered to him. They say he was born twice from Jupiter because in the time of **Deucalion**’s flood <note>the Great Flood in Greek mythology</note>, the vine, along with other trees, perished, but afterwards rose up again. Therefore, they say he was born again from the "thigh" of Jupiter. These fables are written by those who believe Dionysus invented wine. Likewise, those who say this God was a physical man write that he was the first to plant the vine and invent its use. Whether there was more than one Dionysus is uncertain; for some say there was only one who revealed wine and other fruitful trees to the people, traveled the whole world, and established sacred rites, idol worship, and festivals with masked plays <note>original: "fassnaches pil," literally Shrove Tuesday or Carnival plays</note>. Others describe three of them, who lived one after another...

...assigned specific deeds to each. The first is said to have been an **Indian**, and because the earth produced grapevines of its own accord from its richness, he taught his countrymen how to use them, and to plant figs and other fruit-bearing trees and to eat from them. And because it is the custom of the **Indians** never to shave their beards during their lives, he was called **Dionysus the Bearded**. He traveled through the world with a great military host, showing foreigners how they should plant vines and tread out the grapes; for this reason, he is called **Leneus** <note>From the Greek *lenos*, meaning a wine-press</note>. Also, because he taught the people many other things that benefited them, he received divine honors among them after his death. They say that in India, the place where **Dionysus** was born and the cities named after him are still shown to this day. There are many other things that would be too long to recount here which bear witness to this **Dionysus** having been in India.

The second **Dionysus**, they claim, was born to **Jupiter** and **Proserpina** (though some write he was born to **Ceres** <note>Ceres is the goddess of agriculture; this version emphasizes the god's connection to the earth's fertility</note>). They say he was the first to harness oxen to the plow, whereas previously the earth was turned over by human labor alone.

And wherever they set up an image of him, they placed horns upon it as a coat of arms <note>original: "wappen"</note>, to indicate that this **Dionysus**—unlike the previous one—pursued a different way of life and invented much for agriculture.

The third **Dionysus** they call a son of **Jupiter** and **Semele**, the daughter of **Cadmus**, and they say he was born in **Boeotia** at **Thebes**. They tell such a poetic tale as this: **Jupiter** became fond of **Semele** and lay with her many times. **Juno** was envious and became angry; she transformed herself into the likeness of **Semele’s** maid, and to be revenged, she advised her to ask of **Jupiter** that he should lie with her in his full majesty, just as he slept with **Juno**. **Jupiter** consented to do this and came to her with thunder and lightning; at such an unaccustomed sight, she was so terrified that she died and gave birth to the child prematurely. **Jupiter** hid the child in his lap <note>The text says "schoß," but in classical mythology, Jupiter famously sewed the infant into his thigh</note> until it was time for the birth; then he brought it to light and took it to **Nysa**, located in **Arabia**. ## On the invention of certain arts that
### may be recorded in writing.

It is said that the first **Linus** discovered numbers and melody among the Greeks. **Cadmus** first brought the letters there from Phoenicia, put the Greek language into writing for the first time, and gave names to all things. Likewise, he gave a form to the letters as to how they should be written; and because they came from Phoenicia, they were all called **Phoenician**. But since the **Pelasgians** were the first to use them, they were called Pelasgian. Linus had many highly learned pupils in all the arts, especially in poetry, among whom three were the most prominent: **Hercules**, **Thamyris**, and **Orpheus**. When Hercules was supposed to learn the harp, but had no head for the art and was therefore beaten by Linus, he snatched the harp and struck his teacher dead with it. Thamyris had a proud mind <note>original: "glůrnigen kopff", implying a glaring or arrogant disposition</note>; he learned music quickly, and when he had become quite skillful in it, he is said to have claimed that he sang much more lovely than the **Muses** themselves. This moved the goddesses to anger, so that they took from him all the art of music along with the harp, as Homer also writes when he recounts what ships from Pylos and its associated cities Nestor led when departing against Troy. He speaks thus:

> Then they set out upon the journey
> Those of the Neleian lineage
> Who dwelt in Pylos and in Arene
> Whose fields are so well-tilled, and those of Thryon <note>A poetic translation of the "Catalogue of Ships" from Book 2 of the Iliad</note>

<image-desc>A large woodcut depicting a battle scene. In the foreground, numerous dead or wounded bodies lie on the ground. Behind them, soldiers on horseback with lances and banners are engaged in combat or moving across the field. The Titans lay defeated and fled to the places they had previously seized from Hammon <note>A Libyan deity often identified with the Greek Zeus or Roman Jupiter; in this history, he is depicted as a king and the father of Dionysus.</note>. Dionysus marched into the city of Nysa with the captives, acting as if he intended to put them all to death. When he had them all surrounded by soldiers in an open square, he spoke out sharply against the Titans' actions. However, he declared the captives free and gave them the choice: they could depart to wherever they found suitable, or, if they wished to join his campaign, they could remain with him as his own soldiers. At once, they cried out that they wished to remain his soldiers; because he had unexpectedly spared their lives, they honored him as a god. He then provided a good drink of wine to everyone and took an oath from them that they would remain loyal to him through grace and death.

As he set out from Nysa to wage war against Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Titan Cronus, here portrayed as the rival to Hammon and Dionysus.</note>, it is said that his governor Aristeus <note>Aristaeus, a culture hero associated with agriculture and bee-keeping, here serving as Dionysus’s lieutenant.</note> was the very first to offer a sacrifice to him as a god and show him divine honors. The most noble men of Nysa also provided aid and marched with him; these are called Sileni <note>Followers of Silenus, often depicted as elderly, drunken satyrs, though here presented as a noble lineage.</note> after their king, Silenus. (This Silenus had once ruled among them, but his lineage is unknown due to its great antiquity.) These men all wore a tail girded around their waists according to their custom, which they inherited from Silenus. 

Thus Dionysus set forth and passed through desolate and desert lands, which were full of harmful

There he found a wild beast of that same nature, called a Capes <note>Likely referring to a "Cebus" (an exotic animal mentioned by ancient writers) or a variation of the monster Campe killed by Dionysus in other versions of the myth.</note>, which also caused great harm to the inhabitants. He quickly dispatched it, for which he was highly honored and praised by the citizens. To ensure eternal fame for the killing of the beast, he had a great mound built and the deed recorded upon it, which remained standing for a long time thereafter. In this manner, he advanced further against the Titans, yet he marched with such restraint that he caused no harm to anyone, giving to everyone proof...

made it known that he had set out only to punish evil, so that everyone desired to do good. Through this reputation, he managed to make the Libyans recognize his virtue and noble spirit, so that they provided enough food for his army and even joined him as allies. When he drew closer to the city of Hammon <note>Also known as Ammonium, the site of the famous oracle of Amun in the Libyan desert.</note>, Saturn <note>The leader of the Titans and father of Jupiter.</note> gave him battle near the city wall, in which Saturn was defeated. During the night, Saturn set fire to the city, intending to burn the palace of Dionysus’s father, took his wife Rhea and several Rhaetians <note>original: "Rhät"; likely referring to Saturn's followers or a specific tribe.</note>, and fled secretly. However, they were all discovered and captured. Dionysus did not act toward Saturn and Rhea as they deserved for their crimes, but instead forgave them and comforted them; he honored them in place of his own parents for the rest of his life. In return, Rhea loved him like her own child as long as she lived. Saturn, however, was never truly well-disposed toward him, though he pretended to be. While in captivity, Saturn and Rhea gave birth to Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, whom Dionysus raised with great honor; later, through his boldness, this Jove brought the entire world under his rule. Before the battle, the Libyans had told Dionysus that at the time his father Hammon was driven out, a prophecy had been made: that he, Dionysus, his son, would reconquer the kingdom along with the whole world, and finally be worshipped as a god. Dionysus then impressed this image upon his descendants, so that they believed this god was horned. Now that

From his father <note>Through the oracle of Hammon.</note>, he received the answer that because of the good deeds he showed to mankind, he would become immortal.

### Concerning the Jupiter who was also named Olympus.

Following this answer, he became all the more joyful and marched into Egypt. He made Jove, the son of Rhea and Saturn, a king there. Since Jupiter was still a child, Dionysus gave him Olympus to be his guardian, teacher, and disciplinarian; thus, Jupiter was later also called Olympus. He showed the Egyptians how they should plant grapevines, make wine, and use other fruits. As he now came into great renown everywhere because of his power—so that no one dared to resist him, but instead everyone surrendered to him—they sacrificed to him and honored him as a god. He planted the lands with cultivated crops in all places so that the people would have nourishment, whereby he earned great praise from every man and was held as a god. Indeed, even though men sometimes do not think the best of the other gods, there is an eternal memory of Dionysus as their benefactor among them. For there is neither Greek nor Barbarian <note>In the classical sense, "Barbarian" refers to anyone who did not speak Greek, rather than a comment on their level of civilization.</note> who has not received some benefit and welfare from him. The reason is that even if a land was unsuitable for growing vines, he taught them to brew beer from barley <note>The text refers to "Bier auß gersten," highlighting that Dionysus was credited with the invention of beer in regions where wine could not be produced.</note>, which in truth has very little less sweetness than wine. They say that as he moved from India toward the sea, the Titans besieged and captured all the Hammonians on the island of Crete. Some claim that as the Titans pursued Hammon and besieged him in Crete, Jupiter <note>Often referred to as Jove/Zeus.</note> came from Egypt with Dionysus and Minerva, as well as others who are called gods, to Hammon's aid; they gave battle to the Titans, in which Dionysus killed all the Titans and held the victory.

Now when Hammon and Dionysus passed away and the Titans had been wiped out, Jupiter took the chief rule of the world, and no one dared offer him resistance. This is what the Libyans say of the first Dionysus, who was a son of Hammon and Amalthea. The second was a son of Jupiter and Io, the daughter of Inachus; he ruled in Egypt and established priestly rites. The third Dionysus was fathered by Jupiter through Semele among the Greeks, and he strove to match the glorious deeds of the others; for he also traversed the whole world with a military host, set up victory monuments everywhere, and pillars that gave witness to his campaign. Likewise, he planted many desolate places and led women with him into war, just as the first Dionysus led the Amazons. He applied great diligence to establishing temple ceremonies <note>original: "kirchen gepräng"; the author uses the 16th-century German word for church to describe ancient pagan temples.</note> and the worship of idols, to ordaining priests, and improving the old foundations. And since the deeds of the previous two Dionysuses were unknown, he let all such things be attributed to himself, and thus achieved great fame.

Furthermore, this did not happen to him alone, but also occurred to Hercules. The reason is that before him, there were also two others. They say the first was born in Egypt, conquered a great part of the world with the sword, and set up a pillar in Libya. The second was a Cretan, highly renowned for strength and skill, who established the Olympic Games. The last one, born just a little before the Trojan War to Jove and Alcmene, also traveled through almost the entire world at the command of Eurystheus; when he had overcome all danger, he set up a sign-pillar in Europe <note>This refers to the "Pillars of Hercules," usually associated with the Strait of Gibraltar.</note>. Thus, the last Hercules, who lived after those two, attained the deeds and fame of them all, as if there had been no more than one Hercules. That there were many Dionysuses may well be shown by the battle of the Titans, for in that same battle, Dionysus came to the aid of Jupiter. However, Semele is not so old that she could have lived at the time of the Titans; likewise, Cadmus, the son of Agenor <note>original: "Agenoris"</note>, cannot be as old as the Olympian gods.

# Diodorus the Sicilian / and most famous historian / of the beginning of the
### World / until its habitation / and the glorious reign of occurring events. Fifth book.

->Preface.<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'I' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and vine patterns.</image-desc>

It is no secret to us <note>The author, Diodorus, is using the "editorial we" common in classical and Renaissance writing.</note> that those who wish to describe ancient history must occasionally err. For vast antiquity makes history doubtful and tangled, and the description of time—which is not known to everyone—often robs the writer of his credibility, for one cannot always hit upon the exact time and number of years. Furthermore, one cannot discover the true origins and lineages of the heroes and gods, or of other famous people, with complete certainty. Added to this (which is the greatest burden of all) is that in the histories and poems of the ancients, the writers often disagree with one another. From this it follows that many of them have omitted the oldest tales <note>The original German uses "märlin," a diminutive of "Mär" (tale/myth), suggesting these ancient legends were viewed as somewhat legendary or "fable-like" by the translator's era.</note> and have devoted themselves only to more recent events. Ephorus of Cyme <note>Ephorus (c. 400–330 BC) was an influential Greek historian; his "Universal History" was a major source for Diodorus.</note>, a pupil of Socrates, when he undertook to write his book of history, remained silent regarding the deeds of the ancients and began his account from the time of the Return of the Heraclidae <note>The "Heracliten zeit" refers to the legendary return of the descendants of Hercules to the Peloponnese.</note>. Callisthenes and Theopompus, who lived at the same time, never considered the ancients at all. We, however, have undertaken this burden and wish to set down the ancient, vanished matters in writing. For there are many glorious and honest deeds performed by the ancient heroes and men regarded as gods—as well as other brave people—for which they were rightly honored by their descendants; these are well worthy of memory and should be recorded in the chronicles. And because we have described in the three preceding books the histories of foreign nations, what they claim regarding their gods, and the situation and region of each, along with their wild game, animals, and other wonders worthy of memory, we now wish in this book to speak of the Greeks, their heroes, and the men honored as gods who were held in high esteem by them in ancient times, and also of the wars they waged. And we shall add what they invented in times of peace for the benefit and discipline <note>The term "zucht" here implies moral education or civilized conduct.</note> of mankind, and what laws they prescribed for their people. We shall begin with Dionysus, who is above all a very ancient hero and who showed much goodness to mankind. It was mentioned above that certain barbarian nations boast that this god had his birth and lineage among them. For the Egyptians say he is their Osiris, whom the Greeks call Dionysus.

# Regarding the Greek
## tradition. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with intertwined vines and foliage.</image-desc>
They say that Agenor sent his son out from Phoenicia to search for his sister Europa, with the condition that he must either bring the maiden back with him or never return to his land. But as Cadmus found her nowhere despite his search, he left his fatherland and remained in Boeotia. There, at the command of the gods, he built the city of Thebes and took Harmonia, the daughter of Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; the Greek goddess Aphrodite</note>, as his wife. From her, he fathered Semele, Ino, Autonoe, Agave, and a son named Polydorus. Semele, because of her beauty, was seduced by Jupiter <note>original: "Juppiter"; the Greek god Zeus</note> in human form. Believing herself to be despised by Jupiter, she begged that he would no longer come to her as a man, but rather to have dealings with her just as he did with Juno. Thus, Jupiter took on his divine power, and as she could not endure the thunder and lightning, she gave birth to the child before its time and thus died in the fire. Jupiter had the child led by Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"; the Greek god Hermes</note> into the cave of Nysa, located between Phoenicia and the Nile, and commanded the nymphs to raise him diligently. For this reason, he was named Dionysius <note>The name is traditionally explained as "Dio-" (from Zeus) and "Nysa" (the place of his upbringing).</note> after Jove and Nysa, as Homer testifies in his hymn of praise, saying: "Nysa is on a high, greening mountain in a forest located not far from Phoenicia by the waters of Egypt." The Greeks write that he was raised by the nymphs, invented wine and its use in the world, traveled nearly everywhere, planted fruitful trees everywhere, and for that reason was highly honored by everyone. He showed the people where grapevines might grow and where they might not; he taught them to make a drink from barley which is called <term>Zythum</term> <note>A type of ancient beer or barley wine common in Egypt and other regions where grapes were scarce.</note>, which is not entirely unlike wine. He led an army with him, composed not only of women but also of men. He punished wicked, useless people and the evil. He spared all the cities in Boeotia because he had left his fatherland free, and he also built a free city therein and declared it free. Afterward, he traveled into India, where he spent three years roaming, and brought a great haul of spoils back with him to Boeotia. He was the first to ride in as a victor, specifically upon an Indian elephant. The Boeotians, other Greeks, and also the Thracians established a festival in memory of his three-year expedition, which they call <term>Triatēridēn</term> <note>original: "Τριατηρίδην"; referring to the Trieteris, a biennial festival (reckoned every three years by inclusive counting) dedicated to Dionysus.</note>. And for this same reason, the women whom they call <term>Bachides</term> <note>The Bacchantes or Maenads, female followers of Dionysus known for their ecstatic rituals.</note> gather every three years and carry the young—

It is said that with him was his tutor and schoolmaster, a man who makes people learned, named Silenus; he brought great advancement to Dionysus in virtues, honors, and in matters of war. In war, he was accustomed to wearing armor; in peace, he dressed in panther skins. On feast days and high, holy days, he wore flowery, soft, and delicate clothes. Whenever he drank so much that it shook his brain, he would put on a headband, for which reason he is also called *Mitrophoros* <note>Greek for "turban-wearer"</note>. However, later kings made it a custom to wear a band around the head, rather than a cap. He was also called *Dimitora* <note>from the Greek 'Dimetor', meaning 'of two mothers'</note> because two Dionysiuses had one father and two mothers. But the deeds of the first were also attributed to the last; because of this, those who came after did not know the truth and were deceived by the similarity of the name, believing there had been only a single Dionysus. This led to them becoming discordant and sometimes wounding or even beating each other to death with clubs (for at that time, they carried clubs). Pure, unmixed wine makes one frantic, but mixed with water it brings joy and cheerfulness and protects against drunkenness. Two gods are honored by men above all others for the usefulness of their discoveries: Dionysus and Ceres; for the latter invented the noble drink, wine, and the former invented corn-farming <note>Ceres is the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note>. Yet the Greeks write of a Dionysus who is much older than this one, born of Jove and Proserpina. He is called by some Sabazios <note>transcribed as "Sebastis"</note>. This one is honored with certain shameful services, performed only at night and in secret. Out of great wisdom, he was the first to yoke oxen to the plow and sowed with their help; therefore, he is depicted with horns. But regarding the one born of Semele, they say he lived long after the first; he was a man who took good care of his body, handsome in form, and very devoted to women. He led entire armies of armed women with him, and their weapons were wrapped with vine branches. Furthermore, the nine virgins called the Muses, who were learned daughters, traveled with him. And he held them in high regard, both for their lovely singing and for their artistry. Traveling with him was his tutor and schoolmaster, a man who makes people learned named Silenus; he brought Dionysus great advancement in virtues, honors, and in matters of war. In war, he was accustomed to wearing armor; in peace, he clothed himself in leopard skins. On holidays, high days, and consecrated days, he wore flowered, soft, and delicate clothes. When he occasionally drank too much so that his brain was shaken, he put on a headband <note>or turban</note>, for which reason he is also called Mitrophoros <note>Greek for "turban-bearer"</note>. Although later kings made it a custom to wear a band around their head, rather than a hood or cap. He was also called Dimitor <note>original: "Dimitora"; Greek for "of two mothers"</note>, because two versions of Dionysus had one father and two mothers. But the deeds of the first were also attributed to the last; therefore, those who came after did not know the truth and were misled by the similarity of the name, assuming there had only been a single Dionysus. They attribute the vine <unclear>reben</unclear> to him for the following reason: in the beginning of wine-drinking, people did not mix water into it. When they came together at feasts and on wedding days and drank until they were quite full, satisfying their craving with unmixed wine, it happened that they occasionally fell into disagreement. Sometimes with clubs (for at that time they carried clubs), they wounded one another or even beat each other to death. To prevent this, Dionysus issued a decree that wine should be drunk moderately, and that they should carry only small rods <note>thyrsi</note>. In summer, many kinds of—

Some call him Bacchus because of the women. From the wine-press <note>original: "weintrottten"; the name Leneus is derived from "lenos," the Greek word for wine-press</note> he is called Leneus. Bromius from the thunder that occurred at his birth. For that reason, he is also called the Child of Fire.

It would take a long time were I to recount all his surnames, and it does not belong in this book. He is depicted in two different forms, as there have been two Dionysi. The first had a long beard, according to the custom of the ancients who let their beards grow. The other is somewhat handsomer, young in appearance, and delicate. Some say he was painted in two forms because wine, through its fullness, can make one either cheerful or angry. They say he had Satyrs with him, in whose leaping and playing he found great delight. For the sake of their art, he loved the Muses; for the sake of their jesting and pastime, he loved the Satyrs; thus he lived continually in revelry, made joyful by them. Some claim he also invented the huts and playing-tents, as well as the competition of the poets.

Those in his entire following who were skilled in music he set free from all duties, and his successors followed this custom regarding Dionysus; for all musicians <note>original: "Musici"</note> were free and relieved of all burdens. But so that we may bring an end to the recounting of the deeds, homelands, and birth of this Dionysus, and not say too much about one alone, we shall let it suffice to remember him no further, and direct our writing to that which follows immediately after Dionysus regarding Priapus, according to some who write of him.

### Of Priapus.

The ancients say Priapus was a son of Dionysus and Venus, and truly they have no unlikely suspicion; for those who are constantly devoted to wine are also more inclined to impurity <note>referring here to lust or sexual desire</note>. Some also say that when the ancients did not wish to speak too indecently of the male member, they called it Priapus. Some call them the reproductive organs, for they are the cause of the incarnation of humanity, wherefore they also honored them with immortal honor. The Egyptians, speaking of Priapus, write thus: When the Titans had secretly murdered Osiris, they cut his body into many pieces and each secretly carried one away; and because no one wanted to take the male member, they threw it into the water. But when Isis later avenged her husband's death upon the Titans, sought out her husband's body, put the limbs back together, and restored him to human form, she gave the pieces to the priests to bury and commanded that Osiris be honored as a god. Because she could find the male member nowhere, she commanded that temples hang up an image of its likeness and worship it as a god. That is the Egyptian tale of Priapus and his origin. The guardian of the vineyards and gardens is honored because he punished those who stole from gardens. Thus, people offer sacrifices to this god with laughter and jesting, not only during the festivals of Dionysus but also in nearly all other sacrifices to the gods.

## Concerning Hermaphroditus.

A similar origin is attributed to one whom they call **Hermaphroditus**. They say he was born of Venus <note>the goddess of love, Aphrodite</note> and Mercury <note>the messenger god, Hermes</note>, from whom he also received his name <note>a combination of Hermes and Aphrodite</note>. They regard him as a god and say he was both boy and girl; in form and appearance, he was like a delicate woman, yet he performed manly deeds. Some say such a birth is a miracle that occurs very rarely, and that it signifies something, bringing either good fortune or disaster with it.

## Concerning the Muses.

And since we mentioned the Muses during the deeds of Dionysus, it seems to me we should write more clearly about them. Many, including the most famous writers, say they are the daughters of Memory <note>original: "Memorie"; the Greek goddess Mnemosyne</note> and Jove <note>original: "Jouis"; Jupiter or Zeus</note>. A few among the poets—among whom is Alcmeon—say they are the daughters of Heaven <note>original: "Cæli"; Uranus</note> and Earth <note>original: "Terræ"; Gaia</note>. Likewise, they disagree on their number: some say there are three, some nine. However, the number of nine has prevailed through the testimony of the most famous, namely Homer and Hesiod. Homer says they are beautiful beyond measure. Hesiod recounts their names: **Clio**, **Euterpe**, **Thalia**, **Melpomene**, **Terpsichore**, **Erato**, **Polymnia**, **Urania**, and **Calliope**, the last of whom is the most noble of all.

To each of them, they attribute certain qualities suitable for music, such as composing poetry, leaping, dancing, stargazing, and other arts. Some say the fact that they were virgins signifies that the arts of virtue should be incorruptible and pure. Likewise, the name "Muses" comes from the fact that they teach people things that are good and useful, which the ignorant and unlearned do not recognize.

The name of each comes from her specific office. For **Clio** is named from the fame <note>original: "lob"; the name is derived from the Greek "kleos," meaning glory or renown</note> that results from the writings of poets. **Euterpe** is named from the pleasure <note>original: "wollust"</note> felt by those who listen to honorable things. **Thalia** because the fame won by poets flourishes <note>original: "grünet"</note> for a long time. **Melpomene** is named for the voice with which listeners are delighted. **Terpsichore** because the listeners of the good arts are delighted by the benefit that springs from them. **Erato** because learned people are loved by many. **Polymnia** because, through the sweetness of song, she endows poets with immortal honor. **Urania** because she raises learned people up to Heaven; for in investigating heavenly things, she elevates them with honor and wisdom. **Calliope** comes from the fact that she surpasses all others in the sweetness of her voice, for which reason she is more highly regarded by listeners. And since we have now spoken of the Muses, we will now turn to **Hercules**.

# Concerning Hercules and the Most Notable
## of His Deeds. Chapter 2.

It is not hidden from me what a great burden they take upon themselves who undertake to describe the ancient deeds of **Hercules**. For many say that they are so great and glorious that they surpass all deeds ever performed by any man. It is truly difficult to describe the actions of Hercules in a way that is worthy of them; and because his deeds received an immortal reward for their greatness, one cannot easily speak of them so grandly as to match those brave acts. For those who attempted to report them—on account of their antiquity and the magnitude of the wondrous deeds performed—feared that few people would believe their writing. Thus, out of necessity, they omitted the greatest parts so that they would not write things that were entirely incredible.

The reason for this is that some have an unfit judgment when reading; for when they read ancient, long-past histories, they compare them to current events, weighing the past against their own times. Thus, they wish to compare the strength and vigor of Hercules perhaps against the strength of people today, but they find something else that is much greater; therefore, they can never rightly give credence to the past. Truly, if one seeks the literal truth in ancient histories and poems as if measuring with a string <note>an idiom meaning "with absolute precision"</note>, it is in vain. For in the plays <note>theatrical performances or spectacles</note> appear the **Minotaur**, the three-bodied **Geryon**, and others that we know were not formed in such a way, yet we believe in them for the sake of the gods.

So it is also quite unfair—since Hercules cleared the world of the most unfortunate and destructive monsters and showed much good to the whole human race—that one should wish to diminish his praise regarding his glorious deeds. Also, because his descendants, on account of his virtue and with the consent of all good-hearted people, attributed immortality and great fame to him, it is unfair that we do not wish to follow our own ancestors in all godliness. But let us leave that aside and present what we find described of his deeds, both by the poets and others.

They say that from **Danae**, the daughter of **Acrisius**, and from **Jove** <note>original: "Joue"; Jupiter or Zeus</note>, **Perseus** was born. He fathered **Electryon** by **Andromeda**, the daughter of **Cepheus**. Electryon took **Eurydice**, the daughter of **Pelops**, and she bore **Alcmene**. The same woman Jupiter deceived with tricks and fathered **Hercules** upon her. Thus they trace the lineage of Hercules into the line of the highest gods, and his bravery is praised not only for his deeds but also for his ancestry.

They write that Jupiter made three nights out of one when he lay with Alcmene, thereby giving a sign that the child must become strong, since he devoted so much time to fathering a child. For he did this not out of love for women—for he loved others more—but for the sake of the child. And since he had it in his mind to sleep with Alcmene, but knew that she was a pious and steadfast woman who could not be persuaded to break her marriage, he deceived her with tricks and transformed himself into the shape of **Amphitryon**, her husband.

When she was about to give birth, they say Jupiter said in the presence of all the gods: "The child who is born on this very day shall become the king of the **Persides** <note>the descendants of Perseus</note>." This annoyed **Juno** <note>Hera</note>, who immediately sent **Lucina** <note>the goddess of childbirth</note>, her daughter, to [prevent] the birth of Alcmene...

# On Hercules and his most distinguished
## deeds. Chapter 2.

I am well aware of the great burden those take upon themselves who undertake to describe the ancient deeds of Hercules. For many say that they are so great and magnificent that they surpass all deeds ever performed by a man. Truly, it is difficult to describe the acts of Hercules in a way that is worthy of them; and because he received an immortal reward for their greatness, one cannot easily speak of them with such splendor that it matches those brave deeds. For those who undertook to report these things—due to the antiquity and the scale of the performed wonders—feared that not many people would believe their writing. Out of necessity, they have left out the greatest parts so that they might not write without any credibility at all.

The reason for this is that some have a poor judgment when reading; for when they read old, past histories, they weigh them against current events and measure them against their own times. Thus, they wish to compare the strength and joyfulness of Hercules against the power of modern men, but they find something else that is far greater; therefore, they can never truly believe the things of the past. Truly, if one wishes to follow old histories and poems strictly by the letter <note>original: "der schnür nach"</note>, it is in vain. For in the plays there appears the Minotaur, the three-bodied Geryon, and other things that we know were not shaped in that way, yet we believe it for the sake of the Gods. 

So it is also quite unjust—since Hercules cleared the world of the most unfortunate and destructive wonders and showed much good to the entire human race—that one should wish to diminish his praise regarding his magnificent deeds. Furthermore, since his descendants, because of his virtue and with the consent of all good-hearted people, have granted him immortality and great fame, we should not refuse to follow our own ancestors in all godliness. But let us leave that aside and show what we find described of his deeds, both by the poets and by others.

They say that from Danae, the daughter of Acrisius, and from Jove <note>original: "Joue" — Jupiter</note>, Perseus was born. The same Perseus had Electryon <note>original: "Electrionem"</note> by Andromeda, the daughter of Cepheus. Electryon took Eurydice, the daughter of Pelops, and fathered Alcmena. Jupiter dishonored her with trickery and fathered Hercules by her. Thus, they place the lineage of Hercules into the lineage of the highest gods, and his bravery is praised not only for his deeds but also for his ancestry. 

They write that Jupiter made three nights out of one when he lay with Alcmena, thereby giving a sign that the child must become strong, as he spent so much time on the creation of one child. For he did this not out of love for women—of whom he loved many others—but because of the child’s future deeds. ## Hercules' seventh deed.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting Hercules, identifiable by his club and muscular build, standing beside a large wooden wine barrel. In the background, a centaur is approaching or observing.</image-desc>

It happened after this that **Hercules** fought a battle against the **Centaurs**; the conflict occurred in this manner. A Centaur lived by Mount **Pholo** <note>Mount Pholoe in Greece.</note>, from which he also took his name; he hosted Hercules during his travels and gave him wine to drink that had long lain buried in a barrel. For **Dionysius** <note>Also known as Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> had previously, in the fourth generation before, gifted a barrel of wine to one of the Centaurs and commanded him never to give the wine to anyone until Hercules came to them. Mindful of this command, they had kept the wine. But now as the wine was brought out, such a good aroma came from it—due to its age and its excellence—that the surrounding Centaurs were driven wild by it; thus they stormed **Pholus's** house all at once with a great clamor, wanting to drink as well. Pholus fled from the crowd and hid himself; Hercules alone offered them brave resistance. Even though he had to fight against those who were semi-divine on their mother’s side <note>In mythology, the Centaurs were the offspring of Ixion and Nephele (a cloud goddess).</note>, who were as fast as horses, possessed the strength of two bodies, and the reason of humans. The Centaurs tore up trees along with their roots; some threw entire rocks at him; others struck at him with large, heavy battle-axes; but Hercules was not at all terrified by this; he did not want to lose his honor, but fought bravely as he always had before. **Nephele** <note>The cloud goddess and mother of the centaurs; the original German "Nebel" means mist or cloud.</note> stood by her sons in this struggle; she poured down a great rain that made the ground slippery, so that Hercules could hardly stand; they, however, being four-footed, found easy footing. Yet it did not help the Centaurs; Hercules prevailed, killed many of them, and put the others to flight. Those who perished were the most prominent: **Daphnis**, **Argeus**, **Amphion**, **Hippotion**, **Orias**, **Isoplos**, **Malanchetes**, **Tereus**, **Derpos**, **Phrypus**; and those who had already fled had to suffer in the end anyway, for **Omas**...

This brought Hercules much more fame than all the memorial pillars that could ever be erected for him. For this mountain has ever since been called **Pholoe**, named after no other, so that the name of the mountain is nothing other than an epitaph for the deceased. In this same manner, **Chiron**, a famous physician, also perished after being wounded by one of Hercules' arrows. <note>Chiron was a wise Centaur and tutor to heroes; because he was immortal, the poison caused him eternal agony until he was allowed to die.</note>

### Hercules' eighth deed and fourth struggle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing a large stag with majestic, multi-branched antlers leaping through a landscape. Below the stag, a smaller deer (hind) is seen drinking from a river or stream. Following this, Hercules was commanded to bring back alive to **Eurystheus** a wonderfully swift stag that bore golden horns. <note>The Ceryneian Hind, a creature sacred to Artemis.</note> To accomplish this, Hercules used his agility, which is sometimes no less useful than strength. Some say he caught it in a net. Others say he followed it for so long that he caught it while it was sleeping. Still others say he wore it out through a long pursuit. In short, he completed this struggle with cunning, and not with brute strength.

## Hercules’ ninth deed / and fifth struggle.

Now Hercules was tasked with driving the desert birds out of the **Stymphalian Lake** <note>original: "Symphaler See"</note>; this he also accomplished with great skill. He drove a countless flight of these birds—which had been laying waste to the surrounding land—out of the lake. Because of their great number, he could achieve nothing against them by sheer strength alone; instead, it required great wisdom to frighten them all away. Thus, he fashioned a bronze plate <note>The "krotala" or rattles made by Hephaestus in classical myth.</note>; when this was struck, it gave off such a loud clanging that the birds were terrified and would not remain anywhere in the region. Thus, the lake was cleared of the waste.

## Hercules’ tenth deed / and Eurystheus' 
## sixth command.

But to show his contempt for Hercules, **Eurystheus** commanded that he alone should muck out the **Palace of Augeas** <note>original: "Pfalz Augie"; typically known as the Augean Stables.</note>, for it had not been cleaned in many years and was filled with a vast amount of filth. Hercules did not wish to perform such a lowly task with his own hands; instead, he diverted the river **Peneus** <note>original: "Pignio"</note> into it, which washed the manure away in a single day. Thus, the ingenious Hercules was much to be admired; though he was assigned a task intended to be insulting, filthy, and disadvantageous, he completed it with great honor, and yet did nothing in the process that would be unseemly for his immortality.

## Hercules’ eleventh deed - and seventh 
## Eurystheus' command.

Afterward, he had to lead the bull that **Pasiphae**, the Queen in **Crete**, loved <note>Refers to the Cretan Bull, which Pasiphae was famously enamored with, leading to the birth of the Minotaur.</note> to Eurystheus. So he sailed to the island, and with the help of King **Minos**, he brought the bull across the sea over a long distance into the **Peloponnese**. After this deed, he established the competitive festival in **Olympia** <note>original: "Oympo"</note>; for he saw that this region was well-suited for hosting many people because of the meadows situated by the river **Alpheus**. He also dedicated this same festival to his father **Jupiter**, thereby exalting him, for Hercules himself had also earned the gratitude of mankind through his virtue. He won every contest of this festival, so that no one else dared to come near him.

...any kind of combat with him. For it is quite hazardous for wrestlers or fighters to try to overcome a runner; moreover, it is very difficult when those who are already highly regarded in simple combat wish to strive against those who have performed such great deeds. For this reason, one should rightly hold the athletic games <note>The Olympic Games</note> established by Hercules to be the most excellent, because they were founded by the most excellent man. It is also not to be kept secret here with what gifts Hercules was endowed by the gods at that time. For when he sought to have a period of rest and a holiday from war, the gods honored him in the presence of all men, each with a special gift. **Pallas** <note>Athena</note> gave him a robe <note>original: "schleyer", literally a veil or shroud, but here referring to a garment</note>; **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note> gave him the club and the breastplate. Both of these gifts these two gods had made themselves with great skill; Pallas gave him that which he might use in peace, and Vulcan that which he might use in war. **Neptune** <note>Poseidon</note> presented him with several horses. **Mercury** <note>Hermes</note> gave him a sword. **Apollo** a bow, and taught him how to shoot with it. Likewise **Ceres** <note>Demeter</note> instructed him in the religious rites <note>original: "Götzendienſt"; likely referring to the Eleusinian Mysteries</note> by which he might atone for the death of the Centaurs. One must also hear with great wonder the lineage of Hercules. **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note> lay with **Niobe**, the daughter of Phoroneus, who was the first mortal woman with whom he had business. The last was **Semele**, who was born in the sixteenth generation of Niobe's lineage. Thus, Jupiter ceased to father children through mortal women in the same family line where he had begun. For thereafter, he mingled with no more mortals, regarding none as noble enough, and wishing no longer to mix the good with the evil.

# The twelfth deed of Hercules.

Afterward, when the **Giants** stirred up a war against the gods near the island of **Pallene**, Hercules came to the aid of the gods and slew many of the enemy, achieving great fame. Jupiter named all the gods who had stood by him by the common name **Olympians**, so that through this honorable title, he might distinguish the good from the evil. He never honored anyone born of a mortal woman with this title except for **Dionysus** and **Hercules**; and that not only because they were born of him, but because they had striven to follow him in performing great deeds, and because each had shown much goodness to mankind.

# The thirteenth deed of Hercules.

Jupiter had bound **Prometheus** in chains for the reason that he had given fire to men, and had assigned an eagle thereto, which ate from Prometheus's liver every day. Hercules was moved to pity that he should suffer so, since he had nonetheless shown goodness to men through his misdeed <note>The "misdeed" refers to the theft of fire from the gods.</note>. He shot the eagle, reconciled Jupiter, and released his companion.

# Hercules’s fifteenth deed and ninth 
## command of Eurystheus.

It was immediately imposed upon him that he should bring the belt of the Amazon queen, **Hippolyta**, to King **Eurystheus**. Thus, he set out against them with the strength of an army, sailing through the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note>. He traveled upstream following the flow of the **Thermodon** <note>A river in northern Turkey associated with the Amazons</note> until he reached the city of **Themiscyra**, where the Queen of the Amazons had established her camp. He first demanded the belt from her with kindness; however, when she refused, he saw clearly that he must resort to weapons. When the battle began, the noblest among the **Amazons** all aimed for Hercules; each one desired to see him dead. **Aella** <note>original: "Aella"; the name means "Whirlwind" in Greek</note>, being the swiftest (from which her name is derived), stepped forward first, but she was also the first to be stabbed to death. **Philippis** ran after her, but she was laid low with a single stroke. **Prothoe** <note>OCR: Parthoes</note> wished to avenge them, as one who had previously emerged victorious seven times in single combat, but she also fell. **Eurybia** also tried her luck; she desired no help, relying on the fame she had achieved for her skill in all wars, but she found a stronger man in Hercules than she was. Afterward, **Celaeno**, **Eurybia**, **Phoebe**, and **Artemis** the huntress <note>These were members of the Amazonian guard, not the goddess Artemis herself</note> were stabbed by him, as were **Deianeira**, **Asteria**, **Marpes**, and **Tecmessa** <note>OCR: Thermessa</note>. **Alcippe** <note>OCR: Adippes</note> had vowed to keep her virginity for her whole life; she kept that vow, but she was forced to leave her life behind. **Melanippe**, who ruled the Amazons and was widely famed for her strength, cast her kingdom aside and gave the belt to Hercules to save her own life. And when the noblest had all been laid low and the others fled, he utterly destroyed them. From the prisoners, he gave **Antiope** as a gift to **Theseus**.

### The twentieth deed of Hercules.

Before this, Hercules had also performed similar works. There was a vast, large swamp and marsh at the place called **Tempe** <note>a valley in northern Thessaly, Greece, famous for its beauty</note>, which frequently flooded that pleasant region. There, he had a large trench or pit dug, so that the water flowing out of the marsh irrigated all of **Thessaly** as far as the **Peneus** River <note>original: "Peneum"; the principal river of Thessaly</note>.

### The twenty-first deed of Hercules.

In **Boeotia** <note>a region in central Greece</note>, he did the opposite, for he dammed up the **Minyan** waters <note>original: "Mineum"; referring to the waters near Orchomenus, which Hercules reportedly diverted to flood the land</note>, ruined the land everywhere, and turned it into a lake. What he did in Thessaly was done for the benefit of the Greeks, but he ruined Boeotia out of love for the **Thebans** <note>the inhabitants of Thebes in Greece, the city of Hercules's birth</note>, so that he might take revenge on the **Minyans** <note>original: "Boetiern"; here referring specifically to the Minyans of Orchomenus</note>, who had previously brought the city into servitude. When he departed again from **Iberia** <note>the Spanish peninsula</note>, he entrusted the kingdom to the most pious men and traveled with his army through **Celtogallia** <note>Gaul, or modern-day France</note>. He traversed the land everywhere and abolished the unjust, cruel custom they had of killing all foreigners who came to them. Because many people from all sorts of lands followed him in war, he built a city there and named it **Alexia** <note>modern-day Alesia; the city became famous centuries later as the site of Julius Caesar's final victory over the Gauls</note>. It was willingly inhabited by many local people, and because the foreigners were more numerous, it soon adopted foreign customs. The **Celts** still hold this city in great honor today as their capital, and the city remains free to this day. However, since it was conquered by force by **Gaius Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar, who was deified after his death</note> (who, because of his manly deeds, was called a god), it has come under the **Roman Empire** like other Celtic nations.

Hercules then traveled from there across the mountains; he made a road over them so large and wide that all loads and military equipment could pass over, even though it had previously been such an impassable place that it was almost impossible for a single man to walk across it. he rooted out those who stood in his way, practicing robbery and other mischief, and he put their princes to death. Among the **Ligurians** <note>ancient people of north-western Italy and south-eastern France</note> he emerged from the mountains and moved toward what is now called **Galatia** <note>original: "Galatia"; here referring to the land of the Gauls, as the Greek term for Gauls was Galatae</note>, a rough, hard region which, even though the inhabitants worked it heavily, yielded no fruit. For this reason, it produced strong and swift people. The cause was the meager food and constant exercise in plowing the soil, which made them light and nimble, and especially brave in war. They are constantly occupied with farming, and they hire one another for money so that they may help each other complete their planting. Even the women there involve themselves in the work of the fields. There once occurred an event which would seem very strange to our women, almost like a miracle. A woman was standing at her daily work alongside other men, and when she suffered the great labor of childbirth, she went into a thicket, delivered the child—letting out no cry at all during the process—wrapped it up, and hid it. She then went back to work and said nothing of her giving birth. However, when the child began to cry, the farmer would not let her leave the work for a long time, until at last he took pity on the child, gave the mother her wages, and let her go. Now, when Hercules had traveled out of **Liguria** and through **Tyrrhenia** <note>Etruria, the land of the Etruscans in central Italy</note>, he came to the **Tiber**, where **Rome** now stands, though it was built there by **Romulus** the son of **Mars** only much later. At that same time, the **Aborigines** <note>the earliest legendary inhabitants of central Italy</note> lived there; they had a small town on the site where the **Palatine** <note>original: "Pfalz"; referring to the Palatine Hill in Rome</note> is now. Two of the most prominent citizens, one named **Potitius** and the other **Pinarius**, received Hercules as a guest and gave him great gifts. The memory of their names still lasts in Rome, and the **Pinarii** are considered the most noble and ancient family. On the Palatine, there is a spiral path <note>original: "schneck"; likely referring to the Scalae Caci or a similar landmark</note> called **Potitia**, because it stands not far from where the house of the **Potitii** once was. When this city had shown him great honor, he told them that those who—after he was taken up among the gods—offered sacrifices to him and established a tithe <note>a tenth part of one’s goods</note> of all their property, would strive in great prosperity. This has remained true until this time, for many—and not the least, but indeed the richest Romans—have established a tithe for Hercules from their goods. Thus, as they increased more and more over time, they have sacrificed about four thousand **talents** <note>an ancient unit of weight and value</note> to Hercules. **Lucullus**, the wealthiest of all Romans, continually gave a tithe of his appraised wealth to Hercules, constantly held church-consecrations in his temple, and was very generous toward the god. The Romans have built him a beautiful temple on the Tiber, where they sacrifice to him from the tithe.

### The twenty-third deed of Hercules.

Like **Mount Etna** in **Sicily**, it spewed out fire; it is now called **Vesuvius** <note>original: "Vesuutum"</note> and has many ancient signs of fire. When the Giants became aware that Hercules was passing through, they all marched out against him in battle formation, so strong were they, and engaged in a battle. They say the gods came to Hercules’s aid, so that he killed them all and cleared that same region. ### The twenty-fourth deed of Hercules.

Afterward, one evening when he was tired, he fell asleep under that tree; then the cord from which the boar’s head hung gave way, and it fell upon the hunter, striking him dead. ### The Twenty-Fifth Deed of Hercules.

But good fortune met Hercules on account of his godliness; for when he came to the borders of the **Rhegians** and **Locrians** <note>peoples inhabiting the "toe" of Italy</note>, he was weary and could not rest because of the grasshoppers or crickets. This annoyed him greatly, and he called upon the gods to drive the grasshoppers away. His prayer was heard, so that neither then nor ever since have any grasshoppers been found there. Afterward, he traveled to the sea lying opposite **Sicily**, where it is very narrow, and as **Timaeus** <note>an ancient Greek historian, c. 345–250 BC</note> writes, it was no more than thirteen **stadia** <note>about 1.5 miles</note> wide. There, some of his oxen swam across to the island; he himself, however, took hold of the horn of one of the oxen and likewise swam across. Hercules had a desire to travel around the island, and when he had come from Mount **Pelorus** to the shores of **Eryx**, two **Nymphs** brought forth warm water for him to refresh him from his weariness. Each of these springs was named after their dwelling place; one was called **Himera**, and the other **Gepteo**.

### The Twenty-Sixth Deed of Hercules.

**Eryx**, the king of that place—a son of **Butes** the king and **Venus** <note>original: "Veneris," the Roman goddess of love</note>—when he heard that Hercules was there, challenged him to a wrestling match. However, they first quarreled over the wager—what each would lose if he should lose the match. Eryx offered up his land, and Hercules offered up his oxen. At first, Eryx looked down upon this, because Hercules valued his oxen so highly as to compare them to the Kingdom of Eryx. Hercules replied that he valued them more than his life, for if he lost them, he would be deprived of his immortality. Upon this, Eryx accepted the combat and lost his land. Hercules, however, gave it back to the inhabitants to possess freely, but with the condition that they should make use of it until one of his sons or grandsons should come to rule it, which happened later. The cause was that many years afterward, **Dorieus** sailed from **Lacedaemonia** <note>Sparta</note> into Sicily and built the city of **Heraclea** therein. When this city increased greatly in wealth and reputation in a short time, the **Carthaginians** became annoyed; they feared the city might grow over time and destroy the empire of the **Phoenicians**, so they besieged it with a great army, captured it, and destroyed it. Of that, more in its proper place. Now, when Hercules had traveled through the island as far as **Syracuse**, and heard what was said regarding the abduction of **Proserpine** <note>the daughter of Ceres, taken to the underworld</note>, he held a festival for the gods there and sacrificed the most beautiful oxen to them at **Cyane**. He also instructed the subjects and inhabitants there that they should hold an annual festival at Cyane and perform such sacrifices in honor of the goddess.

### The Twenty-Seventh Deed of Hercules.

With his oxen, he then traveled into the middle of the country. There, the **Sicanians** <note>an ancient people of Sicily</note> came against him with a well-armed host. He delivered a fierce battle to them and slew many of the enemy, among whom were many heroes who have received heroic veneration <note>cult worship given to deceased Greek heroes</note> down to our own time. Their names were **Leucaspis**, **Pedicrates**, **Buphonus**, **Glichates**, **Buteus**, and **Crytides**. Thus he moved forward into the **Leontine** region, which pleased him exceedingly...

He was also magnificently received by them, for which reason he left behind an eternal memory of himself. The **Agyrinaeans** <note>the inhabitants of Agyrium, a very ancient city in the heart of Sicily</note> honored him as an **Olympian God** and offered sacrifices to him; this he allowed to happen, although he had previously refused and forbidden such honors to many others. But because his spirit had now given him a true sign, he permitted it. For as he was traveling a path not far from the city—which was almost entirely solid rock—his oxen stepped into the stone as if it were wax; the same happened to Hercules himself. Therefore, he thought that in ten years of labor he had now well deserved some divine honor; for this reason, he accepted such annual sacrifices as a good thing. Now, so that he would not be ungrateful to them, he had a lake dug not far from the city, four **stadia** <note>about 740 meters or nearly half a mile</note> wide, and he gave his own name to it and to the place where the oxen had stepped so deeply. He also erected a temple, which the citizens still honor. For his nephew **Iolaus** <note>Hercules's faithful companion and charioteer</note>, he also built a temple and taught the locals how they should honor and sacrifice to him annually, which they still practice. All citizens let their hair grow from birth for the sake of Iolaus until they appease him with a rich sacrifice; and this temple is held in such great honor and esteem that those who do not offer the customary sacrifices become mute from childhood and like the dead. However, as soon as they vow to give their offerings and reconcile themselves, they immediately become healthy again. The gate through which these offerings are carried in and out is called the **Heracleium** by the citizens, and they have established certain games, horse races, and wrestling matches, in which both freemen and servants participate. They also have a special dance for their servants, with which they have learned to serve the God. Likewise, churches were consecrated and monuments established to honor the god therewith.

## Hercules’s twenty-eighth deed.

Thus Hercules traveled with his oxen back into **Italy**, and as he traveled along the land, he killed **Lucrinus**, who was constantly stealing his oxen. After he had killed **Croton** <note>in mythology, Croton was a friend of Hercules whom the hero accidentally killed; Hercules promised to found a city at his tomb to atone</note> without any danger, he erected a beautiful grave for him, buried him, and said that a city and a precious dwelling would yet be built in this place, the likes of which there would not be many, and it would be named after the dead man’s name. Thereafter, he traveled on foot along the **Adriatic Sea** into **Epirus** <note>a region in modern-day Greece and Albania</note> and came into the **Peloponnesus**.
