# Hercules’s twenty-ninth deed and
### Eurystheus’s eleventh command.

When he had now completed the ten labors, Eurystheus sent him into Hell to lead out **Cerberus** <note>the three-headed hound that guards the gates of the Underworld</note>. He took counsel on such a deed and requested time for it; he went to Athens and had himself initiated as a priest of the **Eleusinian Goddess** <note>Demeter/Ceres; the Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious rites</note>. Her high priest was **Orpheus**, a son of **Musaeus**. Because we have come to Orpheus here, we wish to say a little something about him.

## Of Orpheus.

Orpheus was by birth a **Thracian**, a son of **Oeagrus** <note>original: "Lagri"</note>, highly renowned in art, poetry, and lovely song, so much so that he surpassed all those who have applied themselves to poetry up until this time. He also wrote a precious, wonderful poem that was so pleasant it brought him a reputation that wild animals and trees came to hear his song. When he had devoted himself entirely to learning and inclined toward sacred scripture, he traveled to **Egypt** and learned many arts there, so that he was held by the Greeks to be the most learned and, in the matters of religious service, sacred scripture, and poetry, the most skilled and highest of all. He was also among the first sailors to travel across the sea. Out of the great love he bore for his wife, he descended into Hell to lead her back out; because of his lovely singing, this was granted to him by **Proserpina** <note>the Queen of the Underworld, also known as Persephone</note>. Previously, **Dionysus** had also brought his mother **Semele** back from Hell to the world, thereafter making her a goddess and calling her **Thyone** <note>original: "Theonem"</note>. Now back to Hercules: when he came into Hell, he was received by Proserpina as a brother <note>both were children of Zeus</note>. **Theseus** and **Pirithous** were released from their imprisonment for his sake. Through the help of his sister <note>Athena, who often assisted him, or perhaps a reference to Proserpina's favor</note>, and along with Cerberus whom he led captive, he showed the hellhound to mankind upon the world—an unprecedented sight.

### Of Hesperus and Atlas.

It is claimed that there were two brothers in Hesperia <note>a name used by ancient Greeks to refer to lands to the West, such as Italy or North Africa</note> who were very famous men; one was named Hesperus and the other Atlas. # The Fifth Book.

He achieved no less praise, and many are of the opinion that he ruled over Hesperia. <note>Hesperia refers to the "Western Lands," typically meaning Italy or the Iberian Peninsula.</note> When Hercules was burdened with these tasks, he gave cause for the Amazons—who lived by the Thermodon river—to invade the Greeks. For they intended to take revenge on the Greeks from whom Hercules came, and especially on the Athenians (whose King, Theseus, had captured Hippolyta, or as some say, Antiope). Those who remained of the Amazons saw no further hope of victory and returned to Scythia. But since we have already written enough regarding the Amazons, we shall return to the deeds of Hercules.

## The Thirty-Second Deed of Hercules.

Now that he had completed all his feats of combat and received a sign from the gods that it would be very conducive to his immortality if he sent people to inhabit Sardinia, he was told he should grant the rule of that land to the lineage of the Thespians. Thus, he sent his nephew Jolaus <note>original: "äncklin," meaning nephew or kinsman; Jolaus was the son of Hercules’s half-brother Iphicles</note> with his sons, who were still young, into Sardinia.

### Of the Thespians.

Now, so that it may be more evident who the inhabitants of Sardinia are, we wish to write more clearly concerning the children of the Thespians. Thespis was a noble citizen of Athens, a son of Erechtheus, who ruled in Thespis. He had fathered fifty daughters from many wives. Hercules, though still a young boy but very strong in power, had a desire to father children from this same lineage. He held a great feast and invited the father of the daughters; he filled him with wine and then called for one daughter after another, lay with them, and fathered fifty sons at once by them. These were collectively called by the surname Hesperides. <note>While the text uses "Hesperides," these sons of Hercules and the daughters of Thespis are more commonly known in mythology as the Thespiadae.</note> Therefore, Hercules resolved that he would send them out to inhabit Sardinia, and he entrusted them to Jolaus, the supreme commander of his fleet. Of the fifty sons, two remained in Thespis, whose lineage is said to be held in great honor even today; seven stayed in Thespis, whom the descendants call <term>Demiuchos</term> <note>From the Greek "demiouros," meaning "guardians of the people" or "public officials."</note>, and some of their lineage still hold power in our times. The remaining twenty-one young boys, and many others who went willingly, were taken by Jolaus to Sardinia. He landed where the island is best, which is still called Jolea after him today. As the land was rich and fertile, he planted it with trees and other things so well that they were even fit for military service; indeed, they became so famous for their fertility that the Carthaginians later suffered much in trying to conquer them, as we shall relate. Once Jolaus had thus settled the land, he sent to Sicily to summon Daedalus, through whose art he had many beautiful buildings erected, which still...

## The thirty-second deed of Hercules.

For as the city-folk grew and increased over time, so that they became more numerous than the rural folk, they adopted the customs of the other barbarian peoples. They also sought dwellings in rugged, mountainous places, built huts, lived on milk and meat, and nourished themselves with sheep and small livestock, of which they had a great multitude. Thus, they led a life that was not much inclined toward war. For this reason, the Romans and Carthaginians <note>original: "Carthaginiser"</note> often attacked them in vain.

## Of the Other Deeds of Hercules.

Now that we return to Hercules: when he had overcome all his labors, he granted to Iolaus that he should take Megara as his wife. The reason was that he feared having more children with her would not be good, as she might still remember how he had killed her previous children <note>Referring to the tragic fit of madness in which Hercules slew his own children by Megara</note>. However, so that children might still come from him, he went where he need not harbor any ill suspicion, and he requested of Eurytus, who ruled in Oechalia, that he should—

...marry his daughter Iole to him. Eurytus feared that Megara would not leave this unavenged because she had been cast out <note>Hercules had previously killed his children by Megara in a fit of madness and, in some versions, gave Megara herself to Iolaus</note>; he said he would deliberate further on the matter. When Iole was refused to Hercules, it vexed him, and he drove all of Eurytus's horses away. Eurytus’s servant, Iphitus, suspected that Hercules had taken the horses; he set out and came to Tiryns, where he climbed up a high tower to see if and where the horses were out at pasture. Hercules sensed his intentions, came to him, and complained that he had been innocently accused of theft; seeing none of the horses there, he threw Iphitus headlong off the tower. Because of this innocent death, Hercules fell into a sickness and traveled to Neleus at Pylos to seek absolution <note>original: "ablaß"; here referring to ritual purification or atonement</note> for the manslaughter. All of Neleus's sons, except for the youngest (named Nestor), advised him not to grant Hercules absolution. Therefore, he went to Deiphobus, the son of Hippolytus, hoping to persuade him to help cure his sickness, but it was in vain. Consequently, he asked Apollo what he should do, and Apollo gave him this answer: it would be an easy thing to make him healthy, provided it was done according to his will.

# Of the Servitude of Hercules and
->what he accomplished during the same.<-

He had to allow himself to be sold as a servant for a reasonable sum of money, which was then to be distributed among the children of Iphitus. Thus, out of necessity, he traveled by ship to Asia with several good friends and allowed himself to be sold as a servant to the daughter of Jardanes—she who ruled the people sometimes called the Maeonians or Lydians; the maiden’s name was Omphale. Whatever price was paid for Hercules was given to the children of Iphitus as compensation for their loss, and Hercules became healthy. While in the service of Omphale, he dealt with the Cecropian sea-robbers <note>original: "mhörrauber"; pirates or bandits who plagued the region</note> who had caused great damage to the land; some he killed, and others he brought captive before Omphale. Sylenus, who used to seize travelers and force them to work his vineyards, he struck to death with a hoe <note>term: "Karst" <gloss>a two-pronged hoe or mattock used in viticulture</gloss></note>.

The Ionians, who constantly raided Omphale’s land, he subdued; he captured their capital city, which was a den of thieves, and completely destroyed it. When Omphale saw such brave deeds from Hercules and heard who he was, she set him free and bore him a son named Lamon. Even before this, while still in servitude, he had fathered a son named Cleolaus with a servant girl.

# Hercules against the Trojans.

After he had returned to the Peloponnese, he marched against King Laomedon of Troy with a great army. Previously, he had traveled with Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece <note>original: "guldin fäl"</note>, and they had been promised certain horses because they had destroyed a sea monster <note>original: "mhörwunder"</note> in that region. However, Laomedon would not keep his word; we shall speak of this when we discuss the first sailors. Hercules remained silent until he was free of other wars, then he marched against Troy again with eighteen large ships—though Homer says there were six. For in the poet’s fifth book of the Trojan War, where Tlepolemus challenges Sarpedon to battle, he says, among other things:

Hercules, having arrived before Troy, marched with a portion of his warriors against the city, leaving Dicleus, the son of Amphiaraus, as the captain in charge of the ships. When Laomedon found himself thus surprised, he gathered whatever forces he could in such a short time and moved toward the ships, hoping that if he burned them, he would bring the war to an end. Dicleus marched against him but was struck down; the others fled back into the ships and cast themselves into the sea. The king then returned toward the city and fought with the main body of Hercules’s troops, where he fell along with many others. Hercules took the city by force and slew whoever resisted him. Priam had previously advised his father that he should give Hercules the promised horses; therefore, treating him as a righteous man, Hercules gave the kingdom back to him. He crowned Telamon for his bravery, as he had been the first to scale the wall, and married him to Hesione, the sister of Priam. Afterward, Hercules returned to the Peloponnese and made war on Augeas <note>King of Elis, famous for the "Augean Stables."</note> because his wages had not been delivered to him.

# What Hercules accomplished in the lands of Greece
->according to his commanded tasks.<-

When he gave battle to the Eleans <note>original: "Gliensern"; referring to the people of Elis.</note> and achieved nothing, he returned to Olenus, whose daughter Hippolyta was being married to Anaxion. While he was being merry with all the others who were at the wedding, he saw that Eurytion the Centaur wanted to violate the bride; therefore, he struck him dead. When he returned again to Tiryns, Eurystheus accused him as if he were plotting against his life. For this reason, he, along with Alcmene, Iphiclus <note>original: "Ephidea"; Hercules's twin brother.</note>, and Iolaus, were banished from the city, and he went into exile to Pheneus in Arcadia. He was greatly angered by this, and when he heard that a procession was coming from Elis to the Isthmus in honor of Neptune, led by Eurytus, the son of Augeas, he killed Eurytus at Cleonae, where the temple of Hercules now stands today. Afterward, he marched against Elis again, slew King Augeas, took the city by force, and handed the kingdom over to Phyleus, the son of Augeas. His father had previously driven Phyleus out because he had spoken in favor of Hercules receiving his wages when he had been appointed as an arbitrator <note>original: "rådings mann"; a person chosen to settle a dispute.</note>. Later, Hercules drove Hippocoon, the brother of Tyndareus, out of Sparta, but the twenty sons of Hippocoon

## Of the birth of Telephus.

**A**fter the war was finished, he returned again to Arcadia. There he stayed with King Aleus and secretly seduced his daughter <note>Auge, a priestess of Athena and daughter of King Aleus.</note>, making her pregnant, and then departed for Stymphalia. Now, when Auge's womb began to swell, her father wished to know who had impregnated her. He would not believe the truth—that Hercules had done it—and gave her to a mariner, who was a good friend of his, with the instruction that he should drown her in the sea. As she was being led to the ship, she went into labor near Mount Parthenion; thus, she stepped into the nearby woods, as if she intended to relieve herself according to nature’s needs, and gave birth to the child. She hid him in a thicket and returned to the ship. When she arrived at the landing near Eudaplio in Arcadia, she was unexpectedly delivered from her fate; for the man who led her did not wish to kill her, but instead gave her to a man from Caria who intended to sail to Asia. This man took her with him and gave her to King Teuthras. The little child, whom she had left lying by Mount Parthenion, was found by certain shepherds of King Corythus, who brought him to their lord. He afterwards raised the boy as his own child and named him Telephus, because a shepherd had suckled him <note>original: "geseigt"; traditionally, Telephus was said to be suckled by a doe (elaphos), which provides the etymology for his name, though this account credits a shepherd.</note>. When he came of age and wished to know who his mother was, he went to Delphi to consult Apollo. There he received the answer that he should travel to King Teuthras in Mysia. There he found his mother and was recognized as her son; and because Teuthras had no son of his own, he gave Telephus his daughter Argiopa in marriage so that he might rule after him. When Hercules had lived in Pheneus for five years, he was deeply grieved by the death of his brother Iphitus and the children of Licymnius, so that he voluntarily moved from Arcadia into the Peloponnese. Many Arcadians followed him from there into Calydonia. As yet he had neither wife nor legitimate children; therefore he took Deianira, the daughter of Oeneus <note>The original text says "Oilei," but contextually refers to Oeneus, the King of Calydon.</note>, as his wife—about which I wish to write something here concerning Meleager.

## Of Meleager and the Calydonian Boar.

**W**hen Oeneus—for the sake of his prosperity and because all things had gone well—sacrificed to all the gods but happened to overlook Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis, the goddess of the hunt, who was famously vengeful when neglected in ritual.</note>, she became enraged and sent the Calydonian Boar into the land. It was of such extraordinary size that it utterly ravaged the countryside. Meleager, who was still young and bold, gathered a company to him to hunt the boar. Whoever shot it was to have the skin as a reward. Atalanta, the daughter of Schoeneus, was also there; he fell in love with her and gave her the skin as if she had killed the boar herself. The others who had hunted with him were very bitter, and the sons of Thestius <note>Thestius was the King of Pleuron; his sons were Meleager’s maternal uncles.</note> were already distressed that a foreign woman should carry away the prize before them. They belittled Meleager’s deed and lay in wait for Atalanta, and as she was traveling back home to Arcadia, they took the hide from her by force. Meleager, moved both by love and by indignation that his deed should be so despised, first warned his opponents (who were all the brothers of his mother, Althaea) that they should cease their undertaking and return to the maiden that which she had won through her own prowess. When they refused, he slew them all. When Althaea heard of the death of her brothers, she sought out her child <note>Meleager</note> and prayed that he might die; her prayer was heard, and Meleager gave up the ghost. Some attach a poetic fable to this: that the Fates <note>The Parcae, or three goddesses of destiny.</note> appeared to Althaea in her sleep and told her that her son Meleager would die as soon as the firebrand which lay before her—and which they showed to her—was entirely consumed by fire. After the child was born, she preserved the indicated brand with diligent care. However, when she was enraged by the slaughter of her brothers, she burned it herself, whereby her son died. She later regretted this so deeply that she hanged herself.

### Of the birth of Thydeus.

In these histories, Hippotus, the King of Olenus, became enraged against his daughter Periboea, who claimed she had been made pregnant by Mars. Therefore, he sent her to Oeneus in Aetolia with the instruction that he should put her to death as soon and as quietly as possible. But Oeneus—as his own wife and son had only recently perished—ignored and disregarded the command of her father and took her as his wife, and she bore him Thydeus. Let this be enough concerning that matter.

## How Hercules diverted 
### the Achelous.

Out of love for the Calydonians, Hercules directed the river Achelous into a different channel, so that the land might be more and better irrigated. From this, some poets write that Hercules fought with a bull named Achelous <note>In Greek myth, the river god Achelous wrestled Hercules for the hand of Deianira, transforming into a bull during the fight.</note>, and when he broke off one of its horns, he presented it to the Aetolians filled with all kinds of fruits, grapes, apples, and other things; this was called the Horn of Amalthea <note>Also known as the Cornucopia, or Horn of Plenty.</note>. This poem may be interpreted as follows: the horn of Achelous is the new trench or canal, and the fact that it is full of oranges and other fruits signifies the fertility that this water brings with its flow, making the land "fat" or productive. The horn is hard, which signifies the great labor with which he accomplished it. Hercules also assisted the Calydonians in a war they waged against the Thesprotians; he captured the capital city, Ephyra, by force and slew their king, Phylas. With the king's captive daughter, he fathered a child named Triptolemus.

## Concerning the Death of Hercules.

Afterwards, he marched from Euboea to Mount Cenaeum <note>Original: "Cineum." A promontory on the northwest tip of Euboea.</note>; there he intended to offer a sacrifice and sent Lichas <note>Original: "Lycam."</note>, one of his servants, to Deianira in Trachis <note>Original: "Trachiniam."</note> so that she should send him his ceremonial wedding garments. When Deianira heard of his mistress Iole, she wished to be the most beloved of his wives; she smeared the tunic and shirt with the substance as Nessus the Centaur had taught her. Lichas knew nothing of the matter. When Hercules put the clothes on, the ointment slowly began to work with a terrible effect, so that Hercules suffered great agony; for the ointment was mixed with the poison of the Lernean Hydra <note>Original: "Leerneischen schlangē." The multi-headed serpent Hercules killed as his second Labor; its blood was a deadly venom.</note>, and it seared his body so that the pain became sharper and more intense as time passed. Thus Hercules grew enraged and killed Lichas, who had brought him the garment. Afterward, he gave his soldiers leave and came to Trachis, where his illness became worse and worse. He sent Licymnius <note>Original: "Licynium."</note> and Iolaus to Delphi so they might seek the counsel of Apollo on how the sickness might be cured. Deianira was terrified by Hercules's misfortune, and since she knew that she was the cause of it, she hanged herself. Apollo commanded that Hercules should be led to Mount Oeta with all his war gear, and there a great pyre should be built around him; the rest would be accomplished by Jupiter. Those who were with Iolaus and heard the answer understood well what the outcome would be. When Hercules saw that there was no other help, he laid himself upon the prepared pyre <note>Original: "feürwerck," literally "fire-work," referring here to the combustible structure of the pyre.</note> and asked those standing around to light it. However, no one was willing to do it except for Philoctetes; to him, Hercules gave his bow and arrows as a reward. Philoctetes set it alight, and thus the pyre was soon consumed amidst great thunder.

The Thebans did the same. But the Athenians were the first who honored Hercules as a God, providing an example to the other peoples on how to rightly revere him. **A**fterward, he traveled from Euboea to Mount Cenaeum <note>Original: "Cineum." They say, however, that Hercules was not included in the number of the twelve gods, as Jupiter had foretold. It would also be unjust to show honor to one by bringing shame upon another. Since we have now written what may be said of Hercules, we wish to say something of the Argonauts, with whom Hercules sailed.

## Concerning the first Sailors
->Chapter 4<-

The King of Thessaly, Pelias, had a brother Aeson, who fathered Jason. Jason surpassed other youths in physical strength and great power; his mind was set on accomplishing something worthy of remembrance. He was incited to this by the deeds of the ancients, especially those of Perseus and others who had achieved eternal fame through military expeditions brought to foreign lands; these examples had ignited his spirit to emulate them. Thus, he revealed his intention to the King, his uncle <note>The German text says "vatter" (father), but Jason was Pelias's nephew; Pelias was the brother of Jason's father, Aeson.</note>. The King encouraged the youth in this undertaking, not because he desired Jason's honor and fame so greatly, but because he believed that through this dangerous journey, the youth would sooner meet his end. The reason was that Pelias had no son, and he feared that in time his brother, with the help of his son Jason, would thrust him from the kingdom. Although he never let this suspicion be noticed, he promised to be helpful to Jason if he wished to wage war against the Colchians and carry away the Golden Fleece from there.

## Concerning the ship that first attempted the high seas, and was named "Argo" after its builder, Argus.

At that time, there lived in Pontus <note>The region around the Black Sea.</note> a very beastly and rough people who hated strangers and murdered whoever came to them. Jason, who wished to be famous, recognized that although it was difficult to do, it was not impossible to tame these peoples. Indeed, the more danger there was, the more praise he would hunt for. He prepared very diligently everything that would be necessary for war and built a ship on Mount Pelion. Never before had one of such size been made, for previously only small skiffs and flat-bottomed boats <note>Original: "nachen vnd weydling."</note> were used.

It is written that Sol <note>The Sun god, Helios.</note> fathered two sons, Perses and Aeetes, both cruel and wild tyrants, of whom one ruled in Colchis and the other in Taurica. Afterward, she took Aeetes <note>Some traditions suggest Aeetes was her uncle, others her husband.</note> and bore him three children: Circe, Medea, and Aegialaus. Circe applied herself to all kinds of poisons and inquired into the powers of roots and herbs. ...was named Draco <note>original: "Draco," Latin for dragon/serpent</note>, the legend of the Lindworm <note>original: "Lindtwurm," a wingless dragon or serpent of Germanic folklore</note> arose. Many fables have also been composed regarding Phryxus; for they say he traveled upon a ship that had a golden ram painted on the prow, and when Helle was unwillingly taken away, she clung to the back of the ship, fell into the sea, and drowned. Others claim that Phryxus was captured by the Colchians along with his tutor (who was named "Ram"), that the tutor was killed, and according to custom, the skin that they stripped from the tutor was stretched out in the temple. King Aeetes was given a prophecy that he must die if that same skin were ever taken away; therefore, he had the temple well-guarded with fortifications and men, and so that the skin would be handled with even greater care, he had it gilded. However, the youth Phryxus was given as a gift to Cambro the Scythian (who had come to him without hostility and had conceived a fondness for the boy); by him, Phryxus was raised as a child and later became a ruling king. From this, let everyone believe what seems best to him.

## How the sailors obtained the golden fleece.

Now Medea led the sailors who had arrived with her to the Temple of Mars, which was built upon a mountain two and a half miles <note>original: "dritthalb meil"</note> from the royal city of Sybaris. And when she came to the gate of the temple, she spoke with the guards in the Taurian language; because she was the King's daughter, she was admitted immediately. Thus the Greeks forced their way in with her and stabbed many of the guards, some of whom fled; but they took the fleece and ran by the nearest path toward the sea. Medea, as the legend says, killed the ever-watching dragon <note>original: "Lindewurm"</note> who guarded the fleece with sorcery and poison, and departed with Jason. When those who had fled reported to Aeetes what had happened, he hurried after the Greeks with whatever men he found already in armor, and he caught many of them on the shore with a skirmish. In this turmoil, Iphitus, the brother of Eurystheus (who assigned the labors to Hercules), was stabbed to death. But when the remaining Greeks ran to aid their own, Aeetes was killed by Meleager. And when the Greeks gained the upper hand, the Colchians all fled; yet the best of the Greeks were wounded, namely Jason, Laertes, Atalanta, and the Thespians, all of whom were healed by Medea within a few days using herbs and roots. When they were healthy again, they sailed from there, and when they reached the middle of the sea, a great storm arose, so that they stood in great danger. Then Orpheus made a vow—just as he had done before regarding Samothrace <note>Referring to the Samothracian Mysteries, to which the Argonauts were often linked</note>—and immediately the winds ceased. And there appeared by the ship the sea god Glaucus for two nights and two days; he escorted them and revealed to them the future struggles of Hercules, as well as his divinity. He also told how Castor and Pollux should be honored as gods and called the Dioscuri. While he addressed them one after another, telling each what his future held, he made it known that Orpheus had obtained from the gods that he [Glaucus] be sent to them now, to show them that when they returned home, they should offer sacrifices to the gods as they had twice vowed. When the ship's companions came to the region of Pontus, where Byzantus ruled and where the city of Byzantium now stands <note>modern-day Istanbul</note>, they erected an altar and sacrificed to the gods according to their vow, just as sailors still do today.

## What happened to the shipmates on their return 
### to Troy.

Afterward they boarded the ships again / through the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> and the Hellespont <note>the Dardanelles</note> they came to Troy. There Hercules sent Iphiclus and Telamon, the brothers, into the city to demand Hesione and the horses <note>Hercules had previously saved Hesione from a sea monster, and her father Laomedon had promised him immortal horses as a reward</note>. Since the other siblings were all set against him / Priam secretly brought weapons to Telamon / and released him / indicating what his father had undertaken / so that they would know how to protect themselves. Telamon and his men stabbed their guards / fled to their own people / reported the treachery of Laomedon / and marched against him as he intended to overwhelm them / thus a great battle took place between them / and the shipmates prevailed. Some of the ancient poets write / that Hercules did not destroy Troy when he arrived with the voyage <note>the Argonautic expedition</note> / but traveled there specifically with six ships for the sake of the horses. As Homer reports in his earlier writings / that Hercules conquered the city for the sake of the horses with six of his own ships / and a few men.

# Medea’s Marvelous Deed.

In this matter, it happened that Medea agreed to bring about the death of Pelias through trickery / for she possessed wondrously powerful ointments / some from her mother Hecate / and others from her sister Circe / which she had never before wished to use for the harm of any human being. But for the sake of Jason / she wished to avenge the insult as best she could / and when she showed them how she intended to do it / she let it be known what signals she would give them from the watch / after the deed was completed / namely, by day with smoke / and by night with fire. Thus she fashioned a hollow image of Diana <note>The Greek goddess Artemis</note> / which she filled with various poisons / she turned her own hair gray / and created large wrinkles / so that she took on the appearance of an old woman. Afterward, she took her token / the image of Diana she had made / and filled it with ointments / stopping and blocking the mouths of the common folk with her charms / and entered the city / which was already devoted to the worship of idols. She acted as if she were half-insane / and exhorted the inhabitants / telling them they should show honor to the Goddess / saying they had come from the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people living in the far north "beyond the North Wind"</note> / for the sake of the people's welfare and the King's benefit. Now when the people all ran toward the Goddess / and acted as if they were possessed / the priestesses brought her into the Palace / so that the King was also immediately seized by a sense of devotion. The daughters of the King / who were burdened with great piety / believed nothing else than that they would receive fortune and salvation from the Goddess / for Medea claimed that she and Diana had traveled through the air on two dragons <note>original: "würmen," referring to the winged serpents that pulled Medea's chariot</note> / around the entire world / and had nowhere found a king who seemed more devout to them than Pelias / therefore Diana had given her the command / that she should rejuvenate Pelias with certain arts / so that he might lead a peaceful life pleasing to the Gods for many more years. The daughters heard this and took it for a miraculous sign / and begged Medea / that she should prove the art upon herself. She ordered one of them to bring her fresh water / and when she had locked herself in a chamber and anointed herself / and through the power of herbs made herself / as she was / young again / at which the King and all who saw it were greatly amazed. For it seemed to them impossible without the special grace of God / that such an old woman / could be turned so quickly into a beautiful young maiden. They also say she created a phantom / so that the King and everyone else believed / she arrived escorted by dragons <note>original: "Lindewürmen"</note>. Since it was supernatural to behold / Pelias held Medea in great honor / believing she spoke the truth / and commanded his daughters / that they should do whatever Medea commanded them / and wait upon her / for it was unseemly that a royal person should be tended to by servants / but rather right / that his daughters should serve the Gods. At night, when Pelias had fallen asleep, she persuaded the daughters / that she would indeed rejuvenate Pelias / but he must first be boiled in a cauldron. When the daughters did not wish to do this / and said Medea should prove it first / she took an old ram <note>original: "wider"</note> and cooked it first / though she had them chop it into pieces first / thus she brought it back to life / and made a young lamb out of it. Then they believed her / except for Alcestis alone / who would not agree to the father being killed / but the others were ready. Now Medea forbade the daughters from touching their father yet / until she had completed her prayers / she took them all / and led them up a high tower / with burning lamps / there she spoke for a long time in the Colchian language <note>The language of Medea's homeland on the Black Sea</note> / delaying the time until everyone in the city had fallen asleep / then she sent the daughters to fulfill her command, which they then did. The shipmates had seen her signal—

## On the Cruel Death of Jason.

Now we will return to Jason. After he had been married to Medea for ten years, he fathered several children with her: Didmus, Thessalus, and later Alcymenus and Tissandrus. During this time, Medea was greatly loved by Jason for her beauty, wit, and other virtues. However, as her beauty began to fade with age, Jason began to woo Glauca, the daughter of Creon <note>Creon was the King of Corinth, not to be confused with the Creon of the Oedipus myth</note>, desiring her as his wife. Her father consented to this and set a date for the wedding. Jason intended to persuade Medea to agree to a willing separation, claiming he did not take Glauca as his wife out of contempt for Medea, but rather so that he might produce children who would inherit the kingdom. 

Medea was greatly aggrieved by this; she reminded him of his oath and the many kindnesses she had shown him. Jason, however, paid no heed to her, drove Medea out of the city, and held the wedding. Medea obtained permission to remain in the city for one more day. During that time, she prepared a certain root <note>original: "wurtzen"</note>—an ointment which, when smeared upon something, would cause it to break into an unquenchable fire. She smeared this upon the palace and burned it to ashes, along with King Creon and his daughter, the bride. Jason escaped. 

Some write that Medea’s children gave the bride gifts of clothing, which, once she put them on, afflicted and tortured her with their poison. When the father ran to help her, the poison clung to him as well, so that he also had to die. Even then, Medea was not satisfied and wished to further avenge herself upon Jason. For love, anger, and fury had so inflamed her that when she heard Jason had escaped the fire, she resolved to kill their children to cause the father pain. Only one of them escaped; she buried the others in the temple of Juno <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Hera</note>. Afterward, taking her most faithful advisors, she fled by night to Thebes to find Hercules. He had previously stood as guarantor <note>original: "bürg"</note> for the promises Jason had made to her in Colchis, and he promised her his help, just as he had pledged before. 

Jason, now having neither wife nor children, was told by everyone that he had well deserved this and had sinned against Medea; unable to endure this any longer, he stabbed himself. Terrified by this tragedy, the Corinthians asked what they should do with the bodies of the children. They were answered that they should offer the children the honors of heroes <term>hero worship: a religious practice of honoring significant mortals after their death</term> at their grave in the temple of Juno. 

Later, Thessalus, who had escaped his mother, moved back to Corinth and from there to Colchis <note>The text likely means Iolcus or Thessaly, Jason's actual homeland</note>, the fatherland of Jason. When he learned that the sons of Pelias had all recently died and that the kingdom belonged to him, he took possession of it and called his subjects "Thessalians" after himself. Although I know there is a dispute among some regarding the name of the Thessalians, we shall speak of that in another place. 

Medea, having found Hercules in a state of great madness—during which he had killed his own children—restored him to health.

Afterward, Theseus came to Athens from Troezen and accused her again of being a

The sorceress <note>Medea</note> was rightly forced to depart from the city. Then Aegeus promised to accompany her wherever she wished; she desired to go to Phoenicia, and he led her there. Afterward, as she traveled through the upper regions of Asia and was wedded to a king, she bore a son from him named Medus. He succeeded his father to the kingdom and named his subjects the Medes after himself. Since then, poets have written great wonders and strange things about her in serious poems. Some said that once Aegeus fathered Medus with Medea, the Athenians accompanied them and the son to Colchis; and as Perses had previously driven out his brother Aeëtes, Medea also killed Perses and made her son Medus the king. He inherited the kingdom located in Asia above the Pontus <note>The Black Sea</note>, which was named Media after him.

## Where and what landmarks the ship-mates
### left behind them.

It would be a long matter to describe everything that has been imagined about Medea, nor is it necessary. We wish, therefore, to say what remains concerning the ship-mates <note>The Argonauts</note>; for not a few of the ancients, including Timaeus, write that after the capture of the Golden Fleece, they performed a deed worthy of memory and wonder when King Aeëtes blocked their return path to sail back into the Pontus. They are said to have sailed up the waters of the Tanais <note>The Don River</note> to its very source, then carried the ship over land into another water, reaching the Ocean <note>The Atlantic or Northern Ocean</note> toward the North. Leaving the land on their left side, they reached the Gadeern <note>The people of Gades, modern Cadiz in Spain</note>, and from there sailed into our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>. A proof of this is that those who live by the Ocean almost all worship Castor and Pollux <note>The Dioscuri</note> as gods. Indeed, even down to our time, it is claimed that the brothers provide help to those sailing in the Ocean. Likewise, there are several places located on the Ocean which take various names from either the ship-mates or the Dioscuri. The narrow straits located between the Gades <note>The Straits of Gibraltar</note> still have clear landmarks. For when the ship-mates sailed toward the Tyrrhenian Sea, they came to an island called Aethalia <note>Modern Elba</note>; there they named the best harbor for their ship "Argoon" <note>After the ship Argo</note>. Similarly, in the Tyrrhenian Sea, twenty miles from Rome, a harbor was named after Telamon. In Italy, not far from Formiae, is Aeta, which was later called Caieta <note>Modern Gaeta</note>.

Afterward, the wind cast them into the Syrtes <note>Dangerous shallows off the coast of Libya</note>, and having been warned by Triton, the king of that place, they escaped once they understood the currents of the sea there. They gave him an ancient bronze vessel inscribed with ancient letters; this is said to still be shown among the Hesperians <note>Peoples of the West</note>. It should also not be kept secret that some write that the ship-mates sailed up the Danube <note>Original: "Abnaw"</note> to its source, and from there entered the Adriatic Sea. Time itself proves that such a thing could not be. Furthermore, the Danube flows into the Pontus through many mouths, while the Hister <note>The lower Danube</note> which flows into the Adriatic takes its name from the region of Istria. Thus the Romans, who campaigned with the peoples in the Danubian lands <note>Original: "Istereich"</note>, learned that the source of the Ister is located a full mile from the sea. This error arises because two waters share one name.

# Concerning the Argonauts and the Children
### of Hercules. Chapter V.

Now that we have related the deeds of Hercules, as well as those of the ship-mates <note>original: "Schiffgnossen," referring to the Argonauts</note>, we also wish to make mention of their children. After the death of their father, the children of Hercules remained with Ceyx, the King in Trachynia <note>Trachis, a region in central Greece</note>. When Hyllus and his brothers reached manhood, Eurystheus <note>The King of Mycenae who had imposed the twelve labors on Hercules</note> feared they might wrest the kingdom of the Mycenaeans from him and resolved to drive them all out of Greece. He gave notice to Ceyx that he must expel all the children of Hercules and Licymnius <note>A half-brother of Alcmene, Hercules' mother</note>. Furthermore, he demanded that he also banish Iolaus and the others who had been at war alongside Hercules from the land. So that no harm would come to Ceyx—as he was too weak to resist Eurystheus—they left the land voluntarily. They went to the most famous cities and petitioned them for citizenship <note>original: "Burgrecht," the rights and protections of a citizen</note> and protection, but none would accept them except for Athens. That city received them heartily and gave them Tricorythum (called the <term>Tetrapolis</term> <note>Meaning "four cities," a district in Attica</note>) to inhabit. Later, when the children of Hercules had all become wise men—as the children of Hercules were known for their foresight—Eurystheus became vexed by their rise. He attacked them with a great force, and the Athenians came to their aid. Iolaus, Theseus, and Hyllus became the commanders and defeated Eurystheus in a battle. He was stabbed to death by Hyllus during the flight, along with many of his men and all of his sons. Thus, by common counsel, the lineage of Hercules together with their war-comrades moved

Alcmene, having traveled to Thebes, was taken up <note>original: "verzuckt," referring to her apotheosis or divine assumption into the afterlife</note> and honored with divine worship. The others, including several of the sons of Hercules, settled in the land given to them by Aegimius, the son of Dorus, as his father had provided; there they established themselves. 

Tlepolemus lived in the field, and when he and Licymnius (the son of Electryon) could not come to an agreement regarding a certain choice <note>original: "wal halbe," likely a dispute over leadership or territory</note>, Tlepolemus stabbed him. Thus, he fled to Rhodes. In that same island dwelt Greeks whom Triopas <note>original: "Thriopatus"</note>, the son of Phorbas, had led there. Tlepolemus built three cities there and, with the advice of the merchants, divided the island into three parts, giving each part a capital city; these were Lindus, Ialysus, and Camirus. Having adorned the island with these cities, settled them well, and provided them with noble civil customs, laws, and practices, he became the lord over the entire island. He was held in high esteem because of his own good reputation and the merits of his father. Afterward, he went with King Agamemnon to the war against Troy.

### Concerning Theseus and his feats of strength. Chapter VI.

Now that we have spoken of the lineage of Hercules, the matter requires that we report something of the deeds of Theseus, who emulated the feats of strength <note>original: "kämpffstücke," or labors</note> of Hercules. His mother was Aethra, a daughter of Pittheus, and Neptune <note>God of the sea</note> conceived him with her; he was raised in Troezen. From his mother's father, Pittheus, he found the tokens—or as others say, found them under a rock—and came to Athens. Afterward, he took to the sea so that he might match the deeds of Hercules, intending to do that which might bring him eternal praise and fame.

This represents his victory over the bandit Sinis, also known as the Pine-Bender.</image-desc>

First, he dispatched Corynetes <note>original: "Chorinetum," referring to the bandit Periphetes</note>, who killed all strangers; he took his nickname from the club <note>original: "harnasch," used here to mean his equipment or armament</note> he carried, which was fit for a weapon. Secondly, he killed Sinis, who lived on the Isthmus and was accustomed to killing people cruelly. He would always bend trees down to the earth, then bind people to them by their hands and feet and let the trees snap back, so that they were torn apart. Thirdly, he killed a great wild sow that caused great damage around Crommyon. He also dispatched Sciron, who...

ccxiii
<header>The Fifth Book.</header>
<meta>catchword: the drought</meta>

[He] ended [his journey] in Megara where the **Scyronian cliffs** still are; from these he threw the passers-by, or he led them to a high cliff by **Chelone** <note>named after the Greek word for a turtle</note> and kicked them with his feet down into the sea. At **Eleusis** he killed **Cercyon** <note>The OCR reads "Creontem," likely a transcription error for the wrestler Cercyon</note>, who forced all passers-by to fight and wrestle with him; whoever he overcame had to die. He also did away with **Procrustes** <note>original: "Procyusten"</note>, who lived near **Corydallus** <note>original: "Curdalo"</note> on the way to Attica. This same man commanded the passers-by to climb onto a bed made for that purpose; whatever extended beyond it, he cut off; those who were not long enough, he stretched them out; from this he received his name, **Procrustes** <note>The name means "the stretcher"</note>. After these deeds, he came to **Athens** and recognized **Aegeus** by certain tokens. Afterward, he brought the **Marathonian bull**, which **Hercules** had led out of **Crete** into the **Peloponnese**, captured to **Athens**; there Aegeus sacrificed it to **Apollo**. And so that we may conclude the deeds of **Theseus**, we must speak of the **Minotaur**, also so that what we write may be clearer, we shall follow the chronology of that time.

# Concerning the Minotaur.

**Tectamus** <note>original: "Tectanus"</note>, a son of **Dorus** and grandson <note>original: "ânitlin," literally "little ancestor" or grandson</note> of **Hellen**, the son of **Deucalion**, when he sailed with the **Aeolians** and **Pelasgians** to **Crete** and ruled that same island, took **Creta** as his wife; by her he fathered **Asterius**. While the latter ruled in **Crete**, **Jupiter** <note>original: "Juppiter"</note> had abducted **Europa** from **Phoenicia** and brought her to **Crete** upon a bull. **Europa** bore **Minos**, **Rhadamanthus** <note>original: "Radamantum"</note>, and **Sarpedon**. **Asterius** had no children; he took **Europa** in marriage and adopted the three sons of **Jove** <note>original: "Jouis," the possessive form of Jupiter</note>. One of these, **Rhadamanthus**, gave the **Cretans** their laws. **Minos** came to the throne, took **Itone** <note>original: "Jeonem"</note>, the daughter of **Lyctius**, as his wife, and fathered by her **Lycastus**, who ruled after him. With his wife **Ida**, the daughter of **Corybas** <note>original: "Ceribanten"</note>, he fathered the second **Minos**, whom some consider the son of **Jove**. This **Minos** was the first among the **Greeks** to assemble a great fleet and rule over the sea. He took **Pasiphae**, the daughter of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"</note> and **Creta**, as his wife; by her he fathered **Deucalion**, **Catreus** <note>original: "Cratenum"</note>, **Androgeus**, and **Ariadne**, besides many illegitimate children <note>original: "banharten," literally "born on a bench" rather than the marriage bed</note>. **Androgeus** was invited [to Athens] with the consent of all **Athenians** while **Aegeus** still ruled; there he stood his ground in all contests and made the acquaintance of the lineage of **Pallas** <note>The "Pallantids," the sons of Pallas who were rivals to Aegeus</note>. **Aegeus** fell into suspicion that the children of **Minos** might eventually drive him from the kingdom with the help of the **Pallantids**; he arranged that **Androgeus** should travel to **Thebes** for a festival <note>original: "Kirchwey," an anachronism referring to a church fair or religious festival</note>, where he was stabbed to death by the inhabitants near **Mount Oenoe** <note>original: "Inoe"</note> in **Attica**. **Minos** mourned his son greatly and came to **Athens**, demanding that the killers of **Androgeus** be executed; the **Athenians** mocked him for this, so he renounced them and cursed them so that they should suffer thirst and a barren year. Thus a great drought came over the **Athenians** and over all of **Greece**, so that all the fruit perished. The leaders assembled to seek counsel from the gods on how to avert this misfortune. They were answered that they should go to **Aeacus**, the son of **Jove** and **Aegina** (the daughter of **Asopus**), and beg that he offer a sacrifice for them. When this was performed, the drought ceased throughout all of **Greece**, except among the **Athenians**; thus they had to seek counsel from the god again. It would not be granted (said the god) unless they did for **Minos** everything he demanded of them on account of **Androgeus**. Thus **Minos** commanded the **Athenians** that they should annually send seven boys and seven girls to the island of **Crete** as food for the **Minotaur**, as long as the beast lived. When they agreed to the matter, [the drought] ended.

## Concerning the Minotaur.

**Tectamus**, a son of **Dorus** and grandson of **Hellen** <note>original: "aniklin Heleni"</note> (the son of **Deucalion**), sailed with the **Aeolians** and **Pelasgians** to **Crete** and ruled that island. She was helpful and gave him counsel so that he might kill the **Minotaur** and come out of the **Labyrinth** again. She fled secretly with him by night, and they came to an island once called **Dia**, now called **Naxos**. There, **Dionysus** <note>original: "Dionysius"</note> loved her so much for her beauty that he took the maiden from **Theseus** and honored her above all women. Out of heartfelt love and mortal honor after her death, he took her crown of pure stars and set it among the constellations. Thus, when the maiden was taken from **Theseus**, it grieved his ship-comrades so deeply that they did not think of **Aegeus's** command, but instead sailed into **Attica** with black sails. When **Aegeus** saw this, he believed **Theseus** his son was dead; he committed a fatal deed and threw himself down from the stronghold <note>referring to the Acropolis in Athens</note>. After his death, **Theseus** reigned; he established several laws and expanded the city greatly with magnificent, costly buildings. Moreover, he brought many people together who wished to dwell in **Athen**, so that the city grew in power and prestige until it became the capital of all **Greece**.

## On the Marriage and Death of Theseus.

Now further concerning **Theseus**. **Deucalion**, the elder son of **Minos**, ruled in **Crete** and allied himself with the **Athenians**, betrothing his daughter **Phaedra** <note>original: "Phedra"</note> to **Theseus**. Previously, **Theseus** had fathered a son, **Hippolytus**, outside of this marriage by an **Amazon**; he sent him to his sister **Aethra** in **Troezen** <note>original: "Threcenen"</note> to be raised. **Phaedra** bore him **Acamas** <note>original: "Athamantum"</note> and **Demophon**. Not long after, **Hippolytus** came to **Athens** for a church-consecration festival <note>The translator uses the contemporary German "Kirchwey" to describe a religious festival</note>, and there his stepmother became very fond of him because of his handsomeness. When **Hippolytus** departed again, **Phaedra** founded a temple to **Venus** in the stronghold from which she could see into **Troezen**. One time she traveled with **Theseus** to **Pittheus**, where she propositioned **Hippolytus** to lie with her. **Hippolytus** was horrified by this vice and would not do it. This vexed the stepmother; when she returned to **Athens**, she accused **Hippolytus**, saying he had tried to shame her by force. **Theseus** doubted this and wished to inquire further into the matter, sending for **Hippolytus** to answer for it. When he heard the false accusation (for the messenger reached him in the field while he was racing with horses), the reins escaped him out of dismay, so that the horses went wild and unmanaged, overturning the chariot in which he stood so that it broke. **Hippolytus** became entangled by his clothes, and the horses dragged him to death. Because of the chaste life he had led among the **Troezenians**, they honored him afterward as a god. Following this misfortune, **Theseus** was also driven out of **Athens** and died in misery. The **Athenians** later regretted the misdeed they had committed against **Theseus**; they brought his bones home and honored him as a god, erecting a temple for him which contained a sanctuary <term>asylum<gloss>a place of refuge where people are free from arrest or harm</gloss></term> and is called the **Theseum**.

# Of the Abduction of Helen and Proserpine
-> affairs of love. Chapter 7. <-

Now we shall speak of the abductions of Helen, and also how Pirithous wooed Proserpine <note>Persephone, queen of the underworld</note>, for all of this is entangled with the deeds of Theseus. When Hippodamia, the wife of Pirithous (the son of Ixion), died and left behind a son named Polypoetes <note>original: "Polipitum"</note>, the father went to Athens to visit Theseus. Theseus was also a widower on account of Phaedra <note>original: "Phedre"</note>, who had passed away. Therefore, Pirithous persuaded Theseus that he should abduct Helen—who was then only ten years old and a daughter of Jove <note>Zeus</note> and Leda—as she was his kinswoman; for she was exceptionally well-bred and beautiful. So they went to Lacedaemonia <note>Sparta</note>, and when it seemed opportune, they carried Helen off to Athens. They cast lots to decide whose wife she should be, with the condition that whoever won her should be bound to help the other obtain a wife. When they had confirmed this with an oath, Helen fell to Theseus. This deed displeased the Athenians greatly; fearing them, Theseus brought Helen to an Attic city called Aphidna <note>original: "Amphideram"</note> and entrusted her to his mother, Aethra, and other friends to guard. 

Pirithous simply wanted Proserpine for his wife and revealed his plan to Theseus. Although Theseus saw that this was a godless undertaking, and urged him to desist, Pirithous persisted and reminded Theseus of his oath; thus, Theseus gave his consent to help him. When they had entered Hell <note>the Underworld</note>, they were both captured. However, for the sake of Hercules, Theseus was later released. Pirithous remained in Hell and received his godless, just reward. Some write that they both became free again. Helen’s brothers, Castor and Pollux, marched against Aphidna <note>original: "Amphydriam"</note>, conquered the city, and brought Helen (still a maiden) and Aethra, the mother of Theseus, back with them to Lacedaemonia.

# Of the Seven Kings who Besieged the City of Thebes
-> the siege. Chapter 8. <-

Time and opportunity now require that we speak of the seven princes who set out to besiege Thebes, and of the beginning and cause of that war. Laius, the King of the Thebans, had Jocasta, a daughter of Creon, as his wife. When she remained childless for a long time, he asked the gods whether he would ever have children, and he was answered: It would not be to his benefit to have children, for if he should have a son, that son would murder his father and bring his whole lineage into misfortune and misery. Despite this, his wife bore a son. He immediately had the child's feet pierced and ordered that he be thrown to the wild beasts in a forest. From this, the child was named Oedipus <note>meaning "swollen foot"</note>. The King's counselors did not wish to cast the child away and gave him to a woman to nurse and raise; she was a servant girl named Polybus's wife <note>original: "Polybia"; likely referring to Merope, wife of King Polybus of Corinth</note>. When Oedipus had become a man, Laius wished to inquire further about the child, and at that very same time, Oedipus—having learned that he was a foundling—traveled to Pythia to discover who his parents were. Thus, the son and father came to the region of Phocis; they happened upon each other as strangers, and Laius haughtily commanded Oedipus to move out of the way, at which [Oedipus] was angered...

## Of the Marriage and Death of Theseus.

Further concerning Theseus: Deucalion, the elder son of Minos, ruled in Crete and allied himself with the Athenians. ## Of the Riddle of the Sphinx
<note>original: "Von der Rätterschen Sphyngis." The word "Rättersch" is an early form of "Rätsel," meaning riddle or enigma.</note>

At the same time, a creature of two forms called the Sphinx came to Thebes. It posed a riddle and a questioning piece, and whoever did not solve <note>original: "errhůet," meaning to guess or discover the answer</note> it was forced to die, a fate that befell many. However, to the one who solved the question, the reward was to be the hand of Jocasta and the Kingdom of the Thebans. No one but Oedipus was able to solve it; the riddle was as follows:

->The earth produces a creature,<-
->Which first has two, then soon four feet,<-
->At last three, with but a single mouth.<-
->In the air, the water, sea, and<-
->The land, no creature carries a similar voice.<-
->Just then it loses<-
->Its speed, the more it has<-
->Of the feet upon which it then walks.<-
->For its strength decreases most<-
->When it has many supports and stays.<-
<note>The riddle describes the stages of a human life: walking on two legs as an adult, crawling on four as a babe, and using a staff as a "third leg" in old age. Curiously, this German translation lists the sequence as 2-4-3 rather than the more common 4-2-3.</note>

For the mother had taken a veil not only for her husband’s death, but for her father’s death <note>The original reads "vaters tod" (father's death), though in classical myth, the bribe usually concerned her husband’s life and her son’s participation.</note>. ->Concerning the Aeolians,<-
->Chapter ix.<-

In former times, Boetus, a son of Arne and Neptune <note>Neptune is the Roman name for Poseidon.</note>, moved into Aeolis and came to the place that is now called Thessaly; he called his subjects Boeotians after himself. Here we also wish to say something about the Aeolians. In ancient times, when some of the sons of Aeolus (who was a son of Hellen <note>The original has "Ellinis"; Hellen was the mythical ancestor of the Greeks.</note>, the son of Deucalion) dwelt in this region, Mimas ruled alone in Aeolis. His son Hippotes fathered Aeolus by Melanippe. This Aeolus had a daughter named Arne, with whom Neptune lay. This so angered her father that he gave the daughter to a stranger from Metapontum (who happened to be in Icaria <note>Original: "Kossien."</note>) with the instruction that he should take her with him to Metapontum. There she bore two sons, Aeolus and Boetus, whom this man of Metapontum adopted in place of his own children, for he had none of his own; furthermore, he had been exhorted by the gods to do so. When they reached manhood, an uprising occurred during the lifetime of the Metapontian, such that the youths came to power. Afterward, Arne and Autolyta <note>Original: "Autolipe."</note> quarreled with one another, and the youths killed Autolyta. This angered the man of Metapontum, so they prepared several ships and fled with their mother and many good friends. Aeolus came to certain islands situated in the Tyrrhenian Sea, which are named the Aeolian Islands after him; there he built a city which he called Lipara. Boetus, however, went to Aeolus, his mother's father, and was raised by him as a son; finally, the kingdom was given to him. He named the entire region after his mother <note>Arne</note>, but the people he called Boeotians. His son Itonus had four sons: Hippodamus, Electrion, Archylicus, and Algenor. From these were born: Hippodamus fathered Eleus; Electrion fathered Leitus; Algenor fathered Clonius; Archylicus fathered Prothoenor and Arcesilaus, who marched to Troy and were the leaders of the Boeotians.

Salmoneus was a son of Aeolus, the son of Hellen, son of Deucalion; he traveled from Aeolis with a great company and came to the region of Elis, by the river Alpheus. After him, he named the city Salmonea. He took Alcidice as his wife, the daughter of Aleus <note>Original: "Eleß"</note>, who bore him Tyro <note>Original: "Tyream"</note>, a beautiful and well-formed daughter. After this lady’s death, he married Sidero <note>Original: "Syderam"</note>, who acted like a stepmother and held a hatred for the daughter. Salmoneus, because of his pride and arrogance, was also hated by his subjects; because of his godlessness, he was struck and consumed by a bolt of lightning from Jove <note>Jove is the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note>. His daughter Tyro, while still a maiden, was ravished by Neptune <note>Poseidon</note>, and she bore Pelias and Neleus. After the death of Cretheus, a quarrel arose between Pelias and Neleus over the kingdom; then Pelias became a king over the bordering frontier of Iolcus <note>Original: "Jolco"</note> and allied himself with Melampus and Bias, the sons of Amythaon and Aglaia, and also with the Phthiotians and Archaeans, marching with a great army to the Peloponnese. Melampus was a <term>seer</term> <note>A prophet or soothsayer who could interpret the will of the gods.</note> and restored to health the Argive women who had become insane through the wrath of Dionysus. For such a good deed, Anaxagoras, the son of Megapenthes, gave him the second part of his kingdom of the Argives. But while he lived in Argos, he accepted his brother Bias as a co-ruler of the kingdom and took Iphianira, the daughter of Megapenthes, as his wife, with whom he fathered Antiphates, Manto, Bias, and Pronoe. Antiphates fathered Oicleus <note>Original: "Jocleum"</note> and Amalthaea with Zeuxippe, the daughter of Hippocoon. Oicleus and Hypermestra, a daughter of Lesbus, produced Iphianira, Polyboea, and Amphiaraus <note>Original: "Amphianum"</note>. Thus Melampus and Bias, along with their descendants, obtained the kingdom of the Argives. Neleus traveled with his people into Messenia and, with the consent of the inhabitants, built the city of Pylos <note>Original: "Pilum"</note>; while he ruled there, he took Chloris, the daughter of Amphion the Theban, as his wife, with whom he had twelve sons, the eldest being Periclymenus <note>Original: "Perydymonus"</note> and the youngest being Nestor, the very same who was in the Trojan War. So much for the ancestors of Nestor.

No one wished to forgive him for his murders, yet at last Jupiter granted him absolution. However, he then lusted after Juno and sought to lie with her. When Jupiter became aware of this, he shaped a cloud to look as if it were Juno herself; from this cloud, Ixion fathered the Centaurs. Because of this and his great misdeed, Ixion was bound to a wheel by Jove <note>Jove is the Roman name for the Greek king of gods, Zeus.</note>, upon which he was driven around in eternal torment after his death. Some say the Centaurs were raised by the nymphs on Mount Pelion, and that these same beings later approached certain mares, from which the <term>Hippocentaurs</term> <note>Literally "horse-centaurs," emphasizing the hybrid nature of the creature.</note> were born. 

But this fable arises from the fact that they were the first to master the art of horsemanship and breeding; thus, people perceived them as half-man and half-horse. These beings, as kinsmen of Pirithous, demanded a portion of the kingdom from him. When he refused them this, they waged war against him. But at last, he yielded to them and, when his daughter Hippodamia was betrothed to Theseus <note>In most classical accounts, Hippodamia is the bride of Pirithous, and Theseus is his guest and ally.</note>, the Centaurs were invited. Filled with wine, they attempted to indulge their lust with several of the women at the wedding. This insult so angered Theseus and the Lapiths <note>A legendary tribe of people from Thessaly.</note> that they slew many of the Centaurs and hunted the others out of the city. Those who were not killed fled partly into Pholoe, a region of Arcadia, and partly into Malea. And as they prospered there, they grew so bold that they troubled all of Greece with their robberies. For this reason, they were eventually completely wiped out by the local inhabitants.

### Of Aesculapius and his
->descendants. Chapter 7.<-

The story goes that Aesculapius was a son of Apollo and Coronis, and being of a most ingenious nature, he devoted himself to medicine. In this field, he discovered many useful things for mankind. He became so eminent in this art that he restored many to health whose lives had been despaired of, and it is even said he raised some from the dead. For this reason, he was accused before Jove by the gods of the underworld, as he was diminishing their realm by bringing many back to life. Enraged by this, Jupiter struck Aesculapius down instantly with a thunderbolt. Apollo wished to avenge the death of his son and killed all the Cyclopes who had forged the lightning bolt; because of this, Jupiter punished Apollo by forcing him to serve in the form of a mortal man. Aesculapius left behind two sons, Machaon and Podalirius, who followed their father’s craft. When they went to Troy with Agamemnon, they achieved great fame by healing many wounded Greeks. Therefore, all civic burdens were afterwards remitted for them.

One daughter was carried away by Apollo <note>original: "Apolline"</note> to the place where the city of Sinope is now built. There she bore a son named Syrus, from whom the Syrians derive their name. Neptune <note>The Roman name for the Greek sea god Poseidon.</note> took Corcyra and brought her to the island named after her; she gave birth to Phaeax, from whom the Phaeacians <note>The text reads "phenicier" (Phoenicians), but in the context of the Odyssey and Alcinous, these are the Phaeacians.</note> descend. Phaeax had a son, Alcinous, who later guided Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> home to Ithaca. Neptune carried away another daughter, Salamis, and brought her to the island that bears her name; she bore Cenchreus, who became the most renowned king in Salamis and killed a great serpent <note>original: "Wurm," which in this period often referred to a dragon or monstrous snake.</note> that had been terrorizing the inhabitants. Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> abducted Aegina from Phlius and brought her to the island named after her, where he fathered Aeacus. Aeacus ruled there and fathered Peleus and Telamon. Peleus was throwing a stave <note>Likely referring to a practice spear or discus; in myth, this was a tragic accident during athletic games.</note> and accidentally killed his brother Phocus. For this, he was driven out of the land by his father. He fled to Phthia, located in Thessaly, where he was granted absolution for the killing by King Actor. Because the king had no children, he adopted Peleus and made him king. From Peleus and Thetis was born Achilles, who fought at Troy. Telamon departed from Aegina for Salamis and took Glauca, daughter of King Cychreus, as his wife, ruling the island after his father-in-law. After Glauca’s death, he took Eriboea, the daughter of Alcathous, with whom he fathered Ajax <note>original: "Eantum"</note>; thereafter, he went to the Trojan War.

## On the lineage of Pelops and
### Oenomaus. Chapter 13.

Now we shall say something of Pelops. In the city of Pisa, located in the Peloponnese, Mars <note>Ares</note> fathered Oenomaus with Aegina, the daughter of Asopus. Oenomaus had an only daughter, Hippodamia. When he sought a prophecy regarding how long he would live, the answer given to him was that he must die once his daughter married. Therefore, he wished to keep her in eternal maidenhood so that she would take no husband, thinking he might thus prolong his life. Since many men desired the maiden, he established a contest: whoever wished to have his daughter had to win her in a challenge, but if he failed, he would have to die. The contest was of this sort: they had to race from the city of Pisa to the altar of Neptune which was erected on the Isthmus of Corinth. When the race began, Oenomaus would sacrifice a ram to Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. The suitor would start first with a small chariot pulled by four horses. Once Oenomaus finished his sacrifice, he would race after them with his charioteer, Myrtilus; whenever he overtook one, he would drive a spear through him. Pelops, the son of Tantalus—though many had already perished this way—beheld the daughter of Oenomaus at Pisa and undertook to win her. He bribed Myrtilus with money so that he was negligent in the race, allowing Pelops to reach the goal first. Oenomaus was greatly terrified, realizing the time foretold to him was at hand, and he stabbed himself. Pelops took Hippodamia and reigned at Pisa. He was a very wise man, and as he settled the land with many people, he called that same region the Peloponnese <note>Literally "The Island of Pelops."</note> after himself.

## Concerning Tantalus and Niobe. Chapter 15.

And since we have mentioned Pelops, it seems necessary to us—so that nothing worthy of memory is left out—to also describe his father, Tantalus, here. Tantalus was a son of Jove <note>original: "Jouis"; the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus.</note>, living in great fame and wealth. He dwelt in Asia, in the place that is now called Paphlagonia, and was well-regarded by the gods because of his noble descent. But he eventually became proud due to his prosperity; whatever secrets he happened to hear from the gods when he was their guest, he gossiped about to men. For this, he was punished while still alive, and after his death—as the poets write—he was cast into hell <note>In the context of Greek myth, this refers to Tartarus, the deepest part of the underworld reserved for divine punishment.</note> for eternal torment. He fathered Pelops and Niobe. Niobe bore seven sons and as many daughters, who were all very beautiful. Because of this, she became proud and boasted that she had more children than Latona <note>The Roman name for Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis.</note> herself. Enraged by this, Latona commanded Apollo to shoot all of the sons, and Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis.</note> to shoot all of the daughters of Niobe. This they did, so that in an instant, Niobe—once so rich in children—was deprived of them all. When Tantalus had enraged the gods, he was driven out of Paphlagonia by Ilos, the son of Tros; we wish to make some mention of him and his ancestors as well.

## Concerning Ilos and the Lineage of the Trojans down to Priam. Chapter 16.

The first to rule in the land of the Troad was Teucer, who was born of the water Scamander <note>A river god.</note> and the nymph Ida. He was a brave man who gave his name to his subjects <note>Referring to the "Teucrians," an early name for the Trojans.</note>. He fathered a daughter, Batea, whom Dardanus, the son of Jove, took as his wife. Dardanus thereby acquired the kingdom, and for this reason he called the inhabitants Dardanians. He also built a city of that name on the shores of the sea. His son Erichthonius first lived in great prosperity and wealth, as Homer says in the twentieth book of the Trojan War, when Aeneas recounts the origin of the Trojans to Achilles:

## Of Daedalus and his Ingenuity.
->Chapter xvii.<-

We wish now to proceed further to Daedalus, the Minotaur, and the war that Minos and Cocalus, the Sicilian king, waged. Daedalus was born in Athens from the lineage of the Erechtheids; his father was named Metion <note>original: "Mitionus"</note>, a son of Eupalamus <note>original: "Epulami"</note>, whose ancestor was Athenian, the son of Erechtheus <note>original: "Erichtei"</note>. Daedalus became a famous master builder. With many others whom he took as his assistants, he completed and crafted many a wondrous structure in many places in the world. In the making of statues, he surpassed all masters, so that he earned the fame that his statues walked and lived; he rendered all the limbs so clearly and so perfectly that many people marveled at them. The sculptors before him also made images, but they always lacked something in the eyes, hands, sides, or legs. Daedalus fled from Athens when he was already very famous, for he had committed a murder and was sentenced to death. A youth named Talus, who was his sister’s son, was taught by Daedalus; this youth discovered through his own contemplation the potter's wheel. And when he happened to step on the jawbone of a snake, he used it to cut a piece of wood; then he fashioned an iron saw modeled after that jawbone. Because of this, he revealed useful tools to the builders in many matters. Likewise, he also discovered the lathe <note>original: "dräzeüg"</note>, which served mankind well, and for which he earned great praise. Daedalus killed this youth out of envy, for it seemed a shame to him that he should be surpassed in his art by his apprentice. When he had buried the boy and was asked, quite mournfully, what he had buried, he answered: "a snake." It will seem a great wonder what I say: the snake, after whose jaw he had fashioned the saw, revealed the murder. When he was accused before a council in Athens, he fled to Crete to those who were afterwards called "Daedalids" after him; and because of his skill, he was welcomed by them and entered the service of King Minos.

## Of the Inhuman Lust of Pasiphae.

They say that when Pasiphae the queen lusted after a bull, Daedalus made her a wooden image of a cow, in which she stood, and was made pregnant by the bull. Long before this time, it was the custom of Minos to annually sacrifice a beautiful bull to Neptune <note>The Roman name for Poseidon, god of the sea.</note>. Now one year, when he intended to sacrifice, he regretted losing the most handsome bull and offered him a lesser one instead. To Jupiter to be a cupbearer.
The son of Ilus, within the memory of man,
Was Laomedon; from him came
Tithonus, whom Aurora <note>The Goddess of the Dawn.</note> took
As a lover. Likewise Priam,
And two more, Lampas and Clytius.
Hicetaon was the fifth; all were men of war,
Widely renowned for their heroic deeds.
Assaracus also fathered Capys,
From whom comes, with might and mind,
The proud Anchises, my father.
Hector the hero, how does he please
You? King Priam, the highly chosen,
Raised that very man.
Do you not think it adds to my glory
That I descend from such ancestors here?

### Of Daedalus and his Ingenuity
->Chapter 57<-

Furthermore, we shall now proceed to Daedalus, the Minotaur, and the war waged by Minos and Cocalus, the Sicilian king. Daedalus was born in Athens from the lineage of Erechtheus <note>A legendary archaic king of Athens.</note>; his father was named Metion <note>Original: "Mitionus"</note>, a son of Eupalamus, whose ancestor was Erechtheus. Daedalus became a renowned master builder. Together with many whom he took as assistants, he completed and crafted many wonderful structures in various parts of the world. In the making of statues, he surpassed all masters, so much so that he earned the reputation that his statues could walk and were alive; so perfectly did he craft all the limbs and features that many were astonished by them. The sculptors before him also made images, but they were always lacking in the eyes, hands, sides, or legs. Daedalus fled from Athens when he was already widely famous, for he had committed a murder and was sentenced to death. 

A youth named Talus <note>Often identified as Perdix in other versions of the myth.</note>, who was his sister's son, was taught by Daedalus; this youth discovered through his own contemplation the potter's wheel. And when he happened to step upon a snake's jawbone, he used it to cut a piece of wood; he then modeled an iron saw after that same jawbone. Because of this, he revealed a useful tool to the builders for many tasks. Likewise, he also invented the compass <note>Original: "dråzeüg," referring to a drawing or turning tool.</note>, which served men well and for which he achieved great praise. Out of envy, Daedalus killed this youth; for it seemed to him a shame that he should be surpassed in his art by his apprentice. Now, when he had buried the boy and was asked, quite mournfully, what he had buried, he answered: "a snake." It would seem a great wonder, what I say: the snake—according to whose jaw he had made the saw—revealed the murder. When he was then accused before a council in Athens, he fled to Crete to those who were afterwards called "Daedalids" after him. Because of his skill, he was well received by them and entered the service of King Minos.

### Of the Inhuman Lust of Pasiphae

The legend says that when Queen Pasiphae desired a bull, Daedalus made her a wooden image of a cow, inside which she stood, and was thus made pregnant by the bull. Long before this time, Minos had the custom of annually sacrificing a beautiful bull to Neptune <note>The Roman name for the Greek sea god Poseidon.</note>. However, one year when he intended to sacrifice, he regretted losing the most handsome bull and sacrificed a lesser one instead. Neptune was enraged at Minos and caused Pasiphae to lust for the bull. When Daedalus then helped her in her undertaking...
