...she bore the world-famous **Minotaur**, who was a bull down to the shoulders and a man from there downwards. To house this wonder, **Daedalus** built the **Labyrinth**, which had such confusing corridors that no one who entered could find their way out again; in that place they imprisoned the beast and gave it seven sons and seven daughters of the Athenians to eat every year, as was mentioned above. Daedalus feared the wrath of **Minos** because he had made the wooden cow <note>Daedalus built a hollow wooden cow for Queen Pasiphae so she could satisfy her lust for a bull, resulting in the birth of the Minotaur.</note>; he fled secretly from Crete with the help of the Queen, who gave him a ship and assistance. His son **Icarus** fled with him, but he fell into the sea and drowned not far from the island which, together with the sea, is named the **Icarian Sea** after him. From there, Daedalus sailed and came to **Sicily**, where **Cocalus** ruled; he was warmly received by him, and because of his great skill and good reputation, Cocalus showed him every honor.

### Concerning the Flight of Daedalus and Icarus

Some say that when Daedalus fell into the disfavor of Minos and **Pasiphae** had hidden him, Minos wished to punish him and had all the ships of the island pulled out of the sea, promising great rewards to whoever might find him. In response, Daedalus fashioned wings for himself and his son, which were fastened with wax. When he put them on himself and his son, and both were hovering over the sea, Icarus soared too high toward the sun, so that the wings became loose and the wax melted, causing him to fall into the sea. The father flew along the sea, often wetting his wings <note>Presumably to keep the feathers from drying out or the wax from overheating.</note>, and arrived on the island of Sicily. Although this is indeed a marvelous tale <note>original: "wunderbarlich gdicht"</note>, I did not wish to pass over it in silence.

Daedalus remained as a famous master craftsman for a long time with **Cocalus** in Sicily. He built several structures on the island that still remain; first, not far from **Megara** <note>The ancient city of Megara Hyblaea.</note>, he built the city of **Lymbethram**. Out of it flows a great body of water into the nearby sea, and it is called the **Alabus**. Near **Agrigento** <note>original: "Acragatina"</note>, at the place called **Camicus**, he built a city upon a rock that was impossible to conquer due to its fortification; for one had to climb such a narrow path to reach it that three or four men were sufficient to guard the road. <column-break/> There, Cocalus established his royal seat, and brought all his treasure there as to an unassailable place. Near the **Selinuntine** shore, Daedalus built a cave <note>original: "hülin" or "höhlein"</note> out of which a warm steam rose from a fire, so that those who stood near it sweated, and yet did not burn themselves, but rather cleansed themselves with great pleasure. On the cliffs of **Eryx**, there stood a temple of **Venus** <note>Mount Eryx in Sicily was famous for the sanctuary of Aphrodite/Venus.</note>; the path leading to it was exceedingly rough, dangerous, and narrow. **Daedalus** widened this path and built walls around it. He also constructed many other buildings in **Sicily**, which have now collapsed due to old age. Furthermore, to honor **Eryx** and **Venus**, he cast a golden **Ram** <note>original: "Wider"</note> with such great skill that many took it to be alive.

### How Minos Invaded Sicily, and Was There Brought to His End.

When **Minos** learned that Daedalus was in Sicily, he resolved—since he was well-equipped with ships—to make war upon **Cocalus**. He set out from **Crete** with his naval fleet and landed near **Acragantina** <note>The ancient city of Acragas, modern-day Agrigento.</note> in Sicily. Having disembarked his army there, he sent messengers to Cocalus, demanding that he hand over Daedalus or else prepare for war. Cocalus requested that the King himself should come to him; when he arrived, Cocalus said he would hand Daedalus over as a prisoner and invited Minos to be his guest. He then shut Minos in a hot bath for so long that he suffocated. Thereupon, he called the **Cretans**, saying their King had wished to bathe and had fallen into the hot water and perished; he then gave them the dead body to bury. His army interred him magnificently and built him a double grave: one part was hidden, where they buried the bones of Minos; the other part was where they built a temple of Venus, so that descendants for a long time thereafter honored it in the name of Venus. 

Later, when **Theron** <note>OCR reads "Thunus," likely referring to Theron, the tyrant of Acragas (r. 488–473 BC).</note> ruled over the Acragantines, the true grave of Minos was found, the bones were sent to Crete, and the structure was torn down. The Cretans who had remained in Sicily after the death of Minos could not agree on leadership; therefore, they behaved honorably toward the Sicilians with whom they lived, let the others sail home, and some of them built a city which they named **Minoa** after their king. Others sought out another suitable place on the seashore to build a city, which they named **Engyum** after the water that flows into the city. After the destruction of **Troy**, they received the Cretans and their leader **Meriones**—who had arrived there on his return journey—into the city as fellow citizens. Later, they moved out of the city of **Ochyra**, drove out their neighbors, and inhabited the landscape. As they prospered and grew in wealth, they built a temple to the two **Mothers**, **Cynosure** and **Helice**, where they practiced great idolatry.

They say these two once secretly nursed **Jupiter** to hide him from his father **Saturn**, and as a reward, they were placed among the stars as the two **Bears** <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note>. **Aratus** <note>A Greek poet (c. 315–240 BC) known for his poem "Phaenomena" about the stars.</note> testifies to this when he writes of the appearance of the stars at the very beginning, where he says:

> The stars as a whole, of which there are many
> In many a place, without end or limit.
> Eternally they are turned about,
> As is known from experience.

Therefore, it would be unjust for us to keep silent about how these two goddesses <note>Diodorus refers to the "Mothers" or Deae Matres, ancient goddesses of fertility and nursing</note> are honored, and what great wonders they perform. They are held in high regard not only by the citizens but also by foreigners with sacrifices and other honors. Several cities send costly vessels for their church festivals; for they believe, one and all, that things will go well for those who send some offering there. Their citizens offer them much gold and silver, and they have built for them a large and costly temple; for its construction, as they lacked sufficient stone quarries, they purchased stones from Astygion, the King of the Agyrians <note>Agyrium, a town in Sicily near the modern Agira</note>, at great cost, and dragged them more than two and a half miles <note>original: "dritt halb meyl"</note>. When the road proved too rough for them, they had wagons prepared, and with a hundred yokes of oxen, they brought the stones to the site. For although much expense was spent upon it, it was nothing compared to the church treasury they possessed. A little before my time—the time of Diodorus—this church held and possessed three thousand oxen, not counting the fields, from which they received a large annual income and profit.

## Of the Deeds of Aristaeus.
### Chapter xviii.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a man (Aristaeus) in a long robe instructing a woman on food production. He points toward the woman, who is working with a large bucket or churn. In the background, there is a goat and shelves holding several rounds of cheese.</image-desc>

Aristaeus was born to Apollo and Cyrene, the daughter of Hypseus <note>original: "Ipsei"</note>. Concerning his lineage, some say this: While Cyrene was yet a maiden, raised by Peneus <note>original: "Peleo", likely referring to the river god Peneus, Cyrene's father in most accounts</note>, she was wooed by Apollo because of her beauty. He carried her away by force, while she was still a maiden, to a place in Libya where the city of Cyrene now stands, and there she bore him a son, Aristaeus. He gave the child to the Nymphs to be raised, and they gave him three names: Nomius <note>meaning "The Shepherd"</note>, Aristaeus <note>meaning "The Best"</note>, and Argeus <note>meaning "The Hunter"</note>. From these same Nymphs, he learned the arts of making cheese, honey, and oil. Afterward, he also instructed mankind in how they should perform these tasks; for this, he was honored by posterity as a god, much like Dionysus. He came to Boeotia and took Autonoe, the daughter of Cadmus, as his wife. From this union was born Actaeon, whom the dogs later tore to pieces. Some say he [Aristaeus] was the cause. On one occasion, while hunting near the temple of Diana in a mountain range, Actaeon desired to ravish the goddess. Others write that it was because he boasted that he was a more skilled hunter than she. Both causes may have brought the goddess's disfavor upon him, for she truly had no desire for men; had he sought her, she would have been enraged. No less, by wanting to be a better hunter, he also offended her, for otherwise all the gods yield to her in that pursuit. Therefore, it is no wonder if the goddess became angry and transformed him into a beast <note>A stag</note> that the dogs tore apart.

They say Aristaeus, after the death of Actaeon, went to Delphi to inquire of Apollo <note>his father</note> concerning the course of his life, and Apollo answered him. He told him he would yet come to the island of Chios, where great honor would meet him. There is a story of how he sailed there: during the Dog Days <note>The hot summer period associated with the rising of the star Sirius</note> (which are called the rising of the star Sirius <note>original: "Syrischen gstirns"</note>), he held a sacrificial festival. At that time, the death <note>a plague or pestilence</note> in the land of Greece ceased, which otherwise was raging through the whole country. After this, when the Etesian winds <note>original: "Massen Ostwind", referring to the annual summer winds of the Aegean</note> blew, the dying also came to an end. Truly, a wonderful change of fortune for a man who was previously not highly esteemed. For he had before seen his son torn apart by dogs, and yet the Dog Star, which [afflicts] men...

### Of Eryx, Daphnis, and Orion.
->Chapter xix.<-

Eryx, as some believe, was the son of Venus and Butes, an ancient Sicilian king; he was a renowned man who, on account of his noble mother, was highly esteemed among men and ruled in one part of the island. There, upon a high rock, he built a city which he named after himself, and in the same

fortress he established a temple for his mother, which he adorned with precious jewels. Venus was so well-disposed toward this city that she received as much honor from the inhabitants out of love for her son as she did by being called Venus Erycina <note>Venus of Eryx</note>.

The fame of this temple is truly to be wondered at; for while many other temples have risen to the highest honor, they have at times been laid waste or fallen into misfortune; yet the honor and service of this temple, as they were established from the beginning, have never been diminished but were steadily maintained. After them, the Romans, who entirely conquered the island, surpassed all their ancestors with the gifts they gave to this temple. ## Of Daphnis.

Let enough be said here of Venus. Now we wish to speak of Daphnis. In Sicily, there are mountains that men call Erios <note>Likely referring to the Heraean Mountains in Sicily</note>. These are of such a nature that they are pleasant and fruitful the whole year round. Beautiful springs and great oaks,

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicts two figures in a landscape. On the right, a man (Daphnis) sits under a tree playing a bagpipe (Sackpfeife). On the left, another figure stands leaning on a long staff or spear, observing him.</image-desc>

the likes of which are otherwise hardly found, grow there, and other cultivated trees bear much fruit; many grapevines and great heaps of apples grow there. The trees are so very fruitful that they often came to the aid of the Carthaginians <note>original: "Carthaginensern"</note> during great hunger, and sustained them with fruit alone. There, in a pleasant forest, it is said that Daphnis was born to Mercury by a Nymph; he received this name because laurel bushes <note>Greek: *daphne*</note> grew there in great thickness.

Daphnis was afterwards raised there by the nymphs, and because he kept many cattle, he was named *Bucolos* <note>term: Bucolos, meaning "cowherd" or "herdsman"</note> on account of his guarding them. He also possessed a skillful understanding and applied great diligence to providing well for the livestock. He invented the shepherd songs (which are called *Carmina Bucolica* <note>original: "Carmina Bucolica", or pastoral poetry</note>), which are still held in great esteem among the Sicilians today.

They also say that out of love for Diana he took to the hunt and provided her much amusement with the bagpipe <note>original: "Sackpfeiffen"</note> and his composed songs.

A nymph wooed him and warned him that if he knew another woman, she would blind him; and when he later defiled a king's daughter while intoxicated, he became blind according to her prophecy.

For the part that was battered on both sides by the sea and its stormy waves was originally quite narrow; over time, the water wore it away entirely, and the chasm or gap thus carved out was named Rhegium <note>From the Greek word 'rhegnymi', meaning to break or tear asunder; modern Reggio Calabria</note>. A city of the same name was built on that very spot. Some say that the connection between the island and Italy was torn apart by an earthquake <note>original: "Erdbidem"</note>, which allowed the sea to flow through and created an island. However, Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet</note> disputes this opinion, saying that Orion

poured a promontory into the open sea which is called Pelorium <note>Cape Peloro, the northeastern tip of Sicily</note>, upon which he built a temple to his father Neptune <note>original: "Neptuno"; the god of the sea</note>, which the inhabitants always held in high honor. ccxxxiij
<note>page 233</note>

# Of Diodorus the Sicilian and
# most famous historian / from the beginning of the
### world / until its habitation / and the glorious rule
### of occurring histories. Sixth book.

->Preface.<-

<image-desc>A large, ornate calligraphic initial 'G' decorated with intricate scrollwork and floral patterns in the style of 16th-century woodcuts.</image-desc>
To write histories requires much, and among other things, that nothing be omitted concerning the courses of time and the circumstances of those things which one undertakes to bring to light. Additionally, it requires diligent attention to bring forth each matter as the proper order demands. Those who write should conduct themselves just as orderly <note>original: "sondern," here meaning particular or prudent in management</note> people do, who proceed in everything according to a careful arrangement, so that they might increase and maintain their goods. Such an approach brings, above all, great ornament and prestige to history books. The work of some is rightly praised for its ornate speech <note>original: "auffgemůtztẽ red"</note> and the dense inclusion of past events, but therein they have failed: they used greater effort and art in their writing than order. Therefore, many criticize and find fault with their writings. Timaeus <note>Timaeus of Tauromenium (c. 350–260 BC), a Greek historian known for his critical tone</note> promises he will describe time correctly and well and bring many histories to light, yet he is accused of being too eager to reject and criticize the opinions of others. For this reason, he is called the "Naysayer" <note>original: "Neidstich," literally "Envy-sting." Timaeus was historically nicknamed "Epitimoeus," meaning "The Detractor" or "The Fault-finder"</note> by some. Ephorus <note>Ephorus of Cyme (c. 400–330 BC), the first to attempt a "universal history"</note> has written a history book wherein he joins together all matters, both general and specific, in a free order. He is very eloquent in this and divides his books appropriately. We wish to follow his example as much as possible, and have dedicated this book to the islands, among which Sicily presents itself first, surpassing all others in fertility and ancient renown.

<summary>This page serves as the preface to Book Six, where Diodorus discusses the importance of chronological order in historical writing and critiques his predecessors Timaeus and Ephorus. He introduces his focus on islands, beginning with Sicily.</summary>

# The Sixth Book. 235
# Of the Island of Sicily. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A woodcut map of the island of Sicily and the southern tip of the Italian mainland (Calabria). Labels include: Calabria, Siglio, Pharus (depicted as a lighthouse), Messina, Etna (depicted as a smoking volcano), Catania, Syracuse, Pachynus, Agrigenti, Lilybaeum, Drepanum, Palermo, and the Aeolian Islands: Stromboli, Lipari, Saline, Vulcano, Filicudi, and Ustica. The island itself is marked "Sicilia".</image-desc>

This island was once, in long-past times, called "the Three-Cornered" <note>original: "drei ecket," referring to the Greek name Trinacria</note> because of its shape; afterwards, it was named Sicania by its inhabitants, and finally Sicily by the Italians. Its circumference is one hundred and nine miles. Because it is three-cornered, the distances are measured as follows: from Pelorus <note>The northeastern point, Cape Peloro near Messina</note> to Lilybaeum <note>The westernmost point, now Marsala</note> is forty-two and a half <note>original: "vierzig drytthalb"</note> measured miles; from there to Pachynus <note>The southeastern point</note>, the promontory of Syracuse, is thirty-eight and a half miles; and the third side is twenty-nine miles. 

The Sicilians say they have heard from their ancestors that Sicily was consecrated to Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture, known as Demeter to the Greeks</note> and Proserpine <note>Ceres's daughter, also known as Persephone</note>. Some poets write that after the wedding of Pluto and Proserpine, Jupiter gave this island to a nymph named Anacaliptra <note>A name meaning "unveiled," associated with the ritual unveiling of a bride</note> as a gift. 

Furthermore, the most prominent historians claim that the Sicanians, who first lived on the island, were not foreigners but indigenous people, and that these two goddesses first appeared on this island together. Indeed, the claim that grain first grew among them from the richness of the soil is testified by the most excellent poet Homer in the ninth book of the travels of Ulysses <note>The Odyssey</note>, where he relates how Ulysses came to the Cyclopes, saying:

And to this day, more wild wheat grows in the district of Leontini <note>A territory in eastern Sicily, modern Lentini</note>, as well as in other places on the island; and if one asks from where the use of grain first originated, it must rightly be attributed to Sicily.

# Of Ceres and Proserpine, the Two
## Goddesses. Chapter 2.

That these two goddesses brought forth and discovered the use of grain is manifest; for this discovery, they were first held in high honor in Sicily, and are still highly revered to this day. It is also said that Proserpine <note>The daughter of Ceres; known as Persephone to the Greeks</note> must have been abducted from Sicily, for the goddesses especially loved to dwell on the island. Her abduction <note>original: "verzuckung," literally a snatching away or rapture</note> occurred near Mount Etna, in the meadows situated by the city, which bore lilies and other kinds of flowers, as was worthy of the goddess. And there is still such a strong scent of noble flowers there that dogs cannot track scent, for the fragrance takes away their natural sense of smell. These meadows are quite level from the top down, full of leaping springs; at the very top and at the edges, there are high and smooth cliffs. The area below is called the "Navel of Sicily." <note>original: "Nabel Sicilie"; in Latin, *Umbilicus Siciliae*</note>. All around it are forests, lakes, and other wilderness. Moreover, there is a large cavern with a cleft facing North <note>original: "Mitnacht," a traditional German term for the North</note>, where they say Pluto <note>The god of the underworld</note> rumbled down into Hell with Proserpine. All things are green throughout the entire year; the lilies and flowers never fade. It is further added that Minerva <note>Athena</note> and Diana <note>Artemis</note>, these two virgins, were raised together with Proserpine, and it was their custom to spend time there in the month of May <note>original: "sich zuermayen," to enjoy the spring</note>, and they all three together made a garment for Jove, their father. For this reason, all three of them gained a great love for the island, because they had played and lived together there; each chose for herself a small place where she would later be honored. Minerva took for herself the region lying around Hymera, where, when Hercules passed through, the nymphs let warm water flow for him to wash. And the inhabitants dedicated that place and the city to Minerva, where the name still remains. Diana took an island in Syracuse called Ortygia, and it was granted to her by the gods, and the island was so named by her with mouth and bite <note>This likely refers to a folk etymology or a specific legendary naming ceremony involving the goddess</note>. There, the nymphs created a great fountain for her sake—

ccxxxvij
The Sixth Book.

...a spring therein, which is named Arethusa. This spring produced a great abundance of fish, not only in ancient times but also in my own days <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC, often writes from personal observation of his homeland, Sicily</note>, which did not harm people. But if anyone in a time of war was so greedy that he dared to catch those fish, he fell into great misfortune through the displeasure of the gods. Of this, more is said elsewhere.

Proserpine chose for herself this heath around Mount Etna; a great spring was dedicated to her at Syracuse, named Cyanes. But Pluto took Proserpine by force and carried her with him into Hell, not far from Syracuse. The Syracusans hold a great annual festival at the spring of Cyanes; the common man offers what he can afford, while the Council, on behalf of the city, drowns and sinks several oxen in the lake. They do this according to the teaching of Hercules, who, when he brought the oxen of Geryon to Sicily, performed his sacrifices in this same manner. 

They say that when Ceres could no longer find her daughter Proserpine anywhere, she lit a torch at Mount Etna and ran through the world searching for her. Wherever she was received by someone, she taught them out of gratitude how to sow grain and how to use it. The Athenians were the first after the Sicilians who, mindful of this benefit, honored this goddess with costly sacrifices (with the ritual pomp that they call <term>ἐνϑυσία</term> <note>Original Greek: "enthusia," referring here to divine sacrifice or inspired ritual</note>, and which is highly famous for its antiquity and purity). 

Also, when the goddess taught the Athenians how to sow and cultivate the fruit, and thereafter the sown corn thrived well for them, many others came to them to fetch it. The Athenians shared it generously with all people so that they might also sow it, and from there, it spread into the whole world. 

The Sicilians, mindful of the benefits they received from Ceres and Proserpine—in that they were taught by them how to use and cultivate grain—established religious services for both of them, each at a special time of the year. They celebrated Proserpine’s festival during the harvest with such great discipline and diligence as was fitting for such great grace. At the time of sowing, it was the turn of Mother Ceres; with such preparation and costliness for ten days together, they brought forth everything that recalled the ancient world. Jokes and even ribald words were permitted for everyone to use, so that the people would be moved to laughter, and the goddess might forget the sorrow she bore for her daughter.

Now, in this manner, the historians and also the poets write of the abduction of Proserpine. Carcinus, the "Earnest" writer of poems <note>Carcinus was a Greek tragedian who spent time at the court of Dionysius II in Syracuse</note>, often traveled to Syracuse so that he might learn the customs and secrets of the Sicilians regarding this goddess; he writes of her religious service there. He says Proserpine was snatched into Hell by Pluto, and Ceres thereafter grabbed a torch from Mount Etna and sought her daughter with wailing and lamentation, everywhere demonstrating the cultivation of fruit, and for this, she was thereafter held as a goddess.

One should never keep silent about this goddess’s good deeds, for she has shown much good to mankind. Aside from agriculture, she established many just and good laws, by which men may live well and in total peace if they follow them. For this reason, she is also called "The Lawgiver" <note>This refers to the title *Demeter Thesmophoros*</note>. For truly, without her established commands and discoveries, no one would easily have brought forth anything better; the reason for these laws is not only the sustenance of life but also its just and good preservation. But let this be enough of that.

CCXXXVIII
Of Diodorus Siculus

# Of the first Sicanians.
## Chapter 3.

Now back to the Sicanians, who were the first to live on the island, though historians disagree about their origins. Philistus <note>A historian from Syracuse and advisor to Dionysius I</note> writes that they came from Iberia and took their name from the Sicanus river in Iberia <note>The original German text uses "Hybernia" and "Hyberia"; while "Hybernia" usually means Ireland, in the context of Sicanian history, it refers to the Iberian Peninsula (Spain)</note>. Ephorus of Cyme rebukes him for his ignorance, saying that the Sicanians have lived on the island since time immemorial, and they possess many ancient signs of their long history, which need not be recounted here. These ancient Sicanians lived at first in the mountains, which were naturally well-protected and strong; they built cities there to protect themselves from robbers. At that time, they had no king; instead, each noble ruled his own city. Originally, they occupied the entire island,

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a volcanic eruption, likely Mount Etna. Fire and smoke burst from the jagged peak of a mountain. At its base, a fortified town with several towers and houses stands near a body of water.</image-desc>

and they practiced agriculture, which provided their sustenance. Later, when the mountain Etna spewed out fire and damaged the surrounding region for many years together, they fled in fear from the eastern parts and settled largely toward the west. A long time afterward, the Siculi <term>Sicels</term> <note>The Sicels were an Italic tribe who gave their name to Sicily</note> moved from Italy into the island and settled in the region that the Sicanians had abandoned. As they increased in power and wealth, they continually expanded their territory until they frequently clashed with the Sicanians, though they eventually agreed upon borders for the land. Finally, the Greeks also sent people to inhabit several places there; they built many cities along the seacoasts and traded with the others, so that both groups became acquainted and grew accustomed to one another. As the Greeks continued to arrive day by day, the old inhabitants let their own language fall away, spoke Greek, and called themselves Sicels.

# Of Lipari and other islands that are called the Aeolian Islands.
## Chapter 4.

Now follow the islands called the Aeolian Islands, of which there are seven in number: Strongyle, Euonyma, Didyma, Phenicusa, Sacra, Vulcania, and Lipara, in which there is a city of the same name. These islands are situated in a straight line between Italy and Sicily; the furthest is nearly four miles <note>The author uses "meil," an old German unit of distance, rather than modern miles</note> from Sicily, and they are of various sizes. The largest among them is four miles in circumference. All of them spew fire, and their volcanic vents can still be seen today. Even now, a great steam and stench <note>Referring to the smell of sulfur</note> rises from a cleft in the earth on Sacra and Strongyle <note>Modern-day Vulcano and Stromboli</note>. They hurl fiery sand and stones upward, just as happens at Mount Etna. Some say there are certain passages beneath the earth leading from Mount Etna to these islands, and that there is a single source that casts out fire in all of them. They also say that...

cccxxix
### The Sixth Book.

The islands were also not inhabited in ancient times; but Liparus, a son of King Ausonius, having fallen out with his brothers, sailed to the islands with longships and soldiers. He landed there and named the islands after himself; in one of them, he built a city of the same name and afterwards cultivated the fields on the other islands. When he had grown old, Aeolus, a son of Hippotes, came to him with a band of soldiers. Liparus married his daughter Lipara to him, and Aeolus thereafter ruled over the islands. When Liparus sailed back to Italy, he occupied several places near Surrento <note>Modern Sorrento</note>, which he governed with great renown. After his death, he was buried with great honors and achieved such status that his subjects honored him as a hero <term>Hero</term> <note>In the ancient Greek sense: a mortal who has died and is now venerated as a semi-divine protector</note>. The poet Homerus <note>Homer</note> mentions Aeolus in the travels of Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> at the beginning of his tenth book with these same words:

To assist me on my journey home;
I found his diligence unsparing,
For soon he gave me a bag; it was
Made from an ox nine years old.
In it, he thrust the storm winds,
For he has the power (as I have found),
Since Jupiter appointed him
To release the winds, or as it pleases him,
To shut them in, hold them, or drive them.
When I wished to stay no longer,
He placed the bag into the ship,
Tied at the opening <note>original: "pfeiff"; likely referring to the neck or nozzle of the leather bag</note> with a silver cord.

Blow gently for us in a quiet manner,
To carry and lead us safely

For nine days and nine nights we had
Advanced so far that on the tenth day
The fatherland lay just before us:
We could even see our hearth-fires.
And as I had been at the journey's helm,
With the steering oar in my hand
So that we might reach land the sooner,
I would not entrust it to any of my companions.
Thus, I was immensely tired,
Wherefore I drifted into a sweet sleep.
Misfortune then stirred my shipmates;
They began to speak among themselves,
Full of suspicion, and they believed
That Aeolus had gifted me greatly
With gold and silver; therefore,
Each said to the other: "How can it be?
Ulysses is held in high regard by everyone—
Loved, honored, and esteemed
In city and country, by young and old,
Wherever he goes. Moreover, he has
Plundered many jewels from Troy
And brings home a great treasure.
Look how fortune treats us!
Even though I travel in the same danger
Back and forth with him,
Yet I come home with empty hands,
While he is rich. Is it not a shame?
Look at what Aeolus has given him!"

There we stepped onto land again,
Drew water, and immediately sat
In the ship, consuming <note>original: "zächten" — to feast or drink together, often implies finishing off remaining rations</note> what we had.
We deliberated on what we should do;
I took my herald and a companion with me
And by the nearest path I walked to the court.
I found Aeolus with his wife and children
At the table; we quickly sat ourselves on the ground.
They were filled with great wonder at me there.
Aeolus spoke: "How so, how so?
Do you come back, Ulysses? Tell me:
Tell me, you thoughtless man,
What the devil troubles <note>original: "reüth" — to regret or to be plagued by something</note> you? Now, I have
Already once, completely and securely,
Dispatched you toward your house and home."
How I felt more anxious than anyone! "Truly,"
(I said) "my shipmates, and then
A miserable sleep overcame me.
They bring me into this burden;
Have mercy on me. I beg you earnestly,
All of you, help. You certainly have the power to do so."
My plea was full of good words,
Such that I brought the household’s mind
To compassion and kindness.
Only the father <note>referring to the patriarch Aeolus</note> lashed out at me.
He said: "Oh, be shamed, you lazy man!
Be gone quickly from the island! Look,
The earth never bore the like of such a rogue;
Even the gods are against you.
I do not wish for anyone to help you home;
Therefore, no one shall offer help to this man..."

Diodorus Siculus

-> Against those whom the gods rage, <-
-> Let the misfortune of your journey stay with you; <-
-> Every curse has brought you back to me. <-
-> I was cast out, and it was no jest, <-
-> Full of sorrow with a sighing heart. <-

We read elsewhere that Aeolus was a righteous and pious prince, who received strangers kindly and taught sailors how to attach the sail. From the fires of Etna <note>original: "Aethne"</note> he observed when and what winds would be certain to blow; for this reason, it is said of him that he had power over the winds. Because of his excellent fear of God, he was called a friend of the gods. He fathered six sons: Asthiotus, Xuthus, Androcleus, Feremon, Locastes, and Agathyrsus, who were held in great honor by all men for their virtue and piety, following the example of their father. Locastes ruled the territory around Regium <note>modern Reggio Calabria</note>; Feremon and Androcleus reigned over that part of Sicily that stretches from the Strait <note>original: "Far" — the Strait of Messina</note> to Lilybaeum <note>modern Marsala</note>. In that region, the Sicels <note>original: "Siculer"</note> lived toward the East <note>original: "Offgang"</note> and the Sicanians <note>original: "Sicani"</note> lived toward the West <note>original: "Nidergang"</note>. They waged war with one another, yet they surrendered to the sons of Aeolus, both because of their father’s goodness and their own diligence and loyalty. The land lying toward the Leontines was under Xuthus and is still called Xuthia after him today. Agathyrsus held power in the place that still bears his name, along with the city. Asthiotus ruled in Lipari <note>original: "Lypara"</note>. All these sons followed their father’s example in Sicily in piety and goodness, attaining great praise, and their lineage ruled for many years until it finally died out. Then the Sicels gave power to their noblest and most pious men. The Sicanians, however, quarreled among themselves for the lordship.

### Which foreigners inhabited Sicily. Chapter 5.

But many years later, when the island's population decreased, some came from Cnidus <note>original: "Gnido"</note> and Rhodes, who had been too heavily oppressed by the authorities in Asia, to occupy and cultivate a part of Sicily. Their leader was Penthatlus of Cnidus, who traced his lineage back to Hippotas, the son of Hercules. During the fiftieth Olympiad, when Epistheliades was the victor, they were sent to the promontory of Lilybaeum. Since the Egestaeans <note>original: "Egester"</note> and the Selinuntines <note>original: "Selinunter"</note> were at war with each other, they allied themselves with the Selinuntines but lost the battle; Penthatlus their leader perished along with many of his men. Those who survived the war wished to depart from there and appointed Gorgus, Theston, and Epitherses, the counselors of Penthatlus, as their leaders. When they came to Lipari, they were welcomed. Five hundred of them remained on the island because the Tyrrhenians <note>original: "Thyrener"</note> were blocking the sea with their piracy. Some built ships to protect themselves, and others worked the land so that they might live in common <note>The author describes a communal or "socialist" system where the Liparians shared labor and property</note>. One part fought against the enemies and helped the others; they lived from a common treasury for a long time. And when they later became the lords of the city of Lipari, they used the fields of the other islands in common. Later, they cast lots to decide who should possess or farm this island or that, for they had divided themselves so that everyone should live there with his people for twenty years. They eventually defeated many of the Tyrrhenian pirates and sent a tithe of the booty to Delphi <note>original: "Delphos"</note>. It is fitting that we describe the causes from which the prosperity and the growth of such high honors for the Liparians arose.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a large, ornate multi-tiered fountain where several figures, including children and adults, are bathing. First, the nature of the land is adorned with beautiful heaths; it has many healing baths that bring health and pleasure. For this reason, many Sicilians <note>original: "Siculer"</note> burdened with illness travel there, enter the baths, and recover their health. In addition, the island has a special mineral which they call Alum <note>original: "Alumen" or "Alant," a mineral salt used historically in dyeing and medicine</note>, from which the Liparians <note>residents of the island of Lipari</note> and Romans receive a large annual income. Since Alum grows in no other place in the world, these islands bring great profit. This island is not large, but it is fertile in everything that a person might enjoy; it has all kinds of fish and sweet fruits from the trees. Beyond Lipari toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang," literally "the going down" of the sun</note> lies a very small island,

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a small island with trees, surrounded by water. The base of the landmass is encircled by a gruesome mound of human skulls and long bones, arranged in distinct rows.</image-desc>

which is desolate and called Osteodes <note>original: "Osteodis," from the Greek "Osteodes" meaning "bony" or "full of bones"</note>. At the time when the Carthaginians fought against the Syracusans, they sent a large host of infantry <note>original: "fůßvolck"</note> with a great naval fleet to Sicily. Because they had such a diverse rabble of many different tongues among them, the soldiers often became restless and rebellious. They ran before the tents of the Captains <note>original: "Hauptleüth"</note> demanding their pay, threatening that if they were not paid, they would pay themselves <note>implying they would loot the area</note>. After the Captains reported this to the Council, they were secretly commanded to act as if they intended to lead them into battle against one another, but instead to separate the rebellious from the rest of the host, put them on ships, and lead them to this island. Thus they were led there and left without any food until they all died of hunger. Because of the great many bones <note>original: "gepeyn"</note> of the dead humans found there, the island received its name.

# Of the islands of Malta, Gozo, Methalio,
### Kerkenna, and others. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a group of islands in a sea. Several large, multi-masted sailing ships with rigging and flags are navigating between the islands. The islands feature fortified towns with high towers, walls, and various buildings. In the distance, mountain ranges rise from the horizon. The foreground shows a coastline with trees and a small cluster of houses.</image-desc>

**As** we have now also described these eight Aeolian Islands <note>original: "Aeolider Inseln"</note>, we wish to see what other islands are situated nearby. Toward the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally "midday," the direction of the sun at its peak</note> lie three islands, all of which have good, safe harbors. Located two miles <note>The text says "zwo meyl," though Malta is significantly further from Syracuse; the author likely uses a large historical league or follows a specific manuscript tradition</note> from Syracuse, they are very easy to reach by land. The inhabitants there are well-provided for, as they practice all kinds of crafts; they make good linen cloth that is quite soft and pure. Given the suitability of the location, they build handsome houses finished with gypsum <note>original: "gypß"</note>, and this island is almost like a palm garden, for many grow there. Whoever sails toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang," the setting sun</note> finds a refuge on this island, as it has many good places to harbor; this brings the inhabitants great profit and honor because of the kindness they show to the merchants. There is also another island called Gozo <note>original: "Gaulos"</note>, which has many convenient harbors and is also full of palms. After that is Kerkenna <note>original: "Cercinna"</note>, which lies toward Libya, in which there is a noble city with a good sound <note>original: "Sund," a strait or harbor</note> that was quite convenient not only for merchants but also for warships. Also, extending from Lipari <note>original: "Lypara"</note> there are other islands located in the Tyrrhenian Sea, among which one is called Aethalia <note>The ancient name for the island of Elba</note> opposite Populonia <note>original: "Populania," an ancient Etruscan city</note>, located nearly two-and-a-half miles' journey from the land. This island takes its name from its king. There, iron ore <note>original: "eysen-artz"</note> is dug in great heaps, and they smelt large cakes <note>original: "kūchen," referring to iron ingots or "pigs"</note> from it, which the merchants later carry into foreign lands. They also make tools from it for agriculture, as well as weapons and other things that they offer to foreigners for sale.

# Of the Island of Corsica. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>A woodcut map showing the Italian peninsula and the surrounding Mediterranean islands. The map is labeled with several cities and regions, including Milan, Venice, Genoa, Italy, Rome, Naples, Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily. To the right (East), the regions of the Wends <note>original: "Windon," referring to Slavic-speaking areas</note>, Bosnia, and Dalmatia are indicated. A small sailing vessel is depicted in the Tyrrhenian Sea between Italy and Corsica. The landscape is illustrated with stylized mountains and architectural representations of cities.</image-desc>

Seven and a half miles <note>The "mile" here refers to a historical German league, much longer than a modern mile</note> from there lies another island, called *Cyrnos* <note>original: "Cyrnos"</note> by the Greeks, though the Romans and the inhabitants call it *Corsica*. It is easy to reach by ship and has a beautiful harbor which they call *Syracusium*. Within it are two cities, Calaris <note>likely Alalia, a Phocaean colony</note> and Nicea. Calaris had its origins with the Phocaeans, who were later driven out by the Tyrrhenians <note>The Etruscans</note>. Nicea was built by the Tyrrhenians who live by the sea, and they have subjected other islands lying in that sea to their rule. When the Tyrrhenians brought the island under their control, they imposed an annual tribute of resin, wax, and honey, of which the island produces a great deal. The subjects <note>original: "knecht," which can mean servants or slaves; historical sources note that Corsican slaves were uniquely valued for their honesty</note> who are on this island have a very different way of life from others, and this is by their very nature. It is a wide, broad island, quite mountainous and full of forests, and it has a great deal of water with which it is irrigated. The people live among one another virtuously and friendly; they nourish themselves on milk, honey, and meat, of which they have plenty. Honeycombs are found in the trees, and every person keeps whatever they find. Everyone marks their own sheep and lets them go to pasture, and no harm comes to them. It is a wonder what an honorable and pious life the common man leads there. They also have a strange custom <note>This practice is known as the "couvade"</note> when a child is born: when the woman gives birth, she does nothing for the child <note>meaning she does not take a period of rest</note>; instead, the father, just as if he himself had suffered the pains of birth, stays at home for the duration of the confinement and performs the housework. A large forest of nothing but yew trees grows on this island, from which a bitter honey is produced. The inhabitants have a particular language of their own that is not easy to understand. There are about thirty thousand people on the island.

Sardinia is located not far from this island and is about as large as Sicily. The Iolaeans inhabit it and boast that their lineage descends from Iolaus and the Thespians. For at the time when Hercules performed his Labors, he sent his sons, whom he had fathered by the daughters of Thespius <note>The "Thespiades" were the fifty daughters of King Thespius, all of whom bore sons to Hercules</note>, along with many Greeks and other people—at the command of the gods—to settle Sardinia. When Iolaus, the nephew <note>The original German uses 'äncklin', which can mean grandson or descendant, but mythologically Iolaus was the nephew and companion of Hercules</note> of Hercules, observed this, he also came to the island, built several beautiful cities, conquered the land entirely, and named the subjects after himself. Many theaters, temples of the gods, and other things beneficial to mankind—the traces of which are still present—were established by him. And as it had been prophesied that the inhabitants' possession of the land would last forever, this has remained true even to my time, Diodorus. For even when the Carthaginians had already conquered this island, they still could not rule over the Iolaeans, for they fled into the mountains; there they dug caves and lived in them, subsisting on the cheese, milk, and meat of their livestock, of which they had plenty. They abandoned farming on the plains and lived in the mountains in peace; although they were frequently attacked by the Carthaginians, the latter were forced to desist because of the ruggedness of the terrain and leave them free and unburdened. Indeed, the Romans could gain nothing from them. Once Iolaus had arranged everything pertaining to the possession and settlement of the land, he returned to Greece. After the Thespians had ruled the island for a long time, they finally sailed to Italy and occupied the region around Cuma; those remaining on the island chose the most prominent among the people as leaders, abandoned their coarse ways, and have lived in freedom until this day.

# Of the Oceanic Islands.
### Cap. v.

## Of English tin.

We shall now speak of the tin that is mined among them. The Britons who live around the promontory of **Belerio** <note>modern-day Land's End in Cornwall</note> are somewhat more civil than the others; this is because many merchants visit them for the sake of the tin that is mined there. They dig it out of stony ground, the veins of which can be excavated without great difficulty. They then transport the tin to an island situated near Britain called **Icta** <note>likely St. Michael's Mount, which is reachable by foot at low tide</note>. This place is an island because, when the tide goes out, it leaves the ground so dry that they can transport the tin there on wagons. The islands located between Europe and Britain have a unique nature: during the incoming tide they are islands, but during the outgoing tide they are not. At this location, the merchants collect the tin and carry it into **Galatia** <note>referring here to Gaul, modern-day France</note>. In thirty days, they bring it as far as the mouth of the **Eridanus** <note>here likely referring to a trade route terminus rather than the river Po in Italy</note>. So much for tin.

[...amber is] otherwise found nowhere else in the world. For some poets and historians say that **Phaeton**, the son of the Sun <note>original: "Solis"</note>, while still a child, begged his father to let him lead the chariot of the sun for a single day. Phaeton fell into the waters of a spring, which was then called the **Eridanus** <note>the mythological name for the Po River</note>. These same trees still drip every year at that same time, and from this is made the amber, which is more precious there than anywhere else. But because experience has shown that this is merely a poem <note>original: "gdict"</note>, we wish to write the truth. On the island of which we have spoken, the amber grows, and it is brought by the inhabitants to the nearest lands, and from there it is brought to us. Furthermore, because we mentioned nothing in previous books about the peoples who border **Europe**, we wish to remedy that deficiency here.

# Diodorus Siculus

[She was] beautiful; she despised all who desired her as a wife, believing that no one was worthy of her. Now when **Hercules** undertook the war against **Geryon** <note>original: "Geryonem." In Greek mythology, Geryon was a giant with three bodies whose cattle Hercules was tasked to steal</note> and came into **Celtica** <note>The ancient territory of the Celts, primarily modern-day France and surrounding regions</note>, where he had built the city of **Alesia**, she felt a desire for Hercules because of his manhood and brave spirit. She obtained permission from her parents to sleep with him and conceived a son by him, whom she named **Galatus**. This son surpassed all his peers in joyfulness and strength of body. 

Now, when he had become a man and was established in his grandfather’s kingdom, he conquered many surrounding places with his skillful military maneuvers. And as he became proud because of this, his subjects had to be called **Galatians** <note>Diodorus here uses the term Galatians to refer to the Gauls</note> after him, and the land was also named after him. Now, **Galatia** is inhabited by various peoples, who are quite distinct among themselves in number. **Greater Galatia** is capable of fielding two hundred thousand men; **Lesser Galatia** has about five thousand. This people alone has always maintained friendship and alliance with the **Romans** consistently up to this time. 

It is a cold land because it is situated almost toward the **Midnight** <note>A historical term for the North</note>. In winter time it has no rain but is covered with snow; indeed, there is such great cold there that even the waters freeze so that one may walk across them, not only with goods and wagons, but entire armies can be led across without harm. Many large waters with strange courses flow through Galatia; some spring from the mountains, others from lakes. Some flow into our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>, others into the **Ocean** <note>The Atlantic or Northern seas</note>. Of those that flow into our sea, the **Eridanus** <note>The Po River in Italy, often identified with the mythical Eridanus</note> is considered the largest; it rises in the **Alps** and flows through five branches into the sea. The largest that flow into the Ocean are the **Rhine** and the **Danube**. In our time, **Gaius Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar</note> bridged the Rhine with wonderful labor, led his infantry across, and defeated the Galatians who live across the Rhine. Many other navigable waters are in Celtica, which we will not mention for the sake of brevity. However, they all freeze over in winter time; people strew them with straw so that they are not so slippery, and then they walk across safely. But it is almost unbelievable to write that in the summer time, the winds from the North and the West blow so strongly in Greater Galatia that they hurl stones as large as a handful, as if they were sand, in a heap. Sometimes they tear the clothes and armor from a person's body, or even throw a rider from his horse.

## Concerning the drink of the ancient Germans.

Likewise, there is such great cold and harshness of the air that neither wine nor oil grows there; therefore, the people must boil a drink from barley that they call <term>Beer</term> <note>original: "Bier"</note> or <term>Zythum</term> <note>An ancient Greek and Egyptian term for beer</note>. Likewise, they also use water and honey, from which they make a drink called <term>Mead</term> <note>original: "Meth"</note>. They drink wine so gladly and are so greedy for it that when the merchants bring it to them, they drink it with very little restraint, pouring it down without water. From this, they become so full that they fall asleep or become senseless. This is why the **Italian merchants**, chasing profit, travel by both road and water to carry wine there; sometimes, for one **amphora** <note>A large ceramic jug</note>—about half an **Augsburg pail** <note>A local German liquid measurement</note>—of wine, they receive a handsome boy or a chamber-servant in exchange.

# The Sixth Book.

All of **Galatia** <note>original: "Galatien." Referring here to Gaul, modern-day France</note> has no silver, but they have gold enough without the need for art or labor. For the waters that flow down from the mountains have many bends; when they reach the plains, they overflow the banks and cast up sand. There, they measure the nuggets that glisten, crush them, and wash them with water. Once the dirt is removed, they place them in a smelting furnace, cast them, and once poured and purified, they use the gold for adornment for both men and women; for they make from it rings for the fingers and neck, arm-guards, and great golden chains. Likewise, they decorate their breastplates and weapons with gold. The great **temples** <note>original: "bannsen." Likely referring to sacred enclosures or temple precincts where treasures were kept</note> have a special manner and custom in their **idolatry** <note>original: "Götzendienst." A common Early Modern term for non-Christian religious practices</note>; for when they offer sacrifices, they scatter gold about. Although these people are otherwise greedy for gold, yet no one is so daring that he would venture to pick it up.

## On the form and appearance of the Germans.

<note>While the text says "Teütschen" (Germans), the descriptions that follow are historically attributed to the Gauls or Celts by Diodorus Siculus; the author here uses the terms somewhat interchangeably for the northern "barbarian" tribes</note>

They are delicate, white-skinned men, straight of body, and although they have red hair by nature, they dye it to make it even redder. With a spindle, they curl their locks of hair and pull them so that they fall back over their 

<image-desc>Two woodcut portraits: the left shows a man with shoulder-length wavy hair and a long beard wearing a flat cap; the right shows a man with a large mustache wearing a head wrap or turban.</image-desc>

shoulders, so that they look exactly like **Satyrs** <note>Nature spirits from Greek mythology, often depicted with wild hair</note> and children. They make the hair thick with great effort, so that it is almost like a horse's mane. Some shave their beards; others do not. The nobles shave their cheeks very close, but let their **mustaches** <note>original: "Knebel"</note> grow so long that they cover their mouths, so that they even soil them while eating, and their drink passes through them like through a **pipe** <note>original: "kånel." Referring to the way the mustache acts as a filter or channel</note>.

## On the feasts and tables of the Germans.

They all sit at their meals, not on chairs, but on spread-out skins of dogs or wolves. Young boys serve them at the table; the fire is near them, and around it stand pots full of meat, and spits full of roast. They set the best piece of meat before the most prominent and distinguished guests, just as one reads in **Homer** was done for **Ajax**, one of the captains, when he had withstood **Hector** in a fight; there, among other things, it is said:

> On the other side they hurried with a shout
> Through the whole camp everywhere
> To the King Agamemnon,
> For Ajax, who had done so well in battle,
> The best [portion], which made them more joyful.
> When he was brought before the hero's tent,

When they invite guests, they do not tell them what business they wish to conduct until after the meal is finished. It may also happen that after the meal, they come together in such heated words that blows follow, and even death.

### On the opinion of the ancient Germans concerning the soul.

They hold the opinion of Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras of Samos was an ancient Greek philosopher who taught the "metempsychosis," or the transmigration of souls into new bodies after death.</note> that souls are immortal and travel from one body into another; for this reason, they do not value life so highly. Some even venture to throw letters into the fire where the corpse is burned, as if the deceased would be able to read them.

### On the war equipment of the ancient Germans.

Across the field, in battle, they use small-wheeled chariots; these are guided by the [driver] who sits within them. In battle, they shoot from the carts, then [jump] down and immediately fight on foot with the sword. Some fear death so little that they fight entirely naked. The [poorer] men are appointed by the rich as bodyguards to [serve] them in war and carry their shields. Before the battle lines, the nobles step [forward] and challenge the boldest of the enemy to combat, clattering their weapons to [terrify] the foe and instill fear.

### On the heroic songs of the Germans.

If someone has conducted himself well in war, they compose a song about him and his ancestors and sing his praise. But whatever the enemy does, they [insult]. Indeed, they highly praise all those who are bold in war. When they hack off the heads of their enemies, they hang them from the necks of their horses. The plunder that is sprinkled with the blood of the enemy must be hung before their houses by the servants with great rejoicing, just as if it were a trophy taken from wild animals. But where they have hacked off the head of an enemy commander, they embalm it and show it to their guests; they will not release it for ransom to either friends or enemies. Even for its weight in gold, they would not exchange it; for this, many mock them, as if it were an unrefined sort of pride. For although the tokens that show a man has behaved honorably in war are not for sale, it is nevertheless a boorish thing to continue to wage war against the dead.

### On the clothing of all Germans.

Their clothes are made of rough wool and have many colors, so that they might appear more fearsome; they call these breeches <note>original: *Brůech*; these are the characteristic trousers of the Northern tribes, which the Greeks and Romans found distinctive compared to their own tunics.</note>. They wear striped cloaks, lined in the winter time and thin in the summer.

### On the household goods and weapons of the Germans.

They use thick, decorated earthenware drinking vessels. Their defense consists of a shield as long as a man, which is decorated according to each person's individual taste. Some have bronze figures of animals upon them, both for the better protection of the body and for greater ornament and dignity. Without helmets or cheek-pieces, they wear upon their heads ornaments and coverings shaped like horns, birds, or four-footed animals. Their trumpets have a harsh and terrifying sound. Their breastplates are made of iron, though some take the first thing at hand with which to defend themselves, fighting even while naked <note>Historical accounts often claimed that certain Gallic warriors fought naked to demonstrate their courage and lack of fear of death.</note>. Instead of knives, they have long iron swords which hang on their right sides from bronze chains. Some gird their coats with gold or silver belts. They fight with spears which they call lances; the iron point upon them is about a cubit long, or even longer, and two spans wide. Their swords are no shorter than the boar spears of other nations, and the iron points of their spears are no shorter than other people's swords; their swords are sometimes curved, sometimes straight, suited for both the thrust and the stroke.

### On the language of the Germans, their song,
->and stringed instruments.<-

These are people who have a stormy countenance and a coarse, rough manner of speaking. They speak with short and obscure words, and sometimes intentionally say uncertain things. They are inclined to boast of themselves and to disparage others. They make use of threats and envy; they hold themselves in high regard, have sharp wits, and are not unsuited to the arts. They also have speakers and master-singers who use a certain manner of song; because of their poetry, they call them Bards <note>term: <term>Bards</term> (original: *Bardos*); ancient poets and musicians who recorded the history and genealogies of their people.</note>. These men have instruments like organs <note>likely referring to the lyre or harp mentioned in classical Greek sources, which the 16th-century translator interprets through the musical technology of his own time.</note> to which they sing instead of the fiddle, praising some and scolding others.

### On the learned men who were among the ancient
->Germans.<-

Those among them who are skilled in sacred writings and the knowledge of natural things are called Saronides <note>term: <term>Saronides</term>; a name used by Diodorus Siculus for high-ranking Druids or philosophers.</note> and are held in great honor. They have soothsayers who, by the flight of birds and by sacrifice, announce future events; these are held in high esteem by the common people.

### On the counsel-taking of the ancient Germans.

When they wish to handle a significant matter and take counsel upon it, they have a strange custom that is almost unbelievable. They stab a man to death with a sword. From the way he falls, turns, writhes, and bleeds, and from all other signs, they determine from ancient experience what they ought to do.

# On the Divine Worship of the Ancient Germans.

They never perform sacrifices unless a <term>natural philosopher<note>original: *Natur Künstler*; in this context, the author refers to the Druids or priests who were believed to understand the laws of the physical and divine worlds.</note></term> is present. For they say it is proper that such offerings occur in the presence of those who are knowledgeable of the divine nature and are pleasing to the gods. They believe that through the intercession of these men—whose advice they employ in both times of war and peace—their prayers may be granted all the sooner.

## How Highly the Arts are Held Among the Germans.

Their <term>speakers<note>original: *Sprecher*; these are the Bards, the poet-historians of the Celtic and Germanic tribes.</note></term> are held in such high honor among them that even when two parties are armed for war and standing in battle formation with bared weapons and lowered spears against one another, should these men run between them, both friend and foe cease their fighting. Thus, even among the roughest of peoples, the arts are held in such high esteem that they calm their anger; even <term>Mars<note>The Roman god of war, used here to represent the spirit of battle.</note></term> fears and honors the <term>Muses<note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note></term>. Now we shall describe a matter that is little known.

...be called <term>Galatians<note>original: *Galathe*.</note></term>. The Romans call them all by the common name <term>Gauls<note>original: *Galates*; the author is conflating the Galatians of Asia Minor with the broader Celtic/Gallic peoples.</note></term>. Their women are as large as the men and possess a manly strength. While they are still children, they are somewhat pale, but as they reach maturity, they take on their <term>fathers' coloring<note>original: *vätterliche farb*; likely referring to a ruddy or tanned complexion acquired with age.</note></term>. Even now, according to ancient custom, they devote themselves to murder and robbery; they do no work and earn nothing, but take only what belongs to other people. These are the fellows who conquered Rome, later plundered the <term>temple of Apollo at Delphi</term>, and made a large part of Asia pay them tribute, occupying the lands they seized there. Those who moved from there into Greece were all called <term>Gallo-Greeks<note>original: *Gallogreci*.</note></term>. They also slaughtered great and mighty armies of the Romans. Just as they are otherwise wild, so too are they god-

less. And they use wild things in their idolatry. Those who have forfeited their lives through crime are kept for five years, then fed as a sacrifice to the gods; they are then taken and thrown into a fire along with other first fruits. Some take both the cattle and the people they capture from their enemies and burn them alive or torture them in other ways. And even though they have beautiful wives, they prefer the company of boys. They sleep on the ground upon spread-out skins of wild animals; the rich have guards on both sides. There is a particularly indecent trait among them: they shamelessly show their handsome and naked bodies in public and consider it a disgrace if someone does not wish to have relations with them in front of everyone. Enough of that.

## On the Celtiberians or Spaniards. Chapter xv.

Now we shall turn to the <term>Celtiberians</term>. In former times, the <term>Celts</term> and <term>Iberians</term> quarreled over the land, yet they made peace, divided the territory, intermarried, and from this community they obtained their name. Thus, as these two powers became friends in such a fertile land, they made the name of the Celtiberians widely known; in the end, they could hardly be defeated even with the heavy wars the Romans waged against them.

# On the Bravery and War Weapons of the Spaniards.

<image-desc>A woodcut map of the Iberian Peninsula showing the regions and major cities of Spain and Portugal. Labeled locations include Gallicien, S. Iacob (Santiago de Compostela), Burgus (Burgos), Nauar (Navarre), and Der Ronceuall (Roncesvalles) in the north; Portugal, Lisbona (Lisbon), and Tolet (Toledo) along the Tagus river (labeled Tarus fl.) in the center; Aragonia and Barfalon (Barcelona) in the northeast; and Granat (Granada), Sibilia (Seville), and Valenz (Valencia) in the south. The island of Mallorca is shown off the east coast. The landscape is depicted with mountains and architectural icons for cities.</image-desc>

Whether on horseback or on foot, they are a warlike people, and they can endure all hardship better than other nations. They wear short, black clothes made of wool that resembles goat hair. Some of the <term>Celtiberians<note>A group of Celts inhabiting the central-northeastern Iberian Peninsula.</note></term> carry <term>targes<note>original: *tartschen*; small, round shields.</note></term> and others carry <term>bucklers<note>Small shields held by a handle.</note></term> as large as shields; they wrap their legs with <term>felt boots<note>original: *filzstifflen*.</note></term>, and on their helmets, they stick palms. Their swords are also made of polished iron, a <term>span<note>A unit of measure, about nine inches.</note></term> in length, which they use once the battle has begun. They have a unique way of forging iron armor: they bury iron plates in the earth and leave them lying there until rust consumes the weakest parts. The better part remains, from which they make the finest weapons and armor, which neither helmet, shield, nor anything else can withstand. They carry two swords on horseback; once they have chased the enemy, they leap down and assist the infantry.

# On Personal Care among the Spaniards.

They have a most strange custom that makes them quite unappealing and uncouth, though they are otherwise clean in their conduct and eating. They bathe their whole body in <term>urine<note>original: *pruntz*.</note></term> and also wash their teeth with it, saying that this cleanses the body best of all.

# How the Spaniards Conducted Themselves Toward Others.

Enemies and useless people lose their <term>necks<note>original: *hals verlhorn*; an idiom for being executed or killed.</note></term> among them. However, they treat strangers and guests well. They take in pilgrims, provide them lodging, and each man strives to show more honor to his guest than the next. He who is followed by many strangers gains great fame, and they consider him a friend of the Gods.

# On the food of the Spaniards.

They nourish themselves with many kinds of meat and make a drink out of honey, of which the land is full. They drink wine that is brought to them by merchants. No neighbors are dearer or more welcome to them than the <term>Vaccaei<note>A Celtic people of the northern plains of the Iberian Peninsula, known for their communal farming.</note></term>. Every year they divide the land; each man knows what he is to cultivate, and when it comes to the harvest, everyone is entitled to his share. If anyone steals anything from a peasant, he must die immediately.

# On the Lusitanians.

->Chapter 16<-

Among the Celtiberians, the <term>Lusitanians<note>An Indo-European people of the western Iberian Peninsula, inhabiting what is now Portugal and parts of western Spain.</note></term> are considered the most spirited. They carry <term>targes<note>original: *Tartschen*; small, round shields.</note></term> made of <term>sinew<note>original: *gäder*; refers to cords or animal guts used for strength and flexibility.</note></term>; with these, they cover their whole bodies in war. They are so skillful and light with them that they can parry all blows and shots. They have arrows with points and wear helmets and swords just like the Celtiberians.

## On the agility of the Lusitanians.

They draw out battles for a long time; their lightness of foot allows them to flee the enemy quickly and then pursue them just as swiftly. However, they cannot endure as much as the Celtiberians. In times of peace, they dance and jump with great speed and light leaps. Marching in step, they enter battle and sing a song of joy when they catch sight of the enemy.

## On the brigandage of the Spaniards.

When the Iberians and Lusitanians reach manhood and are pressed by poverty—their bravery and strength being their only help—they dig great caves in the mountainous places of <term>Tiberia<note>Likely a reference to the mountains of the Ebro (Iberus) region or perhaps the Carpetanian mountains; the original German text uses "Tyberien".</note></term>. They settle there and, acting as robbers, being lightly armed and making use of the agility of their bodies, they run through neighboring lands. Once they have taken booty and are well-laden, they run back to the mountains, relying on the rugged terrain so that no army can reach them. The Romans frequently campaigned against them and tamed them somewhat, but they could never stop them from their robbing.

Now we shall speak of the abundance of fine silver that is mined among the **Iberians**. In the deeds of **Hercules**, it is mentioned that the mountains of **Iberia**, which are called the **Pyrenees**, surpass all other mountains in height and size. For they lie from the southern sea to the Northern Ocean, dividing the **Gauls** <note>original: *Galater*; referring here to the Celtic peoples of Gaul.</note> from the **Iberians**. They stretch into **Celtiberia** for about seventy-five miles. Because they were thick with forests, it is said that in ancient times, shepherds set fires there that burned the entire mountainous region, and from this, the mountains were named **Pyrenees** <note>The name is traditionally derived from the Greek word *pyr*, meaning fire.</note>.

As they burned together for many days, it is said that streams of silver flowed forth, which the inhabitants did not recognize. They gave this silver to **Phoenician** merchants in exchange for goods of little value. The merchants carried it to and fro into **Asia** and **Greece** and became wealthy from it. Their greed drove the merchants to such lengths that, when their ships were fully loaded with silver, they replaced their anchors and other weights made of lead with silver, casting the lead away. Thus the **Phoenicians** became rich and sent people to inhabit desolate places in **Sicily**, **Sardinia**, and other nearby and adjacent islands, as well as in **Libya** and **Iberia**.

A long time afterward, when the **Iberians** learned to recognize silver, they began to dig mines. Finding many veins of silver, they obtained great wealth from them. **Gold**, **silver**, and **copper** <term>copper<note>original: *speiß*; likely referring to copper or a bronze-like alloy found during the smelting process.</note></term>, the three most noble ores, are found there, such that a quarter of the earth is ore. The masters of the mountains can obtain an <term>Euboean Talent<note>A standard unit of weight and currency in the ancient Greek world, roughly 26 kilograms or 57 pounds.</note></term> in about three days. The countryside is so full of silver that it is a marvel how the earth can bear it and how the inhabitants can perform the labor. The first who worked these mines became wealthy, for the silver was found in heaps. 

Later, when the **Romans** conquered **Iberia**, the **Italians** who took over the pits and the venture were also not made poor by it; for they put their purchased slaves to work there. These slaves dug many miles deep into the earth, seeking the silver veins and making deep and wide tunnels from which they brought out much gold and silver. This mining is much easier to perform and brings more profit than that in **Attica** <note>Referring to the silver mines of Laurium in Greece.</note>, for there, people spend great wealth in vain, as they either find nothing or, if they do find something, it does not cover the costs. In **Spain**, the mine owners do not have to worry so much; they find more, for the quality of the mine consistently yields large amounts of gold and silver, and it is nothing but ore. 

Sometimes they find water in the pits, which they must drain away if they wish to avoid damage. They do this in a most wonderful way, driving the water out with certain pumps or winches which they call <term>Egyptian screws<note>Also known as the Archimedean screw; a machine historically used for transferring water from a low-lying body of water into irrigation ditches or for draining mines.</note></term>, thereby drying the pits. This tool is said to have been invented by **Archimedes** when he came to the **Egyptian** mines. Truly, the skill of this **Archimedes** is to be marveled at, not only in this matter but in many other works he performed in other parts of the world. We shall speak of these when we come to the time in which he lived. The slaves who work there gain great wealth for their masters, for they labor at the work day and night without ceasing; some are worn out by...
