### Diodorus Siculus

**cclxxij**

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'N' at the beginning of the text, decorated with classical foliage motifs.</image-desc>

Now we will speak of the great quantity of good silver that is dug up in **Iberia** <note>original: *Hyberiern*</note>. As was mentioned in the deeds of **Hercules**, the mountains of Iberia—which are called the **Pyrenees** <note>original: *Pyreneos*</note>—surpass all other mountains in height and size. For they lie from the southern sea to the Ocean in the North, dividing the **Galatians** <note>Gauls</note> from the **Iberians**. They stretch into **Celtiberia** for about seventy-five miles <note>The "German mile" used by 16th-century translators was much longer than a modern mile, roughly 7.5 kilometers</note>. Because these mountains are thick with forests, they say that in ancient times, shepherds set them on fire, burning the entire mountainous region, and from this event, the mountains were named **Pyrenei** <note>The author derives the name from the Greek word *pyr*, meaning fire</note>.

As they burned together for many days, it is said that little streams of silver flowed out, which the inhabitants did not recognize. They sold this silver to **Phoenician** merchants for a meager price. The merchants carried it here and there into **Asia** and **Greece** and became very wealthy from it. Their greed led the merchants so far that, when their ships were fully loaded with silver, they replaced their anchors and other weights made of lead with silver, throwing the lead away. Thus, the Phoenicians became wealthy and sent people to inhabit desolate places in **Sicily**, **Sardinia**, and other nearby and neighboring islands, as well as in **Libya** and Iberia.

But a long time later, when the Iberians learned to recognize the silver, they began to dig mines. Since they found many veins of silver, they obtained much wealth from them. Gold, silver, and copper <note>original: *speiß*; likely referring to copper or a bronze-alloy ore</note>—the three most noble ores—are found there, such that the ore often makes up a fourth part of the excavated earth. The mine owners can sometimes obtain an **Euboean Talent** <note>A Greek unit of weight, roughly 26 kilograms or 57 pounds</note> in just three days. The landscape is so full of silver that it is a wonder how the earth can bear it and how the inhabitants can endure the labor. 

The first to build these mines became rich, for the silver was found in heaps. Later, when the **Romans** conquered Iberia, the **Italians** who took up the mines and the fortune were also not made poor by it. They brought their purchased servants <note>enslaved laborers</note> there, who dug the mines many miles deep into the earth, searching for the silver veins and making deep and wide passages from which they brought out much gold and silver. 

This mining is much easier to manage and brings more profit than that in **Attica** <note>The silver mines of Laurium in Greece</note>, for there, many spend their great wealth in vain; they either find nothing, or what they find cannot cover the costs. In **Spain**, the mine owners do not have to worry so much; they find more, for the quality of the mine always yields large clumps of gold and silver—it is nothing but ore. Sometimes they find water in the pits; this they must lead away if they wish to avoid ruin. They do this quite wonderfully by driving the water out with certain pumps or winches, which they call **Egyptian screws**, and so they dry the mines. 

This tool is said to have been invented by **Archimedes** <note>The Archimedean screw is a machine historically used for transferring water from a low-lying body of water into irrigation ditches or for draining mines</note> when he went to the Egyptian mines. It is truly right to marvel at the skill of this Archimedes, not only in this piece but in many other works he made in other parts of the world, of which we will speak when we come to the time in which he lived. The servants who work there gain great wealth for their masters, but they labor day and night without ceasing; some are worn out <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page</note>...

For the **Carthaginians** arranged it all in this way, and through the diligence they applied to the silver, they established these operations during the time they ruled in **Iberia** <note>original: *Hyberie*</note>. They thus brought together a powerful army and waged many wars against their enemies. By these means, they often placed the **Romans**, the **Sicilians**, and also the **Iberians** in the greatest danger, solely because of their wealth, which they had amassed in gold and silver to pay the wages of these foreigners. [The Iberians] were considered by the ancients to be a prudent and lucky people in gaining wealth; but the Italians yield to no one in this same regard. Likewise, there are tin mines in Iberia <note>ancient name for the Spanish Peninsula</note> which were found not by chance (as some write) but through great labor, just as silver and gold are refined. Above Lusitania <note>modern-day Portugal</note> in the islands of the Ocean, much tin is found, and for this reason the islands are named the **Cassiterides** <note>literally "the Tin Islands," likely referring to the Scilly Isles or the coast of Cornwall</note>. However, much tin is also brought from the island of **Britain**, which lies opposite Gaul, which the Celtic merchants bring on pack-horses through Massalia <note>modern Marseilles</note> to Narbonne; these are the best and most convenient cities for the merchants' trade in that region, having been built and settled by the Romans. But so much for the Gauls and Celtiberians.

->Of the Ligurians and Tyrrhe-<-
->nians. Chapter 17.<-

Now we will proceed to the **Ligurians**; they live in a harsh and infertile land and support themselves with great, bitter labor. For the region is almost entirely covered with trees; some are occupied with woodcutting, others with plowing, which is very difficult due to the stones, for no one can dig up a clod of earth without hitting a stone. They are well-accustomed to this work; their bitter life causes them no distress, and although they work hard, they gain little profit. Constant work and exercise make their bodies lean but strong. The women work just as hard as the men and are accustomed to working alongside them. They are constantly occupied with hunting, and what the farming does not provide, the wild game makes up for. They are well-accustomed to the snow and the rough mountains, becoming agile and healthy from them. Some, because they have no grain at all, eat partly domestic and partly wild animal meat; water is their drink. Herbs that the region bears are also their food; in short, the two most useful gods, **Ceres** <note>Goddess of agriculture and grain</note> and **Dionysus** <note>original: *Dionysius*; the God of wine and revelry</note>, have never visited them. They lie on the bare earth, rarely under a roof or in huts; some creep into caves or hollows made by nature or by hand, which serve as their shelter; thus they live like the ancient world, without any sort of luxury. The women have the strength of men, and the men are like wild animals in power and boldness. They say that in wars, a fat Gaul has often been challenged to single combat by one of these Ligurians and slain. They carry lesser weapons than the Romans; a long targe <note>a type of shield</note> covers their body, which is made in the shape of the Galatians' shields; they wear tucked-up tunics and decent swords. Their armor is sometimes made of wild animal skins. Some who have made acquaintance with the Romans conduct themselves after the Roman manner. They have sharp wits and are daring not only in war but in all of life. They engage in trade, sailing the Sardinian and Libyan seas, willfully putting themselves in great danger; for they have barques <note>small, light ships</note> that are not as well protected as the merchant ships of other sailors, which is why they are often lost in storms. # Diodorus Siculus

[They] held command and lordship, were a brave and high-spirited people, and built many rich and magnificent cities. Also, they were powerful upon the sea, ruling it for a long time; and that part which touches Italy is named the Tyrrhenian Sea after them. They also commanded a very large force of infantry well-trained in warfare, and they invented the war trumpets <note>original: "Hörthorn," likely referring to the *tuba* or *lituus*</note> which are perfect and useful in battle. They honored their commanders with many marks of distinction, giving them lictors <note>original: "bittel," the ceremonial attendants who carried the fasces</note>, an ivory chair <note>original: "helffenbeininen stůl," the *sella curulis* or magistrate's seat</note> upon which they sat, and red purple robes to wear. On their houses they built porticos <note>original: "vorschöpff," referring to the architectural style of the atrium or vestibule</note> where the servants remained while waiting for their masters. In these matters, the Romans followed them and improved upon them. They also applied themselves to the noble arts, exploring the things of nature; they also diligently studied divine writings, being especially skilled in prophecy, which they interpreted from thunder. So it is that even to this day, these men are held in honor by everyone, and they are employed for this art <note>The practice of the *Etrusca Disciplina*, or Etruscan divination</note>. They dwell in a fertile land, which they improve with diligence and cultivation. They eat twice a day and live well; they wear embroidered <note>original: "gepluempte," meaning flowered or patterned</note> clothes and have various golden vessels and a great number of servants and slaves. Not only slaves serve them, but also free men. At last, they abandoned their bravery and spirit, gave themselves over to laziness and gluttony, and lost the glory in war attained by their ancestors. This was partly the fault of the land, which was so fertile that they fell into luxury and laziness because of it. The Tyrrhenian land has wide fields, divided by small hills, and when cultivated they are entirely fertile, for they have enough water not only in winter but also in summer.

# The Sixth Book.

[Some] mountains, the others situated in valleys and wide fields. Capital cities, which are more exquisitely built than others, well-fortified and settled with wealthy citizens. The whole land has many heaths and pastures, and an abundance of livestock; the plains are well watered by large streams so that they might be more fertile; and for this reason, this part of Arabia is called the Blessed <note>original: "die Sålig," referring to Arabia Felix</note>. Now, there in the Ocean, many islands are situated opposite it, three of which deserve to be described. In one of these, one may not bury the dead, and it is called Sacra <note>original: "Sacra," meaning "Holy Island"</note>. The second is situated about a quarter of a mile away; there they carry the deceased. Sacra has no fruit other than frankincense <note>original: "Weyrach"</note>; of this, so much grows that it is exported to the whole world for sacrifices to the gods; it also bears myrrh <note>original: "Myrrhen"</note> and other fragrant spices.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a tree with a thick trunk and visible roots, with sparse branches and clusters of leaves, representing a myrrh tree. It is positioned on the left side of the following text block.</image-desc>

They collect the frankincense thus: it has a small stalk on which it grows, appearing like white Egyptian grain. It has leaves just like the Rockrose <note>original: "Cithea," likely the Cistus plant</note>, and a gold-colored flower; from the stalk, the frankincense drips just like tears. The myrrh tree resembles the mastic tree, yet it has more and thinner leaves. And when one digs the earth away from the roots, it flows out into the rich soil.

Twice a year it yields fruit; in the spring <note>original: "im glenzẽ," referring to the shining season</note> and summer. The first is red, which the dew produces; the second is white. They also collect the seeds of thistles, which they use both in food and drink for digestion <note>original: "zů dem stůlgang," literally "for the stool"</note>. They have various trades, but the King has the best portion; they give him a tenth of everything the island produces.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a resinous plant, possibly illustrating the frankincense plant or its harvest. It features several upright stems, some tied or bundled together at the top, with foliage at the base. It is positioned on the right side of the preceding text block.</image-desc>

The island is five miles wide. The Pancheans <note>original: "Pancheer," the legendary inhabitants of Panchaea</note> dwell there and carry frankincense and myrrh over into Arabia; the Arabs buy it from them, and the Phoenicians come to get it from the Arabs, as do the Egyptians and Syrians, and from there it is brought to all the world. A third of a mile and no more away lies the third island, somewhat towards the east, and it is many stadia <note>A Greek measure of distance</note> long from the mountains situated toward the west. On this island dwell both Pancheans and foreign peoples—Indians, Scythians, and Cretans—who travel there by sea. On it (so it is said) one may see the mountains of India, and it is called Panchaea, having many wonders to describe. An exceedingly beautiful city is there, which they call Panara; it is held in high honor. It has a sanctuary <note>original: "Stifft"</note> of Jupiter, where the temple servants are called Triphylians <note>original: "Triphily"</note>. These alone who dwell there are free; they have no king but live according to their own laws. Every year they elect several judges; these punish evil, but they do not pass judgment on life and death <note>original: "über das blůt," literally "over the blood"</note>, for that belongs to the priests. From the city lies the temple of Jupiter Triphylius <note>original: "Jouis Triphilij"</note>, a good mile and a half or more away in a long, level field; it is wonderful by the nature of the place, by its antiquity, and by its exquisite construction.

The forests and farmland all around this temple bear and produce such a great variety of trees that it brings to those who look upon it a special and wonderful delight, alongside the enjoyment of so many sweet fruits. The most beautiful and largest cypresses <term>Cyparissen: Cypresses</term>, the broadest and most pleasantly shaded plane trees <term>platani: Plane trees</term>, healthy laurel trees, and fragrant myrrh are at their greatest here, according to the nature of this land, because of the abundance of water with which it is irrigated. It has birds of strange colors that nest in the trees, delighting the eyes with their color and the ears with their song. Many pleasure gardens, meadows with many kinds of flowers, and ever-green heaths make the island so pleasant that only gods should dwell therein. Likewise, the large palm trees bear fruit in abundance, and their kernels provide food for the inhabitants. Also, the grapevines, which have grown high, bear beautiful shoots and much fruit. 

The temple is vast, built of white stones, supported by large stone columns that are handsomely carved. Its length is two *Jucharten* <term>Jucharten: An old German unit of land area; here the translator uses it as a measure of length, roughly equivalent to 60-70 meters</term>, and the width is almost the same. The temple has an enclosure or courtyard <note>original: "einfang oder Freyhoue"</note> of four stadia <term>stadia: An ancient Greek unit of distance; four stadia is approximately 740 meters</term> in circumference, and a width of one *Juchart*. At the base of the temple flows a great body of water from many springs, which is white in color. This water they call the River of the Sun <note>original: "Sonnen fluß"</note>.

Those among them who carry out the farming work diligently and well are accepted among the Tens <term>Zehner: decurions or overseers of groups of ten</term>, for they always have ten who instruct the others in the work and distribute the fruits equally. The herdsmen have their number and weight of what they must give to the priests and the community at each time. No one has any private property, except for a house and garden; whatever is left over, whether it is income or goods to be shared, all goes to the priests, who then distribute to each what he needs; they themselves receive two portions. They all wear delicate clothes, for the sheep there bear very fine-haired wool. Both women and men wear gold ornaments, necklaces, earrings, and, like the Persians, bracelets, as well as shoes of always new and strangely dyed colors. The warriors guard the land with their faithful defense, for on the shores, pirates do great damage to the farmers. The priests live foremost in the house of the god with all delicacy and pleasure; they wear the purest clothes made of linen, and sometimes they also make coats from the delicate wool. They wear golden caps and have boots of strange colors, artistically made. They wear all golden ornaments besides earrings, just like the women. They are faithfully devoted to the service of the gods <term>Gōtzendienst: literally "idol-service," referring here to their religious rites</term>, singing much and praising the gods. They say their lineage comes from Crete; Jupiter led them there when he moved to Panchaea, at the time when he lived among men and ruled the world. They deduce this from their language, in which many Cretan words <note>original: "Cretische whörter"</note> are mixed; they have also shown great love to the Cretans since the time of their ancestors and have shown them all goodwill. Likewise, they show founding charters which Jupiter wrote when he built the temple. The land is full of gold, silver, ore, tin, and iron, and they are not permitted to export any of it from the island. So too, the priests must not go outside the consecrated area; if they step beyond it, anyone who finds one may kill him. They have precious jewels...

## Of the Islands situated toward Greece and the Aegean Sea. Chapter XIX.

Since we have finished recounting the islands located in the Arabian Ocean, we will now turn to those lying toward Greece and the Aegean Sea, and begin with Samothrace. This island, as some claim, was called Samos in ancient times, and later received its name from the ancient Samothrace, which was located not far from the island.

First, the Aborigines (these are the native-born inhabitants <term>Aborigines: from the Latin 'ab origine', meaning those who have been there from the beginning</term>) lived there; for one cannot say of them that there were ever any earlier leaders or marriages there, or that they came from elsewhere. Some write that the island was called Samos in ancient times, after which those who came out from...

# The Sixth Book. 271

...moved into the same [region], they called it Samothrace. The original inhabitants <note>original: "Aborigines"; a term used for the earliest known inhabitants of a land.</note> kept their own language there, of which many words still remain as a sign in their religious ceremonies.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting an ark-like covered boat floating on water near a shoreline. In the background, a coastal city and mountains are visible. On the left shore, figures are shown engaging in activities, possibly related to the post-flood settlement mentioned in the text.</image-desc>

The Samothracians say that before the flood of Deucalion <note>In Greek mythology, Deucalion was the survivor of a great flood sent by Zeus, a figure often compared to Noah.</note>, there was an even greater deluge among them. This first rose from the Cyanian <note>Referring to the Symplegades or "Clashing Rocks" at the entrance to the Black Sea.</note> inflow, then increased from the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait now known as the Dardanelles.</note>, and the sea in the Pontus <note>The Black Sea.</note> surged like flowing water, so that with its overflow it devastated and submerged the largest part of Asia <note>Referring here to Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> lying by the sea; even the plains in Samothrace were destroyed.

For fishermen later pulled up several capitals of columns with their nets, which led to the assumption that when the city of Samothrace in the plains was ruined by the water, the people fled to the mountains. Afterward, when the water receded, the inhabitants established sacrifices to the gods and attained a reprieve; therefore, they set up boundary stones all around the island along with several altars upon which they still sacrifice to this day, providing certain proof that this island was inhabited even before the Great Flood. Afterwards, they say that Saóna <note>Commonly known as Saon in classical mythology.</note> was born among them to Jupiter and a nymph—though some say to Mercury and Rhea. He gathered the scattered people together again, gave them laws, and named the island Saóna after himself. He created five tribes from this people and named each after one of his sons. At that same time, Dardanus, Jasius, and Harmonia are said to have been born to Jupiter and Electra. Dardanus was a very wise man; he traveled to Asia by ship, built the city of Dardania, and established a kingdom there which his descendants called Troy; he called his subjects Dardanians. He expanded his power over many peoples and settled Dardanians there in place of Thracians.

## Of Jasius, Cadmus, and Their Deeds.

Jupiter desired that his other son, Jasius, should also attain high honors, so he taught him to establish certain religious ceremonies <note>These are the famous "Samothracian Mysteries," secret rites dedicated to the Cabiri gods.</note> that none but the priests were permitted to perform. Afterward, as Cadmus was searching for Europa, the daughter of Agenor, he came to Samothrace, learned the same priestly work, and took Jasius's sister Harmonia (not, as the Greeks falsely invent, the daughter of Mars) as his wife. The gods attended this wedding. For Jasius's sake, Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture and grain.</note> presented bread made from grain. Mer—

What secrets are used in this religious service <note>referring to the famous Samothracian Mysteries.</note> are known only to the priests. These gods work many healing miracles and do much good for those who call upon them. They also say that whoever joins their brotherhood becomes immediately more just, pious, and better. For this reason, the famous lords and heroes of old generally enrolled themselves in this brotherhood together. Jason, Castor, Pollux, Hercules, and Orpheus were all in this order; for that reason, they had great luck in wars and attained high fame.

There in Naxos, he brought him forth and entrusted the daughter of the nymph Coronis, as well as Cliedi and other nymphs, to nourish him. 

Jupiter had struck Semele with thunder before Dionysus was born so that he would not be born of mortal humans, but rather of two gods, and would be a god from the very moment of his birth. Furthermore, Jupiter granted the inhabitants of the island this grace—as a reward for Dionysus being raised among them—that they should be more excellent at seafaring than others and have a good livelihood on land. ### Of the Heliades and their sins.

The Heliades were very skillful people, especially in the knowledge of the stars and their courses, and they introduced many arts to seafaring. Likewise, they described the geography of the world. The most talented among them was Tenages; his brothers murdered him out of envy, and when the deed came to light, the perpetrators fled. Macar fled to Lesbos, Candalus to Cos, and Actis to Egypt, where he built a city, Heliopolis, in honor of his father and taught the Egyptians the course of the stars. 

Later, when Greece was covered by the deluge, many people perished and all writings were destroyed. The Egyptians knew nothing of this water, and for that reason, they continued in their arts. Thus, because all the Greeks' books of art were ruined in the water, while the Egyptians' writings remained, the Egyptians gained the fame of being the first to have discovered such things. Likewise, when the Athenians built a city in Egypt called Sais, and it too was destroyed in the water's peril, it led to the opinion (held by all writers misled by ignorance) that only many years later did Cadmus <note>original: "Cadamus"</note>, the son of Agenor, bring the alphabet to Greece. # The Sixth Book.

Those who bore no guilt for the killing <note>Referring to the murder of Tenages by his brothers, mentioned on the previous page</note> remained in **Rhodes**; they lived in **Ialysos** and built a city there, which they named **Achaea**, at the place where **Cyrbe** was later situated. After a great flood had destroyed and laid waste to **Cyrbe**, they divided the land among themselves, and each built a city named after himself. 

Later, when **Danaus** fled from **Egypt** with his daughters, he arrived in the territory of **Lindos**. Having been well received by the citizens, they erected a temple to **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena</note> and set up a large statue within it, which he dedicated to the goddess. He was cast onto **Rhodes** by a great storm; and because he had made a vow during the tempest, and having been welcomed by the citizens, he built a temple to **Neptune** <note>The Roman name for the Greek sea god Poseidon</note>. Thus, priests continued to be drawn from their lineage thereafter. 

Among other treasures, **Cadmus** gifted the **Lydian Minerva** a bronze basin <note>original: "basen"; likely a ritual bowl or cauldron</note> that was wondrously crafted. Therefore, they sent to **Delphi** to ask how they might prevent this disaster. They received the answer that they should take in **Phorbas** and his household as citizens; he was a son of **Lapithes** and was then wandering in **Thessaly** seeking a home. Thus they summoned him, according to the god’s instruction, and gave him a portion of the island. There, despite his poverty, he rooted out all the serpents and delivered the island from its anxiety. Furthermore, he was a pious and good man, for which reason he was honored as a **Hero** after his death. 

After these events, **Althaemenes**, the son of **Catreus** the King of **Crete**, came to **Apollo** <note>the Oracle</note> to learn of certain matters; he was told that he would kill his own father. Later, when **Greece** was covered by the deluge, many people perished, and all writings were destroyed. The **Egyptians** knew nothing of this flood; therefore, they continued in their arts. Thus, because all the Greeks' books of art were ruined in the water, while the **Egyptians'** writings remained, they claimed the glory of being the first to invent such things. Similarly, when the **Athenians** built a city in **Egypt** called **Sais**, and it was also destroyed in a water disaster, it led to the opinion (among all writers misled by ignorance) that it was only many years later that **Cadmus**, the son of **Agenor**, brought letters to **Greece**. **Triopas** came to **Caria** and occupied a headland named **Triopion** after him. # The sixth book.

Those who had no guilt in the killing remained in **Rhodes**; they lived in **Ialysos** and built a city there which they called **Achaia**, at the place where **Cyrbe** was later located. Under them ruled the eldest son **Ochimus**, who took a nymph named **Hegetoria** <note>original: "Egeteriam"; in Greek mythology, she is often associated with the early rulers of Rhodes</note>, by whom he fathered **Cydippe**. His brother **Cercaphus** took her as his wife and ruled after him. When they had passed away, their sons **Lindus**, **Ialysus**, and **Kamiros** reigned. When a great flood <note>original: "wasserguß"; referring to a deluge or destructive torrent of water</note> destroyed **Cyrbe** and laid it waste, they divided the land among themselves, and each built a city named after himself. Later, when **Danaus** fled from **Egypt** with his daughters, he came to **Lindos**; being well received by the citizens, they built a temple to **Minerva** <note>Athena</note> and erected a large statue within it, which he dedicated to the goddess. At this time, **Cadmus** came into **Europe** seeking his sister; he was thrown onto **Rhodes** by a great storm. Because of a vow he made during the tempest, and since he was welcomed by the citizens, he built a temple to **Neptune** <note>Poseidon</note>. He established certain **Phoenician** priests there, who became friends with the people of **Ialysos** on the island and remained with them. Thus, from their lineage, priests have continued for generations. Among other treasures, **Cadmus** gifted the **Lydian Minerva** with a bronze cauldron <note>original: "öhrinen hafen"; a vessel made of brass or bronze</note> of wondrous workmanship. Upon it was writing (in **Phoenician** letters, which he later taught to the Greeks and made known, naming them **Phoenician**). It was foretold that the island of **Rhodes** would be destroyed by serpents; therefore, they sent to **Delphi** to ask how they might prevent this disaster. They received the answer that they should take in **Phorbas** and his followers as citizens; he was a son of **Lapithes** and was traveling through **Thessaly** seeking a home. So they invited him, following the god's sign, and gave him a portion of the island. There, through his diligence, he rooted out all the serpents and freed the island from this worry. Otherwise, he was also a pious and good man, for which reason he was honored as a hero after his death. After these events, when **Althaemenes**, the son of **Catreus** the King of **Crete**, came to **Apollo** to learn of certain matters, he was told that he would kill his father. ### Of Chersonesus and the fortified cities

Since we have mentioned the **Rhodians** and also mixed in something regarding **Chersonesus**, and because this place lies exactly opposite the island, we wish to write something about it. This **Chersonesus** <note>a peninsula in ancient Caria, modern-day Turkey</note> has its name, as some write, from the nature of its location, which is called an **Isthmus** <note>original: "Isthmon"; a narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses</note> or a curve of the sea, or as others say, from one who ruled there. After whose reign, five **Curetes** <note>mythological attendants of the mother goddess Rhea</note> from **Crete** took possession of the province. They sailed with a great army to this place, drove out the **Carians** <note>original: "Cares"; the indigenous inhabitants of western Anatolia</note> who lived there, took the land entirely for themselves, and divided it into five parts, each building a city of his own name. When he had searched for her in many places for a long time and in vain, he traveled from **Caria** into **Chersonesus** and left his fatherland behind. Afterward, he persuaded some and forced others to accept him as King, and he built a city of his name. He looked after the public good very well and was held in great honor by his subjects. He drove them out and received the land of the **Dorians** as a reward. Now they had raised a piglet, which ran into the chamber while they slept and broke the vessel, spilling the wine. When one sacrifices to her, the best honeyed wine is poured out, in memory of the fact that they let the wine be spilled. Whoever touches a pig or eats garlic is not permitted to enter the temple. And the devotion to this temple became so great over time that not only the inhabitants but also many foreign peoples have bestowed gifts upon this temple. But the greatest gift ever sent there was that the **Persians**, when they ruled in **Asia** and plundered all the temples of the **Greeks**, yet left the church of this demi-goddess untouched. Likewise, other robbers who left nothing behind in any other places never attacked this temple, even though it was not protected by any wall and they could have easily captured it. They speak of great benefits this goddess bestows upon mankind; for in sleep she teaches the sick what they should use to become healthy. She also helps many who believe they must die. To pregnant women in labor, she gives help in great danger.

From this, she has received a great church-treasury from those who regained their health, and such things remain safe not only through guards but through devotion. So much for **Rhodes** and the **Chersonesus**. Now we wish to move on to **Crete**.

# Diodorus Siculus on Crete or Candia. Chapter 23.

[Image: A woodcut map of the island of Crete, oriented with north roughly to the left. The map includes several labels in Latin: "Candia or Crete island" in a banner at the top, "Cydonia" on the western coast, and "Here above is the Labyrinth" near a central mountain. Several smaller islands are shown off the coast with names like "Dia" <note>original: "Standia"</note>, "Adelfi", "Spira", "Cortone", "Christiana", "The Furious Ones" <note>original: "I furioni"</note>, and "Igaderoni". The landscape is depicted with many small mountains and coastal towns.]

The Cretans say they are a native people born in this same island, having lived there from time immemorial, and are called <term>autochthones</term> <note>original: "abochthones"; from the Greek, meaning "sprung from the earth itself," implying they were the original inhabitants rather than migrants.</note>. Their first king was **Cretas**, who invented many things for human sustenance and welfare. Likewise, it is fabled that many gods originated from them; these are called "gods" because of their discoveries—which served humanity so well. We wish to speak of these gods and recall them one after another, as we find them described by others who have made mention of the Cretans.

->**Of the Idaean Dactyls.**<-

The first ones of whom they can speak lived on **Mount Ida** and were called the **Idaean Dactyls** <note>original: "Idaei Dactili"; "Dactyl" comes from the Greek word for finger (*daktylos*). Legend says they were born from the dust when the goddess Rhea pressed her fingers into the earth while giving birth to Zeus.</note>. Some say there were a hundred of them, while others say there were ten, receiving their name from the fingers of the hand—for they had ten fingers—and this is what **Ephorus** <note>A prominent Greek historian of the 4th century BCE.</note> writes. Others write that these people came from the **Ida** located in **Phrygia**, and later moved into **Europe** with **Mygdon**, where they taught people divination and the service of the gods. In **Samothrace**, they established wonderful things, and at that same time **Orpheus**—who had a great passion for poetry and all the arts—became their pupil and learned from them how to arrange songs and <term>religious rites</term> <note>original: "Kirchen dienst"; literally "church service," though here referring to ancient pagan ceremonies.</note>, and was the first to establish them in **Greece**. 

Likewise, they are said to have discovered and demonstrated the use of fire in **Berecynthia** <note>A mountain in Phrygia associated with the mother-goddess Cybele.</note>, as well as how to forge iron and ore, and what benefits each provides. And because they showed people such great benevolence with these gifts, they deservedly attained divine honors among them. One among them was named **Hercules**, and because they generally came into such great prestige and fame, they established the **Olympic Games**. However, later generations were deceived by the shared name, believing that **Hercules**, the son of **Alcmena**, was the one who first established them. Of this, there are still many ancient and current signs. For

## Of the Curetes.

Following these Idaean Dactyls, there were nine **Curetes**, who, as some claim, were born of the Earth <note>original: "Terra"</note>, while others say they were from the lineage of the Idaean Dactyls. They lived in mountains and valleys that were full of trees, and because neither clothing nor houses had yet been invented, they lived according to nature. As they were wise and foresighted people, they invented many things for the welfare of mankind. First, they made folds for cattle and tamed sheep, goats, oxen, and other animals. After that, they taught how to shoot with the hand-bow and how to hunt wild game. Furthermore, they persuaded people to gather together and established good laws for them to live by. The sword, the helmet, and—along with other weapons—dancing, are their inventions. By the tumult of their dancing, Saturn was deceived <note>This refers to the myth where the Curetes clashed their shields and spears to drown out the cries of the infant Jupiter, preventing his father Saturn from finding and eating him.</note>. They also say that Jupiter was entrusted to them by his mother Rhea to be raised secretly; and since we wish to write particularly about them later, we must write something further back in time.

## Of the Titans.

The Cretans write that at the time of the Curetes, the **Titans** lived in **Knossos** <note>original: "Gnossen"</note>; they still show as evidence some foundations of the house where Rhea was raised, and an old grove of pure cypresses <note>original: "Cyparillen"</note>. These Titans were six men and five women. Some write that their parents were Sky <note>original: "Coelum"</note> and Earth <note>original: "Terra"</note>. Others say one of the Curetes was their father and Tithea their mother, from whom their name comes. They were **Saturn**, **Hyperion**, **Coeus** <note>original: "Comis"</note>, **Iapetus**, **Crius**, and the last, **Oceanus**. The sisters were **Rhea**, **Themis**, **Mnemosyne** <note>original: "Memoria"</note>, **Phoebe**, and **Tethys**. Each of them discovered something useful for the human race, for which they attained great honor and fame.

## Of the Kingdom of Saturn.

The eldest among them, **Saturn**, became King; he brought the people out of a crude, beastly state to a well-mannered life and gave them good laws. And because he received a beloved name among the masses, he traveled through many lands of the world, exhorting them toward justice and bravery of life, making a well-disciplined people out of his subjects—especially those to whom things went well because of their piety. He reigned mostly in the places located toward the West <note>original: "Nidergang"; literally the "going down" of the sun.</note> and was held in great dignity, both by the Romans and Carthaginians, as well as other peoples who offered him many special and heartfelt sacrifices. Many places bear his name. Under his rule, humans lived in peace and prosperity, for they were obedient to the laws, and no injustice was suffered; such is testified...

**Hyperion**, however, showed the people the course of the sun, the moon, and the other stars, and also divided the hours; therefore it is said he is the father of them all, as an investigator of Nature. From **Saturn** <note>In traditional Greek mythology, Latona's parents are the Titans Coeus and Phoebe; the German translator here substitutes Saturn.</note> and **Phoebe**, **Latona** was born. From **Iapetus** came **Prometheus**, who, as some write, stole the fire from the gods and gave it to mankind. He also discovered [the use of] wood and burning things that maintain the fire.

**Memoria** <note>The Titaness Mnemosyne.</note> demonstrated how one should speak in an orderly fashion and gave names to all things, although some ascribe this to **Mercury**. Furthermore, they attribute Memory to this goddess, from which she takes her name. **Themis** delivered prophecies, established the worship of deities <note>original: "götzendienst," literally "service of idols," used here by the translator to describe ancient religious rites.</note>, and showed what serves a quiet, peaceful life; she gave the lawgivers their names, for which reason they are still called lawgivers and protectors of the Church <note>original: "Kirche schirmer"; the translator uses contemporary 16th-century terminology to describe those who defend religious and legal order.</note>—those who, following her example, devote themselves to the fear of God and honesty. They say when **Apollo** wished to give an answer <note>i.e., an oracle.</note>, he first consulted Themis, as if she were able to prophesy. 

And because these gods invented such useful things for mankind, after their death they were not only held as immortals, but were esteemed as those who possess the heavens. **Saturn** and **Rhea** begat together **Vesta**, **Ceres**, **Juno**, **Jupiter**, **Neptune**, and **Pluto**. Among these, **Vesta** taught the people how to build houses, for which reason Jupiter afterward commanded the whole world that, for this cause, she should be honored by mankind as a goddess.

The Sixth Book.

### How the sowing and preparation of grain was discovered.

**Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture and the harvest.</note> instructed the people on how to use the grain that previously grew by chance among other grasses, and how they might sow, harvest, and store it. At the time she began teaching the people these practices, **Proserpina** <note>Also known as Persephone.</note> was not yet born. Later, after **Pluto** <note>The god of the underworld.</note> had carried her daughter away, Ceres—out of both envy toward **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note> and the deep grief she bore for her daughter—burned all the crops. However, once she found her daughter again and was reconciled with Jupiter, she gave the seeds to **Triptolemus** <note>A mythical prince of Eleusis whom Ceres taught the arts of agriculture so he could spread them across the world.</note>. She commanded him to share them with every part of the world and to show everyone how to work with them.

Some write that she also gave laws by which she brought the people to justice. From this, she earned the name **"The Lawgiver"** <note>original: "Gsatz geberin," referring to the Greek title *Thesmophoros*.</note>. Because she provided the cause for such great and high welfare for all the human race, she attained great honor and divine worship—not only among the Greeks and the barbarians <note>In the classical sense, "barbarians" referred to any non-Greek speaking peoples.</note> to whom the knowledge of such blessings came, but from the entire world.

Others write differently regarding the discovery of crops, claiming that the goddess first appeared among them and showed them the nature, cultivation, and use of the same. These are the **Egyptians**, who say their **Isis** and Ceres are the same goddess, and that she first brought grain to Egypt, which possesses a precious soil watered by the **Nile** for all fruitful things. Although the **Athenians** never deny this discovery of crops, they nonetheless claim the grain came to them from elsewhere; they call the place where it first grew **Eleusis** <note>original: "Eleusiniam"</note> because the seed was brought there from foreign lands.

The **Sicilians**, because the sacrifices to Ceres and Proserpina—as well as the highest divine service—are held among them, argue that they should rightly be given the prize. They claim the goddesses gave their gifts first at the place where they are most dearly honored. They argue it is not believable that Ceres, who claimed this island for herself and saw it was otherwise fruitful, would have gifted it last with such small things—especially since her daughter was abducted from this very island, and it was naturally fruitful on its own, so that (as **Homer** said, as mentioned above) it bore barley and corn untilled. But so much for Ceres. Now of the other gods who were born of **Rhea** and **Saturn**.

### Of Neptune.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration depicting four figures in a simple wooden boat or raft navigating a body of water. They appear to be using poles or oars. In the background, there is a hilly landscape with a castle or fortified structure and some trees.</image-desc>

The **Cretans** say that **Neptune** <note>Poseidon.</note> was the first to invent navigation; he rigged the ships and was made a captain upon the sea by Saturn. From this, posterity has claimed that Neptune ruled over the sea, and sailors brought him sacrifices and made vows to him in times of distress. To this they add that Neptune was the first to bridle horses and established the cavalry; for this reason, he is called **Hippius** <term>Hippius: a Greek title meaning "of the horses," reflecting the god's role as the creator or tamer of horses</term>.

<image-desc>Two woodcut illustrations side-by-side. **Pluto** was the one who invented the making of graves, the burial of the deceased, the conducting of funeral processions, and other rites for the soul <note>original: "seel gerädt," referring to religious services or funerary customs for the departed</note> which were not in use before. For this reason, the saying arose that he rules over the dead, and the ancients attributed such dominion to him.

## Concerning Jupiter.

Regarding the lineage of **Jove** <note>Another name for Jupiter or Zeus.</note> and his kingdom, people are of divided opinion. Some write that after **Saturn** <note>The Roman name for the Titan Kronos.</note> joined the gods, Jove took over the kingdom and did not overthrow his father by force, but ruled justly and by right of inheritance. Others argue against this, saying that as soon as the child **Jupiter** was born, it was prophesied to Saturn that he would be driven from his kingdom by force by this son. This moved Saturn to kill many of his children. **Ceres** <note>In this context, Diodorus or the translator likely identifies Ceres/Demeter with Rhea, the mother of Zeus, who saved him from Saturn.</note> was vexed by this, and since she could not quiet the man with good words, she sent Jupiter secretly to **Mount Ida** to be raised. Thus, he was raised on goat's milk (the goat was named **Amalthea**) and honey.

They also say that many other signs of Jupiter’s lineage and upbringing are found on this island <note>Crete.</note>. When the **Curetes** <note>Mythological armed guardians who protected the infant Zeus by clashing their shields to drown out his cries.</note> were carrying the child, they say the *Omphalus* <note>The "navel-stone," a sacred object marking the center of the world.</note> fell near the river **Triton**. Therefore, that place is still called the **Holy Omphalia** because of what happened there, and the surrounding field is called the **Omphalian field**. The cave in Mount Ida wherein he was nourished is consecrated, and the meadows surrounding it are never mown.

Furthermore, one should not omit the wonderful thing said here about the **bees** <note>original: "Immen." In myth, bees fed the infant Zeus with honey.</note>. Jupiter made them gold-colored as an eternal sign of the love he bears for them, whereas they had previously been the color of iron. And although this mountain is very high and situated in a rough, windy location with much snow, none of this harms the bees, nor does it bring them any loss. The goat whose milk nourished him was shown great honor, and the place where she stood was called **Aegiochus** <note>A title of Zeus meaning "Aegis-bearing," derived here from *aix*, the Greek word for goat.</note>.

<center>### The Sixth Book. ###</center>

When he had reached maturity <note>literally "come out of the boy's skin," an idiom for reaching manhood</note>, he built a city on Mount Ida where he was born; the ruins of its walls still remain even after it was destroyed. This god was more courageous and virtuous than all the others; for when he gained the kingdom after **Saturn**, he showed great kindness to humanity. He was the first to train the people not to do wrong to one another, and he abolished violence and dishonor. Wherever discord and strife arose, it had to be settled by law. Whatever served the peace and welfare of a unified life, he established; he encouraged the good toward virtue and tamed the wicked with punishment and fear. He traveled through almost the entire world, waging war against the ungodly and the robbers, and instituting fairness and justice.

## Concerning the Giants and Tyrants.

At that time, he also fought the **Giants**. In **Crete**, he slew **Mylinus**, and in **Phrygia**, **Typhon**. Before the battle he waged in Crete against the Giants, **Jupiter** sacrificed an ox to **Sol** <note>the Sun</note>, to **Caelus** <note>the Sky</note>, and to **Terra** <note>the Earth</note>, which sacrifice signified the victory of Jove. It indicated first his strength, then the defection of people from his enemies, and thirdly the end of the war. For at that time **Musaeus** <note>A legendary polymath and poet</note> defected from the Giants to him, for which he attained great honor. The gods struck down the enemies, and it is also clear that others gave help to the gods in the war against the Giants: the **Macedonians** at **Pallene**, and the **Thessalians** on the plain that is called **Phlegra** <note>original: "Phlegeum"</note> due to the burning, and later named **Cyme**. The reason Jupiter fought against the Giants was this: they relied on the size and strength of their bodies, disregarded all law, committed every kind of wantonness against the poor, made slaves of their neighbors, and dared to wage war against those who were held to be gods because of the benefits they had shown to humanity. They say that Jupiter not only rooted out the godless and evildoers, but also showed great honor to the gods, heroes, and men who did good for the people. Because of this merit, the gods—with the common consent of humanity—gave him the sovereignty of the world, an eternal kingdom, and a dwelling in **Olympus**. Afterward, more precious sacrifices and indeed higher divine service were established for him than for the others. Also, when he was taken into heaven, his memory remained so firm and fast among men because of the kindness he had shown them, that they believe whatever happens in the sky—whether it be rain, thunder, or lightning—he directs it all there. And because he provides the rain, whereby the fruits ripen and which is a cause for human life itself, they have called Jupiter a "helpful Father." And they called him "Father" because he takes heed of all people and cares for them with great goodness; indeed, he was their Prince, who taught them their welfare in life. He is called a King and **Emperor** <note>original: "Keyser"</note> because of the greatness of his power; a counselor and provider because of the wisdom in his judgment.

## Concerning the children of Jupiter.

They also say that in Crete, **Pallas** <note>Athena</note> was born of Jove at the springs of **Triton**, and therefore she has the name **Tritonia**. And one sacrifices

### Vulcan’s Instruction.

**Vulcan** taught how one should work with ore, iron, silver, and everything that must be forged in the fire. Therefore, the smiths and those who deal with ore offer sacrifices to this God; and in eternal memory and gratitude, they call the fire "Vulcan." <note>The text highlights the ancient practice of metonymy, where the name of the god represents the element they control.</note>

### The Arts of Mars.

**Mars** was the first to arm soldiers with forged armor for battling and fighting. He instructed and encouraged people to strike down those who set themselves against the Gods.

### Apollo the Physician.

**Apollo** invented the harp and the art of music, as well as medicine, prophecy, and soothsaying. The sick were brought to him first of all to be healed. He was also highly skilled in shooting with the bow, and he was the first to teach this to others. Because of this, the **Cretans** took a special delight in the bow and called him **Scythum**. <note>The name Scythum likely refers to the Scythians, who were legendary archers in antiquity.</note>

### The Works of Aesculapius.

**Aesculapius**, who was born of **Apollo** and **Coronis**, learned much from his father in the art of medicine. Beyond that, he also invented surgery <note>literally "wound-medicine"</note> and the power of herbs, as well as the mixing of medicines. He raised the art to such a high level that he was regarded as its very author and inventor.

### The Character of Mercury.

To **Mercury** are attributed the tasks of messaging, legal defense, treaties, and truces, as well as making peace during wars. Likewise, heralds and messengers of peace are dedicated to him, as if they make use of his protection and are therefore granted safe passage by everyone. For this reason, he is called everyone’s friend, because he brings benefit and peace to both sides of a conflict. They say he invented the scales, weights, and measures, and whatever serves the dealings of merchants. Stealing and trickery <term>finantzen: in the 16th century, this referred to cunning, fraud, or deceptive cleverness rather than modern banking</term> are also his arts. He is the Herald of the Gods, a good messenger who diligently carries out his commands, for which reason he is also called the **Interpreter** <note>German: "Dolmetsch"</note>. This is not because he invented names and speech, as some claim, but because he fulfills his commands more diligently than others. He was the first to teach wrestling and he invented the lyre <note>German: "Geygen," literally "fiddles," but referring to the classical lyre</note>. Previously, **Apollo** had made one from the shell of a snail <note>The Greek myth specifies a tortoise shell; the German "schnacken" implies a shell of that type</note>, and later defeated **Marsyas** through the favoritism of the judges. After Marsyas was killed, Apollo felt a sense of remorse, smashed the lyres, and did not play upon them for a long time until Mercury restored them.

### The Good Deeds of Dionysus.

**Dionysus**, they say, invented the grapevines and instructed people on how to make wine from them; he also advised them on how they might preserve the fruits for a long time.

may be preserved. He is also said to have been born in **Crete** from **Jupiter** and **Proserpina** (as Orpheus says) and was torn apart by the **Titans** at a sacred festival. However, we have diligently described that there were many of the name **Dionysus**. The **Cretans** conclude that this God was born among them because two curved islands called **Didymus** <note>original: "Dydimas," likely referring to the Twin Islands</note> near them were named **Dionysia** after him, a thing he did in no other place in the world. They say **Hercules** lived a long time ago, born of **Jove**; before him who was born of **Alcmena**, there was no certain mother known. All that is known of him is that he was physically very strong, traveled the world, tamed harmful wild animals and monstrous beasts, and was so invincible and without fear that he brought freedom to humanity. Therefore, because of his good deeds, immortal honors were shown to him. Afterward, the **Hercules** born of **Alcmena** wished to imitate the feats of battle and glorious deeds of the first **Hercules**; through these, and because he shared the same name, he was held to be the first, and the former's deeds were attributed to him because the truth about the first was not known. They also say that some signs of this first **Hercules** are still witnessed in **Egypt**, for it was there that he built the city of **Brittomartim**.

## What Dictynna Taught.

**Dictynna** is also said to have been born in **Crete** from **Jove** and **Acharmide**, the daughter of **Eubolus** and granddaughter of **Ceres**. She invented hunting nets, from which she also received her name. <note>The name Dictynna is traditionally derived from the Greek word "diktyon," meaning "hunting net."</note> She has much in common with **Diana**, which is why many have considered the two to be one. The **Cretans** erected a temple to this Goddess and established annual sacrifices. However, some wish to derive her name from the story that **Minos** chased after her to lie with her, and she hid herself in the sea or under the fishermen's nets; these people are mistaken. For it is not easily believed that a Goddess would come to such great need that she must seek the help of humans, especially since she was the daughter of the mightiest among the Gods. Furthermore, one unjustly accuses **Minos** of such godlessness, as he has been praised before the whole world as a just and pious man.

## Pluto’s Discovery.

They say **Pluto** was born in **Crete** on the **Trifius**, born of **Ceres** and **Jasius**. They report two things regarding his origin. For some claim that as **Jasius** sowed the soil and applied such great diligence to farming that he received much fruit from it, he was called "the Rich" or "**Pluto**" by those who saw this. Thus, among posterity, one who was wealthy was held to be someone to whom the God **Pluto** was gracious. Others say that **Jasius** and **Ceres** fathered a child together who led a lawful and brave life and taught people to gather money together and keep it as a precaution. Now, this is enough regarding the Gods who were said to be born among the **Cretans**. But that their mysteries, honors, consecrations, and other services arose from them and spread to others is evidenced by the fact that the **Athenians**, in their most excellent...

Furthermore, what others consider a great and hidden secret <note>Referring to the "mysteries," such as the Eleusinian Mysteries, which were usually kept secret from the uninitiated.</note>, anyone among the **Cretans** is permitted to know. They also say that many gods were born among them, who then traveled from there through the entire world. These gods showed great kindness to the human race and shared the beneficial things they had discovered for the good of all people.

# Concerning the Special Dwellings of the Gods.

**Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture.</note> taught the art of farming and the use of grain first in **Attica**, then in **Sicily**, and afterwards in **Egypt**; for this reason, she is held in great honor by everyone. **Venus** lived in **Sicily** near **Mount Eryx**, in **Cyprus** and **Cythera**, and around **Paphos**; she also lived in **Asia** near **Syria**. Because of her travels, she is called **Erycina**, **Cytherea**, **Paphia**, and **Syra**. Likewise, **Apollo** had his dwelling mostly around **Delos**, **Lycia**, and **Delphi**. **Diana** <note>The Roman name for Artemis.</note> lived at **Ephesus**, in the **Pontus** <note>original: "Poto," likely referring to the Black Sea region</note>, in **Persia**, and in **Crete**. Because of their deeds and dwellings, these two are called **Pythius**, **Delius**, **Ephesia**, **Cressa**, **Tauropolia**, and **Persea**, even though both were born in **Crete**. **Diana** is highly honored by the **Persians**, and the "Barbarians" <note>A term used by Greeks and Romans for any non-Greek people, here specifically the Persians.</note> established a special divine service for her. It is the same with the other gods, though it is not necessary to say much about them here.

# Concerning the Hero Minos.

A long time after the birth of these gods, many heroes were born in **Crete**. The most noble of these were **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus**, begotten of **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> and **Europa**, the daughter of **Agenor**. They say she was carried to **Crete** on a bull by the arrangement of the gods. **Minos**, the elder son, was the first to rule in that same island, and he built many of the most prominent cities there. Toward **Asia** he built **Knossos**; toward the south, **Phaistos** <note>original: "Vulcanuam," likely referring to the city near the temple of Hephaestus/Vulcan</note>; and toward the west and the **Peloponnese**, he first established **Cydonia** on the island. He gave many laws to the **Cretans**, pretending that he had devised them in a cave <note>According to legend, Minos received his laws directly from Zeus in a sacred cave every nine years.</note>. He was also the first to prepare many warships to attack the neighboring islands, and he was the first among the **Greeks** to rule the sea. Because he attained great fame for virtue and justice, he went to war against **Cocalus** in **Sicily**, which war we mentioned in the life of **Daedalus**.

# Concerning Rhadamanthus.

**Rhadamanthus** is said to have been the greatest lover of justice, who severely punished murderers and other evildoers. He ruled over many islands and possessed a large part of **Asia**, for everyone willingly accepted him as a lord because of his fairness.

He <note>Referring to Rhadamanthus, mentioned on the previous page.</note> gave the kingdom to his son **Erytheus**, from whom the **Erytheans** are named. After that, he appointed **Oenopion**—the son of **Bacchus** <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine.</note> and **Ariadne**, daughter of **Minos**—as king in **Chios**. Some wish to identify him as **Dionysus** himself, saying he taught the people the use of wine just as his father did. To each of his sons, he gave either an island to rule or a city: to **Thoas** he gave **Lemnos**; to **Anius**, **Cyrnus**; to **Pamphilus**, **Peparethos**; to **Evander**, **Maronea**; to **Alceus**, **Paros**; to **Anion**, **Delos**; and to **Andreus**, the island that retains his name, **Andros**. Because of his exceptional justice, the ancients fabled that he is the judge of the pious and the wicked in the Underworld <note>original: "inn der Hell"</note>. **Minos** also attained a similar office for the sake of his equal justice. His third brother, **Sarpedon**, set out for **Asia** with many ships and conquered **Lycia**. He had a son named **Evander** who ruled after him and took **Deidameia**, the daughter of **Bellerophon**, as his wife. From her, he fathered the **Sarpedon** who went with **Agamemnon** to **Troy**, though some call him **Jupiter's** son. **Minos** had two sons, **Deucalion** and **Molus**. **Deucalion** fathered **Idomeneus**, and **Molus** fathered **Meriones**, who came to the aid of **Agamemnon** at **Troy** with ninety ships. Their tomb is in **Knossos**, bearing this inscription:

->This is the grave. Behold it well. From **Molus**<-
->**Meriones** was I born;<-
->Right here beside him, they have buried me.<-

The **Cretans** offer sacrifices to these noble and most famous heroes and call upon them in times of war.

### Concerning the foreign peoples who came to Crete.

Now we wish to recount other peoples who settled in **Crete** at various times. We have said first that the original inhabitants born in **Crete** were called **Eteocretans** <note>Meaning "True Cretans."</note>. However, many hundreds of years later, the **Pelasgians**—who were driven out by rebellion and war—came to **Crete** and occupied a part of the island. The third group were the **Dorians**, who also took the island with their leader **Dorius**; they are descended from **Tectamus**. These gathered mostly around **Mount Olympus**, having been enticed there in part with gifts from **Achaea**, which lies in **Laconia**. The fourth who came there were called **Migades** <note>From the Greek word for "mixed."</note>, a crude people who soon learned Greek customs along with the language and became subject to **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus**. Finally, when the **Argives** and **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans.</note> brought the **Cycladic** islands under their power, they also took these and other islands, and thereafter lived in several cities they built. But no one should wonder why much that is contradictory has been written about the **Cretans**, nor why we do not describe every single opinion. For we have followed only the most credible writers here: some things drawn from **Epimenides**'s knowledge of holy scripture, some from **Sosicrates**, and some from **Laosthenidas** <note>original: "Laoschermide"</note>. And so much for **Crete**.

# Of Lesbos, Chios, Samos, and other Islands
## which were settled by the Rhodians. Chapter 25.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a coastal landscape. In the water on the right is a two-masted ship with a full sail and a smaller rowboat nearby. The shoreline is rocky and mountainous. Now we shall turn our attention to **Lesbos**. This same island has been occupied many times by various peoples who sailed there, and while it was still desolate, the **Pelasgians** were the first to cultivate it. For **Xanthus** the Pelasgian, a son of **Triopas** and King of those who departed from **Argos**, was appointed as a lord <note>original: "zum herzen auffgeworffen," an idiomatic way of saying he was elevated to leadership.</note> in a certain place in the region of **Lycia**. From there, he turned to the uninhabited island of **Lesbos**, divided the land among the **Pelasgians**, and named the island **Pelasgia**, which was previously called **Issa**. And when afterwards, in the seventh generation of his lineage, in the time of **Deucalion**, many perished there through floods <note>The Great Flood of Greek mythology, similar to the story of Noah.</note>, the island became completely abandoned.

Later, **Macareus** arrived, and since the beauty of the island pleased him well, he remained there. This **Macareus** was a son of **Cyrene** and **Jupiter** <note>original: "Jouis", the Latin name for Zeus.</note>. He dwelt in **Olenus**, a region which at that time was called **Jados** <note>likely referring to Ionia</note>, but is now called **Achaia**. Thus he took some of his subjects—the **Ionians** and other peoples—with him, and sailed to **Lesbos**, where he rose to great prominence through just and good rule, aided by the fertility of the island, and he divided the land among them. 

Afterward, some years later, **Lesbus**, the son of **Lapithes** <note>The OCR reads "Jabithi," but this refers to the hero Lapithes.</note> (this **Lapithes** was a son of **Aeolus** <note>The OCR reads "Cocli," likely a corruption of Aeoli.</note> and grandson of **Hippotas**), was prompted by the command of the gods to sail to this island with his good friends. He took the daughter of **Macareus** as his wife, who was named **Methymna**. He thus remained on the island. When he had earned a great name through glorious deeds, he named the island and its inhabitants after himself <note>The island of Lesbos is named after the hero Lesbus.</note>. **Macareus** had two daughters, among others: one named **Mytilene**, the other **Methymna**, after whom he named two cities. He also undertook to bring other islands under his control; he sent some people to **Chios**, whose captain was his son, and had it settled. To **Samos** he sent his other son, named **Cydrolus**, who ruled there. To the third island <note>Likely Cos.</note>, he gave **Ceaneandrus** as king. Likewise, to **Rhodes** he sent **Leucippus** with many people, who were by the **Rhodians** up-

[They were] accepted because there were few people to cultivate the land, and they were granted a portion of the territory on the island. Now, a great flood <note>original: "güss", referring to the catastrophic rains associated with the Deluge of Deucalion mentioned previously.</note> caused immense damage to the mainland lying opposite the islands. Because of the constant dampness, all the crops rotted, the air became poisonous, and nothing would grow; from this, a great plague <note>original: "sterbend", literally "a dying" or mass mortality.</note> arose in the cities. The islands, however, because they enjoyed constant favorable winds and were fertile, were called "blessed" and "fortunate" by their inhabitants. Due to their great abundance, they were named the **Fortunate Isles** <note>original: "Fortunate". Indeed, all these islands—not only in ancient times but also in our own—are praised above all others near the mainland for their good soil, pleasant fields, and healthy air, and thus they are rightly called the Blessed or Fortunate. Furthermore, **Macareus**, who reigned in **Lesbos**, wrote a law for them that was highly beneficial to the public good. He called this law "The Lion," signifying its power and strength, modeled after the nature of that beast.

## Of the Island of Tenedos. Chapter 31.

Sometime later, after the island of **Lesbos** was settled, **Tenedos** was also inhabited in the following way: **Tenes**, the son of **Cycnus**, ruled in the **Troad** <note>The region in northwest Asia Minor surrounding the ancient city of Troy.</note> and was a renowned man. He gathered his subjects together and left his fatherland with them, sailing to a desolate island then called **Leucophrys**. There, he divided the land among his companions and built a city, naming it **Tenedos** after himself. Because he ruled there piously and well, he lived in great honor; on account of the prosperity he brought, he was loved by everyone, and after his death, he was regarded as a god <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the full word is "regarded".</note>

## Concerning the Islands of the Cyclades
### Chapter 36.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration showing a maritime scene. Various islands are visible, each featuring fortified cities with towers and cathedrals. Now we wish to speak of the smaller islands, since we have previously described the large ones. Because these islands of the Cyclades were entirely desolate, Minos—the son of Jupiter <note>original: "Jouis"</note> and Europa, who ruled in Crete and was powerful upon the waters—sent out many people to occupy them; he conquered many of them and distributed the land. In Asia, he also acquired many dominions, which is why many of those islands, as well as several harbors and landing places, still bear the name "Minoes" <note>referring to the various ancient ports named Minoa.</note>.

When Minos <note>original: "Minois"</note> obtained his brother Rhadamanthus <note>In mythology, Rhadamanthus was known for his extreme justice and later became a judge of the underworld.</note> as a companion in the kingdom—who was a pious and upright man—Minos sent him to the outermost reaches of his realm out of secret envy. <image-desc>A large decorative initial 'D' containing a figure of a person, possibly a scholar or scribe, seated and engaged in work.</image-desc>Dictys the Cretan <note>original: "Candiot," referring to the island of Crete, formerly known as Candia</note>, who was a soldier under Idomeneus, left behind a daily record in the Greek language of those things that occurred during the siege and conquest of Troy. However, the reason he used Phoenician letters for this purpose was that they had been newly introduced by Cadmus and Agenor <note>legendary figures credited with bringing the alphabet to Greece</note> and adopted by the Greeks. And this writing of his was discovered in this manner: After many years had passed, once Dictys had departed in death and been buried near the city of Knossos (which was always the royal seat of the kings there), his grave collapsed from old age. Several shepherds happened by chance upon the collapsed structure; beneath the rubble, they found a tin casket <note>original: "todtenbaum," literally "death-tree," a term for a coffin or sarcophagus</note> which was well-sealed. They believed God had provided them with a great treasure and smashed the chest, but they found therein neither gold nor other loot, but only a book written on linden bark. Since their hopes were dashed, they brought the chest to the governor <term>Praui<gloss>a corruption of "Praxis," the name given in Latin manuscripts for the governor of Crete under Emperor Nero</gloss></term>. He found that it was written in the Greek language, yet with foreign characters. He transcribed it again into Greek letters and brought it to Nero, the Roman Emperor, who rewarded him regally for it. When this writing came into my hands—since I had previously desired to truly understand the authentic history of Troy—the desire also came upon me to translate this writing, as it stands, into the Latin language. To this end, I took heart, believing that I could well accomplish it, and thereby refresh my otherwise unburdened mind. Thus, I have left the division of the first five books—in which it is reported how the war was begun and carried out—as they were. The remainder—how the Greeks departed and traveled home—I have condensed into one book, which I am sending to you herewith. It is therefore my friendly request to you, dear Rufinus <note>Septimius addresses his friend Quinto Aradio by the cognomen Rufinus</note>, that you might look favorably upon my undertaken labor.

## Of the Trojan Feud

...having been driven off by storms, he <note>Alexander, also known as Paris, the son of King Priam of Troy</note> also led his ships with him and, having put out to sea, first landed in Phoenicia, at the court of the Sidonian King <note>Sidon was a major city in ancient Phoenicia, in modern-day Lebanon</note>. The King received him in a friendly manner; however, Alexander arranged it so that his host was murdered that very night. He could no more restrain himself here than he had at Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>; he threw the entire royal court and household into turmoil, plundered it, and whatever the King had brought out to honor him, he snatched up and had it packed onto his ships. But when the cry and wailing of the court servants over their dead master became too great—so that some were able to flee in time—and a riot broke out in the city, many people rushed to the court. However, Alexander had almost completely cleared out what he desired and hurried to the ships. The Sidonians pursued him immediately, so that it came to blows, and it went quite violently; for many on both sides remained on the battlefield, because the Sidonians were very embittered and firmly set on avenging their master, while the others were intent on bringing away their fine, fat booty. In the chaos, two ships were struck; the remaining Trojans, through manly counsel, exhausted the enemy and made their escape.

In the meantime, the envoys in Troy were not idle either. For Palamedes—who at that time was considered the wisest among others both at home and in war, and gifted with good plans—stepped before King Priam. A council was also assembled for him, where he, before everyone, first recounted what gross wickedness Alexander had committed. Afterward, he lamented how, by this very example, the loyalty and fatherly duty between host and guest were diminished. He diligently warned them of what great ill-will could arise between kingdoms because of this. He let the examples of Ilium <note>Troy</note> and Pelops <note>the ancestor of the Greek kings Menelaus and Agamemnon</note> be mentioned among others, who for the same reasons came to blows until many lands were destroyed and laid waste.

Finally, he recounted what great hardships war brought with it, and conversely, how much benefit peace created. Thus, it was hidden neither from him nor others that such a villainous act <term>Bubenstück<gloss>a piece of knavery or a rogue's trick</gloss></term> created a loathing in almost all the world, so that everyone would distance themselves from such wrongdoers, and the vengeance would grow over their heads and break out.

Just as he, heated in his speech, wished to continue, Priam interrupted him. "Eh," he said, "proceed slowly, my Palamedes. It would not be consistent with justice to condemn one who is absent. Above all, it is necessary, if that person were present, that he be given the chance to explain himself regarding what he is accused of, or to answer for it well." With these and more words, he ordered such complaints to be postponed until the arrival of Alexander. For he saw well that all the counselors were already somewhat won over by Palamedes’ words, being horrified by the recounted deed of his son; moreover, even with disguised faces and remaining silent, they seemed to judge the matter as a failure. For the speech was so elegantly composed in all its parts, and the words of the Greek were almost all directed toward stirring up compassion. Nevertheless, nothing was decided in the council that day.

When they had departed from one another, Antenor was there—a man more hospitable and friendly than others, who dearly loved justice and honor.
