### The First Book.

He invited the envoys of the Greeks, and as they were willing, he led them home with him. A few days later, Alexander, with his aforementioned companions, set anchor in the harbor and landed, bringing Helen with him.

He had no sooner arrived than a murmur arose in the city; for some cursed him because of the villainy he had committed, while others grumbled that he had so greatly provoked Menelaus <note>The King of Sparta and Helen’s husband</note>. No one thought it right; finally, many became indignant, and the commoners gathered in a rowdy crowd. Priam <note>The King of Troy and Alexander’s father</note> became anxious; he called his sons together and asked them how this matter should be handled. They all answered as one: Helen should be kept. For they looked upon the great wealth she had brought with her, all of which would have to be given back if she were surrendered. Furthermore, they were moved by the beautiful women in her chamber who had arrived with her; each son had already chosen one for himself whom he wished to have. Now, their understanding brought them to a point where—just like their speech—it was so coarse that they acted neither with counsel nor reason; they were intent only on how they might scrape wealth together and fulfill their wantonness with women. Priam, considering their advice not to be for the best, called the elders among his advisors and revealed to them his sons’ opinions, inquiring how they should proceed. But before the council could be polled (as was the custom), the young princes burst into the council chamber and, in a brazen manner, threatened everyone with death if anyone should suggest anything contrary to their wishes. The common man stood outside, bearing great displeasure at the outrage; he voiced this and other grievances with a great clamor.

Alexander, pursuing his will in a reckless manner, feared the people might strike out with their fists or otherwise cause him harm. He took his brothers to his aid, with whom he—thus armed—overpowered the gathered crowd and even stabbed several in the throng. The rest were led away without further harm through the intervention of the Council and the protection of Antenor <note>A wise Trojan counselor who often advocated for peace</note>. Thus, the common man, who had little influence there, had to retreat home in great misery and ruin.

On the following day, on the advice of his consort Hecuba, King Priam went to Helen. He received her very graciously and comforted her, saying she should now be without worry. He requested that she reveal to him who she was and where she came from. Helen answered that she was a kinswoman <note>original: "baß"</note> of Alexander, claiming a closer relation to Priam and Hecuba than to the sons of Plisthenes <note>The lineage of Agamemnon and Menelaus</note>. She recounted her lineage from the beginning: how Danaus, of her own line, and Agenor, the ancestor of Priam, were of one origin <note>original: "vrhab"</note>. She claimed that Electra was born of Pleione, the daughter of Danaus and wife of Atlas. This same Electra, having been made pregnant by Jupiter <note>The king of the gods in Roman mythology, equivalent to the Greek Zeus</note>, had brought Dardanus into the world. From Dardanus, Tros was fathered, and from him the succeeding kings of Ilium <note>Troy</note>. Likewise, Agenor had fathered Taygete, who with Jupiter had Lacedaemon; he fathered Amyclas, nicknamed "the Little Mouse" <note>original: "das Måußlin"</note>, from whom came Argalus, the father of Oebalus. Now, Oebalus was the father of Tyndareus, and she was the daughter of that same Tyndareus. Afterward, she ran through how Hecuba was related to her on the maternal side, for Phoenix, the son of Agenor...

### Of the Trojan Conflict

...had divided the kinship <note>The text refers to a familial connection</note> between the elder Hecuba and her mother Leda.

And as she recounted this outwardly and without reservation, she began to call out kindly with tearful eyes that they should not deliver her up—she who had once received their promise of faith and protection. The goods she had taken from the house of Menelaus <note>The King of Sparta and Helen’s husband</note> and brought with her were her own property; she had taken nothing further from anyone else. Whether Helen said this out of the burning love she bore for Alexander <note>The Trojan prince also known as Paris</note>, or otherwise out of fear that if she were returned, she might meet with ill treatment from Menelaus because of her departure, could not be discerned. Indeed, it reached the point where Hecuba used all her diligence to ensure that she did not lose this kinswoman who was so closely related to her and who so dearly wished to be with her. For though Priam and the other princes, his sons, had already agreed that they should no longer delay the envoys of the Greeks so as not to be entirely contrary to the common people, it was Deiphobus <note>Another son of Priam</note> alone (who was no less fond of Helen than Alexander himself) who stood by and would not let his desire be turned away by useful counsel. So Hecuba lay constantly in the ears of King Priam and then her other sons, pleading that they should let Helen remain with her. Yes, beyond that, no one could tear or bring her away from Helen, whom she constantly held by the arm; no one could persuade her nor with any kind of advice restrain her from stopping her purpose, so that eventually everyone yielded to the Queen's will and, ultimately, the common welfare was neglected for the sake of motherly love.

The following day, Menelaus came to the open square before the entire assembly along with his fellow envoys. He demanded his spouse back, along with the goods that had been taken from him. Priam, who stood in the midst of the leaders, commanded silence. Then Helen came and was led before the common people. There he gave her the choice: whether she wished to travel back home. To this, she is said to have answered: she did not wish to go to her fatherland, for she had never been able to have a rightful marriage or peace with Menelaus. Upon this, Ulysses <note>Also known as Odysseus</note>, although he clearly perceived that he could accomplish nothing, yet to more quickly warn his own people, he recounted everything that Alexander had committed against the Greeks. He also openly advised that it must shortly be avenged. Menelaus became indignant, and with a wrathful face, he threatened all manner of hostility and uprooting, and he stepped out of the assembly, whereupon everyone withdrew.

When the speech of the Greeks reached the young princes—for they well considered (as the outcome also brought to pass) that if the envoys returned home with the matter unresolved, they would persuade and incite all the Greeks to great preparation and war—they secretly took counsel among themselves as to how they might execute the envoys with hidden treachery. Anthenor, of whose piety <note>Or "uprightness"</note> mention was made above, went to Priam and said there was a mutiny at hand, which was directed by his sons against him, and not against the envoys. He said he would not suffer it. Soon he also let the envoys know of these plots, saw that they were well and truly guarded, and at the first best opportunity, he sent them away unharmed.

While the matter was thus prolonged in Troy, and yet in Greece...

Once the matter had been fully discussed, the *descendants of Pelops* <note>The "Pelopider" refers to the house of Atreus, including Agamemnon and Menelaus, who were descendants of Pelops.</note> all convened and bound themselves by solemn oaths. A specific time was appointed for them to meet again to further deliberate on how the war should be conducted. The meeting place named was *Argos*, in the kingdom of *Diomedes*.

So everyone returned home again to make themselves prepared and ready with weapons, travel gear, and other equipment. All of Greece was in armor; weapons, artillery <note>original: "gschütz" — in this 16th-century context, this refers to siege engines, bows, or early projectile weapons rather than modern gunpowder cannons</note>, horses, and ships were prepared over the course of two consecutive years. Many capable youths went there willingly and enlisted; the others did not wish to be outdone by the best, but rather sought to be warlike. The most important labor during all this time was the building of ships, so that the many thousands of men assembling from all places could be transported without delay.

After the passage of two years, at Aulis (which was the designated meeting place), the naval armaments were prepared by every king according to his full capacity. Among these, the following arrived in the name of the Supreme Commander. Their captain was Agapenor.

<header>Concerning the Trojan Campaign</header>

Philoctetes, the son of Poeas, who was a former companion of Hercules; after whose death he received the arrows and quiver of the same as a special gift from the gods because of his swiftness.
Nereus from Syme, who was considered the handsomest man.
Mnestheus of Athens.
Ajax, a son of Oileus, from Locris.
Amphilochus from Argos, the son of Amphiaraus.
Sthenelus <note>original: "Schelenus"</note>, the son of Capaneus.
Euryalus, son of Mecisteus.
Thersander, the son of Polynices, from Aetolia.
Demophoon and Acamas <note>original: "Achamis"</note> were the last two.

Now, all of these were of the lineage of Pelops, and as has been told, each led a great following from his own land and domain—consisting of various kings or envoys from princes and lords—whose names it is quite unnecessary to recount one by one.

When all these lords had arrived at Argos, Diomedes hosted and received them very well; he provided them with fodder, meals, nails, and iron <note>Likely referring to materials for horseshoeing and repairing weapons or armor</note>. Agamemnon had brought a great treasure of gold from Mycenae, which he distributed among everyone, and to each specifically, so that he might make them more willing and ready for the impending war. But when the council met to discuss conducting the war, and the plan and agreement had been made, it was decided that they should bind themselves once again with an oath. This oath was sworn as follows:

Calchas, a son of Nestor <note>In standard mythology, Calchas is the son of Thestor; the author here links him to the wise King Nestor instead</note>, who was considered a seer, ordered that a boar be brought into the middle of the square. He divided it in two, hanging one piece toward the East <note>original: "Morgen"</note> and the other toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang"</note>. All the princes had to walk through the gap with drawn, naked swords, smearing the tips of the same with the blood of the boar and performing other rituals belonging thereto. Then they swore by their highest oath with great devotion to take up the feud with Priam and to be his enemy, and never to make an end to the war until they had first destroyed Troy and the entire kingdom. Upon this, they "baptized" themselves <note>original: "taufftẽ sie sich" — used here in the sense of a ritual initiation or purification rather than Christian baptism</note> and offered sacrifices to Mars and Lady Concordia, with humble prayer that they would grant them assistance. Immediately thereafter, in the temple and foundation of Juno at Argos, they proceeded to the election of who should be the Supreme Commander <note>term: "Veldherr" (Field Commander)</note>. Everyone who had a vote wrote on a small slip of paper the name of the one he judged useful and good for such a command. Thus, in African letters <note>This may refer to the "Phoenician" characters from which the Greek alphabet was derived, or perhaps a specific formal script used for sacred documents</note>, the name of Agamemnon was named and submitted more often than all others. Thereupon, because of his good reputation, he was unanimously recognized as the Commander. He willingly accepted this heavy responsibility for the sake of his brother Menelaus, whom the war concerned most and for whose sake it had begun. Thus, he was not unfairly elevated, as he was considered the most prominent and best equipped in wealth and power among the other kings in Greece.

Afterward, Achilles, Ajax, and Phoenix were appointed as captains over the naval armament.

In the field, the highest offices were held by Palamedes, Diomedes, and Ulysses, who were watch-masters and camp-masters, overseeing all necessary things day and night.

Then everyone returned home again to make themselves ready and prepared with weapons, travel gear, and other supplies. All of Greece was in armor; weapons, artillery, horses, and ships were prepared over the course of two consecutive years. Many capable youths went there willingly and had themselves enlisted; others also did not wish to be left behind, desiring rather to pursue glory and be warlike. The most important labor <note>original: "vnmüß" – literally "un-leisure," meaning a busy or difficult task</note> during all this time was the building of ships, so that the many thousands of men who gathered from all places could be transported across without delay.

# Of the Trojan Feud

->These total 1,280 <note>Roman numeral M. CC. lxxx.</note> ships.<-

Now, all the ships were well-laden with all kinds of grain, and furthermore quite richly provided with fodder and other nourishment, by the command and order of the Supreme Commander Agamemnon, so that such a great multitude of soldiers would not have to suffer a lack of food and maintenance. For there was a mighty number of horses, travel-wagons, and war-chariots; however, the infantry <note>original: "füßvolck"</note> far exceeded them in number. This was because in all the land of Greece, one cannot easily find enough pasture and fodder for horses; for this reason, fewer horses were available later on. Furthermore, one had to have many men who were fit for the ships, for the oars, and for other duties in sailing.

In the meantime, Phalis, the King in Sidon, attempted—with great entreaties and rich gifts—to entice Sarpedon, the Duke in Lycia, and to persuade him to join the power of the Greeks and fight against Troy. However, it was in vain; Priam <note>The King of Troy</note> had previously bribed him with even greater gifts. Whatever the Sidonian promised him, Priam offered him twofold, so that Sarpedon remained his friend.

For five consecutive years, preparations were made for this voyage, until this great and weighty host could be fully readied and assembled from all across Greece. When the army no longer lacked for anything, the lot and the signal <note>original: "loß vnnd Kryden" – refers to the formal call to arms or military orders</note> were given, and the place where they were to gather was appointed, so that on a single day, everyone appeared at Aulis. In his haste, Agamemnon the Supreme Commander ran out to look around and was separated somewhat from the crowd near a grove that was consecrated to Diana. There, he saw a roe deer grazing; not knowing that it was dedicated to the goddess, he dismounted, struck, and killed the animal. 

The goddess was enraged by this deed and poisoned the air, so that a plague <note>original: "schelm" – an archaic term for pestilence or a rogue disease</note> fell upon the host. The longer it lasted, the more fiercely it spread; each day it struck down many thousands of both people and livestock. There was no ceasing; every place was full of dead corpses, and everything tumbled into heaps. When the distress finally grieved the high officers and captains and made them anxious as to what should be done and from whence this misfortune came, a sorceress <note>likely referring to the seer Calchas, though the text uses the feminine "zaubererin"</note> appeared and revealed that it was the wrath of Diana, brought about by the misdeed of Agamemnon. The goddess would not be easily appeased regarding her deer, which had been quite dear and familiar to her; she could not be pacified unless the wrongdoer who had committed this offense sacrificed his own eldest daughter in place of the deer. 

When this report reached the ears of the common crowd, a delegation of the officers was sent to Agamemnon to first entreat him—and if he were not willing, finally to compel him by force—to take this burden from the people, and to do so speedily. Agamemnon would do nothing of the sort; he could neither be persuaded with kind words nor frightened by threats into consenting. Because of this, he was poorly spoken of <note>original: "außgebüppet"</note>, and he was removed and stripped of his command as Supreme Commander. Yet, so that such an innumerable multitude would not be without a head and so that military discipline would not fail entirely, they appointed Palamedes in his place.

# The First Book.
<meta>catchword: maiden</meta>

They gave him furthermore Diomedes, Ajax the Telamonian, and Idomeneus; thus the host was divided into four parts and commands according to number and insignia. Yet the dying <note>Refers to the plague mentioned on the previous page.</note> did not cease because of this.

Ulysses acted and behaved as if he were incensed by the stubbornness of Agamemnon <note>original: "Agamemnonis"</note>; he allowed a rumor to go out publicly that he wished to return home. But under this pretense, he arranged a great, healthy, and useful matter for the whole host, which no one would have expected. He traveled directly to Mycenae—no one knew his plan—taking several forged letters with him as if they had been written by Agamemnon. He brought them to Queen Clytemnestra, and they read as follows: That she should send him the elder of her two daughters, Iphigenia, as soon as she possibly could, as a bride royally provided for and outfitted for a wedding; for she was betrothed to Achilles, and he could not sail against Troy until his promise was fulfilled. And to all of this, Ulysses applied a very beautiful color with invented words to further his plan.

When Clytemnestra heard this, she had a longing for Helen, so that she might be recovered all the sooner, and also because her daughter was to be married to the most famous young man; therefore she did not delay the matter long. With joy, she sent Iphigenia away with Ulysses. Within a few days, he returned to the host and unexpectedly appeared with the maiden in the shrine <note>original: "than" — referring to a temple or sacred grove</note> of Diana.

When Agamemnon heard this and well understood that his daughter was to be sacrificed, he could not, out of fatherly love, bring himself to it; and so that he would not have to look upon the death of his child, he wished to depart with his armor. When Nestor noticed this (who was otherwise a friendly man, agreeable to all the world, and a sharp-witted hero among the Greeks for speaking above all others), he went to Agamemnon and spoke at great length with him until he persuaded him to desist from such a shameful departure and turned him away with good counsel. Meanwhile, according to their orders, Menelaus, Ulysses, and Calchas <note>original: "Chalcante"</note> prepared themselves, without any others being present, to sacrifice Iphigenia. Then the bright sky began to grow dark, and clouds moved over it; suddenly came lightning, thunder, and bolts; upon the water was a great tempest, and upon the land an earthquake, so that through this disruption of the air, a darkness also fell. Immediately there followed a great storm with driving rain and hail that would not cease. Menelaus and his companions who prepared the sacrifice were terrified; they did not know what to do for fear, for they held the sudden and violent change of weather to be a sign of God's wrath; yet the rogue of the soldiery <note>likely referring to the pressure from the restless army</note> forced them so that they did not wish to stop. In that moment, they heard a voice from the shrine, which they heard during this contrary action and understood in this way: The Goddess rejected this sacrifice, therefore one should leave the maiden's body unharmed, for she had compassion for her. However, the Goddess would make the matter difficult enough for Agamemnon on his return home because of the misdeed he had committed. Therefore, they should slaughter and sacrifice that which stood before them and was offered as a sacrifice, in place of the maiden.

...maiden. Immediately the weather, the thunder, lightning, and a great noise in the air began, then ceased and settled down gradually.
   While they were walking about in the temple <note>original: "than" — referring to a sacred grove or sanctuary</note> in this manner, Achilles received letters along with a great amount of gold, which Clytemnestra had delivered to him; in these, she faithfully entrusted Iphigenia and all her family and kin to him. When Achilles had read the letters and understood what Ulysses had orchestrated <note>Ulysses had forged letters from Agamemnon to lure Iphigenia to the camp under the pretense of a marriage to Achilles.</note>, he set all business aside, hurried to the temple, and with a fierce voice, he spoke to Menelaus and his companions, saying they should take heed and leave the maiden unharmed; if any of them bent a single hair on her head, it would cost him his life. They were greatly terrified, having already been stunned by the storm; then Achilles arrived, and as it became a little clearer, he snatched the maiden out of their hands. And as they stood there, looking around for what or where the thing might be that they had been commanded by the voice to sacrifice, a beautiful dog, quite large and smooth, leaped to the altar and stood still there, willingly offering itself for sacrifice. Then they understood well that this was indeed the beast they had heard of; they seized it and sacrificed it. Then the rogue <note>original: "ſchelm" — likely referring here to the tempest or the divine ill-will</note> relented, and the sky became like beautiful summer weather.
   It so happened that the King of Scythia was in the camp; therefore, Achilles and those who had intended the sacrifice entrusted the maiden to that same king, so secretly that no one knew where she had gone. But when the captains noticed that the storm had ceased and the winds were favorable for sailing, and that things were in their proper state, they all went with joy to Agamemnon. He was mourning for his daughter (for he believed she had been put to death); they comforted him with good words and restored his previous command and royal honor with the rejoicing and agreement of the entire host; for the soldiers loved and honored this Agamemnon as their father and as the wisest man in all the war. Perhaps General Agamemnon had secretly discovered how the matter stood, or else, as a wise lord, he could well measure and understand human frailty and sorrowful accidents; for this reason, he was better able to comfort himself and bear the adversity with a firm heart. He acted as if no sorrow had befallen him, took up his command again, and on that same day, he invited all the officers as his guests. After a few days, every captain had prepared and disciplined his folk so that they all, with good readiness, boarded the ships when they had a following wind. They also loaded all kinds of the finest things brought to them by the inhabitants—grain, wine, fodder, and other nourishment—given to them by Anius <note>Anius was the King of Delos and a priest of Apollo; his daughters were said to have the divine gift of producing food and wine.</note> and his daughters, and everything else the priests deemed necessary. # Dictys of Crete on
## the Trojan War
### The Second Book.

When they had departed from Aulis and arrived near the region of Mysia <note>A region in northwest Asia Minor, near Troy.</note>, they positioned themselves there, anchoring all their ships close to the shore. As they intended to disembark, the Greeks were resisted by the local soldiers stationed in the coastal towns to guard the province. Their commander was Telephus <note>The King of Mysia and a son of Hercules; he was originally a Greek but was now defending his own kingdom.</note>, who had secured the harbors, sounds, and landing places along the sea against pirates. Thus, they would not allow the Greeks to disembark or step onto land until they had informed Telephus who they were and where they had come from.

The Greeks at first paid no heed to these words or justifications; every man wanted to be the first off the ship. The guards and garrisons would not permit such pride and began to resist with defiance and force as strongly as they could. When the Greek leaders saw that their men were being treated with such indignity, they decided it was time to avenge this with their own hands. They drew their weapons, leaped ashore, and with angry hearts, they struck, stabbed, and killed many of the local people, putting them to flight. They did not spare those who fled; whoever they caught had to die.

Those who were best able to run and escape the Greeks came to Telephus, telling him that many thousands of enemies had landed, that the watchmen and guards had been driven from the land, and that everything had been conquered—out of fear, they greatly exaggerated the situation. Telephus, with the people he had with him and all those he could gather in haste, marched quickly against the Greeks. There, both sides rushed together with strongly formed battle lines, and so a clash began. Each man struck down the nearest foe; each looked out carefully for his comrades and allies, doing the best and most effective work he could. In this turmoil, Thesander <note>Son of Polynices of Thebes; he was one of the "Epigoni" who had earlier conquered Thebes.</note> exerted himself greatly and killed many of the enemy. Boldly, he even charged at King Telephus himself. The King was enraged because Thesander had stabbed his companion and bodyguard (whom he had appointed as a captain for his bravery and skill) by his side. Thus, in a singular combat, Thesander was slain. For the youth, having been successful at first, believed he would never fail; he therefore attempted even greater deeds, which led to his downfall. Diomedes snatched up his body, which was still fair to look upon, and carried it on his shoulder out through the enemy. He remembered how they had been raised together since childhood and the friendship and companionship they had shared. He had the body burned and buried what remained in the ashes according to the customs of the land.

But when Achilles and Ajax the Telamonian <note>Ajax the Great, son of Telamon, famed as the strongest Greek after Achilles.</note> heard and saw how the war and strife were being prolonged to the great disadvantage of their men, they divided the multitude into two parts. As much as time permitted, they also exhorted their own men...

<page-num>xiiij</page-num>
# Of the Trojan Feud

...their men, and they themselves as the captains followed those who were retreating; against those who attacked them, they stood their ground as unmoving as a rock. Now at the front, then among the foremost, they allowed their manhood and bravery to be seen, so much so that they earned praise and fame even from their enemies.

Teutratius, a son of Teutras and—on the side of his mother, Auge—a half-brother to Telephus <note>In some traditions, Teutratius is considered a full brother; the text clarifies he is a "right" or full brother through their mother.</note>, seeing how Ajax raged among his men and won great honor to his own side's injury, pressed forward against Ajax himself. As they fought, he was run through and killed. Telephus was not a little grieved by the death of his brother and set out to avenge him. With an embittered spirit, he attacked Ajax and put everything before him to flight. Ulysses <note>Also known as Odysseus.</note> escaped from him into a vineyard; Telephus pursued him so recklessly that he stumbled over a grapevine and fell to the ground. When Achilles saw this from afar, he cast a javelin <note>original: "handpfeyl" - literally a hand-arrow or small spear.</note> at him; it struck and passed through Telephus's hip. Telephus quickly scrambled up again and pulled the arrow from the wound. His men ran to him, protected him, and fended off the stabs and blows so that he was delivered from this danger and his life was saved, though it was a narrow escape.

This battle lasted long into the day. The soldiers of both sides were now winning, then being pushed back, sparing themselves nowhere, guided by their noble and most courageous captains, so that it remained an even struggle. For the presence of Telephus had greatly terrified our men <note>The "our men" refers to the Greeks, as the narrator, Dictys, is framed as a Greek participant.</note>, who were already exhausted from many days of sailing. He was the son of Hercules, of upright stature and great strength; with his innate bravery, he nearly matched the heroic and divine deeds of his father. When night began to fall, both sides desired rest; they ceased fighting, and the Mysians retreated to their homes while our men returned to the ships. But in that same struggle, many people from both sides were slain, and a great part were wounded; none, or very few, escaped without receiving blows.

Then, on the following day, messengers were sent back and forth from both sides regarding those who had perished in the previous battle, as each side desired to bury them. During the agreed-upon truce, the corpses were gathered together, burned in fire, and afterwards buried. In the meantime, Tlepolemus and Phidippus, along with his brother Antiphus (who were descended from Thessalus, the grandson of Hercules, as mentioned before), realized that Telephus, the King and lord of these lands, was their blood relative. Therefore, out of the good trust of friendship, they went to him, made themselves known, and explained with whom they had arrived. After they had spoken with him at length, our men also rebuked him sternly for behaving in such a hostile manner toward his kinsmen. They explained how Agamemnon and Menelaus were descended from Pelops <note>A legendary king of Mycenae and ancestor of the Atreid line.</note> and were not foreign people, but had gathered a host of soldiers solely from their own lineage. Then they informed him how Alexander <note>The Trojan prince Paris, often called Alexander in classical and medieval texts.</note> had shamed Menelaus in honor and property and had carried Helen away. Therefore, they argued, it would be fitting for him, for the sake of friendship and because Alexander had violated the laws of hospitality in the places where he had been well-received, to come to the aid of the Greeks on his own accord, by

# The Second Book

For this reason, many memories of the noble deeds of Hercules himself <note>Telephus was the son of Hercules, which explains the shared history between him and the Greeks.</note> were still preserved throughout all of Greece. Regarding these matters, Telephus—although he was weakened beyond measure by the pain of his wounds—nevertheless answered in a friendly manner. He said that what had happened was more through their own fault, for he had not known that his best friends and well-wishers were sailing to his kingdom. Had he known, he said, messengers should have been sent ahead so that he might have learned of their arrival; he would then have gone out to meet them with rejoicing, welcomed them as guests, presented them with generous gifts <note>original: "schwänckungen" — likely referring to parting gifts or tokens of hospitality given to departing guests.</note> (had it pleased them), and allowed them to travel on. Furthermore, he stated he did not wish to wage war against Priam <note>The King of Troy.</note>, for Astioche, Priam’s daughter, had been given to him in marriage; Eurypilus was born of her, and he was the greatest bond of kinship between them. Immediately after this, he ordered his subjects to cease their efforts, and thus he gave our men full authority to leave their ships.

Afterward, they exhorted their people according to the circumstances of the time; meanwhile, Tlepolemus and those who had come with him were handed over to Eurypilus. The others, once they had accomplished the things they desired, went to the ships and announced to Agamemnon and the other princes that there was peace and unity with Telephus. When they heard this, they joyfully allowed the military order of battle to be dissolved. Thereafter, Achilles and Ajax, by a resolution of the council, came to Telephus and comforted him as he suffered in great pain, asking him to endure the injury manfully. But Telephus, as the pain eased a little, rebuked the Greeks for not having sent an embassy ahead to announce their coming. 

Next, he asked which and how many of the lineage of Pelops <note>Pelops was a central figure in Greek mythology; his descendants, the Pelopids, included many of the leaders of the Greek expedition, such as Agamemnon and Menelaus.</note> were in this expedition. Once informed, he requested with great earnestness that they all come to him; our men promised him they would do everything he wished. They announced the King's desire to the others, and consequently, all those descended from Pelops (except Agamemnon and Menelaus) gathered together and came to Telephus, causing the King great rejoicing and joy by their presence. Subsequently, they were presented with rich gifts and provided with lodging. Furthermore, the servants who remained by the ships were not excluded from this royal generosity, for grain and other necessary provisions were carried out to them in sufficient quantities, according to the number of ships. 

When the King noticed that Agamemnon and his brother were not there, he earnestly entreated Ulysses <note>Also known as Odysseus.</note> to go and fetch them. Thus they also came to Telephus, and according to royal custom, they exchanged and received gifts among one another. Afterward, they called for Machaon and Podalirius, the sons of Aesculapius <note>Aesculapius (Asclepius) was the god of medicine; his sons served as the primary physicians for the Greek army.</note>, to heal the wound. When they saw the affliction, they immediately applied skillful medicine or plasters over the injury. 

However, after several days had passed, the season for sailing was hindered; the sea began to rage daily with contrary winds. They went to Telephus and asked him about the favorability of the season, and they were instructed by him that the right time would be at the beginning of spring...

-># Of the Trojan Feud<-

Some wished to sail toward Troy, but others were opposed. Thus (as they all eventually desired) they turned back toward Boeotia; there, each man took his ship to a specific place and withdrew to his own kingdom to remain there over the winter. During that period of rest, Agamemnon had the time to harbor enmity toward his brother Menelaus on account of the sacrifice of Iphigenia <note>Agamemnon’s daughter, who was sacrificed (or nearly so) to appease the goddess Artemis to allow the winds to blow for the Greek fleet.</note>, for it was believed that Menelaus was the instigator and the very cause of Agamemnon's great mourning.

At that same time, when the news of the conspiracy of all Greece against Troy became known (through the messengers who traveled with the foreigners who commonly traded their wares throughout the entire Hellespont and moved to and fro), a sudden fear and sadness came over them all. This was especially true for those who had from the beginning disliked the misdeeds of Alexander <note>original: "Alexandri" — refers to Paris, the son of Priam, who sparked the war by taking Helen.</note> and admitted that a great evil had been committed against Greece; they feared they would be overwhelmed by a common ruin because of the wickedness of a few. Since they were so anxious about these things, many were chosen with great diligence from every rank to gather support from the neighboring regions, sent out by Alexander and other wicked advisors. They were also commanded to return as soon as they had carried out their business. This was most encouraged by the sons of Priam, so that they might gain time by quickly preparing an army and ensure the entire war being readied was brought over into the territory of Greece itself. While these things were happening at Troy, Diomedes became aware of their intentions and traveled in great haste through all of Greece. He spoke to all the princes and presented the Trojan designs to them, reminding and exhorting them to prepare themselves as quickly as possible with the necessary things for war and to hurry to the ships. Not long after the matter became known, they all came to him at Argos. There, Achilles was angry with the King <note>Agamemnon</note> because he had called off the voyage on account of his daughter; however, he was brought to agreement by Ulysses <note>Odysseus.</note>. For Ulysses had for a long time now brought to Agamemnon's mind—which was sad and overcome with lamentation—what had transpired with his daughter, and he restored his spirit and dignity to a new state. Therefore, when they were all together, and although none of them neglected the requirements of the war, Ajax Telamonius and Achilles, along with Diomedes, took upon themselves the highest care and diligence in organizing the war. They also decided to prepare several ships to accompany the gathered armada, with which they were to raid the enemies' territories; thus they assembled a fleet of fifty ships, equipped with all kinds of supplies. Although this war had been started eight years ago and delayed until this time, it was now entering the ninth year. When the armada was fully prepared and the sea was favorable for sailing, and nothing more hindered them, they hired the Citians <note>original: "Citas" — likely referring to people from Citium in Cyprus or a general term for seafaring merchants used as mercenaries.</note> who had traveled there for trade, and chose commanders over those same garrisons.

At that same time, Sarpedon of Lycia—the son of Xanthus <note>original: "Kanti"; Sarpedon's parentage varies in myth, sometimes cited as a son of Zeus or Xanthus.</note> and Laodamia—arrived, encouraged by Priam, who had sent one messenger after another to him. He came with a large company of armed soldiers. When he saw from afar that a great force of ships was approaching the shores <note>original: "ländin"</note>, he realized the situation and immediately organized his men and attacked the Greeks as they attempted to step out onto the land. Not long after, the sons of Priam, as they became aware of the matter, ran toward them with drawn weapons. During this time, the Greeks—on whose necks the hateful enemy lay in every way—could not come ashore without great destruction, nor could they yet defend themselves, because they were running into one another and thus one hindered the other. Yet finally, those who had been able to arm themselves in that same haste encouraged one another and bravely charged at the enemy. But in that same struggle, Prothesilaus (whose ship was the very first to reach the land) was fighting among the foremost when he was finally shot by Aeneas's arrow and fell to the ground. Two of Priam's sons also perished, and the rest of the multitude on both sides did not remain inexperienced in battle. But Achilles and Ajax Telamon <note>original: "Aiay Thelamonius"; referring to Ajax the Greater.</note>, through whose bravery the Greeks were preserved, fought with great honor; they struck fear into the enemies and gave heart to their own men, and they could no longer be resisted until those against whom they marched gradually withdrew and were finally all driven away. Thus, the Greeks, in a time of safety from the enemy, pulled their ships onto the shore and secured them one after another in an orderly fashion. Afterward, they chose Achilles and Ajax Telamon (in whose virtue they placed their hope) to be guards, assigning them the protection of the ships and the army's passage, around the sides and at the forward points.

And not long thereafter, while our men were much occupied with the burial of Prothesilaus <note>Prothesilaus was the first Greek hero to die in the Trojan War, killed as he leaped ashore.</note> and at such a time feared nothing from the enemy, Cygnus—whose dominion lay not far from Troy—having learned of our arrival, attacked the Greeks secretly and with deceitful ruses. ### How the Greeks attacked and conquered several 
### cities that were allied with Troy.

Furthermore, the captains were careful and anxious regarding the many deaths and damages that had often befallen them from the enemy's assaults. It was then decided that they should first march with a portion of the army against the cities nearest to Troy and attack them by all means. Thus, they first took the land of Cygnus and laid everything waste. However, when they had captured the city of the Metorensers <note>Likely referring to the people of Methymna on the island of Lesbos.</note>—which was called the capital of the whole realm and the nurse of Cygnus's children—and since no one resisted them, they began to kindle fires. The citizens of that city begged them with great prayer and weeping to desist from their purpose, entreating them by all things human and divine on bended knees that they should not let the innocent citizenry—who soon after became loyal to them—pay for or suffer the guilt of that most wicked prince. In such a manner, through pity, the city was preserved. But the King's children, Cobis and Corianus, and their sister Glauce, they delivered to the Greeks as they had requested. This daughter they granted to Ajax <note>Ajax the Greater, son of Telamon.</note> because of his noble deeds, after taking the rest of the booty. Not long after, the Metorensers came seeking peace from the Greeks, promising them friendship and to do everything they were commanded or ordered. After these things were done, the Greeks attacked and won Cylla, yet did not touch Corone (which lay not far away) out of favor for the Maeandrians, who were neighbors of that city and have remained loyal and best friends to us until this time.

At that same time, a prophecy of the Pythian God <note>Apollo, whose oracle was at Delphi.</note> was brought to the Greeks, directing that a sacrifice be held for the Sminthean Apollo <note>original: "Smyrnischen Apollini" — likely a reference to Apollo Smintheus, the 'Mouse-God' worshipped in the Troad.</note> by Palamedes. This matter was pleasing to many because of the skill and love of the man which he showed toward the whole army, though it pained several of the princes <note>Palamedes's growing popularity caused jealousy, particularly in Ulysses (Odysseus).</note>.

Furthermore, a sacrifice of a dog-like animal <note>original: "hundt thierē"; this refers to an ancient Greek purification ritual involving the sacrifice of dogs to cleanse an army</note> (as mentioned above) was held for the whole army. Chryses, a priest of that place, presided over the rite. In the meantime, Alexander <note>The Trojan prince Paris, often called Alexander in classical texts.</note> became aware of the matter and came with a gathered troop to prevent it. However, the two Ajaxes <note>Ajax the Greater and Ajax the Lesser, two prominent Greek heroes.</note> drove him away before he reached the temple and slew many of his men. But Chryses—who, as we noted before, was a priest of the Sminthean Apollo <note>Apollo Smintheus, or "The Mouse God," a title of Apollo particularly associated with the region of Troy and the Troad.</note>—feared the enmity of both armies. Regardless of which party came to him, he acted as though he were on their side. During this time, Philoctetes, who stood not far from the altar of that same temple, was bitten by a snake. Thereupon a cry arose from all those who had noticed it, and Ulysses <note>Odysseus.</note> ran toward him and killed the snake. Not long after, Philoctetes was sent with a few men to the island of Lemnos to be healed, for the inhabitants say that the high priests of the cult of Vulcan dwell there, who commonly heal such poisonings.

At that same time, Diomedes and Ulysses took counsel together on how they might kill Palamedes. For human nature is such that it is weak against the sorrows of the mind and full of envy; it cannot well endure that a better man should surpass it. Therefore, they pretended that they had found a treasure in a draw-well <note>original: "galgbrunnen"; a deep well, often with a hoist.</note> which they wished to share with him. They told everyone to stay away and advised Palamedes that he should be the first to climb down. Thus, fearing no treachery, he was lowered on a rope. They then quickly snatched up stones that lay around and threw them down upon him with great force. In this way, a very pious man, who was greatly beloved by the army, was betrayed and unjustly perished at the hands of those who should never have done such a thing to him. However, there were some who said that Agamemnon was also not ignorant of their counsel, because of the favor the prince <note>Palamedes, who was a brilliant strategist and often rivaled Agamemnon in popularity.</note> held with the army. It was also because Palamedes desired to rule the greater part of the force and openly said the command should be given to him. Therefore, his body was burned in a fire by all the Greeks as a public loss and buried in a golden vessel. 

Meanwhile, Achilles considered that the nearest city to Troy would become a servant and a workshop for the war. He took several ships with him and attacked Lesbos, taking it without any difficulty. He slew Porgaritas <note>Likely Phorbas, mentioned in other accounts as a king of Lesbos.</note>, the king of that place, who had undertaken many things as an enemy against the Greeks, and led away Diomedea, the king's daughter, with a great hoard of booty. Afterward, at the desire of all his subjects, he attacked the cities of Pyrrha and Hierapolis, which were full of riches, with great force and destroyed them in a few days without effort. Furthermore, wherever he went, the fields—which were full because of the long peace—were plundered by him and afflicted in all ways. Nothing remained belonging to the Trojans that was not ravaged and devastated. When the neighbors became aware of these things, they came to him of their own accord with peace offerings, promising half of their crops if their fields were not ravaged. Thus, the pledge and trust of peace was vowed and accepted by him.

<header>Of Trojan Damage</header>

# How Achilles besieged and took several cities, and 
->how King Brises, in a state of desperation,<- 
->hanged himself.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' featuring floral motifs and scrolls.</image-desc>
After these events had occurred, Achilles returned again to the host <note>original: "hör"; refers to the gathered Greek army</note>, bringing with him a great company—or a great force—along with honor and booty. At that same time, the King of the Scythians, who had become aware of our arrival, came with great gifts. However, Achilles, not content with the deeds he had already performed, also attacked Cilicia and within a few days won Lyrnessus by storm. Afterward, he slew Eetion <note>OCR reads "Factionem," a misspelling of Eetion, the King of Lyrnessus and father of Andromache</note>, who ruled in those parts, loaded the ships with great riches, and carried away Astynome <note>also known as Chryseis</note>, the daughter of Chryses, who at that time was married to the King. And shortly thereafter, he began to wage war against Pedasus and the city of the Leleges. But Brises, their king, when he perceived that our men were so fierce, thought to himself that he could not withstand the enemy with any force, nor could his people be sufficiently protected. Therefore, out of despair of all refuge and fortune, he went home and hanged himself while the others were occupied against the enemy. And not long after, the city was taken, many people were slain, and Hippodamia <note>better known to history as Briseis</note>, the King’s daughter, was led away. At that same time, Ajax, son of Telamon, ravaged the Thracian Chersonese with all his might. But when Polymnestor, their king, recognized the virtue and fame of the man, and despairing of his own affairs, he surrendered himself. Thereafter Polydorus, the son of Priam (whom the King had sent to him to be raised in secret when he was a newborn), was handed over to him as a price for peace. Enough gold and other such gifts were also surrendered to appease the minds of the enemies. Afterward, he also promised the whole host enough grain for the entire year and loaded the "hunger-ships" <note>supply ships intended to relieve the army's famine</note> that Ajax had taken with him for that purpose. With many great oaths, renouncing Priam’s friendship in favor of the Greeks, he was accepted by them into peace and loyalty. After Ajax had transacted these things, he directed his path against the Phrygians and, having entered their land, slew Teuthras, who alone fought against him as the lord of that place. And after a few days, he destroyed and burned the city, carrying away a great force of booty and Tecmessa, the King’s daughter.

# The Second Book

...and praise was raised, and in the middle [of the camp] they set up [the spoils], crowning them with olive branches. Afterwards, a council was held to decide how they should divide the booty and how to distribute it. **Nestor** and **Idomeneus** <note>Nestor and Idomeneus were among the oldest and most respected Greek leaders, often acting as advisors and administrators.</note> served as the chief officials; for this reason, they brought before **Agamemnon**, out of royal honor, everything from the entire booty that Achilles had brought—except for **Astynome** <note>original: "Astynome"; more commonly known in Greek mythology as Chryseis</note>, the wife of Eetion <note>The OCR reads "Factionis," a corruption of Eetion, the King of Cilician Thebe</note>, who, as we mentioned above, was the daughter of **Chryses**.

But **Achilles** kept for himself **Hippodamia** <note>Better known as Briseis, the captive woman whose later seizure by Agamemnon sparks the central conflict of the Iliad</note>, the daughter of Brises, along with **Diomedea**. Since the two women were of the same age and had been raised together <note>original: "einerley narung"; literally "of the same nourishment," implying they grew up in the same household</note>, they could not be parted from one another without great sorrow. For this reason, they had previously fallen at the knees of Achilles and had beseeched him with great prayer that they not be separated. The rest of the booty was distributed to everyone according to each man's merit.

Afterward, **Ulysses** and **Diomedes** also brought into the midst of them the things that **Ajax** had brought, doing so at his request. From these spoils, as much silver and gold as seemed sufficient was given to King Agamemnon. Then, on account of his noble deeds and labor, they allowed Ajax to have **Tecmessa**, the daughter of **Teuthras** <note>King of Phrygia, killed by Ajax</note>. Thus, whatever was still remaining was divided among them all, and the grain was issued to the entire army.

After they had accomplished these things, he <note>Agamemnon</note> also recounted the terms of the pact and promise that had been made between him and **Polymnestor**, and how **Polydorus** <note>The youngest son of King Priam of Troy, sent away for safety but captured by the Greeks</note> had been handed over to him. Because of this matter, it was decided by them alone that Ulysses and Diomedes should travel to **Priam** to demand the return of **Helen** and the things that had been carried away, while also offering to return Polydorus. 

As they journeyed there, **Menelaus** (for whose sake this entire affair was conducted) also joined the aforementioned men in the duty of the embassy. Thus, they came to the Trojans, having Polydorus with them. When the common people saw that distinguished men of great name had arrived, they immediately brought together all the old men (whose counsel was usually taken there), while Priam kept only his sons at home. 

Therefore, when the others were present, Menelaus spoke among the Greeks, saying that he had now come for the second time regarding this one matter, even though many other things had been done or shown against him and his house. He was forced to complain of this with great sighing: that his little daughter <note>Hermione, the daughter of Menelaus and Helen</note> was now a motherless child <note>original: "weislos kind"; literally "orphan-like," referring to the absence of her mother Helen</note> because of his wife’s absence. All these things had happened to him through the man who had been his good friend and guest, and not according to what he deserved. The elders heard this excessive lamentation with weeping eyes; and whoever spoke, they bowed their heads toward him as if they had compassion for his disgrace. Following this, Ulysses stood in the midst of them and gave such a speech:

"I hold that you Trojan princes have good knowledge that the Greeks are not accustomed to undertaking anything wanton or unreasonable, and how the same has always been demonstrated and proven by us since the days of old..."

# Of the Havoc of Troy

## How Achilles Besieged and Captured Several Cities, and How King Brises Hanged Himself Out of Despair.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring stylized floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

After these events, Achilles returned to the army, bringing with him a great multitude—or rather, great power, honor, and booty. At that same time, the King of the **Scythians**, who had become aware of our arrival, came with great gifts. But Achilles was not satisfied with what he had already accomplished; he attacked **Cilicia** as well, and there, in a few days, he also won **Lyrnessus** by storm. Afterward, he slew **Eetion** <note>original: "Factionem"; this refers to Eetion, the ruler of Cilician Thebe and father of Andromache</note>, who ruled in those parts, loaded the ships with great riches, and led away **Astynome** <note>Better known as Chryseis</note>, the daughter of **Chryses**, who at that time was married to the king. 

Hurrying on after that, he began to wage war against **Pedasus** and the city of the **Lelegians**. But **Brises**, their king, when he noticed how fierce our men were, thought to himself that he could not withstand the enemy with any force, nor could his people be sufficiently protected. Thus, out of despair for all refuge and good fortune, he went home and hanged himself while the others were busy fighting the enemy. Not long after, the city was taken, many people were slain, and **Hippodamia** <note>Better known as Briseis</note>, the king's daughter, was led away. 

At that same time, **Ajax Telamonius** ravaged the **Thracian Chersonese** with all his might. When **Polymnestor**, their king, recognized the virtue and fame of the man and, distrusting his own situation, surrendered himself. Afterward, **Polydorus**, the son of **Priam** (whom the king had secretly sent to be raised by Polymnestor when he was a newborn), was handed over by him as a price for peace. Sufficient gold and other such gifts were also given to appease the minds of the enemies. Polymnestor then promised the entire army enough grain for the whole year and loaded the provision ships <note>original: "hungerschiff"; literally "hunger-ships," used to transport food to the starving army</note> that Ajax had brought with him. With many great oaths, renouncing his friendship with Priam in favor of the Greeks, he was accepted by them in peace and loyalty. 

When Ajax had concluded these matters, he directed his path against the **Phrygians** and entered their land, where he slew **Teuthras**, the lord of those parts, in single combat. After a few days, he destroyed and burned the city, carrying away a great force of booty and **Tecmessa**, the king's daughter.

# Of Trojan Harm

...so that one should rather praise their stories and deeds afterward, than shame them. And so that I may let past good advice pass, one may now well recognize the immeasurable way in which Greece was previously justly insulted by us through the disgrace of Alexander <note>The name "Alexander" is frequently used in these texts to refer to Paris, the son of King Priam who abducted Helen</note>, and how we did not immediately run to take up arms, which is usually the refuge of anger. For by the council's decision, we came as ambassadors with Menelaus (as you well know) to take back Helen, and nothing was given to us by Priam and his young sons except haughty, threatening words and secret ambushes. Therefore, since we could achieve nothing, it was surely appropriate (as I judge) to set out with armed hands and demand our justice by force, which could not be obtained through friendship. 

Therefore, although we have raised an army from all of Greece, with so many brave and illustrious princes, it was nonetheless not our intention to enter into conflict with you, but rather to follow our custom and usual moderation. Now for the second time, we have come back to entreat you regarding the previous matter. The other things lie in your hands, dear Trojans, and it should not regret us that we have advised you for the best (if you are otherwise of good sense) and wish to improve the previous evil plans with good, wholesome undertakings. 

Consider, for God's sake, in your minds what bloodshed and, like a pale sickness following this example, will come upon the whole world. For who would there be (where there is otherwise a manly heart) who would not find it necessary to be suspicious and wary of himself above all things, and also to fear for his friends, when he thinks of the misdeed of Alexander? Or which brother would open door and gate to another anymore? Who would not fear them more as a guest or kinsman than as an enemy? 

Finally, if you should praise this—which I do not expect—then all laws of oaths and loyalty among the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarier"; in the classical context, this refers to all non-Greek peoples, including the Trojans</note> and Greeks will be completely barred. Therefore, dear Trojan princes, it is good and useful that the Greeks be sent home in friendship (as is only right), returning all things that were taken from them by force. For so many of you are held in high regard and are undeserving, and completely uninvolved in that guilt, yet because of the unchastity of a few, you will soon have to suffer punishment for the vices of others. 

Or are you the only ones who do not know how the cities near here and allied with you have been treated, and what is daily done even to those that still stand? You surely know how Polydorus <note>Priam’s youngest son, often depicted in medieval accounts as being captured or sent away for safety</note> was captured and is being held by the Greeks, who might be returned unharmed to Priam if only Helen, along with the other stolen things, were now given back. Otherwise, the war can in no way be delayed any longer, and there will be no end to it, unless either all the princes of Greece (each of whom alone would be sufficient to destroy the city) lose their lives, or (as I rather hope) the city of Troy is taken, burned with fire...

# On the Trojan Destruction
<meta>catchword: burnt/</meta>

...so that one might praise their stories and deeds hereafter rather than shaming them. ## The Second Book

->...be burned, and also left as an example of true villainy <note>original: "schalckheyt"</note> for those who come after. Therefore, while you still have the matter entirely in your hands, consider it well.<-

And after he had finished speaking, and each man (as is common in such dealings) waited for the other's opinion—since no one felt himself prepared enough to be the first to speak—Panthus spoke among them with a clear voice: "Ulysses, you speak words here which we (except for our good will) have absolutely no power to assist with deeds." After him, Antenor said: "All these things you have recounted here, we shall have to suffer while knowing and seeing them; nor would we lack the good will to strive for what is right, if only the power were left to us. But those men hold the highest authority in all things (as you see), who value their own heads more than what is useful and good." And when he had spoken these things, he ordered all the Princes—those who were there for the sake of friendship with Priam <note>King of Troy</note> and those who were also hired for money—to be led in with their armies to help.

When these same men had entered, Ulysses began another speech, calling them all entirely unjust and no different from Alexander <note>original: "Alexandro"; another name for Paris, the prince who abducted Helen</note>, for they had fallen away from what is good and honorable and were following those who cause evil vices. He said all men knew well that if such a shameful injustice were praised, it would eventually happen that—once this evil example was spread among the people—even those who were not far from it would do such things, or perhaps even worse things hereafter. These matters, as they were cruel in themselves, they all considered within themselves in silence, and they were moved by the shamefulness of the things and felt a horror at such an example. 

Afterward, when they asked for the opinion of all the Elders, they all unanimously recognized that Menelaus had suffered this injustice through no fault of his own; only Antimachus <note>a Trojan advisor who, according to legend, was bribed by Paris to argue against returning Helen</note>, against them all, cried out in favor of Alexander. And immediately two men were chosen and sent to announce everything to Priam, who, among other things commanded to them, reported to him concerning Polydorus <note>Priam's youngest son, who was at this time held captive by the Greeks</note>. When the King heard these things, he was greatly terrified by the message concerning his son and fell down before the sight of them all. Afterward, he was slightly revived and raised up by those who were around him. 

When he wished to go into the Council, he was prevented by the young Kings <note>his sons</note>. For they themselves abandoned their father and broke into the assembly by force. And just as Antimachus had let fly many shameful words to insult the Greeks, he said they should only then let Menelaus go. If Polydorus were delivered to them, they must hold to one and the same case, one and the same end, with one as with the other. Against these things, Antenor alone (while all others remained silent) held the opposing side and fought with great force against such a decision being recognized. But after they had exchanged many words and their dispute had come to blows, all those who were there denounced Antimachus as a meddler and a rioter and thrust him out of the Council House. Even Alexander <note>original: "Alexander"; another name for Paris, the Trojan prince who sparked the war</note> would have achieved not a little in satisfying his desire, even if he truly did have a love for Helen; therefore, one must keep in view the presence of the Greek kings, their honorable deeds, and the new glory they attained when they destroyed the cities of Troy's very best friends. When Hector had heard these things, he became somewhat troubled by the memory of his brother's misdeeds and, out of sorrow, let his tears fall; yet he in no way intended to give Helen back, for she had sought the protection of his house, and therefore one must protect and defend her according to his sworn word. Against him, Aeneas also spoke: "Yes, one should not even give you the things mentioned, if I am to speak against it, or if I and the others who are related to me by marriage and friendship and who have advised Alexander for his benefit, have our way. And so that I do not admit that this was the first such abduction, Io was carried out of the land of the Sidonians and moved all the way to Argos. Hitherto we have dealt with you with words; but if you do not flee from these places immediately with your entire armada, you shall now experience Trojan bravery in its place. We have, with God’s help and grace, an abundance of young men skilled in war, and the number of those standing by us increases from day to day." 

When he had finished speaking, Ulysses said with a soft voice: "Truly, now you shall..."

He brought the bloody Polydorus, entirely crushed by stones, back inside to his mother, Hecuba.

## Ajax besieges the cities that are in league with the Trojans, and takes
## **ALL** of their cattle.

Meanwhile, Ajax Telamonius <note>Ajax the Greater, son of Telamon, known as the strongest of the Greek warriors after Achilles</note>—so that nothing peaceful should be left in the lands neighboring the city of Troy or among those allied with her—attacked them as an enemy. He captured the cities of Boryram and Cylla, which were noble in their riches. Not content with this, he also ravaged Gagarum, Marisba, Geniti, Scepsis, and Larissa with wonderful speed. Afterward, having been informed by the inhabitants how much livestock was kept on Mount Ida <note>original: "berg Jde"; a mountain near Troy sacred to the gods</note>, and as all those with him desired it, he went up the mountain with a swift company, slew the guards of the herds, and drove away a great force of cattle. Then, as no one at all offered him resistance, he put everyone he encountered to flight and, when he deemed the time right, returned to his people with great booty.

At that same time, Chryses (whom we have learned above is a priest of the Sminthean Apollo <note>original: "Smyntischẽ Apollinis priester"; Apollo Smintheus was a specific title for the god, often associated with protection against mice or plagues</note>), having discovered that his daughter Astynome <note>More commonly known in literature as Chryseis</note> was with Agamemnon, came to the ships. He took comfort in the religion of such a deity, carrying the image of the god before him along with certain ornaments of that same temple, so that he might more easily bring his dignity to the minds of the Kings through the memory of such a god. Subsequently, he brought many offerings of silver and gold, desiring the ransom of his daughter. He begged that they hold the presence of the god in high esteem, who, for the sake of his own priest, had come with him in person to entreat them. But he also recounted what sort of hostile and hateful things had been done by Alexander <note>Another name for Paris</note>...

He replied that he saw clearly what the cause of the sickness was, but he dared not speak it freely, as it might cause him to suffer the displeasure of the most powerful king. 

After these things, Achilles went to all the kings so that they might confirm to one another with a sworn oath that they would not allow him to be harmed for this reason. Once Calchas was reassured by their collective spirit, he spoke out: it was the wrath of the God Apollo, for the God was an enemy to the Greeks because of the insult to his priest, and he thus demanded punishment from the army. 

Afterward, when Achilles searched for a cure for the sickness, Calchas answered that it would end if the young woman were returned. ## How the Trojans fight with the Greeks, and how Menelaus fights alone with Paris, who carried away his wife, the beautiful Helen.

Afterward, when they had spent several days in good rest, both armies prepared themselves to march out again. They readied the field that lay in the middle between the city of Troy and the ships. When the time seemed right to battle, the soldiers were equipped for defense with great diligence; they stepped forward, sharpened their points <note>referring to spears or pikes</note>, and both enemies were thus arranged. They fought with one another, the Greeks each in particular according to the orders of their captains. In contrast, the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarier"; the text uses this term for the Trojans and their allies.</note> came splashing in without any measure or order. Many people from both parties perished in the battle because no one would give way to the other, and each one endeavored to match his honor with the most valiant men standing near him. Meanwhile, several of the princes who were severely wounded had to withdraw from the fight. Among the Barbarians: Aeneas, Sarpedon, Glaucus, Helenus, Euphorbus, and Polydamas. Among our men <note>The narrator identifies with the Greek side.</note>: Ulysses, Meriones, and Eumelus.

But when Menelaus caught sight of Alexander <note>Paris is frequently referred to as Alexander in classical accounts.</note> without danger, he charged at him with all his might. Alexander, always retreating, could no longer defend himself against him at length and took flight.

When Hector saw this from afar, he and Deiphobus ran toward him, seized his brother, and went through him with words and heavy cursing. He finally compelled him to step into the middle of the enemies and challenge Menelaus to fight him alone, while letting all the others rest in the meantime. Thus, there was a sudden change of spirit that came upon our people and the enemy.

Afterward, the Greeks believed the Trojans would no longer dare to act as enemies against them; thus they lived in good rest and without any care.

## How King Rhesus came to Priam’s aid and was slain in his sleep by the Greeks during the night, and his people with him the following day.

At that same time, Rhesus, the son of Croneus <note>In classical mythology, Rhesus is usually the son of Eioneus</note>—who was not a stranger to Priam’s friendship—arrived from Thrace with a large company for a promised reward. When night fell, he lingered for a while near the island of Den <note>Possibly Tenedos, an island near Troy</note> (which bordered the territory of the city lying opposite) and, at nearly the time of the second watch, moved into the Trojan fields, pitched his tents, and waited there. When Diomedes and Ulysses <note>The Latin name for the Greek hero Odysseus</note>, who were guarding the watch there, saw this from afar, they thought the Trojans had been sent to spy. They immediately drew their weapons, surveying everything, and approached that place with very quiet steps. The guards there were sleeping because they had become quite weary from the journey; thus these two crept inside and strangled the King in the tent. Afterward, they decided they should not attempt anything further, yet they took his chariot, with the most magnificent ornaments, and the horses, and brought them to their ships. Thus each spent the remaining time of the night in their tents in good rest. As soon as it became day, they came to the other princes and informed them of the deed they had undertaken and accomplished. They also expected the Barbarians <note>A common term in this period for the Trojans and their foreign allies</note>, inflamed by the King's death, would soon arrive; thus they commanded everyone to be constantly ready with weapons and to await the enemy. And not long after, the Thracian men, as they from the—

Afterward, the other princes also—as each had taken up a position—slew them all; and wherever they stood together, two or more gathered, our men broke them apart with their assault and soon scattered them, and those who dared to defend themselves were strangled, so that no more were left there whom one could have slain further. There, our men fell upon every place and took away their weapons, horses, the King’s riches, and finally whatever else fortune gave them. In such a manner, the Greeks as victors—after they had annihilated all the Thracians along with their king—withdrew back to their ships, well-laden with booty and triumphs. Yet all the while, the Trojans watched this from the city walls and dared not attempt anything for their allies, so greatly did they fear them, no less within the city itself. Therefore, the barbarians <note>In this context, a term used for non-Greeks, specifically the Trojans and their allies</note>, being quite overcome by so many adverse things, sent their ambassadors (who were to request a truce) to the Greeks; and as soon as our men had accepted the agreement, they offered a sacrifice and thus confirmed the faith of the vow.

At almost the same time, Chryses (whom we mentioned above as being the priest of Smintheus Apollo <note>original: "Smynthij Apollinis"; an epithet of Apollo meaning "Lord of the Mice," often associated with the plague</note>) came to our camp to give thanks for the matters that had been settled with him by our men. Through this, he had regained his daughter, and because of such great matters, and also because he had seen how tenderly his daughter Astynome <note>Commonly known in other traditions as Chryseis</note> had been held, he brought her back with him and delivered her to Agamemnon. And not long after, Philoctetes—along with those who had also brought a portion of the booty to Chryses at Lemnos—returned, still so weak that he could not yet walk well.

# Dictys of Crete regarding
## the Trojan War,
### The Third Book.

During this time, the Greeks—having postponed the war for a season by mutual agreement—spent the entire winter diligently attending to all matters required by the war during such a lull. Thus, the entire multitude, including the captains and the other folk behind the bulwarks, prepared for war in various ways, each assigned to his office according to the best custom. On one side, they crafted arrows like spears <note>original: "pfeyle wie die spieß" — likely referring to heavy javelins or bolts</note>, which were neither light nor small; and those who did not have these used fire-hardened wood. On the other side, they practiced shooting at one another with other arrows long into the day, while some used stones for practice. Among the marksmen, Ulysses, Teucer, Meriones, and Menelaus were the best; and there was no doubt that Philoctetes now surpassed the others, for he was the master of the arrows of Hercules <note>In mythology, Hercules gave his poisoned arrows to Philoctetes, which were prophesied as necessary to win the Trojan War</note> and was wondrous in the art of hitting whatever he wished.

But the Trojans and their allies, being negligent of the war and unconcerned for their army, lived much more idly. Hoping for safety from any secret ambush, they called upon the Thymbrean Apollo <note>original: "Tymbreischen Apollinem" — Apollo of Thymbra, a valley near Troy where a famous temple stood</note> with many sacrifices. During those same days, news arrived that nearly all the cities of Asia had fallen away from Priam and utterly cursed his friendship. For the Trojans were now viewed with suspicion by all peoples and lands—due to the example of the evil deed committed in the guest house <note>A reference to Paris violating the laws of hospitality by abducting Helen from her husband Menelaus's home</note>—and as they became aware that the Greeks had been victorious in all battles, the destruction of many cities even in their own land made them hateful in their hearts; and finally, a heavy enmity had come upon the King’s sons and his kingdom.

But on a certain day, as Hecuba <note>The Queen of Troy</note> happened to be praying before Apollo, Achilles (who wished to see the practice of their ceremonies) also arrived with a few companions. Furthermore, many honorable women were with Hecuba—the wives of her most prominent sons—some of whom showed honor and service to the Queen, while others wished to pray for themselves in such an undertaking. Additionally, Hecuba’s unmarried daughters were there: Polyxena, and Cassandra, the high priestess of Minerva and Apollo. Cassandra was dressed in strange, foreign clothing <note>original: "neüwen Barbarischen kleydung"</note> with her hair flowing all around; Polyxena also prayed and handed over the equipment for the sacrifice. But as Achilles by chance turned his eyes toward Polyxena, he was captivated by the maiden’s beauty. And as his desire increased over several hours and his heart was not eased, he withdrew to the ships. And he claimed the guilt lay not only with Agamemnon, but much more with the other Greeks, who had forgotten his good deeds and remained silent during his disgrace. 

When he finished speaking, Diomedes said that one must now let go of what is already gone, for a rational person should not dwell on things that have already happened, since you cannot bring them back (even if you wished to). Meanwhile, Phoenix and Patroclus, who stood around him, kissed the young man's cheeks and his whole face, and also his hands, and they grasped his knees so that he might become one with them again and relent in his spirit—not only for the sake of those who had come to plead with him, but for the sake of the entire army, which had also deserved well of him. Thus, Achilles was moved by the presence of such men, the prayers of his relatives, and the memory of the innocent army; finally, he said he would do what they desired. 

And upon the advice of Ajax <note>Latin: Ayacis</note>, he then went for the first time back among the Greeks and to the assembly, where he was received in a kingly manner by Agamemnon. As the other princes also showed him their favor, everyone became full of joy and courage. Therefore, Agamemnon, leading Achilles by the hand, brought the other princes with him to supper. And soon after, as they were cheerfully inviting one another, the King sought out Patroclus so that he might lead Hippodamia back to Achilles' camp, along with all the finery he had given her. Then Patroclus willingly and gladly performed that task. Furthermore, during that same winter time, the Greeks and Trojans—either alone or in groups, as it happened by chance—often walked among one another without any worry in the forest
