# **Dictys of Crete on**
## **the Trojan War,**
### **The Third Book.**

In the meantime, the Greeks—having suspended the war for a period by common agreement—spent the entire winter diligently attending to all things required for war during such a respite, focusing their hearts with great industry. For the entire multitude, including the commanders and the other ranks, remained behind the bulwarks <note>The "bollwerck" refers to the fortified camp and ramparts the Greeks built to protect their ships.</note> preparing for war in various ways; thus, every man was assigned to his office according to the best custom. On one side, they fashioned arrows that were like spears, being neither lighter nor smaller; and those who did not have these used sharpened wood. On the other side, they practiced shooting at one another with other arrows long into the day, while some used stones for practice. Among the archers, **Ulysses**, **Teucer**, **Meriones**, and **Menelaus** were the best; and there was no doubt that **Philoctetes** now surpassed all others, for he possessed the arrows of **Hercules** <note>original: "Herculis pfeylen" — According to legend, Philoctetes inherited the bow and poisoned arrows of Heracles, which were destined to be essential for the fall of Troy.</note> and was wondrous in the art of shooting whatever he aimed at.

But the Trojans and their allies, being negligent of the war and showing no concern for their army, lived in much idleness. Trusting without any fear of secret ambushes, they called upon the **Thymbraean Apollo** <note>original: "Tymbriſchen Apollinem" — Apollo had a famous temple in Thymbra, a plain near Troy.</note> with many sacrifices, now one group and then another. During those same days, news arrived that nearly all the cities of Asia had fallen away from **Priam** and utterly renounced his friendship. For they had become suspicious of the Trojans—who were now held in contempt by all peoples and lands because of the example of the evil deed committed in the guest house <note>This refers to Paris abducting Helen while he was a guest of King Menelaus, a supreme violation of the ancient laws of hospitality.</note>—and also because they realized the Greeks had been victorious in all battles. The destruction of many cities in that same land weighed heavily on their hearts, and finally, they had come to feel a burdensome enmity toward the King’s sons and his realm.

However, on a certain day, while **Hecuba** was praying safely before **Apollo**, **Achilles** (who wished to observe their ceremonies) also arrived there with a few companions. In addition, many noble women were with **Hecuba**, the wives of her most prominent sons; some were showing honor and service to the Queen, while others wished to offer prayers for themselves in such an undertaking. Also present were **Hecuba’s** unmarried daughters: **Polyxena** and **Cassandra**, the high priestess of **Minerva** and **Apollo**, dressed in strange foreign <note>original: "Barbariſchen" — used here to describe the non-Greek, Trojan style of dress.</note> clothing with disheveled hair, praying all around. **Polyxena** handed over the equipment for the sacrifice. But when **Achilles** by chance turned his eyes toward **Polyxena**, he was captivated by the maiden’s beauty. And as his desire increased over several hours and his heart was not eased, he withdrew to the ships. But after a few days had passed, and his love increased longer and more firmly, he had the Au...

This was done because it was believed that a fleeting faith and hearts not rightly tested—and such a sudden reversal—could not be without some deceit.

## How Patroclus and Sarpedon fought alone with one another in one place, and Sarpedon perished.

## How the Trojans began to fight with the Greeks on the first day, but were attacked and struck down on the next day.

But after a few days, when the princes had refreshed themselves after the labor of keeping watch, the army was led out into the field as soon as day appeared, and spent the whole day in armor or weapons, waiting for the attack of the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarier"; in these texts, this typically refers to the Trojans and their non-Greek allies.</note>. While our men were focused only on avoiding the missiles or arrows, the Barbarians <note>In the context of Greek epic literature, "Barbarians" refers to the Trojans and their allies.</note>, having spent the whole day shooting their arrows, became weary. Immediately afterward, he threw the young kings to the dogs to be torn apart, and vowed that he would not stop sleeping on the bare earth overnight until he had avenged himself with blood upon those responsible for his great mourning.

## How Achilles waited for, killed, and dragged Hector, who had previously slain his best friend Patroclus.

Not many days had passed when it was hurriedly announced that **Hector** had gone out with a few men to meet **Penthesilea**. She was a Queen of the **Amazons**; it is unknown whether she came to help **Priam** for money or out of a desire for war. They were a warlike people, undefeated by their neighbors and quite famous for their military equipment among all people. Therefore, **Achilles** took a few of his trusted men with him and went out in haste to wait for him in secret, coming upon his enemy who suspected nothing from him—

# Of Trojan Loss

...and there, as he intended to wade into a river, he fell upon them; and so he unexpectedly slew him and all the others who had accompanied the King’s son, as they had known nothing of such a ruse. But he captured one of the sons of **Priam**, immediately cut off his hands, and sent him into the city so that he might announce what had happened. But Achilles, because of the killing of his greatest friend <note>A reference to Patroclus, whose death at the hands of Hector sparked Achilles's rage.</note> and because of the memory of his mourning, so wildly despoiled the enemy; he soon bound the feet together, fastening them to the chariot with a rope. Afterward, as he sat upon it, he commanded **Automedon** <note>Achilles's charioteer.</note> to give the horses their reins. Thus, he raced through the field with the chariot running, where he could best be seen, and dragged his enemy about in a wondrous and terrible fashion—a nearly new and pitiless way of punishing.

But in **Troy**, as they saw the despoiling of **Hector** from over the walls—which the **Greeks**, by the King's command, had carried before the eyes of the enemy—and as he whose hands had been cut off gave word of such a savage matter, recounting the deed as it had unfolded, such a lamentation and such a cry was raised through the entire city that one would have thought the birds in the air had fallen down, terrified by the voices; and our men shouted back with great rejoicing. Immediately, while everyone was crying out in all places, the city was barred. The order of the realm was made hideous, and the faces of the citizenry were shut up in a mournful and deathly manner, and they all gathered together in one place. Those who feared him (as commonly happens in such dealings) immediately fled here and there without any reason; at times there was great and many-voiced lamentation, followed quickly by a silence born of their ignorance and despair. Amidst these things, many also believed their last hope was gone, thinking the **Greeks** would take the city as soon as night fell and destroy it, now that they were made safe by the death of such a prince. Some also held it for certain that **Achilles** had brought to his side the host (which had come with **Penthesilea** <note>The Queen of the Amazons who came to aid Troy.</note> to the aid of **Priam’s** cause). At last, they held all things to be adverse, hostile, and perished; their riches were already taken from them, and no hope remained now that **Hector** had been killed. For he alone, among all in that same city, had always fought with varied fortune against so many thousands and against so many captains of the enemy. He was far more valiant than all our own captains, had he possessed the luck; he was famous among the nations for the praise of his warring, yet strength was never enough to overcome fate <note>The original German "vernunfft" here likely refers to the "reason" or "order" of the world/fate.</note>.

# How a contest of games—including racing, archery, running, fencing, jumping, stone-throwing, wrestling, club-fighting, etc.—was held by the Greeks to honor Achilles.

Meanwhile among the Greeks, when Achilles had returned to the ships and the dead body of **Hector** lay before all their eyes, their grief (which they had received not long before due to the death of **Patroclus**) was laid to rest by the death of the terrifying enemy, and for that reason, a special joy was proclaimed. Then it pleased them all that—since they no longer had any worry regarding the enemy—a combat with the customary games should be held in his <note>Though these are historically the funeral games for Patroclus, the text frames them as a celebration in honor of Achilles' victory.</note> honor. Nevertheless, the other troops who were not participating in the games, but had come only to watch, were to remain armed with their weapons and stay ready. This was done so that the enemy (though defeated in all things) might not, according to their usual custom, secretly set an ambush and break in.

Therefore, **Achilles** ordered prizes to be set out for those who performed best. And when everything was prepared, he ordered all the lords to sit down, with him in the middle as the highest among them all. There, first, **Eumelus**, racing with four harnessed horses, was declared the victor before all others. The prize for the chariot with two horses was earned by **Diomedes**. After him, the second was **Menelaus**. But those who most excelled in the art of shooting with the bow were **Meriones** and **Ulysses** <note>The Roman name for Odysseus.</note>; they had two masts set up, to which a very small thread was tied and pulled across, fastened at the top of both, and in the middle a dove hung down. There was the greatest struggle over who would hit it. Then (while the others exerted themselves in vain) **Ulysses** and **Meriones** hit the target. To them, **Philoctetes**—who was shown favor by the others—promised that he would shoot not the dove, but the very thing it was tied to with his bolt. And when the lords afterward marveled at the impossibility of this, he confirmed the truth of his promise just as skillfully as he did fortunately; and as the cord broke, the dove fell down amidst a great cry from the people. From this same contest, **Meriones** and **Ulysses** carried away the prizes, but Achilles presented **Philoctetes** with two kinds of gifts, outside of the regular prizes. Among those who ran the race, **Ajax**, the son of **Oileus** <note>Known as Ajax the Lesser to distinguish him from the son of Telamon.</note>, was accepted as the best. After him, **Polypoetes** was the second. **Machaon** was one of four <note>Original: "selb vierdt," an archaic expression meaning he was one of a group of four competitors.</note> to fence, and **Eurypylus** was one of two. **Tlepolemus** was considered the best in jumping and stone-throwing. But the winners of the wrestling remained undecided, for **Ajax** seized **Ulysses** around the middle and threw him down, but in falling, **Ulysses** became entangled around his foot. Thus **Ajax**, who had almost already conquered, fell to the earth because of the obstruction and the entangled embrace. As for the clubs, and whatever other combats were fought with the hand, that same **Ajax Tela-** <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the name is Ajax Telamonius, or Ajax the Great.</note>

Afterward, when the prizes of the combat had been distributed, **Achilles** first presented a gift to **Agamemnon**, which he considered the most heartfelt. Secondly to **Nestor**, then to **Idomeneus** thirdly, after whom gifts were given to **Podalirius** and **Machaon** <note>The two primary physicians of the Greek army.</note>. Following this, the other captains also received gifts according to their merit. And finally, gifts were given for their companions who had perished in the war, with orders that these should be brought to their kinsmen when time permitted. After the fighting and the awarding of prizes were concluded and evening fell, they departed from one another, each to his own tent.

But as soon as it was day, **Priam** arrived, piteously attired in a garment that—due to his great misery—left him with no royal honor nor any other appearance of such a name and reputation. With pleading hands and face, he came to **Achilles**. With him came **Andromache**, just as much an object of pity as Priam himself, for she was disfigured in many ways by her grief. She brought before her two very small sons, **Astyanax** (whom some have called Scamandrius) and **Laomedon**, to give to the King <note>Priam</note> as helpers in his pleading. Priam, sinking down toward the earth out of sorrow and old age, leaned upon the shoulders of his daughter **Polyxena**. Behind them came wagons full of silver and gold and precious jewels, while the Trojans watched from the walls, following their King’s companions with their eyes. When this was seen, a silence immediately sprang up from the wonder of it, and the hearts of the Greeks raced to meet them, greedy to know the reason for his arrival. When Priam saw that they were near him, he immediately fell upon his face and sprinkled the dust and other filth of the earth upon his head. Then he begged that they should have mercy on his misfortune and go with him to Achilles as intercessors. **Nestor**, considering Priam’s age and misfortune, mourned for him. Conversely, **Ulysses** pursued him with harsh words and reproached him for the things he had said in Troy against the embassies before the war began. After these things were announced to Achilles, he ordered Priam to be summoned through **Automedon**. Meanwhile, Achilles was placing the bones of **Patroclus** into a vessel <note>original: "schoß," literally lap or bosom, here referring to a funerary urn or container.</note>. As our captains entered with Priam, the King embraced the knees of Achilles with his hands and said: "You are not the cause of this my misfortune, but rather some God who has led my final old age (on which he should have had mercy) into these disasters, which is now entirely consumed and defeated by the lamentation for so many of my sons. For they, comforting themselves in the Kingdom through their youth, while desiring to fulfill their heart's desires in whatever form they wished, brought destruction upon themselves and me. No one doubts that old age is despised by youth. And if it is the case that others will moderate such evil deeds because of my ruin, then I will also (if it pleases you) surrender myself to the punishment of death, which for me, poor man..."

### How Andromache, the wife of the perished Hector, together with her children, also pleaded with Achilles for the dead body of her husband.

Afterward, Andromache threw Hector's two small children down before Achilles and with piteous weeping begged him that she might at least be allowed to look upon her husband's dead body. During these pitiful events, Phoenix <note>The tutor of Achilles.</note> and Nestor, while speaking, lifted Priam up and urged him to take heart. Afterward, when the King had revived his breath a little, he fell upon his knees and, tearing at his head with both hands, he says: "Where is the mercy now that was once so prominent among the Greeks? Or is it only denied to Priam, or not understood?" And as they were now all moved to sorrow, Achilles said: It would have been well-fitting for him <note>Priam</note> at the beginning to have forbidden his sons such vices as they had committed, and not, by his consent, to have become a participant in such a misdeed. But ten years ago he was not so consumed by old age that he would have been scorned by his own people. Rather, the desire for the property of others had possessed their hearts—and not only because of the woman <note>Helen of Troy.</note>, but coveting the riches of Atreus and Pelops <note>Ancient kings of the Greek territories; Achilles implies the Trojans were motivated by plunder.</note>, they had gone forth in a shameful manner to steal; for which things it is entirely just that they should suffer such punishment or even more. Until that very time, the Greeks had followed the very best customs of war, for they had dutifully arranged to bury all those whom they had killed in battle. Against this, Hector had transgressed all human ways, he who had dared to drag Patroclus <note>Achilles’ beloved companion, whose body Hector had attempted to desecrate.</note> out of the fight, namely to mock and insult his dead corpse, which example with her...

## Of the Trojan Damages

...punishment and torment had to be paid. This was done so that the Greeks and other nations, mindful of the revenge taken, would henceforth uphold the customs of human society. For such an expedition would not have been endured—leaving behind houses and small children, staining the homeland with blood (both one's own and the enemy's) amidst so many dangers of war—merely for the sake of Helen or Menelaus. Rather, they wished to learn whether the <term>Barbarians</term><note>The Greeks referred to all non-Greeks, including the Trojans, as "Barbarians."</note> or the Greeks would achieve supreme power over all things. Although it would have been a just cause to wage war over the woman; for just as men find joy in the plundering of foreign things, so does it cause pain to those who have lost the same. In addition to all this, he <note>Referring to Achilles.</note> wished many unlucky and cursed things upon Helen, and also vowed that as soon as Troy was taken and destroyed, he would be the first of all to take punishment from her for such a crime with her own blood. For because of her, he had left his fatherland and his parents, and had also lost Patroclus, his comfort, who had stood by him when everyone else had abandoned him. 

Afterward, he stood up and went to council with the other princes, who were all of one mind: namely, that he should accept the gifts that had been brought and allow the dead body to be returned. Since this pleased them well, they all retired to their tents. And Polixena <note>Priam’s daughter, who accompanied him to the Greek camp.</note>, as soon as Achilles entered, clasped his knees <note>A traditional gesture of extreme supplication in the ancient world.</note> and willingly promised that she would become his handmaid in payment for the dead body. This spectacle so moved the young man that—despite being the greatest enemy of Priam and his kingdom because of Patroclus's death—as he thought of his own daughter and father, he could not stop himself from weeping. He reached out his hand and raised Polixena up. 

After this, he spoke to and commanded Phoenix <note>original: "Phenici"; Phoenix was Achilles's tutor and a Greek Chieftain.</note> to apply himself to comforting Priam and making his time easier. But the King said he could forget neither his mourning nor the heaviness of his labor. Then Achilles promised him that he would not grant his request unless he put on a better garment and ate with him. Thus, the King, fearing that by his refusal he might hinder the things he believed he had already obtained, resolved to do everything that was commanded of him. Therefore, after the dirt was dusted out of his hair and he had been thoroughly bathed, he and those who had come with him were invited to the table by the young man. Afterward, when they all had enough, Achilles spoke thus:

"Dear Priam, tell me now: what was the great reason—since your soldiers decrease daily and notable damages and great misfortunes increase—that you nevertheless intend to keep Helen to this day? Why do you not prefer to cast her away from you like a hereditary disease or an unlucky omen? For you must have realized how you have surrendered your fatherland, those present here, and your closest brothers, which is the most shameful thing of all. For these men here, seeing her evil deeds, did not wish to swear to us in the war; namely, so that those who did not wish her well would not seek to return home through her. Therefore, since you have seen that she has come into your city with the misfortune of you all, why..."

## The Fourth Book.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
Now when it was revealed to the Trojans that the king had finished the negotiations unharmed and had returned with his entire company, they marveled and praised the Greeks' kindness, exalting it to the heavens. For in their hearts they truly believed there was no hope of obtaining the dead man. They also feared that he, along with those with him, would be detained by the Greeks, mostly because of the memory of Helen, whom they had not sent back. But when they saw Hector's body, all the citizens and allies came running together and began a weeping, tearing their hair and disfiguring their faces with long scratches, among such a multitude of people. Therefore, no one should place good hope or trust in his own bravery, seeing that he has perished who was of such famous renown, known to all nations for his conduct in war and of praiseworthy wisdom also in peace—from which he gained no less praise than from his other skills. Meanwhile, they buried him not far from the burial place of King Ilus <note>Ilus was the mythical founder of Troy and the grandfather of King Priam.</note> of old. Afterward, a great wailing arose, and they performed the final rites of a funeral; the women on one side mourning with Hecuba, and on the other side the Trojan men mourning in return, and finally the people of the allied lords. These things, as they were granted a ten-day truce <term>truce</term> <note>original: "kriegs fristung", a temporary suspension of hostilities to allow for the burial of the dead.</note> from the war, were carried out by the Trojans from sunrise until evening, and nowhere

<header>The fourth book.</header>

# Queen Penthesilea: How she came to Priam's aid with a great army
## of Amazonian women, yet was overcome by the Greeks and perished along with her people.

Meanwhile, Penthesilea (of whom we spoke before) arrived during those very days with a great host of Amazons and other neighboring peoples. When she understood that Hector had perished, she was so dismayed by his death that she wished to return home. However, she was eventually persuaded by Alexander <note>original: "Alexãdro"; also known as Paris</note> with much silver and gold to remain there. After spending several days there, she prepared her banners and troops with weapons. Relying on the strength of her own warriors alone, she marched out to battle from a position near the Trojans. She protected the left wing with archers, the other with infantry, and placed the cavalry <term>reisigen: mounted soldiers</term> in the middle. Our men met them in this way: Menelaus, Ulysses, and Meriones—along with Teucer the archer—and the two Ajaces <note>the "two Ajaces" refers to Ajax the Great and Ajax the Lesser</note>, Diomedes, Agamemnon, and Tlepolemus, along with Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, were positioned against the infantry. Achilles, together with the other captains, was to fight against the riders.

Thus, with the armies prepared on both sides, they clashed; many were struck down by the Queen's archers, though the Trojans fought just as well. Meanwhile, the two Ajaces and the other foot soldiers with them struck those they were positioned against. They pushed those who resisted away with their shields and immediately slew them as they fell, not ceasing until the infantry hosts were entirely destroyed. Among the cavalry, Achilles brought Penthesilea before him. He struck her with his spear and—treating her with no more weight than any other woman—threw her down from her horse. He seized her braids with his hand and, having wounded her severely, dragged her back and forth. When this was seen, the enemy finally realized there was no more hope in arms and took to flight. As the city gates were barred, our men pursued those whom flight had saved from the battle and cut them to pieces; however, they stayed their hands from the women and spared the female form.

Afterward, each man, having slain those he went against, turned back. They viewed the half-dead Penthesilea and marveled at her boldness. In a short time, everyone ran together to that same place. It pleased them—since she had dared to overstep nature and the characteristics of her female kind—that she should be thrown into a river or to the dogs to be torn apart while she still felt the last remains of life. Achilles wished to bury the slain woman, but Diomedes prevented him. For when Diomedes asked those standing around what should be done with her, he—by the unanimous agreement of them all—dragged her by the feet and threw her into the river Scamander <note>original: "Scamandrum"</note>, as a punishment for her final despair and folly. In such a manner, the Queen of the Amazons, having lost the people with whom she had come to help Priam, finally provided a worthy spectacle of her character.

## How King Memnon came to King Priam’s aid with an unspeakable multitude by land, and sent just as many by water under Phala the captain, whom the soldiers on the island of Rhodes stoned and whose goods they divided among themselves.

**But** on the following day, Memnon—the son of Tithonus and Aurora <note>original: "Tithoni und Aurorae"; Aurora is the Roman goddess of the dawn</note>—arrived with a great power of Indians and Ethiopians, of whom there was much report. Moreover, many thousands of armed men with various weapons were gathered there, more than Priam had requested or hoped for. Everything around Troy, and further than the eye could see, was full of men and horses, gleaming with the shine of their colors and coats of arms. All of these he had led down from the peak of Mount Caucasus toward the city of Troy. The others, no less in number, he had sent by sea, having given them Phala as a captain. When these men noticed Rhodes—and because the island was in league with the Greeks—they became concerned that if the Rhodians took notice of the situation, they would set their ships on fire. Therefore they waited there and immediately divided themselves into Camirus and Ialysus <note>original: "Camiram vn̄ Galisam"; these were ancient cities on the island of Rhodes</note>, two wealthy cities. 

And not long thereafter, the Rhodians accused or condemned Phala, because not long before, Alexander <note>Paris</note> had destroyed Sidon <note>original: "Sidonem"</note>, and Phala intended to come to the aid of the one who had insulted them. Then, as they stirred the minds of the army, they also said it was plain to see they were no different from barbarians if they wished to protect such a shameful deed—and many other things besides, which incensed the common people and served their own purpose. This was not in vain, for the Phoenicians <note>original: "Phenicier"</note>—many of whom were among that same crowd—were moved by the complaint of the Rhodians. Afterward, out of a desire for the goods they had brought with them, they chased after Phala with stones and slew him. And as they were distributed in the aforementioned cities, they also divided the gold and other booty among themselves.

Meanwhile, the host that had marched with Memnon camped there in the level places (for such a force of soldiers could not have been contained within the city walls). They practiced in various ways, each according to his nation, and their appearance was not uniform or of the same shape, but all according to their own skill—rather, as each was accustomed to the customs of his own land. Their weapons were also made in different manners. The various forms of their shields and helmets presented a terrifying sight of war. When, however, several days had passed and the soldiers desired battle, the entire army was led out to the fight at daybreak according to the given signals. With them went the Trojans and whatever other allies were in the city. But on the other side, the Greeks also prepared, awaiting the time of war, yet somewhat terrified in their hearts for fear of this great and unknown enemy. Therefore, when they had come within about a crossbow <term>armbrost: a medieval weapon used here by the translator to describe distance</term> shot’s distance of each other, the barbarians [charged], as if it were a mountain

### How King Memnon arrived to aid King Priam with a countless army by land, and how just as many were sent by water under the commander Phala, whom the soldiers on the island of Rhodes stoned to death, dividing the goods among themselves.

But on the following day, Memnon—the son of Tithonus and Aurora <note>In mythology, Tithonus was a Trojan prince and Aurora was the Goddess of the Dawn</note>—arrived with a massive force of Indians and Ethiopians, of whom there was great renown. There were many more thousands of armed men with various weapons than Priam had requested or hoped for; all the land around Troy, further than the eye could see, was full of men and horses, glinting with the reflection of their colors and coats of arms. He had led them all down from the heights of Mount Caucasus <note>original: "Caucasi"</note> to the city of Troy. 

The other half of the force, no less in number, had been sent by sea under the command of Phala. When they reached Rhodes and realized that the island was in league with the Greeks, they became concerned that if their presence were noticed, their ships would be set on fire. Therefore, they waited there and immediately divided themselves between Camira and Galisa <note>These refer to Camirus and Ialysus, two of the three ancient cities on the island of Rhodes</note>, two wealthy cities. 

Not long after, the Rhodians accused or condemned Phala, noting that Alexander <note>Another name for Paris, the prince of Troy</note> had not long before destroyed Sidon, his father’s land, and yet Phala wished to come to the aid of the man who had offended him. Therefore the Greeks, once there was a pause, being terrified among themselves and now despairing of all things, spent the entire night burying those they had lost in the battle. ## How the Greeks, in their armor, challenged the Trojans to battle; how the Trojans marched out against them but fled shamefully without attacking, and were slain and drowned in their flight.

After a few days, the Greeks, equipped with their war gear, stepped forth into the field and challenged the Trojans to come out and strike them, if they were bold enough. Alexander <note>The name used in the text for Paris, the Trojan prince</note>, acting as a captain with his other brothers, ordered the soldiers and marched out against them. But before the front lines even met, and before the throwing of arrows or spears had even begun, the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarier"; a term used by the Greeks for the Trojans and their allies</note> broke their formation and took flight. Many of them were slain or driven headlong into the water, as the enemy fell upon them from all sides and cut off their escape.

Also captured were Lycaon and Troilus, the sons of Priam. They were led into the midst of the army, where Achilles ordered them to be strangled. He was filled with disdain <note>original: "verschmacht", suggesting a mix of bitterness or unsatisfied vengeance</note>, for he was not yet satisfied with the matters he had negotiated with Priam. When the Trojans saw this, they began to weep and, with piteous cries, mourned the fall of Troilus in a most miserable manner. They thought of his youth, for in the first years of his childhood he had grown up with modesty and virtue, and was especially beloved and pleasant to the common people because of his physical beauty.

A few days later, the festival of the Thymbrean Apollo <note>Thymbra was a plain near Troy containing a famous temple to Apollo</note> occurred, and the unrest of war was suspended by a truce. Then, while both armies attended to the divine service, Priam found an opportune time and sent Idaeus with a message to Achilles concerning Polyxena <note>Priam's daughter, whom Achilles wished to marry</note>. Achilles heard the matters proposed to him by Idaeus alone in the woods, separated from the others. But when the matter became known back at the ships, a suspicion arose against the "renegade" captain, which finally turned into contempt. Rumors of treason had previously sprung up like a folly, but now they were brought forward as if they were the truth. Because of this, and to quiet the angry spirits of the soldiers, Ajax, Diomedes, and Ulysses went to the woods and stood before the church <note>original: "Kirchen", here referring to the Temple of Apollo</note>, waiting for Achilles to come out so they could tell the young man what was being said and frighten him away from the others, so that he would not hold secret conversations with the enemy. 

Meanwhile, Alexander had secretly set an ambush with Deiphobus. He girded himself with a dagger and prepared to attack Achilles, acting as if he intended to confirm the promises Priam had made to him. He stood immediately by the altar of Apollo so that the enemy would not notice the plot directed by our prince <note>The text likely refers to the Trojan leadership here</note>. Then, when the time seemed right, Deiphobus embraced the unarmed young man—who, being at the sacrifice and service of Apollo, feared nothing from the enemy—kissing him and rejoicing over the things he had allowed to happen to them. He would not be pulled away from him, nor would he let him go...

When they saw that he was cut down with wounds, they burst out at another place—not where they had entered—and, having accomplished such a great deed beyond all their wishes, they ran back into the city.

## How Ajax and Ulysses, the two Greek captains, found Achilles slain in the temple, and intended to carry him to their camp; the Trojans intercepted them and began a skirmish with the Greeks, yet were defeated by them.

When Ulysses saw them, he said, "It is not for nothing that they have mixed among one another and scurried out so fearfully." Afterward, they went into the grove <note>original: "wald"; refers to the sacred grove of the temple of Thymbraean Apollo</note> and inspected everything. There they saw Achilles lying on the earth, powerless and half-dead. Then Ajax said, "It was a known truth among men that no man could be found who could overcome you with true honor, as is now evident; but your reckless daring <note>original: "fräuel"; refers to a rash or impious act</note> has cost you your life." 

Then Achilles, who was in his final throes, said, "Deiphobus and Alexander have overcome me with secret treachery, because of Polyxena." As he gave up the ghost, the two princes embraced and kissed him with great lamentation, and blessed him for the last time. Finally, they took the deceased upon their shoulders and carried him out of the grove. 

When the Trojans noticed this, they all rushed out from the gates, intending to seize Achilles from them and lead him into the city—desiring, according to their usual custom, to vent their arrogance upon the dead body. Against this, the Greeks became aware of the situation, grabbed their weapons, and stepped out to meet them, gradually bringing forward all their banners. Thus, in a short time, the battle intensified on both sides. Ajax handed over the dead body to those who were with him, and then hideously slew Asium, the son of Dymantis and brother of Hecuba <note>Hecuba was the Queen of Troy and Priam's wife</note>, who was the first to encounter him. Afterward, he slew many others as they were placed within the ranks, among whom were Jastes and Amphimachus, who ruled over Caria. 

And now the two captains, Ajax son of Oileus <note>original: "Ayax Oilei"; to distinguish him from the greater Ajax</note> and Menelaus, joined together, struck down the enemy, and forced them to flee. Therefore the Trojans—since so many of their own were slain and they had no hope of making a stand in any proper order—scattered and, retreating, ran toward the gates, believing they had no better luck than what lay within the walls. Consequently, a great force of the enemy was hacked to pieces by our men who hurried after them.

...once the gates were barred and an end was made to the slaughter, the Greeks brought Achilles to the ships. And while every heart mourned the fall of such a man, many of the soldiers neither grieved nor were moved with sorrow (as the cause demanded). For they had firmly believed in their hearts that Achilles had often consulted with the enemy to surrender the army. Yet, now that he had perished, the *summa* <term>summa: the essential weight or main point</term> or greatest concern of the war had become "fatherless," and much hope was lost. He who was so brave in war had received no honorable death, nor could he die anywhere except in silence or darkness. Therefore, they gathered a great heap of wood from Mount Ida and built a funeral pyre for him at the same place (where Patroclus had been before). After the body was laid upon it and the fire was stoked beneath, they held the funeral rites for the soul. Ajax <note>original: "Ayay"; referring to Ajax the Greater</note> was especially devoted to this; he kept a constant watch for three nights in a row and did not leave until the remains were gathered together. For he alone, more than all the others and almost beyond human measure, was utterly stricken in his heart by the death of Achilles, whom he had loved from his soul and held in honor with all kinds of service; for he knew that Achilles had been most favorable toward him and was a kinsman of his lineage. Furthermore, Achilles had surpassed all others in bravery. Conversely, great joy and jubilation came upon everyone among the Trojans because such a terrible enemy had perished. They praised Alexander’s <note>Paris</note> discovery to the heavens—namely, that he had stifled so many through treachery, which he would not have dared to attempt against a warrior in open combat.

Amidst these very joyful things, a message also came to Priam that Eurypylus, the son of Telephus, was marching there. The King had previously enticed him with a great sum of money and finally secured his loyalty by offering his daughter Cassandra. Among other very beautiful things he sent him, he included a grapevine <note>the legendary "Golden Vine" of the Trojan royal house</note> or vine-branch, of which there was great talk among the nations. Furthermore, Eurypylus, renowned for many virtues and equipped with the Mysian legion, was received by the Trojans with the highest praise and joy; he turned all the hope of the "Barbarians" <note>meaning the Trojans and their allies</note> toward the best. Meanwhile, the Greeks placed Achilles' bones into a coffin or vessel and added them to the bones of Patroclus, burying them in Sigeum. Ajax arranged for a memorial to be prepared for him by those who lived in that place for a fee, and he rebuked the Greeks for not showing any proper mourning among themselves over

# Of the Trojan City

## How Pyrrhus Neoptolemus, after his father Achilles' death, came to the Greeks' camp and was received; and how after the third day he fought against the Trojans and prevailed.

At that very same time, Pyrrhus (whom men call Neoptolemus <note>In Greek mythology, he is known by both names: Pyrrhus meaning "red-haired" and Neoptolemus meaning "new warrior."</note>, the son of Achilles by Deidamia, daughter of Lycomedes) arrived there and found the grave for the most part already built. Afterwards, he inquired about his father’s death and was informed of the details. He strengthened the Myrmidons <note>The elite soldiers of Achilles, known for their discipline and ferocity.</note>—a brave people, famous in war—both in their weaponry and in their spirits. He appointed Phoenix <note>original: "Phenici"; Achilles' old tutor and foster-father.</note> to oversee the necessary work. Then he went to his father’s ships and tents; there he found Hippodamia <note>In many medieval accounts of the Trojan War, this name is used for the woman known in Homeric tradition as Briseis.</note> tending to Achilles' things. As soon as his arrival became known, all the princes ran together to that place and prayed that he would be patient in his grief. To them, he answered kindly, saying that it was not unknown to him that all things which happen through God <note>The text uses the singular "Gott," though referring to the divine fate or the gods of antiquity.</note> should be endured with a brave spirit and heart, and that no other law was given to any man than to live according to divine providence. For a long life of old age would be shameful and cursed for brave men, whereas it is something to be wished for the weak. Furthermore, his sorrow was made lighter because Achilles had perished neither in the heat of battle nor in the light of war; for he had not wished that any man braver than himself should now be present, and indeed there had been none, except for Hercules alone. He added that Hercules had been the only worthy man of that time, at whose hands it would have been fitting for Troy to be destroyed. Nevertheless, he did not refuse what had remained unfinished by his father; that it might yet be accomplished by him and those standing around him.

After he had finished speaking, the battle was announced for the following day. All the princes, as the time seemed right to them, went to Agamemnon for dinner. Among them went Ajax with Neoptolemus, as well as Diomedes, Ulysses, and Menelaus; they also took a place to sit together. While they were eating, many noble feats of battle performed by the father were recounted to the youth, and as they remembered his bravery, they extolled him with praise. These things gladdened Neoptolemus not a little and made him eager for such skill; he answered that he would endeavor with all diligence and effort so that his father’s merit would not remain unhonored. Afterward, they went away to sleep, each to his own tent.

But on the next day, at the first light of dawn, the youth stepped out before the tents. He found Diomedes with Ulysses, whom he received and asked what the reason was for their coming. They said that the war must be delayed for a while to refresh the soldiers and their spirits, for their limbs were still stiff from the long journey across the sea, and for that reason they might

## How Alexander and Philoctetes fought against each other alone with bows, and Alexander was killed, after which a skirmish arose between the enemies and the Greeks prevailed.

Then Ajax Telamonius <note>Ajax the Great, known for his massive size and strength.</note> hurried after the fugitives and advanced up to the gate, where he slew a great multitude of the enemy. While the Trojans struggled among themselves—each wishing to be the first to get inside—they were all the more hindered at the entrance by their own crowd. Meanwhile, many who had escaped first lay upon the walls, gathered stones from everywhere, and threw them down upon the shield of Ajax; they even gathered much filth <note>original: "Kots"; mud or waste.</note> and poured it down from above, namely to drive away their enemy. ## Anthenor displays his good will toward the Greeks through the Trojan embassy, through which they should understand that he would gladly have surrendered the city, as then happened.

Anthenor then began a long speech and said that the lords of the city of Troy have always received punishment from God for their evil designs. Afterward, he also added the attempted injustice of Laomedon <note>The father of King Priam, known in mythology for refusing to pay Hercules and the gods for building the walls of Troy.</note> against Hercules, and how the destruction of himself and his kingdom followed thereafter. At that time, Priam was still very small and entirely uninvolved, and by the request of Hesione, he was placed over the kingdom. Even then, he had been wickedly foolish, and a common persecutor of everyone with bloodshed and other injustices—vile, ill-mannered, and greedy for the property of others. From this example or pattern—just as if from a hereditary sickness—his sons were also directed, and they refrained from neither spiritual nor worldly goods. Furthermore, he <note>Anthenor</note> claimed to be of the same kinship with the Greeks as that to which Priam was related, yet his heart never wished to harmonize with Priam. For Hesione, the daughter of Danaus, had borne Electra, from whom Dardanus was born; he married the daughter of Teucer and raised Erichthonius by her. From that same line came Tros, and from Tros came Ilus, Ganymede, Cleomestra, and Assaracus. From Assaracus came Capys, the father of Anchises. Afterward, the same line bore Tithonus and Laomedon. From Laomedon were also born Icetaon, Clytus, Lampus, Thimeres, Bucolion, and Priam; and conversely, Lyersus was born from Cleomestra. Furthermore, he claimed Priam had trodden all rights of friendship underfoot and directed his arrogance and envy most of all against his own people. After he had finished speaking, he requested—since he had been sent by the lords of the council as an embassy of the enemy—that they should give him several from their number with whom he might hold a discussion regarding such dealings. And Agamemnon, Idomeneus, Ulysses, and Diomedes were chosen. These men, in secrecy from the others, arranged the treachery. It also pleased them that Aeneas (if he would keep trust and faith) should have a portion of the booty and his entire house should remain unharmed. But to Anthenor himself, half of Priam’s goods should be given, and the kingdom should be delivered to one of his sons whom he chose. When they felt they had negotiated sufficiently, they let Anthenor go back into the city. There, he declared to his people that many other things had been established by them than was actually the case. # Dictys the Cretan’s
## Account of the Trojan War,
### The Fifth Book.

Once Anthenor and Talthybius had arrived in the city, all the commoners and the allies also became aware of the matter and came running together in haste, desiring to know what had been achieved with the Greeks. Anthenor postponed his answer to them until the following day. Thus he allowed the assembly to disperse, and everyone went their separate ways. Then, during the meal, while Talthybius was also present, Anthenor exhorted his sons, saying they should guard nothing in their lives so much as making a dear friendship with the Greeks alone. Afterward, recounting the piety <note>original: "from[m]keit"</note>, trust, or faith, and goodness of them all in particular, he marveled at it. Thus, after the evening meal was finished, they departed from one another. But at daybreak, as they were all waiting to hear if perhaps some measure of their misfortunes might be settled, he arrived with Talthybius, and not long after him came Aeneas, then Priam with the remaining young kings. Once they had called upon him to tell what he had heard from the Greeks, he spoke in this manner:

> "A heavy thing, my Trojan lords, and you allies—yes, a heavy thing it is for us that we have begun a war against the Greeks; but much heavier and much harder still that on account of one woman, our best friends should have been offended by us, especially since they are descended from Pelops <note>Pelops was a legendary figure whose descendants, the Atreidai (Agamemnon and Menelaus), led the Greek forces. Anthenor is arguing that the Greeks and Trojans share ancient ancestral ties.</note> and are related to us by the laws of friendship. For it is necessary to touch upon at least a few of our misfortunes. When has our city, completely weighed down by great calamities, ever had rest? Have we ever lacked for weeping? Or have the miserable losses of our allies been diminished? When have we not lost our good benefactors, our closest friends, our elders, and finally our children in this war? And so that I may recount the memory of other people's sorrows from my own experience, what have I suffered with my son Glaucus? # The Fifth Book.

When Helenus perceived this, he urged Neoptolemus to be of good heart and to be certain of his secrecy, for he intended to remain with them in Greece for a long time, even after the destruction of his fatherland. Therefore, as it pleased Helenus, many materials that were thought suitable for that work <note>This "work" refers to the construction of the Trojan Horse.</note> were brought forth by Epeius <note>The master carpenter of the Greek army.</note> and Ajax, the son of Oileus.

Meanwhile, the confirmers of the agreed-upon peace entered into Troy: their ten chosen princes—Diomedes, Ulysses, Idomeneus, Ajax Telamonius, Nestor, Meriones, Thoas, Philoctetes, Neoptolemus, and Eumelus. When the common people saw them at the market or the square, they lifted up their hearts joyfully, believing their misfortunes had finally come to an end. Thus, each person individually, or many together as they met them, came to them in a friendly manner, receiving them and kissing them in jubilation.

Then Priam entreated the Greeks on behalf of Helenus and, with great earnestness, commended his dearest son to them; he favored Helenus above the others, most especially because of his foresight.

Afterward, when the time seemed right, a communal feast was begun to honor the princes and the established peace; during this time, Antenor served the Greeks at the table and provided all things most kindly.

But as soon as it was daybreak, the elders or councilors gathered together in the Temple of the Goddess Minerva, among whom Antenor announced that ten chosen men had been sent by the Greeks regarding the pacts or the unification of the mentioned peace. When it pleased them to lead these men into the temple as well, they all reached out their hands to one another and agreed among themselves that on the following day, in the middle of the field and before the eyes of all people, they would set up certain altars upon which they would confirm the good faith of the peace with the religion of an oath. When these preparations were completed, Diomedes and Ulysses began to swear that they would abide by what they had agreed upon with Antenor; as witnesses to this, they called upon the highest God Jupiter, Mother Earth, the Sun, the Moon, and the Sea. Afterward, they divided the sacrifices into two parts—which had been prepared for this purpose—so that one part faced toward the Sun and the other toward the ships, and they walked through the middle of them. <note>Walking between the halves of a sacrificed animal was an ancient and solemn way to seal a covenant; it implied "may I be split like this animal if I break my word."</note> Subsequently, Antenor confirmed his agreement with the very same words, and after the transaction was finished, everyone returned to their own people. Furthermore, the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarier"; in classical accounts, the Greeks often referred to the Trojans as barbarians.</note> extolled Antenor with the highest praise, and each person honored him as he approached as if he were a god, for they believed he alone was the cause of the established peace.

# On the destruction of Troy
<meta>catchword: with</meta>

Minerva / who also led Cassandra away as a prisoner. When the Barbarians <note>A term the Greeks used for the Trojans and their allies.</note> together with the city were being destroyed in this manner, they began to take counsel concerning those who had fled to the altars of the gods and had prayed for the sparing of their lives. Thus they all decided that they should be dragged out by force and strangled, so deeply had the injustice pained them, for which reason a desire to extinguish the Trojan name had come upon them. Thus the prisoners who had escaped the torture of the previous night were slaughtered, trembling just like cattle. Afterward, according to the custom of war, everything was robbed or looted through all the temples <note>original: "kirchen," literally 'churches,' here referring to pagan temples</note> and half-burned houses; and for many days thereafter, a diligent search was made so that no enemy might escape. In the meantime, they also arranged for convenient places to bring together the silver and gold, and others besides, on account of the precious jewels.

### How the Greeks divide the spoils.

**S**<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring leafy patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>ubsequently, once they were sated with Trojan blood and the city was completely leveled by the fires, they first began to pay for the war with the spoils, starting with the captive women and small children. Among them, Helen was first of all returned to Menelaus without any drawing of lots. Afterward, Polyxena—on the advice of Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>—was sent by Neoptolemus to his father Achilles as a sacrifice for the dead. Cassandra was given to Agamemnon, since he was so encompassed by love for her that he could not hide it; he then confessed his desire. Aethra and Clymene were taken by Demophoon and Achamas. For the others, they began to draw lots, and Andromache fell to Neoptolemus; additionally, they gave him her children to honor such a prince. Then Hecuba fell to Ulysses. Thus far, the servitude or service of the noble women was settled; the others each had their portion, either from the booty or from the captives, as the lot fell to each, according to what was due for their service.

Meanwhile, a great dispute arose among the princes regarding the statue of the Palladium <note>A sacred image of Pallas Athena believed to protect the city; its theft was a key turning point in the war.</note>, which Ajax Telamon desired that they should grant to him, on account of the things he had proven through his virtue and skill toward each man individually and toward them all. For this reason, nearly all were persuaded so that the spirit of such a man would not be offended, and they allowed it to go to Ajax; for they had not yet forgotten his honest deeds and his watchfulness or care for the army in their hearts. Only Diomedes and Ulysses spoke against it, who argued in return that the statue had been carried away through their own diligence. Against this, Ajax pointed out that this had not happened through their effort or honesty, for Anthenor—out of regard for their common friendship—had brought it away. Then Diomedes, out of shame, yielded his honor and desisted from the dispute. For this reason, Ulysses [spoke] against Ajax...

[Ajax] had fought with all his might, but on the other hand, Agamemnon and Menelaus endeavored to let Ulysses obtain [the prize] on account of his cleverness—and because of Helen, whom he had preserved for them with his diligence. For when Ajax, after the city of Ilium <note>Troy</note> had been taken, considered how much they had suffered and endured for such a long time because of that same woman, he was the first who ordered her to be killed. And although many of the pious men praised Ajax’s counsel, Menelaus, still having love for his wife, won them all over and pleaded for her. Ultimately, so much was achieved that through the intercession of Ulysses, Helen was delivered to him unharmed. On account of these things—as if by the judgment of both [kings] who recognized the service—they gave the image of the Palladium <note>A sacred wooden statue of the goddess Athena, believed to ensure the safety of whichever city held it; it was a highly contested trophy of the war.</note> to Ulysses, while war was still at hand and many of the nations who were hostile to us still murmured here and there. This was done without regard for the brave men, and also in disregard of Ajax’s many honorable deeds and the grain which he had brought from Thrace and distributed among the entire army <note>original: "hůr," an archaic spelling of "Heer," meaning army or host</note>. Therefore, all the captains who were mindful of Ajax’s virtues recognized that no one should be held above him; but those who followed the favor of Ulysses became diligently partisan and united [against Ajax].

In the meantime, Ajax was filled with contempt and, overcome by the sorrow of his heart, he publicly announced or threatened to the faces of those who had been against him that he would yet avenge himself upon them with blood. Consequently, Ulysses, Agamemnon, and Menelaus kept themselves under close guard, and so that they might be safer, they watched with total diligence. But as the night was already at hand, they [the soldiers] all unanimously insulted both kings in their departure, and did not hold back any bitter words, for they considered the kings' impurity and desire for a woman to be greater than the greatest concern of the war.

But early the next morning, they found Ajax dead in their midst; and as they later searched to see by what death he had died, they discovered that he had perished amidst the army <note>Historical accounts vary on Ajax's death; some claim suicide, while others suggest he was murdered during the night by his rivals.</note>. Afterward, a great disagreement arose among the captains and the common crowd, and soon after a riot followed, as they complained bitterly how not long before Palamedes <note>A Greek hero known for his ingenuity, who was famously framed as a traitor by Ulysses and executed by the Greeks.</note>—a man highly prudent in the ways of war and at home—and now Ajax as well, famous for so much clamor [in battle], had both been wickedly brought into the net through their [the kings'] cunning. On account of these things, the aforementioned kings feared that they might yet face an even worse turn of fate from the army; they remained locked away at home, strengthened by their good friends. Meanwhile, Neoptolemus <note>The son of Achilles, who took a leadership role after his father's death.</note> brought wood there and burned [the body of] Ajax, and gathered the remains in a vessel, and applied himself so that they might be buried on Mount Rhoeteum. Also soon thereafter, he erected a tomb and had it consecrated to honor such a prince. These things, had they happened before the taking of the city, would in truth have aided the enemy’s cause, and a great doubt would have been cast upon the most important concerns of these matters. Thus Ulysses, fearing the violence of the offended army, fled secretly away by sea, and so left the Palladium to Diomedes.

However, the sons of Ajax—Acantes, born of Glauca, and Eurysaces, born of Tecmessa—were entrusted to Teucer.

### How the Greeks Departed.

AFTERWARD, the Greeks were concerned that if they delayed, they would be blocked or hindered from sailing by the intervention of winter (which was already approaching with force). They led the ships into the sea, loaded them with oars and other naval gear, and so everyone departed with the things and the spoils they had acquired over those many years.

Aeneas remained at Troy. These things were made known to Antenor by a messenger who had preceded him; when Aeneas returned toward Troy, finding the matter unsettled, they never let him back in. ### Concluding Remarks.

These things I, Dictys of Knossos, companion of the captain Idomeneus, have described, using the same language which I was most able to achieve and obtain—even when speaking among many different tongues—using the Punic letters <note>original: "Punicischen bůchstaben"; referring to the Phoenician-derived script which legends say Cadmus brought to Greece</note> brought forth by Cadmus and Danaus. It should also not surprise anyone that although they are all Greeks, they live or deal with one another with many different ways of speaking, since we ourselves, coming even from one island, do not use the same tongue, but rather many different and mixed ones. Therefore, knowing all the things that happened to the Greeks and the Barbarians <note>In the ancient sense, "Barbarians" refers to the non-Greek Trojans and their allies</note> in the war—having suffered the greater part of them myself—I have released this into memory. Regarding Antenor and his kingdom, I have also recounted what I heard. Now I will write how our people returned home.

# Of the Trojan losses

...containing the man’s death. Meanwhile, Orestes arrived and became aware of the whole situation; he also urged Menelaus to follow through with his previous intentions, for it pained him deeply that Neoptolemus had carried off or intended to marry Hermione. <note>Hermione was the daughter of Menelaus and Helen, and had been promised to Orestes before being given to Neoptolemus.</note> Therefore, he began to secretly lay wait for him. To this end, he first sent some of those whom he considered his most trusted confidants to Delphi to spy on Neoptolemus’s arrival. When Menelaus became aware of this, he wished to avoid being part of such a crime and retreated to Sparta. 

However, when those who had been sent out returned, they reported that Neoptolemus was no longer at Delphi. Consequently, Orestes was compelled to go there himself to seek the man. The day after he had departed, he returned with the matter unresolved, as was the talk among the people. A few days later, a rumor arrived that Neoptolemus had perished; and according to everyone’s report, he had been lured into a trap through Orestes' treachery, as was spread among the common folk. Thus the young man (as it became known regarding Neoptolemus's end) took back Hermione, whom he had previously been wedded to, and traveled to Mycenae. 

Meanwhile, when Peleus and Thetis <note>Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis were the grandparents of Neoptolemus and the parents of Achilles.</note> heard of their grandson's death, they went out to search for him and discovered that he was buried at Delphi. There they had him sung over or held funeral rites <note>original: "seelgerädt," referring to prayers or services for the soul of the deceased</note> for him, as was the custom. They also learned that he had died in those places where it was said Orestes had never been. Yet the common people gave no credit to this story, so firmly was the belief in Orestes' secret plot fixed in their hearts. Furthermore, when Thetis saw that Hermione had been disposed to Orestes, she sent Andromache—who was pregnant by Neoptolemus—home to the Molossians, avoiding Orestes and his wife so that they would not destroy the child.

## The Sixth Book.

had come, and that he had taken this command upon himself and separated the two of them. Everyone who was present testified to him orally that this was a fatal omen, and they further told him he should guard himself against his son’s treachery. Thus, Ulysses became suspicious of Telemachus’s intentions and sent him away to the estates in Cephalonia, placing him under the care of very trustworthy guards. In addition to this, Ulysses also withdrew to hidden and secluded places, striving to avoid the power of the heavy dreams. At that same time, Telegonus (whom Circe bore to Ulysses and raised on the island of Aea) had grown up and set out to find his father. He arrived at Ithaca carrying a spear in his hands, the point of which was tipped with the bone of a sea turtle-dove <note>original: "mör turteltüblins." This refers to a stingray; in classical mythology and medieval lore, the spine of a stingray was said to be the weapon that killed Ulysses</note>, which was the crest <note>original: "wapen"</note> of that same island where he was born. After he was informed where his father Ulysses lived, he finally came to him. There, he was initially not permitted to enter by those who guarded the estate or fields, as they were suspicious of him. As he persisted more loudly and firmly, he was pushed back; then he began to cry out that it was a dishonorable thing that a man should not be allowed to embrace his father. Thus, as they believed Telegonus had come for the purpose of doing violence to the King, they resisted even more fiercely, for no one knew that Ulysses had another son. But when the youth saw that he was being pushed away longer and more firmly with force, he grew enraged out of grief and killed many of the guards or otherwise wounded and weakened them. When these things were made known to Ulysses, he believed the youth had been sent there by Telemachus, his legitimate son, and he stepped out and threw the spear (which he was accustomed to carrying for his own protection) at Telegonus. But as the youth escaped such a throw without any danger, he also shot a fine arrow or small spear at those present, and very fortunately hit his mark. But when Ulysses fell down from that same blow, he rejoiced in his fortune and confessed that it had gone well for him, that he had perished by the hand of a foreign man and had thus released his most beloved son Telemachus from the paternal crime of parricide <note>original: "vätterlichs todtschlags"</note>. Afterward, while he could still draw his last breath, he asked the youth who he was and from where he was born, who had dared to kill Ulysses (the son of Laertes, a man most famous in counsel and the paths of war). Then Telegonus, when he understood that this was his father, tore at his head with both hands and began to weep most piteously, becoming entirely distressed that he had brought death upon his father. So he showed Ulysses, as he had requested, his name, and his mother’s, and also the island where he was born, and finally the crest of his small spear. Thus Ulysses, as he thought of the heavy dreams that the soothsayers <note>original: "waarfager"</note> had previously shown him—signifying the end of his life—was wounded by the one he had least feared. Three days later he passed away, already old and well-advanced in years, and yet

# The First Book of the ancient and
# highly esteemed Egyptian priest Horapollo
-> of the city of Nilopolis, concerning the signs of sacred writing. <-
-> First Book. <-

### Eternity.
<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Sun and the Moon, both depicted with human faces, representing eternity.</image-desc>
When the Egyptians wished to signify infinite eternity and represent it to others, they depicted the Sun and the Moon, because these two orbiting lights have burned since the world began.

#### Eternity.
<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a crowned snake (basilisk) coiled in circles, representing another symbol of eternity.</image-desc>
They also use another symbol to show Eternity: namely, the serpent called the Basilisk <note>original: "Basiliscum". In Egyptian iconography, this refers to the Uraeus, the rearing cobra often seen on the crowns of pharaohs and gods.</note>, which is colored gold and surrounds certain gods with its blackness and its beak. They say this signifies eternity because, while there are three types of serpents, all others of their kind die, yet this one is immortal; it alone kills other animals with its breath, without any bite at all. Since life and death are thus equally in its power, it is fittingly used to enclose the gods.

### The World.
<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ouroboros: a serpent coiled in a circle, biting its own tail.</image-desc>
To represent the world, they paint a serpent that is scaly and glimmers with many colors, which also eats its own tail and holds it in its mouth. Here, the scales represent the stars. The animal is slow-moving, just like the world, in proportion to its great size. And because it is so bright or smooth, it signifies water. Furthermore, because it sheds its skin annually and thereby casts off its old age, it sufficiently shows in what manner and how the changing course of the years constantly renews and rejuvenates itself. That it feeds upon its own body is intended to show that everything produced in this world through divine providence is also brought to destruction by the world itself.

### The Year.
<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a star positioned above a seated woman (Isis), who is pointing upward.</image-desc>
The goddess Isis, depicted as a woman, was painted to signify the Year; for among the Egyptians, Isis is the star called Sothis in their language, known to the Greeks as the <term>Dog Star (Astrokyon)</term> <note>original Greek: ἀστροκύων. This refers to Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, whose rising heralded the flooding of the Nile.</note>. Because this very star dominates the other stars to some extent, appearing now large, then small, sometimes dark, and sometimes bright. Additionally, from its first rising, predictions are made and observations are taken regarding...

# Signs of Sacred Writing
<meta>catchword: Excellence.</meta>

...to see how the whole course of the year will be; thus they not unfairly represent Isis as the year.

### Year.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a palm tree with twelve distinct branches, representing the twelve months of a year.</image-desc>

They take another meaning for the Year from the aforementioned palm tree. For, unlike the nature of all other trees, it sprouts a new shoot at the time of every new moon, so that in twelve months, twelve branches grow, and from this, a whole, complete year is determined. <note>In Egyptian hieroglyphs, a notched palm branch represents the word 'renpet' (year).</note>

### Month.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a single palm branch arching over a crescent moon, symbolizing a month.</image-desc>

To indicate a month, they paint one of these palm branches, or else a new moon turned upward with its horns. The reason for the palm branch has been shown before. The moon is turned upward because as soon as it becomes new, fifteen of its parts stand empty, which it must still fill. Once full, fifteen parts must again be diminished, so that in thirty days it turns its horns downward.

### Leap Year.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing a portion of a tilled field, representing a quarter-year or leap year calculation, with a small tree on the left.</image-desc>

To indicate a leap year, they paint a quarter-part of a field. A field among them <note>The ancient Egyptians.</note> measures one hundred and fifty feet. They use its quarter to signify the year because from the first rising of the star of Isis <note>original: "Isidis". This refers to the heliacal rising of the star Sirius, which signaled the flooding of the Nile and the start of the Egyptian year.</note> until its next rising, a quarter of a year passes. They say the year contains three hundred and sixty-five days; therefore, every fourth year they count the remaining parts together, for four times a quarter makes one whole day.

### God.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an eagle with its wings spread, standing on the ground.</image-desc>

To represent God, they paint this bird, the eagle, because it is so fertile and long-lived. <note>While the original Greek text of Horapollo likely referred to a vulture—a symbol of the goddess Mut and motherhood—Renaissance translators often substituted the eagle as a more familiar symbol of majesty.</note>

### Sun.

Furthermore, they believe that the eagle is the image and symbol of the Sun, for more than any other kind of bird, it looks straight into the rays of the Sun. For this reason, physicians use a herb for eye pain (I also read here of a stone called aetites <note>original: "aetites", also known as the 'eagle stone.' It was a hollow geode believed to be found in eagles' nests and possessed of magical and medicinal properties.</note>). Therefore, they sometimes paint an eagle to signify the Sun as the lord of sight. Additionally, they compare the eagle to the Sun for this reason: the female is said to be so devoted that as often as the male entices her with lust—which happens perhaps thirty times—she obeys. Likewise, the Sun, when it completes a cycle of thirty days, fills the Moon and makes it bright.

### Excellence.

When they wish to indicate someone highly esteemed and a person of distinction, they also paint an eagle. This is because all other birds, when they wish to soar into the heights, must rise sideways and in curves, whereas the eagle ascends straight upward.

### Oppression.

Conversely, the eagle also signifies the misery of one who is oppressed, who was once held in high regard and suddenly falls into disregard. For just as other birds descend from the air gradually and clumsily, the eagle shoots straight and directly downward.

# Of the first book of Horapollo.
<sig>J J ii</sig>
<meta>Catchword: ...together gathered</meta>

### Nobility.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an eagle perched on a branch, facing left with its wings slightly spread.</image-desc>

If they wished to represent someone who is higher and more excellent than other people, the Egyptians used the eagle to indicate this through its own nature, as it is held to be the noblest among all birds.

### Bloodshed.

And because the eagle (as it is said) quenches its thirst with blood alone and drinks no water, they intended to signify great bloodshed through its image.

### Victory.

This eagle is invincible and superior to all other birds; therefore, they chose to represent victory through its likeness. If another bird should ever overpower it, the eagle throws itself upon its back and defends itself with its claws while lying in this position. In this way, the enemy can never reach it and is chased away or overcome by the one who appeared to be defeated.

### Soul.

The Egyptians call the soul *Baieth*, and yet this little word has two meanings when it is divided: for *Bai* signifies the soul, and *Eth* signifies the heart. <note>In ancient Egyptian, "Ba" refers to the soul or spirit, and "Het" or "Hat" refers to the heart; Horapollo suggests that the soul is literally contained within the physical heart.</note> The Egyptians believe that the soul is enclosed within the heart, so that this word *Baieth* sounds like "Heart-soul." Therefore, they judge the eagle to be of the same nature as the soul, because it drinks no water but only blood, upon which the living soul in man also nourishes itself.

### Marriage.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two eagles standing on the ground, facing each other with wings slightly raised.</image-desc>

The Egyptians take the sign of Mars <note>original: "Martis"</note> for the man, and the sign of Venus <note>original: "Veneris"</note> for the woman. Therefore, they also paint two eagles facing one another to describe marriage. For other animals are not always in a state of desire, nor is the female always submissive to the male; however, the eagle, like the human, allows itself to mate as often as the male feels the urge.

### Fidelity of Spouses.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two birds, possibly crows or ravens, standing on the ground and both facing towards the left.</image-desc>

When the Egyptians paint two crows, they wish to describe thereby the loyalty and duty of the state of marriage. For this bird gives birth to only two eggs, from which a female and a male usually hatch. If, however, (which happens but rarely) two males are hatched together, or two females, the male will not take any other female, nor will the female attach herself to any strange male. Instead, they live alone. For this reason, those whom a single crow flies toward may conclude that they shall finish their time in a state of widowhood.

### An Only Son.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a scarab beetle and a ball of dung.</image-desc>

They paint a dung beetle <term>Roskäfer: a scarab beetle (Scarabaeus sacer)</term> when they wish to indicate an only-born son; for this beetle is brought forth and generated by itself, without a female or any conception. <note>Ancient naturalists believed scarabs were all male and reproduced by rolling balls of dung.</note>

### Procreation.

To signify procreation through this symbol, they observe the nature which the beetle has. When this beetle wishes to bring forth young, it seeks out cow dung. From this, it creates a small ball which is round like the heavens; then, when it has ...together gathered a small lump of the same...

once gathered, it leans against it with its back and rolls it toward the setting sun, while it continues to look toward the rising sun, pushing it along until it becomes as round as the heavens. The sun also runs from its rising toward its setting, while the other stars, through a contrary motion, are driven about from setting to rising. Now, once the beetle has rolled such a little ball, it buries it and lets it lie for twenty-eight days, during which time the moon completes its circuit through all the signs of the <term>Zodiac</term><note>original: "Thier zürcks"; an old term for the Tierkreis or circle of animals.</note>, and the young little beetles also come to life. On the twenty-ninth day, when the beetle believes the sun and moon are joining their light together and the world is being born anew, it strikes the little ball open and casts it into the water; then the young beetles come crawling forth.

### A Father.

<image-desc>Woodcut of two beetles, likely scarabs, oriented horizontally one above the other and facing in opposite directions.</image-desc>

Because this animal is said to be produced by the male alone without any mother, they use it to provide the sign for a father.

### The Circuit of the World.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a single beetle (scarab) facing downward.</image-desc>

To describe the circuit of the world through the form of this animal is not as unfitting as they hold it to be, since it has such a nearly identical manner of birth.

### A Man.

They know no better way to signify a man than with this animal, because in its kind there is no female. There are, however, three types of dung beetles. The first is cat-colored and light; therefore, it is dedicated to the sun. For they say that the cat changes its pupils according to the course of the sun: at sunrise they are elongated, at midday they are round, and they become dark brown toward sunset. For this reason, in Thebes, the City of the Sun, an image of a god was erected that looks like a cat. A beetle has thirty little fingers, which signify the thirty days in which the sun completes its course in each of the twelve signs. Another kind of beetle has horns like a bull and is dedicated to the moon; for this reason, the Egyptians also assign the Bull among the stars in the heavens to the moon. The third kind of beetle has only a single horn, resembles no other creature, and—just like the ibis bird—is dedicated to Mercury.
