## The Mothers.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a large bird, possibly a vulture or eagle, perched on a branch.</image-desc>

If they wish to write the word for "mothers," they paint a vulture, for among these birds no male is found. It conceives its young in this way: when it becomes lustful and desires to lay eggs, it exposes its reproductive organ to the <term>North Wind</term><note>original: "Bißwindt"; historically referring to the biting north wind or Boreas, which was mythologically believed to fertilize vultures.</note> and remains standing there for five days, enduring without eating or drinking; in this manner, it conceives. There are some vultures that do not conceive from this wind but otherwise lay eggs that are good to eat, though they are useless for brooding.

<page-num>92</page-num>
<header>Of the First Book of Horapollo. 92</header>

### Sight.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a vulture (or eagle) standing on the ground, facing left. The bird is depicted with detailed plumage and a sharp, curved beak.</image-desc>

And because this bird has a sharper sight than other animals, looking from the rising of the sun to its setting, and likewise from the setting toward the rising, recognizing from afar where it might find carrion, they chose to have **sight** represented by this bird.

### A Goal.

For a goal <note>In this context, "zil" refers to a destination, target, or a fixed point in time/space.</note> and the indication of the same, this bird has also been depicted. For seven days before a battle takes place, it arrives at the battlefield where the event is to occur.

### Foreknowledge.

And for this very same reason, it is also used where one should understand that someone has **foreknowledge** of future things. This is all the more precise because it always turns itself toward the side that is destined to be defeated <note>Literally "the part that shall lie beneath."</note>. Indeed, it gazes upon the place where the most people are destined to perish. For this reason, in ancient times, kings sent out their scouts to learn toward which direction the vultures turned.

### The Year.

It also serves to indicate the **year** with its image, because this animal or bird divides the three hundred and sixty-five days of the year in this manner: For one hundred and twenty days it remains on the earth, so that it never soars into the air or leaves the ground, but broods and raises its young. For two hundred and forty days it looks after itself, neither nourishing others nor receiving nourishment, but preparing itself only for the future receiving and laying <note>Referring to the reproductive cycle.</note>; the five remaining days it spends in its conception, as has been mentioned.

### Mercy.

It might seem like a consistent interpretation that one would want to signify **mercy** with this bird, even though this very bird spares no other animal. But their reasoning comes from this: during the one hundred and twenty days that it broods, it almost never leaves the nest or flies out. If it lacks food to nourish the young, so that they do not die of hunger, it pecks and tears its own thighs open and lets them suck out the blood. <note>This myth of self-sacrifice is more commonly associated with the pelican in medieval bestiaries, but Horapollo attributes it to the vulture.</note>

### The Upper and Lower Hemispheres of Heaven.

The Egyptians attribute the upper visible circle <note>The celestial hemisphere.</note> to **Pallas** <note>original: "Palladi"; referring to Pallas Athena.</note> and the lower one in the heavens to **Juno**. It seems quite unfitting to them that the heavens should be represented with a masculine name, since the birthing of the Sun and Moon, along with other stars, comes from and is accomplished by female power and contribution. Now, the vulture is said to be only female, and they hold it to be the king of other birds for that very reason; therefore, they wish to signify the aforementioned and every other goddess through this bird.

### A Mother.

When they wish to indicate a **mother**, they paint this bird, for the sole reason—as often mentioned—that there are no males among the vultures. Thus, every mother is represented by a female figure.

<page-num>94</page-num>
<header>Signs of Holy Scripture</header>

->Unity.<-

<image-desc>Small woodcut of a bird resembling a vulture or eagle, standing and facing left.</image-desc>

Among the Egyptians, two handfuls are taken for one <term>quincelin</term> <note>Original: "quincelin." This likely refers to a "quincunx" or a specific unit of weight or measure, which Horapollo associates with the concept of unity or the number one.</note>, and that same thing is taken for unity or a single number. This number is the beginning of all other numbers. Therefore, they represent the single number quite appropriately with this bird, the vulture, because the beginning and the Mother <note>Horapollo asserts that all vultures are female and conceive by the wind, making them symbols of "Mother" and "Nature."</note> can well be taken to represent unity.

->God’s Providence.<-

<image-desc>Small woodcut of a five-pointed star.</image-desc>

When they wish to represent God, they paint a star; for through divine providence, all the stars and even the movement of the entire world are guided, and without God, nothing can have any permanence at all.

->Chance.<-

They attribute all the movements and courses of the stars to God’s regard; therefore, when they wish to indicate a stroke of luck or **chance**, they also made a star.

->Five.<-

The number **five** they represent with a star; for although there are many stars in the heavens, there are only five stars—excluding the Sun and Moon—that are mobile in the heavens and are called **planets**, and they direct all the courses of the world.

->The Course of the Moon.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut of a standing dog-headed humanoid (Cynocephalus), hairy with a tail, gesturing with its hands.</image-desc>

The Moon and its course they describe with a painted **dog-headed ape** <note>The "Hundßkopffaffen" refers to the Cynocephalus or baboon, which was sacred to Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom and the moon.</note>. For this animal's behavior changes almost exactly according to the course of the moon. When the moon wanes, the male among these animals eats nothing and sees nothing; he is entirely sorrowful and stares constantly at the ground as if he were mourning that the moon had been snatched away and removed. The female, in addition to all that is described above, also has her flow <note>Referring to menstruation.</note>. For this reason, the Egyptians constantly kept dog-headed apes in their schools and temple courtyards, which they raised so that they could determine when the moon was new or full by observing them.

->The Circuit of the Earth.<-

Furthermore, through this animal, they wish to signify the **circuit of the earth**. The reason is that such a circumference of the earth is divided into seventy-two stages <note>Original: "stapfflen." This refers to the 72 quinaries or divisions of the zodiac.</note>. This animal, when raised diligently within the temples, does not die all at once like other animals, such that it would perish in a single day. Instead, every day, as it were, one of its parts dies; tomorrow another, which the priests bury, while the rest of the body remains in health. This continues for seventy-two days in a row, at which point it is completely finished.

->Writing.<-

Literal **writing** is understood through the painting of this animal; for the art of writing is born naturally into this very creature. As soon as a dog-headed ape is captured and brought to the temples of the Egyptians, the priest places a writing tablet along with a stylus before it—or otherwise ink, pens, and paper—to test if it is of the kind that is inclined toward writing. Thereupon, the animal writes what it wishes.

<page-num>95</page-num>
<header>From the First Book of Horapollo</header>

### Swimming.

Swimming is signified by this animal <note>Referring to the cynocephalus or baboon discussed on the previous page.</note>; the reason being that all other animals living on earth become somewhat soft and wrinkled from much swimming and bathing, but this animal alone becomes glistening and beautiful from it.

### Wrath.

Above all others, this is a wrathful animal; therefore, wherever it is depicted, the meaning of **wrath** is also understood.

### New Moon.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a cynocephalus (baboon-like creature) standing upright on its hind legs, facing left, with its front paws raised towards the sky and wearing a small crown.</image-desc>

When they wish to indicate that the moon is new, they depict one of these animals standing upright and lifting its front paws toward heaven, with a royal crown upon its head. It is as if it were giving thanks to God that the moon has overtaken the sun and begins to shine itself, and is no longer hindered in its brightness by the sun's glare.

### The Equinox.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a cynocephalus seated on the ground, facing left, with its paws near its face.</image-desc>

When they wish to show how, in springtime and also in autumn, day and night are of equal length, they paint a <term>cynocephalus</term> <note>Original: "Hundskopff" (dog-head). In Egyptian lore, the baboon was sacred to Thoth, the god of time and measurement.</note> crouching on the earth. For this animal urinates once every hour of the day, and does the same at night. For this reason, the Egyptians also depict this animal on their water pipes and let the water run through its penis, because, as said above, it indicates every hour by urinating. 

However, so that the water pipe on the <term>water clock</term> <note>Original: "vhr." Specifically a clepsydra, which used regulated water flow to measure time.</note> is neither too small nor too large, which would cause errors in the hours, they pull a hair from the outer part of this animal's tail; and as thick as that hair is, they make an iron nozzle of that same thickness. This ensures nothing fails in the outflow, which they manage with good calculation and skill, as they do with other things. Furthermore, because it howls twelve times a day—once every hour—at the time of the equinox (which no other animal does), it is also depicted to represent that specific time.

### Joy, Wrath, and Fury.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a lion sitting on its haunches, facing right.</image-desc>

Where they wish to signify these three things, they paint a **lion**. It has a large head, fiery eyeballs, and a round body; its hair resembles the rays of the sun, so radiant <note>Original: "zwitzerecht." This refers to the mane appearing like the "frizzled" or radiating rays of the sun.</note> is it. Therefore, this animal is also painted on the throne of the sun to indicate that it has a resemblance to the sun.

### Manhood.

<image-desc>Woodcut showing the front half of a lion, facing right.</image-desc>

The front part of the lion is painted when someone wishes to indicate **manhood** <note>In the sense of "bravery" or "fortitude."</note> or strength of mind, for the lion's chest is broader than its other limbs.

### Vigilance and Protection.

<image-desc>Woodcut showing the head of a lion, facing left.</image-desc>

The lion's head alone, when painted, signifies a vigilant person who keeps good watch. For the lion has its eyes closed when it is awake, but when it sleeps, it has them open; this is a sign of wakefulness. Therefore, it is not without reason that lions are placed in the precincts of churches to guard them.

<header>Signs of Sacred Writing</header>

### A Dreadful Person.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a lion sitting on its haunches, holding a long scepter or staff upright in its right paw.</image-desc>

They depict this very animal when they wish to give a sign for a person whom everyone dreads. For this animal strikes a certain fear into every person it encounters.

---

### The Flooding of the Nile.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a seated lion similar to the one above, though slightly different in detail.</image-desc>

The Nile is called **Nun** <note>original: "Nun". Likely a reference to the Egyptian primordial waters, "Nu" or "Nun."</note> by the Egyptians, which signifies as much as **innovation** or **renewal**. To report its overflowing, they sometimes depict a lion, and sometimes three water jugs. They use the lion because the Nile overflows most significantly when the Sun enters the zodiac sign of the Lion <note>the constellation Leo</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut of three ceramic water jugs or jars, arranged with one balanced on top of two others.</image-desc>

They depict three water jugs—no more and no fewer—because three distinct causes are given for the flooding of the river. First, it is said that the Egyptian soil itself produces such an abundance of water. Second, they claim that the Great Ocean which surrounds the world—called the <term>Oceanus</term>—does this through the back-pressure of its own course; as it draws the power of the waters to itself, it causes the Nile to swell. Thirdly, it is proposed that it comes from constant rainy weather which occurs all at once in the region of Southern Ethiopia. That such a great swelling of water comes from the Egyptian soil itself is argued by the fact that in other parts of the globe and all other lands, floods come in winter time from great and immoderate rains; however, Egypt—which lies in the middle of the earth like the **apple of the eye** <note>Meaning the pupil of the eye; a metaphor for something central and precious.</note>—sweats out this abundance of water from itself.

---

### Zeal.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a hanging censer or thurible emitting smoke, with a heart symbol depicted on its side.</image-desc>

They depict a censer that burns and contains a heart to show that just as the heart of a zealous <note>The German "Eyfer" implies both fervor and a heated, jealous passion.</note> person constantly glows, so too does this constant and internal fervor make one fruitful for the procreation of children.

---

### An Untraveled Person.

<image-desc>Woodcut of the head and neck of a donkey or ass in profile, facing right.</image-desc>

They depict the head of a donkey to signify a person who has never traveled abroad. For such a person cannot give any credit to writings that tell of past histories; likewise, he believes that whatever travelers say is unbelievable.

---

### Protection Against Terror.

<image-desc>Woodcut of two human heads, a man and a woman, shown in profile within a window frame looking in opposite directions.</image-desc>

When they wish to indicate that protection and a turning away of terror is at hand, they depict the heads of two people: one shaped like a man's face looking into a window, and the woman's face looking out of the window. They say that no misfortune can strike where there is the faithful vigilance of both, even if there is little other skill present.

## A Malformed Birth.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a frog sitting on the ground.</image-desc>
They paint a frog when a malformed birth <note>original: "Mißgpurt." This refers to a deformity or a creature not fully formed.</note> is to be indicated, and this is because its generation takes its origin from mud and water. It often happens then that the frog did not have enough moisture in its beginning; and since it is in part an earthly and in part a watery animal, if the moisture then leaves it, it must also die and does not fully emerge.

---

## Speech.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a human tongue and a human eye.</image-desc>
When they wish to indicate speech, they sketch a tongue and also a wounded eye. For although the tongue is granted to be the most necessary and prominent part of speech, the eye nevertheless also belongs to it. For what the heart is full of and wishes to speak, one can see in a person's eyes—how serious they are in the matter—by the movement of the same.

---

## Utterance.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'D' incorporating a tongue and a hand.</image-desc>
They also interpret speech and spoken proclamation <note>original: "außsprüchlichen fürtrag." Referring to a formal delivery or command.</note> with a painted tongue, beneath which is a hand; for although speech or a spoken command may first be indicated with the tongue, the hand must nevertheless be obedient in the same to carry out the order.

---

## Silence.

<margin>1095 <note>The Roman numeral M. LXXXXV. translates to 1095.</note></margin>
<image-desc>The Roman numeral M.LXXXXV. printed inside a rectangular border.</image-desc>
This number, 1095, which encompasses the total of the days that appear in three years, they paint to indicate Silence <note>original: "Verschwigenheit." Can also mean secrecy or taciturnity.</note>. The year has 365 days, and when that is tripled, it brings the number of days in which one can clearly observe whether a child—if it does not start to speak—will be and remain a mute, even if it indeed has a tongue.

---

## Something Open.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a running hare.</image-desc>
They paint a hare for this, because this animal has its eyes open continually <note>It was a common ancient belief that hares slept with their eyes open.</note>.

## A Far-Reaching Voice.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing clouds with rain and a bolt of lightning striking the earth, symbolizing thunder.</image-desc>
This signifies to the Egyptians the clap of thunder or the voice of the air. Therefore, when they wish to indicate that a voice is heard from afar, yet one does not know from whom it comes, they paint a clap of thunder; for nothing echoes more terrifyingly, loudly, and quickly than the noise of the same.

## Sensual Pleasure.

<image-desc>The Roman numeral XVI printed inside a rectangular border.</image-desc>
When they wish to give understanding of a sensual pleasure <note>original: "Wollust." In this context, it refers to sexual maturity and carnal desire.</note>, they record the number 16. For in the sixteenth year of their age, humans begin to know one another, procreating and giving birth.

### A Dreadful Person.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a lion sitting on its haunches, facing left. Inside the woodcut frame, at the top left, is a large decorative letter E.</image-desc>

They depict this very animal when they wish to signify a person who is dreaded by everyone. For this animal instills fear in every person it encounters.

### The Flooding of the Nile.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting three ceramic vessels or jars arranged with two above and one below. Inside the woodcut frame, at the top left, is a large decorative letter D.</image-desc>

The Nile is called *Nun* <note>The author likely refers to the Egyptian concept of "Nu" or "Nun," the primordial waters, though here it is interpreted as "Newness."</note> by the Egyptians, which signifies as much as "Innovation" or "Renewal." To signal its outflow, they sometimes paint a lion, and sometimes three water jars. They use the lion because the Nile overflows most forcefully precisely when the sun enters the zodiac sign of Leo <note>original: "Löwen" (the Lion).</note>. They use three water jars—no more and no less—for the reason that three causes are given for the flooding of this river. First, it is said that the Egyptian soil itself provides such an abundance of water. Second, they believe that the ocean that surrounds the world, called *Oceanus*, causes this through the back-pressure of its course; as it draws the power of the waters to itself, it causes the Nile to swell. Thirdly, it is claimed that it comes from constant rainy weather, which occurs at that time in the regions of southern Ethiopia. However, regarding the great swelling of water from the Egyptian soil, they wish to prove that while in other parts of the globe and all other lands, floods come in wintertime from heavy and immoderate rain, Egypt—which lies in the middle of the earth like the "apple of an eye"—sweats out the abundance of water from itself.

### Zeal.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting an ornate censer or chalice with a heart inside it, from which flames and smoke emerge. Inside the woodcut frame, at the top left, is a large decorative letter E.</image-desc>

They paint a censer <note>A vessel for burning incense.</note> that is burning and in which a heart lies, to show that just as the heart of a zealous person <note>original: "yferenden." This can mean one who is jealous, eager, or full of passionate zeal.</note> is constantly roasting, so also this constant and internal fervor makes them fruitful for the procreation of children.

### An Untraveled Person.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a donkey's head, shown in profile facing right. Inside the woodcut frame, at the top left, is a large decorative letter E.</image-desc>

They paint a donkey's head to signify a person who has never traveled abroad; for such a person can give no credit to writings that tell of past histories, and he believes that what travelers say is unbelievable.

### Protection against Terror.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting two human heads joined at the back, one male and one female, looking in opposite directions through window frames. Inside the woodcut frame, at the top left, is a large decorative letter W.</image-desc>

When they wish to indicate that protection and the warding off of terror are at hand, they paint a double human head, where one is shaped like a man's face looking in through a window, and the woman's face looks out through the window. They say that no accidents can strike where, even if there is little skill, the faithful vigilance of both is present.

### Speech.

<image-desc>Woodcut showing a human tongue above and an eye with wound-like markings below.</image-desc>

### A Terrifying Person.

They depict this very animal when they wish to represent a person who terrifies everyone. For this animal instills fear in every person it encounters.

### The Flooding of the Nile.

THE Nile is called *Nun* by the Egyptians, which signifies "Renewal" <note>original: "Neüwerung." The author likely references the Egyptian concept of "Nu" or "Nun," the primordial waters, associated here with the annual rejuvenation of the land.</note>. To signify its flooding,

<image-desc>Woodcut of three water jugs or pitchers, two positioned above one.</image-desc>

they sometimes paint a lion, and at other times three water pitchers. They use the lion because the Nile floods most when the sun enters the zodiac sign of Leo. They use exactly three water pitchers—no more and no less—for the reason that this flooding is said to have three origins. First, it is said that the Egyptian soil itself provides such an overflow of water. Secondly, they claim the "Great Ocean" <note>original: "Mhör Occeanus"</note> that surrounds the world causes it by the counter-pressure of its own current; as it draws the power of the waters to itself, it causes the Nile to swell. Thirdly, it is proposed that it comes from constant rainy weather, which occurs at that time in the regions of Southern Ethiopia. Regarding the claim that such great water springs from the Egyptian soil itself, they argue that while in other parts of the world <note>original: "stapfflen des Erdkreyß," literally "steps of the earth-circle"</note> and all other lands, floods come in winter from excessive and immoderate rain, Egypt—which lies in the middle of the world like the pupil in an eye—sweats out its own overflow of water.

### Zeal.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a suspended, ornate censer or incense burner with a heart visible inside its perforated dome.</image-desc>

A burning censer <term>censer: a vessel used for burning incense</term> in which a heart lies is what they paint to show that, just as the heart of a zealous person <note>original: "yferenden," referring to someone filled with ardor, passion, or jealousy</note> constantly burns, so too does this steady and internal fervor make one fruitful in the procreation of children.

### An Untraveled Person.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a donkey's head in profile, facing right.</image-desc>

They paint the head of a donkey to signify a person who has never traveled <note>original: "nie auß kam," literally "never came out"</note>; for such a person cannot give credit to writings that tell of past histories, believing that whatever travelers report is unbelievable.

### Protection from Terror.

<image-desc>Woodcut of two human faces, a bearded man and a woman, side-by-side as if looking through a window or frame in opposite directions.</image-desc>

When they wish to indicate a safeguard and the warding off of an imminent terror, they paint a double human head, where one is shaped like a man’s face looking in through a window, while the woman’s face looks out through the window. They say that no misfortune can strike where, even if there is little skill, there is the faithful oversight of both parties <note>The image suggests a domestic vigilance where both internal and external threats are watched for.</note>.

### The Flooding of the Nile.

<image-desc>A woodcut of three water jugs or urns stacked vertically.</image-desc>

The Nile is called *Nun* <note>original: "Nun." <page-num>xcviij</page-num>
# Signs of Sacred Writing

->The Union of Man and Woman.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a square frame containing the Roman numerals XVI.</image-desc>

**W**hen one wishes to indicate the intermingling <note>original: "vermischūg," referring to sexual union or procreation.</note> of man and woman, they set this number XVI <note>The Roman numeral 16.</note> thus doubled; for children are conceived with pleasure, and this delight is twofold, shared by both the woman and the man.

---

->Ancient Lineage.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a cluster of papyrus plants or reeds growing out of water.</image-desc>

**I**n bundles of papyrus or Nile reeds, they depict what is meant to show an ancient lineage or origin. By this, they give it to be understood that humans first nourished themselves from the sap of these very roots before any other kind of food was invented anywhere else on earth.

---

->Tasting.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a human head in profile, with the tongue extended forward.</image-desc>

**W**hen they wish to indicate the perfect sense of taste with which we sample a thing, they paint a throat or a gullet <note>original: "Kragē oder schlund." The illustration shows a tongue, but the text specifies the throat as the seat of taste.</note> down to its beginning, for that is where the sense of taste has its sensitivity.

---

->Imperfect Taste.<-

**T**hey signify imperfect taste with a tongue placed between the teeth; for with both of these together, every flavor is tested and recognized.

---

->The Longevity of the Soul.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a phoenix bird standing and looking back over its shoulder.</image-desc>

**S**ince the Phoenix is a bird that lives an exceedingly long time—longer than all other creatures—they wish to indicate the longevity of the soul through its image.

---

->The Inundation of Water.<-

**J**ust as the inundation <note>original: "Wassergüß," referring to the annual flooding of the Nile.</note> of water fills and seeks out all things, so too does the Sun, which is the greatest of all creations, penetrate, seek out, and fathom all things in the circumference of the entire world. Because this bird is also dedicated to the Sun, they have presented and painted this bird to represent the floods.

---

->A Late Homecoming.<-

**I**f someone has traveled across the land and is to remain abroad for a long time and return home slowly, they describe this again with this bird, the Phoenix. For only after five hundred years, when it nears its death, does it return again to Egypt, as if it wished to anticipate its own death. For there, it is honored with certain mysteries, and it is shown a unique honor encountered by no other animal. And beforehand, it rejoices in the Sun, which is hottest and most powerful in Egypt, such that its heat causes the Nile to rise and overflow.

<meta>catchword: Heart-</meta>

<page-num>xcix</page-num>
# Of the First Book of Hori.

### Heart.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an Ibis, a long-necked bird, standing in profile facing left.</image-desc>

**W**hen they write of the heart, they paint an Ibis bird <note>original: "Ibuogel"</note>; for this same bird is dedicated to Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the god of wisdom and writing</note>, who is considered the master of all reason and the heart. This bird also possesses a heart larger than other animals in proportion to its size and limbs. Much is said of this bird in Egypt.

### Skill.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a thick cloud in the sky with rain or dew falling from its center onto the ground below.</image-desc>

**W**hen they wish to indicate cleverness or skill <note>original: "Gschicklicheyt"</note>, they paint a cloud in the sky that dews. This signifies how the dew awakens and softens every bud and root that it moistens, provided they are of a nature that can be softened; but for those things that are naturally hard and will not yield, it accomplishes nothing. In the same way, all cleverness offers itself to mankind, but only the noble-natured <note>original: "gschlachtẽ," meaning those of a refined or receptive disposition</note> and the ingenious can grasp it—just like the dew, which the ignorant let pass by.

### Egyptian Writing.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting writing implements: a small inkwell with a lid, a round sieve, and several Nile reeds or pens.</image-desc>

**T**o signify Egyptian letters or writing, they paint an inkwell, a Nile reed <note>original: "Nilrhoz"</note>, and a sieve. For they write with the reed, having no other pens. The sieve signifies that this tool, first made from reeds, is used to sift flour or to separate it. This also implies that those who make their living by devoting themselves to writing should not have to rely on other labors or the work of craftsmen. Therefore, among them, the art or skill was called *Sbo* <note>Coptic for "instruction" or "teaching"</note>, which may be translated as "Full of Food," as if the Art requires a person who does not have to worry about their daily bread.

### Priest or Scholar of Holy Scripture.

**A** priest <note>original: "pfaff oder priester"</note> may also be designated with these same items, as they are those who know how to decide what is useful for life or for death. For their priests have a book they call *Sacra ambris* <note>The "Book of Ambres," a legendary Egyptian medical or magical text</note>, in which it is written whether a sick person shall recover or die.

### The End.

**T**hey paint "The End" with these same three items, for they hold that he who knows how to read and write may well spend his life in rest and in peace, having escaped all human misfortune.

### The Scribes of Mysteries.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a lean dog or hound walking towards the right, looking forward.</image-desc>

**W**here they wish to signify one of their keepers of mysteries or a scribe of the same, they paint a Dog <note>original: "Hũd"</note> in his place. For he who wishes to be a good, well-informed, and perfect scribe must be very reflective, give no one a direct answer <note>meaning to be discreet with secrets</note>, bark at everyone, be uncourtly <note>original: "vnhöfflich," implying a lack of sycophancy</note>, and do nothing merely to please others, just as dogs are accustomed to do.

### Prophet or Soothsayer.

**T**he Soothsayer <note>original: "Weyffager"</note> is also noted and signified by the form of the dog; for when a dog runs through a temple, he gazes at the idols <note>original: "Götzen"</note> more fixedly, more intently, and longer than any other animal. Thus, the Prophet must and shall take more heed of divine things than other people.

<summary>This page describes hieroglyphs representing the heart, skill, writing, and the priestly class, emphasizing the intellectual and spiritual requirements of the Egyptian scribal tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Ibis, Mercury, dew, Egyptian writing, Sbo, inkwell, sieve, priest, Sacra ambris, dog, scribe, prophet, Horapollo</keywords>

# Signs of sacred writing.

### The Spleen

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a dog standing and looking to the left.</image-desc>

To describe the **spleen** <note>original: "miltz." In early medicine, the spleen was believed to regulate the "black bile" humor, influencing mood and health.</note>, they also use the form of a **dog**. This is because the dog has a very light spleen, smaller and more slight than other animals. Because of this, dogs frequently suffer from rabies, madness, frenzy <note>original: "daubsucht," likely referring to a state of being dazed or having a fit</note>, and even death. Furthermore, the servants who wait upon a sick dog often become afflicted with "spleen-sickness" <note>The author suggests that the dog’s spleen-driven diseases are contagious to humans.</note>.

### Smell, laughter, and sneezing.

**Smell**, **laughter**, and **sneezing** <note>original: "strauchen oder nüessen"</note> are also indicated by the image of a dog, since those who suffer from a stinging or diseased spleen can neither smell, laugh, nor sneeze.

### A Councilor or Official.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a man standing in a long cloak (royal mantle), with a small dog sitting at his feet looking up at him.</image-desc>

With the image of a dog, they also describe a **Councilor** <note>original: "Rhatß herren"</note> or another high-ranking **official**. However, they place a naked figure in a royal mantle opposite him. This is to signify that, just as the dog gazes directly at the images of the Gods, so too did the councilors of old attend solely and plainly to the King's command <note>original: "gheyß"</note>, which is represented by the royal mantle.

### A Bishop.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a man sitting on a bench in front of a building with a large, reinforced wooden door.</image-desc>

They paint a **watchman** or a **house-guard** when they wish to indicate a **Bishop** <note>In this context, "Bishop" refers to the Greek *episkopos*, meaning "overseer."</note>. This is because he must keep everything belonging to the sanctuary pure and well-protected, just as a guardian protects a house.

### The Hour-Caller.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a man in historical attire, holding or blowing into a horn.</image-desc>

In place of this, they paint a human who "eats the hours" <note>original: "vhren frißt." This refers to the *Horoscopus* or priest who monitored the hours of the day.</note>. This is not because anyone actually swallows time—for that is impossible for a human—but rather because people prepare their meals at those specific times and hours.

### Ignorance.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting flames of fire rising above stylized waves of water.</image-desc>

**Fire** and **water** are painted here, because these two elements bring about all decay and corruption.

### A Villain.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large fish swimming in the water.</image-desc>

When they wish to signify an **evil person** or a **villain**, they paint a **fish**. This is because the fish is neither used nor permitted in any spiritual sacrifice. Furthermore, every fish destroys whatever it encounters and does not even spare those of its own kind.

<meta>catchword: Hare.</meta>

# From the first book of Horapollo.

### Hatred.

<image-desc>A small woodcut of a fish swimming in water.</image-desc>

Likewise, and for this very reason, they use the image of a **fish** to signify **hatred**; for the fish is a friend to no one and cannot bear to see another’s well-being <note>original: "wolfart." This refers to a common medieval belief that fish were cold-blooded in character as well as body, lacking social bonds.</note>.

---

### The Mouth.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a coiled serpent with its head raised.</image-desc>

They paint an **adder** <note>original: "Nater"</note> when they wish to indicate the **mouth**, for that creature has no other limb that it can use or achieve anything with except for the mouth.

---

->A well-mannered person.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut of a proud breeding bull standing.</image-desc>

They paint a quite proud and beautiful **breeding bull** <note>original: "Pfarren." A term for a stud bull kept for the community.</note> when they want to show a **tame, well-mannered person**. This is because this animal has such a heated and very hot reproductive organ <note>original: "gepär glid"</note> that when it mounts a cow, it releases its seed without any excessive movement. Indeed, it is so powerful that if it slips to the side, it may even wound the cow. Yet it is so well-behaved and self-restrained <note>original: "abbrůchlich"</note> that once the cow is impregnated <note>original: "geladen"</note>, it never mounts her again.

->A strong person.<-

To signify a **strong person**, they record it with the same animal for the reasons mentioned above.

---

### Hearing.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an animal's ear, likely belonging to an ox.</image-desc>

To record the sense of **hearing**, they paint the **ear of an ox**. For the cow, when she is in heat <note>original: "spilt," literally "playing"</note>, is in season for no longer than exactly three hours, at which time she lows loudly. If the bull comes, all is well; if not, she closes her womb <note>original: "Můtter"</note> until another time. But such a thing rarely happens, because due to his excellent hearing, the bull hears her from afar, and when he perceives that she is ready for the bull <note>original: "rinderig," a specific agricultural term for a cow in heat</note>, he leaps upon her, which no other animal does in such a manner.

---

->The male fertile organ.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut of a goat leaping towards the left.</image-desc>

To signify the **male organ** which is **fertile**, they paint a **goat** and not a bull. For the bull only begins to mate after a year, but the goat does so on the seventh day after he is born <note>original: "gworffen," the term for an animal being dropped at birth</note>. And although at that time he has no seed suitable for reproduction, he is nonetheless more lustful <note>original: "geyler"</note> and performs the act while so young, which no other animal of such a young age can imitate.

<header>Signs of Sacred Writing</header>
<sig>C ii</sig>
<meta>Catchword: To know</meta>

### Sin.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an oryx, a wild animal with one long, straight horn, standing in a simple landscape with a small plant.</image-desc>

The **Oryx** <note>original: "Orypist," likely a contraction of "Oryx ist."</note> is a wild animal that some compare to a goat, except that it has only one horn and its hair grows toward the head, whereas other animals have hair growing toward the tail. They paint this animal to signify **Sin**. This is because, at the rising of the moon, when the animal catches sight of it, it screams—not out of devotion or reverence, which is easily understood by a certain specific symbolic sign: it scratches the ground with its front feet and hides its head, as if it were annoyed by the moon and did not wish to look upon its rising. It does exactly the same at the rising of the sun. For this reason, the ancient Egyptian kings, when the astronomers had shown them at what hour the full moon should appear, kept this animal with them as a certain and reliable sign of the exact hour and time the moon reached its full, which the clattering of this wild goat <note>original: "wildegeyß"</note> naturally indicates. 

Furthermore, among all the sacrifices, the priests do not eat of this animal because they believe it bears enmity against this Goddess <note>The Moon, often associated with Isis.</note>. Also, if it finds a spring in the desert and has drunk from it, it scratches filth and waste into it so that the water cannot be used by other animals; it has a nature so shameful and malicious toward the gods and other creatures. In this, it sins greatly, for through the course of the Goddess or the Moon, all plants grow, and thus the entire world's benefit arises from it.

### Destruction.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a mouse or rat facing right.</image-desc>

They paint a **mouse** when they want to indicate **destruction** <note>original: "Verdörbung"</note>; for the mouse destroys all things, gnawing and consuming everything.

### Judgment or Verdict.

If they wish to indicate **Judgment** or a **verdict**, they paint a mouse once again. The reason is that among many types of flour and piles of bread, this animal always gnaws and applies itself to the best and tastiest. From this, the people of the court should take their example: to always seek out the best and judge accordingly.

### Shamelessness.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a fly or similar winged insect on a ground line.</image-desc>

They paint a **midge** or **fly** to signify **shamelessness** <note>original: "Vnuerschampte"</note>; for no matter how often it is driven away, it always returns.

<summary>This page describes the symbolic meanings of the oryx (representing sin and lunar enmity), the mouse (representing both destruction and the discernment of a judge), and the fly (representing shameless persistence).</summary>
<keywords>Oryx, Sin, Moon, Egyptian Kings, Mouse, Destruction, Judgment, Fly, Shamelessness, Hieroglyphics</keywords>

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>From the First Book of Horus</header>

### Knowledge.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an ant, used to symbolize industrious wisdom and knowledge of one's surroundings.</image-desc>

They paint an **Ant** <note>original: "Ometssen," an early German variant of "Ameisen."</note> to signify **Knowledge**, for this tiny creature knows how to tread out safe paths and dwellings for itself. Furthermore, it understands the habits of other animals; when it carries its nourishment to provide for itself during the winter, no matter how far it wanders, it never loses its way and knows how to return home again.

### A Son.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a waterfowl, likely a snow goose, illustrating parental sacrifice.</image-desc>

The **Snow Goose** <note>original: "Schneegaß."</note> is a creature that loves its young beyond measure. If a hunter chases after it and flushes out the young, the mother willingly allows herself to be caught so that she may distract the hunter, allowing time for her young to escape. For this reason, the Egyptians wish to compare this animal to a **Son**, because a son would be dearly loved by his parents in the same way.

### A Foolish Man.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a pelican in its ground-nest, surrounded by smoke as it tries to extinguish a fire with its wings.</image-desc>

Among the species of **Pelicans**, there is a type of water bird that nests in the wilderness. Now, through the water-pelican, one signifies a **Foolish** or **Delusional Man** <note>original: "Whanwitzigen."</note>. For although this bird could easily nest in high places like other birds, it instead makes a small hole in the ground to lay its eggs. Bird-catchers soon become aware of this; they surround the place where the nest is with cow dung and set fire to it. As soon as the pelican sees the smoke, it tries to extinguish the fire by flapping its wings, but this cannot be; instead, the flapping fans the fire more and more. Thus, it burns its wings, can no longer fly away, and is easily captured. Because the bird does and endures this for the sake of its young or eggs, the Egyptian priests do not eat it at all, holding it to be a sin. While the common people do not care much about this, the priests believe the bird does not act out of a knowledgeable, natural love for its children, but rather out of **folly** <note>original: "totheyt," meaning stupidity or senselessness.</note>.

### Gratitude.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a bird with a crest, identified as a Cucupha or stork, symbolizing filial piety.</image-desc>

They paint a **Dulc** or **Cucupha** <note>A mythical bird often identified in Renaissance natural history with the hoopoe or the stork.</note>—called the **Stork** by some—to indicate a **Grateful Person**. This animal alone among all others does good for its parents in their old age when they are no longer capable. In the very place where it was hatched, it makes a nest for the old ones, plucks out their old feathers so that new ones may grow, and brings food to them until they are renewed with fresh feathers and can gather food for themselves again. For this reason, the Egyptians also decorate the staves in the hands of the **Gods** with this bird.

### An Ungrateful Man.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a hippocampus or sea-horse, depicting the upper body of a horse with fins.</image-desc>

They paint the two front quarters of the **Sea-horse** <note>original: "Mhör oder Wasserroß." Though the image is a hippocampus, the description of the behavior matches the hippopotamus in Horapollo's original Greek text.</note> in a bent posture to signify the ungrateful. For when this animal has grown up, it tests itself to see if it is stronger than its father. If the father yields, the son leaves him space and does not kill him. But if the father will not allow the son to mate with the mother, the son kills him, as he has become stronger and more capable than the old one. Now, to warn men...

<page-num>104</page-num>
<header>Signs of Holy Scripture</header>

...that they might consider the benefits received and repay them, in contrast to the wretched state of this ingratitude.

### Ingratitude.

<image-desc>A small bird with a crest (resembling a hoopoe) perched on a branch.</image-desc>

When they wish to show that someone is **ungrateful** <note>original: "vnerkantlich," meaning unthankful or unrecognizing of favors.</note> toward those who have shown him much kindness, they paint a **Hoopoe** <note>original: "Räutter," a dialectal name for the hoopoe, known in Latin as *upupa*.</note>. For when the Hoopoe grows stronger, it drives its father out of the nest and mates with its mother. Otherwise, this is considered a clean bird, for when a plague or sickness <note>original: "schelm," referring to a pestilence or murrain.</note> goes about and all other animals are plagued by it, this bird does not touch the pigeons. For this reason, in times of pestilence, no food other than pigeons would be prepared, and the same were also cooked for the **Pagan Priests** <note>original: "Götzen Pfaffen," literally "Idol Priests."</note>. Beyond this, it is written that this little animal possesses bile.

### The Impossible.

<image-desc>A pair of human legs and feet standing in a tub or small pool of water.</image-desc>

They paint **two human feet** walking in water, or treading upon the water, to signify a matter that is **impossible** to do, thereby marking that which cannot be. Likewise, they also paint a man who walks but is **without a head**; for they hold it to be impossible that a man might walk without a head, which is why it is not at all unusual that they paint it in this way.

### An Exceedingly Evil King.

<image-desc>A man standing inside a circle formed by a snake biting its own tail (Ouroboros).</image-desc>

They paint a **snake** that has its tail curled into its mouth <note>This is the Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of eternity or the cycle of nature, though here used specifically for a ruler.</note> to signify an **exceedingly evil king**. They write the name of the king in the middle of the circle, wishing it to be understood that a king is a lord over everything. However, the nature of this snake is of the kind called **Mest** <note>original: "Mest," likely a corruption of the Egyptian *Meis* or *Mehen*.</note> by the Egyptians.

### A Vigilant King.

<image-desc>A man in classical armor standing beside a large, alert snake with wide-open eyes.</image-desc>

They paint a **watchful, diligent King** as a snake that constantly keeps watch with wide-open eyes. A watchman is used in place of the King's name to signify that a King—as a protector and guardian of the entire realm—should and must be vigilant.

### A Victorious King.

<image-desc>An Ouroboros (snake biting its tail) encircling a large house or palace building.</image-desc>

Again, they paint a **circular snake**, in the middle of which is a house and a great **Palace** <note>original: "Pfalz," referring to a royal residence or seat of power.</note>.

<page-num>105</page-num>
<header>From the first book of Horapollo.</header>

### Obedient subjects.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a domed beehive with bees swarming around it.</image-desc>

They paint bees <note>original: "Bienen oder Immen"; "Imme" is an archaic German term for a bee.</note> to signify a people that is obedient to its lord <note>The OCR reads "herzen," but contextually this refers to "Herren" (Lord/Master).</note>. For among all animals, this one alone has a king <note>In the Renaissance, the leader of a beehive was mistakenly identified as a king rather than a queen.</note> whom the entire swarm follows and obeys, just as humans obey their kings.

### A Prince.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting the front half of a serpent, severed in the middle.</image-desc>

If someone is not the lord of the whole world and king over the entire land, but perhaps holds a princedom <note>original: "Fürstenthumb"</note>, they paint him as half of a serpent. The serpent signifies a king, but the fact that it is split in two and only one part is shown indicates that he is not a lord over the entire earth.

### A Victor in all things.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a whole, coiled snake.</image-desc>

Conversely, with a whole serpent, they signify one who is a conqueror <note>original: "Überwinder"</note> everywhere.

### A swift man.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a man with wings on his feet walking across a body of water.</image-desc>

To describe such a person, they have two winged feet painted, with which he treads upon the water. This is similar to **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio," the messenger of the Roman gods, famous for his winged sandals (talaria).</note>, whom such a man resembles in his dealings and deeds.

### A predatory yet fruitful and senseless man.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a crocodile on the ground.</image-desc>

They paint a crocodile when they wish to indicate a predatory <note>original: "raubgierigen"</note> yet fruitful and, at the same time, senseless and raging man. This is because this animal is very prolific <note>original: "fruchtpar," referring to high fertility.</note>, but if it is deprived of its prey, it rages against itself and becomes furious.

### The Rising of the Sun.

<image-desc>A woodcut of two eyes, one above the other, representing crocodile eyes.</image-desc>

To signify the rising of the sun, they paint two eyes of a crocodile, because those eyes shine <note>original: "glastend," meaning gleaming or glittering.</note> most powerfully.

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>Signs of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Heyliger gschrifft warzeichen." This is a literal translation of the Greek word "hieroglyphics" (hieros: holy; glyphic: writing).</note></header>

### The Setting of the Sun.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a crocodile coiled into a perfect circle, biting its own tail.</image-desc>

They paint a coiling crocodile to signify the sunset, for when this animal wishes to give birth <note>original: "gpärn." While the German text refers to giving birth, the classical interpretation of this symbol often relates to the animal's ability to curl into a circle.</note>, it is exactly circular <note>original: "synnwel," an archaic German term for perfectly round or spherical.</note> and gives birth in a mingled fashion.

---

### Darkness.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a crocodile's tail lying on a patch of grass, separated from the rest of the body.</image-desc>

The crocodile's tail is so strong that the animal has all its power within it; it cannot overcome anything it attacks unless it has first beaten <note>original: "erpleüwet," meaning to strike, pummel, or bruise.</note> and exhausted it with its tail; only then is it the master. Therefore, because death is dark <note>original: "finster."</note>, and the animal kills with its tail, they paint a crocodile tail to signify Darkness. Now, this animal has many other characteristics, but let enough be said here in the first book.

# Determination of the symbols along with their meanings, contained in the second book <note>original: "Noti," likely an abbreviated or Latinized reference to "notes" or a specific edition's commentary.</note>.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|----------|------------|

<page-num>106</page-num>
<header>Symbols of Holy Scripture <note>In this context, "holy scripture" refers to hieroglyphs, which were historically viewed as sacred, divinely inspired characters.</note></header>

### Setting of the Sun.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration depicting a crocodile coiled in a circle, biting its own tail.</image-desc>

They depict a coiling crocodile to signify the setting of the sun; for when this animal is about to give birth, it becomes perfectly circular <note>original: "synnwel." This refers to the crocodile curving its body into a round shape, which the author links to the disc of the sun.</note> and reproduces in a mixed manner.

---

### Darkness.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration showing a crocodile's tail emerging from a landscape with a simple horizon line.</image-desc>

The crocodile's tail is so strong that its entire power is contained within it; it cannot overcome anything it pursues unless it has first bludgeoned <note>original: "erpleüwet," meaning to beat or strike repeatedly until bruised.</note> and exhausted it with its tail; only then is it the master. Therefore, because death is dark and this animal kills with its tail, they depict a crocodile's tail to signify darkness. Now, this animal possesses many other traits, but enough has been said here in the first book.

->End of the First Book of Horapollo. <note>original: "Hori." This refers to Horapollo Niliacus, the legendary author of the "Hieroglyphica," a work that attempted to explain Egyptian symbols through a Greek lens.</note><-

<summary>This page concludes the first book of the treatise by explaining how the crocodile's body and tail serve as symbols for the sunset and darkness/death, respectively. It emphasizes the perceived physical power and reproductive habits of the animal as the basis for these meanings.</summary>

<keywords>crocodile, sunset, darkness, death, Horapollo, Hieroglyphica, symbolism, natural history</keywords>

# Of the Ancient and Sacredly Esteemed
# Egyptian Priest Horapollo of
## Nilopolis / concerning the symbols of sacred
## writing / The Second Book.

->God.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an eight-pointed star enclosed within a square frame.</image-desc>

Now that the first book has ended, I will bring forth further things in the second and display the true meanings. First, I set down those <term>hieroglyphs</term><note>The German text uses "warzeichen," literally "truth-signs" or "omens," to describe the Egyptian symbols.</note> that do not have their explanation elsewhere. Among these is the star, by which they signify God.

->Night.<-

At times, Night is also indicated with a star.

->Time.<-

Time is also occasionally signified by them with a star.

->Human soul.<-

Likewise, with this image of a star, they wish at times to indicate the soul of a human—specifically, of a man.

->Equinox of day and night in Autumn.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing two human feet and lower legs standing straight and parallel on a ground line, enclosed in a square frame.</image-desc>

They paint two human feet that stand stiff and parallel to signify the equality of day and night <note>The autumnal equinox, when day and night are of equal length.</note>, which occurs at the time of Autumn.

->Virtuous speech.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a human head and neck positioned above a heart, enclosed in a square frame.</image-desc>

They paint a heart at a throat <note>German: *Schlund*; referring to the gullet or esophagus.</note>; with this, they wish to give to understand the speech of a virtuous man.

<meta>catchword: Stomach.</meta>

# The Second Book of the Ancient and Holy Esteemed Egyptian Priest Horapollo of Nilopolis, Concerning the Symbols of Holy Writing.

### God.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an eight-pointed star within a square frame.</image-desc>

Now that the first book has ended, I will bring forth further symbols in the second and show their truest meanings. First, I shall set down those signs that have no other explanation <note>Referring to symbols whose meanings are considered primary or self-evident in this tradition.</note>. Among these is the **Star**, through which they signify **God**.

### Night.

At times, **Night** was also represented with a **Star**.

### Time.

**Time** was occasionally signified by them with a **Star** as well.

### The Soul of a Man.

Likewise, with this same image of a **Star**, they wish at times to indicate the **soul of a human**, specifically that of a **man**. <note>In ancient Egyptian thought, stars were often associated with the souls of the deceased, particularly justified individuals or royalty.</note>

---

### The Autumnal Equinox.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing a pair of human feet standing parallel and upright on a patch of ground.</image-desc>

Two **human feet** that stand stiffly and evenly <note>In a symmetrical or parallel pose.</note> are painted to signify the equality of day and night <term>Equinox</term> which occurs during the **autumn** season.

---

### Pious Speech.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a human head with a protruding tongue or throat connected to a heart symbol below it.</image-desc>

Inside a **throat** <note>original: *schlund*, meaning the gullet or maw</note> they paint a **Heart**; they wish thereby to make understood the **speech of a pious man**. <note>This reflects the ancient belief that the heart was the seat of intelligence and morality, and that true speech must proceed directly from it.</note>

<summary>This page opens the second book of Horapollo's Hieroglyphica, introducing the star as a multi-layered symbol for God, time, and the soul, alongside anatomical symbols for the equinox and piety.</summary>
<keywords>Horapollo, Hieroglyphics, Star symbol, God, Night, Time, Human Soul, Autumnal Equinox, Heart, Pious Speech</keywords>

--- Page 846 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded with descriptions of symbols for God, the soul, and the equinox. It ended with the catchword "Magen" (Stomach), which is the first entry on this page, continuing the anatomical series of hieroglyphs.</meta>

<page-num>cxij</page-num>
->**Signs of Holy Scripture**<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a human finger pointing upwards, enclosed in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

### Stomach.

To signify a human **stomach**, they also paint a **finger**. <note>In this symbolic tradition, certain body parts or gestures were thought to correspond to internal organs or their functions.</note>

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a hand covering male genitalia, enclosed in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

### Temperance.

They represent restraint and **temperance** by a painted **male member** that is covered and concealed by a **hand**.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a poppy flower with its stem and a seed capsule, enclosed in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

### Illness.

Through the painting of a **poppy-head** <note>original: "Ölkolbens," literally an oil-bulb, referring to the seed pod of the opium poppy from which oil and medicine were derived</note> or **poppy** blossoms and flowers, they give it to be understood that **illness** is at hand. At this point, I cannot hide that <term>Cälius Calcagninus</term> <note>A 16th-century Italian humanist scholar who wrote on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> uses the <term>Anemone</term> (that is, the **windflower**) instead of the poppy blossom; after it sheds its petals, it also develops a small pod like the oil-poppy. However, instead of illness, he sets down the meaning of **Chastity**. Since I have no **Greek manuscript** <note>original: "Exéplar"</note> at hand, you may choose for yourself what seems best to you, or perhaps accept both according to their respective logic.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a human spinal column (backbone) set against a minimal landscape background with birds, enclosed in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

### Loins and Kidneys.

Whenever they consider the **loins** or **kidneys** as things belonging to **childbirth**, they paint a **backbone**. For according to some sayings, the **seed** <note>Referring to semen.</note> descends from the **brain** down through the backbone and there it reaches maturity.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a bird's beak, identified in the text as a quail's beak, enclosed in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

### Firmness and Security.

**Security** and **firmness** are indicated by a **quail's beak**, for the reason that this bird is not easily injured in that part, nor does it easily rot.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of two men in 16th-century aristocratic dress standing and talking, enclosed in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

### Unity.

When **Princes**, who wear the signs of their power, speak with one another in a comforting and friendly manner, they have painted this to signify **Unity**.

### Confusion.

Where a **confused** or otherwise **turbulent** matter <note>original: "unrhüwige sach," referring to unrest or lack of peace</note> is at hand, they paint an **archer** with a **bow**, who is well-armed and equipped.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a human finger, slightly curved and pointing upwards.</image-desc>

### Measurement.

Also, to signify **measurement**, they paint a **human finger**. <note>A reference to the "digit" or finger-breadth, an ancient unit of measure used across many cultures.</note>

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a sun split vertically in half, positioned above a cluster of seven stars.</image-desc>

### A Bride.

A **divided sun**, painted together with the **seven stars** <note>original: "siben gstirn," commonly referring to the Pleiades constellation</note>, signifies among them a **married woman** or **bride**.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an eagle flying upwards through clouds above a horizon.</image-desc>

### Wind.

To describe **great winds** and **airy weather**, they use an **eagle** that flies toward the **sunrise** <note>original: "Auffganng," meaning the East or the rising sun</note>, or otherwise soars in the air with **outspread wings**.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing thick curls of smoke rising from an unseen source.</image-desc>

### Fire.

**Smoke** that rises toward heaven they take as an indication of **fire**; for where there is smoke, there must also be fire.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a bearded man's head in profile, with two curved horns growing from his forehead.</image-desc>

### Great Work.

Where they wish to indicate **great work** and **labor**, they paint a **man’s head with horns**. <note>Horns were often used in Renaissance symbolism to denote strength, power, or the heavy burden of significant tasks.</note>

### Revenge.

Likewise, when they wish to indicate **revenge** <note>original: "Raach," meaning vengeance or retribution</note>, they paint a **woman's head** with **horns**.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut of a man shown from the waist up, holding a naked sword upright in his hand.</image-desc>

### The Wicked.

When they wish to indicate and signify a **wicked person** <note>original: "Gottlosen menschen," literally a godless human</note>, they paint a **man** visible down to the **navel**, who holds a **drawn, naked sword** in his hand.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut of a "water horse" (hippopotamus) emerged partially from the water.</image-desc>

### Splendor.

To signify **splendor** <note>original: "Glentz," referring to radiance, shine, or brilliance</note>, they paint a **hippopotamus** <note>original: "Wasserroß," literally water-horse; in Renaissance emblem books, the hippopotamus was often associated with time or injustice, but here it represents radiance or prominence</note>.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut of a stag with large antlers leaping across a hilly landscape.</image-desc>

### Long Life.

When someone is to have a **long life**, and they wish to indicate this, they paint a **stag**, which becomes very old and grows a new addition to its **horn** every year, or as some say, pushes out **new horns**. <note>A reference to the annual shedding and regrowth of antlers, which was a common historical symbol for rejuvenation and longevity.</note>

---

<image-desc>Woodcut of a hare leaping through a field while looking backwards over its shoulder.</image-desc>

### Refusal.

Where one will not grant an audience, or wishes to **reject** and **refuse** someone something, they paint a **hare** looking **behind itself**. <note>This likely refers to the hare's keen hearing and its tendency to flee, symbolizing a person who is "turning a back" or already in flight from a request.</note>

---

<image-desc>Woodcut of a dog standing and looking around its shoulder.</image-desc>

### Low Esteem.

When someone is of **low esteem** <note>original: "vnwerd," meaning unworthiness or lack of value</note> and not held in such **regard** among people as he would like to be, they paint a **dog** looking **around itself**.

### Battle.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a crocodile on a riverbank, representing a battle.</image-desc>

To signify a **battle**, in which many have perished, they paint a **crocodile**.

---

### Shedding of Blood.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large flying insect, like a wasp or hornet, representing bloodshed.</image-desc>

A **flying wasp**; wherever they paint it, they wish to give it to be understood as a **great shedding of blood**.

---

### Death.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an owl perched on a tree stump at night under a crescent moon and stars, representing death.</image-desc>

They paint a **night-raven** <note>original: "Nachttrappen"; likely referring to an owl or a nightjar, which were traditionally birds of ill omen</note> when they wish to indicate **death**. For the same falls so unexpectedly upon its young, just as death ambushes humans in an unforeseen manner.

---

### Love Affair.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a rope tied into a complex decorative knot, representing love or a love affair.</image-desc>

A painted **double-knot** <note>original: "zweifelkstrick," referring to a decorative or intricate knot like a "lover's knot"</note> signifies **love**, or as one says, a **love affair** <note>original: "Bülschafft," an archaic term for courtship or a romantic relationship</note>.

---

### Antiquity.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a thick, ornate book with metal clasps, tightly closed, representing antiquity.</image-desc>

When they wish to signify that something is utterly and **ancient**, they paint a **prayer book** <note>original: "Betthbuch," literally a book for prayers</note> that is **closed and secured**.

---

### Siege.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a flight of stairs or a scaling ladder, representing a siege.</image-desc>

Whenever a **stairway** <note>here likely referring to a scaling ladder used in warfare</note> has some height and is prominent, they wish to represent a **siege** through it.

<header>Signs of Sacred Writing</header>

### Poetry.

<image-desc>A woodcut of two fingers (index and middle) pointing upwards, with letters A through G labeled on the tips and joints.</image-desc>

To signify **poetry**, they paint two fingers marked with **seven letters**. <note>The seven letters likely refer to the seven vowels of the Greek alphabet, which were sometimes associated with the music of the spheres or poetic harmony.</note>

### Coarse People.

By **coarse, unrefined churls** <note>original: "Knollen," literally "clods" or "lumps," a derogatory term for the uneducated or boorish</note> they also wish to signify that the more wonderful a thing is, the more it differs from what came before.

### Peril of Death.

With this same sign <note>referring to the fingers mentioned above</note>, they wish to give the **peril of death** to be understood.

---

### Ten Flat Lines or Strokes.

<image-desc>A woodcut box containing ten horizontal parallel lines.</image-desc>

By drawing one line or stroke over the other, they wish to signify **ten flat strokes**.

---

### A Paternal Inheritance.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing a swallow-like bird standing on the ground near a small mound of earth.</image-desc>

When great wealth and riches come to boys as a **paternal inheritance**, and they wish to signify this, they paint a **swallow**. For when the swallow is about to die, it first lays itself in the mud to make little lumps <note>referring to the mud pellets used in nest building</note> so its children or young can build their nests.

---

### Widow.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a bird, likely a turtledove, perched on the ground.</image-desc>

For a **widow**, or a woman who never takes another husband until her death after the passing of her first man, they paint and compare her to a **turtledove**. For this bird also never pairs again after the loss of its mate.

---

### Weak Man.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a long-tailed rodent, identified in the text as a "Nile mouse."</image-desc>

A **weak man** who requires the help of others is indicated by a painted **Nile mouse** <note>original: "Nilmauß"; in ancient lore, this often referred to the ichneumon or mongoose, known for its cleverness in fighting snakes</note>. When it encounters its enemy, the adder, it does not attack it immediately; instead, it gathers many of its kind together with its chirping, and only then attacks the enemy when it deems itself strong enough.

---

### To Drive Away Ants.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a flowering plant identified as "marjoram" or "oregano."</image-desc>

As soon as you lay **marjoram** <note>original: "wolgemütt," an archaic name for Origanum vulgare, known today as wild marjoram or oregano</note> upon an anthill, they all flee from it. Therefore, when they wish to show that this creature is driven away, or how it may be driven away, they paint marjoram.

->Enemy against Enemy.<-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration showing a scorpion and a crocodile facing each other in a desert landscape.</image-desc>

When they wish to signify two mortal enemies who have come upon one another, they paint a **scorpion** and a **crocodile** fighting. For when they clash, usually both of them perish. If they wish to indicate that one of them prevailed and finished off his enemy: if it happened quickly, they paint the **crocodile** on top; if it proceeded slowly, they paint the **scorpion** on top. This is because the crocodile is swift <note>The crocodile was often associated with sudden, lightning-fast strikes despite its size.</note>, whereas the scorpion is slow.

---

->A Brave Woman.<-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration of a small animal, possibly a weasel, on a patch of grass.</image-desc>

To signify a bold and brave woman, they paint a **weasel**. For this creature endures the male’s member even though it is made of bone. <note>This refers to the *baculum* or os penis found in weasels; medieval and Renaissance lore suggested this made mating painful for the female, thus making her "brave" for enduring it.</note>

---

->A Destructive Person.<-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration of a pig or sow standing on a small plot of land.</image-desc>

When they paint a **sow**, they wish to indicate that an evil, destructive person is at hand; for the sow ruins and uproots everything in its path.

---

->Immoderate Anger.<-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration of a lion striking its small cubs with its tail.</image-desc>

To indicate such a fierce anger and embittered spirit that it brings on a sickness from its very poison, they paint a **lion** striking its young with its tail. The elder lion does this out of its own wrath; the young are struck for the reason that their limbs, when rubbed together by the blows, produce heat <note>original: "sewi," likely an archaic form referring to the "sap" or vital heat generated by friction</note>.

---

->An Old Singer.<-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration showing a swan swimming in water.</image-desc>

When they wish to signify an **old singer**, they paint a **swan**; for when it grows old, it sings most sweetly. <note>The "swan song" is a classical motif, suggesting that the bird sings most beautifully just before its death.</note>

---

->Where Woman and Man Have to Do with Each Other.<-

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut illustration showing two crows, one perched and one in flight.</image-desc>

To indicate that a man and woman are joined together <note>This can refer to marriage or sexual intercourse</note>, they paint **two crows**; for these birds relate to one another just like human beings do.

## Enemy against Enemy.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a scorpion and a crocodile in combat on the ground.</image-desc>

When they wish to represent two mortal enemies who have encountered one another, they paint a **scorpion** and a **crocodile** fighting. For when they clash, they generally both perish. If they further wish to indicate that one of them prevailed and finished off his enemy: if it happened quickly, they paint the crocodile on top; if it happened slowly, they paint the scorpion on top. This is because the crocodile is a fast creature, whereas the scorpion is slow.

---

## A Brave Woman.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a small, slender four-legged mammal, possibly a weasel or ermine.</image-desc>

To represent a bold and brave woman, they paint a **weasel**. For this animal endures the male’s member, even though it is made of bone. <note>In ancient and medieval natural history, it was a common belief that certain animals, like the weasel or the wolf, possessed a "baculum" or os penis (a literal bone in the male anatomy), which was used here as a metaphor for the female's endurance or strength.</note>

---

## A Destructive Person.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a pig or sow standing near a patch of grass and water.</image-desc>

When they paint a **sow**, they wish to indicate that an evil, destructive person is at hand, for the sow roots up and destroys everything in its path.

---

## Unseemly Anger.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a lion standing over its young cubs, with its tail raised and flicking.</image-desc>

To signify such fierce anger and a bitter spirit that it brings on a sickness like poison, they paint a **lion** striking its cubs with its tail. The old lion does this because of his rage, and the cubs are struck because their own limbs, when rubbed together by the blows, are said to produce fire. <note>This refers to an ancient legend that lion cubs were born "dead" or motionless and were awakened by the father's roar or by the friction and heat created by his tail.</note>

---

## An Old Singer.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a swan swimming in the water.</image-desc>

When they wish to signify an old singer, they paint a **swan**, for when that bird grows old, it sings most beautifully. <note>This is the origin of the "swan song" trope—the belief that the swan, normally silent, sings a beautiful melody just before death.</note>

---

## Where Man and Woman Have to Do with Each Other.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of two birds, likely crows or ravens, perched together on a branch.</image-desc>

To show that a man and a woman are united or have business with one another, they paint two **crows**. For these birds [behave] toward each other just like humans. <note>Crows and ravens were often used as symbols of marital fidelity in the Renaissance because they were believed to mate for life.</note>

<page-num>118</page-num>
<header>Symbols of Sacred Writing</header>

### One who is sick from the heat of the sun.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a fish jumping out of the water towards a rocky shoreline under a sky with a sun or clouds.</image-desc>

There is a fish in Egypt that they call the <term>Cantharum</term> <note>original: "Cantharum"; likely referring to the Black Sea Bream or a similar species described in ancient bestiaries</note>, which is blinded by the radiance of the sun, so much so that it must die. Therefore, when they suspect a person is sick from the heat of the sun, they paint such a fish to indicate his suffering.

---

### Barrenness.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a donkey or mule with a pack saddle standing in a landscape with a mountain in the background.</image-desc>

To signify a barren woman, they paint a **female mule**, for she is barren for this reason: her <term>womb</term> <note>original: "beermütter"</note> lies crosswise and tangled within her body.

---

### When a woman gives birth to a daughter or a son.

<image-desc>Woodcut of an ox or bull facing to the left.</image-desc>

With this, they wish to make it understood that a woman has born a daughter if they paint an **ox** that turns its head toward the left side. However, if the woman in labor has born a son, they indicate it with an ox that turns its head toward the right side. The reason for this: the <term>bull</term> <note>original: "Farz"</note> or ox, when he has leaped upon the cow, indicates what the offspring shall be—a heifer or a bullock—by his dismounting. For if he dismounts toward the left side, it will be a heifer; if toward the right, a bullock.

---

### Wasps.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a horse carcass lying on the ground with insects (wasps) swarming around it.</image-desc>

When they wish to signify **wasps**, they paint the **carcass of a horse**, for many wasps are born out of such remains. <note>This refers to the ancient theory of "spontaneous generation," specifically the belief that wasps or bees were born from the decaying flesh of large animals.</note>

---

### A woman whose pregnancy has failed.

<image-desc>Woodcut showing a horse and a wolf interacting in a landscape.</image-desc>

When a woman’s birth has failed <note>implying a miscarriage or a difficult labor</note>, they paint a **mare** treading upon a **wolf**; for the mare is corrupted not only if she treads upon a wolf, but even if she treads upon its tracks.

---

### A forewarned person who takes care.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a bird perched on a branch, holding a sprig of laurel in its beak.</image-desc>

When someone is warned of an evil or a sickness, and advice is given to him by the gods or doctors as to how he might turn away his misfortune, and he follows that advice; they then paint a **magpie** or a **jay** <note>original: "Häzen oder Azlen"</note> that carries a small **laurel branch** in its beak. For this bird, when it is sick, places laurel leaves in its nest, from which it becomes healthy again.
