<page-num>cxix</page-num>
<header>The Second Book of Horapollo.</header>

### Gnats.

<image-desc>A square woodcut depicting worms or larvae on and in the ground.</image-desc>

To indicate that many **gnats** <note>original: "Schnacken"; in this period, the term could refer to gnats, mosquitoes, or crane flies</note> are at hand, they paint many worms, for gnats grow out of those same worms.

---

### A kind man who is provoked to anger.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a dove standing on the ground, with its tail feathers fanned upwards and its head turned back towards its tail.</image-desc>

When they wish to indicate someone who is by nature gentle and without anger, yet is moved to wrath and reproach by others, they paint a **dove** that raises and ruffles its feathers at the rear. The reason is that this bird has that which moves it to anger in its hindquarters <note>the text reflects an ancient belief that the gallbladder or the source of "choler" (anger) in doves was located near the tail rather than the liver</note>.

---

### A person who dwells securely in the cities.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an eagle flying with a large, heavy stone clutched in its talons.</image-desc>

To signify a man who dwells securely in cities <note>original: "Stätten"; can also mean "fixed places" or "towns"</note>, they paint an **eagle** carrying a large **pebble** <note>original: "kißling stein"</note> in its talons. For the eagle carries stones into its nest so that it is weighed down and made more secure against the wind.

---

### A weak man who is pursued.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a long-eared owl (Scops or Horned owl) perched on a branch above a horse that is walking or running.</image-desc>

The **horned owl** <note>original: "Schleyereüle"; though literally "Barn Owl," the text specifies it has ear-tufts like ears on its head, indicating a Long-eared or Scops owl</note>, which has little feathers standing up on its head just like ears—this same bird they paint together with a **horse** when they wish to signify a faint-hearted, weak person who flees from one who hunts him. For as soon as this bird catches sight of a horse, it flies away.

---

### One who calls for the heart's help in vain.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing an owl and a smaller bird, likely a sparrow, perched together on a gnarled tree branch.</image-desc>

When they paint a **great owl** <note>original: "Huhu"</note> or owl together with a **sparrow**, they wish to signify a person who seeks help from his own heart <note>likely meaning seeking help from one's own kind or a supposed protector</note> but finds none there. For when the sparrow flees from the bird-catcher, it retreats to the owl, where it stands in just as much danger.

---

### A weak person who blushes in flight.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a bat with its wings fully spread.</image-desc>

The **bat**, although it has no feathers, nevertheless flies. Thus, when they wish to describe someone who is too weak, yet has blushed <note>original: "erröthet"; here implying shame or a physical flush from the exertion of fleeing</note> with flight before his enemy, they paint the bat.

<header>cxv Symbols of the Sacred Script</header>

## A woman who suckles and nourishes well.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a bat-like creature with a human woman's torso, featuring prominent breasts and large wings.</image-desc>

They depict the **bat** to represent a woman who suckles and nourishes well. This is because, among all other creatures that fly, the bat alone has teeth and breasts <note>original: "dutten"; an archaic term for teats or breasts. Ancient natural history often grouped bats with birds because they fly, but noted their mammalian features as unique "signs."</note>.

---

## A dancer.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a bird, identified in the text as a turtledove, standing on a small patch of ground.</image-desc>

When they wish to represent a person who has a desire for dancing and piping <note>original: "Pfeyffen"; refers to playing a flute or pipe</note>, they depict a **turtledove**. This is because that bird very gladly hears piping and loves to watch dancing.

---

## A discreet person.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a grasshopper or locust in a landscape with grass and plants.</image-desc>

To indicate a **discreet** and secretive person, they depict a **grasshopper**. For the grasshopper does not sing with its mouth, but rather chirps quite lovely sounds from its shoulders.

---

## A solitary, stern King.

<image-desc>Woodcut of an eagle with its wings partially spread, perched and looking towards the right.</image-desc>

To indicate a **solitary**, harsh King who has no mercy for any poor evildoer, they depict him with an **eagle**. The eagle nests in the wilderness <note>original: "einöde"</note> and soars into the air higher than any other feathered creature.

---

## Eternal renewal.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a phoenix bird sitting in a nest of rising flames.</image-desc>

When they wish to show that a change or renewal is at hand—one which revives those things that are meant to endure—they depict the bird called the **Phoenix**. For when it appears, it is like a restoration of all things. The Phoenix grows or is created in this manner: When the old, solitary Phoenix wishes to die, it hurls itself out of the air so violently and strongly that it falls to the ground and wounds itself. From the blood that it sheds, a young Phoenix is born. As soon as its feathers have grown, the young bird, along with the old one, flies to **Thebes** <note>original: "Thebe"; likely referring to Heliopolis, the "City of the Sun," which was often confused or associated with Thebes in Renaissance hermetic texts</note>, the City of the Sun in Egypt. There, as soon as the sun rises, the old one dies. After this death, the young one flies back to its homeland from whence it came. Following this, the Egyptian priests bury the old one who has died.

---

## The love of children toward their parents.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a stork standing on one leg among small plants.</image-desc>

To indicate **filial love** <note>original: "kindtliche liebe"</note> toward parents, they depict a **stork**. For as soon as the stork is raised by its parents, it never leaves them again; it remains with them until death and provides nourishment for them when they are feeble <note>original: "vnuermöglichen"; meaning those who are physically unable to care for themselves</note>.

<header>From the second book of Horapollo.</header>

<image-desc>A woodcut of a coiled snake or viper.</image-desc>

->An aggressive or man-hating woman.<-

A woman who is obedient and willing to her husband only in bed, but otherwise so rebellious that she even plots against his life, is depicted as a **viper**. This is because when the male mates with her, he places his head into her mouth; but eventually, when the male thrusts his head into her throat, she bites it off and kills him <note>This reflects an ancient biological myth about the viper (Vipera aspis) recorded by writers like Pliny the Elder, suggesting the female kills the male during mating.</note>.

->Children who are rebellious toward their mother.<-

With this same animal, they also wish to indicate children who cause their mother suffering and are rebellious against her. This is because the young of this **viper** do not come into the world through the proper place like other animals; instead, they tear open the mother’s body and thus come to light through her death.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a Basilisk, a mythical creature with a crown-like crest on its head and a serpent-like body with wings.</image-desc>

->A person who speaks ill of everyone.<-

An evil mouth that has a literal sickness for speaking ill of many people is represented by the image of a **Basilisk**. For that creature kills the nearest snakes simply with its hissing <note>original: "pfeysen"; refers to the deadly breath or hissing sound associated with the legendary king of serpents.</note>.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a salamander in a landscape with water and flames.</image-desc>

->A burnt person.<-

The **Salamander** lives in fire and water, and also perishes in both <note>original: "Kompt auch in beiden umb." While folklore often claimed salamanders were fireproof, this text suggests they are uniquely defined by these elements to the point of perishing in them, making them a symbol for one consumed by fire.</note>. Therefore, they paint it to signify a burnt person.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a mole emerging from the ground next to molehills.</image-desc>

->A blind person.<-

They paint a **mole** to signify a blind person; for the mole has no eyes, and it sees nothing else besides.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing an ant on the ground and a detached bat wing above it.</image-desc>

->One who is away from home for a long time.<-

When someone is away from home for a long time and has no regard for returning, they paint an **ant** and a **bat’s wing**. This is because if one places a bat's wing upon an anthill, no ant will ever enter it again.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a beaver on a riverbank near a tree stump, looking back at its hindquarters.</image-desc>

->One who does harm to himself.<-

When the **beaver** is hunted, he bites off his own testicles <note>original: "geylin"; an archaic term for testicles. This refers to the "Castor and Pollux" myth where the beaver, hunted for its medicinal castoreum, castrates itself to escape hunters.</note> and throws them to the hunters, leaving them behind him. Therefore, wherever someone causes himself harm, they paint a beaver there.

In early modern German, this could refer to either a grasshopper or a cricket.</note>, because it never sings with its mouth; rather, it chirps lovely sounds out from its shoulders <note>This describes stridulation, where the insect rubs its wings or legs together, which was historically perceived as singing from the back or shoulders.</note>.

To indicate filial love toward parents, they depict a **stork**. For as soon as the stork has been raised by its parents, it never leaves them; it stays with them until death and provides nourishment for those who are infirm <note>The "Law of the Stork" (Antipelargosis) was a common classical and Renaissance belief that young storks repaid their parents by carrying them and feeding them in their old age.</note>.

<header>From the Second Book of Horapollo.</header>

### A Man-Hating Woman.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration depicting a coiled serpent or viper.</image-desc>

To represent a woman who is obedient and willing to her husband only in bed, but otherwise so rebellious that she even seeks to take his life, they depict a **viper** <note>original: "Vippernater." In Renaissance lore, the female viper was believed to kill her mate during conception.</note>. For when the male mates with her, he places his head into her mouth; but at the end, as the male thrusts his head into her mouth, she bites it off and kills him.

### Children who are Rebellious against their Mother.

With this same animal, they wish to indicate children who cause their mother suffering and are rebellious against her. For the young of these vipers do not come into the world at the proper time like other animals; instead, they tear open the mother's body and thus come to light through her death <note>This ancient biological myth suggested that because the female viper killed the male, the young "avenged" the father by eating their way out of the mother's womb.</note>.

### A person who speaks ill of everyone.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of a winged basilisk, a dragon-like creature with a long tail.</image-desc>

An evil tongue that has a persistent habit of speaking ill of many people—as if it were a sickness—is indicated by the image of a **basilisk**. For this creature, with its whistling <note>original: "pfeysen"; refers to the deadly hissing of the basilisk which was said to kill at a distance.</note> alone, destroys all the nearby snakes.

### A burned person.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of a lizard-like salamander sitting amidst flames.</image-desc>

The **salamander** lives in fire and water, yet also perishes in both; therefore, they depict it to signify a burned person <note>The salamander was famously believed to be fireproof or to live within flames, but here the author notes the paradox of its destruction.</note>.

### A Blind Person.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of a mole standing on a small mound of earth.</image-desc>

They depict a **mole** <note>original: "Maulwerff."</note> to signify a blind person; for the mole has no eyes, and besides this, it sees nothing at all.

### One who is long away from home.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration depicting a bat's wing hovering over what appears to be an ant or an ant-hill.</image-desc>

If someone is away from home for a long time and has no intention of returning, they depict an **ant** and a **bat's wing** <note>original: "Flädermauß fettich"; *fettich* is an archaic term for wing.</note>; for if one lays a bat's wing upon an anthill, no ant will ever enter it again.

### One who does himself harm.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of a beaver by a stream, depicted in the act of biting its own hindquarters.</image-desc>

When the **beaver** is hunted, he bites off his own testicles <note>original: "geylin." This refers to the beaver's scent glands, or castoreum, which were highly prized for medicine. Folklore held that the beaver would castrate itself to offer the hunters what they wanted in exchange for its life.</note> and throws them to the hunters, leaving them behind him. Therefore, where someone does himself harm [to save his life], they depict a beaver.

<page-num>xxij</page-num>
<header>Symbols of Sacred Writing</header>

### A Father who reluctantly has his Son as his Heir.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a man in a landscape chasing an ape. The ape carries one young one in its arms while another follows behind on foot.</image-desc>

The ape always gives birth to two young at once. One of these she hates, but the other she loves dearly. The one she loves, she constantly carries about, hugging and pressing it so closely to herself that she accidentally smothers it to death. Meanwhile, the one she hates is left to run behind her; because it is left to fend for itself, it is nourished and survives <note>This was a popular medieval and Renaissance fable about the "over-attentive" mother ape whose misplaced affection leads to the death of her favorite child.</note>. Therefore, they depict an ape with a young one running behind it when they wish to represent a son who has inherited from his father, even though the father never intended for him to receive the inheritance.

### One who wishes to hide his shame.

When an ape urinates, it hides its urine. For this reason, they depict an ape when they wish to represent someone who conceals his own disgrace or shame.

### Sharp-hearing.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a goat standing on a small mound of earth.</image-desc>

To represent a person who possesses a sharp sense of hearing, they depict a **goat** <note>original: "Geyß."</note>. For this animal is believed to hear not only through its ears, but also through its neck and throat.

### Fickle.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a long, serpent-like creature with a small head and tail, representing the "Schlangen Hyena."</image-desc>

To describe a fickle person who does not remain steadfast in one opinion—but is now joyful and bold, then despondent and fearful—they represent him with the **Serpent Hyena** <note>original: "Schlangen Hyena." This refers to the ancient (and incorrect) belief that the hyena could change its sex at will, making it a symbol of instability or deceit.</note>. For this creature is said to be now female and then male.

### When the Superior is slain by the Inferior.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of two animals, one on top of the other. The top animal appears to be a hyena, and the bottom one is a spotted leopard or panther.</image-desc>

When one wishes to show that the superior is overcome by the inferior, they depict two hides: one of a hyena and the other of a **leopard** <note>original: "Pard."</note>. This is because the leopard's skin loses its hair <note>original: "harrt sich"; likely "haart sich," meaning to shed or go bald.</note> when it is near the hyena's skin, while the hyena's skin remains unchanged.

### One who overcomes his enemy.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a knight in plate armor holding a spear, standing over a slain spotted animal, likely a hyena.</image-desc>

He who overcomes his enemy—the victorious one—is depicted with a hyena on his right side. However, he who is overcome by his enemy has the hyena on his left side. The reason for this is that when this animal is pursued by an enemy and turns itself toward the right side, it kills the pursuer; but if it turns toward the left side, it must suffer and will perish.

<header>Of the Second Book of Horapollo.</header>

### An unlucky soul who endures it all.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a hyena's spotted skin hanging from a tree branch in a simple landscape.</image-desc>

**W**hen it is said that someone carries or wears a hyena skin or hide about them, they are able to pass through the midst of enemies unharmed and without any worry. Therefore, when they wish to represent a person who is treated as a "Jack-I-care-naught" <note>original: "Hans ich acht sein nitt." This is a period idiom for someone who is disregarded, ignored, or treated with indifference by others.</note>, yet to whom no misfortune can be done, they paint a hyena skin.

---

### That one might outwit his enemy.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a wolf in a field, looking back towards its shortened tail.</image-desc>

**I**f someone gets the better of his enemy without special harm—prevailing and ensuring that the enemy can do him no damage—they paint a wolf with a docked tail. For when the wolf perceives that hunters are in pursuit of him, he casts away the hair and the tip of his tail <note>Ancient natural histories often claimed the tip of a wolf's tail contained a tuft of hair with aphrodisiac or magical properties, which the wolf would bite off if it felt it was about to be captured.</note>.

---

### To be secretly afraid.

<image-desc>A woodcut showing a wolf standing in a landscape with a small round stone depicted in the air above it.</image-desc>

**I**f someone is anxious about a secret danger that might befall them, to indicate this, they paint a stone and a wolf. For the wolf fears neither iron nor spear, but only stones. To prove this does not take much: let one throw a stone at it. Furthermore, if a wolf were hit by a stone, worms would grow in the wound <note>original: "würff," likely referring to the site of the hit or the resulting sore.</note> so that he must perish.

---

### Punishment by fire.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a lion being threatened by a hand holding a flaming torch.</image-desc>

**I**f someone is to be punished with fire or burned, they paint a lion and several torches. For the lion fears nothing worse than a burning torch; one cannot otherwise tame or restrain him except with such as these.

---

### A sick man who heals himself.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a lion devouring a monkey.</image-desc>

**S**hould the lion have the "shivers" <note>original: "ritten," an archaic term for a fever or ague.</note> and he is able to get an ape to eat, he is immediately made healthy. Therefore, where they wish to indicate a sick person who helps himself, they paint a lion eating an ape.

---

### One who is tamed by misfortune.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a bull tied to a wild fig tree by its neck.</image-desc>

**W**henever a proud fellow is so overtaken by great misfortune that he is tamed and well-subdued, they paint a bull tied to a wild fig tree. For even if a bull is wild and bellowing, when tied to this tree, he becomes entirely tame.

<page-num>114</page-num>
<header>Symbols of Sacred Scripture</header>

<image-desc>A woodcut of an ox or bull with one of its front legs tied up or hobbled.</image-desc>

->**One who is suspected of unchastity.**<-

**I**f someone is slandered as though he does not lead a particularly modest or chaste life, they paint an ox with its right knee tied; for when bound in this way, he will not mount a cow. Otherwise, the ox is always presented to represent temperance <note>original: "mässigkeit"</note>, for after the cows are pregnant, he never approaches them again.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut showing a flock of sheep or goats grazing on a hillside.</image-desc>

->**A shepherd who neglects the livestock.**<-

**A**n undiligent shepherd or farm manager <term>Meyer: a bailiff or overseer of a manor’s livestock</term> who neglects the animals, such as sheep and goats, is indicated by a painted herd of said livestock eating Thunderwort <note>original: "Dounerwurtz." Likely referring to a species of Hellebore or perhaps a local plant believed to cause dehydration in livestock.</note> in a pasture; for if the livestock eats of it, they die of thirst.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut of a crocodile with its mouth wide open.</image-desc>

->**Eating.**<-

**T**o indicate that a person is eating, they paint a crocodile with its mouth agape.

->**A lazy and predatory person.**<-

**T**he crocodile is a predatory worm <note>term: "wurm" was a common Early Modern German descriptor for any creeping creature, including reptiles and dragons</note>, and if you but touch it with a feather of the Ibis bird, it can no longer move. Therefore, when they wish to indicate a lazy, greedy person, they paint the worm with an Ibis feather on its head.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut of a lioness standing in profile.</image-desc>

->**A woman who has brought forth only one birth.**<-

**T**he lioness never conceives a second time; therefore, when they wish to indicate a woman who has only experienced one birth, they paint a lioness.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut showing a bear licking a small, unformed lump (her cub).</image-desc>

->**A misshapen birth.**<-

**W**here a misshapen child is born, who only becomes handsome and well-formed as he grows up, they signify this by painting a mother bear giving birth. For at first, she gives birth to a packed-together clump of blood <note>original: "plütknolle"</note> that is entirely formless, which she then licks and brings into the shape of the animal with her tongue.

---

<image-desc>A woodcut of an elephant standing near a tree, its trunk raised.</image-desc>

->**A brave and resourceful person who provides useful things.**<-

**T**o indicate a brave person who provides useful and good inventions, they paint an elephant with an extended snout or trunk <term>ranß: an archaic term for a trunk or proboscis</term>; for with its trunk it examines <note>original: "erschmückt," here meaning to feel out or investigate</note> all things, and thus it perceives whatever pleases it.

It notably features the "licking into shape" myth regarding bear cubs and the crocodile’s supposed paralysis by Ibis feathers.</summary>

<page-num>115</page-num>
<header>From the Second Book of Horus.</header>

### A king who flees from folly.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a sheep and a stag facing each other.</image-desc>

The stag, as soon as he catches sight of the ram, flees from him; therefore, when they wish to indicate that a ruler or king flees from folly <note>original: "torheit"</note>, they paint these two animals.

### A king who hates useless chatter.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting an elephant and a pig.</image-desc>

To indicate that a king hates roguish fools and useless chatter, they paint an elephant together with a sow. For the elephant flees from the squealing <note>original: "kürren"</note> of the sow.

### One who flees quickly without cause.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a stag leaping away from a coiled snake.</image-desc>

A good runner who leaps away quickly, yet flees without cause, is indicated by the depiction of a viper and a stag. For the stag flees as soon as he sees a viper.

### One who is anxious regarding his grave.

<image-desc>A woodcut depicting a stag scraping the ground with its head to bury its antlers or teeth.</image-desc>

When someone applies great diligence to how he wishes to be buried, and also spends much cost upon the funeral, they represent him by painting a stag, who by nature scrapes in and buries his teeth <note>While the text says "zån" (teeth), in the context of stag lore, this refers to their antlers, which were mythologically believed to be hidden by the animals when shed.</note> that have fallen out.

### Self-awareness.

The elephant knows for what purpose humans so gladly use his teeth <note>meaning his ivory tusks</note>, and how gladly they seek his life for their sake; therefore, he buries them when they fall out of his mouth.

### A good old age.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a crow or raven standing on the ground.</image-desc>

They paint a crow when they wish to indicate that a person has reached his old age and has lived out his days. For the crow lives a hundred Egyptian years; however, one year among us is reckoned as four years among the Egyptians <note>This refers to an early misconception regarding the Sothic cycle or the Egyptian "short year" often discussed by Renaissance humanists.</note>.

### Hiding malice.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a spotted leopard or panther (Pard) stalking forward.</image-desc>

One who undertakes to hide his malice and cunning <note>original: "boßheit vnd list"</note>, and so to disguise it that it does not become known to others, they wish to indicate with a painted leopard <term>Parden: a historical term for a leopard or panther</term>. For that animal hunts other beasts solely through cunning so that he may catch them, one after another, so that the others do not become aware of how fast and well he can run; thus, remaining ignorant, they worry or guard themselves less against him in the pasture.

<page-num>cxxxi</page-num>
<header>Signs of Sacred Scripture</header>

### Deception by Flatterers.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a man in a tunic playing a pipe to lure a stag towards him.</image-desc>

If someone is seduced and deceived through fawning and flattery, they depict a stag with a piper; for the stag allows itself to be fooled and enticed by the sound and the piping, forgets itself, and is thus captured.

### Foreknowledge of a Good Harvest and an Abundance of Wine.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a hoopoe bird perched on a branch.</image-desc>

They paint a hoopoe when they wish to predict that much wine will grow and the autumn harvest or vintage will be good. For when the hoopoe begins to sing before the grapevines are dry <note>meaning before the buds have withered or the vines have matured</note>, it is a certain sign of a good supply, and there will be much wine that year.

### When Someone Becomes Sick from Eating Grapes.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a bird standing on a stone wall, pecking at a plant.</image-desc>

If someone takes medicine and wishes to heal themselves because they have eaten too many grapes which cause them pain, they paint a hoopoe eating rue <note>original: "Maurrautten," referring to herb-of-grace or wall-rue, historically used as an antidote</note>; for when this same bird feels sick from eating grapes, it swallows this herb and recovers.

### Vigilance Against Enemies.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of three cranes; the one in the foreground stands on one leg, holding a stone in its raised claw, symbolizing vigilance.</image-desc>

If someone acts with careful vigilance <note>original: "Gwarsame"</note> to escape his enemies and flee their traps, they paint a crane on watch <note>The original OCR reads "Kranck" (sick), but the context and image confirm it is "Kranich" (crane)</note> to signify him. For this bird keeps watch the whole night, with the guard duty being rotated. <note>In medieval lore, the crane held a stone so that if it fell asleep, the stone would drop and wake it.</note>

### The Violation of Boys.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of two partridges on the ground.</image-desc>

To signify the vice of violating boys <note>original: "Knabenschändung," a historical term for pederasty or sodomy</note>, they paint two partridges; for these birds [commit this act] with one another if they lose their females.

### An Elderly Person Suffering from Hunger.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an eagle with a severely curved upper beak that prevents it from opening its mouth to eat.</image-desc>

Where one wishes to represent an elderly person suffering the distress of hunger, they paint an eagle with a crooked beak. For this bird’s beak curves so much in old age that it can no longer eat, and thus it must die of hunger.

<header>From the Second Book of Horus. 127</header>

### A constantly restless, angry person.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a crow or raven standing on its nest in a tree.</image-desc>

A person who is constantly angry and restless, so much so that they cannot eat with ease or peace, is compared by them to the **crow**, which they depict with its young; for as long as she broods over them, she is perpetually restless and fierce.

---

### One who knows Divine mysteries.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a crane flying high above the ground and a fence.</image-desc>

The **crane** flies so high that it touches the clouds, let alone sees them; they depict this bird in flight to represent a man who possesses knowledge and investigation of **Divine mysteries**. <note>The crane was often a symbol of vigilance and high-mindedness in Renaissance emblem books.</note>

---

### Casting out one's children due to poverty.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an eagle in a nest atop a rocky outcrop, with one chick remaining and two others falling away or being cast out.</image-desc>

The **eagle** lays three eggs; it breaks two and throws them out of the nest, brooding only one. The reason for this is that at that same time it molts, so that its feathers fall out and its claws fail, and it cannot nourish many young at once. They depict this bird brooding in this manner to indicate those who, out of **poverty** and inability, must cast out their children and give them away into service. <note>This "natural history" fact was a common medieval myth used to explain the hardships of parenting and the necessity of apprenticeships or domestic service for the poor.</note>

---

### One who walks slowly, dragging their feet.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a camel walking across a landscape.</image-desc>

When someone drags their feet and is unwilling to move from a spot, they depict a **camel** to represent them; for this animal, among all others, crooks and bends its limbs strangely when it walks.

---

### A sharp, lustful face.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a frog sitting on the ground near a tree and a body of water.</image-desc>

The **frog** has no blood except in its eyes; and those who have blood in their eyes are considered shameless. Therefore, **Homer** says in the first book of the *Destruction of Troy*: <note>original: "zerſtörung Troie." This refers to the Iliad. The quote is Achilles' famous insult to Agamemnon.</note>

> Wine-guzzler, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer,
> Drunk, shameless, and cowardly before the sword of war.
> <note>original: "Weinſauffer/ hunds aug/ hirtzen hertz/ Voll/ vnuerſchämpt/ zag in kriegs ſchwertz."</note>

And for this reason, they depict the creature of a **frog** to signify a sharp, lustful, or lecherous face.

---

### One long bedridden, yet recovered again.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a frog in the water, with only its head and upper body visible.</image-desc>

Also, to signify a sick person who has lain long in bed, unable to move, but who is walking abroad again, they depict a **frog** that has no front feet. For frogs first grow without front legs <note>referring to the tadpole stage</note>, which then gradually develop later on.

<header>Signs of Holy Scripture</header>

->The Deception of Flatterers.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a man in a feathered cap playing a flute to a bird perched on a tree branch.</image-desc>

If someone is misled and betrayed through coaxing and flattery, they depict a **stag** with a **piper**; for the stag allows itself to be fooled and lured by the sounds and piping, forgets its own safety, and is thus captured. <note>In European folklore, the stag was thought to be so enchanted by music that it would stand still for hunters.</note>

---

->Foreknowledge of a good harvest, indicating there will be much wine.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a bird (a hoopoe) perched on a branch.</image-desc>

They depict a **hoopoe** <note>German: *Widhopff*</note> when they wish to predict that much wine will grow and that the autumn harvest or vintage will be good. For when the hoopoe begins to sing before the grapevines have dried, it is a certain sign of a good supply, and there will be much wine that year.

---

->When one has made themselves sick by eating wine grapes.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a bird eating berries or grapes from a plant.</image-desc>

If someone takes medicine and wishes to heal themselves because they have eaten too many wine grapes—which cause them pain—they again depict a **hoopoe** eating **meadow rue** <term>Maurraunten: likely meadow rue (Thalictrum) or common rue (Ruta graveolens), traditionally used as an antidote</term>; for when this bird has made itself sick by eating grapes, it swallows this herb and recovers.

---

->Vigilance against enemies.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of three cranes by a shoreline; one stands on one leg, a traditional symbol of vigilance.</image-desc>

If someone acts with great care and caution to escape enemies and flee their traps, they depict a **crane** standing guard to represent them. For this bird keeps watch the entire night, alternating the guard with others. <note>Legend says cranes hold a stone in one foot while standing on the other; if they fall asleep, the stone drops and wakes them.</note>

---

->The corruption of boys.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing two birds (partridges) standing together on the ground.</image-desc>

To signify this vice of the corruption of boys, they depict two **partridges**; for these birds will mate with one another if they lose their females. <note>original: "Knaben schändung." This refers to historical moralizing views on same-sex behavior among animals, often used in bestiaries to warn against "unnatural" acts.</note>

---

->An old person suffering from hunger.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an eagle with a sharply curved beak that prevents it from eating.</image-desc>

Where one wishes to represent old people suffering the distress of hunger, they depict an **eagle** with a crooked beak. For in this bird’s old age, its beak becomes so extremely curved that it can no longer eat, and it must therefore die of hunger. <note>This myth appears in many medieval bestiaries; it was sometimes said the eagle could only survive by breaking its beak against a rock.</note>

### A Constantly Restless and Wrathful Man.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a bird, likely a crow, sitting on a nest with its young in a wooded landscape.</image-desc>

A man who is constantly angry and so restless that he cannot eat with leisure or peace is esteemed by them to be like the **crow**. They depict it with its young, for all the while it broods upon them, it is constantly restless and fierce.

---

### One Knowing Divine Mysteries.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a large bird, perhaps a crane or stork, flying high above a simplified landscape with a small structure.</image-desc>

The **crane** flies so high that it touches the clouds, let alone sees them; to represent a man who inquires into divine mysteries <note>The crane's high flight was often used as a metaphor for spiritual contemplation and the search for "high" or hidden knowledge.</note>, they depict the bird in flight.

---

### Casting Out Children Because of Poverty.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an eagle in a nest atop a rocky outcrop. It appears to be pushing eggs or young birds out of the nest.</image-desc>

The **eagle** lays three eggs, but it breaks two and throws them out of the nest, brooding only one. This is because at that same time it molts <note>Original: *mauſet*</note>, so that its feathers fall out and its claws fail, and it cannot provide for many young at once. They depict this bird brooding in such a way to signify those who, out of poverty and inability <note>Original: *onuermüglickeyt*</note>, cast out their children and give them away to serve others.

---

### One Who Walks Slowly and Drags the Feet.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a camel walking across a sparse landscape.</image-desc>

When they wish to represent someone who drags their feet and does not want to move from their place, they depict a **camel**; for this animal, among all others, bends and bows its bones while walking.

---

### A Sharp and Lustful Countenance.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a frog on the ground in a landscape with a single tree in the background.</image-desc>

The **frog** has no blood except in its eyes, and those who have blood in their eyes are considered shameless. For this reason, Homer says in the first book of the *Destruction of Troy* <note>The author refers to the *Iliad*. This specific insult is spoken by Achilles to Agamemnon in Book 1.</note>:
> Wine-guzzler, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer,
> Drunken, shameless, and a coward in the games of war.
And for this reason, they depict the creature as a frog to represent a lustful <note>Original: *hůeriſch*, literally "whorish," used here to mean lecherous or devoid of shame.</note> and sharp countenance.

---

### One Long Bedridden, Yet Recovered.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a small frog or tadpole near a body of water, notably lacking front legs.</image-desc>

To signify a sick person who has long been bedridden <term>Betthriß: literally a "bed-tearer" or someone confined to bed by infirmity</term> and could not move, but who is now walking abroad again, they depict a **frog** that has no front legs. For frogs first grow without front legs, which gradually come to them later.

<page-num>cxxviii</page-num>
<header>Signs of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Heyliger gschrifft warzeichen," here meaning hieroglyphs or sacred symbols.</note></header>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an eel swimming in water.</image-desc>

->A hater of people.<-

To report that someone is a hater of all the world and can endure no one around him, they paint an **eel** <note>original: "Aal"</note>; this same fish prefers to be alone from other fish, and one does not easily find it among other kinds of fish.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large fish (Narca) swimming.</image-desc>

->A good mariner.<-

There is a fish named **Narca** <note>original: "Narca," the torpedo or electric ray, though here given a helpful nature</note>; when it sees that the other fish in the sea are overcome and almost exhausted by the tide so that they can no longer swim, it comes to their aid and preserves them. They paint this to signify a good mariner who has helped many people in the perils of the water.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an octopus-like sea creature (Mörspinne).</image-desc>

->One who squanders good and bad alike.<-

The **polyp** or **sea-spider** <note>original: "Mörspinne," an early name for the octopus</note> is a fish that eats much and immoderately, and takes in all sorts of good and bad; but as soon as it is full, it casts out the good and bad alike. They paint this fish to indicate a wasteful, prodigal person who, along with the good, also pays no heed to the useless.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lobster or crab-like creature (Carabus) next to an octopus.</image-desc>

->One who is the chief among his kind.<-

The **carabus** <note>original: "Carabus," a species of spiny lobster or crayfish</note> is of the nature of the polyp, much like the sea-spider, or perhaps the sea-spider itself; they paint it alongside or near a polyp to indicate when someone is the preeminent one among his lineage, or when he oppresses all others who belong to him.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large seashell (Mörschnecke).</image-desc>

->A husband.<-

The **sea snails** are produced within their shells, and they also mate within their little houses or mussels; therefore, when one wishes to signify a husband, one paints a sea snail.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing a snail shell with a crab-like creature interacting with it.</image-desc>

->One who takes no care for himself.<-

Where someone is so negligent in his affairs that his own people must constantly drive him for his own benefit, and one wishes to make mention of him, they paint a **sea snail** and a **crab** together. For the crab dwells continually with these shell-snails, so that it is called the "shell-guardian" <note>This describes the symbiosis between the Pinna bivalve and the pea crab (Pinnotheres pisum), often mentioned in classical natural histories.</note>. Now, when the sea snail is hungry, it gapes open; then, when the little fish swim into it, and the crab sees this, he nudges the snail with his claw, so then [the snail] clamps

<meta>catchword: clamps</meta>

<keywords>eel, torpedo fish, octopus, lobster, sea snail, crab, husbandry, misanthropy, symbiosis, social roles</keywords>

...Then he sticks fast, the little fish are caught, and the snail is fed.

### Regurgitating food.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a water creature, described as a "water weasel," swimming in a river with a landscape and building in the background.</image-desc>

People who constantly gorge themselves until they overflow, and then immediately begin to stifle themselves anew, are compared by the ancients to a **water-weasel** <note>original: "Wasserwiseln"; likely referring to a species of shrew or a legendary aquatic animal</note>. To represent such people, they paint this animal for this reason: this fish releases its spawn through its mouth, and later, when the little fish come forward, it eats them again while swimming.

### Adulterers.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an eel or moray (Murena) in the water.</image-desc>

They also compare adulterers to the **moray** <note>original: "Murenen"</note>, for that same fish runs out of the water and mates with the **viper** <note>original: "Vippernater"</note>, and immediately returns to the water. Therefore, where this animal is painted, they wish to signify an adulterer.

### A murderer who is punished.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a turtle dove resting in a woven, basket-like nest.</image-desc>

When the **turtle dove** <note>original: "Turteltaub"</note> is caught in a snare or with birdlime, it sheds the primary feathers in its tail. To signify a murderer, they paint this bird—specifically one who has received punishment for his malice.

### One who ruins himself and others with him.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a multi-limbed sea creature, identified as a "Pulpen" (polyp/octopus).</image-desc>

Many consider it an art, once they have squandered their own property, to ruin the goods of other people as well. Such people are regarded as **polyps** <note>original: "Pulpen," referring to the octopus</note> and are signified by its image. The reason: after this fish has exhausted its prey, it eats its own <term>zasen</term> <note>tentacles or feelers</note> and its tail.

### Aspiring to honor, even with danger.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a cuttlefish (Sepia) characterized by a bulbous head and long tentacles.</image-desc>

The **Sepia** is a fish with a puffed-up hood for a head, which stands between two long tails that it uses in place of feet; it also has a "blackness" <note>ink</note> instead of blood. When the fisherman hunts it, it releases that same blackness and clouds the water so that the fisherman can no longer see where it has gone. Now, when they wish to indicate a man who strives for honor, even through much endured danger, they paint this fish. This signifies that such a man must also suffer much and pull himself through with skill, letting "talk pass by his ears" <note>ignoring rumors or slander</note> if he wishes to achieve his purpose.

<meta>Catchword: Unchastity.</meta>

<summary>This page describes various animals and fish used as symbols for human behaviors, including gluttony, adultery, and the pursuit of honor through adversity. It draws on natural history myths, such as the moray eel mating with vipers and the octopus eating its own limbs.</summary>
<keywords>water-weasel, moray, viper, turtle dove, octopus, cuttlefish, adultery, gluttony, honor, symbolism</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page concludes the second book of symbols, continuing from the previous page's discussion of animal behaviors—such as the eel and the turtle dove—as metaphors for human morality. It transitions from animal-based symbols to musical instruments and human anatomy to represent social traits and wisdom. This text is part of a larger tradition of interpreting "hieroglyphs" based on the work of Horapollo.</meta>

# Sacred symbols of Holy Scripture

### Unchastity.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration depicting two sparrows on the ground in a sparse landscape with hills in the background.</image-desc>

To indicate this vice, they paint a **sparrow**, because it is so lustful and possesses such a great desire for "birding" <note>original: "vogelt"; a German pun or colloquialism where the word for bird is used as a verb for copulation</note> that it mates seven times in a single hour. Furthermore, relative to its small size, it releases an abundance of seed.

---

### A consistent life.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of a stringed instrument, likely a violin or fiddle, shown diagonally with its bow resting across it.</image-desc>

There is a proverb: "You remain forever and ever on your same fiddle." If someone leads a stubborn or very disciplined and orderly life, the ancients painted a **fiddle** <note>original: "Geygen"</note> to represent this, because it always maintains the same tone.

---

### Where one becomes wise through his own harm.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of a transverse flute or fife, shown diagonally.</image-desc>

Where a person has committed a transgression or oversight due to his own folly, but later becomes wise <note>original: "gwizigt"; here meaning to become sensible or "learned a lesson," rather than being humorous</note> through the resulting harm—so that he now takes good care of his affairs—they paint a **transverse flute**. This is because the instrument causes a person to reflect deeply on the things he has done, and it also possesses a fine, lovely sound.

---

### To give everyone what is theirs.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration of an ostrich standing in profile with its wings slightly raised.</image-desc>

The wings of the **ostrich** <note>original: "Strauſſen"</note> are equal in their squareness on all sides. They paint these wings to represent a person who gives to every man that which belongs to him <note>This is a classic symbol of justice or equity, suggesting that the bird's feathers are perfectly balanced</note>.

---

### To signify a person who is industrious.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration featuring a central eye surrounded by three detached hands: one above pointing right, one below pointing left, and a third hand at the bottom right.</image-desc>

They paint a person's **hand** to indicate an industrious man, because manual labor and work are accomplished mostly through the hands.

->End of the second book of Horapollo.<-

<summary>This page concludes the second book of emblematic symbols, using sparrows, musical instruments, and ostriches to illustrate human traits like lust, consistency, wisdom through experience, and justice. It emphasizes the "hieroglyphic" tradition where natural and man-made objects serve as moral lessons.</summary>

<keywords>unchastity, sparrow, consistency, fiddle, wisdom, transverse flute, justice, ostrich, industriousness, hand, Horapollo</keywords>
